Friday, June 1, 1951 

LEATHER FINDERS IAC 

Members of the Leather Finders Industry Advisory Committee, meeting with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization for the first time today, discussed a possible tailored regulation for their industry. Coakley-CPS-GPR-516 

Supplementary Regulation 29, under which the industry now operates, was explained by Eleanore Kerber, Branch counsel, and the committee agreed that while this regulation would be helpful to their industry, work should be started on a tailored regulation which would more adequately fit the requirements of the industry, and that this tailored regulation should follow along the general lines of SR 29.

This industry covers many items in addition to leather, but today's meeting was confined solely to the subject of leather. 

When questioned on their opinion of a freeze-type regulation, industry members stated that such a regulation would foster inequities and distortions in pricing within the industry. 

Dickson Stauffer, chief, Leather, Fur and Fibres Branch, Consumer Soft

Goods Division opened the meeting which was conducted by Daniel W. Keeler, Branch consultant. Other OPS representatives were Thomas L. Karsten, assistant director for Consumer Soft Goods; Leonard Kurvin, Branch economist; John

Neumann, Branch counsel; Thomas W. LaVenia, Enforcement Division; Charles B. 

Conway, Office of Accounting and Harry Spack, Office of Industry Advisory Committees. 

Members of the committee are Eugene Schaefer, E. K. Leiber Leather Co., St. Louis; Morris Levey, Philadelphia Leather Co., Omaha, Neb., absent; 

John Blaufox, Brooklyn, N. Y.; Edgar Lebow, Samuel Lebow Co., Boston; Raymond

Washington TATTERSALL APPOINTMENT 

Coakley-OPS-GPR-517  

Appointment of Wilbur K. Tattersall as chief of the Cotton Section, Textile 

Branch, Consumer Soft Goods Division, was announced today by Michael V. DiSalle, director, Office of Price Stabilization.

Mr. Tattersall replaces William H. Brayer who resigned the post to return to his position as vice president of Cone Export & Commission Co., Inc., New 

York. Mr. Brayer had been on leave of absence from his company to head the OPS 

Cotton Section and will continue to serve on a part-time basis as consultant. 

Before coming to OPS in March as a consultant in the Cotton Branch, Mr. 

Tattersall was assistant sales manager in the colored goods department of Wellington Sears Co., New York City. He had been with that company 14 years. He joined the army in June, 1943, served overseas and was discharged in October, 1945. 

Mr. Tattersall, 34, attended Trinity College, Hartford, Conn. He is married and has two children. The family home is in Forest Hills, N. Y. 

In accepting Mr. Brayer's resignation Mr. DiSalle expressed his regret and wrote, "I want you to know that your efforts in behalf of the Price Stabilization Program are sincerely appreciated. Your task has not been an easy one but I believe you have done a most satisfactory job under very difficult conditions. "I am glad to know that you will still be available to us on a part-time basis as a consultant. We will probably have numerous occasions to call on you for assistance on cotton matters so as to benefit from your knowledge and from the experience you have gained with us during the past few difficult months. In re- turning to the Cone Export and Commission Company you carry with you my best wishes for success and happiness. 11 GPO-O-OPS 930

PRESS RELEASE INNEDIATE RELEASE 

Monday, June 4, 1951 

 Tempo E -Hashington Barkley-OPS-GPR-519  Re: CIGAR IAC The Cigar Industry Advisory Committee today recommended to the Office of 

Price Stabilization the adoption of a price regulation setting forth dollars and cents ceilings at the manufacturing, distributive and retail levels to meet the needs of the industry.

The Committee, in its first meeting with OPS officials, expressed opposition to imposition at this time of a maximum average price regulation such as that provided under the World War II Office of Price Administration. 

However, industry committee members said they would be agreeable to such a regulation in the event that a shortage of cigars developed. 761 Committeemen said the industry would be willing to file quarterly reports of sales in order that OPS might be able to keep tab on the trend of cigar prices and to put a maximum average price regulation into effect if one became necessary.

OPS officials announced a survey will get underway shortly on the cost and earnings of 23 cigar manufacturers to determine how much relief, if any, the cigar industry is entitled to under the earning standard proclaimed by Adminis trator Eric Johnston of the Economic Stabilization Administration. 

The Committee will be called to Washington for a second meeting when the results of this survey are available.

The Committee also proposed that the cigar regulation should limit the prices of new brands and new sizes of cigars to prices which are in line to those allowed for comparable cigars already being manufactured. 

Representing OPS at the meeting were George Mehren, assistant director, food and Restaurant Division; 0. W. Woods, chief, Grocery Branch; Elmer Hallowell, head of the Sugar and Tobacco Section; C.C. Benedict, Consultant; John Paschke, economist, and Israel L. Sonenshein, attorney. 

Members of the Advisory Committee are:

Washington GROUNDWOOD SPECIALTY PAPER IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-520  

The Groundwood Specialty Paper Industry Advisory Committee at its third meeting with OPS officials today made detailed recommendations for revision of the old OPA Price Regulation 449 as the basis of a new tailored regulation for the industry.

The regulation spelled out dollars and cents ceilings for standard grades of specialty papers and set forth differentials for variations in finishes, tints, sizing and other particulars.

The committee recommended that two additional categories be added to the five previously recommended for their industry, namely, A Offset No. 1 and

A. Offset No. 2. Those previously recommended were groundwood hanging papers, special end use groundwood converting papers, general converting grades of groundwood paper, groundwood book paper and coated groundwood papers. 

Committeemen recommended that a subcommittee be named to work with the Bookpaper Industry Advisory Committee because of the overlapping of interests in bookpaper.

Committeemen discussed a proposed form which OPS will employ in obtaining cost information from industry in preparing the regulation. Pricing in the various categories will be determined by cost studies of representative key items in each category.

Committeemen discussed the need of making adjustments for changes in specifications occurring over the interval of cost studies. 

Groundwood papers are widely used by the printing industry and are so described because they contain substantial portions of mechanically produced pulp in contrast to chemical pulps.

The meeting was conducted by Daniel H. Keck, industrial cosultant for groundwood and book paper.  John H. Vogel, economist; William L. Soboroff, counsel; Laurie M. Streeter, Office of Enforcement, and Walter R. Moulton, Office of Advisory Committees. 

Members of the committee who were present: Samuel Pruyn, vice president, Finch, Pruyn and Company, Inc., Glen Falls, N.Y.; E. J. Doonan, sales manager, Gould Paper Co., Lyons Falls, N.Y.; Robert Faegre, Minnesota & Ontario Paper Co., Minneapolis, Minn.; Paul Mahony, sales manager, Groundwood Specialties Division, International Paper Co., New York, N.Y.; Fred W. Mears, Great Northern Paper Co., New York, N.Y.; E.G. Murray, vice president, St. Regis Paper Co., New York, N.Y.; and J.R. Atwanter, Mead Sales Corp., Dayton, 0.

PRESS RELEASE    

Re: WILLIAM C. BURT Coakley-OPS-GPR-521 

Appointment of William C. Burt as an Assistant Chief Counsel for the Office of Price Stabilization and Division Counsel for its Food and 

Restaurant Division was confirmed today by Harold Leventhal, Chief Counsel. 

Mr. Burt formerly served as chief of the Rates Division, Civil 

Aeronautics Board, where he began service in 1941. He began his legal career in the office of Gerald C. Snyder, attorney, Waukegan,

Ill., in 1938 and in December 1940 accepted a position as attorney with the Federal Home Loan Bank Board in Washington. He served with the 

U. S. Marine Corps during World War II. 

A native of Freeport, Ill., Mr. Burt, 35, attended the University of Illinois where he took a B. S. Degree in the College of Commerce in 

1937 and an LL. B. Degree in the College of Law in 1939.

IMMEDIATE RELEASE 

Monday, June 4, 1951 

Huff-OPS-GPR-522  

Re: FABRICATED STRUCTURAL STEEL SHAPES, PLATES, AND BARS IAC Members of the Fabricated Structural Steel Shapes, Plates, and Bars 

Industry Advisory Committee, meeting with OPS officials for the first time today, urged a specific regulation setting ceiling prices on their products to supersede CPR 30 which now covers them.

The committee presented a proposed outline of a pricing formula which was considered within the scope of OPS policy and requested another meeting 

June 19.

The tentative formula would regulate margins on the basis of dollars per ton obtained in the last quarter of 1950 on the contract most comparable to the one being priced. CPR 30 calls for a pre-Korean base period; the industry was in a depressed state of activity at that time. 

Committee members stressed not only the difficulty of making necessary calculations and filing required data under CPR 30 but also the difficulty of arriving at a meaningful cost increase factor because of the variability of materials cost components.

The industry's business is largely on a contract basis, with constant switching to new types of products as opportunity arises. A company making bridges at the present time may produce blast furnaces under its next contract, and steel or alloy materials used might shift from one extreme to the other as far as cost is concerned.

Wide variations in relative materials costs would lead to great pricing discrepancies under CPR 30, while fluctuations in field engineering and field erection costs if only for geographical reasons would create another pricing problem, industry representatives said.

Consequently, individual companies having little or no experience with products on which they wish to submit bids for manufacture six or eight months hence would have to apply repeatedly for OPS approval of separate pricing formulas, a procedure bound to impose a serious administrative burden on manufacturers and OPS alike.

Howard Needham, consultant in the fabricated products section of the OPS Metals Branch, led today's meeting. Other OPS representatives were Sam 

Ewing, acting assistant director of the Industrial Materials and Manufactured 

Goods Division, Robert J. Benes, Metals Branch counsel, C. R. Wasson and 

Jeanette Carey, branch economists, S. H. Burgess, branch industrial analyst,

W. H. Dupka, Chief of the iron and steel section, and Harry Spack, Office for 

Advisory Committees. 

Members of the committee, all present today, are:

Washington Scott-OPS-GPR-523 

Re: APPALACHIAN HARDWOOD INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE The Appalachian Hardwood Industry Advisory Committee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss pricing problems of the industry.

The committee represents hardwood lumber producers in the Appalachian area, which embraces eastern Tennessee, southeast Kentucky, western North 

Carolina, western and southwestern Virginia, western Maryland, the west half of Pennsylvania, and all of West Virginia. Because of the geographical situation, quality grading and pricing of hardwood lumber produced in the area is somewhat different from other hardwood producing areas. 

Committeemen stated that, generally speaking, industry pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation has been satisfactory. Members said pricing under GCPR has not resulted in prices substantially higher than those in effect in June 1950. Some members estimated price increases under 

GCPR not to exceed 8 or 10 percent above June 1950 levels.

The committee felt that a tailored regulation using GCPR pricing as a starting point would be feasible, since these prices would reflect normal trade differentials and are not out of line with pre-Korean price levels. 

The committee felt that overall dollars-and-cents ceiling would not be feasible and would restrict maximum production and disrupt normal distribution.

It was recommended that a sub-committee be appointed to advise further with OPS officials as to a workable basis for setting up a tailored regulation. The following members were named to serve as a sub-committee: John 

B. Veach, E. P. Vaughn, Guy H. Hughes, Charles Bringardner and John C. Turner.

The committee went on record as favoring decontrol of log prices. 

The meeting was conducted by Norman 0. Cruver, chief, Lumber and Wood 

Products Branch, and Lawrence D. Kellogg, chief, Hardwood Section, OPS. 

Other OPS officials attending were: Dante Galotta and Charles Evans, legal staff; Thomas W. McKinley, price economist; James A. Gilmore and J. P. 

Moyer, consultants; and, Walter R. Moulton, Office for Advisory Committees. 

All members of the advisory committee were in attendance as follows:

Re: SOUTHERN HARDWOOD INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE The Southern Hardwood Industry Advisory Committee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization, to discuss a tailored pricing regulation for this segment of the industry. 

Committeemen stated the industry has not experienced any serious difficulties in currently pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation.

In considering a tailored pricing regulation, the Committee strongly favored overall dollars-and-cents ceiling prices, as far as feasible, patterned along the general lines of World War II Office of Price Administration regulation 

MPR-97. 

The committee agreed that a sub-committee be appointed to advise further with OPS officials on the principal details of a tailored regulation and the type of industry data that would be required and available. Members asked that the sub-committee be given the opportunity to review carefully the old OPA regulation MPR-97, with a view of suggesting desirable changes, including factors for freight adjustments and other current trade pricing practices. 

Members appointed to serve as a sub-committee are: Richard P. Baer, II, Sam C. Cursey, W. C. Hanafee, Winthrop M. Hallett, Jr., Henry W. Jones, S. M. Nickey, Jr., Charles H. Proetz and C. R. Ransom. 

P. 0. Box 109 

Edenton, North Carolina

The Committee favored the decontrol of log prices. Members stated there is such a wide variation in log sizes and in methods of grading and measuring, that price control on a fair and equitable basis is practically impossible. 

The committee felt that proper control of lumber prices will control log prices. 

The meeting was conducted by Norman 0. Cruver, chief, Lumber and Wood 

Products Branch, and Lawrence D. Kellogg, chief, Hardwood Section, OPS. Other 

OPS officials attending were: W. S. Ingram, Acting Director, Forest Products 

Division; Carlton F. Diskin, Division Counsel; Dante Galotta, legal staff;

Members of the Plastic Products Industry Advisory Committee today asked the Office of Price Stabilization for a price determining method tailored to the particular needs of the custom segment of the industry. They maintained that the mechanics of CPR 22, now covering the industry, are practically unworkable for the custom molders in pricing new items. 

PLASTIC PRODUCTS IAC 

They estimated that 25,000 applications for new goods pricing would be filed per month with OPS under CPR 22, since the custom molders produce innumerable items according to the individual specifications of their customers. The industry representatives also asked that a subcommittee of the button industry, comprising members other than those on the Plastics Products Committee, be set up to study specific problems of the button manufacturers. 

Robert E. Bell, chief, Toys, Plastics and Miscellaneous Section, Home Furnishings Branch, OPS Consumer Goods Division presided at this second meeting of the group. Other OPS representatives were Ernest W.

Heilman, as sistant director, Consumer Durable Goods Division; Robert Faragher, division counsel; Pauline Heller, Cecelia Goetz, branch attorneys; Carl Kresl, chief, Home Furnishings Branch; Fernley Fawcett, branch economist; Nat Grinder, enforcement; Frank S. Kaulback, Jr., accounting.

  Re: COMMERCIAL MOTOR VEHICLES MANUFACTURES IAC 

Huff-OPS-GPR-527 

An advisory committee representing the Commercial Motor Vehicle Manu facturers industry recommended today that the Office of Price Stabilization prepare a ceiling price regulation designed to meet its current needs with the old OPA MPR 610 as a model. 

Commercial motor vehicles, unlike passenger automobiles, are now covered by the OPS machinery order (CPR 30).

Committee members urged that premiums now being paid for conversion steel should be fully reflected in determining materials cost adjustment factors under CPR 30 not now generally permitted -- and suggested monthly reporting of the amount of premium steel indicated in costs so that adjustment factors could be refigured in the event of a decrease in its cost.

Washington FINE PAPER MERCHANTS LAC WRAPPING PAPER MERCHANTS TAC Moore-OPS-GPR-528 

Wholesale paper distributors today recommended to OPS officials that a special regulation be written adapting the principles of SR 29 to the General Ceiling Price Regulation to the practices and problems of their industry. 

SR 29 permits distributors to pass on increases in manufacturers prices put into effect under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, and obtain relief in instances where their ceilings did not provide a normal mark-up.

The paper distributors, members of the Fine Paper Merchants Industry Advisory 

Committee and the Wrapping Paper Merchants Industry Advisory Committee, said SR 29 seemed to be a workable instrument but definitions should be more sharply drawn to fit the paper trade, covering such items as net invoice costs, bracket pricing, and differentiation between commodities. 

A combined task force of three members from each of the committees was appointed to work over SR 29 paragraph by paragraph with OPS officials at a meeting tomorrow.

The two advisory committees met separately today. The meetings were conducted by M. C. Walsh, deputy chief, Pulp, Paper and Paperboard Branch, assisteč by William G. Luke, Jr., industrial consultant for fine and wrapping paper merchants. 

The committees represent the wholesale distribution of a great many paper products sold to printers, industrial houses and retailers. Fine papers include writing, printing and publishing papers. Wrapping papers are coarse papers used by commercial houses and manufacturers for packaging and industrial uses.

Washington PICKLE IAC Barkley-OPS-GPR-529 

A ceiling price regulation to become effective for the pickle industry when the 1951 harvest is completed next fall was discussed with Office of Price Stabilization officials June 5 by members of the newly formed Pickle 

Industry Advisory Committee. 

Until that time, industry members said they would be satisfied to remain under the Manufacturers Ceiling Price Regulation (CPR 22). Goal for the special regulation is September or early October. 

Because of the variety of the products and time lapses to permit curing of certain types of pickles, multiple base periods were recommended for the purpose of establishing ceiling prices. 

As an example, should the 1948 harvest year be chosen as the pre- Korea year to be used in establishing base periods, the base period for fresh pickles would be the 90 days immediately following the first sale after processing, while the base period for dill pickles would be a 90day period starting three weeks after the first sale and the base period for sweet pickles the 90-day period starting six months after first sale.

This, it was explained, is because time is required for curing certain types of pickles.

To the base period price for each type would be added such factors as raw material cost increases and other allowable direct cost increase incurred since the base period. These would be considered on an area basis. GPOO-OPS 954

The Fruit and Vegetable Branch of the OPS Food and Restaurant 

Division will make a cost and profit survey of the industry to enable it to reach decisions on these factors. The Committee did not reach a decision on which pre-Korea year it would recommend, but expressed the view the year should be far enough back to allow for the time lapses between processing and marketing in establishing base periods.

The industry will express its view by letters to OPS on the year considered the best to be used. 2 - Representing OPS at the meeting were W. G.. Carberry, chief of the Fruit and Vegetable Branch; H. K. Draper, W. K. Batchelder and

W. C. Glover of the Branch; John H. McVay, Branch counsel, and Walter Moul ten of the Office of Advisory Committees. R. P. Callaway of the U. S.

  Re: PRIMARY COPPER LAC 

Huff-OPS-GPR-530 

Chief topic of discussion at a meeting today with OPS officials of the Primary Copper Industry Advisory Committee was the effect of recent advances in the world copper price on domestic producers still operating under the general freeze of January 26.

The world price has risen to reflect the three-cent increase in the price of Chilean copper recently negotiated between the Chilean and U. S. governments. The Chilean price is now 27 1/2 cents, against the domestic ceiling of 24 1/2 cents, with a two-cent import duty eliminated.

Industry representatives pointed out that some domestic custom smelters with outstanding contracts for the purchase of Chilean concentrates would be squeezed if they were not able to pass the increase on to their U. S. customers. There was a general realization, however, that the domestic price cannot follow the foreign figure indefinitely under present pricecontrol policy.

Subsidies or premium price plans for high-cost producers were discussed although these questions do not fall within OPS jurisdiction. The point was made that even a three-cent rise in the present ceiling would not be enough to induce copper mining expansion with existing facilities in the face of the current world shortage or to guarantee additional tonnages of foreign copper. It was also brought out that the Chilean price increase does not necessarily give foreign producers any advantage since the Chilean government collects most of it in taxes. 

The committee may meet again about June 15 when many members will be in Washington for a conference with the National Production Authority.

Today's meeting was conducted by Sam Ewing, acting assistant director of the OPS Industrial Materials and Manufactured Goods Division. Other 

OPS representatives included William Kerber, chief of the Metals Branch, A.F. 

Norling and C. C. Rieth, branch consultants, R. J. Benes, counsel, R. C. Brown, attorney, C. R. Wasson and Jeannette Carey, economists, and Harry Spack of the Office for Advisory Committees.

Washington Re: SUPPLIES OF BEEF Barkley-OPS-GPR-531 

The Office of Price Stabilization today announced the details of its coast-to-coast check of the Nation's meat counters. 

The check, made late in May, shows that in general supplies of beef were about as large under OPS dollars and cents ceilings prices as they were before the program went into effect last May 14.

In general, the report showed a lesser supply of lower grade meats, compared to a month earlier, while the availability at retail of good and choice, the types largely sold at retail, were about even, in some cities being above normal and in some below.

OPS officials pointed out that the survey was not a total one, and was based on spot checks of representative markets, but said they believed it gave a reasonably accurate picture of the situation. 

Two reasons were suggested for the comparative shortage of utility and low commercial meat: 1. This time of the year, with gress plentiful, fewer low grade cattle are sold since growers can keep them on gress for additional fattening until the dry period begins. This seasonal trend is true each year, it was said. 2. Recent high beef prices have stimulated the demand for sausage and other low grade products, and have taken an unusually large supply of the commercial and utility supply from the markets. 

An OPS official estimated that from 80 to 85% of all beef normally sold at retail was top commercial grade or better. 

The survey covered a cross-section of cities ranging in size from 15,000 population up and was made by OPS Regional and District Offices at the request of Price Stabilizer Michael V. DiSalle.

The check was made as of May 28, 1951, against the same date a month earlier.

Mr. DiSalle said that while the information furnished by the field offices was not sufficiently complete to permit final conclusions in all cases, it did disclose some salient points.

G.P.O.-O-OPS 949

These facts seem apparent: 

1. In general, the availability of beef in the larger cities is almost as great or greater than it was a month ago. 2. 

There is an adequate supply of beef of the most popular retail grades (choice and good) in almost all cities surveyed, but a general shortage of commercial and utility grades. 

3. One major area reporting rather acute shortages in lower grade beef, and some decrease in the better grades was the Chicago region, where the meat packing industry is heavily concentrated. This was not true in all cities of this area, however. Madison, Wis., reported better grade beef 10% more plentiful than a month ago, as did several small towns checked in Illinois. 

4. The New York region showed that availability of beef was greater than it was a month earlier.

Supplies of beef on May 28, were found to be about 18 percent more in the 

New York area than on April 28; about 5 percent more in the Philadelphia area; and about the same in Washington, Richmond, Detroit, Miami, Cleveland, Cincinnati, Kansas City, St. Louis, Denver, Seattle and San Francisco.

The check indicated supplies in Boston were about 20 percent less; about 

10 percent less in Pittsburgh; 5 percent less in Baltimore; about 5 percent less in Los Angeles; 10 percent less in Phoenix, Ariz., and 10 percent less in Dallas.

In Chicago, the check indicated supplies of better grades of beef--choice and good-- were about 25 percent less than a month earlier, while commercial and utility grades were less by about 50 percent. 

Milwaukee supplies of better grades were about 10 percent less, it was estimated, while commercial and utility were down by about 30 percent.

Washington 

Re: 

RUBBER SUNDRIES IAC Moore-OPS-GPR-532 

Members of the Rubber Sundries Industry Advisory Committee at their fourth meeting today with OPS officials discussed the effect of pricing formulas contained in the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regula tion, CPR 22, on their industry.

Nearly complete data from the industry indicated CPR ceilings will average very close to GCPR ceilings, perhaps slightly above. 

The committee had previously requested a tailored regulation be written for the industry employing weighted average percentage cost adjustment factors.

Members indicated that if the adjustments under CPR 22 were very close to GCPR prices, they would prefer to retain the latter. 

They pointed out that if the factors worked out at 100 percent this would mean the new ceilings under SR 2 of CPR 22 would be the same as GCPR ceilings. SR 2 is an alternate formula to CPR 22 which permits adjustments to GCPR prices rather than base period prices. 

OPS officials indicated a tailored regulation would be issued prior to the effective date of CPR 22 July 2, so the industry can avoid pricing temporarily under CPR 22. 

OPS officials present at the meeting were: Chester Conner, chief of the Rubber Branch; H. J. Haflin, industrial consultant, and D. C.

Corridon, economist. Western Wiles of NPA was present.

PRESS RELEASE    

Re: NEWSPRINT 

Moore-OPS-GPR-533 

Michael V. DiSalle, Director of Price Stabilization, today invited

American newsprint manufacturers and representative newspaper publishers to confer with him next week on prospective increases in newsprint prices. 

Seven manufacturers were asked to consult with the director at 9:30 a. m. Tuesday, June 12, while 24 newspaper publishers were invited to meet at 2 o'clock that afternoon.

The conferences were decided on after the Abitibi Power & Paper Co., Ltd., of Canada, announced a $10 per ton increase in the price of newsprint, effective July 1, which will bring the New York price to $116 per ton. 

Director 

DiSalle has asked Canada to suspend the increase pending discussion with U. S. 

The manufacturers will constitute a newsprint Industry Advisory Committee to OPS. The publishers will not be named formally as an advisory committee because newspapers are not subject to price control. 

In inviting the publishers DiSalle said he understood their industry had been "disturbed" by the announced increase and expressed a desire to to consult with leading newsprint consumers.

Newsprint manufacturers will be asked what price action they contemplate, if any, under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, which becomes effective July 2, 1951, or before if the manufacturer elects. 

Newsprint manufactured and sold in the United States has been controlled since January 26, 1951, under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, which is being superseded for newsprint manufacturers by CPR 22. GPO-O-OPS 957 3

It is possible American manufacturers may increase their prices under CPR 22 formulas. These permit a manufacturer to increase his pre-Korea price by his material and labor cost increases since that time up to certain cut-off dates. These are March 15, 1951, for labor and domestic woodpulp, April 6 for imported woodpulp, and December 1, 1950, for other materials. 

OPS expects, however, that any increase which domestic manufacturers will be allowed under CPR 22 will be substantially less than the increase announced by the Canadian concern.

American and Canadian newsprint historically have sold at approximately the same level. About 85 per cent of newsprint consumed in the United States comes from Canada.

Both Canadian and domestic manufacturers put a 6 per cent increase in price in effect in October, 1950, which was reflected in GCPR ceilings on American newsprint. Whether a manufacturer's ceilings under CPR 22 will roll forward or backward from GCPR prices depends on whether his allowable increase in costs since pre-Korea have been more or less than 6 percent. 

American manufacturers must file their newsprint ceilings under CPR 22 by July 2. An American manufacturer could continue selling at his present prices if his ceilings under CPR 22 are higher than under the GCPR, but would have to roll back to the new ceilings if they are lower than GCPR prices. He may not increase his prices until 15 days after filing higher ceilings under 

CPR 22. 

OPS has no control over prices of Canadian newsprint. However, newsprint has been declared as "essential material" in Canada and as such is subject to control by the Canadian Department of Defense Production.

Crist-OPS-GPR-534  

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers 

RE: QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS ON THE GENERAL MANUFACTURER'S REGULATION 

CPR-22 The Office of Price Stabilization today issued a series of questions and answers on the general manufacturers' regulation (CPR 22) and a statement regarding common errors which have been found on the public form (Form 8) which must be filed under the regulation. 

Experience to date in processing Form 8's submitted by manufacturers, OPS officials said, has revealed these common errors: (1) The code number for Item 1 is omitted. Manufacturers are required to enter the appropriate six digit code set forth in Amendment 1 to CPR 22, for the particular category or product line covered by the Form 8. This code number is used in OPS to direct the Form 8 to the appropriate division for processing. 

Omission of the code number may delay processing. (2) Item 1 calls for a description of the particular category or product line covered by the report. Many manufacturers submit instead a general description of the nature of their business which does not permit any identification of the particular category or product line. (3) Item 2 calls for identification of the base periods used for the particular category or product line covered by the report. This should be any one of the following: (1) July 1, 1949, to September 30, 1949; (2) 

October 1, 1949, to December 31, 1949; (3) January 1, 1950, to March 31, 1950; (4) April 1, 1950, to June 24, 1950. (A significant number of reports are received in which dates other than those permissible are shown, rendering these reports inacceptable and requiring a request to the manufacturer for a corrected report.) (4) Item 3 for estimated 1950 dollar sales should be sales for the particular category or product line. Many manufacturers submitting Forms 8 for several categories have been showing on each Form 8 their estimated 

1950 dollar sales for their entire business. (5) Item 4 on the labor cost adjustment factor must be shown as a percentage which has been derived from a multiplication of the percentage of factory payroll to net sales (labor cost ratio) by the percentage of increase in wage rates (wage increase factor). Many manufacturers have been entering a dollars and cents figure. 

Others have been entering either the labor cost ratio or the wage increase factor. (6) Item 5 on Form 8-materials cost adjustment factor-is composed of two parts and requires that only one be filled in, depending on which method you have used. The left-hand portion deals with a factor derived under either methods 1, 3, or 4. In all cases this must be shown as a percentage and the appropriate check box for the particular method used must be checked. The right-hand portion of Item 5 is to be used only if method 

2 is used. In this case, the manufacturer must show, for the best selling commodity in the particular category or product line, the name of the commodity, its base period selling price and the dollars and cents material cost adjustment computed for that commodity. Common errors have been entries shown in both the left- and the right-hand portions of Item 5, dollars and cents figures shown for methods 1, 3, or 4 and a percentage shown for method 2. (7) Item 6 on the price-adjustment ratio is to be filled in only if a price-adjustment ratio has been computed under the provisions of Supplementary Regulation 2 of CPR 22. Where appropriately computed, this ratio is to be applied uniformly to all of the GCPR prices of commodities in the particular unit of business for which you maintained separate records, category, or product line. If the price-adjustment ratio indicates a uniform increase over GCPR prices, it should appear as a figure higher than 100 percent. If the price-adjustment ratio computed indicates a uniform decrease in GCPR prices, it should appear as a percentage somewhat less than 100 percent. Common errors in connection with this item have been to show in Item 6 the total of the labor-cost adjustment factor and material-cost adjustment factor shown in Items 4 and 5 or the inclusion in Item 6 of a dollars-and-cents figure. In many cases a figure such as 10 percent is incorrectly shown for price-adjustment ratio, and no indication is given as to whether this is meant to be a 10-percent increase or a 

10-percent decrease to be applied to GCPR prices. . (8) Item 7, or the certification regarding proposed ceiling-price increases over GCPR, must be signed on every Form 8 by an officer or authorized agent of the firm submitting the Form 8, together with his title and

the date, whether or not you have calculated and shown increases over GCPR prices in Item 8 of Form 8. 

Many Forms 8 have been received without the required certification necessitating requests for a corrected filing. (9) Item 8-Proposed ceiling price increases.-The data required in Item 8 of Form 8 must be supplied for each item in the particular category or product line covered by the report for which a ceiling price higher than the GCPR ceiling price is calculated. Many reports have been received showing data for only one item in a category or product line with indications on the form that the percentage increase shown for the particular item is to be applied to other items in the category or product line. The data required by Columns 8 (a) through 8 (g) should be shown for each item in the category or product line for which a ceiling price higher than a GCPR ceiling price is calculated; 8 (h) should be filled in only if method 2 has been used to derive the materials cost adjustment. (10) Item 8 (a).-The name and specification of the item are frequently given in such a manner as to be meaningless to the OPS reviewer. For example, Lot No. 100. The physical unit priced is often omitted. The name and specification should be sufficiently specific so as clearly to identify the item and the physical unit priced. For example, per each, per dozen, per ton, etc., should always be shown. (11) Item 8 (c).-Separate estimated 1950 dollar sales are often omitted in 8 (c) or sales for many items are shown lumped together. (12) Item 8 (f)-Proposed price.-The proposed price is the proposed ceiling price calculated by applying the appropriate labor cost increase and material cost increase factors to the base period price of the item. 

For example, the proposed ceiling price for an item whose base period price is $1 with a labor cost adjustment factor of 5 percent and a materials cost adjustment factor of 5 percent is $1.10. The proposed price is commonly misconstrued as the proposed selling price so that manufacturers who have calculated total labor and materials increase factors of 10 percent, for example, show proposed prices which are only 6 percent above the base period prices. Other manufacturers whose total labor and materials factors are 10 percent, for example, "proposed" prices which are 25 percent higher than their base period prices. Wherever a manufacturer finds himself able, under the regulation, to calculate proposed ceiling prices higher than his GCPR prices, he should complete Item 8 of Form 8 for each such item in his category or product line. This establishes the ceiling price. The manufacturer may at all times use a lower selling price. A manufacturer is not permitted to "propose" on Form 8 ceiling prices any higher than can be calculated through the application of his total labor and materials cost adjustment factors to his base period prices. (13) Item 8 (h).-Figures should be shown in this column only if method 2 is used in calculating the materials cost adjustment. If shown here, figures should be in dollars and cents. 

[The following are the series of questions and answers on CPR 221 

OPTION OF USING GENERAL CEILING PRICE REGULATION 

Q. I am a new manufacturer and have not completed a fiscal year's operation prior to the effective date of CPR 22. My gross sales have been less than $250,000. May I elect to price my goods under GCPR?

A. A manufacturer who has not completed a fiscal year prior to the effective date of CPR 22 must price his commodities under CPR 22 no matter how small his sales have been in his period of actual operation. Any such manufacturer who has established prices under Sections 3, 4, or 6 of the GCPR will have to re-apply under Sections 33 or 34 of CPR 22. 

Q. If I elect to remain under the GCPR because my gross sales in my last complete fiscal year prior to the effective date of CPR 22 were less than $250,000, may I subsequently alter my election and come under CPR 22? 

A. The subsequent election to price under CPR 22 is permitted. When a manufacturer so elects, he must file his Form 8 and wait 15 days from the time of its receipt by OPS before putting into effect any prices which he may calculate at a level higher than his GCPR prices. 

Q. If I elect to price under GCPR because my gross sales for my last fiscal year were under $250,000, may I price some of the commodities which I manufacture under CPR 22 if I can show that under the latter regulation I can calculate higher prices for them than under GCPR? 

A. If you elect to remain under GCPR, you may not use CPR 22 for any of your commodities. 

Q. If I elect not to use CPR 22 because my gross sales for my last complete fiscal year of commodities 

I manufactured were less than $250,000, what ceiling prices do I use? 2

A. You continue to use GCPR for commodities which would otherwise be covered by CPR 22. 

Q. For purposes of determining whether or not I may elect to remain out of the coverage of CPR 22, I am supposed to look at my gross sales in my "last complete fiscal year." Does this mean prior to the date of issuance of CPR 22, or is it prior to the effective date of the regulation? 

A. The last complete fiscal year for a manufacturer for the purpose specified is his fiscal year ending prior to the effective date of CPR 22.

Q. If my gross sales in my last complete fiscal year exceed $250,000, but my gross sales of commodities covered by CPR 22 were less than $250,000, may I elect to remain under GCPR? 

A. No. The $250,000 figure comes from total sales of all commodities manufactured by you regardless of how much of such commodities are subject to CPR 22, GCPR, or any other regulation. 

Q. If I elect to use GCPR instead of CPR 22 because my gross sales in my complete fiscal year were less than $250,000, do I have to file a Form 8 with OPS? 

A. No. A manufacturer who elects to use GCPR instead of CPR 22 is not required to file any report of such election.

FORM 8's 

Q. Must I submit a Form 8 on commodities which I manufactured in the period July 1, 1949, to June 24, 1950, but which I am no longer manufacturing?

A. On such commodities, the filing of Form 8 is not required. However, when a discontinued base period commodity is to be used as a "comparison commodity" for establishing a ceiling price for a new commodity under Section 32, the report under that section requires that you calculate and show a CPR 22 ceiling price for the "comparison commodity." Therefore, you must obtain its base period price and must figure the applicable labor cost adjustment and materials cost adjustment factors. The Director of Price Stabilization may direct that you submit your calculations.

Q. If I intend to use my CPR 22 base period prices and therefore do not calculate either my labor cost adjustment or materials cost adjustment factors, do I have to file Form 8? 

A. Yes. The filing of a Form 8 is nevertheless required by Section 46 (b). In such a case, the manufacturer should supply, in addition to his name and address, the information required by Items 1, 2, 3; should insert "None" in Items 4 and 5; should sign the certification in Item 7; and should indicate on the form that he has elected to use his base period prices. In the event that base period prices are higher than GCPR prices, Item 8 of Form 8 must also be completed.

Q. If I calculate my labor cost adjustment factor for my entire business, do I file only one Form 8? 

A. Not necessarily. You are required to file a Form 8 for each category or product line which you produce. Thus, a manufacturer of five categories of commodities must file five Forms 8, even though his labor and/or materials adjustment factors are calculated on the basis of his entire business. 

Q. If, as permitted by CPR 22, I elected to forego the calculation of my labor and materials cost adjustment factors at the time I filed my Form 8 (my base period prices and GCPR prices were identical and I was satisfied with them) may I, at a later date, go up to the ceiling prices I could have proposed? 

A. Yes, a manufacturer who elected to forego the calculation of labor and/or materials cost adjustment factors at the time of submitting his Form 8 initially, will be permitted to file a new Form 8, at such time as he may select. If in such report he appropriately calculates prices higher than his GCPR prices, he will be permitted to use them 15 days after a new report is received by OPS. 

Q. At the time I filed my Form 8 I misunderstood the requirements of CPR 22 in connection with "proposed prices." I thought I was supposed to propose selling prices rather than ceiling prices. Accordingly, although I showed on Form 8 labor and materials cost adjustment factors which totaled 10 percent, I only applied an increase of 6 percent to my base period prices and showed the resultant "proposed prices" in Item 8 of Form 8. May I, at some later date, go up to the ceiling prices I could have proposed? 

A. Yes. However, since the Form 8 did not actually show the allowable ceiling prices, such manufacturers should file a new Form 8 at such later date as he may select. This will make clear that his labor and materials cost adjustment factors as shown on his first report were not erroneous. He will be permitted to use his appropriately calculated ceiling prices 15 days after his new report is received by OPS.

Q. If I propose an increase over GCPR ceilings in Item 8 of Form 8 for only 2 out of 10 commodities which 

I produce in a category, may I retain my GCPR prices for the other 8? 

A. Clearly not. If the CPR 22 calculated ceiling prices are lower than GCPR, the CPR 22 ceilings must be used. You are prohibited from selling above the CPR 22 ceiling prices. 

EXEMPTIONS 

Q. If the commodities which I manufacture are exempted from CPR 22 under Appendix A or under Section 

1, am I thereby exempted from price control?

A. As a rule, no. The commodities exempted from CPR 22 under Appendix A or under Section 1, are still subject to price control under such other regulations as may be applicable. 

Q. I am a manufacturer who sells the same commodity both at wholesale and at retail. CPR 22 exempts my retail sales. Am I also exempt on my wholesale sales? 

A. No. Goods produced by a manufacturer and sold by him at wholesale are covered by CPR 22. When the manufacturer sells at retail, he is covered by such other regulations as may be applicable. 

Q. If I produce a new item which is covered by CPR 22 but I do not expect to have total net sales of the new item which will exceed $10,000,, am I exempt from price control on the new item? 

A. No. A new item produced in a category in which a manufacturer has base period sales experience (July 1, 1949 through June 24, 1950) must be priced under Section 32 by reference to a comparison commodity. 

If it is anticipated that total net sales of a new item will not exceed $10,000, no report under Section 32 is required and the manufacturer may sell at the price he determines pursuant to Section 32 immediately. However, if sales of the new item have increased to the point where additional sales will exceed $10,000, sales must cease until a report pursuant to Section 32 is filed with OPS, and may not be resumed until 15 days after the report has been mailed.

MATERIAL COSTS 

Q. If I manufacture commodities covered by CPR 22 in more than one plant and I maintain separate accounting records for each plant, may I calculate my materials cost adjustment factor for each plant separately, using method 1 in each case?

A. Yes. Although a manufacturer is prohibited from lumping his manufacturing data from several plants in calculating a materials cost adjustment factor under method 1, he may use method 1 for each plant separately if he regularly maintains separate accounting records for each plant. 

Q. If I manufacture items in the same product line in more than one plant, may I develop a single materials cost adjustment factor to apply to the base period prices of all the items in the product line? 

A. Yes. You may determine your materials cost adjustment (dollars and cents) for the best selling item in the product line and then apply the percentage, which that adjustment bears to the base period price, to the base period prices of all the items which you manufacture in the product line regardless of the fact that they are produced in more than one plant. However, you are not required to do this. You may develop a separate materials cost adjustment factor for the product line in each of your plants. 

ROLLBACKS 

Q. If I file a Form 8 with OPS and do not propose any prices higher than GCPR on any of the items in a category even though the regulation permits me to use such higher prices on some of the items, may I keep my 

GCPR prices on the other items in the category?

A. Clearly not, if CPR 22 requires rollbacks on the other items. Sales at above CPR 22 ceiling prices are prohibited.

EFFECTIVE DATE 

Q. When must I place CPR 22 rollbacks into effect?

A. On the effective date of the regulation. This may not be later than July 2, 1951. However, it may be any earlier date which you select between May 28, 1951 and July 2, 1951. After the effective date you may not sell any commodity unless you have filed a Form 8 for the category or product line into which it falls. 

In addition, if you have calculated ceiling prices higher than those under GCPR, you may not put them into effect until 15 days after OPS has received your report.

Moore-OPS-GPR-535  

Re: HARDWOOD PLYWOOD LAC Members of the Hardwood Plywood Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials declared they desired a tailored regulation for their industry combining the features of wartime OPA 

regulations MPR 501 and MPR 568. 

MPR 501 applied to Small Dimension Hardwood and employed a formula embodying base period prices plus allowable increases in costs. MPR 568 fixed dollars and cents ceilings for hardwood plywood.

Committeemen agreed that dollars and cents prices would be feasible for standard stock-size panels but said the only practical way to price custom built and architectural panels would be by formula. 

A subcommittee was appointed to study these regulations and report recommendations thereon to OPS officials.

Committeemen said they knew of no practical way of placing ceilings on face veneers, which are thinly sliced, peeled or sawn from select logs and used on the visible surfaces of furniture, cabinets, doors and interiors. Face veneers are priced on the quality of the grain and the yield of matched patterns of grain. The yield of any log cannot be determined before it is cut. 

Committeemen likewise said they knew of no practical way of controlling logs which are now under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, because their is no way of enforcing precise scaling and grading. 

Control of the finished product, they said in effect controlled the price which manufacturers could pay for logs and face veneers, as ordinarily manufactures would not pay prices that would make their operations unprofitable.

WEDNESDAY, June 6, 1951   Re: 

WIRE AND CABLE TAC 

Huff-OPS-GPR-536 

 The Wire and Cable Industry Advisory Committee of the Office of Price Stabi lization, holding its second meeting today, was informed by OPS officials that the agency is weighing the possibility of removing wire and cable from its machinery price regulation (CPR 30) and ultimately placing them under a specifically designed order, leaving them in the interval under the general freeze. 

Industry representatives have advised these steps because of their low profit status in the pre-Korean base period stipulated by CPR 30, together with their extraordinarily complicated price structure and the difficulty of scheduling preparation of a tailored regulation. Price wars and the squeezing of some producers who voluntarily refrained from advances, plus higher Chilean copper prices, have left the industry's quotations in a confused situation.

Recommendations were made for a ceiling regulation based on price lists filed with OPS. The argument was put forward that the industry is essentially a mill industry and does not belong under the machinery order at all. 

Ceiling prices at levels not above those maintained by the highest priced segment of the industry under the General Ceiling Price Regulation were discussed. 

A. F. Norling, OPS Metals Branch consultant, presided at today's meeting. 

Other OPS representatives were William Kerber, Branch chief, R. J. Benes, counsel, and C. R. Wasson, economist.

G. E. Ralston attended for the National Production Authority.

Washington Scott-OPS-GPR-537  Re: EASTERN AND CENTRAL WOODEN AGRICULTURAL CONTAINER LAC The Eastern and Central Wooden Agricultural Container Industry Advisory 

Committee today asked Office of Price Stabilization officials for a quick interim pricing regulation, to relieve a more or less serious price squeeze under the General Ceiling Price Regulation.

The industry produces wooden baskets, hampers, crates, etc. used in the marketing of fruits and vegetables.

Committee members stated the industry generally experienced a depressed price situation during the December 19, 1950 to January 25, 1951 base period under GCPR, and for a considerable period of time before the base period, due largely to numerous crop failures. 

Committeemen pointed out several major factors which have brought about the present price squeeze. For some time before the GCPR base period, they said, the industry generally had accumulated heavy inventories, produced at labor and material costs substantially lower than current costs. As these inventories have been liquidated, the industry is now producing stocks on the basis of greatly increased labor and material costs, and is held to low base period ceiling prices under GCPR.

Existing prices are based on previous low minimum wage rates and low material costs. Current labor costs not only reflect an increase in the minimum wage rate, but also a lowering of labor efficiency due to the draining off of efficient labor to defense industries. The current cost of lumber and logs, the principal raw materials, is not reflected in current ceiling prices. 

The committee asked for an interim pricing regulation to give the industry immediate relief until a tailored regulation can be issued. 

The committee favored a tailored dollars-and-cents ceiling price regulation patterned along the general lines of the old OPA regulation MPR-320. Members said OPA regulation MPR-320 was equitable and workable, and fairly well reflected the industry's normal pricing practices. 

A sub-committee was appointed to advise further with OPS officials on an interim regulation and a tailored regulation. Members appointed as a subcommittee are:

C. H. Kinney, E. C. Hulett, W. C. Haggard and S. C. Lampert.

PRESS RELEASE   

 Re: RUBBER ADHESIVES IAC Moore - OPS-GPR-539 

Members of the Rubber Adhesives Industry Advisory Committees at their second meeting today with OPS officials stressed the need for a tailored regulation in their industry which would permit them to calculate increased costs of research in computing their ceilings. 

Committeemen said their industry was obliged to make heavy expenditures for research to develop new cements and find substitute materials, and in some instances research ran higher than factory labor costs. The Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, they said was not satisfactory in this respect because it did not permit inclusion of increased research costs.

The committee also pointed out that substantial increases in their prices caused by increased material and labor costs forced them to pay increased commission on sales which they had to absorb to the extent of materially effecting their returns.

Rubber adhesives are used in many industries such as the automobile, shoe and construction industries. They are made to many specifications depending on their particular uses. The industry is currently faced with the necessity of making many substitutions in their compounds. # # # # # # # # #

GPOO-OPS 961

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers 

TEMPO E-WASHINGTON RE: BEEF CONTROL PROGRAM 

The only alternative to price control on beef is soaring beef prices, Director Michael V. DiSalle of the Office of Price 

Stabilization told Congress today.

He filed a formal report on the beef price control program with the Senate Banking and Currency Committee, before which he recently appeared to urge extension of the National Defense Act. 

Mr. DiSalle pointed out that many critics of price control on beef had argued production is the way to bring down prices. 

Answering these critics, Mr. DiSalle declared: "We would like to make it perfectly clear that the alternative to price control on meat is soaring beef prices. Increased production will not keep prices down. This can be demonstrated by the following facts: "First, from June 1950 to April 1951 there was a substantial increase in cattle production. Prices of beef cattle during that period rose 25 percent. Production did not keep prices down.

Barkley-OPS-GPR-540 

 "Second, in January 1951 the OPS placed controls on the price of meat at wholesale and retail but not on live cattle. 

Despite meat price controls at wholesale and retail levels, prices of live cattle increased 12 percent between January and 

April 1951. Production did not keep prices down. "Third, in 1946 when the meat price controls of OPA were lifted the price of beef increased about 50 percent in one month. 

The high production of that year did not keep prices down." 

Mr. DiSalle said rising cattle prices made price control on the live animals essential. "Between January 1950, the date of the wage-stabilization base, and March 1951, the prices of cattle rose more than five times as much as the wages of manufacturing workers, over four times as much as prices paid by farmers, over five times as much as the index of consumer prices, and over three times as much as the prices of food items," Mr. DiSalle said. "It was obvious to the Office of Price Stabilization that unless the price of live cattle was adjusted to a level more nearly in line with other prices and wages, there would be irresistible economic pressures to raise wages and other prices to the level of cattle prices. * *"" "Accordingly, we decided to try to create a beef program which would be fair to all segments of the cattle industry, from the farmer through the feeder; to all segments of the beef industry, from the packer through the retailer, and to the consumer." 

Mr. DiSalle said the program was broad enough to encourage continued increased production and to be enforceable. 

He quoted from the statement, before the House Agriculture Committee, of Secretary of Agriculture Charles F. Brannan that the program, at the producer and feeder level, gave "reasonable incentive for the continuing production of beef animals." 

Even after the last roll-back contemplated on October 1, Mr. DiSalle said cattle prices would be sufficiently high to make cattle production and cattle feeding profitable. Cattle Prices after October 1951, will be 25 percent higher than January 1951, he said, while prices paid by farmers have increased only 13 percent. 

While there is a "great deal of theoretical appeal to the argument" that the program will lead to "regimentation” against which the cattle industry will rebel, Mr. DiSalle said this argument "loses its validity" because of the prices fixed by the regu lation. 

953517-51-1 "While cattlemen, like everyone else, dislike controls," he said, "they are in business for profit and if, as will be demonstrated, the OPS prices make it profitable for them to produce or feed cattle, cattle will be produced and fed." 

The price stabilizer said a major criticism of the program is that beef will not be sold in regular channels at ceiling prices but will be sold in the "black market" at higher prices and, therefore, the entire beef program is meaningless. 

Mr. DiSalle emphasized that OPS has advantage of OPA experience in dealing with black markets. he pointed out, was primarily caused by lack of slaughter control and by poor distribution of meat-problems that have been 

The black market, overcome in the OPS program by registration of slaughterers and monthly quotas to allocate the available supply of animals equitably among the registered slaughterers.

The objective of the slaughter quota system for allocating available supplies of livestock among slaughterers is two-fold: 

1. To assure a fair division of available supplies of livestock among existing slaughterers. 

2. To prevent irresponsible operators from obtaining supplies of livestock and diverting meat into the black market. (1)

MEMORANDUM ON BEEF CONTROL PROGRAM INTRODUCTION 

During the past few weeks the representatives of the meat packers and cattle raisers have come before various committees of the Congress urging an end of price control on their products. They have testified that they are opposed to price control in principle on beef and cattle because in their opinion it is unworkable, leads to a decline in production, and creates black markets that destroy all respect for law. They have also testified that they are opposed to the beef and cattle price regulations because in their opinion the regulations are unfair and will create losses. 

I. PRICE CONTROLS ON BEEF ARE CRUCIAL 

In passing the Defense Production Act of 1950 Congress did not see fit to exempt beef and cattle from price control. 

Nor should such an exemption be made in the legislation extending the price control powers. and isolated commodity for which the decision to price control or not to price control can be made on the basis of the ease or

Beef occupies a crucial position both in the consumer's cost of living and in the

Failure to control beef prices would thus result in wrecking controls on all food prices. And with no controls on food prices-which account for a third of the consumers' price index-the wage stabilization program would become unjust and unenforceable. With wage control out of the picture, it is easy to see that we would have to give un price control on the industrial sector, as well as on the agricultural sector of the economy. production will not keep prices down.

He stated that he couldn't give the public "any damn insurance that prices won't go up" if meat controls were ended.

We would like to make it perfectly clear that the alternative to price control of meat is soaring beef prices. Increased during that period rose 25 percent.

THE BEEF PRICE CONTROL PROGRAM IS FAIR AND WORKABLE 

Since the beginning of 1950 the prices of live cattle have risen far out of proportion to wages, and to other prices. A brief comparison of cattle prices with other prices clearly shows the disproportionate increase in cattle prices.

1950 1951 Thus, between January 1950, the date of the wage stabilization base, and March 1951, the prices of cattle rose more than five times as much as the wages of manufacturing workers, over four times as much as the prices paid by farmers, over five times as much as the index of consumer prices, and over three times as much as the prices of food items. 

It was obvious to the Office of Price Stabilization that unless the price of live cattle was adjusted to a level more nearly in line with other prices and wages, there would be irresistible economic pressures to raise wages and other prices to the level of cattle prices-that faced with the rises in price of beef that would have to be made to reflect the increased price of cattle, labor unions would have a compelling case for further cost-of-living increases which would in turn cause pressures for price rises by their employers. Accordingly, we decided to try to create a beef program which would be fair to all segments of the cattle industry, from the farmer through the feeder, to all segments of the beef industry, from the packer through the retailer, and to the consumer-a program which would encourage increased production, and which would be enforceable. After many months of intense study, including extended conferences with all major segments of the beef and cattle industries and other interested government agencies, we achieved a program, embodied in Distribution Regulations 1 and 2 and Ceiling Price Regulations 23, 24, 25, and 26, which it is believed will accomplish each of these objectives. This program- 

1. Will encourage the production of beef cattle. 

2. Will be fair to the cattle industry. 

3. Will be fair to the beef industry. 

4. Will be fair to the consumer.

A. The general level of cattle prices is profitable 

In his testimony before the House Committee on Agriculture on May 17, 1951, the Secretary of Agriculture said: "Judging from actual experience of the rate at which cattle numbers were increased in 1949 and 1950, average cattle and calf prices at about the 1950 level, which will still be allowed by the OPS ceilings, should still constitute a reasonable incentive for the continuing production of beef animals. We must bear in mind, however, that costs of farm and ranch operations are increasing and that again this is a situation which needs to be carefully watched." 

There are sound reasons supporting the Secretary's conclusion that there will be a "reasonable incentive for the continuing production of beef animals.” The basic reason, of course, is that the prices even after the last roll-back will be sufficiently high to make cattle production and cattle feeding profitable. This is demonstrated by the following facts: 

First. The prices after the last roll-back will be about 25 percent higher than January 1950—yet the Department of 

Agriculture index of prices paid by farmers, including feed, interest, taxes, and wage rates have increased only 13 percent.

Second. The prices after the last roll-back will be more than 20 percent higher than parity-and parity was revised as late as January 1950 to substantially increase parity for beef cattle and lambs relative to other products. 

Third. The prices after the last roll-back will be higher than the June 1950 prices. The June 1950 price was so high that it stimulated a substantial increase in beef production. 

Fourth. The prices after the last roll-back are higher than the highest average annual price for any year prior to Korea. 

The highest average annual price prior to Korea was $22.40. The lowest price set by OPS is about $24.00 or 7 percent higher than the highest historical price. 

B. Price regulation will not deter production 

The opponents of the OPS beef program have stated that the mere fact of control will be sufficient to cause a decrease in production. In effect they say that the cattle industry will rebel against OPS "regimentation" and curtail production 

While there is a great deal of theoretical appeal to this argument, it loses its validity if the prices fixed by the regulation make cattle producing and cattle feeding profitable. For while cattlemen, like everyone else, dislike controls, they are in business for profit and if, as will be demonstrated, the OPS prices make it profitable for them to produce or feed cattle, cattle will be produced and fed.

Moreover, under OPA, price regulation did not deter production. Here is what happened under OPA: 

First.-Total meat production reached a record high that was never equalled before or after the OPA. 

Second.-Beef production increased to a record high which has only been equalled in one year since OPA. 

Third.-Total cattle numbers reached an all-time high which has not since been equalled. 

Fourth. There were more beef cattle and calves on the farm than ever before or since. 

The OPA didn't cause this record production but it didn't stop it either.

II. THE OPS PROGRAM IS FAIR TO THE CATTLE INDUSTRY 

A. It is fair to the producer 

This memorandum has previously compared the lowest prices set by OPS in relation to farmer costs generally, in relation to parity, and in relation to historic cattle price levels. All of these general indices demonstrate that the OPS prices are fair and profitable to the producer.

This conclusion is also supported by Department of Agriculture studies of specific producer costs which show that under the lowest prices set by OPS the return to the cattle producer will be substantial and will equal his historical profit. Studies by the Department of Agriculture of cattle operations in the intermountain region show that the return of cattle growers for the year 1947 amounted to $7.25 per cwt, or $50.75 per 700-pound animal. Subsequent studies, bringing the original publication down to date, show that the return for the year 1950 was $7.96 per cwt, or $55.72 per 700-pound animal. A similar analysis, by the Department of Agriculture, and applied by OPS to the level of cattle prices to be in effect after October 1 (the lowest price proposed by the regulation), shows that producers will realize a return of $7.49 per cwt, or $52.43 animal. The Department of Agriculture study is confined to the intermountain region, but there is no reason to suppose per 700-pound that the costs of operation in that region are lower than those in any other part of the country. 

It should be pointed out that the 1951 calculation of the Department of Agriculture actually understates the producers' margin by about $9.00 per animal.

Since it is clear that feeders will make liberal profits under the October ceilings, it is clear that they will have a sufficient incentive to continue the production of well-finished cattle. $117.30 117.30 117.30 117.30 117.30 117.30 

The second question is whether, when prices are rolled back, losses to feeders on their present inventory of cattle will be so substantial as to make a roll-back unfair. This question was carefully considered prior to the issuance of the regulations. 

In fact the desire to protect the feeder against inventory losses was the sole reason why the roll-backs were delayed. The delay gave the feeder a chance to dispose of his cattle at higher prices and the final roll-back was timed to coincide with the period when the number of cattle in feed lots is normally at a relatively low level. 

Under the present program feeders will not incur over-all inventory losses though some losses will be sustained on cattle purchased since January. There are two major groups of feeders, the farmer feeder and the commercial feeder. The farmer feeder usually purchases cattle in the fall and sells during the next spring or summer. To the extent that he followed this normal practice he is not adversely affected by the roll-back, because he did not purchase his cattle at the recent high prices but at the lower prices that prevailed last fall. The commercial feeder usually purchases the year round but tends to concentrate his purchases in the fall when prices are normally most favorable. His losses on the relatively small number purchased since January should be more than offset by his profits on his large fall purchases.

III. THE OPS PROGRAM IS FAIR TO THE BEEF INDUSTRY 

There have been relatively few complaints of the theoretical fairness of the beef regulations, Ceiling Price Regulations 23, 24, 25, and 26, to the beef industry. Indeed, The Washington Post reported on May 16, 1951, that the attorney representing the National Association of Meat Processors and Wholesalers "complimented OPS for 'regulations under which we can live.'" 

Such criticism of the OPS regulations as the Congress has received from the beef industry has centered around these two major questions:

Save for those members of the beef industry who are opposed to price controls under all circumstances, it appears that the other members of the industry-packers, wholesalers, retailers, and other distributors—would have no serious complaints concerning the OPS regulations if they do not curtail beef-cattle production and if they are workable and enforceable, that is, if under the OPS regulations they will receive an adequate supply of beef at or below the ceiling prices established for their sources of supply. Both of these points are discussed at length in this memorandum.

IV. THE OPS PROGRAM IS FAIR TO THE CONSUMER 

Under the OPS program, there are three sets of ceiling prices. The first set, the May level, is designed to restore prices to the January level and relieve the squeeze on the beef industry caused by the post-January rise in cattle prices. This reduction in the price of live cattle will have little or no effect on the average beef prices at consumer levels. The reductions in live cattle prices of approximately 4½ percent in August and 4½ percent in October will be reflected in reductions in the prices at retail stores. The last reduction will reduce retail beef ceiling prices about nine percent and restore them close to the levels of May-June 1950. As has previously been pointed out, the roll-backs were timed to minimize inventory losses of feeders.

V. THE OPS PROGRAM IN ENFORCEABLE 

Rib roast (7-inch cut) $0.88 8888 86 82 78 

Chuck roast Hamburger $0.74 .76 73 69 $0.66 .67 .64 .61 

A major criticism of the program is that beef will not be sold in regular channels at ceiling prices but will be sold in the "black market" at higher prices and, therefore, that the entire beef program is meaningless. 

The OPS has the advantage of OPA experience in dealing with the black market. Thus we should be able to do a more effective job. The black market was primarily caused by lack of slaughter control and by poor distribution of meat. The 

OPS program to deal with these problems is as follows: 

First: Slaughter registration.-OPS issued its slaughter registration and quota regulation, Distribution Regulation 1, in

February. This early issuance date was determined upon in order to keep black marketeers from entering the slaughter field. 

OPA did not effectively register slaughterers until 1945. By that time, some black marketeers had entered the slaughtering business, and it was difficult in most instances to prevent their registration. By starting early, OPS can limit distribution to legitimate slaughterers and keep beef distribution in their hands. The slaughter control program, by setting quotas each month based on last year's slaughter, effectively apportions the total available supply fairly among all slaughterers. Thus, if in a given month, estimates indicate that hog slaughter will be 110 percent and the cattle slaughter will be 95 percent of the 1950 slaughter, each slaughterer's quota for that month is established at 110 percent of his 1950 hog slaughter and at 95 percent of his 1950 cattle slaughter.

Second: Allocation.-In Distribution Regulation 2, OPS provided for record keeping which might serve as the basis for meat allocation when and if meat shortages should develop. If necessary, OPS can allocate meat to areas, to assure fair supplies to each area through legitimate dealers, or can allocate meat to distributors to assure a fair supply to each distributor. 

By allocating, if necessary, OPS can keep meat in legitimate channels and make it unnecessary for legitimate businessmen to go into a "black market" to get supplies.

Third: Prices adequately cover transportation costs.-The OPS beef regulations more adequately reflect transportation costs than did the OPA regulations, thereby making it equally profitable to sell meat in all parts of the country. Since all areas of the country will thus have access to an adequate supply of beef, it will not be profitable to set up area black markets. 

Fourth: OPS beef regulations do not squeeze legitimate businesses.-OPS regulations provide more liberal dollar margins for slaughterers and wholesalers than OPA allowed. These wider margins have but little effect on what the consumer pays, but make it profitable for businessmen to comply with the program. 

While OPS should do a better job in dealing with the black market than OPA, the extent of the black market under OPA has been very much exaggerated. Those who have expressed concern about the black market have primarily pointed to experience in the middle of 1946 when price controls were crumbling. They have ignored the fact that during most of 

OPA, meat black markets were not a serious problem. 

A study made by OPA covered the monthly purchases during 1944 and 1945 by 21 packing companies covering over 100 plants and about 58 percent of the total volume of federally inspected slaughter. The total cost of their cattle was, on the average, the maximum cost permitted by the cattle regulations, and exceeded the maximum permissible cost in relatively few 

This is shown in the following table: cases.
