Even in the spring of 1946, there was substantial compliance with the OPA meat regulations. A survey conducted in 27 representative cities in March 1946 collected 4,473 meat prices from 857 retail stores. Of these, 83 percent were found to be in compliance. Another survey, conducted in Washington, D. C., in April 1946, revealed that overcharges were made in only 

3% percent of the purchases. The same situation existed in slaughtering plants. An OPA survey covering almost 2,000 plants, which slaughtered between 1.2 and 1.4 billion pounds per month, disclosed that the cost of cattle at these plants averaged 

15 cents below permissible cost in January 1946; 5 cents below in February 1946; and 4 cents below in both March and April 

1946. Moreover, the survey showed that out of the 170 zone and market reports for the five months, there were only 10 instances where the actual cost exceeded the permissible cost by more than one percent. It is clear that during most of OPA there was little black marketing at either the wholesale or retail level. However, beginning in 1946, when it became increasingly probable that controls would end on June 30, cattle were withheld from market and black market operations increased. The increasing violation in 1946, however, were caused not by price control but by the prospects of decontrol. 

VI. THE OPS PROGRAM IS WORKABLE 

Various witnesses have testified that the OPS program is unworkable for various reasons. below.

A. Uniform grading is practical 

There has been some testimony that uniform grading cannot be achieved. Uniform grading under standards prescribed by the Department of Agriculture has been used since 1916. For many years all beef purchased by the armed forces has been 

The major charges are discussed

Government graded. Some large chain stores, such as Safeway, have for many years purchased only Government graded beef. The OPS merely applied these well accepted grading standards to all beef. 

The OPA used uniform grading all during World War II. Not only was the grading practicable and workable but it received the support of the meat industry itself. A special Congressional Committee, the so-called Boren Committee (H. 

Rept. No. 808, 78th Congress, 1943) was established to investigate grade labeling and found that grade marking of meat was supported by the industry. In its report, the Committee stated: "In its price regulations the Office of Price Administration sets ceilings for these meats at various sales levels according to these grades. This system had the support of the industry from the outset. Prior to the issuance of OPS Regulation No. 1, continuation of meat grading and labeling was urged by the War Meat Board representing the meat industry. "No opposition against this system of grading and labeling of meat was voiced at any time in testimony before the subcommittee." 

B. Standard cuts are practical 

The OPS, to avoid evasion of the beef regulations, has prescribed a uniform system of cutting beef. These cuts are said to be impractical. The uniform cuts used by OPS are identical with those prescribed by OPA and were successfully in use during all of World War II. The cuts were defined and formulated for the OPA in accordance with the recommendations of industry representatives. OPS has used these same definitions and has also permitted additional cuts in accordance with the recommendations of industry advisory committees and its industry consultants, who recommended the standards for the new cuts.

C. There are a sufficient number of Federal graders 

Another criticism of OPS was that the beef program would not work because there were not enough Federal graders available. Prior to May 7, 1951, the effective date of Distribution Regulation 2, it was believed that there would be an adequate supply of Federal graders. When it became apparent, on May 9, that there were certain areas which did not have an adequate number of graders, Distribution Regulation 2 was promptly amended, on May 11, to permit self-grading for all grades if Federal graders were unavailable. This authority lapsed after May 20, when the temporary shortage of Federal graders ended.

D. The OPS program will not cause premature sales 

There has been some testimony that the OPS program will cause the premature liquidation of stock, thereby eventually causing a decline in beef-cattle production. The reports of cattle marketings following the issuance of beef regulations on 

April 30 show that there has been no premature liquidation. In each of the next three weeks for which reports have become available, fewer head of cattle were marketed than in the corresponding week of 1950 and the average weight of the cattle marketed was heavier than the average in the corresponding week of 1950. Inasmuch as these three weeks were immediately prior to the first and sharpest roll-back of cattle prices, it might have been anticipated that any substantial liquidation would have occurred during this period.

The result was to be expected because under the OPS regulations it does not pay to market prematurely. Holding cattle for a longer time is advantageous to the producer and the feeder, for the heavier and better grade animal brings a higher price. 

Then, too, any premature rush of cattle to market would drive prices below OPS ceiling prices, and it is unlikely that cattlemen will kill their market by glutting it with cattle.

I. OBJECTIVES OF THE PROGRAM 

The OPS slaughter quota system is a method for allocating available supplies of livestock among slaughterers.

It has the 

1. To assure a fair division of available supplies of livestock among existing slaughterers. 

2. To prevent irresponsible operators from obtaining supplies of livestock and diverting meat into the black market. 

These objectives are important for three reasons: -Y First: Experience in World War II demonstrated that there can be no equitable distribution of meat among areas, or to consumers, or to meat processors or distributors unless livestock is kept moving in normal channels to the slaughterers who 22

E tie

BI 

have customarily handled such livestock.

Slaughter quotas are the foundation of any program for equitable distribution of meat. 

Second: It is an essential requisite of any system of controls that the businesses regulated be assured of an opportunity to make a fair profit. In the absence of slaughter controls, established slaughterers might not be able to get adequate supplies of livestock and would therefore be unable to earn a fair return. !

Third: Unless meat is controlled at the slaughter level, the task of controlling the black market becomes very difficult. 

In World War II black market sellers frequently obtained their supplies from irresponsible operators who invaded the slaughtering business and diverted supplies from legitimate slaughterers. Moreover, legitimate and established businesses which do not get their fair share of livestock or of meat are under constant economic pressure to go into the black market in order to survive.

II. TECHNIQUE OF THE ORDER 

The method used in Distribution Regulation 1 to achieve these objectives is basically simple. 

Packers are prohibited from slaughtering in any given month a greater proportion of the total available livestock than they slaughtered in 1950. Thus if a packer slaughtered in June 1950 one percent of the total live weight of cattle slaughtered in that month, he may slaughter in June 1951 only one percent of the live weight of all cattle slaughtered in June 1951. 

This result is accomplished by giving each slaughterer for each month a quota base for each species of livestock equal to the amount he slaughtered in the corresponding month of 1950. Then an estimate is made of the livestock which will come to market in a particular month. This estimate is based on information from various sources, including Department of 

Agriculture data.

If it is estimated that marketings of a particular species of livestock in a particular month will be 110 percent of what they were in the same month last year each slaughterer has a quota equal to 110 percent of his quota base. If the estimate for that species in that month is 90 percent, each slaughterer's quota for that species is equal to 90 percent of his quota base. 

III. OBJECTIONS TO THE QUOTA SYSTEM 

Two general objections have been made to the slaughter quota program. The first is that it is designed to limit livestock marketings and will result in shortages. The second is that the order is unfair to persons who want to enter the slaughtering business. These objections will be considered in order. 

First: It is obvious from the explanation above that the quotas are not a limitation on livestock marketings but only a method for dividing livestock brought to market, equitably among slaughterers. Quota percentages are fixed on the basis of estimated marketings. If the percentage proves to be too low, the regulation provides for an increase. Also individual quota increases are granted in local situations when marketings are running higher than the national average. 

When, as in the month of May, cattle quotas were set at 90 percent the question is sometimes raised as to what will become of the other 10 percent. As explained above, there is no other 10 percent. The quotas in any given month are set at a level sufficient to absorb all cattle brought to market in that month. 

When quotas are set at 90 percent, the percentage is not 90 per cent of current marketings but rather 90 percent of last year's marketings. This is because the number of livestock being marketed in a particular month is that much less than the number marketed in the corresponding month of 1950. 

Second: The slaughter control order also provides in effect that new operators will not receive a quota for livestock except in certain situations. Thus, adjustments have been granted under Section 9 of the order in cases where slaughterers made investments in facilities prior to the date of the order even though they did not slaughter any livestock in 1950. Adjustments have also been granted where facilities have been expanded. 

Also Section 10 of the order provides that new entrants into the slaughtering business will be registered and granted quotas where they show that their operations are essential to meet civilian needs in the area to be served, that the products to be produced cannot be obtained from any other source, and that the operation of the new establishment will promote the National Defense by facilitating the production and orderly distribution of meat. 

These provisions obviously will keep out potential black-market operators but permit the entry of persons whose proposed operations serve a genuine need and contribute to the National Defense. 

In brief, the slaughter quota program is a method of assuring equitable distribution of livestock and of meat, of protecting legitimate enterprises in the meat business and of preventing the growth of the black market. It is not a restriction on production nor a device to limit marketing of livestock. 

CONCLUSION 

The OPS beef program is fair to all segments of our economy and is workable and enforceable. As the Secretary of 

Agriculture stated to the House Agriculture Committee on May 17, 1951: "In view of the mutual stake of farmers, consumers, labor, and business in economic stabilization, I believe we should give the price orders a fair chance to work, or those who now complain should come forward with a better plan."

PRESS RELEASE    

Re: NORTHEASTERN HARDWOOD IAC Moore-OPS-GPR-541  Members of the Northeastern Hardwood Industry Advisory Committee today recommended that a dollars and cents ceiling price regulation be tailored for their industry.

They told OPS officials at their first meeting that they would be willing to accept ceilings spelled out on the basis of average ceilings established by the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, under which lumber manufacturers are still operating.

They said GCPR prices reflected most of the cost increases in labor and stumpage which occurred after the outbreak of fighting in Korea and up to the time the GCPR went into effect, but they were apprehensive about further cost increases in the future.

However, they agreed it was impractical in the lumber business to work out costs for various grades and dimensions under the provisions of the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, and felt it would be better to accept GCPR prices as a reasonable approximation rather than undertake the complicated cost studies which would be required under CPR 

22 formulas. 

Members of the committee were unanimous in their belief that it was not practical to maintain ceiling prices on logs, which are also under GCPR. They felt sufficient uniformity in scaling and grading could not be obtained to enforce ceilings on logs.

Committeemen suggested that prices be spelled out on the basis of finished lumber delivered to the consumer. They felt customary marketing practices would maintain lower differentials on rough green lumber cut by many small mills which is usually sold to larger yards. 

The meeting was conducted by Norman O. Cruver, chief of the Lumber and Wood Products Branch, and Lawrence D. Kellogg, head of the Hardwood section.  W. S.

  Scott-OPS-GPR-542  SATURDAY CLOSING OPS FIELD OFFICES 

Michael V. DiSalle, Director of Price Stabilization, issued instructions today to all Office of Price Stabilization regional and district field offices for Saturday closing to the public, beginning June 16. 

On February 2, Mr. DiSalle ordered all OPS field offices to remain open on Saturdays for the convenience of the public and to care for the work load entailed in getting the price stabilization program organized and under way. # # # # # # # # # # # # # "We have reached the point in our organizational program and in our public information effort", Mr. DiSalle said, "where the volume of Saturday business does not justify the added expense of keeping field offices open on that day. We can and will order field offices to remain open on Saturdays when the need arises."

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers 

TEMPO E-WASHINGTON Crist-OPS-GPR-543 

RE: BUSINESS LICENSING 

A memorandum has been filed with the House and Senate Banking and Currency Committees by the Office of Price Stabilization setting forth in detail the reasons why the agency is seeking licensing authority. 

This memorandum makes it clear that every business firm would have "an absolute right to a license," that it would not give OPS the authority to prevent persons from going into business, and that only the courts would have the power to suspend a license.

The proposal to grant the OPS licensing authority is contained in a pending amendment to legislation extending the Defense Production Act of 1950, on which hearings are currently being held. "This amendment, which is offered as a general enforcement device for price control only, provides that a license must be given as an absolute right to anyone engaged or desiring to engage in business," the memorandum points out. "No license can be required under the amendment of (a) farmers and fishermen, or (b) newspapers, radio, and television stations."

The OPS memorandum points out that the agency is not seeking an unprecedented power, but that more than 20 Federal statutes having no relationship to wartime emergencies contain licensing provisions as a necessary aid in securing compliance, and that the amendment follows almost word for word provisions contained in the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942. 

Only a court, the memorandum points out, would have the power to suspend a license, and then only after "a legal proceeding which is designed to give the licensee every safeguard. . . 

Stressing the need for flexibility in enforcement provisions, the memorandum states: "The proposed licensing system provides a method whereby there can be taken into account in connection with each violation the degree of willfullness involved, the seriousness of the violation, the nature of the violator's business, and the importance of his business to the community as a whole."

The memorandum concludes by pointing out that the licensing system is not designed to punish the initial violator, but to "restrain the persistent violator." The mere existence of this authority, it contends, would prove a major deterrent to violations, especially in the case of "a small group of willful businessmen who regard financial penalties as merely 'taxes' to be paid for a continuing unlawful profit. 

From the inception of price control in 1942 through March 31, 1945, there were 32,118 license warnings issued, but as of May 1, 1945, only 325 license-suspension suits had been filed in court; out of 116 suits completed on that date, 101 resulted in orders of suspension varying from two days to one year. 

MEMORANDUM ON LICENSING 

This memorandum is designed to clarify the purpose and applicability of the licensing amendment, and to correct certain misunderstandings that have arisen regarding its scope and effect. 

1. Everyone has an absolute right to a license.—OPS would not be given the power to keep persons from going into business. 

This amendment, which is offered as a general enforcement device for price control only, provides that a license must be given as an absolute right to anyone engaged or desiring to engage in business. 

No license can be required under the amendment of (a) farmers and fishermen, or (b) newspapers, radio and television 

2. Only a court would be enabled to suspend a license. The licensing amendment provides specifically that suspension would be determined only by the courts and not by Government officials. Only after a legal proceeding which is designed to give the licensee every safeguard could a license be suspended. (a) Full court hearing and requirements of warning notice after violation. The procedure spelled out in the amendment grants the price violator every opportunity to avoid a court proceeding. After the first violation, a warning notice only would 

Even in the absence of wartime stresses, Congress has recognized that licensing is necessary in many cases to secure compliance with regulatory legislation. 

Indeed, more than 20 Federal statutes, which are listed in Appendix A, having no relationship to wartime emergencies contain licensing provisions as a necessary aid to securing compliance. Under these statutes a license can be suspended by administrative action. The proposed amendment, on the other hand, allows suspen. sion only by order of a court. (1) 953516°-51

5 be sent. If a person continues flagrantly to violate price regulations after a warning has been issued, the Director of Price 

Stabilization would have the right to petition a court for suspension of the license. After a full judicial hearing, the court could suspend the license for any period up to one year, after taking into consideration any extenuating circumstances. Furthermore, a license which has been suspended by the court may be restored upon such terms and conditions as the court finds reasonable. The right of appeal is guaranteed and a stay may be granted pending appeal. 

3. Licensing provisions afford enforcement flexibility.—The proposed amendment which follows almost word for word provisions contained in section 205 (f) of the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942, affords an opportunity for tailoring enforcement to the needs of each particular case. Just as, because of the complex nature of the American economy, price regulations must be flexible in order to fit the divergent needs of individual industries; enforcement measures must also be flexible in order that substantial justice be achieved in each case and hardship be minimized, wherever possible. The present criminal and civil sanctions of the Act do not by themselves provide a sufficient degree of flexibility. Where there are initial infractions of law, in some cases wholly innocent, criminal penalties may be too harsh. On the other hand, resort to treble damage actions or injunctive proceedings may likewise be inappropriate.

The proposed licensing system provides a method whereby there can be taken into account in connection with each violation the degree of willfullness involved, the seriousness of the violation, the nature of the violator's business, and the importance of his business to the community as a whole. 

As the Senate Banking and Currency Committee stated in 1942, in approving licensing provisions similar to those recommended here:

Nor are criminal prosecutions or injunction suits sufficiently flexible to assure substantial justice in the particular case. 

Licensing, on the other hand, in many cases, will provide . . . the flexibility which is essential to avoid hardship to the law-abiding businessman. American experience during the last war shows that both compliance and flexibility are attainable goals. That experience arose primarily out of the licensing provisions of the Lever Act. Under that statute, Mr. Herbert Hoover, as Food Administrator, was given broad licensing power which was extensively and effectively used. On the other hand the Fuel Administration did not at first have the powers to license, but it was soon discovered that such power was necessary; the result again was enforcement which, though highly effective, caused no hardship to business. 

In 1917, when he was Food Administrator, Mr. Herbert Hoover said:

The licensing system, however, is the backbone of all control. Without compulsion there will always be a few slackers in every trade who will profit by the patriotism of the majority and prevent any effective control. 

4. Licensing serves as an effective deterrent to price violations.—The licensing system which is requested is not designed to punish the initial violator. Its purpose rather is to restrain the persistent violator. The mere existence of a sanction to suspend a seller's right to sell a commodity or commodities for a limited period of time would have great deterrent effect upon persistent violations.

This would be especially true in the case of a small group of willful businessmen who regard financial penalties as merely "taxes" to be paid for a continuing unlawful profit. 

The effective nature of licensing is evident from the experience of the Office of Price Administration. From the inception of price control in 1942, through March 31, 1945, there were issued 32,118 license warning notices. However, as of May 

1, 1945, only 325 license suspension suits had been filed in court. Out of 116 suits completed on that date, 101 resulted in orders of suspension varying from two days to one year, depending on the nature of the violation. 

The fact that resort was had to the courts in so small a percentage of the cases is a clear indication that the warning notices had their intended effect-to prevent recurrence of violations. 

This conformed with the experience of the Food and Fuel Administrations during World War I. The reports of these agencies reveal that it was rarely necessary to suspend a license. The threat of suspension was a sufficient deterrent in substantially all instances in obtaining compliance.

Scott-OPS-GPR-544 

Re: USED TEXTILE BAG DEALERS IAC 

An industry advisory committee representing the used textile bag dealers today told officials of the Office of Price Stabilization that a dollars-and-cents ceiling pricing regulation for the industry is of great The industry is concerned with the buying and selling of second hand burlap and cotton bags used principally in marketing agricultural crops. 

Committee members previously met with OPS officials informally on April 6. At that time industry members felt it would be difficult to set dollars-and-cents ceiling prices on used burlap bags, because of the disturbed situation in the import prices of burlap, which basically control the price of used burlap bags. Since then dollars-and-cents ceiling prices on imported burlap have been set by Ceiling Price Regulation 40, issued and effective 

May 24, 1951.

Used burlap bags represent a substantial percentage of total dealer volume and the committee recommended that OPS set dollars-and-cents ceilings for used burlap bags on the basis of 75 percent of the ceiling price cost of import burlap, Members contended this formula would reflect the historical pattern of pricing used burlap bags and would, generally speaking, reflect a rollback of dealers current ceiling prices under GCPR. 

The committee strongly favored a tailored dollars-and-cents ceiling pricing regulation patterned after the old OPA regulation MPR-55. Members said this regulation was equitable and sound. 

The committee pointed out the urgency of drafting and issuance of a tailored regulation at the earliest date possible. They said the heavy harvesting season is immediately ahead, but dealers feel it is economically unsound to make heavy committements in buying and selling until dollarsand-cents ceilings are set.

The committee will meet with OPS officials again tomorrow to advise on the industry data that will be required to expedite the drafting of a tailored regulation.

Huff-OPS-GPR-545 

Re: RATE CASE INTERVENTION, CALIFORNIA ELECTRIC POWER COMPANY 

The Office of Price Stabilization has petitioned the California Public Utilities Commission for the right to intervene in commission proceedings on the California Electric Power Company's application for a general rate increase, the agency announced today.

Public hearings on the case have been scheduled for June 27 in Riverside, California. OPS will be represented by a member of its chief counsel's staff. 

OPS said intervention was desirable at least for the purpose of placing evidence in the record to demonstrate specifically what effect a rate increase might have on the Federal government's price stabilization program. 

The agency stated to the commission that approval of the proposed increase might have a tendency contrary to the purposes of the Defense Production Act. 

The California Electric Power Company advised OPS by letter of March 12 

that it had asked the California Public Utilities Commission on March 6 for a general increase in rates and charges for electric service, including service to certain customers for resale to the Public. 

In a letter of April 20, the company consented to OPS intervention in proceedings before the commission. OPS is legally concerned only with resale rates; it believes higher rates in this instance might have to be passed on to ultimate consumers.

Section 402 (e)(v) of the Defense Production Act exempts rates charged by common carriers and public utilities from OPS price control but requires notice to OPS 30 days before the effective date of higher rates for property or services sold for resale to the public, along with consent for "timely intervention" before the appropriate regulatory body.

PRESS RELEASE   

Re: 

 BEAUTY AND BARBER SERVICES Huges-OPS-GPR-546 ST. 4200, Ext. 3491 

Post-Korean prices in the 845-million-dollar barber and beauty shop trades have outrun the general increase in the cost of living and probably would go higher if controls were removed, according to an Office of Price 

Stabilization report to Congress.

A memorandum on these trades has been filed by OPS with the Banking and 

Currency Committees of the Senate and House. 

Charges for barber shop and beauty shop services are controlled by the general services regulation - Ceiling Price Regulation 34. This regulation keeps services at the general level of the period December 19, 1950-January 

25, 1951.

In reporting to Congress on the necessity of controls in this field, the OPS memorandum notes that charges for service in barber and beauty shops are a significant factor in the cost of living. In 1948 there were nearly 92,000 barber shops, more than 74,000 beauty shops, and more than 2500 combination shops in the country-a total of 168,500. Receipts in these establishments reached nearly $845,000,000. In 1950, barber and beauty shop services absorbed 1.3 per cent of all consumer dollars spent in that year. 

To indicate the disproportionate rise in prices in these trades following the Korean outbreak, OPS cited the Cost-of-Living Index as of December 1950, the latest date on which figures are available for the service trades. 

At that time the general index stood at 178.8, a 78.8 per cent increase over the 1935-1939 base, which is treated as 100. The index for all services (not including rent) was 152.5. The index for men's haircuts was 231.8; for shampoo and wave sets in beauty shops 266.5, and for beauty shop services, 189.7. 11 "It can be seen from the foregoing figures, the OPS memorandum says, "that barbering and beauty shop service prices have increased far in excess of the general increase in prices in the service trades and in excess of the increase in the cost of living. In short, these groups are not in an adverse position because of the increase in the cost of living for the reason that their prices have outpaced the general increase. The above figures indicate that the inflationary pressures in the barber and beauty shop fields exceed the pressure in the nation generally and, if anything, control over them is at least as necessary as for other businesses 'whose charges enter into the cost of living index.

GPOO-OPS 969

"If these services are freed from controls it is possible, in view of current trends, that the prices for such services will continue on an upward and unchecked movement, thereby bringing about not only a distortion of price control, but also a disproportionate claim upon the consumer dollar.' ?? The OPS memorandum also points out that if, despite the general price rise in barber and beauty shop services, individual hardships exist, relief can be sought under Section 20 or CPR 34. vides that if prices in a particular area are, on the whole, too low, correc- In addition, the regulation protion can be applied for under Section 24 of CPR 24.

Tempo E 

Washington Re: BARBER AND BEAUTY SERVICES 

Hughes-OPS-GPR-546X  

CORRECTION 

A recent OPS press release was incorrect in stating that prices for beauty and barber shop services have risen disproportionately since the Korean outbreak, the Office of Price Stabilization said today. 

The release correctly pointed out that, with 1935-39 as a base of 100, the index for men's haircuts stood at 231.8 in December 1950, for shampoo and wave sets in beauty shops at 226.5, and for beauty shop services at 

189.7. These figures compared with a general cost of living index of 178.8 and an index for all services (not including rent) of 152.5. 

The wording of the original press release indicated, however, that much of the increases had taken place since Korea, which is incorrect. Most of the increases over the 1935-39 base actually took place during World War II when beauty and barber shops were left free from OPA controls. After Korea, up to December, hair cuts advanced 8 percent.

Hughes-OPS-GPR-548 ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 Re: 

Re: INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEES EFFECT OF REGULATIONS ON EXISTING CONTRACTS 

In issuing price control regulations, the Office of Price Stabilization has given careful attention to the effect of such regulations on existing contracts for future delivery, the Agency has reported in a memorandum to Congress.

The memorandum was submitted to the House and Senate Committees on Banking and Currency as a comment on allegations that OPS has "not paid any attention" to a section of the Defense Production Act of 1950 directing that consideration be given to existing contracts. 

While the Defense Production Act grants the power to cut across contracts, the memorandum notes, it does direct that "the President shall make appropriate provisions to prevent hardships and inequities to sellers who have bona fide contracts in effect on the date of issuance of any such regulation or order for future delivery of materials in which seasonal demands or normal business practices require contracts for future delivery. IT As evidence of the fact that due attention has been given to the matter, the OPS memorandum cites 12 regulations which have permitted preexisting contracts for future delivery of materials to be carried out at contract prices higher than the ceiling price established. Commodities so affected included coal, fats and oils, exported commodities, cotton, coke, coal chemicals, coke oven gas, wool yarns and fabrics, American Upland Cotton, blackstrap molasses, scrap metals, imported commodities, marine feed products, and burlap.

In addition, OPS has issued five regulation which contain provisions for adjusting upward the ceiling prices established in the regulations, based on contracts. These regulations cover anthracite; cattlehides, kips, and calfskins; manufactured goods in general (CPR 22); machinery, and shoes. 

In still other instances, the memorandum notes, provision has been made in regulations to relieve a manufacturer who, as a result of his applicable ceiling prices, has been or would be forced to operate at a loss with respect to his over-all manufacturing operations. The relief provision is applicable to pre-existing contracts for future delivery. GPO-O-OPS 971

Moreover, the absence of a specific provision validating pre-existing contracts does not prevent a seller or group of sellers from obtaining relief. Price Procedural Regulation 1 Revised provides the machinery for petitions for amendment and for protests. A change in Ceiling Price Regulation 8 for example validating certain cotton shippers' contracts in effect when CPR 8 was issued - resulted from such a petition. 

Industry Advisory Committees 

Another memorandum filed by OPS with Congress reports that by June 1, 1951 OPS had appointed 263 industry advisory committees. Of this number, 225 had a total of 263 meetings, of which 15 were held in February, 60 in 

March, 77 in April, and 111 in May. Thirty-eight committees have 'not yet held meetings, but dates are being arranged. GD The memorandum outlines the authority (as contained in the Defense 

Production Act) for the appointment of industry advisory committees, and their proper functioning, as outlined by the Department of Justice in relation to the antitrust laws. OPS procedure, the memorandum says, has followed the requirements of the Defense act and of the antitrust laws. 

To be eligible for membership on an industry advisory committee, a person must be presently employed "with a firm in the business or industry affected in an advisory, managerial, or technical capacity related to the production, distribution or use of the material or service." Elected officials of a trade association eligible by this standard are frequently appointed to membership. Full-time trade association executives are not eligible under this requirement.

OPS obtains nominations for membership from many sources, including trade association officials. No committee may be approved by OPS unless the proposed membership parallels in proportional distribution the characteristics of the industry as a whole within a reasonable degree. It must include a fair representation of small, medium and large businesses. "These industry advisory committees," the memorandum says, "have contributed invaluable advice and recommendations. However, the responsibility for reaching final decisions must rest with OPS." 

The memorandum adds: 

"In the present emergency, OPS was confronted with the urgent necessity for making many important decisions as rapidly as possible. Far from being unwilling to cooperate with industry through advisory committees, or to consult with industry and trade associations OPS is using the committee function to the fullest extent permitted by existing law, and has consulted industry and trade associations in every way practicable."

  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in All Editions SUNDAY, JUNE 10, 1951 

POSTING OF SERVICE CEILINGS 

Milliken-OPS-GPR-552 

ST 4200; Ext. 6029

Family expenses will be better stabilized and budget makers will know better where they stand next Friday, June 15, when several hundred classes of retail services are required to post their ceiling prices. 

The many different service trades, used from day to day by the 

American public, have been under ceiling price Regulation 34 since May 16.

Next Friday they are required to post their ceiling prices in their places of business where customers can see them.

The ceiling price regulation affects more than $10,000,000,000, annually of personal and commercial services. Over a million establishments throughout the United States are involved.

While it is expected to make few material changes in the going prices that American pay in many diverse offices and business places every day, it will roll back any unjustifiable increases since the base period of December 19, 1950 to January 25, 1951. Equally important, it will stabilize and hold a substantial group of prices that add up in the course of a year to a substantial bit out of the family budget. 

Among the many classes of services are: adding machines, air conditioning maintenance and repair; and ambulance services. Automobile repairs are covered, as are like services for boats, trucks, tractors, appliances, refrigerators, typewriters, vacuum cleaners, watches and washing machines. 

Do you need a haircut, or your wife a permanent? Look for the posted ceiling price in your favorite shop. The same goes for that Tuesday night bowling engagement. Pay no more than the posted prices. 

What have you been paying for cleaning and dyeing? The posted ceiling price at your neighborhood cleaner tells you that you can expect to keep this important budget item at a fixed figure per month. The same goes for shoe repairs, the rental of a dress suit for that wedding and developing and printing the snapshots of the ceremony. 

Businessmen, who require numerous services, can know that there is a visible, ascertainable ceiling price on bookkeeping and financial services, brokerage in commodities and buying and selling commissions. Cash register services are included in the regulation as well as credit information services, investment counsel, and public relations and publicity counsel. GPO-O-OPS 978

Idea behind Regulation 34 is, simply, that services rendered in trade, commerce and industry, services integrated with such services as well as personal services all vitally affect the national economy. 

All persons engaged in professional services and the many trades and business activities covered by the regulation are urged by OPS to get in touch with their nearest District OPS Office for the answer to any problem. # # # # # # # # # # # # #

PRESS RELEASE    

Moore -OPS-GPR-555 

Re: WOOD PRESERVING IAC Members of the Wood Preserving Industry Advisory Committee today recommended to OPS officials that an interim regulation be written which would relieve members of their industry caught in a squeeze between the higher costs of forest products which they buy and contract prices on the treated products they sell.

They told OPS officials their products are frequently sold against large volume contracts, and consequently their selling prices were not adjusted to rising costs as rapidly as the raw products which they purchase. 

Hence some were caught in a squeeze under the General Ceiling Price 

Regulation which governs their industry.

Relief could be obtained, they said, if they were permitted to pass through the cost to them of the raw forest products--ties, bridge timbers, poles and piling--merely maintaining their customary margin. They suggested this be done in an interim regulation. 

The committee gave some attention to the old OPA regulation MPR 491, governing the pressure preservative treatment of forest products and the products themselves as the basis of a future tailored regulation. This regulation fixed dollars and cents ceilings on the services performed by the industry on the basis of cubic feet of content, and also prices of poles and piling and other products, but not ties, which were covered by another regulation.

A price survey of the brewing industry is being prepared by the Office of Price Stabilization to aid in drafting a price regulation for beer from brewery to the consumer, the agency announced today.

Washington Moore-OPS-GPR-558 ST. 4200: Ext. 3491 TIGHT COOPERAGE LAC Members of the Tight Cooperage Industry Advisory Committee today recommended to OPS officials that a tailored regulation be written for their industry that would fix dollars and cents ceilings on barrels, but leave staves and headings uncontrolled.

Committeemen suggested that the weighted average of the January freeze ceilings be employed to arrive at a dollars and cents ceiling on whiskey barrels, and that the ceilings on tight chemical and food barrels reflect the same proportionate relationship with whiskey barrels that existed under old OPA regulation MPR 424.

They estimated this would produce ceiling prices for 50 gallon whiskey barrels of between $26.00 and $30.00 and for chemical and food barrels from $13 to $14.

Members of the committee said control on the price of barrels would establish indirectly ceilings on the price of staves and headings, and provide a flexible relationship between prime produced stock and "off falls" from white oak whiskey barrel stock used in producing chemical and food barrels. 

Committeemen explained that normally the competition of steel drums keeps prices down to a point where it is uneconomic to manufacture wooden chemical and food barrels from stock produced primarily for that purpose. Such barrels have been manufactured mainly from white oak staves and headings rejected for use in whiskey barrels.

With the tightening of the supply of steel drums due to demand and NPA controls, there is a growing market for wooden chemical and food barrels. But existing ceilings, predicated on containers manufactured from off falls of the whiskey barrel industry, committeemen reported, are not high enough to make it economic to produce such containers from staves and headings cut primarily for chemical and food barrels.

Committeemen said the most practical way to determine prices which would make chemical and food barrels a self-sustaining industry was to go back to the old price relationship that existed under OPA. This would result in prices, they said, which would encourage production of staves and headings for chemical and food barrels from other species, such as red oak, gum and ash. 

A sub-committee was named to work out details of the problem with OPS 

GPO-O-OPS 994

Re: TOY INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE Scott-OPS-GPR-560 

At its second meeting today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization, the Toy Industry Advisory Committee discussed recommendations for a tailored pricing regulation for the industry.

The committee was told that OPS will issue as soon as possible, an order putting retail toy sales under the retail price regulation, CPR 7, which will remove retail toy sales from the General Ceiling Price Regulation. 

The committee was also told there is little possibility, if any, that toy manufacturers would be given the privilege of pricing under GCPR rather than under the manufacturers' price regulation CPR 22, except in the case of small manufacturers with sales volume under $250,000. who can elect to price under 

GCPR as now provided by CPR 22.

The committee asked OPS to give further consideration to the industry's recommendation that toy manufacturers be permitted to remain under GCPR until a tailored pricing regulation can be issued. 

Members pointed out that, generally speaking, between 50 and 60 percent of the total volume of toy manufacturers' business for the current year will have been shipped at GCPR prices or less by July 2, when CPR 22 pricing becomes effective. 

Members stated that figures of a representative number of industry members indicates that pricing under CPR 22, generally speaking, will result in a substantially greater roll forward in ceiling prices than in roll backs. 

Members said a change in industry pricing from GCPR to CPR 22 at this time, when the industry has already shipped more than 50 percent of the current years business, will result in serious price confusion within the industry, without resulting in any material benefit at the consumer level. 

It was suggested the committee, or the sub-committee already appointed, be asked to meet again with OPS officials at an early date, to advise further on specific provisions needed in a tailored regulation for the toy industry. 1 GPO-O-OPS 989

ST 4200; Ext. 3491 Moore Members of the Envelope Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee today recommended a tailored regulation be written for their industry which would employ the method of pricing prescribed in SR 2 to CPR 22.

Under this method, they recommended an industry-wide weighted average percentage cost adjustment factor be developed which would be applied to price lists and formulas frozen under the General Ceiling Price Regulation. 

They reported that CPR 22, the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, was not suitable for their industry because it would result in widely scattered ceilings between competitors in a highly competitive trade. 

Moreover, ceilings established under CPR 22, they said, would not return their industry the 85 percent earnings of the best three out of four years from 1946 to 1949 inclusive. It is agency policy to consider relief if ceilings are not high enough to yield that much return.

PRESS RELEASE   ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers WEDNESDAY, June 13, 1951 Re: LIVE CATTLE PRICES Barkley-OPS-GPR-563  

Price Stabilizer Michael V. DiSalle today cautioned livestock slaughterers against over-bidding for live cattle.

He warned that some slaughterers may be headed toward violations of the Office of Price Stabilization's price ceilings at the end of the June accounting period. 

Unless these slaughterers stop overbidding the price of cattle, he added, they may find themselves out of compliance with the regulation and subject to its penalty provisions, including civil and criminal actions as well as reductions in their July slaughter quotas. "I want to go on record right now while this program is just getting started that violations of cattle price ceilings will not be condoned any more than the violation of any other price regulation, " Mr. DiSalle said. "Live cattle prices have, been under ceilings only since June 4, but from the reports we are receiving some slaughterers may find it rough going when they try to "even out" during the remainder of the June accounting period. "I want to caution them now to get back in line and to cooperate in this program. " 

Mr. DiSalle said some slaughterers appeared to be paying $1 to $1.50 a hundred pounds above ceilings. To average out in compliance with the ceilings they will have to buy cattle later in the month at less than ceiling prices. 

The regulation does not set ceiling prices on individual cattle, but it establishes a "maximum permissible price" which slaughterers, on the average, can pay for animals. A slaughterer is in compliance so long as his average price paid for all cattle is at or below the ceiling at the end of each accounting period.

GPO-O-OPS 999

Slaughterers who are now paying above maximum prices are gambling on the chance of getting cattle below the maximum later in the accounting period. 

OPS Enforcement Director Edward P. Morgan has instructed his agents to keep a close check on cattle sales at various markets, both large and small, and to send daily reports to the National Office in Washington. 

Agents at such markets are sending in reports on the names of purchasers, the quantity of cattle purchased, disposition made of the cattle and whether slaughterers of cattle purchased, either directly or through brokers, paid more than the maximum price. 

If there are violations at the end of the accounting period, Mr. Morgan said the "penalties provided by the law will be invoked. " 

He joined Mr. DiSalle in urging slaughterers who are over-bidding for cattle to get in line so it will not be necessary to take such action. # # # # # # # # ". # # #

Re: NEWSPRINT IAC Moore -OPS-GPR-565 ST. 4200: Ext. 3491 

Members of the Newsprint Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials indicated their industry would be entitled to increases of from $3.00 to $5.00 per ton in their newsprint ceilings under the 

Manufacturers General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. 

They reported their current prices under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, are running from $105 to $110 per ton, including various freight allowances, and are several dollars under Canadian prices. 

Committeemen discussed whether spelled out dollars and cents ceilings or an upward adjustment of base period prices by a specified industry-wide differential would be the more satisfactory method of control. 

They indicated that the old OPA MPR 130, which placed dollars and cents ceilings on newsprint, would provide a possible means of price regulation, but a majority felt the old zoning system outlined in MPR 130 was outmoded and unsatisfactory.

The alternative proposal, which committeem en favored, would be for each manufacturer to adjust his GCPR ceiling prices upward by a fixed amount around $3.00 or $4.00 which would be uniform for the whole industry. 

Committeemen said they preferred to have a flat increase industry-wide rather than to calculate individual ceilings under CPR 22, which would leave individual manfacturers with divergent ceilings in a highly competitive industry. 

The suggestion was made that uniform increases might be effected under CPR 22, if, after manufacturers file their new ceiling prices, which they must do by July 2, OPS would allow all manufacturers identical increases. 

The question whether to fix ceilings on imported newsprint from Canada was discussed. Manufacturers pointed out that if American newsprint was controlled and Canadian newsprint uncontrolled it would create a hardship on newspaper publishers dependent wholly on Canadian newsprint. 

Michael V. DiSalle, Director of Price Stabilization, told the committee that control of newsprint prices was one of the most important problems before 

OPS. 

(over)

GPO-O-OPS 996

"The spirit of cooperation shown here in your discussions," he told members of the committee, "indicates that it will not be as difficult to reach a solution as in some other industries. "The relationship between Canadian and American newsprint is one of the problems we must solve. We have both a supply and a price problem. "We want to preserve the ordinary business practices existing in the industry as much as possible during this period of restraint made necessary while we expand our productive capacity in order to meet both our civilian and defense needs." 

The meeting was conducted by M. C.

Walsh, deputy chief, Pulp, Paper and 

Paperboard Branch. Other OPS officials present included Price Director 

DiSalle; Walter J. Damtoft, assistant director, Forest Products Division;

Re: CONFERENCE ON EARNING STANDARDS 

Top officials of the Office of Price Stabilization are holding conferences this week to develop methods of carrying out the industry earning standards announced in April by Economic Stabilizer Eric Johnston.

Under Mr. Johnston's directive on earning standards, ceiling prices for "an industry shall be considered 'generally fair and equitable' under the Defense Production Act if the dollar profits of the industry amount to 85% of the average for an industry's best three years during the period 1946-49, inclusive." 

In his directive of April 21, Mr. Johnston concluded by saying he understood the "OPS will develop in greater detail the methods for applying the above standard and also standards for permissive increases justified by exceptional reasons of public policy. 11 Meeting with OPS officials to help develop these methods are five former 

OPA officials: Geoffrey Baker, general sales manager of Nestle Co., Inc.; 

Richard Heffelbower, professor of economics, Northwestern University; 

Joseph Steiner, Cincinnati businessman; James F. Brownlee, partner J. H. 

Whitney Co., New York; and Henry Hart, professor of law, Harvard Law

School.

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today that the date for posting official OPS retail beef price ceiling lists has been changed from

GPO-O-OPS 998

Re: NEWSPAPER PUBLISHERS MEETING Moore-OPS-GPR-569 ST. 4200: Ext. 3491 

Michael V. DiSalle, Director of Price Stabilization, today met with 21 newspaper publishers and told them he wanted to have their recommendations before taking price action on newsprint.

The meeting was called after a Canadian firm recently announced a $10.00 increase per ton in the price of newsprint, effective July 1. 

Elements of the situation were discussed, during which time it was recognized that the problem was one both of price and supply. 

DiSalle told the publishers he had requested a meeting with Canadian officials to discuss the matter. 

As a result of today's meeting it was decided OPS would take no price action on newsprint pending consultation with Canadian officials. 

One publisher stated that he felt maintenance of good relations between Canadian manufacturers and American publishers should be fostered. Another interjected that increasing prices $10 a ton was not a good way to foster such relations.

Canada supplies 5,000,000 of the 6,000,000 tons of newsprint used annually in the United States. The industry is so important to Canada that the proposed price increase, DiSalle disclosed, had been discussed at cabinet levels.

Although Canada at this time has no price controls, it has established a Department of Defense Production, DiSalle pointed out. R.M. Fowler, head of the Canadian newsprint industry, is now serving as head of the paper and newsprint division.

There was a great deal of discussion among the publishers of the methods of resolving the problem and the recommendation to attempt negotiations was generally supported by the publishers.

PRESS RELEASE 

  Re: COLLAPSIBLE TUBES IAC 

A newly appointed advisory committee representing the Collapsible Tube Industry conferred with Office of Price Stabilization officials today on a price regulation specifically designed for their products. 

Collapsible tubes--tin, lead, and aluminum containers for dentifrices, medicinal salves, greases, and similar consumer items now fall under the general manufacturers' order (Ceiling Price Regulation 22). Factors peculiar to the industry make pricing difficult under the formulas in the regulation, committee members said.

Primarily, the difficulty lies in the fact that historically the industry has based prices on the cost of converting metals into containers and not, except for aluminum, on the cost of the metals themselves. The selling price is then reached by including the cost of the metals on the day the customer places his order. The committee believes this practice is not feasible under CPR 22. 

Seth G. Malby

Aluminum Co. of America 

Edgewater, New Jersey

Huff-OPS-GPR-570 

ST. 4200: Ext. 3491 

A specific regulation for collapsible tubes would probably establish dollars-and-cents ceilings for conversion costs in a selected base period the same as provided by CPR 22 -- April 1 to June 24, 1950, or any one of the three preceding calendar quarters. 

W. H. Dupka, chief of the iron and steel section of the OPS Metals Branch, conducted today's meeting. Other OPS representatives were Karl P. Fuhrmann, container section consultant, C. R. Wasson and Jeannette Carey, branch econo mists, and Harry Spack, Office for Advisory Committees.

Washington Scott-OPS-GPR-572 

Re: NORTHERN HARDWOOD INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE The Northern Hardwood Industry Advisory Committee today recommended a dollars-and-cents tailored pricing regulation for this segment of the industry at its first meeting with Office of Price Stabilization officials. 

The committee told OPS that, except for a few hardship cases due to contracts made before January 25, 1951, industry pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation was currently satisfactory and there is no urgency for a tailored or interim regulation.

The committee felt members should be given an opportunity to further study industry pricing problems and meet again with OPS officials late in July or early August, at which time the committee would be prepared to make specific recommendations for a tailored regulation.

The committee suggested that northern softwoods be covered by the committee, since most northern hardwood industry members also produce softwood lumber and the committee could very well advise and recommend in regard to a tailored regulation for both northern hardwood and softwood, as its cost data embraces both products. 

The committee felt that consideration should be given to including dollars-and-cents ceiling prices on imported lumber in a tailored regulation, and the matter of freight adjustments should be taken up for discussion at the next meeting.

The committee favored a tailored dollars-and-cents pricing regulation patterned along the lines of the old OPA regulations MPR-222 and MPR-223, with ceilings spelled out on the basis of average ceiling prices currently established under GCPR.

The committee favored decontrol of log prices. Members stated there is such a wide variation in log sizes and in grading and scaling, that price control of logs on a fair and equitable basis is practically impossible. 

The meeting was conducted by Lawrence D. Kellogg, chief, Hardwood 

Section, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: William S. Ingram, director, Forest Products Division; H, B. Kiley, head, Eastern & Southern Soft Wood Section; Dante Galotta and Stanley M. Levy, legal staff; A. F. 

Deneke, consultant; John R. Riggleman, economist; and, Walter R. Moulton,

Office for Industry Advisory Committees.

PRESS RELEASE    

Scott-OPS-GPR-573  Re: PAPER SHIPPING SACK INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE The Paper Shipping Sack Industry Advisory Committee met with Office of Price Stabilization officials today and asked that the industry be permitted to use the first two quarters of 1949 as a base period for determining ceiling prices under the manufacturers' regulation, CPR 22. 

Members said use of a base period between July 1, 1949 to June 24, 1950, as under CPR 22, would result in abnormally low prices, and might result in serious curtailment of production. 

The committee said the industry produced over 2-1/4 billion paper shipping sacks in 1950, used largely for shipping agricultural products, chemicals and building materials. Kraft paper is the basic raw material and the industry used approximately 790, 000 tons out of a total 2, 300, 000 tons of kraft paper produced in 1950, members said.

The committee strongly recommended that the base period for figuring ceiling prices on paper shipping sacks under CPR 22 be extended to include the first and second quarter of 1949, or that the industry be permitted to continue to price under the General Ceiling Price Regulation until a tailored pricing regulation can be issued for the industry. The committee favored a tailored regulation based on a formula patterned after the historical pricing practices of the industry, and pointed out that the industry produces paper shipping sacks in a great multiplicity of sizes, which are usually suited to the individual specifications of a great variety of customers.

The committee felt it could not offer specific recommendations and advise on a tailored regulation until it knew what pricing policies and regulations would be used by the kraft paper segment of the industry in determining ceiling prices. However, the committee felt a start should be made in drafting a tailored regulation and suggested a sub-committee be appointed to advise further with OPS officials in this connection. 

The chairman appointed the following members to serve as a sub-committee: Mr. Scholl, Mr. Sheldon and Mr. Weisberger.

Re: V-BELT SUBCOMMITTEE OF MERCHANICAL RUBBER GOODS IAC Members of the V-Belt Subcommittee of the Mechanical Rubber Goods Industry 

Advisory committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials defined more precisely the seven product lines previously designated by the main committee for v-belts, and recommended an 8th product line for replacement automotive type fan v-belts sold under private brand names.

The committee recommended the proposed tailored regulation for the industry cover all sizes, grades, construction and sections sold to both original equipment manufacturers and to the replacement trade unless otherwise stated, but excluding v-belts made of assembled segments. 

V-belts are power transmission belts, v-shaped in cross-section, which run in grooved pulleys, and contrast with flat transmission belts that run on smooth pulleys.

The seven product lines originally chosen were defined as follows: 

1. Heavy duty industrial type v-belts including multiple and variable speed 

2. Light duty or fractional horsepower type v-belts. 

3. Connector or open-end type v-and round belting except railroad types. 

4. Connector or open end type railroad v-belting. 

5. Agricultural implement v-belts and all round endless belts. 

6. Original equipment or car manufacturers automotive fan type v-belts. 

7. Replacement automotive fan type v-belts except private brand belts.

The committee decided to meet again June 19, by which time it is hoped that sufficient cost data will have been received from the industry for OPS to compute weighted average percentage cost adjustment factors for the industry. 

OPS officials present at the meeting were Chester Conner, chief of the Rubber 

Branch, and Everett D. Hawkins, and William Sheskey, economists.

PRESS RELEASE 

4 1 

   

Wednesday, June 13, 1951

Scott-OPS-GPR-579  Re: HARDWOOD DIMENSION MANUFACTURERS IAC The Hardwood Dimension Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee today urged Office of Price Stabilization officials to provide a tailored pricing regulation for the industry.

The industry is currently required to price under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, since lumber products are exempted from the general manufacturers' regulation, CPR 22.

Hardwood dimension is lumber sold in the form of squares, flat stock, rounds, billets, and sawed or glued blanks for use in the manufacture of furniture, vehicles, implements, caskets, toys, and in radio, television, and other cabinets, such as refrigerators, pianos, etc. These products move in all stages of manufacture from rough square-sawn to completely machined and ready for assembly into a final product. 

Members said the industry produces a vast variety of sizes, usually according to the specification of individual customers. In the great majority of cases, products must be priced on individual jobs or under individual contracts with customers, based on production cost analysis, members said, and for these reasons a formula type of pricing must be followed. 

The committee favored a tailored formula type of regulation along the lines of the old OPA regulation MPR-501, which follows the historical formula pricing practices of the industry, with adjustment factors to reflect increased labor and material costs. Members said overall dollars-and-cents pricing is entirely unfeasible for the industry.

A sub-committee was named to advise further with OPS officials on details of a tailored regulation. Members of the sub-committee are: Omar 

Hilton, David B. Morgan, Jr., C. D. Dosker, James R. May, and J. S.

Horner.

PRESS RELEASE 

1 1 

   

Crist-OPS-GPR-582 

Re: COMMODITY EXCHANGE PENALTIES 

The Office of Price Stabilization today issued an opinion on the legality of settlement costs on commodity exchanges for defaults or failure to make deliveries under futures contracts. 

In a telegram to the New York Cotton Exchange, OPS Chief Counsel 

Harold Leventhal, advised that 1) it is illegal under the Defense Production Act of 1950 to establish a settlement price for defaults in excess of the spot ceiling prices for the commodity set by OPS; and 2) an exchange may require a predetermined penalty for defaults if provided for in the rules of the exchange. 

Mr. Leventhal stated that Section 707 of the Defense Production Act the law under which OPS functions precludes the establishment of a settlement price for default in excess of the spot ceiling price for the commodity involved. 

The legal maximum market value for the commodity, Mr. Leventhal wired, is fixed by ceiling price regulations, and to require a defaulting seller to pay damages based on a market value in excess of the ceilings would be illegal.

If, however, the rules of an exchange require the assessment of a predetermined amount as a penalty, Mr. Leventhal said the exchange could impose the penalty without violating the Defense Production Act or ceiling price regulations.

In such a case, Mr. Leventhal pointed out in his wire, the penalties are not based on any assumption concerning the market price, but are intended to promote the integrity of the exchange contracts. Thus, concluded Mr. Leventhal, the proposal of the New York Cotton Exchange to fix a total settlement price of 45. 81 cents per pound for defaulted sales of cotton, together with a liquidation penalty of 25 points (quarter of a cent a point) per pound is permissible.

Text of Mr. Leventhal's telegram follows: 

GPO-O-OPS 1016

YOUR TELEGRAM JUNE 8, 1951 REQUESTS A RULING FROM OPS AS TO WHETHER THE FOLLOWING PROPOSED ACTION OF THE NEW YORK COTTON EXCHANGE RELATIVE TO DEFAULTED MAY 1951 CONTRACTS WOULD VIOLATE THE DEFENSE PRODUCTION ACT OF 1950 OR OPS CEILING PRICE REGULATIONS. THE EXCHANGE PROPOSES (1) TO FIX A TOTAL SETTLEMENT PRICE FOR THESE CONTRACTS AT 45.81 CENTS PER POUND RESULTING FROM THE ADDITION OF THE AVERAGE PRICE OF SPOT COTTON ON ALL DELIVERY MARKETS UNDER EXCHANGE RULES (45.32) PLUS 49 POINTS FOR THE ACTUAL COST OF COMPRESSION AND CERTIFICATION TO PUT THE COTTON IN DELIVERABLE FORM UNDER EXCHANGE RULES: AND (2) TO ASSESS A PENALTY OF 25 POINTS WHICH LIQUIDATED AMOUNT IS COLLECTIBLE ON DEMAND UNDER THE RULES OF THE EXCHANGE. 

IN RESPONSE TO YOUR REQUEST FOR A RULING, IT IS OUR OPINION THAT THIS PROPOSED ACTION OF THE EXCHANGE WOULD NOT CONTRAVENE THE DEFENSE PRO- DUCTION ACT OR OPS CEILING PRICE REGULATIONS, IN VIEW OF THE FACT THAT THE TOTAL SETTLEMENT PRICE OF 45.81 CENTS PER POUND DOES NOT EXCEED THE SPOT CEILING PRICE FOR THE COMMODITY INVOLVED. 

THAT THE PENALTY OF 25 POINTS HAS BEEN FIXED BY THE RULES OF THE IT IS UNDERSTOOD EXCHANGE AND THAT ITS ASSESSMENT IS MANDATORY IF CLAIMED IN THE EVENT OF DEFAULT. UNDER THESE CIRCUMSTANCES, IT IS OUR VIEW THAT AN ASSESS- MENT OF THIS TYPE OF LIQUIDATED PENALTY IS NOT PRECLUDED BY SECTION 707 OF THE DEFENSE PRODUCTION ACT OF 1950.

Scott-OPS-GPR-583 

Re: OAK FLOORING INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE The Oak Flooring Industry Advisory Committee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a tailored pricing regulation for the industry. 

Members said industry pricing generally under the General Ceiling

Price Regulation is currently satisfactory, and while there is no present urgency for a tailored regulation, the committee agreed it would be desirable to start the drafting of such a regulation without undue delay. 

Generally speaking, the committee favored an over-all dollars-andcents ceiling price regulation patterned along the lines of the old OPA regulation MPR-458, as amended, although some members felt there should be some discussion and consideration of a formula type regulation. 

The committee discussed the matter of a base period for determining ceiling prices and some members expressed the opinion that prices established by the industry during the December 1, 1950 to January 25, 1951 period, would reflect fair and equitable levels. 

Some concern was expressed with respect to ceiling prices to be established for lumber generally, since lumber ceiling prices would have a very direct bearing on ceiling prices for oak flooring. 

The committee favored decontrol of log prices. Members said it is unfeasible and practically impossible to control log prices due to the wide variation in sizes, grading and scaling.

Members felt they should be given an opportunity for further study of industry pricing problems and to meet again with OPS officials at a reasonably GPO-O-OPS 1017

early date, at which time the committee would be prepared to make specific recommendations for a tailored regulation.

Committee members complimented OPS officials on their fair and business-like approach to the industry's pricing problems.

Thursday, June 17, 1951 

Moore-OPS-GPR-584  Re: BOVINE HIDES IAC 

Members of the Bovine Hides Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials discussed proposals in detail for revisions of the present ceiling price regulation on hides, CPR 2, Revision 1. 

The committee considered small lot provisions and classification of different types of hides such as country hides and renderers' hides. 

Committeemen urged that provision should be made for differentials to pernit tanners to sell hides to each other without loss. They pointed out that carload shipments often contain hides which are unsuitable for a tanner's purposes and sound economy requires that he have a practical method of selling to another tanner.

They discussed the advantages and disadvantages of allowing selection premiums on table No. 1 shipments. The committee's sentiment was mixed. 

The committee also considered the advisability of reducing the allowable maximum of No. 2's on table No. 2 to 15 per cent. Table No. 1 covers basic quality hides and table No. 2 covers standard packers. 

Whether a differential should be spelled out for trimmed and untrimmed green hides was explored. Committeemen said it was customary for the trade to discount untrimmed green hides and the custom was being observed under the present regulation, though it makes no differentiation. There was some discussion whether 4, 7 or 10 per cent was the most reasonable differential. 

The question of pricing cut hides was examined by the committee, including allocation of prices between different cuts of hides. Committeemen could suggest no practical means of regulating pricing of the respective cuts, such as bellies and shoulders. The question of commission on the sale of cut parts was also discussed. 

Committeemen considered the legality of escalator clauses in contracts which would permit sellers to receive future increases in prices. A number of such contracts, it was suggested, are of doubtful legality.

PRESS RELEASE   

 Re: CANNED SOUP LAC Barkley-OPS-GPR-586 

Members of the Canned Soup Industry Advisory Committee in their first meeting today proposed to the Office of Price Stabilization that a tailored regulation providing for "line pricing" be adopted for their industry. "Line pricing" is where a group of commodities have the same selling price although the cost of the raw materials may have varied. 

Canned soups are now covered by the General Ceiling Price Regulation. 

Industry spokesmen said canned soup regulation should, in addition to line pricing, permit cost adjustments to cover increased costs of cans, labels, cases and labor, as well as raw materials. 

They urged that action on a regulation be taken as soon as possible as summer vegetables soon will be coming to market.

Their first problem, committee men said, is tomato soup, with the big 1951 pack scheduled to start around July 1. Tomato soup is the biggest canned soup item in volume of business. 

Since the tomato harvest is so near, members said they would like a temporary provision covering this pack, pending the adoption of a regulation for the entire canned soup industry. 

Representing OPS at the conference were George C. Mehren, assistant director of the Food and Restaurant Division; W. G. Carberry, chief, Fruit and Vegetable Branch; H. K. Batchelder, who presided; W. C. Glover, H. K. 

Draper, John McVey, George Goldsborough of the Branch; and William R.

COMMON MOTOR CARRIER IAC Members of the Common Motor Carrier Industry Advisory Committee met with

OPS has no jurisdiction over rates charged by common motor carriers but can protest increases to the Interstate Commerce Commission or State Commissions if such increases are thought to threaten the national stabilization program.

A cooperative arrangement was agreed upon between the Committee and OPS for the furnishing of advance information of any rate increases contemplated through group meetings of representative carriers and OPS in affected territories. At such meetings data and justification to be submitted to regulatory bodies would be reviewed.

"We consider this group of retailers to be one of the most important advisory committees working with OPS, representing as it does over 494, 000 non-food retail establishments with a 1948 sales volume of over 47 billion dollars," Mr. Wess stated, "and we want it to be a working committee with grass roots knowledge of the basic problems of retailers, because next to the consumer the retailer has the greatest stake in inflation and price control".

addition to his Department of Justice posts, Mr. Cohen served as special counsel to the Federal Communications Commission and during part of World 

War II was legal adviser to the War Department Construction Contract Board.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers SUNDAY, June 17, 1951 Tempo E 

Washington Re: NEW DISTRIBUTION DIVISION 

Hughes-OPS-GPR-594 

ST.4200; Ext. 3491 Establishment of a Distribution Division in the Office of Price Operations to handle price control in the fields of non-food retailing and wholesaling of consumer goods was announced today by Director Michael V. DiSalle of the Office of Price Stabilization.

The new division will issue and administer all regulations concerned with price control at wholesale and retail of consumer goods presently under the jurisdiction of the Consumer Soft and Durable Goods Divisions. These goods include apparel, textiles, shoes, leather, furs and fibers, appliances, home furnishings, housewares and accessories, along with many other items. 

The division will be under the general supervision of Harold B. Wess and 

Thomas L. Karsten. Mr. Wess is Director, as well, of the Consumer Soft Goods and Consumer Durable Goods Divisions, and Mr. Karsten is his assistant director for the Soft Goods Division. 

An assistant director will be appointed as operating head of the Distribu tion Division. 

11 

"The size and complexity of distribution operations in the consumer goods field," 

Mr. DiSalle said, "clearly call for handling by a separate division.

With that kind of and organizational set-up we can assign to the work a larger and more diversified staff than would be the case with a single branch. We shall hope to find a man of broad general experience to serve as operating head under Mr. Wess and Mr. Karsten. Mr. Wess himself, as former vice-president of 

Macy's in New York and as an instructor in marketing at Columbia's Graduate School of Business, has a broad understanding of the structure of distribution. 

The divisional form of organization will allow us to give the operating head the assistance of specialists in particular phases of distribution along with the help of division and branch lawyers and economists.' 

The existing Distribution Branch of the Consumer Soft Goods Division will be absorbed in the new division, Mr. DiSalle said. Recruitment of additional staff up to full division strength, he added, will be pushed with all possible speed.

Functions of the New Division 

A major task of the new division, Mr. Wess said, will be to take over administration of Ceiling Price Regulation 7. This is the regulation covering consumer goods whose retail sales run into billions of dollars annually, including GPO-O-OPS 1047

sales of apparel, shoes, furniture, rugs, yard goods, housewares, jewelry, musical instruments, radio and television sets, etc. 

The division will complete and issue the wholesale regulations which have been in preparation for some time. It will devise pricing techniques for different kinds of retailing and wholesaling, and will make necessary revisions of techniques currently in use. It will deal with the special problems of small retailers and wholesalers.

The Distribution Division will also provide expert counsel to other divisions in OPS which are concerned with the pricing of other commodities. In general, Mr. Wess said, the Division will attempt a kind of overall resolution of distribution problems such as was never done under the war-time OPA and which thus far has not been done under OPS.
