PRESS RELEASE  Tempo E ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers SUNDAY, June 17, 1951 

Washington Re: TOY MANUFACTURERS Scott-OPS-GPR-595 ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 

Officials of the Office of Price Stabilization have told industry representatives that toy manufacturers will not be permitted to stay under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, but must price under the general manufacturers' ceiling price regulation, CPR 22.

Harold B. Wess, Director of the Consumer Goods Divisions of OPS, said today he had informed toy industry representatives that without a full survey of their industry there was no proof that pricing under the general manufacturers' regulation would mean higher prices to the consumers than would be true under GCPR. There would be no time for such a survey before 

July 2, effective date of CPR 22, Mr. Wess pointed out.

The contention has been made by industry representatives that the general effect of the manufacturers' regulation would be to increase ceiling prices above current GCPR levels. Only unaudited data from a few companies, OPS officials said, was submitted to support this contention, and they questioned whether it would prove correct for the industry as a whole. 

The policy of OPS, Mr. Wess informed three representatives of the Toy 

Industry Advisory Committee, who had been selected to appeal the decision made three weeks ago to keep toys under the new manufacturers' regulation, was to place as many industries as possible under this interim order so as to eliminate inequities of the general freeze.

Under the general freeze regulation, OPS officials pointed out to the three representatives, manufacturers who had disregarded the President's request to keep prices down had a tremendous advantage over those who had tried to prevent inflation. The new manufacturers' regulation wipes out this advantage, Mr. 

Wess said, adding that an industry which had not advanced prices more than increased costs justified would not be hurt by the new regulation. 

Bion Howard, OPS economist, told the industry representatives that information already received by OPS shows that a number of major companies will have to roll back their prices on toys.

Representatives of the toy industry claimed they had already shipped more than 50% of their commitments for this Christmas and that they could not take GPO-O-OPS 1043

advantage of any price increases which might be permissible under CPR 22. 

They expressed concern over having to make any refunds on toys whose prices were rolled back by CPR 22.

When industry representatives suggested that OPS give them the choice of remaining under the general freeze, Mr. Wess pointed out that if any one industry were allowed to stay under the freeze order the agency would be flooded with requests from other industries wishing to remain under the freeze to avoid rollbacks.

Mr. Wess emphasized that many hundreds of thousands of manufacturers come under the general manufacturers' regulation and similar manufacturing orders for machinery (CPR 30), cotton textiles (CPR 37), shoes (CPR 41) and apparel (CPR 45), and that an exemption for one industry would bring insistent demands for similar treatment of others. It was pointed out to the three toy industry representatives that under an alternative pricing formula to the general manufacturers' regulation (SR 2 to CPR 22) a company could average out increases and decreases, where there was an overall increase, and retain their present pricing structure.

Moore -OPS-GPR-596 

Re: WOOD HEEL MANUFACTURERS LAC Members of the Wood Heel Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee, today told OPS officials at their first meeting that most manufacturers in their industry were in distress because of increased costs which they could not pass on under the General Ceiling Price Regulation.

They stressed the need of prompt relief and indicated an interim regulation on a formula basis would be desirable if available sooner than a tailored regulation.

Members said an interim formula which would permit manufacturers to add their pre-Korea mark-up to current costs would be acceptable to their industry.

It was agreed that OPA MPR 196, covering turned and shaped wood products, might provide a pattern for an interim regulation. 

Committeemen suggested that any interim regulation give individual manufacturers the alternative of retaining GCPR ceilings if they were more satisfactory than those provided by the formula. 

Members said that a tailored regulation patterned after the old OPA MPR 420, Amendment 7, which spelled out dollars and cents ceilings on their products, would be satisfactory if properly revised, after lumber and other material costs are stabilized.

Committeemen reported that some manufacturers put in price increases before the GCPR freeze January 26, 1951, and others who undertook voluntarily to hold the price line did not. Most of those who put in price increases reported they were not sufficient to cover subsequent increased costs. 

Some members reported they were operating at a loss either over all or in certain factories because of mounting costs.

Committeemen reported that all of their materials had gone up substantially except in some instances for blocks which were frozen under the GCPR before prices were increased. They said their other materials frequently were received against orders several months old so that prices of these materials kept creeping up after the freeze.

PRESS RELEASE   ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers TUESDAY, June 19, 1951 

Huff-OPS-GPR-597  

Re: BEDDING MANUFACTURERS' PRICING 

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today it will issue a supplementary regulation to the general manufacturers' order (CPR 22) allowing bedding manufacturers to continue identical pricing of mattresses and box springs if that has been their established practice in the past. 

Customarily, OPS officials pointed out, many manufacturers have charged the same price for box springs as for matching mattresses, but under either method 2 or 3 of CPR 22 the prices are likely to be different since the cost of materials in mattresses has risen more sharply than in box springs.

The summer Furniture Market opened Monday in Chicago, and, OPS officials said, permission to follow the uniform pricing method for box springs and mattresses is being announced in advance to avoid confusion among buyers and sellers there.

The supplementary regulation will permit manufacturers to arrive at a ratio of box springs produced or sold to mattresses produced or sold during the last fiscal or calendar year and to apply this ratio to the prices arrived at under CPR 22 to develop a weighted average uniform price for each of the two items. Crib mattresses, mattresses normally sold or used with flat or folding cots, and Hollywood bed outfits will be excluded.

OPS officials reminded bedding manufacturers it is not now permissible in using method 3 to treat mattresses and box springs in the same product line and to apply the materials cost adjustment factor determined for a best selling mattress to a box spring in order to maintain uniform prices for each. PRESS RELEASE   

 Milliken-OPS-GPR-598 

ST-4200; Ext. 6029

Re: FLUE-CURE TOBACCO IAC OBACCO 

Representatives of the flue-cured tobacco industry were informed by officials of the Office of Price Stabilization that the fundamental interest on a ceiling price regulation for that crop is for the purpose of having a standby regulation in the event new crop prices advance over parity price levels. The 

OPS view was that such a standby regulation should be formulated if possible in advance of the opening of the 1951 market, which starts in Georgia in July. 

Members of the Flue Cured Tobacco Industry Advisory Committee all ex pressed the opinion that a ceiling price regulation was not needed at this time and that the record size expected for the 1951 crop and existing marketing conditions should obviate the need of controls. The committee, which represents buyer-manufacturers, warehousemen, dealers and growers, held its organization meeting today.

The 1950 flue-cured tobacco crop averaged 54. 7 cents per pound. Parity as of May 15, 1951 was 56. 1 cents.

Objections were raised by manufacturers and warehouse representatives, with some manufacturers dissenting, to the OPS proposal that any ceiling price regulation be based on grades. Growers favor regulation by official grades in the interest of encouraging quality production and reflection of maximum possible values for better grades. The opposite view recommended instead that regulation be based on a weighted average of the crop. This position was shared by some manufacturers who stated that it would mean more orderly marketing and eliminate potential collusion as to handling of grades in the markets. 

Growers took the stand that it would be impossible for them to get a parity price if grade ceiling prices were established which would reflect parity exactly, assuming a normal crop. OPS officials pointed out, however, that the grade ceilings would reflect a slight margin over parity. 

The representatives were told that the administration proposed to freeze parity prices of agricultural products for a marketing season, but that this would require legislation to carry out. GPO-O-OPS 1053

Scott-OPS-GPR-599  Re: SOAP, CLEANSER AND SYNTHETIC DETERGENT LAC The Soap, Cleanser and Synthetic Detergent Industry Advisory Committee met today with Office of Price Stabilization officials to discuss a proposed revision of the present manufacturers' ceiling price regulation (CPR 10) covering household soaps, cleansers and synthetic detergents.

CPR 10, issued March 8, covers sales by manufacturers of a wide range of soaps, soap products, cleansers and synthetic detergents customarily sold for household use. Ceiling prices are set at the highest prices established by manufacturers on the basis of bona fide sales or offers for sale during the month of December 1950. 

It is proposed to revise CPR 10 to include sales for industrial, institutional and governmental use, as well as for household use, and to somewhat clarify and more clearly define soaps, cleansers and synthetic detergents covered by the regulation.

Ceiling prices under the revised regulation would be on the same general level as under the present CPR 10, based on December 1950 sales or offers for sale. In addition, the revised regulation would provide that manufacturers of liquid and paste soaps and cleaning specialties, using imported vegetable oils as ingredients, may add any increased costs of such oils over spelled-out dollars-and-cents prices specified in the regulation, or in the case of domestic vegetable oils whose ceiling prices are set under CPR 6 (Fats & Oils) the manufacturer may add any authorized increase in such ceiling prices. 

The revised regulation would also spell out specific requirements for obtaining ceiling price adjustments under certain situations. 

The committee reviewed the proposed revised regulation word by word with OPS officials, and offered suggestions and advice for clarification and minor changes. Generally speaking, the committee felt the proposed revision would be workable and satisfactory to the industry as a whole, and complimented OPS officials on their effort to draft a practical and workable regulation. 

The committee urged that the new regulation be issued at the earliest date possible and that the industry be relieved from pricing under the general manufacturers' regulation (CPR 22, effective July 2) on products and sales not now covered by CPR 10, and which will be covered under the proposed revised regulation. Members said it would work an undue hardship on many industry members if they are required to price under CPR 22, and shortly thereafter are required to reprice under the revised regulation. It was thought that some manufacturers might even suspend sales until the revised regulation is issued, rather than try to price under CPR 22 temporarily. 

(Over)

The committee strongly recommended that on the additional cla. of sales to be covered in the revised regulation, manufacturers be permitted to continue to price under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, rather than price temporarily under CPR 22 until the new regulation is issued. 

OPS officials told the committee every effort possible will be made to issue the new revised regulation before July 2.

Re: BUTTON SUBCOMMITTEE, PLASTIC PRODUCTS LAC The first meeting of the Button Sub-committee of the Plastic Products

Members of the committee stated that operation under the provisions of Ceiling Price Regulation 22 would result in serious hardship to their industry. 

They pointed out that during the entire 12-month period prior to June 24, 1950, the industry was engaged in a price war which forced a number of manufacturers to cease operations.

CPR 22 provides that manufacturers covered by it recompute their ceiling prices by adding to their pre-Korean base period certain materials and labor cost increases. Representatives of OPS advised the committee members that at their request an industry survey would be made. If this industry survey 

If this industry survey indicated that ceiling prices under the General Manufacturers' Ceiling Price Regulation (CPR 22) would reduce earnings below the standard fixed by the Johnston formula, an adjustment would be made. OPS officials suggested that the committee members furnish records substantiating their claim that during all the CPR 22 base periods the industry was in a depressed condition.

PRESS RELEASE 

E 

   

Scott-OPS-GPR-602  Re: RETAIL INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE 

Michael V. DiSalle, Director of Price Stabilization, today told the newly appointed overall Retail Industry Advisory Committee that OPS 

appreciates the substantial support it is receiving generally. from retailers in the fight against inflation. 

At its first meeting today, Mr. DiSalle assured the committee it is the earnest desire of OPS to give the fullest possible consideration to the constructive efforts of the committee to make price control regulations workable and practical at all levels of retail distribution. 

Harold B. Wess, Director of the Consumer Goods Divisions, presided at the all day meeting and repeatedly emphasized the importance of the retailer in the overall pattern of price control.

Mrs. Ethel Gilbert, Director of the Office for Industry Advisory Com mittees, outlined the functions and responsibilities of the committee under the 

Defense Production Act of 1950. 

The committee engaged in a roundtable discussion of the overall retail pricing problems under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR) and the retail ceiling price regulation CPR 7, with special emphasis on the problems of the small retailer. 

Several members said the pricing burden of many retailers would be considerably relieved if OPS could speed up the authorization of the use of manufacturer's retail list prices as provided under CPR 7. Under this provision (Section 43) OPS may upon application by a manufacturer, issue an order establishing dollars-and-cents retail and wholesale ceiling prices for branded articles. Members said a substantial percentage of retail sales under CPR 7 are of branded merchandise that has been historically sold at manufacturer's suggested retail list prices, and the provision in the regu- GPO-O-OPS 1065

lation récognizes this situation. OPS officials told the committee everything possible will be done to speed the processing of manufacturers applications and the issuance of orders setting retail prices under this provision of the regulation.

The committee suggested that a sub-committee be appointed, to be known as a steering committee, to facilitate the work of the whole committee. 

It was suggested the sub-committee function in the following general manner: 

1. OPS will submit overall retail pricing and administrative problems to the sub-committee for suggestions and advice, and the sub-committee will make a report to the committee of the whole with recommendations. Likewise, industry members will submit suggestions and advice, on overall retail pricing problems to the sub-committee, which in turn will make recommendations to the whole committee. In this manner the sub-committee will assist OPS in setting up an agenda for future meetings of the whole committee. 

2. The sub-committee will suggest the manner in which industry data can best be obtained by OPS, and will also suggest the formation of subcommittees to deal with special problems of any segment of the industry. 

3. Where OPS sets up separate commodity industry advisory committees which affect the retail trade, OPS will include members of the retail industry advisory committee to serve on such separate commodity committees. 

4. OPS will keep the sub-committee informed as to important impendingoverall regulations effecting the retail trade, and the sub-committee will advise OPS as to the desirability of submitting such matters to the whole committee. 

Mr. Wess told the committee that such a sub-committee would be appointed within a few days, and that another meeting of the full committee will be called within 30 days.

A member of the committee suggested that a sub-committee be appointed to deal especially with the problems of the small retailer with sales of less than $100,000 a year. Mr. Wess said these retailers represent a large percentage of total retail sales and that such a sub-committee is urgently needed and will be appointed. 

A member of the committee moved that a vote of confidence be expressed by the committee to OPS officials for their fair and understanding approach to the problems of the retailer under price control. A unanimous vote was taken with applause from the entire committee.

Re: EASTERN POLE AND PILING IAC Moore-OPS-GPR-604 ST 4200: Ext. 3491 Members of the Eastern Pole and Piling Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials reported that at their ceilings under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, they are unable to compete with sawmills for stumpage for larger poles and piling 35 feet or more in length.

They were unable to suggest a practical method for placing ceilings on stumpage. They said the way to meet the problem is to fix prices on poles and piling in a competitive relationship with lumber prices. 

Committeemen acknowledged such a solution would have to wait finally on the establishment of dollars and cents ceilings on lumber. At present lumber like poles and piling is under the GCPR.

Members said price control for the industry worked satisfactorily under OPA MPR 559, as amended, during the latter part of the war. It fixed dollars and cents ceilings with differentials for various geographical zones. 

It was suggested relief might be provided by an interim regulation which would permit the industry to apply a pre-Korean margin to current stumpage and other costs. However, the committee decided it was more practical to work for a long-range tailored regulation.

The products of the industry are used by utilities, mines and in harbor installations and construction, and are usually finally sold treated with preservatives.

Ceilings have been frozen, the committee reported, in a manner that favors the use of large timbers as piling rather than as poles. For example, the same log might produce a 45 foot pole, or alternately, a 35 foot piling at the butt end plus a small timber from the smaller end.

PRESS RELEASE   ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers THURSDAY, June 21, 1951 

Re: WOOD PULP 

Moore-OPS-GPR-609  

The Office of Price Stabilization today announced that dollars and cents ceiling on 12 standard grades of wood pulp produced in the United States and four grades of imported wood pulp comprising the bulk of shipments from overseas will be issued Monday.

Ceilings will not be fixed on imports from Canada, which provides a substantial portion of market wood pulp consumed in the United States, by the regulation.

OPS said that the Canadian Department of Defense Production has taken action to stabilize prices of wood pulp sold to United States consumers and assured the United States government that no general price increase will be authorized without prior consultation with the United States. 

Wood pulp is the basis raw material used in the manufacture of paper and paper products, and is also used by the rayon and other chemical converting industries. 

The new ceilings will be set forth in CPR 49, effective June 30, 1951.

For domestic wood pulp they are at levels representing pre-Korea prices plus amounts deemed adequate to cover cost increases since last June, and will result in rollbacks on a substantial portion of market pulp. 

Likewise ceilings on overseas pulp represent the lowest levels of prices during the second quarter of 1951. OPS indicated a cutback in receipts may result. 

The new ceilings will relieve some of the pressure for higher paper prices on paper manufacturers who buy market wood pulp. However, this will be only a minor factor for the whole industry, as most such wood pulp is produced by integrated mills for their own use and never sold as wood pulp.

Domestic manufacturers of special grades of wood pulp and buyers of overseas wood pulp for which prices are not spelled out may file proposed ceilings on such pulp which are "in line" with spelled out prices with due regard for customary quality price differentials. Such proposals will determine ceilings if OPS by order does not establish lower prices within 30 days.

Special grades include: Dissolving, high alpha and special chemical sulphite; dissolving, high alpha and special chemical sulphate; specification glassine and mitscherlich sulphite; specification condenser sulphate, semichemical wood pulp; unbleached soda pulp; bleached groundwood; wood pulp produced in whole or in part from rags, paper stock or any fibrous material other than wood; wood pulp shipped pursuant to N. P. A. orders and produced upon equipment not designed for production of such wood pulp for sale in the open market.

Exports are subject to the same ceilings as domestically sold wood pulp, f.o.b. nearest port of shipment, with allowances for special packing or routing to alternate ports at the purchaser's convenience. Exports represent less than one per cent of domestic production. 

The United States produces about 40 per cent and consumes almost 50 per cent of the world's wood pulp. It purchases about one-third of the wood pulp moving in international trade.

Wood pulp production in the United States is chiefly by integrated mills for their own use in the manufacture of paper and paperboard. About 10 per cent of domestic production is market pulp made for sale.

About 260 U. S. mills produced 14, 800, 000 tons of pulp in 1950. The same year the paper industry purchased 2, 900, 000 tons of wood pulp, of which 900,000 tons were domestic, 1,300,000 tons Canadian and 700, 000 tons overseas, chiefly from Sweden and Finland, while the rayon and other chemical converting industries purchased about 680, 000 tons of special grades of sulphite pulp, about 440, 000 tons from U. S. mills and 240, 000 tons from Canada.

With the outbreak of the Korean war, domestic woodpulp prices rose substantially. Between June, 1950, and January, 1951, domestic bleached sulphite rose from $118 to $135-$165 per ton. Canadian bleached sulphite rose from $118 to $145-$160. Finnish bleached sulphite rose from $118 to $183 and 

Swedish from $118 to $175. Domestic unbleached sulphate rose from $80-$85 to $130-$200 per ton.

American prices were frozen in January but foreign wood pulp continued to advance in price. During the second quarter of 1951, Canadian bleached sulphite ranged from $160 to $170, the Finnish price reached $225 and the Swedish price $275 to $290. Canadian unbleached sulphate ranged from $155 to $170 during the second quarter, Finnish was $200 and Swedish $250 to $275.

Washington Scott-OPS-GPR-611 

INDUSTRIAL BLOCKING & MINE MATERIAL IAC The Industrial Blocking and Mine Material Industry Advisory Committee met with Office of Price Stabilization officials today to discuss a tailored pricing regulation for this segment of the industry. 

The industry is concerned with the production of wooden mine materials such as ties, switch ties, cross bars, cribbing, lagging, post caps, wedges, etc., and lumber and timber used in underground mines, particularly coal and iron mines. It is also concerned with the production of mixed hardwoods sawn to specified sizes and of a grade meeting the requirements of steel mills and like users for bracing and blocking their products for shipment. 

Members pointed out that the industry is turning out products which are highly essential to the production effort in that they are necessary in mining operations and heavy industry steel shipments. Members said ceiling prices on their products must be in line with production costs, if the industry is to produce the quantities required for maximum mine production and large steel shipments.

The committee told OPS officials that industry pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation at present is generally satisfactory, and there is no urgency for a tailored regulation. However, members felt it was desirable to start work on a tailored regulation, because it would take some time to develop the data necessary to write a satisfactory, sound and workable regulation.

Generally speaking, the committee favored a spelled-out dollars-and-cents type of regulation patterned along the lines of the old OPA regulation MPR-558. 

The committee felt the regulation should cover only the producers in the area East of the 100th meridian, except North Dakota and South Dakota. Generally speaking, the 100th meridian is the Western line of what is known as the Middle- 

West farm belt.

Members said it would be difficult to set dollars-and-cents ceiling prices for this segment of the industry, until ceiling prices are set on ties and lumber, since tie and lumber prices have a very direct bearing on wooden blocking and mine material prices.

It was suggested the committee be given an opportunity to study carefully the matter of freight allowances and differentials as related to f.o.b. mill prices, and also the matter of zone pricing. 

GPO-O-OPS 1071

-- · - The committee discussed the desirability of decontrolling log prices. 

Seven members favored decontrol, 3 members were against decontrol, and two members did not want to express an opinion.

Members felt the committee should be given an opportunity to study industry pricing problems further and to meet again with OPS officials in August or September, at which time the committee would be prepared to make specific recommendations for a tailored regulation.

PRESS RELEASE    

Scott-OPS-GPR-613  Re: SHOE LAST MANUFACTURERS IAC The Shoe Last Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee today told 

Office of Price Stabilization officials that a tailored pricing regulation for the industry is urgently needed.

Committeemen said the industry is being squeezed by ceiling prices under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, due to increased labor costs, and that there has been no general increase in price on their product since 

August 1950. 

The industry produces wood shoe lasts, which are used in the process of manufacturing shoes. They take a rough-shaped wood block and carve it to the exact size and style specified by the shoe manufacturer. The shoe manufacturer uses these wood lasts in the process of shaping the shoes being manufactured.

The committee favored a formula type regulation patterned along the lines of the old OPA regulation MPR-196, covering turned and shaped wood products, which provided a formula percentage markup. 

The committee recommended that June 1951 be used as a base period for determining labor and material costs, and that the industry be given the option of using the first two quarters of 1950 and the first quarter of 1951 as a basis for determining historical formula percentage markups. 

The principal raw material used by the industry are rough-shaped wood blocks, which are usually purchased from block manufacturers, and which will be priced under the same ceiling price regulation. Therefore, the shoe last industry feels it should be permitted to use as material cost, whatever ceiling price is permitted on rough-shaped wood blocks. 

The meeting was conducted by Bernard Topkis, deputy head, Miscel laneous Wood Products Section, Lumber & Wood Products Branch, OPS.

Levy, legal staff; David White, economist; and Walter R.

OPS officials informed the committee there was not sufficient time to make the required cost studies in time to prepare the tailored regulation by 

July 2, when the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, becomes effective.

The committee agreed members of the industry should work out and report on their form 8's their CPR 22 prices, using the key item technique and employing the same key items on which the industry will report cost data to 

OPS for the tailored regulation.

Committeemen reported they would be entitled to some roll forwards under CPR 22, but expressed willingness to forego these and remain under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, until a tailored regulation is prepared.

Re: BEEF POSTING 

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today that the June 25 requirement that retail meat sellers publicly post ceiling beef prices would be postponed until August 1.

In view of the fact that mechanical difficulties had forced a delay in the intended June 18 posting date, and that August 1 is the end of the present price levels based on the first 10 per cent roll back of live cattle, it was decided to delay posting of the charges for the brief period of time before that date. On August 1 new lower price levels at retail are scheduled under the present regulation.

In addition, OPS officials said, continued study of the operation of the program indicates that adjustments in prices of some cuts may be necessary, to bring them in line with others in the same region. 

Meanwhile, it was pointed out, the order requires that all prices be listed on the tray in which the beef cuts are displayed, and that these prices must be at or below ceilings prescribed in the regulation. Kosher beef retailers, who were required to post their prices on June 11, must continue to display their charts, OPS said. 

Also, any other retail dealers who desire to post their prices for the benefit of their customers, may prepare their own from the prices in the regulation and post them, it was pointed out.

Re: CONSUMER ADVISORY COMMITTEE 

Formation of a national Consumer Advisory Committee to consult with the Office of Price Stabilization was announced today by Michael V. DiSalle, Price Stabilization Director. "The Purpose of the Committee", Mr. DiSalle said, will be threefold

We want to make certain that the consumer's interest has a definite opportunity to be heard, on an advisory basis, in the formulation of OPS policies and regulations. We want, through their cooperation, to see that the work of OPS is understood by the consumer-minded groups in local communities and by the national offices of the cooperating organizations, and that OPS receives consumer reactions to its program, channeled through the cooperating organizations, to balance the flow of comments and suggestions from industry groups. " 

Representatives of 22 organizations have been invited to attend a meeting with OPS officials in Washington on Monday. Most have already accepted, Mr. 

DiSalle reported. 

An all day meeting is planned to open with an address by Mr. DiSalle at 10 a. m. 

Other speakers will include Edward F. Phelps, Jr., Assistant

Director for Price Stabilization, who will give an over all review of price regulation procedure and policy; Gardner Ackley, Economic Advisor who will outline the economic philosophy underlying the price regulations; Max Hall, Assistant Director for Public Information, who will describe the OPS Program for public education and information, and Mrs. Ethel Gilbert, director, Office of Advisory Committee, who will explain the organization and functions of the 

Industry Advisory Committees. Mrs. Chase Going Woodhouse, a member of Mr. DiSalle's staff, who has been primarily concerned with the formation of the committee, will serve as presiding officer.

Coakley-OPS-GPR-620  PRIVATE BRAND COSMETIC MANUFACTURERS SUBCOMMITTEE 

A ceiling price regulation tailored to the needs of their industry was requested by members of the Private Brand Cosmetic Manufacturers Subcommittee of the Cosmetics and Toiletries Industry Advisory Committee in a meeting to day with Office of Price Stabilization officials,

The committee reviewed OPA regulation MPR 282 which applied to their industry during World War II, and CPR 22, the OPS general regulation for manufacturers. They told OPS that, with some revision, a regulation following the pattern of MPR 282 would more nearly meet their problems. The OPA regulation permitted use of the General Maximum Price Regulation for old products and required producers to apply for ceilings on new products. 

Chief problem cited by the subcommittee was the rising costs of raw materials and labor, and they asked that any new regulation make some provision for reflecting these increases in new ceiling prices.

Industry members recommended a simplified form of regulation, especially with reference to reporting forms, so as to ease the burden of paper work on small manufacturers who comprise the largest segment of the industry. They also requested simplification of information required on applications for adjustment and they objected to requiring their buyers to file statements that any increase in manufacturers' ceilings would not be passed on to consumers. 

Industry members favored reduction of the lapse of time between filing application for new ceilings and the effective date of the new prices, from 20 to 10 days. They objected to any provision requiring them to reveal the names of prospective purchasers on the grounds that the industry is a highly competitive one, and that customers might be lost through such disclosures.

PRESS RELEASE    

Re: RUBBER PRICES Moore-OPS-GPR-623 

The decrease in the government price of natural rubber announced today by the General Services Administration, effective July 1, will be reflected in lower ceiling prices in the rubber industry during the second half of the year as the new rubber goes into production and distribution, Michael V. DiSalle, Director of Price Stabilization, declared today. "If Congress permits rollbacks where they are economically justified, the 14 cents per pound decrease in the price of natural rubber could mean up to $200, 000, 000 in savings annually to the consumer and the tax payer," the director said..

The first effect will be abandonment of certain price increases to which industry was entitled under the pricing formulas of the Manufacturers' General 

Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, effective July 2, This permits manufacturers to add to their base period prices material and labor cost increases up to certain cut-off dates.

The Tire and Tube Industry Advisory Committee at a meeting with OPS 

officials today agreed their industry would waive an approximate 5 percent increase in the ceiling prices on tires and tubes to which it would have been entitled under CPR 22, in view of the impending reduction in the price of natural rubber. The action was taken before the GSA announcement was issued. The potential increases amounted to 4.1 percent on replacement tires and tubes and 5.95 percent on original equipment tires and tubes.

The committee agreed their industry was willing to continue pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation freeze of January 26, 1951, pending the completion of a tailored regulation for their industry and determination of the effect of the rubber price slash. OPS indicated a supplementary regulation would be issued temporarily leaving tires and tubes under GCPR, in view of this development.

GPO-O-OPS 1086

2  It was estimated that the increase to which tire manufacturers were entitled, before the reduction in the price of natural rubber, would have amounted to approximately $75, 000, 000 annually at the manufacturers level. 

Other industry advisory committees have waived potential increase of up to 7 percent under CPR 22. These include footwear, heels and soles, rubber hose and certain rubber drug sundries.

Decreases under GCPR prices are already in prospect on miscellaneous items such as rubber bands, rubber thread, original equipment automotive and farm machinery v-belts and friction tape.

Industry factors are currently being computed for many other rubber products under CPR 22. "The full impact of the price cut cannot be determined for some time on the thousands of rubber items produced by the industry," DiSalle said. "The proportion of natural and synthetic rubber varies from product to product and from month to month depending on the rubber supply. " 

Rubber goods manufacturers have finished or are now in the home stretch of figuring their new ceilings under CPR 22. It was a major accounting problem and it will take some time to make another calculation, such has been contemplated all along under CPR 22.

Today's meeting of the Tire and Tube Industry Advisory Committee was conducted by Hubert H. Peterson, chief of the Tire Section. Other OPS

PRESS RELEASE   

Re: 

 FEED MANUFACTURERS' PRICING Scott-OPS-GPR-625 

The Office of Price Stabilization said today that many manufacturers of "manufactured feed" are mistakenly filing ceiling prices on OPS Form 8 in accordance with the provisions of manufacturers' ceiling price regulation 

CPR 22. 

OPS officials pointed out that manufactured feeds are specifically exempt from pricing under the manufacturers' regulation CPR 22, and that Supplementary 

Regulation 7 to the General Ceiling Price Regulation was issued February 27 to provide a method for establishing ceiling prices on manufactured feeds. 

SR 7 to GCPR provides a comparatively simple method of determining ceiling prices, OPS officials said, and was written with the feed manufacturers' pricing problems in mind. Generally speaking, this regulation permits feed manufacturers to use their highest prices for products sold during the December 19, 1950 to January 25, 1951 base period, with a provision for adjusting ceiling prices to reflect dollars-and-cents increases in the cost of ingredients used in the manufactured feed. # # # # # # # # # # # # # # "Manufactured feed" is defined in the supplementary regulation as a mixture or blend of more than one ingredient for the purpose of feeding to animals or poultry, either in the same form or in combination with other ingredients, including scratch-chick or growing grains consisting entirely of recleaned grains, seeds, grit and shell containing no more than 10 percent of grain flour or screenings that will pass through a No. 20 standard tinned mill wire.

The regu- lation lists certain products not included such as food prepared for household pets, mineral mixtures, feeds containing 50 percent or more of milk solids, animal and poultry tonics and medicants, vitamin products, etc. GPO-O-OPS 1092

Moore-OPS-GPR-627  

Re: WRITING PAPER AND OTHER FINE PAPERS TAC Members of the Writing Paper and other Fine Papers Industry Advisory 

Committee today approved a tentative draft of a tailored regulation for their industry prepared by OPS officials.

The draft was based on old OPA MPR 450 which spelled out dollars and cents prices for standard grades, with differentials for packaging, finishing, trimming volume shipments and other variations customary in the trade. 

The proposed regulation embodied representative prices taken from current price lists and prices under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, reported by members of the industry on OPS Form 8 representing the bulk of production in the industry.

The proposed prices were developed by OPS in line with the principle that when a majority of an industry is entitled under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, to higher prices than existed under the GCPR freeze, the industry may be permitted to maintain GCPR ceilings under an interim or tailored regulation.

This may be desirable in an industry from the standpoint of price stability, particularly if there is a likelihood of future reductions in costs which would bring lower ceilings in event of a future recalculation under CPR 22.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers SUNDAY, June 24, 1951  Re: CONSUMER ADVISORY COMMITTEE Coakley-OPS-GPR-631 

Response from public and consumer-interest organizations to an invitation to consult with the Office of Price Stabilization on problems of price control through a national Consumer Advisory Committee has been most gratifying, Michael V. DiSalle, Price Stabilization Director, said today.

The committee, which will hold its first meeting Monday at 10 a. m. in OPS headquarters in Washington, will serve in an advisory capacity.

Its purpose will be to make available to OPS the reaction of consumers in local communities to the pricing program and carry back to the public, through cooperating organizations, a better understanding of the OPS program and its aims and procedures, Mr. DiSalle pointed out. 

Organizations which have accepted invitations to attend Monday's meeting and their representatives include: National Congress of Parent 

Teacher Associations, Mrs. O. G. Hankins, Washington; National Farmers 

Union, John Baker or Angus McDonald, both of Washington; American Council on Education, Dr. Herbert Moss, Durham, New Hampshire; National Urban

PRESS RELEASE    

Huff-OPS-GPR-633  

Re: BUILDERS HARDWARE IAC An advisory committee representing the Builders Hardware Industry told Office of Price Stabilization officials at a meeting Saturday that the industry would rather remain under the general freeze with normal price relationships than obtain higher but discrepant prices under the manufacturers' order, CPR 22, pending issuance of a specially designed industry-wide regulation. 

Cost computations under CPR 22 would result in price adjustments at levels higher than under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, committee members said, adding that other manufacturers not represented at the meeting will submit evidence substantiating this point before July 2, the effective date of the manufacturers' order. The industry is highly competitive with practically uniform pricing, they said, but CPR 22 would lead to price increases and wide variations since every manufacturer would have separate cost increase factors.

OPS officials told the committee that consideration would be given if this contention proves correct, to remove the industry from CPR 22 coverage for a long enough time to prepare a specific regulation, which would take three weeks or longer. Such a regulation would set forth specific cost increase factors for some 25 categories of products furnished by the committee. Products include metal builders hardware as well as glass and plastic trim. (over) 

Fred Schwarz, chief of the OPS Building Materials Branch, presided at the meeting. Other OPS officials attending were Irving Rubenstein, economist, A. E. Reyman, attorney, L. M. Keller, business analyst, and Harry Spack,

Office for Advisory Committees.

DAĻA IMMARIZ PRESS RELEASE    

Scott-OPS-GPR-634 

Re: HICKORY TOOL HANDLE MANUFACTURERS IAC Members of the Hickory Tool Manufacturers Industry Advisory Com mittee today urged Office of Price Stabilization officials to draft a tailored pricing regulation for this segment of the industry, as quickly as possible. 

The industry is currently pricing under the General Ceiling Price 

Regulation. Committeemen said most industry members are experiencing a steadily increasing price squeeze under GCPR, due primarily to increased labor costs, and an increase in the cost of stumpage and logs, which is the principal raw material of the industry. 

The committee felt the industry urgently needs some fairly quick price relief and recommended that interim relief be granted under the proposed formula price regulation now being drafted for turned and shaped wood products, until such time as a dollars-and-cents ceiling price regulation can be issued to cover hickory tool handles. 

The committee favored a dollars-and-cents pricing regulation patterned along the lines of the old OPA Supplementary Regulation 14 (as revised and amended) to the OPA General Maximum price Regulation. 

The committee reviewed OPA regulation SR-14 to GMPR and offered suggestions and recommendations for changes, deletions and additions to meet current industry pricing problems. The committee specifically recommended that rough-sawn wood blanks sold to domestic manufacturers for making tool handles, be included in the tailored regulation and that dollarsand-cents ceilings for export sales be included. 

A sub-committee was appointed to advise further with OPS officials as to the kind of industry data and other specific information which may be required to draft a tailored regulation.

PRESS RELEASE   ADVANCE RELEASE 

For use in Afternoon Papers

WEDNESDAY, June 27, 1951 

BEDDING MANUFACTURERS Crist-OPS-GPR-636 

The Office of Price Stabilization today reminded bedding manufacturers of two conditions under which they are not required to file a public form under the general manufacturers' order (CPR 22). 

They are not required to file: 

1) for that portion of their business which consists of repairing, renovating and upholstering; 

2) For sales of new products made directly to the ultimate consumer. 

OPS officials said that on the basis of forms (Form 8) filed so far there was considerable misunderstanding on these points. OPS pointed out that all repairing, renovating and reupholstering are considered as "services" and come under CPR 34, and that rates or prices for these services should be posted as well as filed with the nearest District OPS office. 

It was also pointed out by OPS officials that a manufacturer of new products who sells directly to the ultimate consumer at retail does not come under CPR 22, but under the General Ceiling Price Regulation.

CPR 22 defines sales at retail this way: "Sales at retail means any sale to an ultimate consumer other than a commercial, industrial, governmental or institutional user." 

7 GPO-O-OPS 1130

ald-

ALKALI-CHLORINE IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-637 

ST-4200: Ext. 3491 

Members of the Alkali-Chlorine Industry Advisory Committee at their second meeting today with Office of Price Stabilization officials reported for the most part their ceilings under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, would be at or near the prices at which they were frozen in January under the General Ceiling 

Price Regulation, GCPR. 

They requested that industry-wide cost adjustment factors be developed for their industry and applied to their GCPR prices under CPR 22, SR 2, which they predicted would have the effect of maintaining GCPR ceilings for their industry until there is a new recalculation under CPR 22.

They said this automatically would take care of the case of one manufacturer who asked OPS for special consideration because the labor cut-off date under CPR 22 did not permit his company to compute a wage increase which would bring the company up to the level of other manufacturers. Other manufacturers reported their wage increases had been fairly uniform.

Most committeemen reported their ceilings under CPR 22 would work out within one per cent either way of GCPR ceilings, which would permit them to continue pricing at their old ceilings, but they said if any single important manufacturer were frozen. below current prices it would tend to pull down prices for all manufacturers. 

Committeemen felt CPR 22 would not only take care of this particular case, but also of possible future cost increases resulting from wage contracts containing cost of-living escalator clauses. 

Committeemen undertook to expedite returns on their form 8s in order that the industry-wide factor could be computed by OPS. 

The meeting was conducted by George W. Strasser, acting assistant director, Rubber, Chemical, and Drugs Division.

CONSUMER ADVISORY COMMITTEE 

Coakley-OPS-GPR-639  

Price Stabilization Director Michael V. DiSalle today appealed to members of the Consumer Advisory Committee meeting with OPS officials in Washington to help in getting the facts about the price stabilization program to the American people, and in keeping OPS informed as to the public reaction to the program and the fields in which additional understanding and information is needed.

Mr. DiSalle said that the committee is not intended as a "propaganda organization" for OPS, but instead is being asked to advise with the agency on consumer problems. "We would like you to serve as our liaison with the consumer public through your own organizations," Mr. DiSalle said, "letting us know how the public feels about the various control regulations, and helping them to understand and cooperate with our program." 11 In response to a question, Mr. DiSalle said that the agency is not in a position, and does not intend, to agitate for renewal of the Defense Production Act. The agency does have, however, the responsibility of making the facts about its program, and the economic problems it is attempting to meet available to Congress and the public, and the public and Congress must then decide the issues on their merits.

He declared that consumer understanding and support of price controls is vital if the stabilization program is to succeed, and urged members of the committee to feel free to ask any questions which they felt needed further clarification to the public. He also stressed the need for understanding of the fact that the temporary recession now in progress is due to be replaced by strong inflationary pressures as the defense program continues to accelerate. 

Asked why OPS ceilings sometimes are higher than actual selling prices, especially in foods, the director explained that many of the pricing schedules now in effect were necessarily based on average industry factors, and naturally varied from locality to locality as far as actual selling conditions were concerned. However, he said, that in the grocery field it is planned to establish community pricing, with prices reflecting actual local conditions and GPO-O-OPS 1137

practices, as soon as possible. Again, however, he pointed to the fact that heavy inventories and the temporary slump were causing otherwise tight ceilings to be undersold.

Members of the committee said they felt that much pertinent information about the OPS program was not understood by consumer groups, and asked if the agency was hampered by an inadequate staff to bring the facts before the public. 

Mr. DiSalle said that to some extent that was true, but he added that there had been considerable apathy on the part of the public to some of the control problems, and pointed out that much could be done to correct the situation if the organizations represented at the meeting would cooperate in an educational and information program with OPS personnel and their members. 

Edward F. Phelps, Assistant OPS Director for Price Stabilization also stressed the need for cooperation between consumer groups and OPS in working out a public information program. This, he said, was in his opinion the most important function the committee could perform. 

Mr. Phelps traced for the committee the development of the price stabilization program through three phases the voluntary phase in which industry was asked to voluntarily hold prices down; the corrective phase or interim phase during which prices were frozen to stop further price spiraling and interim regulations to relieve inequities were adopted; and the third phase of the program, which will then be directed toward holding the line and preventing further price increases. th 

The Agency is now in the second phase of its work, he declared, and cited the general manufacturers order as an example of it, explaining that OPS intends to follow it as rapidly as possible with tailored regulations for each of the manufacturing industries which it covers. 

Gardner Ackley, OPS Economic Advisor, explained the OPS earnings stand ard, which establishes the policy that the level of price ceilings for an industry shall normally be considered "generally fair and equitable" within the meaning of the Defense Production Act, if the dollar profits of the industry amount to 85 per cent of the average for the industry's best three years during the period 1946-49. the Cost absorption is the cornerstone of stabilization he told the meeting, since it enables us to break through the cycle of rising costs and prices. 

If all cost increases were automatically translated into price increases, cost of living and the farmers parity index would rise, causing further increases in prices, cost of living and parity and the spiral of inflation would continue unabated. Industry must, therefore, absorb some of the costs, he said.

Max Hall, OPS Assistant Director for Public Information, told members of the Advisory Committee that while the Office of Public Information had issued more than 600 press releases about the OPS program other means must also be utilized to get the facts to the public. 

He would not ask the committee to spread propaganda for OPS, nor would his office function as a lobbying organization, he delcared. However, he pointed out, the Office of Public Information would welcome the cooperation of consumer interest groups and would make every effort to furnish factual material for their use.

Mr. Hall described the functioning of the Volunteer Citizens Committees which have been set up in many cities to assist in interpreting the OPS program and cooperate with district and regional office of OPS. 

He also outlined some of the work now being done or in the planning stage for the use of radio, television, films, posters, pamphlets, and other media to explain the OPS program to the public. 

Mrs. Ethel B. Gilbert, director, Office of Industry Advisory Committees, described the functions of the Industry Advisory Committees. They advise the agency on specific regulations affecting them rather than matters of broad policy, she explained. They are asked to supply OPS with technical information about how their industry operates and what its peculiar problems are, so as to guide the agency in writing a tailored regulation which will best serve the ends of price stabilization, and at the same time be least disturbing to the effective functioning of that industry, she said. 

At the afternoon session T. Otis Black, director of the Program Division of the Office of Public Information and Gordon McCloskey, special assistant to Mr. Hall, outlined OPS plans for an information program. 

Members of the committee expressed their desire to have more information about OPS and offered their cooperation in furthering a public information program. 

OPS invited the committee to make recommendations as to how the Agency and the consumer representatives could best work together in the interest of the price stabilization program and the public. 

An executive committee headed by Wallace Campbell, Chicago, Cooperative

League of the United States of America, will be set up to carry on the work of the committee between general meetings. Three other members, residing in 

Washington, will be selected by Mr. Campbell and Mrs. Chase Going Woodhouse, a member of Mr. DiSalle's staff, to serve with them on the executive committee. 

Mrs. Woodhouse presided at today's meeting. 

July 19 was set as a tentative date for the next meeting of the committee.

Members of the Consumer Advisory Committee attending today's meeting were Mrs. 0. G. Hankins, Washington, National Congress of Parent Teacher 

Associations; Angus McDonald, Washington, National Farmers Union; Guichard

Scott-OPS-GPR-641  Re: BROOM AND MOP HANDLE INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE 

Members of the Broom and Mop Handle Industry Advisory Committee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a tailored pricing regulation for this segment of the industry. 

The industry is currently pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regula- Committeemen said the industry generally is experiencing a steadily increasing price squeeze under GCPR, due principally to increased labor costs. 

One member stated his company is urgently in need of relief from GCPR ceiling prices because the company's normal supply of broom and mop handle lumber is obtained in Canada on the basis of contracts entered into last October at increased prices, which are not reflected in current GCPR ceiling prices. Deliveries of lumber under the October 1950 contracts will not start until July, at which time the increased costs will be reflected in current production.

The committee favored a formula type of tailored price regulation patterned along the lines of the old OPA regulation MPR-196, covering turned and shaped wood products. The broom and mop handle industry priced under this regulation, and committee members said that, generally speaking, it was a satisfactory pricing formula for the industry.

OPA-MPR-196 maintained seller's pricing method established under the OPA 

General Maximum Price Regulation, by preserving each seller's formula and applying it to labor and material costs to a specified date.

The committee did not think that dollars-and-cents pricing would be feasible because of the substantial variation in raw material costs in each area as between fir, pine and hardwoods, and also because of substantial variation in labor cost factors in each area. The committee felt that dollars-and-cents ceiling would require a great amount of study, and in the meantime, the industry urgently needs a formula type of regulation which will permit the reflection of current increased labor and material costs.

Members said that when dollars-and-cents ceilings are established for lumber generally, the committee could give further consideration to the feasibility of setting dollars-and-cents ceilings on broom and mop handles.

The meeting was conducted by Bernard H. Topkis, deputy head, Miscellaneous 

Wood Products Section, Lumber & Wood Products Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: 

Norman 0. Cruver, chief, Lumber & Wood Products Branch;

Leonard Perez, head, Miscellaneous Wood Products Section; Stanley M. Levy, legal staff; David White, economist; Glen Converse, consultant; and, Walter R. Moulton,

Washington Re: PRINTING INKS IAC Moore -OPS-GPR-642 ST-4200: Ext. 3491 

Members of the Printing Inks Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with Office of Price Stabilization officials reported that the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, which applies to their industry, was impractical for them and recommended that a tailored regulation be prepared for printing inks using the pricing techniques of CPR 11, the restaurant regulation.

They also said the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, was equally unsuitable for their industry.

Committeemen said there were no standard industry-wide grades or products and no stable long-term formulas. Printing inks, they reported, are mixed to meet requirements of the users and vary not only as to color but also as to drying qualities, stability, absorbability, resistance to chemicals and moisture and other characteristics. 

One member reported the average life of a formula was four months, so that most of the inks produced by the industry are for the purposes of price regulation actually new products. 

The committee agreed to the feasibility of employing a ratio of material costs to dollar sales as a price governing factor similar to the "food cost per dollar of sales" ratio used by restaurants.

The manufacturer would determine this ratio for his base period and maintain it in subsequent periods in his over-all operations. The committee recommended that accounting and adjustment should be made semi-annually and that a tolerance of 5 percent of cost of materials be allowed before a manufacturer would be liable for violation.

Committeemen recommended that a manufacturer should determine his ratio of costs to his sales in his last accounting period prior to June 30, 1950.

They reported it was physically impossible for their industry to comply with CPR 22 because of the pricing problems peculiar to the industry. 

(Over)

Form 8s by July 2 to comply with CPR 22.

PRESS RELEASE    

Wednesday, June 27, 1951

Scott-OPS-GPR-646 

Re: GROCERY AND VARIETY BAG MANUFACTURERS IAC The Grocery and Variety Bag Manufacturers Industry Advisory Com mittee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a tailored pricing regulation for this segment of the industry.

The industry is currently pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation and will be required to price under the general manufacturers' ceiling price regulation, CPR 22, effective July 2.

Members said it has been indicated that ceiling prices under CPR 22 will be generally slightly higher than under GCPR, but that probably few industry members will sell at the higher ceilings.

The committee felt it would be difficult to draft a tailored regulation until a regulation governing ceiling prices on kraft paper is issued. 

Committeemen said it would be highly desirable and urgent that a tailored regulation for grocery and variety bags be issued simultaneously with the issuance of a kraft paper regulation, and in order to accomplish this, the committee felt the industry generally would be willing to hold prices at the GCPR levels, subject to adjustments to reflect current ceiling prices established for kraft paper.

Members said the industry would probably prefer maintaining their individual GCPR prices, rather than conform to a leveling of GCPR prices on an industry wide basis.

Members pointed out that many industry members, who are converters rather than integrated companies, are experiencing serious difficulty in obtaining a sufficient supply of paper of grades suitable for grocery and variety bags, and as a result, will probably suffer a substantial reduction in production, unless kraft paper ceilings reflect weight differentials making it attractive to produce weights suitable for making light grocery and variety bags. 

Members asked that this situation be recognized in determining ceiling prices for kraft paper.

Moore-OPS-GPR-648 

CAMELBACK AND TIRE REPAIR MATERIALS IAC 

Manufacturers' prices on camelback and tire repair materials will be reduced from 4 to 14 per cent under current prices shortly as a result of the recent decline in the government price of natural rubber, it was indicated at a meeting today of Office of Price Stabilization officials with members of the Camelback and Tire Repair Material Industry Advisory Committee. 

Committeemen discussed returns from the industry on OPS Form 15s, reporting computations under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation,

CPR 22. 

These returns, prepared before the rubber price was lowered by GSA from 66 to 52 cents, indicated new ceilings would be 2 to 3 per cent higher on three of the industry's products and from 1 to 4 per cent lower on six products. 

Tentative adjustments of the returns to reflect the new lowered rubber prices indicated new ceilings will range from 4 to 14 per cent under prices established last January by the General Ceiling Price Regulation. 

The industry will be asked to make new reports on natural rubber camelback on the basis of the new rubber price to confirm these computations prior to the announcement of industry-wide percentage cost adjustment factors which will be used to determine the new ceilings. Camelback is the material used in vulcanizing new treads on used tires. 

OPS officials informed committeemen that a postponement of two weeks from 

July 2 would be sought in the effective date of CPR 22 for camelback and tire repair materials, pending issuance of the new cost adjustment factors. 

This indicated that the first of a series of rollbacks resulting directly from the new government rubber prices will be effective by the middle of July, applying to the camelback and tire repair materials industry. The reduced price of natural rubber has already been reflected in the abandonment of possible roll forwards under CPR 22 by several segments of the rubber industry, since such increases would be only temporary in view of the future recalculations of ceilings under CPR 22 reflecting the lower government rubber prices.

The meeting was conducted by Hubert H. Peterson, chief of the Tire Section of the Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division. Other OPS officials present were

Re: INTEGRAL HORSEPOWER ELECTRIC MOTOR AND GENERATOR LAC An Industry Advisory Committee representing integral horsepower electric motor and generator manufacturers discussed relief from the provisions of the machinery ceiling price regulation (CPR 30) at a meeting with Office of Price Stabilization officials yesterday.

Committee members said the National Production Authority has asked for a huge expansion in electric motor and generator output which cannot be accomplished without resort to additional subcontracting and overtime and shift premium labor. They recommended permission for manufacturers to include increased costs of these practices in their cost adjustments under OPS regulations. 

Motors and generators made by this segment of the industry range from one to 500 horsepower. Electric motors and generators are vital for machine tool operation and various industrial processes and thus play a major role in the defense program. 

Industry representatives pointed out at the meeting that they are also encountering other cost increases which are not recognized under CPR 30, mainly resulting from personnel training, labor rotation requirements, production schedule changes, and expanded purchases and sales.. 

They said also that cost adjustment calculations under CPR 30 would confuse prices since manufacturers would come up with many varying factors. They said the years 1936 through 1940 were the most typical period as to normal cost-price relationships. A specially designed regulation was favored by the committee to supersede CPR 30 for their products.

OPS officials asked a subcommittee to meet with them next month to determine what statistics would be needed to clarify the industry's problems. They said the committee's point of view and recommendations would be considered on the basis of this information.

H. M. Jalonack, head of the electrical section of the OPS Machinery Branch, led the meeting. Other OPS officials present were L. J. Carson, branch chief, H. C. 

Thompson, Jr., attorney, and Harry Spack and W. R. Moulton, Office for Advisory Committees. Representatives of the National Production Authority also attended the conference. 

Members of the committee, all present except Mr. Clements, are:

Re: 

 RETAIL TAGGING UNDER CPR 7 

Beginning next Monday stores selling the many articles covered by 

Ceiling Price Regulation 7 must have each article marked or tagged with the selling price, the Office of Price Stabilization said today in a reminder to the nation's retailers.

Ceiling Price Regulation 7 is the "margin control" regulation which covers a wide range of consumer goods, notably apparel and shoes, furniture, floor coverings, yard goods, housewares, radio and television sets, musical instruments, jewelry, silverware and glassware, watches, and clocks, etc.

Hughes-OPS-GPR-650  

The selling price may be marked on the article itself, on a ticket or tag attached to the article, or may be shown on the shelf, rack or bin containing the article. In either case the price must be clearly visible to, and understandable by, the store's customers. 

Beginning Monday, also, each store must post, in a prominent and clearly visible position, a sign reading:

THE PRICES OF MERCHANDISE IN THIS STORE ARE NO HIGHER THAN THE OPS CEIL- ING PRICES OF THE ARTICLES. 

These requirements designed to give store patrons assurance that they issued last February. are not being asked to pay over-ceiling prices were contained in CPR 7 as The effective date of the marking and tagging requirement was then set at July 1, so as to give retailers ample time to figure their ceilings under the regulation and to mark their merchandise with selling prices as required by the regulation. 1011

The National American wholesale Grocers Association has wired Congress an urgent plea for extension of the Defense Production Act in its present form for a year, Michael V. DiSalle, director of the Office of Price Stabilization, said today he was informed.

The association, largest in the wholesale grocery field with members throughout much of the nation, notified Mr. DiSalle that the following telegram had been sent to Senator Burnett R. Maybank, chairman of the Senate Banking and 

Currency Committee, and Rep. Brent Spence, chairman of the House Banking and 

Currency Committee: 

"Ernestly urge extension of Defense Production Act in present form for not more than one year to permit further study and adjustment in line with uncertain international situation."

The telegram was signed by Sherwin A. Hill, president of the association, and president of Lee and Cady Wholesale Grocery Company, Detroit. 

The United States Wholesale Grocers' Association, Mr. DiSalle said, has also called his attention to a resolution adopted by the Association during its 1951 meeting, and forwarded to all members of Congress. 

The Association, a large organization with many southern members, approved a resolution favoring "full support of legislation, taxes, and government orders, necessary for the safety of the nation and designed to curb inflation, to control prices and wages, to allocate critical materials, to establish civilian defense, and to provide manpower and training for the armed forces of the Nation." 

Mr. DiSalle said he had also been informed that the San Francisco, Calif., board of supervisors had voted to urge all congressional representatives of the state and city to support legislation to permit the additional rollbacks of beef prices.

The board's action was taken at the request of the San Francisco Council of Women Shoppers, which presented a petition bearing 3,000 signatures, Mr. DiSalle said he was informed. Mrs. Frances Shaskan, council chairman, was quoted as saying: "A move in Congress to ban all rollbacks threathen collapse of the housewives' pocketbook."

Re: 

PACKAGE LIQUORS IAC Barkley-OPS-GPR-663 

A ceiling price regulation for the off-premise sale of packaged wine and liquors based on a percentage markup was recommended today to the 

Office of Price Stabilization by the Retail Package Liquor Dealers Industry Advisory Committee. 

Such a regulation would be similar to one used by the Office of Price Administration during World War II. The dealers recommended, however, that the new regulation specifically apply the percentage markup to proposed increased Federal taxes on alcoholic beverages. They explained the industry had to absorb a tax increase during World War II. 

The dealers recommended that the percentage markup vary according to the type of alcoholic beverage, with wine being given the largest markup, cordials in between, and whiskeys the smallest. They said this policy was followed by OPA. 

OPS officials told the committee it was contemplated that the new regulation would apply to imported wines and liquors as well as to domestic products. Such action, they explained, would remove imported wines and liquors from the the import ceiling price regulation (CPR 31) and place them under the new regulation for liquors.

The proposed regulation would not cover beer, which is to be included in a regulation specifically for this beverage.

Pending drafting and adoption of a regulation for retail packaged liquors, the industry will remain under the General Ceiling Price Regulation with imported liquors continuing under the import regulation. 

Representing OPS at the meeting were George C. Mehren, assistant director, Food and Restaurant Division; Charles W. Sand of the Alcoholic Beverage 

Section, who presided; Clarence C. Benedict of the Grocery Branch; William R. 

Thomas, jr., of the Office for Advisory Committees; Henry Keiser, attorney; and John Paschke, economist.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers Monday, July 9, 1951 Tempo E 

Washington Re: BALER AND BINDER TWINE Moore -OPS-GPR-664 

Office of Price Stabilization field agents are investigating pricing and distribution of baler and binder twine in a number of key agricultural states in response to reports of price control violations, OPS enforcement officials revealed today.

Sixty field representatives are inquiring into specific cases reported in Texas, Missouri, Minnesota, Iowa and Wisconsin.

In addition, other agents are checking details of manufacturers' shipments in Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Illinois and New York, looking into quantities, prices and recipients of all shipments of twine. Enforcement officials said some violations appeared deliberate and others are due, apparently, to failure to read carefully the applicable price regulations, particularly Supplementary Regulation 29 to the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, which permits wholesalers and retailers to reflect increased prices charged them by suppliers in some instances. 

The inquiries are being pressed because the demand for twine is unusually high at this season. OPS officials said farmers could aid in the inquiry by demanding and preserving receipts for all purchases of twine. 

Indicative of information being received from the farm states, four large retailers not in the business before were reported selling twine at exorbitant prices in Iowa. A new dealer must establish his ceiling prices on the basis of those of his closest competitor, hence his ceilings cannot legitimately be higher than prevailing prices. 

The situation is aggravated by a shortage of such twine which has induced speculative buying. Manufacturers this year received only 35 percent of their normal supplies of sisal, due to defense and stockpile requirements, though they had sufficient inventories to permit above normal shipments to meet the demand.

Behind the rise in twine prices is the world rise in prices of sisal, the principal raw fiber used in baler and binder twine. Sisal is an imported product, brought into this country at uncontrolled prices. A basic prin ciple of the OPS Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, is to allow manufacturers to reflect legitimate materials cost increases in their ceilings. Thus some manufacturers who have begun to price under CPR GPO—0—OPS 21

have been able to establish twine ceilings $3 to $4 higher than their former ceilings.

Another factor entering into higher twine prices is the relief from "squeeze" situations recently granted wholesalers and retailers by OPS.

When all prices were frozen in January under the GCPR, some wholesalers and retailers with substantial inventories of twine had not yet raised their own prices in relation to higher prices put into effect by their suppliers. Thus their GCPR ceilings did not truly reflect the cost to them of replenishing their stocks. To relieve such "squeezes," OPS recently allowed sellers to recalculate their ceilings so as to adapt them to higher prices charged them by suppliers under GCPR. As in the case of other products, this resulted in some legitimate increases in twine prices. 

This adjustment was applicable to a dealer's entire inventory. 

Wholesalers and retailers also are permitted to make a further adjustment of their ceilings based on higher CPR 22 ceilings of their suppliers, but this second adjustment is applicable only to the inventory purchased at prices calculated under CPR 22. 

Information received by OPS indicates that some wholesalers and retailers are repricing their entire inventory on the basis of CPR 22 prices, and thus are intentionally or unknowingly violating the regulations. 

Enforcement officials stated when dealers and retailers can show they unwittingly sold old inventory at CPR 22 ceilings and thereafter sold a compensating volume of new inventory at their GCPR ceilings, this effort at correction would be considered in determining the disposition of their violations. ### ! # # # #

PRESS RELEASE   

Monday, July 9, 1951

Tempo E 

Washington Moore - OPS-GPR-666 ST 4200; Ext. 3491 Re: COTTON, LINEN AND UNDERWEAR CUTTING DEALERS IAC Members of the Cotton, Linen and Underwear Cutting Dealers Industry 

Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials recommended that the language of CPR 28, which sets prices in their industry, be clarified specifically permitting commissions to be paid on sorted cuttings baled in 

Army, Navy and Marine depots.

The committee recommended that no commissions be allowed on unbaled cuttings from such depots or factories, or on cuttings baled by factories. 

There was considerable discussion whether differentials should be established between ceilings on baled and unbaled cuttings. CPR 28 spells out prices for 87 grades of cuttings, without specifying whether the prices are for baled or unbaled cuttings. Committeemen reported that the industry generally accepted the ceilings as applying to baled cuttings and that normal practices in the trade took care of the differentials. (over)

The consensus was that any attempt to prescribe differentials would lead to confusion.

The problem of pricing exports was discussed. CPR 28 provides that the spelled out ceilings apply to exports on dock at port of exit, and that customary charges for packaging and other special services incidental to export may be added to the ceilings.

Committeemen reported this provision was difficult to apply Ordinarily dealers shipping abroad cover the extra cost of special baling, agents commission abroad, travel expenses, licenses, letters of credit, cables and exchange transactions by figuring extra margins of profit. Committeemen suggested the export price should be 10 or 12 per cent higher than domestic prices to cover these contingencies.

GPO--O-OPS 23

- A subcommittee was named to study this problem and recommend a workable formula for computing such costs. Committee men stressed the need of such a formula to permit them to quote prices in response to queries from abroad.
