Re: JOHN K. MESKIMEN Coakley-OPS-GPR-667 

Price Stabilization Director Michael V. DiSalle today announced that he has named as his labor adviser John K. Meskimen, a member of the Brotherhood of Railway Clerks.

The appointment, Mr. DiSalle said, is in line with OPS policy to have all segments of the national economy represented in the price control program. "We have been working on the problem of setting up machinery for a labor liaison program in OPS for some time," he reported. "We have set up industry advisory committees and a consumer advisory committee to consult with us and the appointment of Mr. Meskimen is another step toward assuring a role for every citizen in the battle against inflation."

Mr. Meskimen, who will be an assistant to the director, will maintain liaison between OPS and organized labor. He will keep the unions informed as to OPS policies, practices and progress and give them whatever assistance they need in interpreting the program to their members. He also will consult with the unions so that they may voice their opinions and suggestions for more effective price stabilization, Mr. DiSalle said.

Mr. Meskimen has had wide experience in the field of labor relations. Following five and one-half years' service abroad in the U.S. manpower and labor-relations program in Germany, he returned to this country in October 1950. Since 

February, he has been employed as consultant to the Defense Manpower Administra tion, U.S. Department of Labor. 

Inducted into the Army in 1943, he went overseas with the 766th Railway Shop Battalion and was detailed to the U.S. Group Control Council, Berlin, as labor relations specialist and assigned to the Manpower Division. Following his discharge from the army in Germany in 1946, he was appointed chief of the Labor Dis putes Section, Manpower Division of the U.S. Group Control Council. 

He represented the United States on the Quadripartite Committee on Labor Law, Trade Unions and Labor Relations until the Control Council for Germany collapsed as a result of Russian withdrawal and the blockade of Berlin in April 1948.

In June, 1948, he was appointed chief of the Industrial Relations Branch, Manpower Division, Office of Military Government for Germany, U.S. and in 1949 was named Deputy Director of Labor Affairs in the Office of the U.S. High Commis sioner for Germany by the State Department. 

Mr. Meskimen, 42, is a native of Lawrenceville, Ill. He began his railroad career in 1924 as messenger boy in the general office of the Atchison, Topeka and 6965 GPO-0--OPS 24

Santa Fe Railroad. He held various clerical positions in the Arizona Division of the railroad before entering military service. He served as general chairman of the System Committee of the Brotherhood of Railway Clerks from 1937 to 1943. 

Swearing-in ceremonies for Mr. Meskimen at noon Wednesday in Mr. DiSalle's office will be witnessed by representatives of OPS, organized labor and the 

Department of Labor.

Re: SOUTHERN YELLOW PINE POST LAC  Members of the Southern Yellow Pine Post Industry Advisory Com mittee at their first meeting today with OPS officials recommended that prices of their products should be fixed in an equitable relationship to the prices of lumber.

The committee felt that a tailored regulation for their industry should not be written until prices have been determined for lumber. 

OPS has been working on tailored regulations for the lumber industry, which is still pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation. 

Committeemen reported they were finding it difficult to obtain stumpage in competition with lumber and pulpwood manufacturers at prices which would permit them to sell their products profitably. 

Members recommended that pricing in their industry be based on the price of peeled and rough posts at the producer level.

The committee agreed that the service of treating posts with wood preservatives could be dealt with properly in a separate regulation.

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers

Re: QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS ON GOR 13 

The Office of Price Stabilization today issued a series of questions and answers on the effect of General Overriding Regulation 13 on the general manufacturers' order (CPR 22) and companion manufacturing regulations.

GOR 13 provided that manufacturers continue pricing under the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation of January 26, unless they had put new prices into effect on or before June 30 under CPR 22 and related regulations.

Although drafted in terms of CPR 22, the series of questions and answers apply generally to the other manufacturing regulations: Machinery and Related

Manufactured Goods (CPR 30); Primary Cotton Textile Manufacturers' Regulation (CPR 37); Shoe Manufacturers' Regulation (CPR 41); Apparel Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation (CPR 45); Manufacturers' Prices for Wool Yarns and Fabrics (CPR 18 and CPR 18, Revision 1). 

This series of questions and answers has been issued as a guide to enable manufacturers to determine whether any of these manufacturing regulations were in effect for them on June 30. 7060 GPO-O-OPS 76

1. 2. 3. Q. 

I filed a Form 8 under CPR 22 before June 30, 1951. 

Is CPR 22 automatically in effect as to me on June 30?

A. Q. A. Q. A. 

No. 

The act of filing is not in itself sufficient to establish that the regulation was in effect as to you. 

You must have exercised your option to have put the regulation into effect as to you on or before June 30. 

See Question 2.) 

How may I show that I put CPR 22 into effect as to me on or before June 30, 1951? 

By showing that on or before June 30 you had both complied with all the requirements of the regulation, and had taken action to put it into effect prior to July 1, either by making price increases pursuant to CPR 22 effective prior to July 1, through sales, deliveries, etc., or by other action, such as actual written notification to OPS, or to your customers, that you were putting the regulation into effect prior to July 1, 1951. 

My Form 8 showing price increases was received by OPS on

June 20. In view of the fact that I filed my reports prior to June 30, may I sell under CPR 22 at the higher price on 

July 6 after the 15-day waiting period has elapsed? 

No. If all you did was to file your Form 8 on June 20, you continue pricing under the GCPR. In order to put CPR 22 into effect in the case of a price increase your Form 8 must have been filed more than 15 days prior to selling at the increased price. Therefore, the higher ceiling price under CPR 22 was not in effect on June 30 if the Form 8 was received after 

June 14. If it was not in effect as to you on June 30, it cannot now be made effective simply because the 15-day waiting period has now elapsed. 7010-2

5. 

A. 

I filed a Form 8 proposing a price increase and the 15-day period expired before June 30, but I did not put the higher price into effect before July 1 because of a soft market in my product. May I now use the higher ceiling price under CPR 22?

I put price increases into effect pursuant to CPR 22 on

June 30 for a few of my commodities covered by that regulation. Must I price under GCPR other commodities manufactured by me and covered by CPR 22 but which I did not sell prior to July 1 at CPR 22 prices?

A. 

No. 

If you put CPR 22 into effect on or before June 30 for some of your commodities than the regulation was in effect on June 30 as to you for all of your commodities covered by that regulation. In that event you must price all such commodities under CPR 22, with respect to both price increases and decreases. You must file Form 8's as to all such commodities before making sales, and comply with the 15-day waiting period on all price increases. 

No. Selling at a price below your CPR 22 ceiling price does not of itself establish the exercise of your option to put CPR 22 into effect prior to July 1. A soft market may be one of a number of reasons for not exercising the 

Would one sale, offer or delivery made on June 29 at my increased price under CPR 22 suffice to establish the fact that I exercised my option to put CPR 22 into effect on or before June 30? 

Yes, if made in good faith pursuant to CPR 22 with the intention to put CPR 22 into effect at that time. 7010 - 3

7. 8. Q. A. Q. A. 

CPR 22 was in effect as to me on June 30, 1951 for commodities A, B, C. Now I propose to sell commodity D, which is covered by CPR 22, for the first time. Should I price commodity D, under CPR 22? 

Yes. Since CPR 22 was in effect as to you on June 30 it was in effect as to you for all its provisions, including rollbacks, adjustments, supplementary reglations, filing, etc. Commodities sold by you for the first time must therefore be priced under CPR 22.

Some manufacturers filed Form 8's under CPR 22 as to increases before June 15. However OPS requested additional information before June 30, so that the manufacturers were not using their increased prices under CPR 22 for the commodities covered by the questioned filings. May CPR 22 be used to price these commodities, if: a) All the Form 8's filed by a manufacturer had been questioned? b).

Only some of the Form 8's filed by a manufacturer had been questioned? a) No. If all Form 8's had been questioned and none of the increased prices could have been charged on or before June 30, then CPR 22 was not in effect as to such a manufacturer on or before June 30, so that he uses GCPR for all his commodities. b) Yes, if the manufacturer had put CPR 22 into effect for some commodities on or before June 30. 

In auch case,

CPR 22 was in effect as to him for all his commodities even though OPS had stopped the proposed increases for other commodities. His other commodities must be priced under CPR 22 and he may charge the ceiling price as approved by OPS. 7010 4

11. A. 

On June 20, 1951 I filed Form 8's under CPR 22 for both increases and decreases. At the same time I printed new price lists showing these CPR 22 prices. The new price lists were issued to my salesmen on June 20 with written instructions that all sales were to be made immediately at the prices decreased pursuant to CPR 22. The increased prices were to become effective on July 6, after the 15-day waiting period had elapsed. Was CPR 22 in effect as to me on June 30, and may I now charge the higher prices? 

Yes. The above facts show that you intended to and did put CPR 22 into effect on or before June 30.

I had filed Form 8's showing my new CPR 22 prices on July 14, but had not started using these new prices before 

July 1. I did, however, announce before July 1 that the new prices were to be effective July 3. May I now use these prices under CPR 22? 

No. Your announcement that your new price list was to become effective on July 3 shows that you did not intend to put CPR 22 into effect on or before June 30. Such an announcement is only an advance arrangement for future deliveries which were to be covered by ceilings in effect at the time of deliveries. 

Q. On June 14 I mailed my Form 8 under CPR 22 covering price increases but the Form was not received by OPS until 

June 15. Do I consider my Form filed on June 14 or June 

15? How would I know the date of receipt by OPS? 

A. The date of filing is June 15, the date of receipt by OPS and not the date of postmark. Your registered mail return receipt or other acknowledgment by OPS would show the date on which your form 8 was received. 7010 - 5

12. Q. 

A. 

If I filed as to a price increase under CPR 22 on June 15, wouldn't the 15-day waiting period have expired on June 29 so that I could use the higher price on June 30?

A. 

No. Section 48 of CPR 22 states that you "must wait 15 days after the date of receipt" by OPS before using the higher price. Thereafter you may sell at the increased price "at the end of that 15-day period." Thus, you must wait 15 days after June 15, which carries you through

June 30, and you could not sell at the increased prices on June 30. 

13. Q. How are manufacturers affected by supplementary regulations to CPR 22?

If CPR 22 was in effect as to you on June 30, then it was in effect for all its provisions, including amendments and supplementary regulations thereto. 7010

Form 8's in the usual way whether filed on, before, or after July 1. 

If CPR 22 is not in effect as to you on June 30, OPS will nevertheless continue to process your Form 8's regardless of your date of filing. Such processing is intended, however, only to expedite the establishment of your ceiling prices under CPR 22 at such time as CPR 22 may be made effective as to you by future action of OPS.

The proces- sing would not make CPR 22 effective as to you and you could use your CPR 22 prices only after future action by 

OPS making CPR 22 effective as to you.

 Re: BUTTER TAC Barkley-OPS-GPR-671 ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 Al Members of the Butter Industry Advisory Committee today discussed with 

Office of Price Stabilization officials the possibility of a ceiling price regulation for butter in the event price controls are placed on milk and butterfat.

The farm prices of both milk and butterfat are now below the legal minimum and are not subject to control. However, the commodities would become subject to controls should prices rise above the legal minimum. 

If a butter regulation is issued, committeemen emphasized the need for maintaining a proper relationship between the prices received by milk producers whose milk is used for various manufactured products, such as butter, cheese and evaporated milk.

The committeemen also discussed the feasibility of relating manufacturing milk prices to fluid milk prices. 

(Over) 

Much of the time was devoted to discussing the reduction in butter production which has occurred during the past year. Butter production this year is estimated at 10 to 15 percent below 1950. The reduction was attributed to the disparity between the price of butter and the price of meat. 

It was the Committee's first meeting.

 Re: PASSENGER CAR MANUFACTURERS INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE The Passenger Car Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee, meeting for the first time today with office of Price Stabilization officials, recommended unanimously that the industry be covered by Ceiling Price Regulation 30, the machinery order, in place of the present CPR 1.

Committee members said CPR 30 would enable automobile manufacturers to adjust prices of passenger cars on the same pre-Korea-plus-costs formula that applies to trucks and automotive parts which they also produce. They said it would also tend to equalize prices thrown out of line by the December freeze established by CPR 1 which found some manufacturers with price increases already in effect and prevented others from going ahead with planned increases.

OPS officials pointed out that CPR 30 is an interim regulation not yet in effect and designeŭ largely to provide a pricing formula for various types of industrial manufactured goods until separate regulations could be issued. 

Agency representatives asked the committee to collaborate in obtaining information from all manufacturers showing operating and balance sheet figures. 

They said the earnings position of the industry, now and in the immediate future as altered by defense program requirements, would have to be considered in the light of the so-called Johnston earning standard before any action could be taken to adjust present ceiling prices. The standard specified by Eric Johnston, Economic Stabilization Administrator, establishes the general principle that ceiling price increases cannot be granted unless an industry as a whole demonstrates earnings below 85 percent of the average of the best three years between 1946 and 1949. 

W. LeRoy Jordan, chief of the OPS Automotive Branch, presided at today's meeting. Edward F. Phelps, OPS Assistant Director for Price Stabilization, discussed the general background of price control and the specific problem of automobile pricing. Other OPS representatives at the meeting were Murray D. Smith, director of the Industrial Materials and Manufactured Goods Division, John M. 

Bulkley, assistant director, F. Stewart Stranahan, counsel, Bruce Morris, economist, H. H. Robbins and T. B. Brown, Jr., attorneys, R. W. Orr, business specialist, and W. R. Thomas, Jr., and Harry Spack, Office for Advisory Committees.

DOGWOOD AND PERSIMMON SHUTTLE BLOCK IAC Members of the Dogwood and Persimmon Shuttle Block Industry Advisory

Re: HICKORY DIMENSION MANUFACTURERS IAC Members of the Hickory Dimension Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials recommended a tailored regulation be written for their industry spelling out dollars and cents ceilings for their products.

The committee suggested the ceilings be fixed on a board foot basis, f.o.b. mill, for various categories of dimension hickory, with provisions for a mark-up for concentrators to pay them for their services. Concentrators buy from small mills, dry and grade the products, and ship in carload lots to consumers.

The committee recommended that, pending preparation of a tailored regulation, the industry be placed under an interim regulation being written for the turned, shaped and allied wood products. This regulation would permit manufacturers to adjust their prices to take into consideration allowable increased costs to which they would apply their markups existing during the first quarter of 1951.

Committeemen said their industry was depressed and in need of immediate relief, particularly the smaller mills.

The industry produces such items as picker stick blanks used in the manufacture of picker sticks for textile mills, shunt pole squares used for making shunt poles for the railroad industry in Great Britain, ski billets, handle blanks and ladder rung stock.

Box 393 

Dermott, Arkansas

A subcommittee was appointed to assist OPS in preparation of a tailored regulation for the industry.

Miscellaneous Wood Products Section.

EVAPORATED MILK TAC 

Adoption of a dollars and cents ceiling price regulation for evaporated milk in the event the cost of milk passes the legal minimum was discussed today at a meeting of the Evaporated Milk Industry Advisory Committee with Office of Price Stabilization officials. 

Committeemen proposed that the first six months of 1951 be used as the base period. They said that the gross margin for the industry the difference between the cost of milk received from producers and the price of the finished product-- was lower during this period than in the May-June, 1950, pre-Korean base.

They also recommended that pass throughs be permitted for increases in the cost of milk, transportation and packaging materials such as cartons, cans and labels.

The committeemen emphasized the need for a pricing policy for evaporated milk which would maintain a proper relationship between the prices received by milk producers whose milk is used for other manufactured milk products such as butter and cheese.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers Friday, July 13, 1951  Barkley-OPS-GPR-678 ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 Re: CROP LOSS ALLOWANCES 

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today that the ceiling price regulation now being prepared for processed sweet cherries, apricots and freestone peaches will reflect increases in the grower prices for these items due to severe crop losses in producing states. 

The maximum raw material costs for sweet cherries for canning and freezing and for brining in Washington and Oregon, which if paid may be reflected in ceiling prices, will be $368 per ton for canning and freezing and $345 per ton for brining.

The maximum raw material costs for apricots for canning or freezing, which if paid may be reflected in ceiling prices, will be $106 per ton in 

California and $109 per ton in Washington.

The maximum raw material costs for freestone peaches for canning or freezing, which if paid may be reflected in ceiling prices, will be $102 in Washington and Oregon and $94 per ton in Michigan. 

These adjustments, OPS said, will be made in accordance with the pro visions of Section 402 (a) (3) of the Defense Production Act which requires that appropriate allowances shall be made in ceiling prices for processed agricultural commodities to reflect substantial reductions in merchantable crop yields, unusual increases in cost of production, and other factors which result from agricultural hazards.

The normal legal minimum prices will be adjusted by the percentage of 1951 processing crop loss from the ten year (1940-49) average crop as reported by the U. S. Department of Agriculture for each of the producing states. 7135 GPO-OOPS 49

Washington MAHOGANY IMPORTERS TAC Cole-OPS-GPR-680 (Revised) 

The Mahogany Industry Advisory Committee today recommended to the Office of Price Stabilization that their industry be excluded from the provisions of the interim import regulation now being prepared by the Lumber Division. They also recommended that the industry operate under the General Ceiling Price Regulation until further study of the industry's operating problems. 

Several members of the committee urged complete decontrol for the industry. 

The proposed interim regulation is based essentially on landed costs plus a percentage or a dollar-and-cents markup.

Committee members insisted that it was impossible to make any determination of landed costs as they have no knowledge of costs until the entire contract is completed. Furthermore, they said, such costs depend on too many unpredictable factors including fluctuations of the market and steamship charters. 

In further substantiation of their contention that it is impossilbe to estimate landed costs, they pointed out that all inventories are lumped together by grade and thickness regardless of cost, that contracts are made and lumber sold months before any logs are seen, and that the log season is very short and weather and deterioration must be considered.

In the true or genuine mahogany industry, it was pointed out, the price is determined by market selectivity largely depending upon the end use of the material and the degree of quality required in the finished product. From 10 to 40 per cent of the import volume of the firms represented by committee members is lumber, while the rest is logs. The history of the industry is based on competitive prices which tends to prevent any runaway prices. At present, the market is soft with competition stiff. (over) The meeting was conducted by Norman 0. Cruver, chief of the Lumber and 

Wood Products Branch, and James Owens, head of the Hardwood Plywood and Veneer 

Section. 

Other OPS officials attending were John R. Riggleman, economist; Stanley

Levy and Dante Galotta, counsel; and Walter R. Moulton, Office of the Advisory Committee. 7157 1 GPO-O-OPS 55

  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers MONDAY, July 16, 1951 Re: COMMUNITY PRICING SURVEY 

To lay the basis for a program of posted dollar-and-cent "community prices" in the nation's grocery stores, the Office of Price Stabilization shortly will begin a country-wide survey of wholesale and retail grocery costs and prices, OPS Director Michael V. DiSalle said today.

During the course of the survey expected to last several weeks teams from OPS 84 District Offices will reguarly visit about 2,000 retail food stores and about 1,000 wholesale establishments, gathering information on what grocers pay for foods, and what they sell them for.

Hughes-OPS-GPR-681  

Sample community price ceilings will be computed, for comparison with ceilings established under existing regulations, and with actual selling prices. 

Information gathered from individual sellers will be held in strict confidence. 

The first survey of wholesalers will begin on Monday, July 30. The retail survey will get under way on Thursday August 2. At the outset, establishments will be visited every other week. This may be stepped up to every week if experience indicates a need for more frequent sampling.

A chief purpose of the survey will be to discover whether there is sufficient stability in the prices of a number of standard grocery items to make a "community pricing" program possible. "Community pricing, "Mr. DiSalle explained, "is a system, familiar in World

War II days, under which the country is divided into relatively small 'market areas, and grocery price ceilings are established for each area on the basis of local transportation and other cost factors. These ceilings which are the same in an area for all stores of the same class - are then printed on charts for posting in retail stores where all customers may see them." 

"The community pricing program, "Mr. DiSalle added, "was considered by many to be the most successful, the most important, and the most effective of all OPA programs during World War II. That program made available exact dollar-and-cent ceilings both to consumers and food retailers in the form of price lists which each retailer was required to post. The program had a lot to do in holding the line on wholesale and retail food prices from the time it was started in May 1943 to the end of the price control program. 11 OPS is fully aware, Mr. DiSalle said, of the important part that a community pricing program can play in the stabilization program, of the necessity for having published ceilings for consumers, and of the great help such a program can be to individual grocers in simplifying their pricing problems. 1 GPO-O-OPS 54 7156 (over)

- Thus far, since the agency is prohibited by law from controlling below-parity farm prices, it has not had sufficient assurance that prices have been stable enough to make the printing and posting of ceiling charts practicable. "The process of preparing and printing a chart," Mr. DiSalle said, "take a certain minimum amount of time. Obviously you can't do it sucessfully if prices change so rapidly that a chart is out of date almost from the moment it goes up in the stores. You've got to be sure of a reasonable degree of price stability before you can start. Therefore, before inaugurating a nation-wide program as important as community food pricing, it is necessary that we obtain the specific information about food prices needed to assure the program's success." 

In addition to determining the relative stability of prices of food items subject to change because of parity provisions, the survey will have two further advantages: (1) It will permit a comparison of actual selling prices with ceiling prices as now established under Ceiling Price Regulations 14, 15, and 16 the grocery regulations which provide fixed percentage markups for wholesalers and for small and large retail grocery stores. (2) The process of gathering the needed information will prepare and train the OPS staff which will be responsible for operation of the community food pricing program when such a program actually gets under way. 

In the experimental survey, OPS field staff members will sample prices of at least one grocery item in each of the 36 categories of food listed in CPR 14, 15, and 16. To add to the value of the survey, selected district offices will sample about 130 items, while others will survey only about 36 items. All information gathered will be sent to Washington for tabulation and analysis. TH In preparation for the survey, and in order to assure its success, two members of the Washington OPS staff who were prominent in the war-time community pricing program are visiting each of the 13 OPS regional offices to meet with district office staff members assembled to receive training in the program. The two officials are Julius Davidson, head of the Community Pricing Section in the OPS Food and Restaurant Division, and his associate, W. H. Zimmerman. 41

Thursday, July 12, 1951

Re: POLYVINYL CHLORIDE RESIN IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-684  

Members of the Polyvinyl Chloride Resin Industry Advisory Committee today discussed proposals for a tailored regulation for their industry with OPS officials but withheld recommendations on the type of regulation they prefer pending further deliberation and decision of Congress on control legislation for the coming year.

The industry, which manufactures the resins used a great variety of plastic products-- including table cloths, shower curtains, wire insulation, raincoats, shoes, phonograph records, upholstery materials and beer can linings--is now pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR. 

Committeemen said they were experiencing no hardship under GCPR because the price of their products had been fairly steady and adjustments had ' been made before the price freeze.

Committeemen indicated the industry would experience some rollbacks and some roll forwards under the provisions of the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. Their industry is subject to the latter regulation, but manufacturers had not instituted CPR 22 prices prior to 

June 30, when its effectiveness was suspended by Congressional action.

Committeemen said their industry customarily sold at substantially uniform prices and the effect of CPR 22 would be to disturb this uniformity, which would not be welcome.

Members discussed the possiblity of adopting an industry-wide cost adjustment factor under the provisions of SR 2 to CPR 22, which would give them a uniform percentage adjustment of their GCPR prices. It was estimated the effect of this would be to give the entire industry prices at or close to the present levels.

Committeemen decided they wanted to study the application of this device and the type of information they would have to supply OPS to develop such a factor, and weigh their conclusions against the details of the expected extension of price control by Congress, before reaching a final decision. 7197 The committee recommended that their industry be defined by OPS as including polyvinyl chloride and all polyvinyl chloride copolymer resins having essentially the same use, the copolymers containing 50 per cent or more by weight of polyvinyl chloride, sold in the forms of resins and latices and compounded products in powder or granular states, but not including other forms such as film, sheets, rods and tubes. GPO-O-OPS 61

Strasser, acting assistant director of the Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division.  T. H. McCormack, director of the division; Alfred T. Loeffler, chief, Chemicals and Drugs Branch; John F. Corwin, chief, Plastics, Resins and Adhesives section; Walter L. Bossart, business specialist; Theresa

Re: LEVENTHAL LETTER TO PURCHASING AGENTS 

A reminder that trade buyers unlike domestic consumers, are subject to sanctions under the Defense Production Act of 1950 unless acting in good faith, was contained in a letter of Harold Leventhal, Chief Counsel of the Office of Price Stabilization, published in today's issue of the Bulletin of the National Association of Purchasing 

Agents. 

"The Act, wrote Mr. Leventhal, "is specifically made applicable, in terms of prohibitions, to any person who purchases, in the course of trade or business, in violation of the regulations. The buyer is not subject to the treble damage provisions, but he is subject to the other sanctions of the act, from injunction suits to criminal prosecution in cases of wilful violations." 11 

This provision of the National Defense Production Act, Mr. Leventhal continued, recognizes that in certain situations the buyer, as much as or even more than the seller, may encourage an illegal transaction, especially on commodities in short supply where he feels that "price is no object. 

The ultimate test, Mr. Leventhal wrote, is essentially the "good faith" of the buyer, since frequently there are circumstances under which he cannot know all the facts regarding the legality of a sellers' price. He pointed out, for example, that ceilings under the general manufacturers' order (CPR 22) are "based upon the materials and labor costs of the manufacturer, which in many, or perhaps most, situations would be beyond the knowledge of the buyer or the purchasing agent." 

Mr. Leventhal warned, however, that a buyer cannot hope to obtain immunity "by simply shutting his eyes to the transaction." If a buyer suspects a violation may be involved, Mr. Leventhal offered this advice: "If he has any reason to believe a violation exists, he can ask for a clarification from the seller. Or if he wishes to avoid that approach, possibly because of an indication that supplies might be withheld in retaliation, he can address his inquiries to the Office of Price Stabilization. The name and identification of any person making such an inquiry will be withheld....

IT 7361 GPO-O-OPS 91

As for certificates of compliance, Mr. Leventhal recalled that when he was 

Assistant General Counsel of the Office of Price Administration in 1942 he wrote the association that they might provide "some evidence of good faith on the part of the buyer. But Mr. Leventhal emphasized that what he had in mind was a certificate referring to a particular regulation, not just a rubber stamp saying, "All prices are in accordance with applicable OPA regulations." Such a general statement, Mr. Leventhal contended, "does not really add anything to the invoice itself." 11 11 While a certificate of compliance referring to a particular regulation would represent some evidence of good faith, Mr. Leventhal warned that any such certificate would not outweight any other facts pointing to a violation. 

Mr. Leventhal's letter, addressed to George A. Renard, executive secretarytreasurer of the National Association of Purchasing Agents, summarized a speech he made before the association on June 6.

THOMAS B. WORSLEY Coakley-OPS-GPR-693 

Thomas B. Worsley has been appointed Defense Goods Price Coordinator for the Office of Price Stabilization, Edward F. Phelps, Jr., Assistant Director for 

Price Stabilization, announced today.

Mr. Worsley will be responsible for the development, coordination and clearance of policies and actions relating to the purchases and sales of goods and services by or for government agencies, and for liaison with such agencies. 

Before coming to OPS, Mr. Worsley had served with the Munitions Board, Department of Defense, since March, 1950. His last assignment there was as Chief of the Price Control and Market Analysis Division, Office of Procurement. Earlier, he was attached to the Economic Management Office of the National Security Resources Board and served for some time as Chief of the China Economic Section, Office of International Trade, Department of Commerce. 

He was business economist in the Textile, Leather and Apparel Branch of the Office of Price Administration during 1941-1942 and then entered military service. He was attached to the Army Quartermaster Corps and Air Forces and to the Industrial College of the Armed Forces as an instructor in economic mobilization. Mr. Worsley has taught economics at the University of Georgia and the University of Richmond. At present he is a part-time instructor in Money and 

Banking and International Economics at Georgetown University School of Foreign Service. 

A native of Columbus, Ga., Mr. Worsley, 39, attended the 

University of Virginia, receiving a B. S. Degree and an M. S. and Ph. D. Degree in Economics. He held a fellowship at Brookings Institutions in 1940-1941. 

Mr. Worsley is the author of "Wartime Economic Stabilization and the Efficiency of Government Procurement" and of various magazine articles. Married, and the father of one child, he makes his home in Alexandria, Va. 7382 GPO-O-OPS 89

Re: AGRICULTURAL LIMING MATERIALS IAC Moore-OPS-GPR-694 ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 Members of the Agricultural Liming Materials Industry Advisory Committee today told OPS officials their industry was in need of price relief and discussed the information which might be supplied to OPS to justify increased ceiling prices.

Committeemen reported their product has experienced little change in price over many years. Their prices are now frozen under the General Ceiling Price 

Regulation, GCPR. They said prices have been held down by various influences. 

These include the fact that much agricultural limestone is a by-product in the production of crushed stone, competition in the industry for government contracts, and regulation by local committees under the Department of Agriculture 

Production and Marketing Administration agricultural conservation program. 

Committeemen indicated the industry would experience difficulty in making an adequate showing of the need of relief because some manufacturers were multiple product producers whose division of costs between crushed and agricultural limestone would be arbitrary, and others were local operators with inadequate cost figures. 

Members stressed the need for relief on the cost of hauling and spreading agricultural limestone. This need existed alike for the producer who distributes and for the contract truckers who are also under GCPR, with no present means of getting relief for increased cost of fuel, tires and labor. 

About 10 per cent of the approximately 200,000,000 tons of limestone produced annually in the country is agricultural limestone in finely powdered form. The balance is used in the metalurgical, chemical, construction and other industries, mostly in the form or crushed stone. 

Under the agricultural conservation program, the PMA shares with the farmer in defraying part of the cost of about 90 per cent of agricultural limestone under three plans. In some instances the farmer buys directly and obtains part of the cost later from the government. In other instances the Department lets long-term supply contracts directly to producers. Under the third method in which the Department participates, local county agricultural committees issue purchase orders to farmers at prescribed prices to be obtained from eligible dealers. 

Committeemen urged the need for prompt action to provide their industry a practical means of pricing for the coming year, since the Department of Agriculture normally negotiates contracts at this time of year for the Northeast 

States.

The following letter regarding the "guaranteed profit" amendment to the

Defense Production Act and describing its affects on the stabilization program, has been sent by Michael V. DiSalle, Director of the Office of Price 

Stabilization, to Congressman Brent Spence, Chairman of the House Banking and Currency Committee. 

(over) McClanahan-OPS-GPR-700 2 

Dear Chairman Spence: 

[I have noted with some concern the action of the House yesterday in agreeing to an Amendment to the Defense Production Act introduced by Representative Poage of Texas, which is in effect a "cost-plusguaranteed profit-on every item" Amendment. I am taking the liberty here of setting out to you my views and certain facts with regard to the detrimental effect of this Amendment if it is finally adopted. Ticha 

DASATER 

logo fas It is my considered opinion that the effect of this Amendment would be to destroy the entire price-control program. Its inflationary effect on consumers is far worse than the proposed prohibition against side rollbacks which the House defeated Tuesday. A prohibition against rollbacks, costly as it might be, would still not prevent holding the price line although at a much higher level. This Amendment would open the door wide to increases costing the consumers billions of dollars. 

It would make necessary an immediate and substantial increase in ceiling prices for practically all food items. At the same time the Amendment would unnecessarily guarantee for manufacturers and processors excess profits substantially higher than the highest earnings ever record- o ed by American industry. And since it would require that food prices be based upon parity even when lower prices are actually paid by processors, it would mean an unjustifiable windfall to such processors at the expense of consumers and farmers. 17 Under the Amendment administration of price control would be practically impossible. There are not enough accountants in the world to do the accounting work required by the Amendment to determine costs and allocate profits on each and every single item produced in an industry. 

The net result would be to bury the entire price-control program in an impossible administrative morass and to place the government stamp of approval on an immediate inflationary spiral. 7525 COLE 2000 GPO-O-OPS 118

This Amendment guarantees every manufacturer and processor his cost, plus a profit on every single item sold. The profit allowed for pricing every single item must at least meet the excess profits tax level. Since it is impossible to fix every single price at this minimum, the Amendment in effect guarantees excess profits to every manufacturer and processor. 

Costs for food processors must be computed on the basis of actual costs or the parity price for the agricultural commodity, whichever is higher. 

For a commodity below parity the processor could compute the parity price as his cost no matter how much lower his actual cost might be. 

Industry never made a profit on every item. It is frequently impossible to allocate all costs. But even where it is possible, industry expects to take "losses" on some items, and almost any multiproduct company will freely admit that it never makes a profit on every item. To give a profit on every single item at the same time would establish a condition which industry never was able to reach in a competitive market. Companies already making the highest profits in their history could still get price increases on many of their items--price increases which are entirely unnecessary and unjustified. 

There are many reasons why a company may be willing to make and sell an item without profit or even at a loss. Here are some such reasons: 

1. Taken by itself, an item may bring a loss but it still contributes something to covering total cost of a company's operation. 

2. An item may bring a loss at one time but a profit at another time. 

3. A loss item may help by attracting and keeping customers for profitable items. 

4. A loss item may contribute to a company's prestige. 5. 

Business in a loss item may be built up over the years to the point where a profit will result or the company at least so hopes. 

This Amendment would permit industry to use the present national emergency to assure themselves profits in every such case. The Amendment would create administrative chaos. It sets up requirements that are completely impractical and utterly impossible of effective administration. In the first place, very few processors and manufacturers have adequate cost data. 7525 (over)

The OPA Accounting Department made an extensive survey of cost accounting systems industry by industry, which was published in 1946. 

It found that only 15 percent of the companies could determine total cost for individual items. These 15 percent accounted for no more than 25 percent of total production. Here is a sample of the results: 

Meat - Less than 1% of the companies have adequate cost records. 

Breakfast Cereals About 20% of the companies have cost system... and 25% of these can determine total cost. 

Canned and Frozen Fruits and Vegetables About 2% of the companies have cost system.

Shoes Cigars 

Less than 5% of the companies have cost systems. 

Lumber About 10% of the companies have cost systems determine costs by grade or species.

Bedding cost system.

And they would immediately encounter insoluble problems. 7525 euft fash 1 V♡

DA AEQ-907 Here are some examples of the difficulties incurred in attempting to comply with the Amendment: 

1) A single Douglas Fir log is sawed up into lumber of hundreds of sizes and grades. Each of these is a separate item for which someone must compute total cost and profit not only now but in each of the years 1946 1949. No one has ever done this, and any accountant will tell you that it is impossible. 

2) Each size and thickness and color and grade of paper is a separate item. Many hundreds of them come out of a single "mix" of paper, made perhaps from pulp-wood cut from the firm's own forest lands. 

What is the cost, and what the reasonable profit for each of these items? 

What is the value of the pulp-wood, and how much of this value is the cost of a particular size of envelope? 

3) Thousands of chemicals, dyes, drugs, fertilizer materials come from a single batch of coal tar. How can we compute for each "all costs currently incurred in the processing or manufacturing operation and distribution" of every item including allowances for indirect costs; and what is "for each unit of such item" a profit "not less than 85% of the average profit earned on an equivalent unit of such item during the three most profitable years of the period 1946 1949"? 

4) When a steer is slaughtered, the products included various cuts of beef, the hide, various meat by-products, glue, fertilizer, dog food, cleansers, and hundreds of other items. If it were ever possible to allocate the costs and accountants could argue indefinitely how it would be found that a great many of them were produced at a loss in any period, no matter how profitable the packer's operations might be. (over) 

Any attempt to apply the Amendment would immediately plunge industry and the OPS into a maze of legal and accounting controversy. Clever lawyers and accountants could argue for the next five years what the correct price should be. Any firm accused of a violation could always protest that the price on that item did not cover all costs plus a profit, and the courts would be swamped trying to find out if it did or did not. 

It is extremely significant that permanent regulatory agencies setting maximum rates for railroads and utilities have never tried to set prices on individual services to cover cost plus a profit on every item. Despite the fact that they have had years to perfect their techniques, and that they deal with a relative handful of companies, they look only at over-all earnings. The I. C. C. may separate passenger and freight revenues and costs, but they do not try to set rates that will give the railroads a profit on bananas and watches and iron ore and salt. 7525

sons R Consider the problem that the CAB has had trying to decide the cost [ando 

BERG VID 

of carrying airmail.

Jwow Administrative breakdown could be avoided only by loose pricing. In the face of this fantastic administrative situation, the OPS would have to do one or the other of two things:

A. 

It would be compelled to grant virtually every increase that any industry requested. It could never possibly check the correctness of the industry's claims. 2 B. Or it would have to set up some automatic formula for self-pricing by each manufacturer. Under such a system no real enforcement would be possible because neither the buyer nor the OPS could know or check the calculations that lay behind the price.

Further, OPS would have to allow a continuous upward escalation of all prices to reflect any and every increase in cost. These price increases would constitute cost increases for other sellers, and the inflationary spiral would resume its upward climb. Wages would of course rise, too, and be the source of still further upward pressure on prices. 

Congress has banned the use of cost-plus contracts for military procurement, but this amendment would force OPS to allow it for all manufacturers and processors selling to civilian buyers. (over) 931 Processors of farm products would get an unjustifiable windfall. 

For products made from agricultural commodities, this Amendment requires ceilings to be based on parity whenever the actual price is lower. This is supposed to be necessary in order to permit the agricultural products to come up to parity. In reality, the system now used by OPS places no hindrance in the way of any rise in agricultural products now below parity. 

As agricultural prices go up, processors and distributors may automatically adjust prices of products made from them. They need not wait for any OPS approval. 

In contrast, the Amendment would allow processors to raise their own prices without paying more to the farmers. For example wheat is selling for $2.08 a bushel. The parity price in $2.42. Under the Amendment the ceiling on flour would have to be high enough to include wheat figured at $2.42 plus all other costs plus a profit to meet the excess profits tax base.

This would add about half a cent to the price of each loaf of bread. 

IBNU 

7525

For some other foods, there are much larger differences between the prices actually paid by processors and the parity prices which this Amendment would recognize as their cost. For instance, farmers lately have been receiving 53 for a box of grapefruit and $1.53 for a box of oranges. This

Amendment would let processors continue paying these prices but charging parity as cost $2.02 for a box of grapefruit and $3.71 for a box of oranges. These fictitious "costs" are respectively 287% and 142% larger than the actual costs. 

These differentials would not benefit the farmers but would merely allow a tremendous windfall to processors. 

This parity provision also means, for example, that ceilings for canned food items must be increased every month even though the canner bought his pack at the beginning of the season and has no increases. 

No food price control could be effective on such a basis, and, without effective food price control, wage controls cannot be maintained. 

This Amendment goes farther than any requirement ever previously in the law. The Amendment has been called the same as the "Brown-Bankhead Amendment".

In reality, it is no such thing. The Brown-Bankhead Amendment of 1944 merely required calculation a) for a single industry (cotton textiles) b) by major items not for every item 

c) of prices allowing a reasonable profit - without setting a specific formula for both costs and profits. 2. 

This Amendment really is like the Taft Amendment that was defeated in 1945, was enacted in modified and much milder form in 1946 and then led to the veto by the President.

This Amendment also goes much further and is much more difficult to comply with than the Cole Amendment which was designed to give special advantage to livestock processors. Mr. Cole was careful to point out that the livestock Amendment requires profits on every species but not on every item. 

The purposes of the Amendment appear reasonable. 

They are said to be: 

1. To assure that industry gets reasonable profits, and

To assure that ceilings set for processors do not prevent farm prices from rising to parity. (over) 7525

All of us agree with these aims. That is why this Amendment seems so innocent, and yet why, in its subtle phrasing, it is so dangerous. 

OPS approves of reasonable profits. Its "industry earnings standard" guarantees to every industry that its earnings shall not fall below 85% of its earnings in the best three years of 1946 1949. Over and above this OPS will insure that no major item is produced at a loss, and that no single firm, no matter how highcost a producer it may be, will be forced out of business by its ceiling prices. 

But this Amendment goes way beyond that fair standard. It is like the difference between providing enough taxicabs to carry all the traffic and providing a separate taxi for every person who ever uses one. If everyone who wants a cab can get one when he needs it, there are enough cabs. If an industry is getting handsome over-all earnings, prices are high enough.

The OPS price regulations for processors of agricultural products automatically permit every rise in the price of farm products below parity to be added to the processor's ceiling. Thus processor ceilings can never stand in the way of farm products reaching parity. Thus one object of this Amendment is already attained. 

As pointed out above, it would ignore what the processor actually pays the farmer, but would base the ceiling for the processed product on a fictitious cost, which might be far in excess of what he pays and so penalize the consumer with no benefit to the producer. 

I will appreciate your consideration of the matters set out above. 

With kindest personal regards, I am 

Very truly yours,

Michael V. DiSalle

PRESS RELEASE 

11 

  

 10 

 Re: SODIUM SILICOF LUORIDE IAC 

Moore -OPS-GPR-701 Sufficient production of sodium silicofluoride to supply the mushrooming demand of municipalities for chemicals required for the fluoridation of public drinking water can be brought out by modest upward price adjustments, chemical manufacturers indicated today.

ST 4200; Ext. 3491 ols 

Members of the Sodium Silicofluoride Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting with OPS officials reported their product had experienced repeated substantial price fluctuations in the past and price increases invariably served to stimulate additional production sufficiently to bring prices down again. 

Committeemen explained that a certain volume of sodium silicofluoride was available on a low cost basis as a joint or by-product of processes producing other chemicals. Greater volumes of sodium silicofluoride can be obtained by diverting the components from other end products or by employment of additional facilities. Additional volumes of production become economic at various stages in the price level. (over) Committee men estimated production for 1950 at 11,000 or 12,000 tons and for 1951 if the current rate is maintained at around 18,000 tons. Most of the current production is for industrial purposes and used in connection with the manufacture of laundry sours, ceramics, glass, aluminum, insecticides and rubber.

The pur- Public health officials estimated 50,000 tons a year would be required to fluoridate the nation's drinking water. They said about 90 communities now fluoridate their water and many others, including a number of larger cities, desire to do so once their source of supply of the chemical is assured. pose of fluoridation of drinking water is to reduce dental caries among the users, especially children. 7553 GPO-O-OPS 113

They estimated the new demand of municipalities would require an additional 

10,000 tons this year.

Committeemen reported ceiling prices under the General Ceiling Price Regulation ranged from 5 to 8. 6 cents per pound. They said upward adjustment of ceilings would bring out increasing volume, and pointed out that every manufacturer of superphosphate fertilizers was a potential producer of sodium silicofluoride. 

They said it was difficult to forecast precisely the volume that would result from any particular price, but one member expressed belief that a price between 6 and 7 cents would probably produce most of the anticipated increased requirements for this year. It was pointed out that if prices were raised across the board to bring out the required additional volume, which would require relaxation of existing ceilings, it would impose a hardship on certain existing users. Whether an equitable system of pricing could be developed at two levels, one to cover present production and the other applicable to additional production, was discussed without conclusion. 

Committeement rejected the suggestion that the premium price be paid only for new or additional production, or borne solely by new users. 

The possibility of substitution of other chemicals for sodium silicofluoride by some of the present users was also explored. 

Members indicated that application of the Manufacturers' General Ceiling 

Price Regulation, CPR 22, would roll back some manufacturers from GCPR ceilings. OPS officials indicated the industry would be removed from control 

GPR 22 and left under GCPR pending the writing of a special regulation. 

Today's meeting was conducted by George W. Strasser, acting assistant director of the Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division. 

T. H. McCormack, division director; Hugo E. Weisberger, Division economist;

PRESS RELEASE    

Re: PRESSED STAMPINGS IAC 

An industry advisory committee representing pressed stampings manufacturers discussed a new ceiling price regulation for their products with OPS officials today.

Committee members favored a formula-pricing regulation on the order of the old OPA MPR 136 which took into account the job shop nature of the industry and permitted trial runs to determine actual prices on customers' specifications. 

Pressed stampings would come under CPR 30, the OPS machinery order, pending a specifically designed order.

Industry representative also expressed the view that consideration in relating prices to costs be given to increased use of warehouse, premium, and conversion steel as a result of shortage of mill steel, to modified products, and to wage advances granted since March 15 not recognized under the CPR 30 

formula. 

The industry makes steel, aluminum, brass, and plastic stampings for many purposes, including such things as automobile fenders, hub caps, and dash boards, round-cut washers and washing machine and vacuum cleaner parts.

Huff-OPS-GPR-702  

Today's meeting was conducted by E. L. Norman, head of the cutting tool and industrial supply section of the OPS Machinery Branch. Other OPS representatives were L. J. Carson, branch chief, E. L. Inwood, economist, George Brody, attorney, J. J. McCullough, business analyst, and Harry Spack, Office for Advisory Committees.

Appointment of Rodney L. Perkins as Chief of Military Goods and Government Agency Coordination in the Legal Review and Administration Division of the Office of the Chief Counsel, Office of Price Stabilization, was confirmed today by 

Harold Leventhal, Chief Counsel. 

Mr. Perkins was an attorney with the Pepsi Cola Co., New York City, from 

1944 to 1951. He handled matters pertaining to price controls, priorities and manpower until 1946 and later was assigned to labor relations; contract, corporate organization, franchise and export problems; real estate tax questions and antitrust matters. He also was an attorney with Blaw-Knox Co., Martins Ferry, O., during 1943-1944, handling liaison with the Bureau of Ordnance, Navy Department, as well as problems of price controls, priorities, manpower and labor relations. 

A native of Wheeling, W. Va., Mr. Perkins, 33, attended Ohio University where he received, in 1939, an A. B. Degree, with a major in economics. He received his LL. B. Degree in 1942 from the University of Cincinnati and took a post graduate law course at New York University in 1947. He is a member of the New York 

Bar and the Ohio Bar. # # # # # # # # # Mr. Perkins, who formerly lived in Valley Stream, N. Y., now makes his home at 1644 Crittendon St., N. E., Washington. 7558 GPO-O-OPS 116

PRESS RELEASE   

 AUTO ENFORCEMENT CASE 

In the nation-wide OPS drive to prevent over ceiling prices, under the table payments and falsification of records in the sale of new and used automobiles, the first criminal proceedings in the New York region were filed today against a Manhattan used car dealer by U.S. Attorney Irving S. Saypol in the U.S. District Court, Southern New York District. 

Cole-OPS-GPR-704 

The information is based on the investigation of OPS District Enforcement Director Sol A. Liebman and his staff. It alleges that the GMT Motors Inc. 

1749 First Avenue, New York City, and its secretary-treasurer, Richard Gould, violated the ceiling price regulations in both the purchase and sale of a 1951 automobile at over ceiling prices and further failed to keep proper records as required by OPS regulations. 

Director Liebman stated that "the defendants were caught red-handed by our agents," and that they would be notified of the court action and ordered to appear for arraignment in Federal Court on July 25. If found guilty of the charges, he said, they face possible maximum penalties of a $10,000 fine and one year in jail.

The automobile involved in the case was purchased by the defendant firm, the government alleges, for $2,046 and resold for $2,150, both being over ceiling prices. The resale price, according to the government, includes the sum of $1,975 as indicated by the invoice, and a cash payment to the defendant firm of $175. The ceiling price for this car, according to OPS, is $1,951. 

Cooperating on the case, according to Mr. Liebman, were Samuel S. Burman, Assistant U. S. Attorney; Samuel Reis, attorney from the Department of Justice in Washington; John T. Clancy, special assistant to the U. S. Attorney at the 

District OPS; and Seymour Chotiner, chief, Machinery and Industrial Materials

Enforcement Section, New York District OPS. 

Meanwhile, Edward P. Morgan, assistant OPS director in charge of enforcement, said today that the GMT case is only one of many cases involving new and used car dealers in widely separated sections of the country who face prosecution for ceiling price violations and falsification or records. "There is no excuse for such violations," Mr. Morgan stated. "The OPS regulations are clear, and understood by all of the dealers. The Office of 

Price Stabilization is not going to sit idly by and watch such violations without taking positive action. 11 (over) 7561 GPO-O-OPS 111

G 

The case of the Central Motor Sales of Louisville, Kentucky, arising from two over ceiling transactions and falsification of records, will be returnable in the United States District Court, Western Kentucky District, in Louisville, the first week in October.

Information in this case has been filed in Louisville, naming Donald G. and John T. Ford as partners of the firm, and Guffye W. Fentress, salesman for the firm. Violation of Supplemental Regulation 5 of the General Price Ceiling 

Regulation is charged.

Also under investigation according to Mr. Morgan, are numerous new and used car dealers in Texas and Louisiana who are charged with over ceiling transactions. 

This situation affects many dealers whose pricing of cars does not comply with Supplemental Regulation 5. Several cases have already been referred to the Department of Justice in Washington. One of the cases also involves falsification of records. * Prosecution is to be sought in other cases arising from complaints from people residing in rural areas in several states, Mr. Morgan said. They allege they have been forced to pay over ceiling prices for used cars of pre-World War II vintage, despite the 'soft' market in used cars in other sections of the country.

Re: 

MCDONALD-VAN NOPPEN Coakley-OPS-GPR-705  Appointment of Sterling B. McDonald as chief of the Furniture Section, Home Furnishings Branch of the Durable Goods Division, was announced today by Harold B. Wess, Director of the Consumer Goods Division of the Office of Price Stabilization. 

Mr. McDonald replaces Donnell Van Noppen who has resigned to return to his position as vice president of Henredon Furniture Industries, Morganton,

N. C. He came to OPS on limited leave from his firm in mid-February and helped set up the Furniture Section which he headed. 

Mr. McDonald had served as technical consultant for Kroehler Mfg. Co., Naperville, Ill., furniture company, since 1938 and had operated his own engineering and consulting business since 1933. Earlier, he was associated with Karpen Bros. and Marshall Field and Co. He was employed in the field of architecture and engineering prior to World War I. 

He studied at Cotner University, Lincoln, Neb. and has had specialized courses at the Chicago Art Institute and Armour Institute, Chicago. He is author of two text books, "Color Harmony" and "Color, How to Use It", published by Wilcox and Follett.

Mr. McDonald holds several patents and was design coordinator for the first streamline trains for the Union Pacific and Santa Fe Railroads. He designed the interiors for the American Airlines DC-2 and DC-3 flagships and his designing and departmentalizing of furniture stores is well known throughout the country.

Born in Alvo, Neb., Mr. McDonald is 58. He is married and makes his home in Napersville. # # # # # # # 7563 GPO-O-OPS 112

FEATHER AND DOWN IAC Members of the Feather and Down Industry Advisory Committee today recommended to the Office of Price Stabilization that the ceiling price regulation proposed for their industry include a specific provision for equitable adjustment of outstanding forward contracts for sale of new processed waterfowl feathers and down to government agencies. 

Barkley-OPS-GPR-706 ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 

Processed waterfowl feathers and down such as duck and goose feathers and down are under a freeze issued by the National Production. 

Administration which restricts their sale to the filling of government stockpiling and defense orders.

In view of this, the committee was of the opinion that the pricing regulation should make provision for adjustments in forward contracts held by segments of the industry for future purchase of feathers and down for delivery to the government. 

George W. Gartz, Vice Pres. 

Burton-Dixie Corp. 

27 New Jersey R.R. Ave. 

Newark 5, New Jersey

It was explained that some contract holders may have commitments to buy, for delivery to the government, at prices which may be higher than the ceiling prices which may be adopted. They said the regulation should provide a sufficient lapse of time to liquidate these contracts. 

It was the committee's second meeting with OPS officials. The first was held April 19, 1951. The committee recommended that a third meeting be called in about a month.

Price Stabilization, today notified members of the Retail Industry Advisory Committee that the meeting of the committee scheduled to be held in Washington on July 24, has been postponed. 

At the same time Mr. Wess advised members of the Permanent Subcommittee and the Subcommittee of Small Merchants that the meetings of these two subcommittees scheduled to be held in Washington on July 23, have also been postponed.

Postponement of these meetings is deemed necessary and desirable because of the uncertainties as to the provisions of the forthcoming price control law now being debated by the Congress, Mr. Wess said. It is expected these important meetings can be rescheduled within next two or three weeks and definite dates will be announced later. 

The 36 member Retail Industry Advisory Committee held its first meeting in Washington on June 19. As a result of that meeting, a 7 member Permanent 

Subcommittee was appointed to advise with OPS on over-all retail pricing problems to be considered by and brought to the attention of the whole committee. At the same time, a 7 member Small Merchants Subcommittee was appointed to study the problems of small retailers under price control.

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers MONDAY, July 23, 1951  Re: HUTSON MEHREN 

Director Michael V. DiSalle of the Office of Price Stabilization, yesterday announced the resignation of J. B.

Hutson as director of the agency's Food and 

Restaurant Division. 

Barkley-OPS-GPR-710  

Mr. DiSalle designated George L. Mehren, who has been an assistant director since early in April, to be acting director, pending the appointment of a director. 

Arval L. Erikson will continue as assistant director with supervision of the 

Meat Branch and several other branches of the Division. 

Mr. Hutson, who has been on leave from the presidency of Tobacco Associates, Inc., to head the OPS Food Division, has returned to that association to fulfill previous commitments. He will soon leave for Europe where he will be chairman of one of the committees at the World Tobacco Congress in Amsterdam, Holland, September 17 to 24.

During World War II, Mr. Hutson was president of the Commodity Credit Corporation and Director of Food Production. He was Under Secretary of Agriculture from July 1945 to March 1946. He makes his home in Washington. 

Mr. Mehren, whose home is in Berkeley, Calif., is a widely recognized authority in agricultural marketing and price research work. Before joining OPS, he had been associated with the Giannini Foundation for Agricultural Economics at Berkeley for 13 years.

He has conducted many research projects in such fields as wholesale marketing of produce, market control in various agricultural commodities, statistical demand and cost analyses for farm products and farm price support programs. 

During World War II, Mr. Mehren was Aide and Flag Lieutenant on cruisers and battleships in the Pacific fleet. 

Mr. Erikson has served as assistant director in charge of the OPS meat program for several months and is widely known in meat and agricultural circles. 

He came to OPS from the United Nations' Food and Agricultural Organization, where his most recent assignment was as Chief of the Livestock Products Branch. 

During World War II he was chief of the Office of Price Administration's Meat, Fats and Oils Branch. His home is in Falls Church, Va.

WAGE Moore-OPS-GPR-711 ST 4200; Ext. 3491 Aug AGRICULTURAL PESTICIDES, DDT AND BHC MANUFACTURERS IAC 

If manufacturers of DDT are obliged to roll back prices, it will tend to cut production by the diversion of their limited supplies of chlorine to other more profitable uses, members of the Agricultural Pesticides, DDT and BHC Manufacturers 

Industry Advisory Committee told OPS officials at their first meeting today.

Committeemen expressed the opinion that supplies of DDT would be tight for the next two years, but that there would be ample BHC (benzine hexachloride) for all needs including requirements for export. 

Committeemen said their industry was satisfied to continue pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR. A poll of the committee showed that of 

12 companies represented, eight would experience rollbacks and four roll forwards in their DDT ceilings under the provisions of the Manufacturers' General Ceiling 

Price Regulation, CPR 22. Four companies reported roll forwards and none rollbacks on BHC.

If and when CPR 22 becomes generally effective, dependent on the decision of Congress, the application of CPR 22 to manufacturers of DDT and BHC will still continue to be indefinitely postponed under the provisions of SR 12 to CPR 22.

Committeemen recommended that this postponement be continued at least until October 1, when the current season will be over, to avoid disturbing the existing price structure in line with the purposes of SR 12. Any reductions which might result from application of CPR 22 before that time would apply retroactively in practice to shipments for the entire season, committeemen said, and might force some smaller firms out of business. 

COO 

Committeemen were unwilling to make long-range recommendations for pricing the products of their industry, pending the outcome of the current debate in Congress on extension of price control and its effect on the provisions of CPR 22. 

It was suggested another committee meeting be called after Congress acts. Ist

Both insecticides are employed in dust and spray forms to protect cotton, coffee, peaches, forage and other products. DDT is produced in bigger volume and has a wider range of uses.

Both products are employed against flies and mosquitoes.

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers WEDNESDAY, July 25, 1951 Coakley-OPS-GPR-712  Re: KENNETH LAWTON 

Kenneth E. Lawton has been named special assistant to Edward F. Phelps, Jr., Assistant Director for Price Stabilization, OPS announced today.

Mr. Lawton has been with the Office of Price Stabilization since November, 1950. His early assignments were in the field of recruitment and general organization and more recently he served as Acting Jurisdictions Officer. As aide to 

Mr. Phelps, he will be particularly concerned with contacts with business representatives, business associations and similar groups. 

Before coming to OPS, Mr. Lawton had his own commercial financing business in Chicago. He has had wide experience in the field of banking and finance and as a management consultant to small business concerns. This has given him a close working relationship with sales, distribution and over-all operating policies in many industry fields. He formerly was general manager of the 

Phoenix-Commercial Corp., Washington; sales manager and director of Branch 

Operations, Union Investment Company, Detroit, and assistant regional manager, National Bond and Investment Co., Detroit.

He served with the Office of Price Administration, 1942 1947, where he first headed the Special Projects Section in charge of the new tire war stockpiling program. Later he was field officer of the Industrial Manufacturing Division and during the last three years was on the staff of the Deputy Administrator for Price.

Mr. Lawton, 45, was born in Marion, Indiana. He attended the University of Chicago, receiving a Ph. D Degree in Economics and Business Administration in 1924. He is a member of Phi Gamma Delta Fraternity. Married and the father of one child, Mr. Lawton makes his home in the Edgewater Beach Apartments, Chicago. # # # # # # # # # # # GPO-O-OPS 125

Saturday, July 21, 1951

Washington SAFEWAY ROLLBACK ON PORK 

Housewives in 23 states and the District of Columbia will save an average of two cents per pound on pork and pork products bought at Safeway Stores as the result of a voluntary rollback in prices today, Edward F. 

Morgan, assistant director in charge of enforcement, Office of Price 

Stabilization, announced tonight.

Cole-OPS-GPR-713 

Safeway Stores through J. A. Anderson, manager of the Washington

Division, notified the Richmond, Washington and Baltimore OPS district offices, under date of July 16, that they were raising retail ceiling prices on pork and pork products under Section 11 (c) of the General Ceiling Price Regulation, which allows a pass-through of increases in prices of listed agricultural commodities that are selling below legal minimum prices.

At a conference yesterday afternoon, OPS officials pointed out to Mr. Anderson that the Safeway firm had misinterpreted the regulation and that pork and pork products are not included under the heading of livestock listed in Section 11 (c). Mr. Anderson then announced the voluntary rollback of the increased prices that were in effect this week. 

The widely known chain operates nearly 2,000 retail food stores in 23 states and the District of Columbia. In the Washington area there are nearly 200 stores which sell more than 250,000 pounds of pork and pork products a week. Most of the Safeway stores are in the western part of the country, from Arkansas, Missouri and Iowa west. There are, however, more than 

200 stores in the New York and New Jersey area.

Mr. Morgan pointed out today that the action of the Safeway firm in voluntarily rolling back its price increases will mean savings of many thousands of dollars to consumers.

This action, Mr. Morgan added, represents a commendable attitude, a sense of business responsibility, and a high regard for the consumer, on the part of this organization. The Safeway firm yesterday filed a petition with OPS, asking that Section 11 (c) be amended by inserting the word 'hogs' under the general heading of 'livestock and livestock products'. If this petition is denied, the Safeway firm can take the case to the Emergency Court of Appeals, under the provisions of the Defense Production Act. 

Reasons given by the Safeway firm for increasing its ceiling prices on pork and pork products last Monday include a ten per cent increase in cost of labor and an increase of from two to seven cents per pound in the cost of pork loins. 1 GPO-O-OPS 127

PRESS RELEASE   ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers WEDNESDAY, July 25, 1951 Re: FRANKLIN L. ORTH 

Coakley-OPS-GPR-714 

Appointment of Franklin L. Orth as Chief of Field Operations in the Legal Review and Administration Division of the Office of the Chief Counsel, Office of Price Stabilization, was confirmed today by OPS Chief Counsel 

Harold Leventhal. 

Mr. Orth comes to OPS from the Veterans' Administration where he had been legal consultant on the staff of the Solicitor since 1946. During World War II he served as Colonel, Army of the United States, commanding an infantry combat team in Burma, and later served on the War Department General Staff. 

A native of Milwaukee, Mr. Orth, 44, was a partner in the law firm of 

Orth & Orth in Milwaukee from June, 1931 to December, 1940. He specialized in corporation, real estate and probate law. He has been admitted to practice in the U.S. Supreme Court and the Supreme Courts of the State of Wisconsin and the State of Illinois.

Mr. Orth is a graduate of the University of Wisconsin where he received an A.B. Degree in Economics and an LL.B. Degree. He resides in North Fork, Va.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers 

Thursday, July 26, 1951

 Barkley-OPS-GPR-715 ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 Re: CROP LOSS ALLOWANCE--PRUNES 

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today that the ceiling price regulation now being prepared for processed prunes will reflect an increase in grower's price for this item resulting from substantial crop losses in the producing areas.

The maximum raw material costs for prunes for canning and freezing in Washington, Oregon and Idaho which, if paid, may be reflected in ceiling prices will be $67 per ton, the agency said. 

These adjustments are made in accordance with the provisions of Section 402 (d)(3) of the Defense Production Act which requires that appropriate allowances shall be made in ceiling prices for processed agricultural commodities to reflect substantial reductions in merchantable crop yields, unusual increases in the cost of production and other hazards occurring in connection with the production and marketing of agricultural commodities. 

The normal legal minimum for prunes for canning and freezing was adjusted by the percentage of 1951 processing crop of the 10-year (1940-49) average crop as reported by the U. S. Department of Agriculture in the producing areas. # # # # # # # # OPS also announced that no adjustment in the ceiling price for Bartlett pears for canning and freezing is warranted at this time. According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture July Crop Report, Bartlett pear production is indicated as 93 percent of normal for the Washington-Oregon area. A 7 percent crop reduction, OPS said, would not be considered as substantially below normal. 7678 GPO-O-OPS 140
