PRESS RELEASE   

Monday, July 23, 1951

Tempo E- 

Washington Re: PHOSPHATE ROCK IAC Moore-OPS-GPR-717  Members of the Phosphate Rock Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials reported their industry was caught in a squeeze between long-term contracts under which their product is customarily sold and rising labor and fuel costs.

Phosphate rock is an important fertilizer source, and is sometimes ground and applied to soil directly. It is also acidulated with sulfuric acid to manufacture superphosphate fertilizer.

Sales customarily are on long term contracts of a year or more. 

Florida, Tennessee, Idaho, Montana and Wyoming are major producing states. 

The price of Florida phosphate rock determines the market, and the Florida contracts historically contain escalator clauses which permit adjustment in prices to reflect increases in the costs of fuel and labor. 

There has been an important increase in fuel costs since June 5, 1951 amounting to 82 cents per ton and a new round of wage negotiations in the Florida field, if recognized by the Wage Stabilization Board, will increase labor costs by 9¢ per ton. There is no way to adjust for these cost increases under the freeze provisions of the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR) 

which govern phosphate rock.

Committeemen stressed the need of prompt relief. They rejected the suggestion that this be accomplished with a formula embodying the principles of the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation (CPR 22) saying CPR 

22 would not produce adequate relief.

The committee urged that a tailored regulation be written that would allow contractual escalator clauses to operate. It was pointed out that the contracts for western state producers do not contain the escalator clauses. 

The suggestion was made that western producers be permitted to adjust their ceilings in proportion to the customary relationship to Florida prices. 

The committee agreed to reconvene in the middle of August. 7708-2800 GPO-O-OPS 143

The meeting was conducted by George W.

Strasser, acting assistant director of the Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division.  Hugo E. Weisberger, division economist; Alfred T. Loeffler, Chief, and Wilhelm Hirschkind, technical advisor; Chemicals and Drugs Branch;

Henry A. Huschke, newly named chief of the Agricultural Chemicals Section; 

Philip Travis and Joseph J. Strassman, counsels, Cedric Gran, consultant; 

Susan M. Phillips, economist, and W. R. Thomas, Jr., Office of Advisory

Committees. S. P. Wimpfen, Atomic Energy Commission, Division of Raw Materials, attended.

Monday, July 23, 1951

Tempo E- 

Washington Re: WATCH IMPORTERS AND ASSEMBLERS IAC Scott-OPS-GPR-718 

Members of the Watch Importers and Assemblers Industry Advisory Com mittee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss pricing problems of the industry. 

Industry members import completely assembled watches in cases ready for sale, and also watch movements which are fitted to domestic parts, mountings and cases.

Completely assembled imported watches are now covered by the import regulation, CPR 31. Imported watch movements which are fitted to domestic parts, mountings and cases are covered by the Manufacturers' Regulation, CPR 22. However, most importers are presently pricing under the General

Ceiling Price Regulation, because they have not qualified at yet for pricing under CPR 31 or CPR 22.

Generally speaking, committeemen felt that the industry should be covered under a supplementary regulation to CPR 22, which would recognize the peculiar pricing problems of the industry and give effect to fluctuations in tariff rates and foreign money exchange rates.

The meeting was conducted by Lee McCanne, chief, Housewares & Accessories 

Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: Bion B. Howard, acting assistant director, Consumer Durable Goods Division; Robert Faragher, chief counsel, Consumer Durable Goods Division; Robert Lowenstein, Branch Counsel; 

Henry Wohl, Division Economist; John Muskat, James Falloon, Malvin Cornfield, attorneys; Giles Evans, chief, Accessories Section; Eric Stern, business analyst; Julius Langsner, economist; Nat Grinder, Enforcement Division; 

Javier Cerecedo, acting chief, Export-Import Division; Edwin A. Elbert,

Service Trades Branch; and, Walter Moulton, Office for Industry Advisory Committees.

Tempo E 

 TUESDAY, July 24, 1951 

Washington Barkley-OPS-GPR-720 

Re: 

FLUE-CURED TOBACCO 

The Office of Price Stabilization today emphasized that no ceilings have been imposed upon producer prices of flue-cured tobacco. 

It also stressed that there are limitations upon OPS in the imposition of such ceilings. OPS officials explained that in view of the current state of the market and the anticipated large crop it is not likely to become necessary to impose ceilings at the producer level. 

Flue-cured tobacco is now listed as a below-parity item in the General Ceiling Price Regulation and the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price 

Regulation (CPR 22). 

While this commodity remains so listed in these two regulations, increases in raw material costs may be reflected in ceiling prices of commodities processed from flue-cured tobacco. 

As in many cases for many commodities, stand-by regulations have been prepared in case heavy pressure on prices should occur. There is no indication at the moment that such pressure will immediately occur in the flue-cured tobacco market.

The Agency added that burley tobacco acreage is up 13 per cent from last year. 1952 production is now estimated to be up approximately 20 per cent over both last year and the ten-year average Markets for burley tobacco will not open until about December. No ceiling regulation has been prepared. The same considerations set out above for flue-cured tobacco will apply to burley tobacco. ##########:#### /GPO-O-OPS 152

Tempo E-Washington Re: METAL CUTTING TOOLS IAC Members of the Metal Cutting Tools Industry Advisory Committee told 

OPS officials at a meeting today that they were satisfied with pricing under Ceiling Price Regulation 30, the machinery order, except for problems created by recent wage increases and higher costs of tungsten carbide. 

Industry representatives pointed out that wage increases have gone into effect since March 15, the cutoff date in calculating labor costs for price adjustments, and that OPS-authorized advances in ceiling prices of tungstencontaining materials used in manufacturing cutting tools would cause, a difficult squeeze for many producers. These materials often constitute half the cost of the tools, they said.

OPS officials said both matters would be fully considered as a basis for possible adjustments in the regulation as it applies to the metal cutting tool industry.

PRESS RELEASE   

Tuesday, July 24, 1951

Washington 

Moore-OPS-GPR-722  

AGRICULTURAL PESTICIDES, REPROCESSORS AND FORMULATORS IAC 

Members of the Agricultural Festicides, Reprocessors and Formulators Industry Advisory Committee today told OPS officials they felt that writing a tailored regulation for their industry should await stabilization of prices they pay for their raw materials, notably DDT and BHC (benzene hexachloride). 

Committeemen reported the provisions of the General Ceiling Price Regu lation under which they are now operating are generally satisfactory, though some manufacturers are being compelled to absorb certain increased raw materials cost which had not been reflected in the prices of their products at the time of the freeze.

Some committeemen said they could operate satisfactorily under the Manu facturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. The application of 

CPR 22 to these products was indefinitely postponed by Supplementary Regulation 12 to CPR 22. However, they cited that there had been increased costs of their raw materials since the materials cut-off date of December 

31, 1950, under CPR 22.

Committeemen also stressed the need of some device by which they can price new formulations without awaiting OPS approval. Members of the industry reported they produced up to 150 formulations to be used against pests and combinations of pests under varying weather conditions, and often were called upon to produce a new formula on a few hours' notice. 

They pointed out there was no problem in this respect under GCPR, but for new products CPR 22 required that they file prices 15 days before putting them into effect. There was some discussion of the extent to which this could be avoided under CPR 22 by pricing the new formulations on the basis of relationship of costs to comparable products. 

Committeemen suggested the preferred form of a tailored regulation would be to apply their pre-Korea markup to current costs in computing their ceiling products. They said such a formula could be applied very satisfactorily to uniform dollars and cents ceiling prices on their raw materials, if OPS determines on that type of regulation for DDT and BHC. GPO-O-OPS 157

Committeemen discussed the practicability of placing dollars and cents ceilings on their formulated products. The difficulty of doing this in veiw of the wide variation of their formulas was pointed out, and it was noted that uniform prices for formulations would lead to a reduction of product lines, thereby hurting the consumer. 

The possibility of developing industry-wide cost adjustment factors under CFF 22 was considered, together with the question of what information OPS would require to work out the factors. Committeemen were unable to suggest a mutually agreeable base period to employ in such computations, and agreed to study further the effects of pricing under CPR 22.

It was suggested the committee meet again after the forthcoming scheduled second meeting of the DDT and BHC Manufacturers Industry Advisory committee, following completion of Congressional action on extension of price controls.

B. P. Webster, Vice Pres.

PRESS RELEASE ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers FRIDAY, July 27, 1951   Re: JAVIER H. CERECEDO 

The Office of Price Stabilization today announced the appointment of 

Javier H. Cerecedo as Chief of the Export-Import Branch of the Services, Export-Import Division. 

Mr. Cerecedo, who was born in San Juan, P.R., has been in the field of 

International Trade since 1916. He came to OPS in May as a consultant in the 

Services, Export-Import Division, on leave as a senior partner and general manager of J.H. Cerecedo & Co., New York; president, Cerecedo Hermanos, Inc., San Juan, and overseas consultant for Sollitt Overseas Construction Co., San Juan. 

During World War II, he served in the War Department, Army Security Agency, Intelligence Division and has continued in the active reserve of that Division with the rank of colonel. He heads the Army Security Reserve, Planning and Training, New York Military District.

Mr. Cerecedo attended private schools in Spain, France and Germany where he received a Master's Degree in electrical and mechanical engineering in 1913. He has traveled extensively in Europe, Latin-America and the West Indies. Mr. 

Cerecedo, 58, is married and makes his home in Washington and Puerto Rico. Coakley-OPS-GPR-723  GPO-O-OPS 167

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers THURSDAY, July 26, 1951 

Washington Cole-OPS-GPR-724 

Re: Lumber Enforcement 

Court action is being sought in at least seven cases as a result of the Office of Price Stabilization probe into Virginia's lumber industry, Edward P. 

Morgan, assistant OPS director in charge of enforcement, stated today. The lumber investigation has extended into other states with firms located in North Carolina and Georgia as well as Virginia, facing court action. 

Judge Don Gilliam of the United States District Court, Eastern District of 

North Carolina, has entered a permanent restraining order and consent judgment restraining Hofler and Riddick of Sunbury, North Carolina, from violating any of the provisions of Section 16, General Price Ceiling Regulation, pertaining to re cord keeping on lumber sales for the protection of the buying public. 

The Sunbury firm, wholesale dealers handling only rough cut green lumber, had failed to prepare its ceiling price list, according to District Enforcement Director 

James F. Latham of Raleigh, North Carolina.

Halsey Hardwood Company Inc. of Edenton, North Carolina, will have a chance in the United States District Court in Raleigh on July 26 to show cause why a permanent restraining order should not be issued for failing to maintain records. 

Four more cases have been sent to the Department of Justice this week. 

In one case an injunction is sought to compel a Norfolk, Va., retail lumber and supply company to compile its ceiling price list. Similar action as well as treble damages for over-ceiling charges of approximately $1,500 is asked in a case against a manufacturer in eastern Virginia who has been supplying another mill operator.

In the third case sent to Justice Department, OPS seeks an injunction and single damages approximating $540 against another eastern Virginia manufacturer who handles rough lumber. The fourth case is against an Atlanta Ga., wholesale lumber company for more than 75 over-ceiling violations approximating $300. 

Treble damages will be sought. (over) 

Treble damages will also be sought against another Atlanta firm, a retailer, for more than 160 over-ceiling violations, in an amount still to be determined. 

The probe of Virginia lumber mill operators and dealers was launched by OPS nearly two months ago with special agents being sent into the field from Washington to assist the agents assigned to the Norfolk and Richmond offices. 7816 GPO- -OPS 166

According to OPS officials, the investigation was launched following receipt of complaints from some mill operators that log prices were so high that they are unable to produce lumber profitably. A preliminary inquiry indicated, according to OPS, that both mill operators and dealers have been very lax in keeping records and compiling price lists as required under the General Ceiling Price Regulation. 

Several more cases, Mr. Morgan stated, are now being investigated for failure to keep records and compile lists, and for over-ceiling violations. Court action against the Sunbury and Edenton firms, he said, has resulted in much better compliance with OPS regulations on the part of both mill operators and dealers.

CPR 7 ENFORCEMENT Cole-OPS-GPR-725 

The Office of Price Stabilization today asked the United States District 

Court in Trenton, N. J., to issue an injunction against Binder's Department store of 132 W. State Street, that city, for violation of Ceiling Price Regulation 7 requiring the filing of ceiling price charts showing retail markups. 

Judge Philip Forman, chief judge of the United States District Court of New 

Jersey, issued a show cause order, returnable July 31.

According to Edward P. Morgan, assistant director of OPS in charge of enforcement, in Washington, the Trenton firm which does a business of around $600,000 a year, is one of a number of retail stores throughout the nation which have failed to file the required charts.

The injunction proceedings seek to compel the Trenton firm to file the charts and ask that the firm be restrained from doing business unless or until it files the charts and also keeps other records and sales information as required by OPS. 

Trenton district OPS officials told the United States Attorney that the Binder firm has also ignored a warning letter and failed to give assurance in a conference of counsel that it will comply within the stated grace period. 

Mr. Morgan stated that while the majority of retail stores have filed the required charts, there are still many which have not done so as yet, and that court action will be taken against the dilatory firms to force compliance. # # # # # In issuing this warning, Mr. Morgan observed that retail stores have had a fair and reasonable opportunity to comply and that failure to do so can be attributed only to an attitude of willfulness or indifference which cannot longer be tolerated. 7855 GPO-O-OPS 168

PRESS RELEASE   

Wednesday, July 25, 1951

Re: 

 SUPERPHOSPHATE IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-726 

Members of the Superphosphate Industry Advisory Committee told OPS 

officials today that there will be a substantial shrinkage in the production of superphosphate, essential to the fertilizer industry, unless there is an upward adjustment in prices.

The demand for sulfuric acid, which is used in the manufacture of superphosphate, is so heavy that, unless superphosphate prices are raised, sulfuric acid will tend to find its way into other more profitable uses, committeemen said.

Of six committeemen present, three reported their firms had established new ceiling prices under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 

22, in time to price under it commencing June 30. The other three reported their prices were still frozen under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPF.

Committeemen said most companies normally sold superphosphate on the basis of a contract year ending June 30, and therefore had not raised their prices before GCPR became effective to cover increased costs of sulfuric acid, and were thus caught in a squeeze. Other companies selling on a spot basis raised prices, so that there was an abnormal price disparity between manufacturers under GCPR. 

Members of the committee agreed that the old OPA RMPR 205, which fixed dollars and cents ceilings during the war for various points of production, was a satisfactory price regulation, and urged that a similar regulation be written now. 

Committeemen agreed it should cover superphosphate, triple superphosphate and ammoniated superphosphate.

The members felt that a weighted average of CPR 22 prices, calculated for the various production points, would provide a realistic approach to determine spelled out ceilings, but pointed out there had been important cost increases since the CPR 22 cut-off dates, including freight rates. 

The question of future supply and price of sulfuric acid is also of prime importance, committeemen said. Some members reported they were obtaining sulfuric acid at costs up to more than double the former cost, due to heavy inbound freights on spent acid purchased to supplement curtailed supplies of virgin acid. 7861 GPO-O-OPS 171

Members pointed out that the shortage of sulfuric acid has already forced a curtailment of production which has meant some increase in unit cost. Two members estimated that their increase was about 10 to 12 per cent. 

Industry members expressed concern over the impact of still further sulfuric acid curtailment upon their costs.

Members of the committee indicated their industry could produce substantial quantities of sodium silicofluoride to meet the growing requirements of municipalities for the chemical which is used in fluoridation of drinking water. They agreed to study the potentialities of their industry to meet the demand.

Some 

Committeemen suggested another meeting in mid-August, after the future of CPR 22 is determined by Congressional action. They stressed the need of a prompt solution so their industry can contract for the coming season. committeemen reported they had not renewed contracts but were shipping on a month to month basis, awaiting clarification of the situation, and others reported their contracts were studded with contingency clauses. 

The meeting was conducted by George W. Strasser, acting assistant director, Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs division. Other OPS officials present were T. H. McCormack, division director; Alfred T. Loeffler, chief, Chemicals 

Branch; Wilhelm Hirschkind, branch technical advisor; Philip Travis, branch counsel; Henry A. Huschke, head Agricultural Chemicals section; Cedric Gran, section business specialist; Susan M. Phillips, section economist; Joseph J. 

Strassman, counsel; Hirschie Johnson, Office of Enforcement, and W. R. Thomas,

Jr., Office of Advisory Committees. S. P. Wimpfen, Atomic Energy Commission, also attended.

PRESS RELEASE

OFFICE CF PRICE STABILIZATION 

Tempo E- 

Wednesday, July 25, 1951 

Washington Coakley-OPS-GPR-727 

Re: CONSUMERS ADVISORY COMMITTEE 

The future course of price stabilization in the light of developing economic conditions was discussed today in the second meeting of the Office of Price Stabilization Consumers Advisory Committee. 

Inflationary pressures, which he predicted will follow the present "soft" market, in which prices of some commodities have been reduced, were discussed by Gardner Ackley, OPS Economic Advisor. 

For the last several months, Mr. Ackley pointed out, consumer buying and business buying for inventory have been temporarily depressed below normal levels, in part as a reflection of the overbuying which occurred last fall and winter.

However, he said, we cannot expect this consumer withdrawal from the market to persist indefinitely. Over a longer period, consumer buying tends to move closely with consumer income, and consumer income is bound to rise as employment stays high and wages increase, he said.

Although high taxes and credit controls will tend to hold down the expansion of consumer buying, Mr. Ackley explained, defense spending, rising income and exhausted inventories of goods will operate to produce shortages, rising prices and the familiar price-income-price spiral, unless direct controls are applied.

While there is some feeling among consumers and industry that because prices are low decontrols could be instituted, Mr. Ackley said, all indications are that the condition is only temporary and that by late fall or early winter, inflationary pressures will be felt.

Asked what the economic impact of a truce in Korea would be, Mr. Ackley said he doubted it would change the long-range picture, although if defense spending were cut, it might prolong the period of lowered prices. 

Committee members discussed with T. Otis Black, Director, Programs

Division, Office of Public Information, and Gordon E. McCloskey, assistant to the Director of Public Information, the need for an educational program. The committee agreed that the public should be made aware of the danger of future GIO-O-OPS 172

GAD 

2inflation if controls are relaxed now. They asked OPS to make available to them material which would tell this story. The possibility of cooperation with local CPS Volunteer Committees in this and other educational projects also was discussed.

Harold Leventhal, OPS Chief Counsel and Herbert N. Maletz, chief of the 

Legislation Research and Opinions Division of his office analyzed the various amendments now being considered by Congress in drafting a new Defense Produc tion Act. 

Mr. Leventhal told the meeting that CPS would make every effort to administer whatever controls law the Congress might enact. He said he believed that an effective act can be achieved if House and Senate members of the Conference Committee considering the new act are given adequate information as to the possible effects of proposed amendments. 1 

Irvin Rice, chief of the Livestock and Meat Distribution Branch of OPS dis cussed the implications of the proposal to abandon slaughter controls. He told the committee that slaughter quotas do not limit the marketing of livestock and if they are prohibited it will be impossible to insure normal distribution of meat; to protect legitimate enterprises in the meat business from financial hardship, or to insure compliance with price ceiling regulations. 

Plans were discussed by the Advisory Committee to set up subcommittees to enable members to work more closely on specific problems. Possibilities of enlarging the committee in response to requests from groups not now represented also were discussed. 

Committee members attending today's session, at which Mrs. Chase Going 

Woodhouse, a member of the staff of Price Stabilization Director Michael V. 

DiSalle presided, were: Miss Frances Boyer, National Education Association; 

Mrs. Irma Piepho, National Council of Catholic Women; Wallace J. Campbell, Cooperative League of the United States; Thomas X. Clancy, American Legion;

PRIVATE BRAND TIRE AND TUBE TACS 

Both owners and manufacturers of private brand tires and tubes have approved proposals for a tailored regulation for their industry, and no further meetings of their industry advisory committees are in prospect before preparation of the order, OPS officials said today.

The tentative regulation was discussed with individual manufacturers concerned, and they indicated concurrence.

Members of the Private Brand Tire and Tube Owners Industry Advisory 

Committee at their meeting July 20 unanimously subscribed to the general provisions of the proposed regulation, as explained by Hubert H. Peterson, chief of the Tire Section, and Harry Hinkes, Rubber Branch counsel. 

Three methods of determining prices were defined. OPS would fix certain accounting periods, and the tentative regulation would allow negotiations between brand owners and manufacturers on adjustments for increased or decreased costs. Price control would be maintained by freezing the manufacturer's margin.

Selection of the method of computing the cost was described as the manufacturer's responsibility, while selection of accounting periods would be by agreement between the manufacturer and owner. # # # # # # # # # # # # Committeemen who attended the owners committee meeting were John H. 

Buchanan, Atlas Supply Co., Newark; Vernon Lawrence, Star Rubber Co., Mansfield, Ohio; Wayne W. Letho, National Cooperatives, Inc., Chicago; Arthur

Washington LUMBER ENFORCEMENT Moore-OPS-GPR-729  

The first court test of the question of where records must be kept under provisions of Office of Price Stabilization regulations occurred today at Raleigh, North Carolina, where a federal court consent judgment was issued requiring the Halsey Hardwood Company to maintain its records at its place of business in Edenton, OPS officials said today.

The judgment, issued by Judge Don Gilliam of the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina, ordered the company commencing July 26 to maintain all records required under Section 16 of the General Ceiling Price 

Regulation at its Edenton office.

The Halsey Hardwood Company is a North Carolina Corporation controlled by R.P. Bear & Co., a Baltimore partnership. Representations in court were made showing that the records of the Halsey Hardwood Company, manufacturer and wholesaler of lumber and other wood products, were maintained by the owners in Baltimore. 

It is notworthy, OPS said, that a number of lumber companies operating in North 

Carolina are controlled by out-of-state ownership. An enforcement drive has been under way in the lumber industry in North Carolina and adjacent states. 

The decision, moreover, constitutes a precedent which other federal district courts may follow, the agency pointed out. # # # # # # 7915 GPO-O-OPS 177,

Tempo E 

 THURSDAY, July 26, 1951 

Washington McDonald-OPS-GPR-730 

Re: CONSTRUCTION IAC 

A proposed new regulation permitting contractors to reflect increased labor and materials costs in future ceiling prices was discussed today by Office of Price Stabilization officials with members of the Construction 

Industry Advisory Committee. 

Under the present regulation governing the construction industry, the service trades order (CPR 34), contractors are permitted to reflect certain increases in material costs but are required to absorb recent wage increases in their profit margins. 

OPS officials said the proposed new pricing order would not drastically affect the cost of new construction, paving, painting, renovations, roofing, and the like, since wage increases for this type of work have not been large. 

Committee members told OPS representatives that many contractors are suffering hardship under CPR 34, but the group expressed the view that permitting adjustments for wage increases would do much to eliminate present difficulties.

Two segments of the construction industry requested OPS to remove their operations from pricing regulations entirely: the road building contractors and the electric line contractors. Representatives said road building was almost entirely for federal, state, and local governments, bids are usually a matter of public record, and contractors are faced with regulatory control from the various government agencies letting paving contracts. Electric line contractors presented a similar view.

The committee went on record as opposing any new pricing action which would require contractors to file or report ceiling prices. The committee approved an OPS proposal for a provision making it mandatory for contractors to keep adequate records to show how they arrived at their ceiling prices. 

Today's meeting was conducted by Walter H. Acheson, acting chief of the 

OPS Building Materials Branch. Others in attendance were John Bulkley, Assistant 

Director, Industrial Materials and Manufactured Goods Division; Thomas G. 

Latchworth, head of the construction section: Leo Wasser, branch attorney; 

Irving Rubenstein, branch economist; Arthur Reyman, branch counsel; Bruce 

E. Kent, business specialist; and Harry Spack, Office for Advisory Committees.

 Monday, July 30, 1951   POTASH IAC 

Washington Moore-OPS-GPR-732 ST: 4200; Ext. 3491 Members of the Potash Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with Office of Price Stabilization officials discussed what portion of the products of their industry should be priced under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, and what portion under the Manufacturers' General 

Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. 

Committeemen indicated that there had been some confusion in the industry about where to price the major product, muriate of potash, an important fertilizer. Prior to the issuance of Interpretation 33 to CPR 22, a portion of the 

Industry's production had been contracted for under proposed CPR 22 prices. 

The question hinged on whether production. was an extractive mining process or a manufacturing chemical process. In some instances, it was reported, the production obtained from predominantly mechanical processes was boosted by supplemental chemical processes.

OPS officials held that muriate of potash was a non-metallic mineral produced by an extractive process and therefore subject to GCPR. The chemical grade refined by recrystallization, however, was considered a chemical and along with sulfate of potash, subject to CPR 22.

Committeemen agreed it would be desirable to price the three products under one regulation, and a majority indicated it would be satisfactory to remain for the time-being under GCPR. Contracts are normally entered into on an annual basis in June. It was suggested that after Congressional action is completed on extension of price control, the question of a tailored regulation be explored in ample time to provide for the next contract period if action seems required.

PRESS RELEASE   

Tuesday, July 31, 1951

 Coakley-OPS-GPR-734 

Re: COMMUTER RATE INCREASE PROTESTS 

The Office of Price Stabilization has filed with the Interstate Commerce Commission protests against proposed increased commuter passenger rates requested by 11 railroads.

OPS said the proposed increases would be unreasonable and discriminatory in that the railroads ask, generally, for the same fixed monetary increase on passenger tickets of the same class, between stations, regardless of distance. 

The agency pointed out that the railroads have pending before the ICC a request for a 15% increase in freight rates which includes an alleged passenger deficit as an expense item which would be covered by the 15% increase in freight rates. Thus, if the proposed increases in commutation fares are based upon increased costs, such costs have already been presented for consideration of the Commission. If the proposed increases are not based upon higher costs, OPS said, they are unjustified.

The proposed increases would be inflationary, OPS stated, and would increase the cost of living of commuters, thus increasing their difficulties in carrying on their needed activities during the national emergency. Any widespread increase in the cost of defense workers' transportation hampers the defense effort, the agency pointed out. # # # # # # # # # # # 

Railroads involved are: Baltimore and Ohio, Central Railroad Co. of New Jersey, Delaware, Lackawanna and Western, Railroad Co., Erie Railroad Co., Lehigh

Valley Railroad Co., New Jersey and New York Railroad Co., New York Central Railroad Co., Pennsylvania Railroad Co., Pennsylvania-Reading Seashore Lines, Pittsburgh and Lake Erie Railroad Co., Reading Co. 

GPO-O-OPS 214

Wednesday, August 1, 1951 Re: 

 MIXED FERTILIZERS IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-735  

Members of the Mixed Fertilizers Industry Advisory Committee today told 

OPS officials their industry could price satisfactorily for the present under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. 

Committeemen, attending their first meeting, however, requested that a tailored regulation be prepared for their industry allowing manufacturers to reflect in their ceiling prices certain cost increases beyond the cut-off dates provided in CPR 22. These included increased freight rates, cost of imported ingredients not under price control, and possible increases in the prices of their basic materials. 

The industry prepares numerous formulations which vary in accordance with the soil requirements and the specifications of state regulatory agencies, using such basic materials as nitrates, phosphates, and potash. One committeeman reported his company prepared 60 or 70 formulations and entered some 500 

600 registrations to comply with state regulations.

Committeemen said the old OPA regulation for their industry, which spelled out dollars and cents prices on standard formulations by zones and subzones, worked satisfactorily. However, they expressed preference for a tailored regulation following the principles of CPR 22 but employing industrywide percentage cost adjustment factors which they would apply to their respective base period prices.

They suggested that these factors be calculated by zones along the general pattern of the zoning followed during the war. They also suggested provision be made for pricing new liquid fertilizers which are being developed, particularly in California. (over) Committeemen said their industry customarily priced by seasons, the spring and fall. They said it would be desirable to have any new regulation prepared before November, when it is customary to issue prices for the spring season. 

The committee discussed the type of information that would be required to develop the factors. OPS officials agreed to prepare a proposed questionnaire and submit it to the committee for criticism prior to circulating it to the industry. A new committee meeting was planned soon after the questionnaire is prepared.

GPO-O-OPS 221

It was tentatively suggested that cost studies be developed on the basis of key products rather than on an overall basis.

Thursday, August 2, 1951 Tempo E- 

Washington Re: CAROLINA USED CAR DEALER PROSECUTIONS 

First prosecutions in the Office of Price Stabilization nation-wide drive on used car dealers violating OPS filing regulations were recorded in the Federal District Court in Raleigh, N.C., this afternoon when Judge Don Gilliam signed temporary restraining orders against 16 eastern Carolina used car dealers. 

Cole-OPS-GPR-737 

This action, culminating three months of effort on the part of OPS enforcement agents in Raleigh to secure voluntary compliance, is the most vigorous action taken in any OPS enforcement district to date, Edward P. Morgan, assistant OPS director in charge of enforcement, stated this afternoon.

According to James F. Latham, Raleigh OPS District Enforcement Director, the 16 firms are restrained from selling or delivering used cars until such time as they come into compliance with OPS regulations. Judge Gilliam set August 9 at 11:00 a.m. for the "show cause" hearings.

Named in the temporary injunctions issued this afternoon were Marvin Ham Used 

Cars of Fayetteville; Thomas Woodrow Shirley, Smithville; Gurley Motor Company, Morehead City; Carleton R. Nixon, Winsall; Ernest L. Yoder and Bennie B. Pittman, Sharpsburg; Wrenn Motors, Louisburg; Gupton Service Center, Louisburg; D & E Car 

Exchange, Wilmington; Willetts Motor Company, Boliva; Bradshaw Brothers Used Cars, Wilmington; Morgan Motor Company, Raeford; Pamlico Motor Company, Washington; 

Pembroke Motor Company, Pembroke; Britt Buick Company, Elizabethtown; and Edward

Brothers, Louisburg. 

* Used car dealers throughout the country have been given ample time to comply with OPS regulations, according to Mr. Morgan, who said that OPS would seek injunctions in further violations. The Carolina dealers brought into court this afternoon were charged specifically with failing to file statements with OPS giving required information as to which of several accepted guide books they are using in establishing their ceiling prices.

Planned prosecution of delinquent dealers throughout the country has raised compliance with OPS regulations from a low of 30 percent to a high of approximately 

90 percent at this time, Mr. Morgan said.

For the most part it appeared it would effect little change on the pricing devices now available to this branch of the rubber products industry. 

Certain standard products in the industry are now subject to price control under Amendment 1, SR 8, CPR 22, which sets forth industry-wide percentage cost adjustment factors which are applied to individual manufacturers' base period prices.

Other products are subject to pricing under CPR 22 formulas, unless sales of the respective items were under $10,000 during the 2nd quarter of 1951, in which case manufacturers have the alternative, as provided under SR 10 to CPR 22, to price under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR.

Committeemen said they desired a tailored regulation to cover the products of their industry not priced under SR 8 to CPR 22. These are mostly custom made products sold on a bid basis to other manufacturers. Committeemen said they desired a method of pricing these items by formula similar to the provisions of old 

OPA MPR 149. 

They volunteered to report their pricing methods to OPS so the latter can work out a suitable formula regulation. In general, it was proposed to price such products on the basis of each manufacturer's pricing method in effect during a determined base period.

Washington 

Re: SUBCOMMITTEE OF BOOK PAPER IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-739 

ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 

Members of the Book Paper Industry Advisory Subcommittee at their fifth meeting today with OPS officials endorsed proposals for a tailored regulation for their industry spelling out dollars-and-cents ceiling prices for six or seven key grades of book paper. 

Prices for other grades and weights, and variations in packaging, cutting, finish, etc., would be established by customary differentials. 

It was proposed that spelled out ceilings be based on ceilings filed by individual manufacturers under CPR 22, the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation.

Committeemen suggested that spelled out ceilings be fixed at levels that would be equal or greater than individual ceilings on the bulk of the production in each key grade. 

Analysis of price data submitted to OPS showed that ceilings determined in this manner would average several per cent higher than weighted averages of CPR 22 ceilings. It was shown that weighted averages of CPR 22 ceilings on the key grades represented increases of about 4 to 10 percent over average prices under the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR. 

A parallel study showed that if the cut-off date for all allowable cost increases under CPR 22 was advanced to July 1, 1951, ceilings would be slightly lower than those arrived at using the various earlier cut-off dates specified in CPR 22. 

Increases over GCPR ceilings under this calculation would average from about 3 to 

9 percent.

Basic grades for which it was proposed to spell out prices are: No. 2 Enamel 

70 lb., Enamel 45 lb., A Grade EF Untrimmed 50 lb., M.F. Litho 50 lb., No. 2 Offset 

55 lb., Envelope 20 lb., and Tablet 16 lb.

Committeemen discussed the possible effects of the new Congressional legislation extending price control through the current fiscal year. The opinion was expressed that the new legislation would effect little practical change in the application of price control to their industry. (over) Members of the subcommittee agreed to meet again August 15 and suggested a meeting of the full committee the same day.

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers MONDAY, August 6, 1951  

a:9 Re: 

 BANK CHARGE REFUNDS 

Banks throughout the country which have raised their service charges through a misunderstanding of Office of Price Stabilization regulations, are now cooperating with OPS officials in rolling back their charges and making refunds to customers.

Cole-OPS-GPR-740  

This statement was made today by Edward P. Morgan, assistant OPS director in charge of enforcement, who said the Corn Exchange Bank Trust Company of New York has agreed to roll back its checking account charge and refund approximately $80,000 to holders of such accounts in 77 of its 78 branches. 

The refunds represent a 25-cent monthly service charge instituted March 7, last. Mr. Morgan said this charge is in violation of Ceiling Price Regulation 

34. A similar charge at the Audubon branch of the bank, instituted December 1, 1950 before prices were frozen, is not affected. 

The same problem exists, Mr. Morgan added, in certain other banks elsewhere in the country. A second New York City bank the Hellenic Bank and Trust Company, will refund approximately $6,000 to some 6,000 customers. 

Mr. Morgan again reminded bankers that service charges made by banks, including checking accounts and safety deposit boxes, were frozen by the General Ceiling Price Regulation, Such services, he pointed out, are not included in the list of exemptions under General Overriding Regulation 14. 

Banks are not considered as retail establishments and do not have to post ceiling price lists, he stated. # # # # # # # GPO-O-OPS 232

Tempo E-Washington ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers MONDAY, August 6, 1951 RE: 

COMPLIANCE UNDER CPR 7 Cole-OPS-GPR 741  

Office of Price Stabilization enforcement investigators today launched a nation wide survey to determine compliance on the part of retail dealers in apparel, furniture, household wares, radios, televisions and related fields in the filing of price charts under Ceiling Price Regulation 7, Edward P. Morgan, assistant OPS director in charge of enforcement, has announced. 

According to Mr. Morgan, upwards of 275,000 retail dealers should have filed such charts by May 31. Thus far, he said, many dealers have failed to comply with OPS regulations. 

Compliance with CPR 7 is very important, Mr. Morgan stated, because of the large number of retailers throughout the country who come under the regulation. Mr. Morgan noted that there has been a wide variance in compliance in the various CPS regions, and that more than 25 per cent of the price charts filed have been returned for additional information or correction of errors.

The Department of Justice has instructed United States Attorneys in the field to institute suits to compel filing of the charts in all cases where dealers fail to heed warning letters within the grace period set by OPS, Mr. Morgan said. !! !! !! !! ! !! !! !!_!|_ !! !! !!_IIILILI!_!! nonfiftitit GPO-O-OPS 233

PRESS RELEASE   ADVANCE RELEASE For Use In Morning Papers SUNDAY, August 12, 1951 Crossley-OPS-GPR-742  Re: BOARDS OF REVIEW HEARINGS 

Announcement of two public hearings before Boards of Review--the first such hearings to be held under the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended--was made today by the Office of Price Stabilization. 

Both hearings have been scheduled in response to protests filed against price control of services. Prompt consideration of such protests is given in accordance with Price Procedural Regulation 1-Revised.

PROTEST AGAINST GENERAL CEILING PRICE REGULATION 

As contract carriers by motor vehicle, operating an interstate service, Woodfin Brothers of Richmond, Va., come under coverage of the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation, they have filed a protest against price control of contract carriers, contending that, since common carriers and other public utilities are exempt from price control by virtue of Section 14 (f) of GCPR, they as contract carriers should be accorded similar treatment. 

In their protest, Woodfin Brothers cite increased costs of operation as having required a 10 per cent rate increase "approved" for them by the Interstate Commerce Commission on March 26, 1951. They haul under contract exclusively for Wheeling Corrugating Company of Wheeling, W. Va. 

operating from Richmond to North Carolina and South Carolina. 

Points of issue are the following: (1) Whether there is adequate legal basis for subjecting contract carriers to price control.... (2) Assuming adequate legal authority for subjecting contract carriers to control, whether it is arbitrary and capricious for the Office GPO-O-OPS 242

D of Price Stabilization to maintain controls over the maximum rates of such carriers.

On August 14, 1951, a Board of Review appointed by the Director of Price Stabilization will hear the oral argument on this protest. Members of the Board of Review, meeting in Washington, will be the following:

Herbert N. Maletz, Chief, Legislation Research and Opinions Divisions, Office of Chief Counsel, presiding; Henry L. Duncombe, Acting Division Economist, Transportation, Public Utilities and Fuel Division, Office of 

Price Operations; W. Bryce Rea, Jr., Counsel, Rublic Utilities Branch,

Transportation Public Utilities and Fuel Division, Office of Chief Counsel. 

PROTEST AGAINST SERVICES REGULATION 

Consolidated Currency Exchanges operate 28 places of business in Chicago, providing such services as cashing checks, issuance of money orders and travelers' checks and receipt of public utilities bills, these services being provided on a fee basis. They have filed a protest against price control of their services on the bases that (1) the services are not essential to the National Defense Program, (2) the services are a matter of convenience and are entirely optional and (3) an increase in their fees, necessitated by a recent reduction in their volume of business, would not increase the cost of living.

The protest also pointed out that Consolidated Currency Exchanges operates under supervision of the Auditor of Public Accounts of the State of 

Illinois under provisions of the Illinois Community Currency Exchange Act. 

On August 24, 1951, at OPS Regional Office 7 in Chicago, a Board of 

Review subcommittee --Vaughn Ball presiding--will hear an oral argument on the protest. Subsequently, the entire record of the case, including transcript of the oral argument, will be considered by the entire Board of Review consisting of the following: Vaughn Ball, Deputy Chief, Legislation Research and Opinions Division, Office of Chief Counsel, presiding; Edwin A. Elbert, 

Acting Assistant Director, Services, Export-Import Division; and Robert

Willcox, Attorney-Advisor, Public Utilities Branch, Transportation, Public Utilities and Fuel Division, Office of Chief Counsel. 

OPS Boards of Review make written recommendations to the Director of Price Stabilization on protests which request consideration by such Boards. 

The Director of Price Stabilization may then grant or deny the protest. If a protest is denied, it may be carried to the Emergency Court of Appeals.

PRESS RELEASE    

Friday, August 3, 1951 

Moore-OPS-GPR-744 

Re: AGRICULTURAL PESTICIDES (GENERAL PESTICIDES) IAC Members of the Agricultural Pesticides (General Pesticides) Industry 

Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials reported their industry could operate reasonably satisfactorily under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, which becomes effective for their industry October 1, 1951, under the terms of Amendment 1, SR 12,

CPR 22. 

Of 13 committeemen present, eight reported CPR 22 would give them general price increases above ceilings under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, and five no change or mixed rollbacks and rollforwards. 

None reported that rollbacks were predominant. 

However, several committeemen said they could not take general advantage of higher ceilings because of competitive conditions, while they would still have to take their rollbacks under price control. 

It was suggested that employment of the device provided in SR 2 to CPR 22, under which overall cost increase factors are applied uniformly to GCPR prices instead of to base period prices, might tend to equalize rollbacks and rollforwards. 

Committeemen were apprehensive over the possible effect of future increases in prices on their basic raw materials, and suggested that the possibility of writing a tailored regulation for their industry covering such contingencies be explored.

Committeemen suggested that another meeting be held around November 1, after their industry has completed filing Forms 8 under CPR 22, to determine GPO-O-OPS 240

no whether a tailored regulation might be desirable for their industry and what form it would take. OPS officials reported that few Forms 8 had been received from the industry up to the time its operation was suspended by SR 

12 to CPR 22, and urged members to file before October 1 whenever possible.

Members stressed the desirability of having prices in their industry stabilized around October for the coming season. Committeemen also urged the need of a device for more rapid pricing of new formulations. Under CPR 

22 a waiting time of 15 days after filing proposed ceilings on new products is required.

The committee represented manufacturers of insecticides, herbicides, fungicides, rodenticides and fumigants.

The meeting was conducted by Huge E. Weisberger, division economist, Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers 

MONDAY, August 6, 1951

Washington

MANUFACTURING REGULATIONS 

Crist-OPS-GPR-745  

Firms covered by the general manufacturers' order and related manufacturing regulations must figure their new ceilings under the provisions of these orders as they existed before the new Defense Production Act became effective, on August 1, it was emphasized by Office of Price Stabilization officials in a statement today.

Some confusion has arisen over this point, they said, because of the socalled Capehart amendment to the Defense Production Act, providing that ceilings on materials and services must reflect increases or decreases in costs, including overhead, up to July 26.

It has come to the attention of OPS officials that some manufacturers are under the impression that they may calculate their ceilings on the basis of the Capehart amendment rather than the formulas spelled out in the manufacturing orders.

This impression, they said, is false. The manufacturing regulations, having been issued before the enactment of the amendments to the Defense Production Act, remain in effect. These regulations do not provide for increases in overhead costs.

The Capehart amendment, however, provides that "upon application and a proper showing of ...prices and costs, "the OPS shall adjust ceilings to reflect changes in costs, including overhead, up to July 26, 1951, a somewhat later cut-off date than used in the manufacturing regulations. OPS is now studying methods by which this new requirement can be placed in regulatory form. 

OPS officials said that undoubtedly the provisions of the Capehart amendment will give many manufacturers higher ceiling prices upon application to the agency. 

On the other hand, they pointed out, some manufacturers will not be entitled to any increases because in some fields costs on July 26 were no higher than on earlier cut-off dates used in the manufacturing regulations. (Cut-off date for most materials was December 31, 1951, and for labor March 15.) (over)

So far as overhead costs are concerned, they continued, many of them have decreased between pre-Korea and the present time because of increased volume. GPO-0-OPS 241

Officials said the situation may be summarized as follows: 

1) Manufacturers under the general manufacturers' order (CPR 22), and the machinery order (CPR 30) must file their public forms under these regulations on or before August 13, if they have not already done so. 

2) Ceilings under CPR 22 and CPR 30 and related manufacturing orders must be computed on the basis of the formulas in the regulations. 

3) Any rollbacks called for in these regulations must be placed into effect no later than August 13; except in the case of the apparel order, where the deadline is August 15. 

4) Manufacturers filing forms under CPR 22 and CPR 30 on August 13 would have to rollback prices under these regulations on that day, but would have to wait until 15 days after the forms have been received by OPS before increasing any prices above the levels of the General Ceiling Price Regulation. After that period they may increase the prices, if they have not been disallowed by 

OPS or further information requested. 

5) Manufacturers who have already waited 15 days and are legally entitled to place increases under CPR 22 and CPR 30 into effect before August 13, must also place any rollbacks into effect at the same time. 

All of these regulations were issued many weeks ago. Most of them were to have gone into effect July 2. But when Congress prohibited rollbacks in the 

31 day extension of the law during July, the agency issued General Overriding Regulation 13, providing that manufacturers who had not placed ceilings under these regulations into effect on or before June 30 would continue under GCPR. GOR 13 was revoked July 31, and these various manufacturing regulations again placed in effect, but with an extension of filing time for the various reports and forms required by them. Thus pricing under the regulations is optional until the final deadlines in mid-August. 

The manufacturing orders involved are the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation (CPR 22); Machinery and Related Manufactured Goods (CPR 30); 

Primary Cotton Textile Manufacturers' Regulation (CPR 37); Shoe Manufacturers' Regulation (CPR 41); Apparel Manufacturers General Ceiling Price Regulation 

(CPR 45); and Manufacturers' Prices for Wool Yarns and Fabrics (CPR 18-Revised). # # # # # # # # # # # # # #

PRESS RELEASE ADVANCE RELEASE   For Use in Morning Papers TUESDAY, August 7, 1951 Re: DEPOSIT CHARGES ON CONTAINERS (General Interpretation 2 

Coakley-OPS-GPR-747  

Deposit Charges for Containers)

The Office of Price Stabilization has issued General Interpretation 2 to define conditions under which deposit charges for containers may be instituted or increased. 

Where a seller, during his base period, sold on a container-included basis, the container is considered part of the commodity being sold, OPS ruled. 

Therefore, he may not now sell the product on a returnable-container basis and make a deposit charge, unless he deducts from his ceiling price the present value of the empty container.

If the seller, during his base period, sold on a returnable-container basis, but made no deposit charge, he may now institute a deposit charge without making a deduction from his ceiling price, OPS said. 

The deposit charge must be reasonable, OPS pointed out, and on containers easily lost or broken or easily replaceable, would be generally, the replacement cost of the container. On the other hand, when containers, such as steel drums, are in short supply, the deposit may exceed the replacement cost of the container. # # # # # # # # # # # # GPO-O-OPS 248

Washington SUGAR BEET PULP IAC Barkley-OPS-GPR-748 ST.4200; Ext. 3491 Members of the Sugar Beet Pulp Industry Advisory Committee, in their first meeting with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization, today recommended that proposed dollars and cents ceilings on sugar beet pulp products be closely related to the prices of other feed products such as corn and barley. 

Sugar beet pulp is an important livestock and dairy feed and is also used in the manufacture of mixed feeds. 

Committeemen also urged that provision be made for the industry practice of having seasonal variations in the price of wet beet pulp and dried beet pulp.

It was the general concensus of the group that beet pulp imports, which have been large in recent years, be priced at the same level as the domestic product at point of destination.

Committee members said domestic production of beet pulp is expected to be off probably 50 percent this year.

Monday, August 6, 1951

  Moore-OPS-GPR-749  Re: APPAREL MANUFACTURERS WHO RETAIL 

Nine representatives of apparel manufacturers who retail their own products met today with OPS officials and generally approved the terms of a proposed amendment to CPR 45, the Apparel Manufacturers' General Ceiling 

Price Regulation, which would permit them to obtain a markup on their retail business comparable to that obtained by retailers generally. 

Heretofore such manufacturers who did not carry on their retail business through separate organizations were obliged to price under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, or CPR 45, and thus could not obtain retail markups such as provided under CPR 7, the retail regulation. 

The amendment would provide alternate devices whereunder they could separate their retail operations and determine ceiling prices on the latter by applying markups on increased manufacturing costs. 

The amendment would permit manufacturers who customarily employ transfer prices between manufacturing and retailing operations to use these prices during the base period to compute new ceilings on their manufacturing operations under CPR 45.

Manufacturers who do not customarily use transfer prices between their two operations may employ prices at which they sold to other retailers to determine their base period transfer prices. 

Manufacturers who cannot arrive at base period transfer prices by either of these devices may obtain their transfer prices by employing fixed percentage markups for the respective items set forth in Appendix E, CPR 7, the retail regulation, and working back from their retail prices. 

After the base period transfer prices and the adjustment to these prices permitted for their manufacturing operations are determined, the differences between the transfer prices and the base period retail selling prices form the basis for percentage markups which may be added to the adjusted transfer prices to establish new ceiling prices. 

It was pointed out that in some instances employing the manufacturer's price to other retailers would give a manufacturer an abnormally low margin on his own retail operations, which he would have to maintain in calculating his new retail prices.

The opinion was expressed, however, that most manufacturers could arrive at satisfactory ceiling prices on both their manufacturing and retailing operations by resort to one of the alternatives.

The meeting was conducted by Morris L. 

Branch.

MEAT ENFORCEMENT 

Cole-OPS-GPR-750  

Charges of flagrant and widespread violations of Office of Price Stabilization price and quota regulations on livestock and meat, made by the National Independent Meat Packers Association, are absolutely unfounded and unwarranted, Edward P. Morgan, OPS director of Enforcement, stated today. 11 Commenting on the resolution of the Association demanding that OPS "be more diligent in the enforcement of existing laws, rules and regulations," Mr. Morgan stated that the enforcement personnel in 89 OPS district offices throughout the country have for a long time been concentrating on enforcement of meat regulations. "Enforcement personnel have run down every single complaint received by them and have also conducted hundreds of surveys with a view to locating all possible violations", he added. "Each violation is promptly and effectively investigated. There are now pending over 10,000 investigative cases in the 

OPS Enforcement Division, with a very large percentage of these cases being in the food field, including meats." 11 Mr. Morgan particularly challenged the statement of the Association president, C. B. Heinemann, regarding inadequate enforcement and flagrant and widespread violations, stating: "Mr. Heinemann admitted he did not have information indicating existence of a single violation to bring to the attention of the OPS and added that he would not give such information to OPS even if he did have it because he was not obliged by law to do so." # # #

Re: 

USED MACHINE TOOLS IAC Scott-OPS-GPR-751 

The Used Machine Tools Industry Advisory Committee held its second meeting today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a proposed tailored pricing regulation for the industry. 

The first meeting of the committee was held on May 17.

The committee reviewed the proposed tailored pricing regulation in detail. 

In general, the proposed regulation provides for ceiling prices based on the manufacturer's list price as of a given date for an identical new machine tool, or for a most comparable new machine tool, against a percentage markdown based on the age and condition of the used machine tool being priced. 

Where a manufacturer did not have a list price in effect on a given date, for an identical new machine tool, the seller would determine the ceiling price of the used machine tool generally on the basis of comparable weight. 

The committee was opposed to the weight method of pricing as being impractical and difficult to apply. OPS officials told the committee that careful consideration will be given to the committee's objections in this connection.

Otherwise, the committee felt that the provisions of the proposed regulation were generally acceptable, subject to minor changes and clarifications which were suggested.

The meeting was conducted by Edward L. Norman, chief, Cutting Tools & 

Industrial Supply Section, Machinery Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attend ing were: Leslie J. Carson, chief, Machinery Branch; H. C. Thompson, Legal staff; Charles A. Simons, consultant; Ernest L. Inwood, branch economist; Ralph 

R. Irwin, business specialist; W. Y. Kulp, accountant; William E. Edwards,

Office of Enforcement; and, Harry Spack, Office for Industry Advisory Committees.

Coakley-OPS-GPR-752 

John W. Baker, retired president of the Philippine Refining Corp. of

New York, N. Y., has been appointed chief of the Fats and Oils Branch of the 

Food and Restaurant Division of the Office of Price Stabilization. 

He replaces Nelson H. Eddy who will continue to serve as consultant on a part-time basis for the Foods and Restaurant Division. 

Mr. Baker, who has held the position of president of the firm since 1922, also served with the government during World War II. He was a consultant in fats and oils for both the War Production Board and the War Food Administration.

Re: LIVESTOCK QUOTAS 

Although livestock slaughter quotas have been cancelled since August 1, the Office of Price Stabilization today reminded Class 1 and 2 slaughterers whose quota period did not end by July 31 that they must keep records of their slaughter of each species of livestock through the July 31 termination date.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use In Morning Papers 

SUNDAY, August 12, 1951

 Crossley-OPS-GPR-754 

Re: SMALL BUSINESS 

Michael V. DiSalle, Director of Price Stabilization, today established new policies and standards to safeguard the interests of small business in the pricecontrol program and simultaneously created the position of an Assistant to the 

Director for Small Business and an intra-agency Small Business Affairs Advisory 

Committee.

Appointments have not yet been made, but the committee will consist of a senior official from each major operating department of the agency, Mr. DiSalle said.

The policies and standards outlined by Mr. DiSalle today are based on recommendations of a temporary committee formed to develop an orderly program within OPS for small business. That committee has now been dissolved. 

Mr. DiSalle's statement says "OPS is keenly aware of the many problems confronting the operators of small business enterprises" and "the special problems of small business will continue to be reflected to the fullest possible extent in the basic pricing policies and techniques embodied in the regulations.' 11 If simpler pricing methods can be devised for small business with limited clerical facilities, this will be done to the maximum extent possible, consistent with practicable and enforceable stabilization policies, he said. "Special concern for small business must take the form of writing regulations in the simplest language, with an adequate comprehension of small business problems, so as to help the small businessman understand and comply with them, and to reduce to a bare minimum the clerical burdens imposed," the Director's statement said. Records required are to be no more onerous than those usually kept in establishments of comparable nature and size. 

Mr. DiSalle directed that all industry advisory committees appointed should continue to have fair representation of independent small business and that a senior official of every OPS regional and district office be assigned specific responsibility for handling the problems of small business. (over)

He instructed the Office of Field Operations to obtain a quarterly report from regional offices showing the number of small business complaints and a composite analysis and appraisal of the regulatory points in question. GPO-O- -OPS 358

4 The Office of Public Information will develop specialized material about the participation of small business in OPS, together with guides, trade bulletins, charts, and graphs which will assist small business operators. 

The Small Business Affairs Advisory Committee will provide an intra-agency mechanism for the consideration of special problems of small business and will serve as a device for the development of policies and standards to govern OPS relations with small business. It will advise the Director of Price Stabilization on recommendations originating with the Select Committees on Small Business of the Senate and House of Representatives and other government sources. 

In establishing the committee, Mr. DiSalle in a staff memorandum declared: "In order to assure the utmost attention to the problems of small business there is hereby created within the Office of Price Stabilization a Small Business Affairs Advisory Committee. The purpose of the committee is to provide an intraagency mechanism for the consideration of problems of small business and as a device for the development of policies and standards from time to time to govern our small business relations. "The committee will be composed of the head or senior representatives of the Office of Price Operations, Office of the Chief Counsel, Office of the Economic Advisor, Office of Enforcement, Office of Public Information, Office of Field Operations, Office of Management, Office of Accounting, Assistant to the Director for Special Assignments, and the Office of Advisory Committees. 

"The Assistant to the Director for Small Business shall serve as chariman of the committee. The committee shall conduct periodic meetings and be subject to call of the Director and the chariman of the committee. "The committee is charged with the following functions: 11 (a) The development of proposed policies, standards and precedures to govern small business operations in the Office of Price Stabilization. "(c) Giving advice to the Director relative to recommendations originating with the Select Committees on Small Business of the House and Senate and other governmental sources.

"(f) Considering such problems as may be referred to it from time to time by the Director or the Assistant to the Director for Small Business." # # # # # # # # #

Wednesday, August 8, 1951

Washington NEWSPRINT IAC 

Moore -OPS-GPR-755  

Members of the Newsprint Industry Advisory Committee at their second meeting today with OPS officials discussed provisions of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry and recommended that it provide a flat dollars and cents increase for all manufacturers over their newsprint prices under the General Ceiling Price Regulation to take care of increases in costs since the GCPR freeze. 

Committeemen said this would permit the industry to maintain its customary price structure, including freight allowances and differentials for super newsprint and newsprint made from waste. 

It would also permit continuation so-called "fringe" production which is helping to relieve the current newsprint shortage. This includes newsprint made on obsolete machinery, machinery intended for other types of production, or under other circumstances where production of marginal newsprint became profitable only under inducement of higher prices.

Committeemen said that fixing dollars and cents ceilings (as contrasted to dollars and cents increases over GCPR ceilings) would eliminate fringe production unless individual exceptions were made, and introduce other complications in their price structures. They said zone pricing as promulgated under OPA was impractical now and that they would prefer to continue their individual freight charge practices.

It was disclosed that a number of American newsprint manufacturers have established ceilings under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, of $116 per ton, which is equal to the price of Canadian newsprint. 

About 85 per cent of newsprint consumed in the United States is manufactured in Canada and not subject to price control. Canadian mills recently announced a $10 increase to $116, New York basis.

A number of American manufacturers showed costs under CPR 22 entitling them to ceilings higher than $116, but indicated they would maintain their prices at that level, in competition with Canadian prices. (over) 8675 GPO-O-OPS 359

The question was discussed whether ceilings should be imposed on the price that American consumers could pay, which would in effect be a ceiling price on imported newsprint. Committeemen said American publishers were in a better position to advise OPS on this subject than American newsprint manufacturers. 

They pointed out, however, that because of volume and lower costs, Canadian prices had always determined the price obtained for newsprint by American manu facturers.

Paperboard Branch.  Walter J. Damtoft, acting director, Forest Products Division; Fred Mears, consultant on newsprint; Marvin

Re: USED STEEL DRUM IAC Scott-OPS-GPR-756 

ST-4200, Ext.3491 

Members of the Used Steel Drum Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss proposed changes in the used steel drum ceiling price regulation (CPR 36).

This was the third meeting of the committee. Previous meetings were held on April 3 and July 17. 

Ceiling Price Regulation 36, issued May 11, establishes dollars-and-cents ceiling prices for raw and reconditioned steel drums and ceiling prices for services in reconditioning and lining raw steel drums. 

The committee discussed proposed minor changes in CPR 36 to clarify and make the regulation more workable. 

It was also proposed to amend the regulation to include 5 gallon steel pails, 100 lb. steel grease drums, and 15 gallon steel drums. The regulation at present covers only drums of 30 to 58 gallon capacity. 

Committeemen objected to the inclusion of 5 gallon pails and 100 lb. grease drums under the regulation, but felt that the 15 gallon drums might well be included. Members pointed out that 5 gallon pails and 100 lb. grease drums are a minor factor in the used drum business and usually require special handling under widely varying conditions and that pricing of these items could better be handled under the. General Ceiling Price Regulation.

It was brought to the attention of the committee that numerous complaints were being received by OPS from dealers that ceiling prices in the regulation did not permit them to operate on a sufficiently profitable basis. The committee suggested that OPS make a careful survey and investigation of these complaints to determine whether these dealers are actually in need of relief. 

General speaking, committee members felt that the ceiling prices established in the regulation are fair and equitable. 

The meeting was conducted by Karl P. Fuhrman, business analyst, Metals 

Branch, Industrial Materials and Manufactured Goods Division, OPS. Other OPS 

officials attending the meeting were: Abner Frank, legal staff; Walter R. 

Rogers, economist; Bruce Allen, accountant; Richard B. Buhrman and G. F. Hadlock,

Committees.

THURSDAY, August 9, 1951  Re: MANUFACTURERS' PRICES 

Crist-OPS-GPR-757 

An indefinite postponement of the mandatory effective date of six basic manufacturing regulations was granted today by the Office of Price 

Stabilization. 

The purpose of this action is to preserve the status quo until OPS can issue regulations to carry out the so-called Capehart amendment to the Defense 

Production Act of 1950. 

OPS had previously set August 13 as the deadline for five of the mamu facturers' regulations and August 15 for the Apparel Regulation. 

OPS had expected to issue adjustment provisions to carry out the 

Capehart amendment prior to August 13.

OPS officials said, however, that the problems encountered in trying to work out procedures under this amendment made it impossible to meet that early target date for issuing the adjustment provisions. 

The Capehart amendment provides that "upon application and a proper showing of prices and costs" the OPS shall adjust ceilings to reflect cost changes, including overhead, up to July 26. The OPS manufacturing regulations 

do not take into consideration increases or decreases in ovorhead costs and use an earlier cut-off date for figuring increases in materials and factory labor. 

Today's action extends the compulsory filing and reporting provisions as well as the compulsory pricing provisions.

Affected by today's action are the general manufacturers' regulation (CPR 22); machinery (CPR 30); cotton textile manufacturers (CPR 37); shoe manufacturers' (CPR 41); apparel manufacturers (CPR 45) and wool yarns and fabrics (CPR 18 Revised).

Thus many manufacturers, who have not already started pricing under these regulations, would have been forced to rollback prices under the existing terms of the regulations on August 13, and then permitted to come in at a later date and make application under this amendment for an adjustment which might have reduced or eliminated the amount of the rollback. 

Although today's action indefinitely postpones the compulsory effective date of these regulations, manufacturers at their option may elect to come under them at any time. In the case of CPR 22 and CPR 30, manufacturers who may wish to put increased prices into effect under the regulations, must also put all rollbacks into effect at the same time. Manufacturers who have already put 

CPR 22 and 30 into affect by selling at the increased prices permitted by the regulations must continue to keep the regulations in effect and apply all rollbacks required under them, An amendment to each of the regulations affected was issued,

GPO -OPS 367.

Thursday, August 9, 1951

Re: 

Tempo E 

Washington Moore-OPS-GPR-759  SUBCOMMITTEES OF THE WRAPPING PAPER MERCHANTS IAC AND FINE PAPER MERCHANTS LAC Subcommittees of the Wrapping Paper Merchants Industry Advisory Committee and the Fine Paper Merchants Industry Advisory Committee today made detailed recommendations on a proposed draft of a tailored regulation being prepared for their industry by OPS.

Members strongly recommended a single regulation whereunder paper merchants would determine their ceilings by applying their base period percentage markups to the cost of paper products to them. 

The regulation would follow the pattern of Supplementary Regulation 29 to the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, but would make special provision for practices in the industry with respect to packaging, delivery, size of shipments, services such as trimming and perforating, and other particulars. 

Members recommended that the first quarter of 1951 be employed as the base period in their regulation. Committeemen said their industry was in a depressed period immediately before the outbreak of the Korean war, particularly between 

May 24 and June 24, 1950, the interval mentioned for wholesalers in the new amendment to the Defense Production Act. Competition and need to move inventories had depressed margins. Committeemen made suggestions how data could be obtained to support the selection of the alternate base period. 

Committeemen said it would be impossible to write an equitable regulation based on uniform fixed margins because costs of distribution were higher in populous areas and varied from place to place across the United States.
