Friday, August 10, 1951

  

Re: GEORGIA EXCISE TAXES Scott-GPR-760  Harold Leventhal, Chief Counsel of the Office of Price Stabilization has ruled that sellers of gasoline, cigarettes, beer and wine in the state of Georgia must give effect to the recent 50 percent reduction in state excise taxes. 

Georgia adopted a 3 percent sales tax, effective June 30, 1951. Pending the effective date of the sales tax levy, the existing excise taxes on gasoline, cigarettes, beer and wine were substantially increased. 

These increased excise taxes were in effect during the period of December 19, 1950 to January 25, 1951, the base period under the General Ceiling Price Regulation and the retail gasoline order (CPR 13). When the sales tax became effective June 30, the excise taxes were then reduced by 50 percent.

Indications are that sellers generally have reflected the reduction in excise taxes and reduced their prices accordingly. However, some sellers have not given effect to the reduction and have raised the question of whether failure to reduce prices to the extent of the reduction in excise taxes would constitute a violation of OPS regulations. 

Section 11 of the retail gasoline order (CPR 13) and Section 20 of the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation provide that separately stated excise taxes may be collected by the seller over and above his regularly established ceiling price, but only to the extent of the tax actually in existence and paid by the seller. 

Accordingly, OPS has ruled that a seller would be in violation of OPS ceiling price regulations if he continued to add to his ceiling price, an excise tax which has been reduced (as in the case of the Georgia excise taxes) and which he no longer is required to pay or collect.

It is the general practice for gasoline stations to post a conspicuous sign stating separately the price of gasoline and the amount of Federal or state excise tax per gallon. With respect to cigarettes, beer and wine, each package of cigarettes and each container of beer or wine is stamped or printed or a stamp affixed to show the exact amount of excise tax. (over)

Signs posted by gas stations have customarily served to notify purchasers of the amounts being collected by the seller for Federal and state excise taxes. GPO-O-OPS 370

Such postings constitute a separate statement of taxes within the meaning of Section 11 of retail gasoline order (CPR 13). Similarly, a printed or stamped statement or stamp affixed to each package of cigarettes or each container of beer or wine would constitute a separate statement of tax within the meaning of Section 20 of GCPR. 

This interpretation, Mr. Leventhal said, "is fair and equitable in view of the language and intention of the regulations, gives full effect and consideration to the practices customary in the sale of the commodities involved, and is consistent with the intention of the State of Georgia in reducing the taxes".

RE: OPS PROTESTS PROPOSED ROUND- TRIP RAIL FAR INCREASES. 

A protest against proposed increases in railroad round-trip passenger fares has been lodged, with the Interstate Commerce Commission by the Office of Price Stabilization.

Browne-OPS-GPR-761  

Continuing its efforts to protect the value of the dollar and stem inflationary trends, the OPS asked the I.C.C. to suspend the proposed increases, hold a full public hearing in the matter and institute an investigation to determine whether the proposed increases in railroad fares are 'necessary, just and reasonable."

The proposed increases vary, it was pointed out. For instance, where a one-way coach fare is $20.00 and the round-trip fare is $30.40, it is proposed to increase the round-trip fare to $34.00, an increase of $3.60. Where a one-way first-class fare is $40.00 and the round-trip fare $72.00, it is proposed to increase the round-trip fare to $76.00, an increase of $4.00.

The OPS requests that should the suspension and public hearing be granted by the I.C.C. the agency be afforded an opportunity to appear and participate in the proceedings.

OPS holds that a full public hearing is warranted prior to establishment of the proposed increases since the I.C.C., in authorizing the general freight rate increases granted on August 8 to the petitioning railroads in Ex Parte No. 175, stated that such increases "were and are designed to enable them to meet steadily mounting costs of operation and rising deficits in net railway operating income from their passenger service during the post-war period." "The proposed increases in round-trip passenger fares published in the new tariffs appear to be arbitrary in nature and may be inflationary in effect," warns the OPS in its protest. "This protestant contends that such proposed increases should not be permitted to become effective prior to a full hearing by this Commission concerning the lawfulness of such proposed 

(over)

GPO- 0 -OPS 374

"Full public hearing concerning the proposed increases in round-trip passenger fares will enable this protestant to become fully informed as to the necessity for any increases in such fares thereafter authorized by this 

Commission. 

"The information thus obtained will accordingly make it possible for this protestant to evaluate the potential inflationary effects of any increases that may be granted upon the cost of living generally, and also upon the living standards of particular classes of the public that may be directly affected thereby."

In a separate case, following a similar protest by the OPS, the Interstate Commerce Commission August 9, 1951 suspended proposed increases in commuter passenger fares and promised an early hearing in the matter.

MONDAY, AUGUST 13, 1951 Re: MARINE SUPPLIERS' INDUSTRY MEETING   

Cost increases incurred by the industry in supplying meat to various types of ships, and uncertain cost factors in their operation, were pointed out by members of the Marine Suppliers' Industry Advisory Committee meeting with the Office of Price Stabilization in Washington on Friday, August 3, 1951. 

The industry cited increased labor, meat and storage and freezing costs as requiring special pricing provisions for their industry. The higher costs incurred in serving tankers, foreign ships and tramp steamers pose especially acute problems to the industry. 

Commodities other than meat do not work any special hardships on the industry under OPS pricing provisions, the industry said. OPS representatives agreed to make an accounting survey of the industry to determine costs and to take these costs into consideration.

MONDAY, August 13, 1951 

Washington TEXTILES-CLARIFICATION Crossley-OPS-GPR-764 

The Office of Price Stabilization today issued the following clarifica tion as to the effects on operations of the textile industry of the recently announced indefinite postponement of the effective dates of six basic manufacturing regulations: 

SILK AND SYNTHETICS (Rayon, nylon, orlon, dacron and others)

Until further action by OPS, a manufacturer or converter who is still pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation has the option of continuing to price under the General Ceiling Price Regulation or under Ceiling Price 

Regulation 22. If a manufacturer or converter elects to use CPR 22 for one fabric, he must use it for all fabrics, and take his roll-backs as well as his roll forwards. A manufacturer or converter who prior to this time made 

CPR 22 effective as to him, cannot now return to pricing under the GCPR, but must remain under CPR 22.

COTTON YARNS AND FABRICS 

The above CPR 22 requirements also apply to converters of cotton gray goods.

A manufacturer of cotton goods covered by CPR 37, who is still pricing some or all of his fabrics under GCPR, has the option, until further action by OPS, of continuing to price such fabrics under GCPR or beginning to price them fabric by fabric under CPR 37. Furthermore, he may price some of them under 

GCPR and some under CPR 37. If a fabric is priced under CPR 37, the manufacturer must file the report required under that regulation before delivery under 

CPR 37. 

WOOL YARNS AND FABRICS 

Fabric by fabric, a manufacturer who is still pricing some or all of his fabrics under GCPR may elect until further action by OPS, to use GCPR, CPR 18, or CPR 18, Rev. 1, for those fabrics.

OPS officials pointed out that this clarification does not represent any departure from previous interpretations of these regulations. A manufacturer was required to price all of his products under CPR 22 once he priced any item under it, whereas a manufacturer under CPR's 37 or 18, Rev. 1, always had the option, until the mandatory effective date, of pricing fabric by fabric under the GCPR or, if he elected, the numbered regulation. Today's clarification merely carries forward this difference in the regulations, OPS said. GPO-O- -OPS 391

A practicing member of the New York Bar since 1932, he has done considerable work in the field of legal, governmental and economic research. During 

1947-1950 he served as special consultant to Governor A. E. Driscoll and to 

Chief Justice A. T. Vanderbilt of New Jersey. He was assistant director for 

Public Administration for the Pennsylvania Economy League in Harrisburg, from September 1946 to May 27, 1947. 

Mr. Temple served in the field of administration and programming for the 

War Production Board and the Office of Price Administration and was a staff member of the U. S. National Resources Planning Board during 1942-1943. 

Earlier, he was administrative and legal consultant and director of research for the Constitutional Revision Commission of the State of New Jersey. He did similar work for various county and municipal offices in Cook County and the city of Chicago.

He has been a lecturer in the Department of Government of Brooklyn College and also has lectured for a number of public affairs organizations. 

He has been active in civic affairs in Kings and Queens Counties, N. Y.

Ph. D. degree at New York University.

PRESS RELEASE ADVANCE RELEASE  For Use in Morning Papers 

Tempo E 

Washington Re: INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEES 

Coakley-OPS-GPR-766  

In preparing price control regulations, the Office of Price Stabilization has obtained the advice and counsel of nearly 400 Industry Advisory Committees which comprise a cross section of American industry, a recent report by Mrs. 

Ethel B. Gilbert, director, Office of Industry Advisory Committees reveals. 

These committees, set up by OPS as required by the Defense Production Act, bring together business and government experts who pool their ideas and experience to work out effective pricing action and build a bulwark against inflation. More than 500 such meetings have been held since the first committee was appointed last February.

Many segments of an industry have their own Industry Advisory Committee, Mrs. Gilbert explained. The rubber industry, for instance, is represented by 15 committees, ranging from the Tire and Tube Manufacturers Committee to 

Rubber Soles and Heels, Surgical Adhesive Plasters and Rubber Hose Committees. 

In the Chemicals and Drugs Division there are 24 committees;

Food and 

Restaurant Division, 76; Industrial Materials and Manufactured Goods Division 

(building materials, machinery, metals, automobiles), 81; Consumer Soft Goods 

Division (textiles, apparel, leather, furs, fibres), 66; Forest Products

Division (wood, pulp and paper), 79; Transportation, Public Utilities and 

Fuels Division, 21; Consumer Durable Goods (appliances, housewares, home furnishings), 30; Services, Export-Import Division, 2.

Even within a committee the problems may be so varied that subcommittees are necessary to handle them effectively. OPS has named 26 such subcommittees. 

The Leather Industry Advisory Committee, for example, has a subcommittee for goat, kid and cabretta leather; another for side upper leather and a third for calf leather. The Special Paperboard Industry Advisory Committee is divided into subcommittees on cardboard, food container paperboard, and special indus trial paperboard. The Mechanical Rubber Goods Committee has eight subcommit tees. 

The function of the committees is purely an advisory one and they do not actually draft price regulations. However, their recommendations are given serious consideration by OPS officials and the information they supply as to costs of operation, availability of materials and equipment and problems peculiar to the industry are studied carefully by OPS pricing and accounting experts before a regulation is issued, Mrs. Gilbert said. (over) GPO-O-OPS 387

-- • 

Because OPS regulations must be adaptable to all segments of an industry, the Industry Advisory Committee must be representative of all segments. In naming committee members the agency includes both big business and small business, all sections of the country where the industry is found, members of trade associations and non-members, and representatives of each type of operation within the industry, according to Mrs. Gilbert. As a result, executives from the country's largest department stores share the council table with owners of small-town independent stores and heads of great grocery chains meet with the corner grocers who operate small, family-type stores.

Members of the Industry Advisory Committees often write to Mrs. Gilbert or to Price Stabilization Director Michael V. DiSalle expressing their approval of the way a committee operates or their pleasure at having an opportunity to serve as a members. "1 One industrialist wrote that after attending an Industry Advisory Committee meeting he had lost all criticism of the government's handling of price controls. 

Another reported that ...the meeting which was held on July 23 was on such a plane that there is no doubt in my mind that further relations with the agency can and will be very cordial and cooperative." 

Almost to a man, Mrs. Gilbert reported, the Industry Advisory Committee members seem to come to Washington with a deep sense of responsibility, to do what they can for their country in a national emergency rather than with the idea that they must get the best deal possible for their company or their industry.

Monday, August 13, 1951   Re: KRAFT PAPER IAC Moore-OPS-GPR-767 

Members of the Kraft Paper Industry Advisory Committee at their second meeting with OPS officials today made detailed recommendations on the proposed provisions of a tailored regulation for their industry which would fix dollars and cents ceiling prices on seven key grades of unbleached kraft paper manufactured in integrated mills in the South and West. 

The dollars and cents ceilings would apply to about 60 percent of the unbleached kraft paper produced in the country. Other grades made by these mills, amounting to another 20 percent of the nation's total production, would be determined by differentials from key grades. Historic differentials would also apply to special size rolls and sheets, variations in weight, colors, packaging and small lots.

Under the proposed regulation integrated manufacturers in the Northeast and Lake states, who make about 6 percent of the total production of unbleached kraft paper, would employ as their ceilings the ceilings they had in effect on a specified date, possibly at the level under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR. These mills mostly produce high grades of specification papers at premium prices.

Integrated mills are those mills which manufacture both unbleached kraft pulp and paper, and account for 86 percent of the total national production of kraft paper. 

The balance of 14 percent is produced in non-integrated or converter mills, whose costs tend to be higher because they must purchase market pulp. 

Under the proposed regulation ceiling prices of non-integrated manufacturers of unbleached kraft paper might be fixed at the level of the Manufac turers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. 

The different pricing devices for different segments of the industry were proposed because of the peculiar character of the industry. Mills in the South and West generally are low cost mills operating with modern equipment where pulpwood is abundant. To meet the competition of the low cost mills in the 

South and West, Northeast manufacturers have tended to specialize in quality and specification papers. The converter mills, moreover, could not operate profitably at ceilings which would be adequate for the integrated mills. (over) GPO-O-OPS 390-

The key grades on which it is proposed to spell out ceilings are: 

Wrapping paper, counter rolls. 

Butchers paper, counter rolls.

Grocers and variety bag paper, mill rolls. 

Shipping sack paper, mill rolls. 

Gumming paper, mill rolls. 

Envelope paper, mill rolls.

The proposed prices discussed for these key grades were weighted averages of GCPR prices, which means that the regulation might retain GCPR ceilings for almost 90 percent of the unbleached kraft paper industry.

Unbleached kraft paper is defined as any paper of G.E. brightness of less than 35, containing 75 percent or more of unbleached kraft sulphate fibre in basis weights of 18 pounds or more. The South and West are described as all areas south of Ohio and all territory west of the Rockies. 

Today's meeting was conducted by M. C. Walsh, deputy chief, Pulp, Paper and Paperboard Branch, and J. R. W. Street, industrial consultant for kraft paper.

Washington MECHANICAL RUBBER GOODS IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-769  

Members of the Mechanical Rubber Goods Industry Advisory Committee at their fifth meeting today with OPS officials recommended that their industry be permitted by amendment the option of pricing their products category by category under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. 

Under the terms of Amendment 21 to CPR 22, manufacturers still under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, have the option until further action by OPS of pricing either under GCPR or CPR 22. However, if they elect to apply CPR 22 to any of their products they must apply it to all of them subject to CPR 22.

Committeemen reported that cost increases vary widely from one category to another and that hardships were being experienced in certain categories. 

Because, CPR 22 would result in mixed rollbacks and rollforwards throughout the industry, long line companies were standing on their GCPR prices until the price situation is clarified. This has prevented single line companies in squeeze categories from taking advantage of rollforwards under CPR 22 because of price competition from companies maintaining their old prices. If ap- plication of CPR 22 was permitted by categories, committeemen said it would tend to relieve such situations.

The committee discussed pricing of rubber hose. Under CPR 22 there would be mixed rollbacks and rollforwards in the 23 product lines. The question was explored whether a manufacturer now under GCPR, in the interest of price stability and anticipating CPR 22 would ultimately be obligatory, could sell below his GCPR ceiling and at the same level as his CPR 22 ceiling without putting CPR 22 generally in effect. Committeemen requested a clarifying ruling on this point.. (Over) A report was received from the Molded, Extruded and Lathe-Cut Rubber Goods subcommittee indicating that large manufacturers of such products preferred to price under CPR 22 while smaller manufacturers favored remaining at GCPR prices. The latter expressed doubts whether they could take their rollforwards because of competition, while at the same time they would have to take their rollbacks under price control.

READY MIXED CONCRETE IAC Scott-OPS-GPR-770  The Ready Mixed Concrete Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems. 

The industry is presently pricing under the General Ceiling Price 

Regulation (GCPR). 

The committee was immediately concerned with the critical problem of many industry members who are faced with increased costs for cement and increased transportation costs in cases where it has become necessary to obtain supplies of cement from other than normal sources. 

In many areas a serious cement shortage has developed due to greatly increased construction of facilities incident to the defense program. 

Concrete suppliers in these areas normally obtain their supply of cement from nearby sources. To meet the increased demand it has been necessary for these suppliers to obtain cement from distant sources involving greatly increased transportation costs and in some cases higher f.o.b. mill prices for cement.

OPS officials told the committee that an order is being prepared to give relief in these situations, but that it is designed to give relief only in the case of increased transportation costs. 

The committee recommended that relief should be given to take care of both increased cement cost and increased transportation costs in these situations. In any event, the committee felt that quick and immediate relief should be afforded these suppliers to cover their increased transportation costs on out of area cement purchases. 

The committee discussed the matter of developing a tailored pricing regulation for the industry. Industry operating and pricing practices were discussed in considerable detail. OPS officials advised the committee that a subcommittee will be appointed to work with OPS in the further development of a tailored pricing regulation for the industry. Tuesday, August 14, 1951

  

Barkley-OPS-GPR 771  Re: PORK LAC 

A proposed regulation establishing uniform ceiling prices for sales of dressed hogs and pork products, except at the retail level, was discussed section by section today at a meeting between officials of the Office of Price Stabiliza tion and members of the Pork Industry Advisory Committee. 

Upon the issuance of this regulation, it is contemplated that OPS will make adjustments in retail ceilings to reflect the new dressed pork and wholesale pork ceilings. 

Dressed hogs and most pork products, including hams, bacon and cooked pork products, are now covered by the General Ceiling Price Regulation which froze each seller at his highest selling price during the December 19, 1950-January 

26, 1951, base period.

As a result, ceiling prices among different sellers are now at varying levels. The proposed regulation will supersede these ceilings and establish uniform prices for dressed hogs and for pork cuts. Ceilings on cuts will be established by standardized cuts.

The regulation also will supplant the recently issued ceiling price regulation (SR 47 to GCPR) which established, temporarily, specific ceilings for pork loins weighing 16 pounds or less.

As in the temporary pork loin regulation, the proposed regulation will follow the industry practice of pricing cuts of pork on a basis of weight, with differentials between the lighter and heavier weight cuts and for different types of processing.

The committee was informed that the ceilings will also vary by zones with the base zone being Iowa and parts of adjoining states. Additions to the base ceilings will be permitted in other zones to cover transportation and other costs to encourage shipments from the big hog producing areas to other parts of the nation. It

It is also intended to have additions to the ceilings for local slaughter in some of the deficit hog producing regions of the country. is planned to set up six regions for this purpose, but the regions are subject to revision. 

(Over) 

GPO-O-OPS 401

In general, member of the committee expressed themselves as favoring uniform ceilings. They urged, however, that the price structure be established at a level which would encourage wide distribution of pork products. 

A message was read from a South Carolina group of packers which called for early action on specific dollars and cents uniform ceilings for pork, or the decontrol of pork. 

On one proposal the industry recommended a transition period. This was a provision requiring that cooked wholesale pork cuts be identified on the wrapping as "Cooked Cuts".

Spokesmen said a transition period is needed to give handlers sufficient time to have the words stamped on coverings. It was explained that cellophane is used for many cuts and there have been delays in obtaining supplies.

PRESS RELEASE    

Wednesday, August 15, 1951

RE: 

PRECISION MECHANICAL SPRING IAC Scott-OPS-GPR-772 

The precision Mechanical Spring Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems.

Products of the industry are covered under the machinery ceiling price regulation (CPR 30), but the industry is currently pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR). Committee members said it would be extremely difficult for the industry to operate under the pricing provisions of CPR 30. 

Precision mechanical springs cover a wide range of specifications ranging from hair springs used in delicate instruments, and weighing a minute fraction of an ounce, to large springs used in heavy machinery, ships, trains, guns, etc., and weighing from a pound to several thousand pounds. 

These springs are used as components in a vast range of consumer durable goods and in industrial machinery and equipment of all kinds. 

Most springs are manufactured to individual customer's rigid specifications. Some companies will produce as many as 100,000 different types of springs annually, all on the basis of individual specifications. 

Most spring manufacturers have a formula method of pricing best suited to the individual requirements of their particular type of plant operation. 

The committee discussed in considerable detail the wide range of operating and pricing practices in the industry with a view of determining some basis for a tailored ceiling price regulation. The discussion did not result in any well defined conclusions.

The automatic screw machine industry and the metal stamping industry have pricing problems similar to those of the precision mechanical spring industry. 

OPS officials said that a subcommittee would be formed consisting of four members from each of these three industry advisory committees. This subcommittee will meet with OPS in about two weeks to further consider the pricing problems common to these three industries.

PRESS RELEASE    

Wednesday, August 15, 1951 

Re: BOOK PAPER IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-773 

 Members of the Book Paper Industry Advisory Committee today recommended that the Office of Price Stabilization issue a tailored regulation for their industry which would spell out dollars and cents ceiling prices on seven key grades of book paper. 

Ceilings on other grades and variations in finishing, packaging, trimming, size of shipments and other particulars would be determined by differentials existing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, except for long-term contract prices, which would be determined by the differentials existing from 

January 1 to June 24, 1950. 

The proposed spelled out ceilings would be arrived at by the "bulk line" technique and would be equal or greater than the ceilings on the bulk of production in the respective grades as determined under the Manufacturers' 

General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. The bulk line ceilings recommended would be several per cent higher than weighted average of CPR 22 ceilings. 

Committeemen recommended that there be a clear delineation between coated groundwood and book papers and that manufacturers be permitted to follow their historic pricing customs in determining where to price certain papers that might qualify as either.

Members of a nine man subcommittee met for the sixth time with OPS officials in the morning and made detailed recommendations on the wording and ceilings in the proposed regulation. In the afternoon the main committee met for the second time and approved with minor changes the recommendations of the subcommittee.

If any changes in OPS policy resulting from recent legislation require a major deviation from the committee's recommendations, the committee expressed a desire for further discussions before OPS issues a tailored regulation. 

Committeemen said they could price their products on a reasonably satisfactory basis under CPR 22 and might recommend that their industry continue under CPR 22 rather than a tailored regulation substantially different from that recommended.

Individual members objected to recommending any ceiling prices prior to the establishment of firm ceilings on waste paper used in the manufacture of their products.

The meeting was conducted by Daniel H. Keck, industrial consultant for groundwood and book papers.

Thursday, Aug. 16. 1951

F ICE OF PRICE STABILIZATION  

Re: FOOD DISTRIBUTION IAC 

Plans for a nationwide survey of grocery price markups--at both the wholesale and retail levels--were outlined today by officials of the Office of Price Stabilization at a joint meeting of the Wholesale and Retail Food 

Distributors Industry Advisory Committees. 

Barkley-OPS-0-776 

ST.4200; Ext. 3491 

The survey will be made to determine how une present markups in the CPS grocery Ceiling Price Regulations (CPRS 14, 15 and 16) compare with margins prevailing in the pre-Korea month, May 24, 1950-June 24, 1950, the base period used in the regulation, and with margins and prices prevailing generally from 

January through June of 1950.

George L. Mehren, acting director of OPS' Food and Restaurant Division, of which Food Distribution is a Branch, outlined the general objectives of the survey. Mr. Mehren said that the major goal is revision of the present OPS markups to reflect cost changes and the new requirements of the Defense Production 

Act Amendments of 1951. 

A further goal, he added, is to determine the need for establishing margins for non-food items handled mainly by food dealers such as household supplies. 

Present OPS grocery markups are generally those used for most food cate gories by the Office of Price Administration during World War II with some adjustments. 

When the OPS regulations were issued last March 28, the agency announced a study would be made to determine whether these markups are representative of the pre-Korea period.

OPS said at that time that should the survey indicate that the markups are either too low or too high the regulations would be promptly revised to reflect results of the study.

The survey will be made by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the Department of Labor, with the cooperation of the Food Distribution Branch of OPS. 

BLS is the Government agency which compiles statistics on the wholesale and retail prices of consumers' goods. 1 (over)

an early "test run" of the survey is scheduled in a few typical cities. 

When the results of this test run are studied and the final scope of the survey agreed upon, it will be undertaken on a nationwide basis. 

The survey will include food items covered by the grocery regulations and other foods such as milk, butter and cheese. Markups on non-food items, the household and other supplies commonly handled by grocers, also will be studied. 

Spokesmen for both OPS and the BLS outlined plans for the survey. Recommendations were sought from members of the committees as to what items should be included, what size container should be considered, the proposed method of sampling and what additional questions should be included. 

Markups of institutional wholesalers as well as service wholesalers will be surveyed, along with those of retail dealers. 

Emerson Brown, chief of the Food Distribution Branch, presided at the joint meeting. Lelan Jamison of the Branch, outlined the present status of the grocery regulations and listed amendments which have been adopted since their issuance. He also announced plans for a survey of primary distributors of food and frozen food distributors. 

Julius Davidson of the Branch, told of OPS' part in the survey and Edward D. Hollander, chief, Division of Price and Cost of Living, Bureau of Labor 

Statistics, told of BLS' part.

Mr. Hollander emphasized that data gathered from individuals during the survey will be kept in strictest confidence by BLS.

After the joint meeting, the three groups represented--the Service Wholesalers, the Institutional Wholesalers and the Retailers--broke up into separate meetings for discussion of individual problems. Other OPS officials at the conference included W. H. Zimmerman, E. Lewis 

Cook, Otto Rauschwalbe of the Branch Staff; Alexander G. Hardy, Branch attorney; and W. R. Thomas, Jr., of the office of Advisory Committees.

PRESS RELEASE    

Re: SAND AND GRAVEL IAC Scott-OPS-GPR-778  The Sand and Gravel Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems. 

The committee represents sand and gravel producers. These producers are currently pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation..

Members pointed out that producers in many areas are experiencing a declining market due to the reduction and restriction in construction work. 

Members said that, generally speaking, there is little, if any, pressure on ceiling prices in the industry at the present time. Some members felt there is no need for price control on sand and gravel because of the highly competitive conditions that have always existed in this industry. 

Because inbound and outbound transportation costs generally represent the larger part of the cost of sand and gravel, the committee felt that increased transportation costs since the GCPR base period (December 19, 1950 to January 25, 1951) should be permitted to be reflected in ceiling prices. 

OPS officials said consideration was being given to the matter of granting relief in the case of outbound increased transportation costs based on rate increases granted to common carriers by order of the Inter state Commerce Commission. 

The committee asked that OPS make a study of increased inbound transportation costs and increased outbound contract carrier truck rates. Also that OPS give consideration to increased transportation costs where deliveries are made by trucks operated by sand and gravel producers.

The committee discussed industry operating and pricing practices and made numerous suggestions and recommendations for consideration in the drafting of a tailored regulation.

OPS officials said a subcommittee will be appointed to advise further with OPS on current pricing problems and the drafting of a tailored regulation. (over)

Friday August 17, 1951

Tempo E 

Washington Re: Slaughter Enforcement Cole-OPS-GPR-779 

A nationwide campaign to enforce cattle price ceilings will be undertaken at once, Michael V. DiSalle, Director of Price Stabilization, announced today.

For this purpose a large part of the OPS enforcement staff will be directed to concentrate on enforcing cattle prices and they will be assisted by meat experts from Regional and District offices, who will be used to augment the size and effectiveness of the force to be devoted to the program. 

The Justice Department will be asked to give priority to cases involving cattle and beef ceiling violations, Mr. DiSalle said.

Mr. DiSalle pointed out that since the abolition of OPS's authority to allocate slaughter quotas equitably, the agency has been receiving numerous complaints from packers that they were unable to purchase cattle at the ceiling price.

Under the slaughter quota system, all the available supplies of meat for a slaughter period were divided between all registered slauthterers, on the same percentage basis they had previously slaughtered. The power to continue this allocation system was removed by congress in the Devense Production Act 

Amendments of 1951. 

"Since we are no longer able to channel meat into regular normal channel. through the slaughter quota system, there are growing indications of maldistribution. This situation, of course, puts a strain on legal prices, and threatens to move the available supply into fewer areas where higher--and illegal--prices may be obtainable", Mr. DiSalle said. There are indications that ceiling price violators are outbidding legitimate slaughterers and are extending their operations far beyond normal. As a result honest packers in the absence of slaughter quotas find it difficult to get cattle at the legal prices and they are being forced to reduce their cattle purchases substantially below normal volume..

The program to obtain enforcement of live cattle ceilings will contain the 

1. Teams of OPS enforcement officers and meat experts will inspect plants which have been slaughtering abnormally high amounts of cattle to determine whether these plants have been buying cattle (over) (PO-0--UPS 438

--  at higher prices than are permitted by Ceiling Price Regulation 23, the live cattle regulation. These investigators will check accounting records, weighing methods and weight scales to determine whether there have been any violations. 

2. While at these plants, these investigators will check their records to determine whether these companies have violated Ceiling Price Regulation 24 by selling dressed beef at above ceiling prices. 

3. Immediate enforcement action will be taken against those slaughterers who have violated Ceiling Price Regulation 23, by failing to file promptly their drove compliance reports, OPS Public Forms 13.

Mr. DiSalle further announced that OPS officials will meet with an Industry 

Advisory Committee of beef slaughterers on Wednesday, August 22, to consider steps to be taken with respect to ceiling prices on cattle in view of the abolition of slaugher quotas. 

On the agenda of the meeting will be a review of the operation of the present system of cattle ceilings as well as a consideration of possible alternatives which would make ceilings applicable to sellers as well as buyers and to each individual animal sold, either by rail grading or live grading.

Specifically, the agenda of the meeting will cover the following points: 

1. Whether or not to lower the freight allowance to eastern and far western markets. Inder the present regulation, slaughterers in eastern markets are given up to $1.25 per hundredweight to compensate for the loss of meat weight in cattle during shipment. There is some indication that such allowances are too high and as a result cattle are being drained from the midwest to the east and far west. The Office of Price Stabilization is therefore considering lowering the amount of the allowance. 

2. Review of the compliance requirements for slaughterers who have been unable to obtain a normal supply of cattle. 

3. Establishment of an overriding ceiling for cattle. The present ceiling price cattle regulation does not limit the amount which the buyer may pay for any particular steer. It merely requires that over an accounting period the average purchase price be within the prescribed ceilings. In order to prevent bidding up of prime grades of cattle, consideration is to be given to the use of a top limit which would be the maximum which would be paid for any steer. 4. Investigation of other methods of establishing and enforcing ceiling prices, including ceiling prices on live cattle by grades. OPS officials explained that the present cattle ceilings applied to slaughterers and not to sellers and applied on an average basis to all cattle slaughtered during a month rather than to individual animals. Mr. DiSalle stated that in the absence of quotas the present system of cattle ceilings might prove difficult to enforce and that the abolition of quotas makes it necessary to consider alternative methods of holding cattle prices at reasonable levels. 5. 

A review of the functions and operations of order buyers.

Re: EXPORT PRICE CONTROL 

Browne-OPS-GPR-780  

Office of Price Stabilization today clarified provisions of its export regulation, Ceiling Price Regulation 61, affecting sales made after July 30, 1951 and completed before August 26, 1951.

It did this by announcing that on all such sales, the seller is granted the option of pricing either under CPR 61 or any other applicable regulation, including the General Ceiling Price Regulation.

In making its announcement, OPS restated the provision that all sales made after July 30, 1951, for delivery after August 26, 1951 are subject to 

CPR 61, and that filings of markups under CPR 61 must be made within 15 days after first sale of commodity or product line. A seller may file markups determined under CPR 61 prior to a sale under that regulation. 

CPR 61, the export regulation, provides that American exporters may not add more than their pre-Korean percentage markups to domestic prices in selling abroad.

Monday, August 20, 1951.

Browne-OPS-GPR-781 ST-4200; Ext 3491 

CALIFORNIA POWER RATE INCREASE 

The Office of Price Stabilization today opposed a million dollar increase in electric rates proposed to be established by the California Electric Power Company as "a long, forward step in the upward spiral of inflation, contributing its full share to the threat of runaway, uncontrollable inflation." 

OPS made its position known in a brief filed with the California Public 

Utilities Commission, San Francisco by Director Michael V. DiSalle through 

OPS counsels Bryce Rea, Jr., and John J. Kirby. The California Commission had requested briefs from all parties to the California rate proceeding involving several days of public hearings at which Dr. Allen R. Ferguson, OPS economist, testified on the inflationary aspects of the increase.

The brief maintained that the power company failed to justify an increase at this time either under OPS pricing policies or State Commission rate making standards, and asked the Commission to assist OPS in its battle against inflation by denying the application for a rate increase. "Control of inflation cannot be accomplished unless everybody bears his share of the burden," the OPS brief declared. "The size, scope and extent of any particular increase are irrelevant. Inflation feeds on small increases. 

Their cumulative effect does incalculable harm.' 11 The power company serves an area of the State which has recently had a phenomenal growth in population, caused by the expansion of war industries and war plants since the outbreak of the Korean war. Counties served by the company include Mono, Inyo, Kern, San Bernardino, Riverside and Imperial. 

The OPS brief takes the position that increases in rates should be permitted by regulatory bodies only to the extent necessary to enable a utility to earn a sufficient return to meet the demands of the public for its service.

The brief further enunciates it to be the policy of the Director of Price Stabilization, with respect to prices which are at the general level of fairness and equity established by the Congress in the Defense Production Act, to allow increases only to assure the continuation of essential services and to alleviate existing economic hardship. 9586-2830 GPO-O-OPS 499

"In this case, "the brief declares, "the applicant has not said that its present rates are unfair or inequitable. There is no existing threat to continued service, or indeed to expansion of service. There is no existing economic hardship. If and when the problem of financing which are applicant prophesies arises, or when that prophecy can be substantiated by evidence; when, after a period of operation with its new plant, it has accumulated experience and data as to costs, revenues, volume of sales, and when market conditions can be predicted on a basis in fact, it will be time enough to consider an application for a rate increase." # # # # # #

Re: VARIETY TURNED AND SHAPED WOOD PRODUCTS IAC Members of the Variety Turned and Shaped Wood Products Industry 

Advisory Committee at their second meeting today with OPS officials made detailed recommendations for a proposed tailored regulation which would provide for pricing their products by formula. 

The industry manufacturers a variety of wood products including such items as handles, dowels, skewers, plugs, cores, bushings, spools and variety turnings.

Under the proposed regulation manufacturers would determine their ceilings by formula including material costs, freight, waste factor, labor, direct and indirect expenses and net margin.

Committeemen recommended the latest permissible cut-off date for computing their labor, material and freight costs be adopted, specifically, the date of issuance of the regulation. They said, however, they could operate reasonably satisfactorily using the cut-off date provided in the 

Capehart amendment, July 26, 1951, unless there are future mounting cost increases.

Members said it would be satisfactory to apply the same formulas they employed during the first half of 1950 in computing their ceilings under the proposed regulation, as the formulas generally speaking remain constant.

It was proposed that percentage factors in their formulas for direct and indirect expenses and margin employed during the base period be converted into dollars and cents mark-ups per unit which would be added to allowable costs in determining ceilings under the new regulation. 

If and when dollars and cents ceilings are spelled out for lumber, the lumber ceilings would be used for the material costs in the formula to determine ceilings on shaped and turned wood products. 

It was proposed that the regulation eliminate reporting requirements, and that provision be made for individual hardship adjustments on application to OPS.

The committee discussed whether dollars and cents ceiling prices might be fixed on certain items manufactured by the industry, such as dowels, skewers and paint brush handles. (over)

GPO-O-OPS 500

Committeemen reported that customarily the industry sells these items at uniform prices due to competition and dollars and cents ceiling prices would be welcomed by the industry. It was suggested that subcommittees be named to study dollars and cents ceilings for these items.

Press Release    

Tuesday, August 21, 1951

Moore-OPS-GPR-783  

Re: WOOD HEEL, MANUFACTURERS SUBCOMMITTEE Members of the Subcommittee of the Wood Heel Manufacturers Industry 

Advisory Committee at their second meeting with OPS officials today recommended that their industry be included in the coverage of an interim regulation under which manufacturers of turned, shaped and allied wood products would determine their ceiling prices by formula. 

The subcommittee also recommended that OPS continue cost studies with the objective of writing a tailored regulation fixing dollars and cents ceilings on wood heels, drawn up on the lines of Amendment 7 to 

MPR 420, the old OPA regulation. The subcommittee recommended that wedges be included with heels under the dollars and cents ceilings. 

The committee discussed the type of information that would be required from the industry to determine dollars and cents ceilings. It was suggested they might be determined from pre-Korean prices, current prices under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, and prices to be determined under the proposed interim regulation.

The subcommittee reported their industry had undertaken to make an independent study of costs to assist OPS in drafting such a tailored regulation.

The proposed interim regulation would also cover wood products produced by other industries, including venetian blind wood slats, handles, picker stick blanks, ski billets, shunt squares, tobacco sticks, wood lasts, bowling pins, dowels, skewers, excelsior, clothes pins, rough turned bobbins, plugs, cores, bushings, bungs, shoe pegs, artificial limb blocks, cleat stock, wooden pallets, skids, canvas binder slats, lobster traps, trellises, spokes, axles, rims, tobacco pipe stock, butchers blocks, spools and variety turnings.

Under the interim regulation manufacturers would determine their ceilings by employing a formula that would include material costs, freights, waste, labor, direct and indirect expenses and net margin. 

Committeemen recommended that the cut-off-date on labor, material, freight and expenses correspond with that named in the Capehart amendment, July 26, 1951. Under the formula dollars and cents margins would be determined by the highest dollars and cents margins in effect during the base period. Committeemen suggested the base period be nine months or a year, ending 

June, 1950. (over) GPO-O-OPS 528

- The wood heel industry is divided in two segments. One is composed of manufacturers of the wood blocks and the other finishers who cover the blocks with materials, in many instances the covering materials being supplied by shoe manufacturers. It was estimated that about half of the industry's production comes from integrated operations in which both levels of manufacture are under the same management. Both segments would be covered by the proposed regulation.

Committeemen stressed it would be disastrous for the non-integrated finishers, most of whom operate small businesses, if they could not pass through as part of their material costs the cost of the blocks priced under the regulation by the manufacturers of the blocks. 

It was proposed to meet the problem that finishers be given a cut-off date on the cost of their blocks 30 days after the issuance of the regulation, and the ceiling prices determined by their suppliers under the regulation would become the basis for computing their block costs. Block manufacturers similarly would adjust their ceilings to reflect any changes in their lumber costs if and when dollars and cents ceilings are fixed on lumber. 

Today's meeting was conducted by Bernard H. Topkis, deputy head, Miscellaneous 

Wood Products Section.  Norman 0. Cruver, chief, Lumber and Wood Products Branch; Leonard Perez, head, Miscellaneous Wood 

Products Section; Stanley M. Levy, counsel; H. M. Cleland, economist; J. J.

Wenstrup, Office of Accounting, and Walter R. Moulton, Office of Advisory Committees.

Washington CONSTRUCTION LAC Scott-OPS-GPR-786 

Members of the Construction Industry Advisory Committee held its second meeting today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a proposed tailored ceiling price regulation for the construction industry. 

The committee previously met with OPS officials on July 26.

In addition to committee members attending today's meeting, OPS invited a group of 7 members of the construction industry to attend the meeting for consultation with the committee and with OPS.

A draft of the proposed regulation was read paragraph by paragraph and OPS officials explained the intent and purpose of the various provisions. In turn committee members made numerous suggestions and recommendations for clarification and changes, which in the opinion of committee members, would make the regulation more workable to conform with the traditional operating and pricing practices of the industry.

În general, the proposed regulation would cover any transaction in which a seller furnishes labor, materials and services for building, highway, heavy, railroad, and miscellaneous construction. It would include installation and incorporation of materials or equipment into a building, structure or construction project, including new or additional construction. It would also include the repair, remodeling or alteration of an existing building or structure or construction project.

PRESS RELEASE   For Advance Release Afternoon Newspapers For FRIDAY, August 24, 1951 

Re: 

OPS Enforcement Cases 

Cole-OPS-GPR-787  

Hearings in initial cases under two Office of Price Stabilization regulations will be held in Michigan, Louisiana, Minnesota and North Dakota within the next fortnight as a result of the nation-wide drive to secure full compliance with OPS regulations by all retail stores, restaurants and other eating and drinking establishments.

Scheduled for hearing in the United States District Court in Michigan on 

September 4 is the first case in that state under Ceiling Price Regulation 7 requiring retail stores to file price markup charts. The defendant, the Globe 

Tile Company of Bay City, Mich., is alleged to have ignored an OPS warning of 

July 17 to file such information. This is the fourth civil injunction case filed by OPS under CPR 7 in the country. 

The New Orleans firm of Emblem, Inc., will be given a hearing August 29 in Federal Court in that city for alleged violation of CPR 7, in the first such case in that state. 

North Dakota's first CPR 7 case, against Mrs. Albert Mellem, doing business as Evie's Tot Shop at Devil's Lake, N. D., will be heard August 27 in Federal 

Court in that state. 

The first OPS enforcement actions in Minnesota under Ceiling Price Regulation 11 are slated for the Federal Court in Duluth September 7 with a restaurant and a drugstore being charged with failure to file base period price statements in food and beverages.

The defendants are Wally's Cafe in Grand Marais, Minn., operated by Wallace 

R. Lundquist, and the Buss Drugstore in Aitkin, Minn., operated by Alvin and

Emma Buss. 

Filing of charts and statements as required under CPR 7 and CPR 11 is very important because they constitute a permanent record as an aid in enforcement of OPS regulations to protect the consumer, Edward P. Morgan, OPS Director of 

Enforcement, stated. " he said. "These establishments should have filed statements long ago, "They have had ample warning. Preliminary reports received in Washington in nation-wide surveys indicate that there are still many who are not yet in compliance. Court action will probably be taken against these firms and individuals without any further warning."

THURSDAY, AUGUST 23, 1951 TEMPO E Re: 

Washington EXPORT PRICE CONTROL 

Browne-OPS-GPR-789 

The Office of Price Stabilization today notified exporters that it did not believe it necessary to extend the effective date of Ceiling Price 

Regulation 61, the export regulation, which is August 26, 1951.

Confusion apparently exists within the industry, OPS said, stemming from a belief that sales made after July 30th and before August 26, 1951 must be reported by August 26. Numerous requests have been received seeking an extension of the August 26 date.

To clarify the situation, OPS today stated that reports for commodities sold after July 30th and before August 26th for delivery after August 26th, must be filed by September 10th, which is 15 days after August 26th.

All reports for commodities sold after August 26th must be filed within 15 days after the date of the first sale of a particular commodity. After a seller has once filed his report under CPR 61 for a particular commodity, he uses the mark-up reported for subsequent sales and does not have to make further filings, OPS said.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers SUNDAY, August 26, 1951 

Re: 

 SMALL RETAILERS Crossley-OPS-GPR-790 

As part of an Office of Price Stabilization program to give careful consideration to the pricing problems of the small retail merchant, the agency today announced creation of the position of Special Assistant for Small Retailer Problems in the Distribution Branch.

Rawle Deland, who has served as Special Assistant to the Director of the 

Consumer Soft Goods Division since July 5, 1951, will be the new Special As sistant for Small Retailer Problems. Mr. Deland came to OPS from Thorndike 

Deland and Associates, of New York City, a management recruiting service for the retailing industry.

A first task of the Special Assistant will be to make a basic determination regarding small retailers. This will be a determination as to whether sales volume or other criteria should be used as a basis for deciding when a small store has special problems under price control.

The Special Assistant will work continuously with a permanent standing 

Subcommittee for Small Retailers of the OPS Retail Industry Advisory Committee in planning tailored ceiling price regulations for small merchants, a major part of whose business is in consumer durable and soft goods. Working with commodity pricing personnel of OPS, the Special Assistant will examine the effects of all present and future regulations on the small merchant and will advise the Director of Price Stabilization. He will maintain liaison with other agencies concerned with small retailers such as the National Production Authority and the Select Committees on Small Business of the Congress. Finally, the 

Special Assistant will serve as the contact point within OPS for small merchants and will expedite the handling of their inquiries and problems. 

BACKGROUND 

Today's action is taken in line with the recent establishment of an overall 

Agency Advisory Committee on Small Business Affairs comprised of senior executives of OPS. (See Press Release OPS-GPR-754 of August 12, 1951.) On June 19, 

1951, OPS appointed the Retail Industry Advisory Committee--the first such committee providing overall representation of the retail industry in the history of price control. At the recommendation of that Industry Advisory Committee, a permanent Subcommittee for Small Retailers was appointed. Meetings with the 

Retail Industry Advisory Committee and with the Subcommittee for Small Retailers are scheduled for August 27 and 28. # # # # 1 ### GPO—O—OPS 591

PRESS RELEASE    

Re: BITUMINOUS COAL IAC Browne-OPS-GPR-794  Members of the Bituminous Coal Producers Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting with OPS officials Wednesday recommended that truck mines without rail connections, producing 20,000 tons or less of coal a year be exempted from price control. Most of this coal is sold in communities near the mines.

Some of the Committee representatives suggested that such action would not harm the larger segment of the industry--commercial mines--competitively, nor would it have a significant effect on the general level of coal prices. 

They suggested that if the prices charged by the smaller mines, selling coal from trucks, reached the general level of ceiling prices at retail in particular communities they could be brought under control by promulgation of an area price ceiling.

In further support of decontroling the small mines, it was argued by some of the producers that the excessive cost of obtaining reports under the law would actually outweigh their value to the OPS. 

Some OPS Field Representatives, 18 of which attended the meeting, expressed the feeling that it might be unwise to fully decontrol the small mines at this time. They reported that operators in some regions had objected to such action.

The Price Branch of OPS now has this matter under consideration and will begin a study of the proposals made pending a final decision in the matter at higher levels.

Other topics discussed between the operators and OPS officials included OPS regulations applicable to solid fuels, pricing standards established under CPR 3, the bituminous coal regulation, the current pricing problems under 

CPR 3. 

No date was set for the next meeting of the Committee.

EASTERN AND CENTRAL WOODEN AGRICULTURAL CONTAINER SUBCOMMITTEE 

Members of the subcommittee of the Eastern and Central Wooden Agricultural Container Industry Advisory Committee met with OPS officials today and made detailed recommendations for a proposed tailored regulation for their industry that would spell out dollars and cents ceiling prices on many standard items.  

The committee recommended following in general the provisions of old OPA 

MPR 320, with prices adjusted to current costs.

Determining specific ceiling levels constitutes a difficult problem for the industry because it is seasonal. The industry prices under the General Ceiling 

Price Regulation, GCPR. The base period under the latter is December 19, 1950, to January 25, 1951, which is a period in which the industry was least active. 

Many manufacturers found it difficult to establish realistic ceilings, being forced back to the levels of the summer of 1950, when the industry was in a depressed situation.

The subcommittee was favorable to an approach to the problem which would utilize the level of prices of manufacturers whose operations under GCPR were reasonably satisfactory. Some members suggested these prices would not be far off from prices arrived at under the Capehart formula, under which manufacturers would add cost increases up to July 26, 1951, to their pre-Korea prices. 

The industry produces wooden baskets, hampers, crates, etc., used in the marketing of fruits and vegetables.

PRESS RELEASE ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers MONDAY, August 27, 1951   Re: MANUFACTURERS MEETING 

Crist-OPS-GPR-796  

Tentative proposals for revising the manufacturing regulations to conform with recent changes in the Defense Production Act of 1950 will be reviewed at a meeting of 16 manufacturers and officials of the Office of Price Stabilization, Tuesday in the Archives Building, it was announced today by the Agency. 

Under discussion at the meeting will be a tentative draft of a revised general manufacturers' order (CPR 22). Originally issued April 25, this regulation, allowing manufacturers to add factory labor and material cost increases to pre-Korean prices, set the pattern for various other manufacturing regulations of the Agency.

An amendment to the Act requires the Agency to take into account cost increases or decreases up to a later date than was provided in the general manufacturers' regulation and companion orders. It also requires the Agency to include changes in all costs, including overhead. 

Undoubtedly, OPS officials said, this new draft will result in higher prices for some manufacturers than the original CPR 22, but they will be increases which the Agency would be required to give under the provisions of the amended law. 

Generally, CPR 22 and similar orders covered only increases in factory labor and material costs, specifically excluding increases in overhead expenses, such as general administration, advertising, selling and research.. 

Moreover, manufacturers could figure increases only up to December 31, 1950 on most materials under CPR 22 and labor increases up to March 15, 1951. The new law requires inclusion of cost increases or decreases up to July 26, 1951. 

The tentative draft follows the general approach of CPR 22 for handling labor. and material cost changes, making all the revisions required by the law, such as providing a different base period and the later cut-off date for figuring the cost changes. 

CPR 22 provided optional base periods of April 1 through June 24, 1950, or any one of the three previous calendar quarters. The base period now required by the law is January 1 to June 24, 1950.

With respect to including overhead costs in new ceilings, the tentative draft permits manufacturers who have adequate cost accounting systems to determine their cost increases on the basis of these systems, taking full account of changes in the volume of production or sales since the pre-Korean base period. GIO-O--OPS 600

For manufacturers who do not have complete systems of cost allocations by commodities, the initial draft of the new regulation provides a general formula to permit the necessary computations on overhead costs. 

Act. 

The Agency expects that this revised regulation, whenever it is issued, will contain all of the provisions required by the recently amended Defense Production Consideration is being given to allowing manufacturers the option of retaining ceilings already calculated under CPR 22 for all commodities under the regulation, if they elect to do so. 

As in CPR 22, small businesses would be given the option of remaining under the General Ceiling Price Regulation of January 26. 

Mandatory effective date of CPR 22 and five other manufacturing regulations on August 9 was postponed indefinitely in order to preserve the status quo until OPS could revise the regulations to conform with the amended law. Final effective date was to have been August 13, except for apparel. Deadline for that order was to have been August 15.

Those postponed, aside from CPR 22, were machinery (CPR 30); cotton textile manufacturers' (CPR 37); shoe manufacturers' (CPR 41); apparel manufacturers (CPR 

45; and wool yarns and fabrics (CPR 18 - Revised).

Washington Re: SHOE LAST MANUFACTURERS IAC Moore-OPS-GPR-798  Members of the Shoe Last Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee at their second meeting with OPS officials today recommended that their industry be included in the coverage of the proposed formula price regulation for turned, shaped and allied wood products. 

Under the formula prices would be determined on the basis of costs up to a specified cut-off date, plus the highest dollars and cents margins existing in a specified pre-Korea base period. 

Committeemen recommended that the cut-off date on costs be no earlier than July 26, 1951, the cut-off date provided in the Capehart Amendment, and that freight increases granted after that date also be included in compiling costs.

The committee suggested a base period for computing net margin of approximately nine months, from October 1, 1949, to June 24, 1950.

Members recommended that manufacturers of lasts be permitted to include in their allowable costs the ceiling prices on blocks determined by manufacturers of blocks under the regulation. Members suggested this be accomplished by making the cut-off date on blocks purchased by last manufacturers 30 days after the effective date of the regulation. They said it would be disastrous for last manufacturers who purchase instead of make their blocks if the price of blocks determined under the regulation cannot be passed through as part of their costs. 

A substantial portion of last manufacturers are dependent on purchased blocks, the committee reported.

Committeemen expressed belief that dollars and cents ceilings would not be practical for their industry. They recalled that no satisfactory basis for dollars and cents pricing was found during the war under OPA.

Washington Re: FROG, SWITCH AND CROSSING MANUFACTURERS IAC Scott-OPS-GPR-799 

The Frog, Switch and Crossing Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization and recommended that a tailored pricing regulation be drafted for the industry. 

The industry is concerned with the manufacture of railroad frogs, switches, crossings and other fabricated units for railroad right-of-way installations. 

Presently, products produced by the industry are covered by Ceiling Price 

Regulation 30 (Machinery). 

Committee members were not certain whether CPR 30 pricing would result in an overall rollback of industry prices. They were agreed that the pricing technique of CPR 30 is difficult to apply to the products of this industry and would distort the industry price structure, with the result that ceiling prices would be too high for some products and too low for others. 

It was pointed out that a large percentage of the units manufactured are built to individual specifications required by railroad and industrial customers. 

Labor and material cost ratios will vary greatly, depending on the mechanical and metal requirements of each individual unit being produced. At the same time, the industry does produce a fairly substantial volume of so-called stock or recurring items, and these may represent from 25 to 40 percent of total volume, depending on the particular producer. Committeemen said that, generally speaking, it has been the customary practice in the industry to use a costing formula based on cost plus a varying arbitrary profit, rather than a formula based on cost plus a fixed percentage profit markup. (over) The committee felt that it is important and desirable for the industry to have a tailored pricing regulation without delay and it was suggested that a subcommittee be appointed to confer further with OPS officials in the drafting of such a regulation at an early date.

A 4 member subcommittee was appointed and it was tentatively agreed that the subcommittee would meet with OPS officials in Washington on September 11.

Washington Re: TIGHT COOPERAGE LAC Moore-OPS-GPR-801  

Detailed recommendations for the provisions of a tailored regulation for their industry were made today by members of the Tight Cooperage Industry Advisory 

Committee at their second meeting with OPS officials.

Committeemen recommended that dollars and cents ceilings be fixed on finished tight cooperage stock and that the price of cooperage be determined by markups over the cost of materials used. 

Prices would be on the basis of f.o.b. mill with differentials for delivery and customary markups for dealers and warehousemen.

Committeemen proposed that prices for white oak whiskey barrels and bourbon cooperage stock be fixed at roughly the same levels as General Ceiling Price Regu lation ceilings. 

Prices for prime produced food and chemical barrels would be determined by the general relationship that existed between whiskey and food and chemical barrels in 1945, the last years food and chemical barrels were made in quantities from prime produced cooperage stock.

During normal times, due to the competition of metal drums and containers, "bourbon oil grade" barrels made of offal from whiskey barrel stock are generally sufficient to meet the demand for wooden chemical and food barrels, rending production of food and chemical barrels from prime produced stock unprofitable. 

Owing to the shortage of steel containers at this time there is a growing demand for wooden food and chemical barrels. (over)

THURSDAY, August 23, 1951  Re: BITUMINOUS COAL LAC 

Browne-OPS-GPR-802  

Members of the Bituminous Coal Producers Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting with OPS officials Wednesday recommended that truck mines without rail connections, producing 20,000 tons or less of coal a year be exempted from price control. Most of this coal is sold in communities near the mines.

Some of the Committee representatives suggested that such action would not harm the larger segment of the industry--commercial mines--competitively, nor would it have a significant effect on the general level of coal prices. 

They suggested that if the prices charged by the smaller mines, selling coal from trucks, reached the general level of ceiling prices at retail in particular communities, they could be brought under control by promulgation of an area price ceiling.

In further support of decontroling the small mines, it was argued by some of the producers that the excessive cost of obtaining reports under the law would actually outweigh their value to the OPS. 

Some OPS Field Representatives, 18 of which attended the meeting, expressed the feeling that it might be unwise to fully decontrol the small mines at this time. They reported that operators in some regions had objected to such action.

The Price Branch of OPS now has this matter under consideration and will begin a study of the proposals made pending a final decision in the matter at higher levels.

Other topics discussed between the operators and OPS officials included OPS regulations applicable to solid fuels, pricing standards extablished under CPR 3, the bituminous coal regulation, and current pricing problems under 

CPR 3. 

No date was set for the next meeting of the Committee.

Fuels Branch of the Transportation, Public Utilities and Fuels Division, and T. Reed Scollon, Chief of the Bituminous Section of the Solid Fuels Branch.

PRESS RELEASE 

August 27, 1951 

 Tempo E 

Washington Re: LIVE CATTLE PRICES 

Hughes-OPS-GPR-803 

Due to increases in freight rates which will become effective on August 28, 1951, there will be changes in the maximum ceiling prices which slaughterers may pay for live cattle, the Office of Price Stabilization announced today. 

Ceiling Price Regulation 24 establishes zone differentials hased upon carload freight rates on fresh meats from Denver, Colorado, for shipments west and from Omaha, Nebraska, for shipments east. Freight rate increases (6% in some freight territories; 9% in others) effective August 28, 1951 will therefore change zone differentials on that date more or less throughout the country, except in Zone 1 which is the central part of the country in which the two basing points are located. The increase in zone differentials will result in increases in the maximum calculated prices which slaughterers may pay for live cattle. The increases will 

The new prices will apply to cattle slaughtered in that portion of each slaughterer's accounting period following the effective date of the freight rate increases, whereas the previous prices apply to cattle slaughtered in the first portion of the same accounting period.

Slaughterers may use the price before this change for their entire accounting period or they may, if they wish, file separate Drove Compliance Reports for the cattle slaughtered in each portion of the accounting period for which the two different sets of prices apply. The first report would be for cattle slaughtered up to and including August 27, and the second report would be for cattle slaughtered on August 28 and later. Both reports would be combined for determining the slaughterer's drove cost compliance for the full accounting period. # # # # # GPO-0-OPS 615

PRESS RELEASE    

Monday, August 27, 1951

Re: 

Scott-OPS-GPR-804 

SCREW MACHINE PRODUCTS, METAL STAMPINGS, PRECISION MECHANICAL SPRINGS INDUSTRY ADVISORY SUBCOMMITTEE 

A subcommittee consisting of members selected from three industry advisory committees representing the screw machine products industry, the metal stampings industry, and the precision mechanical springs industry, met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss pricing problems common to these three industries.

The Screw Machine Products Industry Advisory Committee was represented by: 

Asa W. Bonner, Detroit, Michigan; N. A. Hewitt, Elyria, 'Ohio; and, E. W. Schneider, Chicago, Illinois.

The Metal Stampings Industry Advisory Committee was represented by: Owen H. 

Wenning, Worcester, Mass.; G. Glenwood Rose, Philadelphia, Pa.; Ray Nigro, Detroit, Michigan; and, Howard C. Wolf, Salem, Ohio.

The Precision Mechanical Springs Industry Advisory Committee was represented by: E. J. Byrnes, Jr., Worcester, Mass.; J.-D. Culbertson III, McKees Rocks, Pa.; and E. L. Goff, Bristol, Conn.

Because of the job shop nature of these three industries their pricing problems are somewhat similar in that, generally speaking, they produce a wide range of products based on the specifications of individual customers and the ratio of material cost to labor cost will vary greatly on these individual orders. 

These industries are called on to handle a large number of small individual orders which represent only a small percentage of total volume, but which nevertheless present a serious pricing problem from the standpoint of paper work, particularly for the many small producers. 

It was pointed out that they are primarily intermediate suppliers of components used by the manufacturers of a multitude of end products. Historically, they have always been highly competitive and have always operated on a close profit margin, committeemen said.

Committeemen also pointed out that the defense program has not been a boon to these industries and that most companies are currently suffering a 25 to 30 (over) GPO-O-OPS 618

percent reduction in volume of sales under 1950 levels. Any curtailment of civilian production has an almost immediate adverse effect on their business, they said.

Generally speaking, committee members felt that they could live with a tailored pricing regulation patterned along the general lines of the recently issued metal castings ceiling price regulation (CPR 60).

Differences of opinion were expressed with respect to cut-off dates for figuring material and labor cost increases and with regard to the handling of small order pricing.

Committeemen felt that adjustments should be permitted to reflect current metal costs.

In general, CPR 60 establishes ceiling prices on the basis of price lists or the formula for pricing which a producer had in effect on January 25, 1951. 

OPS officials told the committee that a tentative draft of a regulation along the lines of CPR 60 would be prepared and suggested that the committee meet again on September 13 to go over such a tentative draft and make further suggestions and recommendations for a final draft. 

The meeting was conducted by Warren B. Leland, chief, Auxiliary Equipment 

Section, Machinery Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: Leslie J. 

Carson, chief, Machinery Branch; Edward L. Norman, chief, Cutting Tool & Industrial Equipment Section; C. W. Moore, division economist; E. L. Inwood, branch economist; D. S. Otterson and J. J. McCullough, business analysts; George Brody, legal staff; Robert R. Teates, Office of Enforcement; and, Harry Spack, Office for Industry Advisory Committees. Also attending was Walter Schuch of the 

National Production Authority.

MONDAY, August 27, 1951

Re: NATURAL GAS RATES 

Browne-OPS-GPR-805  

Early determination, possibly this week, on an appeal of the Stanolind Oil & Gas Corp., Tulsa, Okla., and the Continental Oil Company, Houston, Texas, from a decision of the Office of Price Stabilization denying an increased natural gas rate in a proposed contract between these two companies and the 

Mississippi River Fuel Corporation, St. Louis, was indicated following a meeting here today between company representatives and OPS officials. 

The buyer in this case, the Mississippi River Fuel Corporation has applied to the Federal Power Commission for permission to increase its rates on the sale of gas to public utility customers. The OPS is intervening in protest to the increased rates sought by the Mississippi River Company in the case before the Power Commission. Hearing date in the latter case in September 5. 

The Stanolind and Continental companies seek approval of a rate of 12 cents per thousand cubic feet measured on the Texas pressure base of 14.65 per square inch absolute at well head for natural gas produced in the Woodlawn. Field, Harrison County, Texas. In a letter order date August 22, 1951, OPS through its Petroleum Branch, denied the request and extablished a ceiling of 10 cents per thousand cubic feet on a basis of 14.65 per square inch absolute at wellhead, in line with other prices in the same general producing area. Today's meeting followed at the request of the companies involved. 

Also attending were representatives of several other independent producers of natural gas in the Woodlawn Field, who have pending contracts with the Mississippi company to sell the gas at the higher price. 

Gas company officials submitted additional evidence supporting their claim for the increased rate, and received OPS permission to produce further documentary evidence by mail. OPS officials told the companies that the additional material submitted by them would be carefully studied and that a decision would be reached as quickly as possible.

One argument made by the gas companies for the increased rate was that the potential reserves of gas in the Woodlawn Field are large and that consequent large investments in equipment justify the hike in price. Further, the natural gas operators argued, their negotiations with the Mississippi River company for the 12 cent rate were completed before the base period (December 19, 1950 to January 25, 1951) even though they had not entered into a formal contract during that time.
