MONDAY, August 27, 1951   Re: Enforcement Training School 

COLE-OPS-GPR-806  

Vigorous enforcement of Office of Price Stabilization regulations will be the program carried out in the future by the Office of Enforcement, Edward P. 

Morgan, OPS Enforcement Director, stated today.

This was his message to more than 60 Special Assistant United States Attorneys and other OPS Enforcement officials attending the fourth OPS Training School which opened at the Department of Justice today. "There is nothing on earth more demoralizing to enforcement officers, nor more undermining to public confidence, than letting off wilful or influential violators with a slap on the wrist," he said. "Equal justice under the law will be our high goal of attainment. I am personally going to see to it that there is no 'tampering' with investigations. 

I'm going to follow up on all important criminal cases from the day of their inception until the day of sentence. I'm going to keep this organization clean. 

There is not going to be any backdoor compromises by influential lawyers, or anyone else, while I am Director of Enforcement."

The basic goal of enforcement, however, he pointed out, will be the maximum of compliance with a minimum of court action. # # # # # # # # # # # The Training School will continue throughout the week. 

Justice officials are assisting on the instructional staff.

PRESS RELEASE    

McDonald-OPS-GPR-807 

Re: RETAILERS INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING 

Working through a series of subcommittee recommendations this afternoon, the Office of Price Stabilization's Retailers Industry Advisory Committee studied proposals for amending existing regulations and issuing new orders to care for hardship cases, increased freight rates, averaging of costs of identical items, rounding of prices to permit retailers to charge their traditional price lines, and proposals for decontrolling some items now under price control.

A subcommittee to study hardship cases reported that a number of retailers who as a result of low markup charts were in a loss position have no basis for relief under existing OPS regulations, and made tentative suggestions for meeting the problem. The over-all committee recommended that the subcommittee continue its study of the problem and consult further with 

OPS on a corrective amendment.

Another subcommittee suggested that retailers who have not traditionally included freight rates in their selling prices be permitted in the future to reflect these increased rates in their ceiling prices because of the recent wave of increasing transportation costs over the country. OPS was requested to take the subcommittee's recommendation under consideration and to consult with its members as to placing the recommendation into effect. 

OPS was advised to go slowly on removing items from price control. A subcommittee, however, will work with OPS in considering items of no importance to the cost of living and which might warrant decontrol. 

Another subcommittee considered the problem of how to price an identical item being purchased at lower cost than an inventory of the same item on hand. It was suggested that the two costs be averaged in order to permit the retailer a higher markup than he would be entitled to on the basis of the new lower cost.

The Committee considered a tentative proposal for a regulation which would simplify the work performed by small retailers in complying with OPS regulations. The proposal that a new pricing regulation be written to care specifically for the problems of small retailers was advanced yesterday at a meeting of the Small Retailers Sub-Committee of OPS's Retail IAC. 

Committeemen voiced the opinion that small retailers should be covered by a separate pricing regulation that would ease the task of record keeping and making reports. The Committee further felt that many existing OPS regulations do not fit the needs of small retailers, and that a simplified procedure should be developed to enable small retailers to establish their ceiling prices with local OPS offices with a minimum of difficulty. The 

Committee stressed that there was no desire to relieve the small retailer from a level of ceiling prices applicable to retailers generally but merely to make the small retailer's task of compliance simpler. 

GPO-O-OPS 630

OPS officials told the Committee that final legal interpretation had not been reached within the agency as to the possible application of Section 402(k) of the Defense Production Act, as amended, to future pricing actions affecting retailers. 

Among problems discussed and still to be worked out was the effect of the Herlong Amendment on retailers who generally reflect increased freight rates and similar cost increases in their selling prices, and on those who customarily absorb these costs as part of their overhead. Further study of this effect was delegated to the subcommittee on freight problems. 

OPS officials pointed out that the Herlong Amendment applies only to regulations issued hereafter. However, it was suggested that certain amendments to existing regulations may have to be issued, for reasons of uniformity with future regulations, taking account of the amendment's provisions. 

OPS officials attending today's meeting included Harold P. Wess, consultant to the Director of Price Stabilization, who acted as honorary chair man and Thomas L. Karsten, acting director of the Consumer Soft Goods Divi sion, who presided as chairman of the meeting. Others attending were: Bion

Re: FIBRE BOX IAC 

Detailed recommendations on the provisions of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry were made today by members of the Fibre Box Industry Advisory Committee at their second meeting today with OPS officials. 

Under the proposed regulation, which would apply to set-up and folding paper and fibre boxes and a variety of converted items such as drums, cones, tubes, bobbins and cores, manufacturers would determine their ceiling prices either on the basis of price lists or formulas employed during a specific basis.period.

If they price by formula, manufacturers would compute their raw materials, converting and delivery costs, and apply the same margins as employed in the base period, which might be either a percentage or dollars and cents margin per unit. 

Committeemen recommended that January 25 to February 24, 1951, be employed as the base period.

Re: MILL WORK IAC 

A tailored regulation fixing dollars and cents ceilings on stock items would be welcomed by their industry, members of the Millwork Industry Advisory Committee told OPS officials today at their first meeting. 

Committeemen reported they have been operating fairly satisfactorily under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, which they attributed to a high volume of production together with the fact that lumber prices have remained fairly stable.

They urged that ceiling prices be spelled out for lumber before fixing them on millwork, and that current and possibly future wage increases be reflected in ceilings on millwork.

Committeemen said spelled out prices on lumber would be a means of insuring them against paying higher than ceiling prices for lumber. 

Members said it would be impossible to put dollars and cents ceilings on custom millwork, recalling this type of millwork was priced by formula under a separate OPA regulation during the war. 

Committeemen recommended individual pricing on hollow core doors because of lack of uniformity of the core structures. 

They said old OPA regulation No. 293 would provide a satisfactory starting point for preparing a new regulation for stock items. 

The question where the line of demarcation should be drawn between pine and fir millwork was discussed. A separate regulation. is being projected for west coast fir products.

The meeting was conducted by Norman 0. Cruver, chief, Lumber and Wood 

Products Branch, and Glen Converse, chief, Millwork Section.

Re: 

MANUFACTURERS' MEETING 

are. Crist-OPS-GPR-810  

A proposed revision of the general manufacturers' regulation (CPR 22) for optional use was discussed today by 17 manufacturers with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization at an all-day meeting in the Archives Building. 

Director of Price Stabilization Michael V. DiSalle told the manufacturers the agency was making necessary changes in the manufacturing regulation to conform with recent changes in the Defense Production Act of 1950. "We realize," Mr. DiSalle said, "that controls create problems for business.

We don't want to make them any more difficult than they necessarily "Every word of the proposed revision is tentative. We don't feel that we have found satisfactory answers for all problems. We do not know how soon we can get this new regulation out, but we won't issue it until we are certain it fulfills the intent of Congress in amending the law and is as workable as we can possibly make it.' 11 Under the tentative draft discussed at today's meeting, manufacturers would have the option of retaining prices already calculated under CPR 22, or of recalculating ceilings and coming under the revised manufacturing order.

While the tentative draft follows the same general approach of CPR 22 for handling labor and material cost changes, it makes the various revisions required by the law, such as a different base period than in CPR 22, a later cut-off date for figuring cost changes, and provisions for reflecting overhead cost changes. CPR 22 specifically excluded increases in overhead expenses.

Many different views were expressed by the manufacturers, who were called in by OPS to thrash out various problems which have arisen in revising the regulation.

Some favored the present approach of the agency of allowing manufacturers the option of retaining their present CPR 22 ceilings or coming under the revised version, but suggested a modification of the revised regulation. 

The current draft provides that if a manufacturer prices one commodity under CPR 22 it must price all commodities under that regulation. A number of the manufacturers suggested that the option be extended to different products of "optional divisions." Thus, for example, a manufacturer might use CPR 22 for chemicals and the revised regulation for cameras. (Over) GPO-O-OPS 628

Other manufacturers suggested the agency drop consideration of a revised manufacturers' order, even though for optional use, and merely amend the present CPR 22 to incorporate the changes required by the recently amended law. Those who favored optional use of the revised CPR 22 opposed amending the present regulation, contending it would force manufacturers to recalculate ceilings even though they were satisfied with CPR 22. 

They maintained that so long as manufacturers had the right to come under the revised CPR 22 at some later date their right to a higher ceiling,. under the provisions of the new law, was protected. 

Another group of manufacturers urged that they be allowed to remain under the General Ceiling Price Regulation of January 26, with the right to make individual application for higher ceilings under the new provisions of the law.

Some objection was raised to the provisions of the tentative draft for handling overhead costs. The current draft would require manufacturers, who chose to exercise the option of using it, to take full account of changes in volume of production or sales since the pre-Korean base period of January 1, 1950 to June 24, 1950.

Thus, for instance, if a manufacturer's volume had risen sharply since pre-Korea he might be forced to reduce prices because unit overhead costs were down.

Various other manufacturing orders of OPS, such as the ones for machinery, apparel, shoes, cotton textiles, wool yarn and fabrics, are also being revised to meet the terms of the new law. OPS officials made it clear that no firm decision had been made to issue revised versions of each of these basic manufacturing regulations. Some other approach, such as amending them, was another possibility, they said. 1 Presiding at today's meeting was Edward F. Phelps, assistant director of OPS. Among other OPS officials attending were Arnold Shaw, an assistant to Mr. DiSalle; Saul Nelson, deputy economic advisor; and Cecelia H. Goetz, general counsel's office.

Re: MOLDED, EXTRUDED AND LATHE-CUT RUBBER GOODS SUBCOMMITTEE Members of the Molded, Extruded and Lathe-Cut Rubber Goods Subcommittee of the Mechanical Rubber Goods Industry Advisory Committee at their fourth meet ing today with OPS officials expressed preference at this time for the comparison product pricing method for their custom made items. 

The industry manufactures thousands of items for machinery, office and household equipment, automobiles and other manufactured products to varied specifications.

The industry is covered by the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. Under SR 10 to CPR 22 items whose volume in the second quarter of 1951 amounted to less than $10,000 in value were left optionally under the 

General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, until September 30, 1951.

Committeemen said they would be satisfied to continue pricing as at present and suggested that the provisions of SR 10 applying to their items be extended beyond September 30. There was some discussion whether the volume limit should be $10,000 at at present or something less per quarter. 

Committeemen recommended that if their industry is taken out from under GCPR and CPR 22 by a special tailored regulation, comparison pricing devices such as are available to them under these regulations be incorporated in the tailored regulation. There was some discussion of formula pricing as an alternative, with ceilings determined on the basis of costs plus base period margin, but the comparison product method appeared to have preference. 

Members will deliberate on these alternatives pending another meeting and clarification of OPS policy in the light of the changes in price control legislation. (over)

  THURSDAY, August 28, 1951 

Washington STEEL IMPORTERS LAC 

Browne-OPS-GPR-812  

Members of the Steel Importers Industry Advisory Committee, at their first meeting today with OPS officials, recommended markups to be applied to steel imports in three separate categories in arriving at their ceiling prices. The recommendations represent the concensus of industry members only, and not of the OPS, which has taken the matter under advisement. 

The suggested categories and the proposed mark-ups, based on today's landed cost, follow:

Category I: Imported steel commodities whose cost is up to $200.00 a ton, a markup of $15.00.

Category II: Imported steel commodities whose cost is from $200.00 to $250.00 a ton, a markup of $20.00.

Category III: Imported steel commodities whose cost is $250.00 to $300.00 a ton, a markup of $25.00 to $30.00.

It was pointed out at the meeting that the importation of steel has increased almost ten times over the quantity imported before the Korean conflict. 

Consequently, there are steel importers and steel warehousemen in the business today who were never in it before and who were not in business during the base period for Ceiling Price Regulation 31, the import regulation, which is July 

1, 1949 to June 30, 1950.

Today's meeting was called to consider markups to cover this situation. 

The suggested markups, the discussion revealed, would apply to two classes of importers, first the importer who has no warehouse and who re-sells to a warehouse, and the warehouse which imports its own steel directly, and resells it to another warehouse in the original condition in which it was received. 

In both instances, the importer and warehouseman may add the markup to their landed cost, under the recommendations.

Committee members discussed ways and means to prevent so-called "ringaroundthe-rosey" deals, during which added costs might be reflected by multiple sales made while the steel was on the high seas. One suggestion to cure this situation was that the import cost, as reflected in the consular invoice, might be used for the sole mark-up applied. (over) 

---

- Several pleas were heard from the industry group for a percentage markup instead of a dollars and cents markup, but OPS officials explained this is impossible, since CPR 31, the import regulation, provides for dollars and cents ceilings. Arguments were also made by some industry members that if OPS insists on dollars and cents markups they should be applied on a sliding scale. Complaint was made by some of the importers against high customs duties, but OPS officials explained that downward revision of tariff rates must be made by Congress. 

Industry members were told by the National Production Authority at the meeting that it is the desire of that agency to bring in as much foreign steel as possible. Every ton added to the domestic supply, it was said, gives that much more freedom in the use of steel in the defense effort. At present, one 

NPR regulation facilitating imports permits a fabricator to take title to steel abroad and bring it in over his Controlled Materials Plan allotment. There is under consideration, it was said, some method of broadening that regulation so that steel brought in by importers will receive comparable treatment. 

The meeting was conducted by K.J.H. Cerecedo, chief of the Export-Import Branch and N. Guccione, chief of the Import Section. Other OPS officials present were 

Merritt R. Kotin, attorney, Enforcement division; Charles Potter, consultant, Metals 

Branch; Joseph B. Hyman, attorney, Export-Import Branch; William R. Thomas, Office of Industrial Advisory Committees; Clifford F. Bolhagen, Enforcement and Edwin A. 

Elbert, acting Assistant Director, Services -Export-Import Division. Present from NPA was J. Joseph W. Palmer, Chief, International Section, Iron & Steel Division.

SECONDARY COPPER REFINERS IAC COPPER AND COPPER ALLOY SCRAP DEALERS TAC The Secondary Copper Refiners Industry Advisory Committee and the Copper & Copper Alloy Scrap Industry Advisory Committee met jointly with OPS officials today to discuss pricing problems common to both industries. 

These two industries are concerned with pricing under the copper and copper alloy scrap ceiling price regulation (CPR 46) and to some extent with the ceiling price regulation covering brass mill scrap (CPR 47).

Several changes in CPR 46 to make it more workable had been suggested and committeemen discussed these changes in detail.

It had been suggested that CPR 46 be changed to include ceiling prices on sales between dealers. Committeemen were opposed to such a change as being impractical and unworkable.

A discussion was held with respect to changes in the quantity premium provisions to lower the quantities on which premiums would be allowed. 

The committeemen also discussed possible changes in the preparation premium 

No definite conclusions were reached in regard to changes in the premium provisions, but OPS officials told members that full consideration will be given to their suggestions and recommendations.

Tempo E 

Washington Re: LEO H. McCORMICK 

1 Coakley-OPS-GPR-814 

Price Stabilization Director, Michael V. DiSalle, has designated Mr. Leo

H. McCormick to assist him temporarily with problems relating to small business in the Office of Price Stabilization.

In this capacity Mr. McCormick will recommend to the Director standards and policies for small business, act as chairman of the Intra-Agency Advisory Committee for Small Business Affairs in the Office of Price Stabilization, represent the agency on the Inter-Agency Small Business Executive's Committee and represent the Director before the Select House and Senate Small Business Committees.

During the past several months he has represented the Director at some 30 hearings and clinics in various parts of the country, conducted by the Select Small Business Committees of the House and Senate. This has enabled Mr. McCormick to study, at the local level, small business problems, with their solutions, which grow out of the entire Defense Program. 

Mr. McCormick was formerly associated with the food and distribution business, having recently served as president of a small distribution firm in

Re: STEEL SCRAP 

(CPR 5, Int. 1 Use of Water Rates in Determination of Shipping Point Prices for Steel Scrap) Scott-OPS-GPR-815 

Shippers of steel scrap may not use water rates in establishing shipping point ceiling prices if it has been the customary well established practice to make shipments by rail.

The Office of Price Stabilization today issued a formal interpretation to clarify this provision under its iron and steel scrap Ceiling Price Regulation 5. 

The interpretation is as follows: 

"It has come to the attention of the Office of Price Stabilization that some confusion has persisted in the iron and steel scrap industry regarding the proper use of vessel rates in computing ceiling shipping point prices for steel scrap under Ceiling Price Regulation 5. "The intent of CPR 5 has been to recognize and make provisions for the shipment of scrap by vessel where such a method of shipment was the well established practice of shippers in a particular locality as of the effective date of the regulation. "The regulation does not permit the use of water rates, even though such published rates are currently available, to determine a shipping point price where, for reasons other than seasonal restrictions, it had ceased to be the customary practice at that point to ship by water and had subsequently become the customary practice prior to February 7, 1951, to ship by rail. 

"Section 21(c) reads as follows: 

'No vessel charge shall be deemed as an established charge within the provisions of this regulation unless regular vessel movement of scrap, except for seasonal restrictions, is being made to the most favorable basing point as of the effective date of this regulation, as a customary business practice.' (over) GPO-O-OPS 634

SEPUTED 88. 

"This provision embodies three basic requirements, all of which must be The first is that shipment of steel scrap by vessel must have been made regularly and as a customary business practice and not merely in a few insolated cases. Secondly, such shipments must have been made to the most favorable basing point as defined in this regulation. Finally, such shipments must have been made as of February 7, 1951, except for seasonal restrictions. The provisions of section 21(c) recognize, however, that normal water movement of scrap might have been temporarily suspended as of February 7 due to bad winter weather, and such temporary suspension due to seasonal restrictions does not in and of itself preclude the use of water rates in determining the ceiling shipping point price in such locations."

Detailed recommendations for the provisions of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry were made today by members of the Folding Paper Box Industry 

Advisory Committee at their second meeting with OPS officials.

Under the proposed regulation manufacturers who price according to price lists would employ as their ceilings their prices in effect during a specified base period. 

Manufacturers who price by formula would employ the formulas they used during the base period and apply the base period margins to costs of materials, conversion and delivery.

There was considerable discussion of the transfer price for materials used by integrated manufacturers-those who make both paperboard and paperboard boxes. For those who transfer their paperboard between the two operations at market prices, it was suggested their transfer price be at existing ceiling prices. For those who transfer at cost, it was recommended the transfer price used in the base period be the transfer price under the formula.

Re: PLATINUM IAC Scott-OPS-GPR-819 

The Platinum Industry Advisory Committee held its second meeting today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a tailored dollars-and-cents ceiling price regulation. 

The committee previously met with OPS officials on May 4. 

The industry is currently pricing under the General Ceiling Price 

Regulation. 

A tentative draft of a proposed dollars-and-cents ceiling price regulation was presented to the committee.

The committee reviewed the proposed draft paragraph by paragraph and offered suggestions and recommendations for changes and clarification to make the regulation more workable. In the main the proposed regulation was acceptable to the committee.

The proposed regulation would cover platinum, platinum scrap, ore and concentrates, platinum alloys and platinum products. 

It was proposed that dollars-and-cents ceilings be set at a level to bring domestic and foreign platinum out of hoarding and into the market. 

It was also proposed to have the regulation prohibit imports at prices in excess of ceiling prices set by the regulation.

Presently, the industry is pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regu- Committeemen expressed the feeling that, generally speaking, pricing under GCPR has been satisfactory. THURSDAY, August 30, 1951. 

Re: 

NATURAL GAS PRICES 

Browne-OPS-GPR-824  

The Office of Price Stabilization today re-affirmed its decision of 

August 22, 1951, approving a ceiling price on natural gas of 10 cents per thousand cubic feet at well head in a proposed contract between the Stanolind 

Oil & Gas Corp., Tulsa, Okla., the Continental Oil Co., Ponca City, Okla., and the buyer, the Mississippi River Fuel Corp., St. Louis, Mo.

The two companies in question had sought OPS approval of a 12 cent per thousand cubic feet rate, included in an April 20, 1951 contract with the Mississippi River Fuel Corporation. The price was measured on the Texas pressure base of 14.65 per square inch absolute at well-head for natural gas produced in the Woodlawn Field, Harrison County, Texas.

Today's action by OPS closely follows an appeal by representatives of the Stanolind and Continental companies, and their letter setting forth added reasons why the increase should be granted, filed by them with OPS August 27, 1951. The action constitutes a re-affirmation of the August 22 decision denying the proposed 12 cent price, and establishes 10 cents as the ceiling price on natural gas sold by the two companies to the Mississippi River Fuel Corpo ration from the Woodlawn Field. 

It was made known in a letter directed to the companies involved by 0. D.

Judd, Chief, Petroleum Branch; Transporation, Public Utilities and Fuels Division, OPS. 

A highlight of the letter to the companies involves statements made by the companies in their appeal that "Woodlawn gas represents between seven and 12 percent of Mississippi River Fuel's total purchase." "You are, of course, aware of the fact," wrote Mr. Judd, "that Mississippi

River Fuel must of necessity incorporate all prices paid for gas incident to the establishment and preservation of their rate structure, and any statements that they might make leading to a contrary impression should be corrected at this time."

Mississippi River Fuel Corporation was not represented at the August appeal meeting. OPS pointed out, however, that the Mississippi River Corporation has applied to the Federal Power Commission to increase its rates on the sale of gas to public utility customers. The OPS is intervening in protest to the increased rates sought by the corporation in the case before the Power Commission. Hearing date in this case is September 5, 1951. (over) GRO-O-OPS 654

The OPS letter concedes points made by the two companies in their effort to justify the price increase sought. Included were the higher values of a large, fully controlled gas reserve; the sharp upward movement of gas prices generally during the past two years, and that United Gas Pipeline Co., one of the major purchasers in the United States, has recognized that the value of large reserves in several large producing areas had reached 10 cents per thousand cubic feet measured on a pressure base of 14.65 per square inch absolute. The letter added that the Agency had given "every consideration" to the companies' estimate of the differential value of gas due to the BTU content. 

The letter concludes, however: "It may be of interest to point out that if the Woodlawn gas was evaluated on a strict comparative price with North Lansing that a ceiling price of 9.02 cents per thousand cubic feet might have been the result. 

However, adding .6 cents per thousand cubic feet to this price, which was your estimate of the weight that should be given to the higher BTU factor, a ceiling price of 9.62 cents per thousand cubic feet might have been indicated. It therefore is evident that the 

Director has taken into consideration other values such as deliverability, large reserves, etc., in fixing this ceiling price at 10 cents per thousand cubic feet." # # # # # # #

PICK-UP AND DELIVERY CHARGES (OPS Protest to I. C. C.) 

The Office of Price Stabilization today protested to the Interstate Commerce Commission the imposition of new charges for pick-up and delivery services on freight moving on less-than-carload and any-quantity rates within Eastern territory.

The OPS protest calls the proposed charges "arbitary, unreasonable and discriminatory," and asks that the tariffs establishing the charges be suspended pending an investigation by the I.C.C., and a full public hearing 'in the matter. 

Since 1935, less-than-carload and any-quantity traffic class rates generally have included pick-up and delivery service as well as line haul transportation service. The proposed elimination of pick-up and delivery services from the published rate, and establishment of separate plus charges for such service on shipments moving less than 300 miles within Official Territory and on all shipments moving inter-territorially having either .origin or destination in 

Official Territory is tantamount to an increase in such class rates, the OPS said. "Therefore, " the OPS protest concludes, "if the proposed tariff goes into effect on September 10, 1951 (as proposed) the results would make such rates unjust, unreasonable and in violation of Section 1 (5) of the Interstate Commerce Act." 27 Section 1 (5) is one of the basic sections of the Interstate Commerce act, and provides that all charges must be just and reasonable. The protest, however, cites three additional sections of the act which it claims would be violated by imposition of these charges.

Territory which would be affected by the proposed charges includes that portion of the United States north of the Ohio and Potomac Rivers and East of the Mississippi River, except the Northern Peninsula of Michigan, the states of Wisconsin and Minnesota, and that portion of the State of Illinois lying North of and West of a line drawn from Chicago to East St. Louis, Ill. 

Arguing that imposition of the charges would be arbitrary, unreasonable and discriminatory not only as between shippers and shipments, but also as between localities, the OPS protest says: (over)

GPO-O-OPS 666

- "If the Commission (ICC) should permit the railroads' tariff to go into effect, thereby authorizing the collection of additional charges for pick-up and delivery service in Eastern or Official Territory, rail carriers in the other Territories will be prompt to follow the lead of the Eastern Territory and will file similar tariffs at an early date. "This will surely constitute an irresistible invitation to non-rail carriers throughout the United States to make upward revisions in their freight tariffs in their respective territories as soon as opportunity permits. "The net result will be a widespread increase in the cost of freight transportation in addition to the surcharges already approved by the Commission in 

Ex Parte No. 175. 

"Thus, failure of the Commission to suspend the instant schedule may very well result in a material and nation-wide inflationary increase in the cost of transporting the nation's products in less-than-carload lots." 

Signing the OPS protest are Harold Leventhal, Chief Counsel, OPS and 

Bryce Rea, Jr., and Paul R. Conway, of counsel. phy YO Ern henend Jelle worth (soldi iscol resul

WEDNESDAY, September 5, 1951. 

 Re: FUEL OIL 

Browne-OPS-GPR-828  

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today the start of a compliance investigation covering the prices received and paid for petroleum products being exported from the East Coast of the United States. 

Preliminary reports to OPS indicate that some East Coast suppliers whose prices were frozen under GCPR and who were not, at that time, selling petroleum products for export have, since mid-June, 1951, been offering, and delivering these products for export.

Many of these suppliers who have entered this new market are independent jobbers whose marketing practices heretofore have been in furnishing fuel oil to householders and industries in New York and New England.

OPS further announced that, in accordance with the present ceiling price regulations, a supplier desiring to sell petroleum products for export must make application for ceiling price for such sales if no ceiling price had been previously established. The OPS policy of establishing equivalent prices for export and domestic sales of petroleum products is designed to prevent a drain of petroleum products from the United States at the expense of the domestic consumer. 

This export situation, if allowed to continue, may mean a shortening of supply in some of the area along the Atlantic Seaboard. Requests have been made to OPS for an increase in ceiling prices for domestic sales by independent jobbers in this area to increase the supply there. These increases would have to be paid by the individual householder or consumer. It is hoped such increases can be avoided by retaining available area supplies for sale to domestic users. This price compliance activity is based on data showing that of the 2,633,500 barrels of No. 2 and gas oil exported from North Atlantic ports during the period under survey, independent jobbers who ordinarily sell mainly to domestic users, supplied 

2,373,500 barrels, or approximately 92 percent. # # # # # # # # GPO-0-OPS 686

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers 

Monday, September 10, 1951

FREIGHT RATES (General Interpretation 3 Increase in Railroad Freight Rates) 

A general interpretation of the effect of recent freight increases on ceiling prices has been issued by the Office of Price Stabilization for the information of sellers operating under price regulations. 

Text of the interpretation (General Interpretation 3, issued) follows: 

"A number of sellers have inquired as to whether they may add to their ceiling prices the increases in railroad rates recently authorized by the 

Interstate Commerce Commission (Ex Parte 175, August 2, 1951). 

Hughes-OPS-GPR-829  "Inclusion of freight in ceiling prices is determined by the specific regulation which may be applicable to the seller, and increases in freight rates may be added to a ceiling price only where such regulation permits this addition. With respect to sellers under the General Ceiling Price 

Regulation, Interpretation 1 under GCPR, issued April 9, 1951, states that increases in freight may be passed along to the purchaser only in the situations specified and only in connection with outbound freight charges." 

(NOTE: Interpretation 1, referred to here, establishes as a general rule that sellers may add freight increases to their GCPR ceiling prices only where a ceiling price was established on an f.o.b. basis or where the ceiling price, in limited situations, is a delivered price reflecting the actual cost of freight.) "Inasmuch as the increases allowed by the ICC could become effective only after August 2, 1951, such freight rate increases would not constitute a cost increase which must be reflected in ceiling prices under Section 104(e) of the Defense Production Act Amendments of 1951, which provides that certain cost increases occurring prior to July 26, 1951 must be reflected in ceiling prices. "It is the policy of the Office of Price Stabilization to afford relief to sellers where cost increases would result in inequities, and various of the regulations issued provide for adjustments in certain cases. Freight costs would constitute "costs" under these adjustment provisions and may, in appropriate cases, provide a basis for relief under the applicable regulations."

Washington Scott-OPS-GPR-832  Re: SMALL PNEUMATIC COMPRESSOR IAC The Small Pneumatic Compressor Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems.

The industry is concerned with the production of small air compressors up to 15 horsepower, not including compressors used in connection with condensing units.

It was pointed out that small compressors are used as a vital and essential common component in a very wide range of commercial and industrial applications and in connection with military, naval and air force equipment and facilities. Many mechanical devices and installations are absolutely dependent upon these compressors. They are also essential and vital to the operation and maintenance of transportation by truck, rail, water and air. 

Compressors are covered under the machinery ceiling price regulation (CPR 30), but the industry generally is currently pricing under the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR). 

Committeemen stated that the industry has not found it feasible to price under CPR 30. Also, that the industry generally is selling at maximum prices permitted under GCPR, but even so some companies are suffering a serious price squeeze which is forcing them into other production. It was pointed out that most companies need price relief to expand production or even maintain present production. 

Members stated that pricing under CPR 30 will not afford the necessary relief due to the depressed condition prevailing in the industry during the 

CPR 30 base period.

Committeemen suggested that OPS establish dollars-and-cents ceiling prices for the industry based on a study of current industry production costs, plus a fair and equitable profit markup. 

OPS officials pointed out the difficulties of using such a pricing technique. However, it was agreed that industry cost and pricing data should be assembled and studied as an initial approach to the industry's pricing problem. Thursday, September 6, 1951

Moore-OPS-GPR-833  

TIRE AND TUBE DEALERS IAC 

A majority of the members of the Tire and Tube Dealers Industry Advisory Committee at their third meeting today with OPS officials indicated a reduction in the spelled out ceilings on passenger tire carcasses would be justified and acceptable to their industry.

Present ceilings are fixed on passenger tire carcasses at $3.50 retail and $2.60 wholesale by Supplementary Regulation 49 to the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR. Proposed new ceilings of $3.00 retail and $2.25 wholesale were discussed. 

Committeemen said that dollars and cents ceiling prices were generally'satisfactory on tire carcasses, which are used tires suitable for recapping or retreading. They suggested either a differential of $1.00 for white sidewall tire carcasses, or an increased service charge for recapping and retreading white sidewall tires to compensate for the extra work of cleaning them. 

Members also recommended a differential of $1.00 be established for 6-ply passenger carcasses over 4-ply carcasses. The committee opposed establishment of differentials between sizes of passenger tire carcasses. 

Committeemen said that truck tire carcasses have risen with demand and threaten to go higher, some of the prices asked being legal under GCPR and others probably not. Prices for truck tire carcasses before Korea ranged from $7.00 to $12.00. Current prices from $15.00 to as high as $40.00 were reported. Many recapping and retreading prices are frozen at levels which prevent them from absorbing such prices on truck tire carcasses. 

Committeemen suggested fixing dollars and cents ceiling on truck tire carcasses would be necessary to stop this trend. They proposed appropriate differentials between sizes of truck tire carcasses, and a spread of 20 to 25 per cent between wholesale and retail ceilings. 

It was suggested that ceilings be fixed for truck tire carcasses at the average level of GCPR prices or at a fixed percentage of about 10 per cent over old OPA spelled out prices.

Committeemen opposed establishment of regional differentials in the ceilings on carcasses to reflect local market differences, suggesting this would tend to cause carcasses to flow to the areas with higher ceilings. 10650 GPO- -O-OPS 696

Committeemen said tire recappers and retreaders are finding CPR 34, the Services Regulation, satisfactory at present as a pricing regulation for recapping and retreading services. 

They said that the CPR 34 prices, at the same level as originally frozen under GCPR, are as much as the market will stand because of the pressure of competition.

They expressed preference for CPR 34 over a proposal to establish ceilings on recapping and retreading services by applying industry-wide cost adjustment factors to individual pre-Korean prices.

The committee generally recommended the drafting of a special regulation for new tire and tube resellers to include these features: 

1. Freeze of the retail ceiling price of new tires and tubes at the brand owners suggested list price in effect January 25, 1951. 

2. Freeze of each brand owner's discount structure in effect during the base period. 

3. Establishing of minimun discounts for all other sellers at wholesale. 

4. Requiring of maintenance of all customary trade-in allownaces, services and discounts to commercial accounts. 

The meeting was conducted by Hubert H. Peterson, chief, Tire Section, Rubber 

Branch. Other OPS officials present were D. C. Corridon, economist; William D. 

Miller and Laurence Williams, business analysts, and Harry Hinkes, counsel.

 FRIDAY, September 7, 1951  

RE: MEAT ENFORCEMENT CASE 

COLE-OPS-GPR 834 ST-4200; Ext.3491 

The Office of Price Stabilization brought its first injunctive action against a subsidiary of a nation-wide slaughterer and packer in the United 

States District Court in Washington, D. C., today.

Jepsen Hotel Supply Company of Washington, wholly owned subsidiary of Wilson & Company, nationally known slaughterer and packer, is defendant. 

On behalf of OPS, United States Attorney George Morris Fay asked the court to grant an injunction to restrain the defendant company from the sale of fabricated cuts of beef under its present schedule of prices to hotels and restaurants.

OPS officials allege that the Jepsen firm is selling its fabricated beef cuts under Schedule 2-A, Section 21, Ceiling Price Regulation 24, which has been established for use solely by hotel supply houses. OPS further alleges that the firm does not meet the definition for a hotel supply house as established under Section 50 (K) of CPR 24. 

The Jepsen firm is charging, according to OPS, prices which run from $1.10 to $5.70 per hundred pounds more on the majority of cuts than is permitted under the next lower schedule for sales to hotels and restaurants. 

The effect of the present pricing situation by the Jepsen firm, OPS officials state, is to cause higher prices in restaurants and hotels serviced by the firm.

The Jepsen firm and four other wholly owned Wilson subsidiaries have filed with OPS a protest, claiming that CPR 24 is discriminatory in banning any firm owned or controlled by a big slaughtering and packing company from being considered in the same classification as an independent hotel supply house, and using the higher price list under Schedule 2-A. No final action has been taken on the protest by OPS as yet.

The Jepsen firm, OPS officials say, has for some time given its customers invoices showing two sets of prices, but has collected the higher price under Schedule 2-A, and has indicated that if its protest is denied by OPS, it would refund the amount of overcharge shown on the invoices. (over) 10688 GPO-O-OPS 700

--  OPS officials further state that the action of the Jepsen firm is an arbitrary and wilful violation of OPS regulations. They also point out that any such refunds by the Jepsen firm would merely be a windfall to the hotels and restaurants, as they would be unable to make corresponding refunds to their customers. 

Edward P. Morgan, OPS Enforcement Director, stated that two similar cases have already been referred to the Department of Justice, and that two others are still under investigation. # # # # # 10688

PRESS RELEASE ADVANCE RELEASE  Tempo E For Use in Afternoon Papers 

GME Washington Barkley-OPS-GPR-836 ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 Re: PRUNES, BARTLETT PEARS & FREESTONE PEACHES 

The Office of Price Stabilization today announced that the ceiling price regulation for processed fruits (CPR 56) would shortly be amended to reflect increases in grower's prices for prunes, Bartlett pears and freestone peaches resulting from substantial crop losses in certain producing states.

The maximum raw material costs for prunes in Washington and Oregon for canning and freezing which, if paid, will be permitted to be reflected in ceiling prices, will be $70 a ton. This is a change from a price of $67 a ton, announced on July 26, 1951, which was calculated on the basis of a production area including Idaho. area.

It has since been brought to the attention of OPS that Idaho prune production does not enter significantly into the processing channels of the Washington-Oregon area and should not be included in the same price OPS has, therefore, recalculated the prune adjustment, considering Washington-Oregon and Idaho separately. Because Idaho 1951 prune production is not substantially below normal, the raw material costs for Idaho prunes to be reflected in ceiling prices of canners and freezers will revert to the normal legal minimum of $63.40.

The maximum raw material costs for Bartlett pears for canning and freezing in Washington and Oregon which, if paid, may be reflected in ceiling prices, will be $102.70 a ton.

The maximum raw material costs for freestone peaches for canning and freezing which, if paid, may be reflected in ceiling prices, will be $97.90 a ton for the states of Indiana, Illinois, Kentucky, Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi and Colorado. (over)

These adjustments are made in accordance with the provisions of Section 402 (a) (3) of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended, which require that appropriate allowances shall be made in ceiling prices for processed agricultural commodities to reflect substantial reductions in merchantable crop yields, unusual increases in the cost of production and other hazards in connection with the production and marketing of agricultural commodities. 

The normal legal minima for the above items in the above states were adjusted by the percentage of the 1951 crops of the 10-year (1940-49) average, as reported by the U. S. Department of Agriculture. 

GPO-O-OPS 706

www The forthcoming amendments to the canned fruit regulation and a frozen fruit regulation soon to be issued will contain raw material adjustment factors for these fruits which processors will use in determining their ceilings. These adjustment factors will be computed by taking the difference between 1948 grower prices and the adjusted 1951 legal minimum prices set forth above.

Friday, September 7, 1951  Scott-OPS-GPR-837  Re: REFRACTORIES INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE The Refractories Industry Advisory Committee met for the third time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a dollars-and-cents ceiling price regulation. 

The committee had previously met with OPS officials on April 27 and

June 21. 

The industry is concerned with the production of heat resisting refractory products such as fire brick, furnace brick, furnace linings, and other special fire and heat resisting brick clay and castables. 

Products of the industry are covered by the manufacturers' ceiling price regulation (CPR 22), but generally the industry is pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR) since CPR 22 is not as yet mandatory. 

OPS had prepared a tentative proposed dollars-and-cents ceiling price regulation which the committee reviewed paragraph by paragraph. Committemen made recommendations and suggestions for changes and clarifications to make the regulation more workable. In general, the regulation would establish dollars-and-cents ceiling prices for a basic product in each category, f.o.b. specified shipping points.

Tempo E 

Washington Re: CHEMICALS IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-838  

Members of the Chemicals Industry Advisory Committee today recommended at their first meeting with OPS officials that their industry be given the option of remaining under existing price regulations after the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, is revised to conform with the provisions of recent legislation.

Certain committeemen said their industry could continue pricing satisfactorily for the time being under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, or CPR 22, and urged that the efforts of OPS be directed towards preparing tailored regulations for the various segments of their industry rather than relying on revisions of CPR 22 as a means of meeting price problems in the industry. 

Committeemen indicated belief that the Capehart formula prescribed in recent legislation would not be generally beneficial to their industry because the volume of production has substantially increased. The Capehart formula requires that both increases and decreases in overhead be considered in computing ceilings.

OPS officials explained that the overhead is figured on a unit cost basis, so that effect of increased volume of production is to lower the unit overhead. 

One committeeman objected that this in effect penalized increased efficiency and recommended that overhead be computed on a rate basis. 

Committeemen examined a tentative draft of the proposed revision of CPR 22 and made certain recommendations for revision based on their brief study at the meeting.

Members felt strongly that the industry should be permitted to exercise the option of pricing under CPR 22 and the revised CPR 22 by categories or divisions. 

At present if a manufacturer elects to price one product under CPR 22 he must price all his products subject to that regulation under it. 

Committeemen pointed out that the chemical industry is in fact many industries and many of the companies operate in widely diverse segments of the industry. (over) It was suggested committeemen study the problem of defining the various segments of the industry which logically price separately and make recommendations to OPS.

GRO-O-OPS 705

Committeemen recommended that the revised CPR 22 retain the four methods of computing material costs that were employed in the original CPR 22. It was suggested that the product line method might be revised to require use of more than one best selling commodity in computing material cost adjustments for the line, in cases where the best selling commodity represented only a small percentage of the total volume. This would meet the objection that this method might yield disproportionately high ceilings when costs worked out favorably for the best selling commodity in a long line that represented only a small part of the line.

Committeemen recommended that provisions for including long-term contract prices in computing their costs, which were added to CPR 22 by subsequent amendment, be incorporated in any future revisions of that regulation. It was proposed that transportation costs for those providing their own deliveries be computed in direct costs instead of indirect costs.

Committeemen also recommended that the provisions of SR 2 to CPR 22, which permits a manufacturer to make an additional computation and apply his cost adjustment factors to his GCPR instead of CPR 22 base period prices, be applicable to the revised CPR 22.

FRIDAY, September 7, 1951  Re: LAMINATED BOTTLE CAPS, IAC 

Browne-OPS-GPR-839  

A proposed tailored ceiling price regulation for laminated bottle caps was discussed by the Office of Price Stabilization officials at a meeting to day with members of the Laminated Bottle Cap Board Industry Advisory Committee. 

Members of the industry are covered by CPR 22, the manufacturer's regulation. 

At this first meeting, the consensus was that a pattern should be formulated, using the measure of square yards in pricing the varied categories manufactured by the industry. The complexity of the problem, dictated by the very large number of the items and their varied price problems, led to the setting of a tentative date for a second meeting September 24, 1951. At that time, further discussion regarding the use of a pricing pattern common to the industry will be held. 

Laminated caps are inserted in metal caps such as those used in the beverage industry, in the dispensing of pharmaceuticals and proprietary medicines and carious other bottled industrial goods. The caps protect ingredients of the product from contact with the metal cap. 

Facts presented at the meeting demonstrate the complexity of the industry. 

Manfacturers laminate or glue 22 kinds of paper facings, foil, aluminum and tin on four different kinds of board and cork, utilizing calipers (thickness) of paper board ranging from twenty thousandths up to sixty thousands of an inch. 

The items are sold three ways: the individual item itself; in strips to be cut in the customer's plant, and in small jumbo rolls to be stripped and cut in the customer's plant. 

Considerations which will be included in the adoption of a pattern include: (1) the fact that the cost per thousand for the same item would be different, whether blanked out in pieces, in strips or in rolls; (2) the cost of various kinds of paper board to be laminated, whether foil, aluminum or tin, etc.

Re: 

Monday, September 10, 1951

GRAPHITE CRUCIBLE MANUFACTURERS IAC Scott-OPS-GPR-841 

The Graphite Crucible Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems.

The industry is concerned with the production of crucibles made from graphite, silicon carbide and certain clays. These crucible pot-like hollow receptacles are use for processing nonferrous metals. 

Graphite crucibles are covered by the machinery ceiling price regulation (CPR 30), but the industry is currently pricing under the General Ceiling 

Price Regulation (GCPR) pending the mandatory use of CPR 30.

Committee members stated that it is not feasible for the industry to price under CPR 30 because of the fluctuating cost of raw materials which are principally imported, particularly graphite. They stated industry members prefer to price under GCPR rather than CPR 30, even though most producers are currently suffering a price squeeze.

The committee said it felt that these products should be removed from price control because the industry has no control over cost of imported raw materials, which represent a large percentage of the cost of production. 

As an alternative the committee suggested that OPS issue a supplementary regulation to CPR 30, permitting an adjustment of increased materials cost to September 15, 1951, and that the industry be given the option of pricing under the supplementary regulation or under GCPR until such time as a tailored regulation can be developed for the industry. 

A subcommittee was appointed to advise further with OPS in the development of a tailored regulation. Members appointed as a subcommittee were: 

Mr. Arensberg, Mr. Behrendt, Mr. Michie and Mr. South, Jr. 

The meeting was conducted by Joseph C. Twinem, chief, Miscellaneous 

Metals and Minerals Section, Metals Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attend ing were: Chester R. Wasson, economist; Richard Appleton, legal staff; and

Harry Spack, Office for Industry Advisory Committees. 

(over) 

Also attending the meeting were: Valentine C. Smith of the National

Production Authority and Frank D. Lamb of the Bureau of Mines.

Re: 

N. Y. MEAT VIOLATION CHECK 

COLE-OPS-GPR-842  

Receipt of a check for $3,770.06 from the Triangle Meat Distributors, Inc., of 440 West 14th Street, New York City, in settlement of the first of several meat violation cases, was announced today by Edward P. Morgan, Enforcement Director of the Office of Price Stabilization. 

Violations of the General Ceiling Price Regulation alleged by the Government in its case against the Triangle firm included the sale of bull meat to a broker who in turn sold it to the United States Army, and the sale of kosher chucks to a non-kosher dealer with the removal of the kosher markings at the request of the purchaser. Both sales, OPS officials charge, were at prices above ceilings. 

Payment of $3,770.06 to the United States Treasury was accepted by 

OPS as compromise settlement of its treble damage action. # # # # # # #

Re: SULPHITE PAPER SUBCOMMITTEE 

Detailed recommendations for provisions of a proposed tailored regulation for sulphite and bleached kraft papers were made today by members of the subcommittee of the Sulphite Paper Industry Advisory Committee at their second meeting with OPS officials.

Under the proposed regulation dollars and cents ceilings would be spelled out for a number of key items, f.o.b. mill, and prices for other weights and grades would be established by customary differentials. 

It was proposed to spell out ceilings on the following: 

Untreated dry finish butchers paper, 40 lb.; machine treated butchers paper, 40-47 lb.; machine finish grocers and butchers paper, 30 lb.; envelope Manila, 20 lb.; regular bleached waxing paper, 25 lb., and bleached bag paper.

It was suggested that prices be fixed at levels equal to or greater than the prices established under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, on the bulk of production of each key item. 

The industry has been asked to supply price lists covering the pre-Korea and CPR 22 period, ceilings under the General Ceiling Price Regulation ceilings.

There was considerable discussion and lack of unanimity on the question of precisely what papers should be covered by the regulation. 

It was suggested that the coverage include such papers as butchers Manila, dry finish grocers, imitation parchment, water finish butchers, blasting, cartridge, die wiping, gumming, newspaper and mailing wrappers, ribbon and ticker paper, shell, silk protection, textile papers, tympan, cash register, foil backing, music roll, machine treated, oiled Manila, soap wrapper and dry wrapping papers.

Coakley-OPS-GPR-844 

 Re: OPS PETITION ON NEW JERSEY RAIL COMMUTATION RATES 

The office of Price Stabilization today intervened in a New Jersey rail rate case on behalf of thousands of commuters threatened with an increase in their cost of living.

The action followed a petition filed September 7 with the New Jersey Department of Public Utilities seeking permission to intervene in proceedings on a proposal by eight railroads operating in New Jersey for increases in intrastate commutation rates. The hearings opened today before the New Jersey Board of Public 

Utilities Commissioners in Newark, N. J. .

OPS is interested in the case, the Agency said, because any increases in intrastate railroad commutation fares in New Jersey have an obvious effect on the cost of living of persons dependent upon the railroads in traveling to and from work, school, and office.

Paul Conway, OPS attorney, is presenting the agency's views as to the railroads' need for additional revenue, the general inflationary effects which might result from any increase, and the effect of any increases upon the living standards of persons directly affected.

Railroads affected are: The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad Co.; 

Erie Railroad Co.; Lehigh Valley Railroad Co.; New Jersey and New York Railroad 

Co.; New York Central Railroad Co.; Pennsylvania Railroad Co.; Pennsylvania 

Reading Seashore Lines; Reading Co.

Washington Crossley-OPS-GPR-845  Re: HOPE NATURAL GAS RATE INCREASE 

The Office of Price Stabilization today asked leave to intervene before the Federal Power Commission to present its views on an increase in natural gas rates which could mean higher gas bills for more than one million consumers in Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York and West Virginia.

Application for a rate increase on gas sold by the Hope Natural Gas Company, of Clarksburgh, W.Va., for resale to public utility companies was filed with the Federal Power Commission on July 25, 1951. Based on figures supplied in the company's application, the increase would amount to an estimated 16 per cent.

In its petition to intervene, OPS said: "If the increase of rates and charges is permitted by the Federal Power Commission, it is probable that the public utility companies which receive natural gas from this company will apply to the various state commissions to pass the increase on the their customers.".

OPS also said that intervention was called for because a large segment of the industrial and domestic economy would be affected by whatever action was taken. Legal basis for intervention by OPS in such cases is found in Section 

402 (e)(v) of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended. 

Principal public utility customers of Hope Natural Gas Company are the following: 

The East Ohio Gas Company serving 66 communities in Ohio, including Akron, Canton and Cleveland. (over)

Pittsburgh, Altoona, New Kensington, Johnstown and Wilkensbury. 

New York State Natural Gas Corporation, a pipeline company serving utilities in New York and Pennsylvania.

The River Gas Company serving Ohio communities including Marietta. 

The Manufacturers Light and Heat Company serving its own retail customers and 27 utilities in Ohio, Pennsylvania and West Virginia, and Mount Morris 

Gas Company serving customers in Mount Morris, Pa.

Coakley-OPS-GPR-846 

ST-4200: Ext. 3491 Re: CONSUMER ADVISORY COMMITTEE 

A formal statement, suggesting that it be given an opportunity to review and offer suggestions on proposed pricing regulations is being drawn up by the Policies and Regulations Subcommittee of the Consumer Advisory Committee of the Office of Price Stabilization, members said today. 

The statement, authorized by the full committee in a meeting Tuesday in 

OPS Headquarters, will be presented to Edward F. Phelps, Jr., Assistant

Director of Price Stabilization. Mr. Phelps told members of the committee that, while he felt the consumer's interest was now represented by OPS officials in deliberations on pricing regulations, he would be glad to consider the possibilities of more formal consumer consultation. 

Mr. Phelps also told the meeting that OPS recognized that, in order to facilitate compliance with ceiling price regulations and assist the consumer in knowing whether or not selling prices are authorized by OPS, the Agency must issue more tailored regulations setting up easily identifiable ceiling prices. This process, he said, is a current goal of the Agency. 

He urged that the Advisory Committee attempt to increase general interest in the problems of price stabilization as a topic of public discussions, forums, civic and club programs.

In line with this suggestion the Committee recommended that plans be drafted to set up voluntary committees in the OPS regions and districts using the organizations which nominated members for the national committee as the nucleus.

The Tuesday meeting also was addressed by Edward P. Morgan, Assistant OPS 

Director for Enforcement. He pointed out that retailers and consumers alike must be educated regarding OPS regulations before an enforcement program can become truly effective. In addition to aiding in a public information program, the Advisory Committee can be of assistance to OPS by bringing to the Agency's attention situations which should be investigated for possible violation, he said, but warned that such reports must be reliable and factual. (over) GPO-O-OPS 722

Mr. Morgan assured the committee that, although his department is not fully staffed, it makes every effort to give each complaint referred to it full consideration and to report to the complainant the disposition of the case. 

Other speakers at the meeting were J. Otis Garber, Assistant OPS Director for Field Operations, and William C. Burt, Assistant Chief Counsel. Mrs.

Chase Going Woodhouse, Executive Secretary of the Advisory Committee, presided. 

Mr. Garber explained the work of his office, which is concerned with liaison with OPS field offices. He invited committee members to consult with these field offices so as to bring to OPS consumer viewpoints at the local level. 

Mr. Burt explained the recent amendments to the Defense Production Act. 

Congress he pointed out, has been asked to reconsider only three provisions of Title IV of the amended Act, the Capehart Amendment which considers all production costs in setting ceiling prices; the Herlong Amendment, which insures resellers their full pre-Korea percentage markup on all items sold regardless of the dollars and cents return, and the provisions abolishing slaughter quotas.

The Advisory Committee approved four subcommittees appointed by Mrs. 

Woodhouse and authorized her to name their chairmen at a later date. The subcommittees are: Washington Steering Committee Wallace J. Campbell, Mrs.

Winfield W. Riefler, Thomas X. Glancy and Boris Shishkin. Information -

PRESS RELEASE   ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers SATURDAY, September 15, 1951 

Re: 43 CPR 7 INJUNCTION ACTIONS 

COLE-OPS-GPR-847  

Forty-three court actions for injunctions have been filed or accepted for filing by United States Attorneys in 12 states as a result of the recent nationwide enforcement survey under Ceiling Price Regulation 7, requiring filing of price charts, Edward P. Morgan, Office of Price Stabilization Enforcement 

Director, stated today. 

United Men's and Boys' Shop of 136 Main Street, Hackensack, N. J., and 

Korettes of 468 Springfield Avenue, Newark, N. J., have been ordered to show cause in United States District Court in Newark, New Jersey, September 24 as to why temporary injunctions should not be issued against them for failing to file price charts.

Filing of price charts, required under CPR 7 on the part of retail dealers in apparel, furniture, household wares, radios, televisions and related fields, is important because until such charts are completed and filed neither the dealers nor OPS are able to ascertain the proper ceiling prices, Mr. Morgan said. 

Thousands of dealers came under compliance as a result of the survey, according to Mr. Morgan who pointed out that OPS is considering criminal prosecution and court action without any warning or grace period in the future as dealers have had ample time to file required charts. # # # # # # Mr. Morgan said that while only a spot check was possible at this time because of the thousands of dealers involved, the limited OPS enforcement staff and the many regulations to enforce, there will probably be many more court actions in the coming months. 

The 43 injunctive cases under CPR 7 are divided as follows: New York 12, California 10, New Jersey seven, Michigan three, Georgia, Louisiana and West 

Virginia two apiece, and California, Maine, Minnesota, North Dakota and New 

Mexico one each. 1 GPO O-OPS 721

Re: NITROGEN MATERIALS IAC Moore-OPS GPR-848 

Advisability of adopting dollars and cents ceilings on their products was discussed today by members of the Nitrogen Materials Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting with OPS officials.

Committeemen reported their products, important fertilizers, were for the most part still being sold under ceilings fixed by the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, which froze prices at the highest levels existing between December 

19, 1950, and January 25, 1951. 

They said under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, they would be entitled for the most part to modest price increases. 

They indicated their industry had not elected generally to price under CPR 22 for two reasons, namely, the competitive condition of the market and the fact that manufacturers of long lines of chemical products would have to price all their products subject to CPR 22 under it if they elected to do so for nitrogen materials.

Committeemen indicated spelled out ceilings at the average level of either GCPR or CPR 22 ceilings would be satisfactory for their products so long as costs remain about as at present.

They questioned whether they might not be foregoing possible future adjustments for increased costs under CPR 22 if they were placed under dollars and cents ceilings now.

They also questioned whether taking nitrogen materials out from under CPR 22 might not adversely affect the ceilings to which multiple product manufacturers would be entitled on their other products in instances where averaging devices are employed in figuring ceilings or costs. 

Committeemen agreed to discuss the question whether to recommend a tailored dollars and cents price regulation for their industry and report back by mail within a few days.

It was suggested any spelled out ceilings should reflect customary differences in prices by geographical areas. 

Committeemen also discussed precisely what products to include in a possible tailored regulation. Inclusion of ammonium-nitrate-lime compounds, ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulphate (synthetic), ammoniacal liquors, anhydrous ammonia, nitrate of soda, nitrogen solutions, urea and urea compounds was suggested. Re: PETROCHEMICALS IAC

Recommendation that their industry continue to have the option of pricing either under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, or the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, was made today by members of the 

Petrochemicals Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting with OPS officials. 

They reported the base periods permitted under CPR 22, from July 1, 1949, to July 24, 1950, represent an interval when the industry was depressed. Ceilings computed on the basis of prices prevailing during that interval would cause rollbacks for many manufacturers and force the industry to abandon many plans for plant expansion sought in the interest of the defense program, committeemen said.

Members pointed out that calculations of ceilings under CPR 22 was difficult for the industry because of many instances of integrated operations involving numerous raw materials, products and by-products at various intermediate levels of manufacture. The complication of computing transfer prices between the various operations existing under CPR 22 is entirely absent under GCPR. 

Committeemen said spelled out prices at GCPR levels would be satisfactory for the present, but they questioned the adequacy of such prices to cover increases in freight and labor costs in the future.

They discussed the type of information that would be required and could be furnished by the industry from which to compute dollars and cents ceilings. 

Committeemen submitted information showing prices in their industry had not advanced nearly as rapidly as their costs or as prices generally. 

It was suggested that if certain petrochemicals were placed under a tailored regulation, manufacturers who had already average costs or ceilings under CPR 22 including such products should not have to readjust their ceilings on the other products remaining under CPR 22.

Members discussed the problem of defining precisely the products to be included under a tailored regulation. They would embrace many chemicals produced from petroleum and natural gas, particularly alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, acids, esters, chlorinated solvents and certain hydrocarbons. (over) GPO-O-OPS 734

Scott-OPS-GPR-852  

Re: FROG, SWITCH & CROSSING MANUFACTURERS IAC SUBCOMMITTEE 

A subcommittee of the Frog, Switch and Crossing manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee today concluded a two day meeting with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to explore the possibilities for the drafting of a tailored pricing regulation for the industry. 

The industry is concerned with the manufacture of railroad frogs, switches, crossings and other fabricated units for railroad right-of-way installations. 

These products are presently covered by the machinery ceiling price regulation (CPR 30), but the industry generally is pricing under the General Ceiling Price 

Regulation (GCPR) pending manatory application of CPR 30. 

Committeemen reviewed for OPS officials the customary operating and pricing practices of the industry and pointed out the difficulties involved in pricing under CPR 30. They felt that the pricing provisions of CPR 30 are not adaptable to this, their industry. 

It was the concensus of the committee that a tailored regulation using the general technique of the castings ceiling price regulation (CPR 60) with some modifications would be suited to the industry. 

Under CPR 60 ceiling prices are determined on the basis of sellers list prices or formula pricing in effect on January 25, 1951. 

OPS officials told the committee that its recommendations and suggestions would be given full consideration in a preliminary and tentative draft of a proposed tailored regulation which will be submitted for consideration by the full industry advisory committee at an early date.

The meeting was conducted by Walter H. Dupka, chief, Iron & Steel Section, Metals Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: S.H.Burgess, analyst; 

R.B.Appleton, legal staff; C.W. Moore, division economist; R.E.Snyder, accountant; 

and Harry Spack, Office for Industry Advisory Committees. 

# # # # # # # # # # # # # Members of the subcommittee are: John Hutchins, Ramapo Ajax Division, American Brake Shoe Company, Chicago; Howard Prentice, Cleveland Frog & Crossing

Monday, September 17, 1951

Tempo E 

Washington Re: BLACKBERRIES Barkley-OPS-GPR-853 

The office of Price Stabilization today announced that the ceiling price regulation for blackberries for canning and freezing will reflect increases in grower's prices for these items resulting from substantial crop losses in producing areas.

The maximum raw material costs for such blackberries in Washington and Oregon which, if paid, may be reflected in ceiling prices, will be 17.9 cents per pound. The legal minimum is 14.1 cents.

These adjustments are made in accordance with the provisions of Section 402 (a) (3) of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended, which requires that appropriate allowances shall be made in ceiling prices for processed agricultural commodities to reflect substantial reductions in merchantable crop yields, unusual increases in the cost of production and other hazards in connection with the production and marketing of agricultural commodities. 

The normal legal minima for blackberries in Washington and Oregon were adjusted to reflect the decrease in the current crop compared to the 10-year, 1941-50, average, as reported by the U. S. Department of Agriculture. 

A forthcoming amendment to the canned fruit regulation and a frozen fruit regulation soon to be issued will contain raw material adjustment factors for these fruits which processors will use in determing their ceilings. These adjustment factors will be computed by taking the difference between 1948 grower prices and the adjusted 1951 legal minimum prices set forth above.

Thursday, September 13, 1951

Re: WEISERT RESIGNATION 

Coakley-OPS-GPR-854 

Edward F. Phelps, Jr., Assistant Director for Price Stabilization, Office of Price Stabilization, has accepted the resignation of his special assistant, John C. Weisert, who is returning to private industry. 

Mr. Weisert, will leave OPS September 17 to open a Washington office for the Magnavox Company of Fort Wayne, Ind.

He has been with OPS since February, 1951 and has been attached to the Office of Price Operations headed by Mr. Phelps. He worked with business associations and industry representatives on special problems relating to price operations.

Mr. Weisert came to OPS from the Scott Radio Laboratories of Chicago where he was vice president and director. He also was president of the Bissell-Weisert 

Piano Co. of Chicago. He is a past president of the Chicago Piano and Organ As sociation, a former director of the National Association of Music Merchants and a member of the Cliff Dwellers Club. He also was a member of Chicago Rotary. 

A graduate of Dartmouth College, he was class agent for the Dartmouth Alumni Fund, 1949-1950. He is an officer in the Marine Corps Reserve. Mr. Weisert is married and has two children.

A tailored regulation for manufacturers of superhosphate which would permit the industry to add a flat increase of so many cents per unit to their pre-Korean prices to cover cost increase since that time was recommended today by members of the Superphosphate Industry Advisory Committee at their second meeting with OPS officials.

Members said the industry committee could furnish figures on increased costs of labor, materials and freight to justify the proposed adjustment. 

Committeemen suggested that the information be submitted on the basis of cost increases per unit. It was proposed that average costs be compared for the year ending June 30, 1950, with those in a period of six months or more ending June 30, 1951. OPS officials undertook to provide a form on which the industry would report the required information.
