THURSDAY, September 13, 1951. 

Washington BROWNE-OPS-GPR-856  

Re: EASTERN POLE AND PILING IAC SUBCOMMITTEE Members of a sub-committee of the Eastern Pole and Piling Industry Ad visory Committee have recommended that a revised version of OPA's old MPR 559, as amended, which formerly covered their industry, be adopted by Office of Price Stabilization in writing a new dollars and cents ceiling price regulation. 

The subcommittee members said that price control for the industry worked satisfactorily under OPA MPR 559 as amended during the latter part of the war. 

It fixed dollars and cents ceilings.

The recommendations were determined at a two-day meeting of the subcommittee with OPS officials, just concluded. It was agreed that the industry would submit further price information to OPS and that the agency would work out a new ceiling price regulation on this basis. At present, the industry operates under the General Ceiling Price Regulation. 

The sub-committee meeting with OPS consisted of taking OPA MPR 559, as amended, and going over it section by section, and recommending changes, deletions and additions to bring the regulation up to date. Many of the changes dealt with new conditions, including the growing importance of trucking in the industry. 

Products of the industry are used by utilities, mines and in harbor installations and construction, and are usually finally sold treated with preservatives. 

The industry subcommittee members recommended that on the basis of information to be submitted by them, ceiling prices will be established at the f.o.b. car level to producers for rough peel products on a dollar and cents basis. Their decision eliminated recommendation of a markup, which would require application of a formula to arrive at the ceiling price. The consensus was that consideration should be given to costs incurred in preparing the tree for the industry intending to utilize it. (over) Further consideration should be given in arriving at the ceiling price, industry members said, to pre-Korean war prices; to prices prevailing during the freeze period and to suggested prices to assure production under the proposed new regulation.

GPO-O-OPS 744

Increased importance of the trucking industry in the transporation field and in important segments of the pile and pole industry is recognized in the sub-committee's consensus. A new recommended section would provide that on shipments by truck the amounts added for transportation in reaching a price may not be more than the published common carrier rates for such a haul, times the estimated weights.

If there is no published rate to the final destination, the producer should use the published rates to the nearest loading point, plus the actual cost of trucking beyond that point to destination, plus the unloading cost. 

Industry members reported that they still cannot compete with sawmills for stumpage for larger poles and piling 35 feet or more in length. Ceilings to be provided in the manner agreed upon, industry members said, might provide a solution. 

The sub-committee recommended adoption of new size specifications for the logs to be priced. The new sizes are contained in the so called Federal or 

Master Specification used by the industry. MPR 559 utilized Navy specifications. 

Territory to be covered by the proposed regulation includes all states east of the 100th Meridian, excepting the states of North Dakota and South Dakota. 

Logs involved include pine, cypress, oak and mixed hardwoods. 

The meeting was under the chairmanship of Leonard Perez, head of the 

Miscellaneous Wood Products Section. Other OPS officials present from the same section were Bernard Topkis, Deputy Head, William S. McKinley, attorney and Carl

W, Fairweather, business analyst. Walter R. Moulton represented the Office of

Friday, September 14, 1951

Moore-OPS-GPR-858  Re: MIXED FERTILIZERS IAC 

Members of the Mixed Fertilizer Industry Advisory Committee at their second meeting today with OPS officials reviewed a proposed cost questionnaire to be submitted to the industry for data required for a tailored regulation. 

The proposed questionnaire underwent substantial alterations as a result of the constructive suggestions made by committee members. 

The suggestions dealt with the selection of base periods for cost comparison purposes, the form in which raw material cost increases were to be submitted, the reporting of the selling prices for mixed fertilizers for both periods and numerous other technical details peculiar to the mixed fertilizer industry.

The industry urged that the revised reporting forms be prepared by OPS as promptly as possible for submission to the industry and that a time limit of 30 days be placed on the replies from industry. 

This urgency was attributed to the need to have new ceilings established by November 1, which marks the beginning of the fertilizer sales season. than 90 per cent of fertilizer is sold between November 1 and May 31. More

After the survey forms have been returned to OPS by industry a further meeting will be held at which the tabulated averages derived from questionaires will be reviewed for development of a tailored regulation. 

At that time, decision will be sought as to whether the tailored regulation will spell out dollars and cents ceiling prices for leading grades of fertilizer in each market area, or whether it will merely spell out percentage adjustment factors to be applied by each mixer to his base period prices to determine his new ceilings.

The meeting was conducted by George W. Strasser, acting assistant director, Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division.

Friday, September 14, 1951

Re: 

 new automobiles.

RETAIL MOTOR VEHICLE LAC The Retail Motor Vehicle Industry Advisory Committee met yesterday and today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss proposed new permanent ceiling price regulations for new and used passenger automobiles. 

Scott-OPS-GPR-859 

Resellers of new and used cars are presently pricing under Supplementary Regulation 5 (SR 5) to the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR), as amended 

September 14.

The committee first reviewed a proposed new regulation covering resellers of In general, the proposed regulation would establish resellers' dollars-andcents ceiling prices on the basis of "Special Orders" to be issued by OPS to cover each make and each body style, line or series, and for extra, special and optional equipment. To these prices the reseller would be permitted to add transportation, Federal excise taxes, State and local taxes, and customary charges for other items and services furnished to the purchaser. 

The committee made numerous recommendations and suggestions for changes and clarification. These were principally as follows: (1) That the reseller be permitted to make a charge to the customer for perparing and conditioning a new automobile for delivery equal to five percent of the basic delivered price, or $150.00, whichever is lower. (2) That resellers not be required to state finance charges, other than is required by Federal or State laws. (3) That the definition of a new car be worded so as to include demonstrators or other cars which the dealers use and which have never been sold. Also, that no mileage restriction be imposed on new cars which have been used by the reseller as demonstrators or otherwise, or that "new cars" must be current models. (4) That resellers be permitted to use a flat average transportation charge for each make and model, rather than the exact amount of transporation applied to each car. (over) 1 GPO-O-OPS 754

· 2- (5) That resellers be permitted to add to the basic price, without markup, any specific cooperative advertising charge made to the seller by the manufacturer. 

Other recommendations and suggestions were in the nature of clarifications and modifications to make the regulation more workable. 

The committee then reviewed the proposed new regulation covering resellers of use automobiles.

The committee also made numerous recommendations and suggestions for this regulation.

It was recommended that no ceiling prices should be established on models produced before 1946, except that such cars cannot be sold at higher than 1946 ceilings. This was felt necessary so that resellers could properly recondition such cars for resale.

OPS officials told the committee that all its recommendations and suggestions would be given the fullest possible consideration and that a subcommittee would be appointed to confer further with OPS as soon as a revised draft of the regulations has been prepared.

The meeting was conducted by W. LeRoy Jordan, chief, Automotive Branch, OPS.. 

Other OPS officials attending were: John M. Bulkley, assistant director, Industrial Materials and Manufactured Goods Division; Erwin Lerten, division counsel; 

Horace Robbins, branch counsel; Ralph Orr and Kirk Metserott, Automotive Branch; 

John B. Day, Hal Woodside, and Dick Kahn, analysts; Nathan Grinder, Office of Enforcement; and Harry S. Spack and William R. Thomas, Jr. Office for Industry Ad visory Committees.

TUESDAY, September 18, 1951  

Re: MEAT ENFORCEMENT DRIVE 

COLE-OPS-GPR-860  

The Office of Price Stabilization today stepped up its meat enforcement drive to include slaughterhouses in major cities throughout the country. 

In announcing the action, Edward P. Morgan, OPS Enforcement Director, stated that a special corps of investigators opened their step-by-step survey of slaughterhouse operations by checking plants in Chicago, Cleveland, Philadelphia and Newark this morning.

Special attention is being paid to grading and yield and whether or not the slaughterer is complying with live cattle ceiling prices. The meat survey is an answer to complaints of several slaughterers who claim it is impossible or them to buy cattle at ceiling prices and remain in business, Mr. Morgan stated. 

OPS ceiling prices on live cattle are based on a certain percentage of yield and also on grade of meat. Packers in buying animals estimate both yield and grade. Complaints received by OPS, according to Mr. Morgan, are that slaughterers buying out of compliance not only boost their estimate of yield to substantiate higher ceiling prices per pound, but also falsify their records and weights on invoices to cover up their illegal practices, thus billing their customers for more meat than they actually receive. Both agents and meat specialists attached to regional and district offices are assisting in the survey. "Immediate injunctive action will be taken in United States District Courts against all slaughterers found violating OPS regulations, "Mr. Morgan said. "We hope by this stepped up enforcement survey not only to curb illegal practices and bring violators to justice, but also to bring the price to live cattle on the market in line so that slaughterers who are in compliance can purchase sufficient cattle to continue in business."

PRESS RELEASE   

Tuesday, Sept. 18, 1951 ·

Tempo E 

Washington Re: HARDWOOD VENEER MANUFACTURERS TAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-861  

Detailed recommendations on provisions of a tailored regulation for their industry were made today by members of the Hardwood Veneer Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee at their second meeting with OPS officials. 

Under the proposed regulation manufacturers would apply the highest net margins they received during a specified base period to their costs for materials, labor, freight and overhead in calculating their new ceilings on commercial veneer, using the same formula they used in computing their prices during the base period.

It was proposed that the base period be January 1 to June 24, 1951. Material costs would be figured at the averages obtained from any quarter in the year from July 1, 1950 to July 1, 1951, and costs for labor, freight and overhead up to a cut-off date of July 26 or July 31, 1951. Committeemen pointed out the difficulty of attempting to control fancy face veneers. These are cabinet wood veneers 1/8 of an inch or thinner, regardless of species, used on exposed surfaces of panels and selected by buyers because of their individual decorative characteristics, from samples in flitch stock form, or manufacturered to buyers' specifications of thickness, size, color and species.

The committee also discussed the problem of aircraft veneers and urged that OPS explore the question with the National Production Authority looking to possible decontrol compatible with the defense production program. A subcommittee was named to deal with aircraft veneers. 

Committeemen questioned the practicability of maintaining ceilings on logs, but expressed belief that the General Ceiling Price Regulation was a better pricing device than a dollars and cents regulation for logs. 

The meeting was conducted by Norman 0. Cruver, chief, Lumber and Wood 

Products Branch, and James Owens, head, Hardwood Plywood and Veneer Section.

TEMPO E - Washington TUESDAY, September 18, 1951. 

Re: Canned Tomatoes 

Browne-OPS-GPR-862  

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today that processors of canned tomatoes in the Eastern Shore area of Delaware, Maryland and Virginia will be permitted to decrease their actual 1948 raw material cost by $7.50 per ton for the purpose of figuring the raw material adjustment required under CPR 55, the canned vegetable regulation. 

The result of this 1948 raw material cost adjustment will be to increase the processors' ceiling price per case of tomatoes in this area by $7.50, divided by the number of cases per ton they have realized as an average yield over the past three years. OPS said this could not be specifically estimated, since yields vary from year to year and area to area, but that normally tomatoes should yield from 30 to 40 cases per ton. 

Increases realized under the forthcoming regulation may be reflected at retail through the pass-through provisions of the grocery regulations, (CPR 

14, 15 and 16.).

The processors affected by an amendment to be issued shortly are those in the State of Delaware, Accomac and Northampton counties in Virginia, and those counties in Maryland east of Chesapeake Bay and the Susquehanna River. 

The amendment is intended to correct the effect caused by an abnormality in 1948 prices paid by canners for tomatoes, when there was a very short pack in this area.

Without the change, CPR 55 would cause an undue hardship on canners of tomatoes in this area.

GPO-0-OPS 772

Tuesday, September 18, 1951

 Re: ALUMINUM SMELTERS IAC Scott-OPS-GPR-863  The Aluminum Smelters Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss pricing problems in connection with aluminum scrap and secondary aluminum ingot. 

The industry is principally concerned with the smelting of aluminum scrap and production of aluminum alloy ingot used mostly by foundries making aluminum castings.

Aluminum scrap and secondary aluminum ingot is covered by Ceiling Price Regulation 54 and today's meeting was devoted mainly to a discussion of proposed revisions in this regulation to meet varying practices of government agencies in the disposal of scrap and surplus aluminum materials, particularly wreacked aircraft.

The committee also discussed minor changes and clarification in CPR 54 to make it more workable.

In discussing the general market situation, it was indicated that one of the reasons for the current short supply of aluminum scrap was due to the feeling on the part of some scrap dealers that ceiling prices for scrap would be increased. 

In this connection OPS officials told the committee that OPS does not have under consideration and does not anticipate the need for any increase in the general level of ceiling prices for aluminum scrap. 

The meeting was conducted by William Kerber, chief, Metals Branch and 

W. N. White, Jr., chief, Aluminum & Magnesium Sections, Metals Branch, OPS. 

Other OPS officials attending were: Alfred Copeland, legal staff; W. R. Rogers, economist; Harry Goldstein, consultant; Carl Allen, accountant, Stanley Blumenfeld,

Office of Enforcement; Harry Spack, Office for Industry Advisory Committees; and 

William E. Haines, Office of Coordinator for government Purchases and Sales.

The meeting was also attended by Lee Lloyd of the General Services Adminis tration and J. C. Nieman of the National Production Authority.

Tempo E 

Wednesday, September 19, 1951 

Washington Scott-OPS-GPR-864  Re: GENERAL MOTORS AUTOMOBILE PRICES 

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today that new factory wholesale price ceilings for General Motors passenger automobiles have been permitted to go into effect beginning today. 

General Motors Corporation filed application with OPS for price increases last Friday, September 14, under provisions of the recent revision of Ceiling Price Regulation 1, and reflect increased production costs they have experienced.

The new ceilings automatically become effective five days after being filed with OPS unless the agency denies them. OPS said the justification figures filed by the company appeared to be correct, and the new ceilings would not be disapproved.

Increases percentage-wise may also be applied to extra, special and optional equipment furnished by the manufacturer with new cars. For instance, General Motors retail price increases on car radios range from $2.81 to $5.20 and increases on car heaters range from $1.54 to $4.12.

The new prices apply only to automobiles and extra, special and optional equipment sold to dealers by the company after Tuesday, September 18. 

The new prices do not apply to cars which dealers already have on hand. 

OPS officials pointed out that the approval was for the factory wholesale price increase, and that retail prices (factory list price) must be computed from them on the basis of the amendment to the resellers' price regulation (SR 5 to GCPR) issued September 14. Using this formula, the new retail prices which can be charged were arrived at (see attached lists). 

New dealer prices can only be applied in the case of General Motors cars to shipments after September 18.

OPS said it had no notification that the company intended to put all or any of the new prices into effect immediately. GPO-O-OPS 778

PRESS RELEASE   ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers THURSDAY, September 20, 1951 Re: SLAUGHTERHOUSE INVESTIGATION 

Cole-OPS-GPR-865  

Office of Price Stabilization special agents investigating slaughterhouse operations throughout the country have extended their activities to nine western cities. Investigators have started checking into plants in 

St. Paul, Salt Lake City, Reno, Spokane, Seattle, Portland, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Sacramento.

Tuesday's investigations of operations uncovered violations in slaughterhouses in New York City, Cleveland and Chicago, according to Edward P. 

Morgan, OPS Enforcement Director. 

Typical violations discovered by OPS agents in the investigation which started Tuesday involve short weighting of customers by operators of slaughterhouses in order to cover up illegal practices such as paying more per hundred weight for cattle than the estimated grade and percentage of yield would permit, Mr. Morgan said. No further information regarding violations uncovered yesterday was given by Mr. Morgan, pending court action against the violators. 2 First grand jury indictment in the country for violation of OPS meat regulations was reported today by Mr. Morgan, in the case of Reisman 

Wholesale Butchers, Inc., of West 29th Street and Red Road, Hialeah, Fla.

The indictment, returned by the grand jury sitting in Miami, charged the Reisman corporation with filing a false and incorrect application for slaughterhouse registration pursuant to OPS Distribution Regulation 1. 

The Reisman plant, operated for several years by Max Reisman and his father, was purchased on Feb. 1, 1951, by Food Fair of Florida, Inc., which then employed Reisman as manager and his father as livestock purchaser.

OPS officials allege that Max Reisman in making application for a Class 2 registration falsified records of his 1950 kill, substantially increasing the total.

Wednesday, September 19, 1951

Re: 

RETAIL COAL IAC SUBCOMMITTEE 

Coakley-OPS-GPR-866  

A decision to defer consideration of a permanent, tailored regulation for their industry until an interpretation of the Herlong Amendment to the Defense Production Act is available, was made today by members of the Retail Coal Sub committee of the Retail Coal Industy Advisory Committee of the Office of Price 

Stabilization.

The group met with officials of the Transportation, Public 

Utilities and Fuels Division of OPS. 

The Herlong Amendment, designed to assure resellers their full pre-Korean percentage markup on sales, is under consideration by the Agency and as yet no definite interpretation as to how it shall be applied and administered has been made.

The Subcommittee recommended that a survey of the retail coal industry be made to determine general conditions and the ability of the industry to absorb cost increases.

Declaring that the recent freight rate increase of 14 cents a ton granted to the railroads by the Interstate Commerce Commission is proving a hardship to many retailers, the subcommittee urged that OPS permit dealers to add this increase to their ceiling prices.

William A. Fullarton, Chief of the Solid Fuels Branch, presided at today's meeting. Other OPS officials there were: J. Atlee Schafer, Chief, Retail Section; 

Irwin Davis, Chief, Fuels, Chemicals and Services Division of the OPS Cincinnati office; M.E. Gardner, Peter Krehel, attorneys, Solid Fuels Branch; Arnold L. Fein,

Committees; J.N. Wagoner, C.F. Luberger, economists, Solid Fuels Branch.

Wednesday, September 19, 1951 

Re: ALUMINUM SCRAP DEALERS IAC 

Scott-OPS-GPR-867  

The Aluminum Scrap Dealers Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization and discussed industry pricing problems and the current short supply of aluminum scrap. 

The committee previously met with OPS officials on June 21.

The industry is concerned with the collection and sale of aluminum scrap for use by aluminum smelters and other consumers. 

Aluminum scrap is covered by Ceiling Price Regulation 54.

There was some discussion as to the possibility of aluminum scrap ceiling prices being increased. OPS officials told the committee that 

OPS is not considering and does not feel there is justification for any increase in the general level of ceiling prices.

The committee reviewed and discussed a proposed revision of CPR 54 to meet varying practices of government agencies in the disposal of scrap and surplus aluminum materials, particularly wrecked aircraft.

The pro- posed changes are the same as those discussed yesterday with the Aluminum Smelters Industry Advisory Committee and the two committees are essentially in agreement as to the changes that are necessary. 

The committee felt that the regulation should be changed to permit sales between dealers at the maximum ceiling provided in the regulation without regard to quantities involved.

The meeting was conducted by William H. Kerber, chief, Metals Branch and W. N. White, Jr., chief, Aluminum & Magnesium Section, Metals Branch,

OPS. 

Other OPS officials attending were: Charles C. Rieth, chief, Lead, Tin & Zinc Section; A. L. Copeland, legal staff; W. R. Rogers, economist; 

Charles Moore, division economist; H. Goldstein, consultant; John Z. 

Kibbler, accountant; Stanley Blumenfeld, Office of Enforcement; and,

Harry Spack, Office for Industry Advisory Committees. 

Others attending were: Lee Lloyd of General Services Administration; 

M. C. Robinson of the Munitions Board; and, Dr. T. F. Ednie, C.

Briel, Amos Brown and F. J. Albertoli of the National Production Authority.

PRESS RELEASE  Tempo E ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers 

Saturday, September 22, 1951 

Washington 

COLE-OPS-GPR-868  

Re: GEORGIA LUMBER PAYMENTS 

Three lumber companies in Georgia have paid to the United States Treasury approximately $5,000 as a result of ceiling price violations uncovered during a three-month enforcement survey of the lumber industry in the southeastern part of the United States, Edward P. Morgan, Enforcement Director of the Office of Price Stabilization, announced today.

Thus far 18 lumber cases seeking injunctive action have been referred to the Department of Justice as a result of the investigation which extended from Washington south and from the Atlantic Ocean to the Mississippi River. The 

Department of Justice has already accepted six of these cases and referred them to the United States Attorneys in the field with recommendations for court action.

The largest lumber check received by the OPS thus far is for $2867.71 from the McEntire Lumber Company of Jasper, Georgia, for a total of 287 overcharges, all involving the same customer. Next in size is the check of $1860.54 from the 

Villa Rica Lumber Company of Villa Rica, Georgia, for 47 overceiling charges.

The third check is for $198.36 from the Covington Lumber Company for four overcharges.

The lumber cases referred to Justice Department involve above ceiling charges approximating $30,000 and several of them also seek to compel the keeping of records required under the General Ceiling Price Regulation. Thus far the majority of the cases are located in two states, Georgia and Virginia. # # # # # Among the cases referred to the Department of Justice, according to Mr. 

Morgan, is one involving a total of one thousand ceiling price violations totaling more than $7,500. Concerns involved in the 18 cases include manufacturers, wholesale and retail lumber dealers, and sawmill operators. 11367-2830 GPO-O-OPS 783

Re: PERSONNEL CHANGES-FOREST PRODUCTS DIVISION 

The Office of Price Stabilization today announced personnel changes in the Forest Products Division, following the resignation of Walter 

J. Damtoft, Assistant Director, and Acting Director for the past three months. Mr. Damtoft has returned to the Champion Paper and Fibre Co. of 

Hamilton, O., as assistant secretary-treasurer and director of the General 

Woods Department. 

Rufus I. Worrell, who has been serving as Chief of the Pulp, Paper and Paperboard Branch since January, has been named Acting Director of the Division. He is on leave from the chairmanship of the board of the Mead Sales 

Co., Inc., Dayton, 0.

During World War II he was a member of the Industry Advisory Committee of the War Production Board and the Office of Price Administration. 

Formerly he served on executive committees of the Sulphite Paper Manufacturers' 

Association, Writing Paper Association and the Book Paper Manufacturers' 

Association, of which he is presently chairman. 

M. C. Walsh, who has served as Assistant Chief of the Pulp, Paper and 

Paperboard Branch since March 1, 1951, has been designated Acting Chief of the Branch. 

Before coming to OPS he was manager of the Trade Research Department of the Champion Paper and Fibre Co., Hamilton, 0., with which he had been associated for 22 years. He also spent six years as senior research fellow of the Mellon Institute, working on shipping container research, and two years as Chief of the Paperboard, Coarse Paper and Converted Proucts Section of the Office of Price Administration. Following two years in the office of the chief of the chemical war fare service during the war. 

Earlier, he was research director of the American Oak Leather Co., Cincinnati, for two years.

Mr. Walsh, a native of Montreal, Canada, is a citizen of the United 

States. 

He received a Commerce Diploma from McGill University, Montreal, and a B. S. and Ch. E. Degrees from Columbia University. His home is in 

Hamilton, 0. (more) GPO-O-OPS 781

Smith Lumber Co., Jackson, Ala., has been named a consultant to the 

Forest Products Division in connection with pricing policies of lumber products.

Tempo E 

Thursday, September 20, 1951 

Washington Moore-OPS-GPR-871  Re: FINE PAPER MERCHANTS TAC WRAPPING PAPER MERCHANTS IAC 

Recommendations that a tailored regulation be adopted for their industry that would employ the same margins that were in effect during the period January 1 to March 31, 1951, were made by members of the Fine Paper Merchants and Wrapping Paper Merchants Industry Advisory Committees at their second joint meeting today with OPS officials.

Under the proposed regulation merchants would apply these margins to current ceiling prices on materials in computing their ceilings. 

The ceilings so fixed would apply to wholesale transactions, namely, sales to manufacturers, commercial houses, printers and retailers, of fine, book, groundwood, specialty, newsprint, glassine, waxed, tissue and other papers, paper products, paperboard and paperboard products, and paper packing materials. 

Members of the two main committees, and also members of subcommittees which met together earlier, stressed the need of employing a base period subsequent to Korea to obtain normal margins for their industry. 

It was pointed out their industry was depressed during 1949 and the first six months of 1950. Moreover, the pricing practices of a substantial portion of the industry during that interval, involving the use of standard pricing books, have been subject to action by the Federal Trade Commission, and cease and desist orders are pending against these practices. 

A regulation which would refer back to the pricing practices of this interval would thus be in conflict with the position taken by the Federal Trade Commission, it was said. (over)

The joint meetings of the main committees and subcommittees were conducted by William G. Luke, Jr., industrial consultant for fine and wrapping paper merchants. 

Other OPS officials who attended the meetings were: Rufus I. Worrell, acting director, and Carlton F. Diskin, division counsel, Forest Products Division; M. C.

Walsh, acting chief, Pulp, Paper and Paperboard Branch; Florence de Haas Dembitz, counsel; Donald K. Weasmer, economist; Charles J. Thursday, September 20, 1951

Moore-OPS-GPR-873  

Re: NORTHWEST LOG IAC 

Proposed dollars and cents ceiling prices for Pacific Northwest logs were discussed today by the Northwest Log Industry Advisory Committee at its third meeting with OPS officials.

OPS proposed ceilings be fixed at levels near those prevailing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation. The ceilings would apply to deliveries in towable waters, f.o.b. car or in the buyer's mill pond. They were computed separately by grades and species for three areas--Puget Sound, Grays Harbor and the Columbia River. Grades would be determined by the three independent grading bureaus in the respective areas. 

There were numerous individual objections to the ceilings proposed for specific grades. Some members objected that the ceilings proposed would not take care of loggers who are obtaining premium prices for quality logs. However, the committee promptly rejected the suggestion that the grading rules might be changed to take into consideration differences of quality within the standard recognized grades. 

Committeemen also objected that available published prices were lower than the market because they included many so-called trade or barter sales. They said the prices at which logs were traded were not always up to date with the market. 

Such a sale occurs, for example, when a veneer mill operator trades sawlogs to a sawmill operator for peeler logs, or when one operator trades off unwanted species for those meeting his requirements.

Various members undertook to submit invoices and other evidence that would tend to establish higher prices. 

The objection was also made that the proposed ceilings would not cover increased costs of labor, stumpage, transportation and equipment occurring recently. 

The meeting was conducted by A. L. Helmer, chief, Western Softwood Section. 

Other OPS officials participating were: M. White Smith, acting assistant director, Forest Products Division; Norman 0. Cruver, chief, Lumber and Wood Products Branch; John R. '  FRIDAY, September 21, 1951 Cole-OPS-GPR-874  Re: SLAUGHTERHOUSE INJUNCTION ACTION 

Office of Price Stabilization enforcement agents have uncovered additional meat regulation violations in slaughterhouses in four western cities in their stepped up nation-wide meat enforcement drive launched Tuesday, Edward P. Morgan,

OPS Enforcement Director, announced today. 

Violations have been uncovered in Spokane, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Fresno. Court action is being prepared in at least one of the cities, while in . the others additional time will be required to complete the investigations. 

The first court action in connection with the current slaughterhouse investigation will be heard in the United States District Court in Newark, N. J., on 

October 8. Defendants are Sidney, Samuel and Sloan Schweid and John Glorstein, doing business as S. Schweid, a partnership, at 238 East Fifth Street, Paterson, N. J.

An injunction is sought to prohibit the Schweid firm, a Class 1 slaughterer, from violating OPS weight and record requirements under Ceiling Price Regulations 23 and 24. Federal Judge Alfred E. Modarelli signed the show cause order, returnable October 8.

Mr. Morgan previously announced that violations had been uncovered in 

Chicago and Cleveland. It is anticipated that a case will be presented in the 

United States District court at Cleveland shortly, and the investigation is being continued in the Chicago case. 

Another meat court case, on the retail level, is being prepared in Spokane. 

This case involves not only above ceiling charges, but also upgrading of meat and the mutilation and obliteration of federal grade markings, Mr. Morgan said.

Friday, September 21, 1951  

Tempo E- 

Washington Moore-OPS-GPR-877  Re: CUPS AND NESTED CONTAINERS IAC 

Speed in preparing a tailored regulation for their industry was urged to day by members of the Cups and Nested Containers Industry Advisory Committee at their third meeting with OPS officials.

Committeemen reported that small non-integrated manufacturers were feeling a squeeze from increased costs of their raw materials, paper and paperboard, and also freight and labor.

They said relief could not be obtained under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, because the larger integrated companies could not obtain price increases under that regulation. Because of the highly competitive nature of the industry, one manufacturer could not obtain higher prices than another even if permitted under his ceilings. 

Returns filed with OPS on Forms 8 showed that the CPR 22 ceilings of the two largest firms, producing more than half of the industry's entire volume, averaged slightly under current prices established under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, whereas the average for 19 smaller companies making the balance was several per cent higher than GCPR prices. 

Committeemen urged that a tailored regulation be prepared as soon as possible with ceilings somewhat higher than weighted averages of CPR 22 prices, without waiting for establishment of dollars and cents ceilings on paper and paperboard. 

They said an increase was imperative for some of the smaller producers if they were to continue production.

Committeemen approved an OPS proposal that prices be spelled out for key items in each of several categories, and that prices of other items in the respective categories be determined in proportion by relationship to GCPR prices. 

Categories and key items proposed were: 

Pleated construction--3 ounce water cup. 

Conical construction--6 ounce soda cup, 3 ounce wedge cup. 

Single wrapped construction--7 ounce soda cold cup, 3 ounce light duty cup. 

Heavy duty construction--8 ounce hot drink cup, 12 ounce squat waxed food container, pint single wrap food carton. 

Lids--3 ounce ice cream cup lid, 12 ounce waxed food container lid.

Dishes--5 ounce. 

GPO-O-OPS 795

-- ·2· G OPS has already requested the industry for price lists effective during the first half of 1950, during the period January 25 to February 24, 1951, and as of August 31, 1951.

Members of the committee will report the weight of the material used per thousand in manufacturing the key items so that OPS can make adjustments for any changes in the ceilings on paper or paperboard which may be issued by OPS. 

From this information, together with that yielded by Forms 8, OPS will undertake to arrive at the spelled out ceilings.

Washington Scott-OPS-GPR-878  Re: BUILDERS HARDWARE IAC The Builders Hardware Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a tailored pricing regulation for the industry. 

The committee previously met with OPS officials on June 25.

The industry is concerned with the production of an extensive line of builders hardware items, including locks and lock sets, padlocks, butts and hinges, cabinet hardware, hangers, track and garage door hardware, overhead door hardware, etc.

Most of the items produced by the industry are covered by the general manufacturers' ceiling price regulation (CPR 22), but generally speaking the industry is pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR) pending mandatory application of CPR 22.

The committee recommended that a temporary interim regulation be issued for the industry providing for an industry wide cost increase factor. 

It was suggested that three separate cost increase factors be provided to be applied to three segments of the industry. The three segments suggested were: (1) Builders hardware; (2) butts and hinges; and, (3) door hangers, track and hardware.

OPS officials told the committee that an analysis of price adjustment information submitted to the agency based on OPS Public Form No. 8 data indicated the following factors..

Information from 21 out of 29 companies was analyzable and covered all categories of the builders' hardware industry, but only a few firms presented their data by category.

This The total 1950 net sales of the 21 companies was $129,418,000. figure represents a substantial percentage of total sales for the whole industry. 

Ten companies had 1950 net sales of less than $2,000,000, and 11 companies reported 1950 net sales of more than $2,000,000. The small companies net sales totaled $9,469,000 and the large companies accounted for $119,948,434 in net sales. (OVER) The price adjustment factor of each company was weighted by the 1950 sales of each firm and an average price adjustment factor of 103.64 was developed. GPO- -OPS 794

Price adjustment factors were also developed for the 10 small and 11 large companies, and these are 104.068 and 103.607 respectively.

Re: SUBCOMMITTEE FOR FARM EQUIPMENT RETAILERS IAC A subcommittee of the Farm Equipment Retailers Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a tenta tive rough draft of a proposed tailored pricing regulation. 

The full industry advisory committee previously met with OPS officials on July 18. The industry is pricing under the resellers' ceiling price regulation (CPR 67), and has indicated that CPR 67 does not lend itself to the general pricing practices of the industry and that a tailored regulation should be developed. 

The committee discussed a rough draft of a proposed tailored regulation which is patterned along the general lines of CPR 67, but with changes to meet industry practices.

It was also proposed that the regulation should also cover sales of used equipment with a markdown from published list prices along the general lines of the old OPA regulation MPR-133.

Monday, September 24, 1951

Barkley-OPS-GPR-880 

ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 Re: KOSHER RIB BEEF CEILING PRICES 

The Office of Price Stabilization today announced it is reconsidering a proposed amendment to the wholesale beef ceiling price regulation (CPR 24) which would have authorized kosher beef slaughterers in wholesale beef zone 4 (a) to take an additional markup of $1.50 a hundred pounds on sales of kosher rib beef cuts.

The agency had announced on Saturday that the amendment was expected to be issued and effective today, Monday, September 24.

Since the announcement, however, the agency explained, decision has been reached to restudy the proposal in the light of later price information which has been made available and in view of the fact the increase in the wholesale kosher rib beef ceiling prices would have had to have been absorbed by retailers. 

The agency now has under consideration a proposed change which would not impose any hardship or price squeeze on kosher retailers but still would equalize the wholesale ceiling prices of kosher and non-kosher ribs in zone 4 (a) so that kosher butchers would be assured of a normal supply of kosher ribs. 

Zone (4) (a) includes New York state, except for western counties; 

Pennsylvania, except for western counties; New England states; New Jersey, Maryland and the District of Columbia. (Note to correspondents: The above supersedes Press Release Nɔ. OPS-0-398issued Saturday, September 22, in regard to proposed Amendment 7 to CPR 24)

MONDAY, September 24, 1951 

Re: 

PHONOGRAPH RECORD IAC 

Browne-OPS-GPR-881  

Members of the Phonograph Record Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss proposals for establishing a specific ceiling price regulation for recordings. 

It was the first meeting of the committee with OPS, and the manufacturers and agency officials explored application to the industry of Ceiling Price Regulation 22, the manufacturers' regulation, or a specific dollars and cents regulation. Record manufacturers today are under the General Ceiling Price 

Regulation or under CPR 22. 

Industry members told OPS officials they felt their prices should not be controlled, since they are part of the show business, which is exempt. In addition, some members argued, there are many costs in the production of records which are not controlled, and placing of ceiling prices on records might bring about a squeeze when these costs rise. 

The record manufacturers said they do not regard their product as a commodity, such as a refrigerator or washing machine. Rather, it was argued, the consumer pays for the voice or music which is recorded in the grooves of the disc.

Several of the committee members made the point that the recordings are educational and cultural and appeal to the consumer at the emotional level. 

One group of the manufacturers has filed a petition with OPS asking that the recording industry be exempted from control. No action has been taken by 

OPS on this petition.

OPS officials told the manufacturers that the agency is seeking some means of applying ceiling prices to records and might not approve any action to decontrol the industry. Committee members were urged to consider either a dollars and cents ceiling price regulation or some other simple type of regulation. 

One argument repeated by the manufacturers was that the record business is highly competitive, and this in itself would make price control unnecessary. 

The industry, committee members said, has fought to keep the prices of records low. One member said that a Beethoven symphony which used to cost $13.50 on a recording now sells as cheaply as from $4.85 to $5.85. GPO-O-OPS 807

RENGS The record manufacturers saw no reason why their product should not be decontrolled under General Overriding Regulation No. 8, which decontrols such products as books and sheet music. The art which is released through a recording is in the same category as these items, it was said. 

OPS officials told the manufacturers that a policy decision is involved in the control question. Concern was expressed by the agency officials as to consumer reaction should record prices go up. Record prices were controlled during the past war, industry members were told, and OPS is considering controlling them now.

James B. Conkling, President Columbia Records, Inc.

Monday, September 24, 1951

Re: 

Moore-OPS-GPR-882  LAMINATED BOTTLE CAP BOARD IAC 

A tailored regulation which would fix ceiling prices in their industry at approximately the weighted average of ceilings determined under the 

Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, was recommended today by members of the Laminated Bottle Cap Board Industry Advisory Committee at its second meeting with OPS officials.

Information available on Forms 8 filed by the industry under CPR 22 would be used to compute an industry-wide percentage adjustment factor. 

Manufacturers would apply the factor to their prices under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, to determine their new ceilings. 

Need of their industry for a tailored regulation that would permit price adjustments reflecting increased costs was stressed by committee members. 

They reported their industry was still pricing under GCPR. It has the option of pricing under CPR 22, but members have not elected that option. Two reasons were suggested by committeemen:

In some cases the board is manufactured by long-line manufacturers who find GCPR more favorable for their entire operations. CPR 22 provides if a manufacturer elects to price under it for one commodity he must price under it for all commodities subject to it. 

In the second place, while CPR 22 would give manufacturers increases over GCPR prices, the advances would be uneven as between various products of the industry and between manufacturers. For competitive reasons, the industry generally sells at uniform prices, and an increase which one manufacturer might be entitled to under CPR 22 is of no avail to him if other members of the industry cannot obtain the same increase. 

Laminated bottle cap board is made of paperboard, pulpboard, cork or felt covered with facings of paper, foil, film or other materials, and is inserted in bottle caps of metal and other materials to keep the contents from coming into direct contact with the caps. 

The meeting was conducted by Harry C. Harvey, industrial consultant for food containers.

Washinton TUESDAY, September 25, 1951 

Cole-OPS-GPR-883  

Re: EXPANDED SLAUGHTERHOUSE PROBE 

Office of Price Stabilization agents today inspected both operations and sales in practically every major slaughterhouse in the country in a move to stamp out illegal practices in the slaughter and sale of beef. 

Expanding the meat enforcement drive now in progress, OPS Director Michael V. Di Salle has ordered all regional and district OPS directors to make immediately available to their respective district enforcement officers every person from all divisions and branches who can contribute in any way to the special livestock and beef enforcement campaign.

Personnel assigned from the other divisions and branches are working in teams with and under the supervision of the enforcement agents in the nationwide check of slaughterhouse operations and sales. These teams called on several hundred packers early this morning, inspecting weights and scales, invoices, etc. 

Mr. DiSalle pointed out that a number of slaughterers have contended that they were unable to buy beef at ceiling prices, and said that the meat enforcement program during the past week has uncovered a number of violations of the control law in slaughterhouses in at least eight cities. 

According to reports received by OPS officials in Washington, the enforcement drive is already having its effect on prices of livestock. One slaughterer reported that for the first time in several weeks he was able to buy livestock in compliance with OPS ceiling prices. "The investigation now being pushed throughout the country should show if slaughterers are recouping their losses by selling at illegal prices when they continue to purchase livestock at above ceiling prices," Edward P. Morgan, OPS Enforcement Director, stated. 

"It has been charged that slaughterers are resorting to numerous devices to cover their illegal purchases," he continued. "Among these devices are falsification of weights and records, side payments, and tie-in sales which are all violations of OPS meat regulations. "Violations have already been uncovered in slaughterhouses in Chicago, Cleveland, Newark, Spokane, San Francisco, Portland, Los Angeles and Fresno.

Court actions have already been started by the United States Attorneys in Newark, Portland and Cleveland. "We plan to continue this meat enforcement program indefinitely in order to bring the price of live cattle within the legal ceiling prices." GPO-O-OPS 810

-- · 2. 

Meantime, injunctive court action is being sought by U. S. Atty. 

Donald C. Miller of Cleveland against nine Ohio meat packers for numerous violations including the sale of ungraded meat, failure to keep records and failure to register with OPS, and to report the number of cattle purchased, prices paid, and number of cattle slaughtered. 

Named by the Government are John A. Tompkins Co., Cleveland; McElrath 

Meat Packing Co., Warren; McMillen Packing Company and Rocky's Meat Market, Kilgore; Arthur I. Fouch, Creston; Kearns Packing Company, Mansfield; B & A 

Meat Company, Lisbon; Troyer's Market, Strassberg; and Lodi Frozen Food Lockers, Medina.

Criminal action has been instituted by U. S. Atty. Lester Luther of Kansas in one of the first OPS "black market" meat cases which will be heard in the United States District Court at Wichita, Kansas, at a later date to be set by the court. Defendants are Bert 0. Persons, doing business as the El Dorado 

Packing Company of El Dorado, Kansas, and Calvin Virgil Adams, doing business as Willard's Fine Meats, Wichita, who are at liberty under bonds. 

OPS officials allege that ungraded and unmarked meat found in Persons' truck was traced to Adams' market and then traced back to Persons' packing house. # # # # # # 44

Washington Re: DOMESTIC WOODPULP CONSUMERS IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-885  

Members of the Domestic Woodpulp Consumers Industry Advisory Committee met today with OPS officials and discussed the levels of prices established under 

Ceiling Price Regulation 49, the Woodpulp Regulation. 

Ceiling Price 49, which has been in effect since June 30, spells out dollars and cents ceilings for 12 standard grades of woodpulp produced in the United States and four standard grades of woodpulp imported from overseas. It does not establish ceilings on woodpulp produced in Canada, principal source of imported woodpulp.

Ceilings on overseas woodpulp are about 50 per cent higher than domestic ceilings. Uncontrolled Canadian prices are 15 to 20 per cent higher than domestic prices.

Committeemen discussed the disparity between domestic, Canadian and overseas prices and the effect on supply that might result from a downward adjustment of overseas pulp ceilings.

Members of the committee, representing paper and paperboard manufacturers, reported no difficulties in the mechanics of operating under CPR 49.

AUTOMATIC TEMPERATURE CONTROLS IAC Members of the Automatic Temperature Controls Industry Advisory 

Committee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems. 

The industry is concerned with the production of an extensive line of automatic temperature and related controls for household and commercial application. In general, these include controls for temperature, pressure, humidity, time, liquid level, and related devices, which are used extensively with household appliances and with heating, air conditioning and refrigeration apparatus and equipment. Not included are industrial process controls, steam specialty controls and aircraft controls. 1 These products are covered by the general manufacturers' ceiling price regulation (CPR 22), but generally speaking, the industry is pricing under the 

General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR) pending mandatory application of 

CPR 22. 

A discussion by committeemen indicated that in general the industry is experiencing a serious squeeze under current ceiling prices, and that there is considerable urgency for issuance of a tailored pricing regulation to give industry wide price relief.

It was pointed out that industry pricing practices will indicate an historically uniform price relationship as between products and companies, which would lend itself to application of a weighted industry wide ceiling price adjustment factor to partially reflect increases in material and labor costs within the criteria provided under CPR 22.

The committee recommended that OPS issue a tailored or supplementary regulation giving the industry a price increase adjustment factor to be applied to GCPR prices.

Officials told the committee that OPS will correlate information submitted by industry members on OPS Public Form No. 8, using the alternative method of determining ceiling prices as provided under Supplementary Regulation 2 to CPR 22, which permits adjustment of ceiling prices established under GCPR rather than base period prices.

Re: EXPANDED SLAUGHTERHOUSE PROBE 

Many additional meat regulation violations uncovered by Office of Price Stabilization agents in a nation wide investigation of slaughterhouses today boosted the number of slaughterers in violation' to 199 in 50 cities throughout the country.

Upwards of 1500 OPS agents will continue indefinitely the exapanded probe of illegal practices in the meat industry ordered over the weekend by OPS 

Director Michael V. DiSalle. 

Commenting on the progress of the meat enforcement drive, Edward P.

Morgan, OPS Enforcement Director, declared: "Indications of wisespread violations of the OPS meat regulations bear out the contention of OPS Director Michael V. 

DiSalle that unethical members of the meat industry are victimizing the American public by sharp practices which must be discontinued. "Although the majority of the slaughterers have accepted this investigation in good spirit, our agents have met resistance on several occasions. Appropriate court action will be taken against all violators."

Typical violations found thus far in the crackdown on illegal slaughterhouse practices include falsification of both weights and records, upgrading of meat, failure to keep records required by OPS, selling ungraded and unmarked beef, shortweighting of customers, faulty scales, improper tagging of meat carcasses, and violation of ceiling prices. 

A temporary injunction has been granted against Landis and Gehman of Norwood, Pa., in the United States District Court in Philadelphia by Federal 

Judge Grim. The injunction restrains the firm from violating Distribution 

Regulation 1 and Ceiling Price Regulation 23. The firm is charged with failure to file required reports and improper grading of meats.

PRESS RELEASE    WEDNESDAY, Sept. 26, 1951 

Re: Browne-OPS-GPR-889  

MAINTENANCE BRUSH MANUFACTURERS LAC Members of the Maintenance Brush Manufacturers Industry Advisory 

Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss proposals for establishing a tailored ceiling price regulation for their products. It was the first meeting of the committee with OPS. 

Manufacturers recommended issuance of a regulation which will permit them to pass on increases in cost of raw materials, 90 percent of which are imported, to the ultimate consumer. Increased labor costs would also be taken into consideration, as would a selected base period and a uniform method for reaching costs.

The chairman appointed a sub-committee of industry members which met today and will meet on future dates with OPS officials to explore the items in the proposed tailored regulation recommended by industry members. 

Sub-committee members are Jack Ganz, President, Empire Brushes, Inc., Port Chester, N.Y.; A. R. McEwen, President, Ox Fibre Brush Co., Inc., New 

York, N, Y., and Clyde A. Porter, Secretary and Treasurer, National Brush Co., Inc., Aurora, Ill.

Following sub-committee meetings, a date will be set for a full committee meeting with OPS officials to consider their findings.

Maintenance brush manufacturers, whose products range from vegetable brushes to sweeping brushes for households and industry, are under either the 

General Ceiling Price Regulation or Ceiling Price Regulation 22, the manufacturers' regulation, if they have elected to price under the latter regulation. 

The industry members said they are caught in a squeeze between the cost of the raw materials used in their product, and what they sell the finished product for in this country. Raw materials are chiefly horse hair and plant fibers. Few bristles are used because of their high cost. The materials are imported from Argentina, Africa, Australia, India, Mexico and China. 

The brush manufacturers said that prices of their basic raw materials have increased from between 25 to 100 percent in recent years. The industry has operated normally on a small margin of profit and is highly competitive. 

Even though CPR 22 provided a measure of relief, they said, brush manufacturers have not generally increased their prices. GPO-O-OPS 835

Meanwhile, they said, OPS has no control over prices of the imported materials. As little as 10 percent of raw materials used in the industry are domestic. 

Industry representatives were asked by OPS officials why they had not used CPR 22 to obtain relief from the high foreign prices. Some members reported that they had increased prices slightly on horse-hair brushes because of the high cost of the raw material. Others said they had not gone up because of instability within the industry if pricing was done under CPR 22. This was said to be due to uncertainty among themselves as to proper application of the four elective pricing formulas in the regulation. Still others said they had been unable to raise prices because of the highly competitive nature of the industry. 

Industry members suggested that a regulation be issued which might include the following: An escalator clause to cover cost increases to assure their normal profits; that CPR 31, the import regulation, be tied into CPR 22 to cover price increases; that provision be made for periodic price adjustments; that a single pricing formula for the entire industry be adopted; that a new cut-off date be established and that a certain small number of specialty brushes be exempted from price control.

The OPS officials said it would be difficult to issue a tailored regulation with an escalator clause and suggested the cost of raw materials might be stabilized if they reach exorbitant levels. It may be possible to provide relief if a regulation which establishes July 26, instead of the industry's earlier cut-off date in March, is issued.

The meeting was conducted by J. H. Randolph, Jr., chief of the Housewares and Accessories Branch, Consumer Durable Goods Division, and Charles M. 

Gilbert, chief of the Housewares and Hardware section of the same division. 

Other OPS officials participating were Ernest Heilmann, Director and Eugene E.

Smallwood, Assistant Director, of the Consumer Durable Goods Division; J.

Office of Accounting, and Walter R. Moulton, Office of Industry Advisory Committees.

THURSDAY, September 27, 1951  

Cole-OPS-GPR-891 

Re: DiSALLE STATEMENT ON MEAT 

Office of Price Stabilization agents engaged in an expanded nation-wide probe of slaughterhouses today reported the number of violators uncovered had risen to 254 in 59 districts throughout the country. The investigation will be continued indefinitely in order to curb illegal practices in the meat industry. 

Eight injunctive actions--two in Los Angeles, one in Newark, New Jersey; three in Shreveport, Louisiana, one in Fresno, California, and one in Dallas--against slaughterers have been filed thus far, with more now being prepared for filing in court. These injunctive actions involve from one to seven violations. 

Meanwhile, OPS Director Michael V. DiSalle today released the following statement through his office in Washington: "The results of this week's beef enforcement drive have already conclusively shown that a portion of the meat packing industry is not cooperating with the OPS program to prevent the price of beef in the butcher shops from rising even higher. "Indeed, the American Meat Institute, in a statement personally attacking me, made it clearer than ever that their objective is the destruction of price ceilings for beef. "The AMI statement was obviously prompted by the speech I made this week before a forum of San Diego consumers and housewives. I pointed out then some of the illegal, immoral and unethical practices that exist in parts of the meat industry. Since that time our Enforcement Division has checked slaughterers and packers all over the country. The results so far show many instances of the unethical practices I described, which now are also illegal under our regulations. "In Los Angeles, the U. S. District Attorney has filed the first two cases growing out of our enforcement drive, asking injunctions against two packers. 

Additional injunctions are being sought against packers in other parts of the country. Here are a few of the violations uncovered in our nation-wide checkup-- "1. In the Pacific Northwest we found upgrading of meat sold at retail to the consumer, overcharges on beef sold to the armed forces, charging transportation where there was no transportation. "2. In Reno, Phoenix, Fresno, Sacramento and Los Angeles as well as in the 

Pacific Northwest we found that slaughterers had failed to keep adequate slaughter and purchase records. There was upgrading of beef bought at over-ceiling prices. "3. In Sacramento, Detroit, Pittsburgh and Chicago, investigation showed short weights on beef deliveries and faked dress weight statements. GPO-O-OPS 840

2. "4. In the Fresno and San Francisco area we found dealers were leaving excess fat, sweetbreads, and extra tail joints on dressed carcasses delivered to wholesalers, "15. In Los Angeles and San Francisco slaughterers had ignored OPS and continuod to charge over-ceiling prices. #6. It was common violation over the entire country to find slaughterers paying over-ceiling prices for beef and recouping by degrading sausage, frankfurters and hamburger by decreasing the beef content and adding illegal amounts of cereal, water and undesirable products. "7. In Sacramento we found that the listed weight of beef carcasses had included part of the tare weight of equipment such as pulleys, shrouds and pins so that the actual animals were being purchased at above-ceiling prices. "8. We found it common over the country to fail to keep adequate records and to file the forms necessary to show that purchases and salos were within the regulations. 

19. In the Boise, Idaho, area we found a serious beef shortage developing because out-of-State buyers were going into the Idaho live cattle market and buying practically all available animals at high prices, so that local packers could not obtain the beef to supply their customers in the area. Two local packing plants were shut down and one large packer is slaughtering only 60 percent of his normal kill. "The assertion by the American Meat Institute that the situation will get worse unless controls are promptly ended is first of all a threat to deprive American families of beef unless we surrender to the selfish interests purporting to represent the meat industry. But far more than that is involved. It is an attempt to break down the entire stabilization program for the sake of exorbitant profits for a few. Let me tell you what would happen if beef controls were removed, "First, beef prices would soar still higher. Second, such a demonstration t that we must give in to one industry which refused to cooperate would destroy the mutual confidence and cooperation that the rest of American industry and our OPS staff have built up together. Violation and defiance of our regulations would be encouraged. It would set off demands for a new round of price and wage incrcases, And under the circumstances, such increases could not reasonably be denied. The cost of living, which has gone up only 9/10ths of one percent in the seven months since the general price freeze, would start an upward sweep again. The cost of defense-a cost borne by every American taxpayer--would go up and additional taxes would have to follow. "American families must not be deprived of the protection of price stabilization. And--a really wild round of inflation would undermine the economic base that is the foundation of our military security. "We cannot permit these things to happen. We, as a Nation, must be strong enough--and big enough to submerge our differences and carry through the defense program so successfully begun. We must restrain the few among us who place profit before patriotism. For here in America we hold--now, today--the fate of the 

Entire free world in our hands."

OFFICE OF PRICE, STABILIZATION  

Crossley-OPS-GPR-892  PROTEST AGAINST WOOD PULP CEILINGS 

A Board of Review hearing on a protest against wood pulp ceiling prices, established under Ceiling Price Regulation 49, was held at the 

Washington Office of Price Stabilization today. 

The protestant was the Gould Paper Corporation, of Lyons Falls, N. Y., which produces printing paper and sells it surplus to other manufacturers. 

Appearing for the protestant were R. G. Dunmore, attorney, and E. J. Doonan, sales manager of the company. Representing R. W. Luether president of Gould. 

Paper Corporation, at today's hearing was the law firm of Ferris, Hughes, Dorrance and Groben, of Utica, N. Y.

Basically, the protest was directed at the requirement of CPR 49 that transportation costs up to $16 per ton of unbleached sulphite and of. groundwood pulp be absorbed by the seller. The company maintained that, in the case of unbleached sulphite, this absorption requirement would result in a ceiling price approximately $3.60 less than the company's actual manufacturing cost. The company also asked that its protest be considered either as a request for amendment to the regulation or as an application for individual adjustment.

The following issued were discussed at today's hearing: 

1. Whether CPR 49' is generally fair and equitable in industry-wide application to the manufacture of unbleached sulphite pulp and groundwood pulp if it results in (a) one manufacturer, who sells to other paper makers the excess of its production of these products not required in its own paper making operations, having a ceiling price for unbleached sulphite pulp less than the total of all manufacturing costs, both direct and indirect, and (b) the same manufacturer having a ceiling price on groundwood pulp which returns a reduced profit less than that required to continue profitable production thereof for sale. 

2. Whether, if the application of CPR 49 requires a manufacturer of these products to use a pricing plan other than that used prior thereto, it compels a change in a business practice or a cost practice, or method in violation of Section 402 (g) of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended. 

3. Whether CPR 49 is arbitrary if its application permits competitive

Canadian manufacturers of unbleached sulphite pulp to sell, at prices higher than the ceiling prices established for domestic manufacturers of the same product. 

GPO-O-OPS 853

As provided under Price Procedural Regulation 1-Revised, an official transcript was made of today's hearing. Members of the Beard of 

Review will subsequently meet to consider the transcript and all other data and render an advisory opinion to the Director of Price Stabilization. 

Members of the Board of Review were: Charles Evans, legal advisor, Forest Products Division, presiding; Lester R. Conley, acting chief, Transportation Branch; and Joseph C. Twinem, head, Miscellaneous Minerals and Metals Section. Also representing OPS was Albert F. Reardon, Office of Boards of Review.

Washington Moore-OPS-GPR-893 

SHOE BOARD AND BINDERS BOARD IAC Members of the Shoe Board and Binders Board Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials explored the question of what type of price regulation would be most suitable for their industry. 

Committeemen expressed the feeling that further price studies in their field should be made before reaching a conclusion and OPS officials undertook to gather the requisite information from 18 companies making shoe board and several companies making binders board. 

Committeemen reported that there was no immediate need for a tailoredregulation because, for competitive reasons, prices frozen under the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, on January 26, 1951, were all the market could stand at present. They said these prices were unsatisfactory, not being in a normal relationship to costs. They reported that some manufacturers had filed ceilings under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, which were higher than they had under GCPR, but that they could not be supported in the present market. Committeemen, however, stressed a desire that a tailored regulation be written so they could obtain normal profit margins whenever the market would support them.

They argued that, with their selling prices fixed, their margins were largely dependent on the prices of waste paper, a basic raw material for them. 

They urged that prices on waste paper first be established and that prices for their industry be related thereto. (over) The industry produces varieties of paperboard used by book binders and by shoe manufacturers, the latter including counter, sole, mid-sole and heeling boards. There are no industry-wide standard grades. Instead, grades vary between manufacturers as to price, quality, weight and other characteristics, and are generally sold under trade names.

Discussion brought out that it would be difficult if not impossible to fix flat dollars and cents ceilings covering the industry, or even for a few selected key grades to which manufacturers might relate the prices of their other grades.

GPO-O-OPS 850

COR 

In the case of binders board, some manufacturers sell direct to the trade and others through jebbers, in accordance with published price lists. 

Prices are ordinarily on a delivered basis, and vary according to areas, reflecting delivery costs.

In the case of shoe board, some manufacturers sell f.o.b. plant and others on a delivered basis, some against published price lists, others against unpublished price lists.

No common denominator could be reached in the discussion to be used as a basis for flat fixed pricing, and no common pricing formula was found. 

Accordingly, it was suggested that a tailored regulation establish prices at the level prevailing for each individual manufacturer as of a specified date, or at a date adjusted by industry-wide percentage cost adjustment factors.

Committeemen concurred with the OPS suggestion that the industry be asked for price lists prevailing immediately before the outbreak of fighting in Korea, under GCPR, and as now prevailing. From these prices it was hoped a pricing pattern might be developed. 

F. S. Madden, Secretary

The Davey Company 

Jersey City 8, New Jersey

RE: PETROLEUM TANKER IAC Members of the Petroleum Tanker Industry Advisory Committee told 

Office of Price Stabilization officials at their initial meeting today that they felt sure the tanker supply was such that domestic trade could be satisfactorily supplied without a tailored pricing regulation for the industry.

Both industry representatives and OPS officials expressed the view that it would be impractical, at this time, to issue a specific regulation for the industry whose rates now are controlled by the General Ceiling 

Price Regulation. 

Without adequate controls in world-wide trade, or resort by the government to requisitioning of ships, specific controls in domestic coastwide trade would tend to jeopardize the supply of ships for domestic trade, industry members said.

Although the GCPR was characterized by industry members as inequitable, because of the variety of rates prevailing at the time of the freeze, it was pointed out that the regulation did provide for adjustments under certain conditions.

Scott-OPS-GFR-895 

 Re: SCREW MACHINE PRODUCTS, METAL STAMPINGS, MECHANICAL PRECISION SPRINGS INDUSTRY ADVISORY SUBCOMMITTEES. 

A subcommittee consisting of members selected from three industry advisory committees representing the screw machine products industry, the metal stampings industry, and the mechanical precision springs industry, met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss the draft of a proposed tailored pricing regulations to cover the products of these three industries. 

This subcommittee previously met with OPS officials on August 27 and 

September 13. 

Three industry members representing the tools, dies, jigs, fixtures and workholding devices industry were invited by OPS to attend today's meeting with a view of determining whether this industry might be covered by the proposed regulation now under consideration. After a review of the proposed regulation it was decided that the operating and pricing practices of the tool and die industry generally would not lend itself to pricing under the proposed regulation and that this industry would probably require a separate tailored regulation. It was suggested that an industry advisory committee be appointed for the purpose of discussing the pricing problems of the tool and die industry. 

OPS officials pointed out that tool and die manufacturers are not covered by the machine tool ceiling price regulation (CPR 30, SR 2, Rev. 1) since that regulation is restricted to specified power driven machine tools. 

The subcommittee reviewed in detail the proposed "job shop" tailored price regulation for the three industries involved. (more) 1 1 GPO-O-OPS 845

In general, the proposed regulation would establish ceiling prices on the basis of pricing formulas which each manufactuber had in effect on January 25, 1951, using material and labor costs as of that date. 

Generally speaking, it was felt that the proposed pricing method would establish ceilings somewhat lower than the general level of prices established by the industry under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR) and at about the same level that might be established under Ceiling Price Regulation 30 (Machinery), if CPR 30 should become mandatory for these three industries. These industries have contended that pricing under CPR 30 is impractical because of the job shop nature of their operations.

The proposed draft exempts small orders from ceiling price requirements. 

This would involve small orders of less than $500 in the case of stampings, of less than $400 in the case of screw machine products, and of less than $200 in the case of mechanical precision springs. This exemption would be limited to a ratio of small orders to total sales established by a selected calendar month between 

November 1, 1950 and January 31, 1951. The committee felt this exemption should be established on the basis of a ratio to total sales to be selected by the seller for any calendar quarter from February 1, 1950 to January 31, 1951.

With the exception to the provision relating the the exemption of small order sales the committee felt that the proposed regulation would be generally satisfactory to the industries involved. 

The meeting was conducted by Warren B. Leland, head, Auxiliary Machinery 

Section, Machinery Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: Erwin Lerten, branch counsel; Charles Moore, division economist; "dward L. Norman, chief, Cutting

Re: CAST IRON BOILER AND RADIATOR IAC The Cast Iron Boiler and Radiator Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a tailored pricing regulation for the industry. 

The committee previously met with OPS officials on May 24.

The products of the industry are covered by the general manufacturers' ceiling price regulation (CPR 22), but generally speaking the industry is pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR) pending mandatory application of CPR 22. 

Industry members contend that pricing under CPR 22 would distort historically uniform price relationships as between products and companies.

The committee discussed the drafting of a tailored regulation to be based on an industry-wide price increase adjustment factor to be applied to prices established by the industry under the General Ceiling Price 

Regulation (GCPR). 

OPS officials reviewed with the committee figures complied by OPS from OPS Public Form No. 8 information submitted by the industry under the provisions of CPR 22. These figures were correlated to price adjustment factors computed under the provisions of Supplementary Regulation 2 to CPR 22, which permits adjustment of ceiling prices established under GCPR rather than base period prices. The industry-wide price adjustment factors indicated by these figures would be about the same as present GCPR prices for cast iron boilers and slightly above GCPR prices for cast iron radiators. 

Generally speaking, the committee, felt that a tailored regulation based on the industry-wide price adjustment factors determined by OPS would be satisfactory to the industry at this time. the urgency for the issuance of such a regulation at an early date.

THURSDAY, September 27, 1951 

Washington Re: STATEMENT BY RICHARD F. COOK 

McClanahan-OPS-GPR-897  

The following statement was made today by Richard F.

Cook, Assistant 

Director for Management, Office of Price Stabilization: 

I am glad to withdraw the staff bulletin cautioning against unauthorized disclosure of confidential information regarding Office of Price Stabilization operations.

It was in no way intended to place any restriction whatsoever on the dissemination of legitimate information on agency activities, decisions or policies which have been formulated or adopted. 

Some information coming to OPS is confidential because it has been obtained from business men on that basis. 

It had also come to our attention that in a number of cases information on matters on which decision is pending and where final policy has not been adopted, has been given out, resulting in confusion and, in some cases, actual inconvenience to businesses mistakenly believing they were final and official. Some legal interpretations which had not been finally approved, had been taken to be official, with consequent confusion and embarrassment. 

In view of this the staff bulletin was issued. 

It has always been Office of Price Stabilization policy to make public all information concerning agency activities which are of public concern. 

This policy continues in effect. 16 GPO--0--OPS 847
