PRESS RELEASE   

Re: 

SURVEY OF GROCERY MARGINS 

Crist-OPS-GPR-900 A nationwide survey of grocery margins will get under way with pre-tests starting today in New York City and Columbus, Ohio, it was announced by the 

Office of Price Stabilization. 

ST-4200; Ext. 5518 

The survey is being made by OPS with the assistance of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (Department of Labor) to determine how the present markups in OPS grocery Ceiling Price Regulations (CPR's 14, 15 and 16) compare with margins of May 24 June 24, 1950.

When completed, OPS will discuss its analysis of the survey with industry representatives, before making any adjustments in its markup regulations. 

During the next few days, the survey plan will be pre-tested in New York and Columbus. The pre-test should take about a week or 10 days, and another 

10 days or two weeks will needed to analyze results, iron out the "bugs" and revise forms and instructions before starting work in a nationwide sample of cities and rural areas. 

It is now planned to use OPS personnel in the various district offices to collect net cost and selling price data for the period of May 24 June 24, 1950, from wholesalers and retailers. 

OPS said its staff members will be used for this purpose because they are already working with the distributors who will be represented in the survey, either in the course of day-to-day administration of the regulations or in collecting the same types of data for the current community food pricing survey. 

The Bureau of Labor Statistics has taken substantial responsibility in developing the design of the survey, and will continue to take an active part in the conduct of the study and in analyzing results. Scientific methods of sampling, OPS officials pointed out, have made tremendous strides since the early 1940's when the original margin survey was made by BLS for the wartime Office of Price 

Administration. 

(over) In the developing the current survey, OPS has had the advantage of assistance from leading statisticians, both in BLS and the Bureau of the Budget. 

Technical problems and objectives of the survey were discussed by OPS and BLS officials with members of three industry advisory groups at a joint meeting on August 16: Wholesale Food Distributors, Retail Food Distributors, and a special group of Institutional Wholesalers. 11872 GPO-O-OPS 863

The counsel of these three groups was sought in order to assure the adequacy of the procedure proposed for the survey and particularly the proper selection of items to represent the several food categories which are subject to the various mark-ups in the ceiling price regulations. 

The suggestions made by the advisory committees indicated the need for reconsidering the tentative plans, particularly the method for selecting the items to be studied, and to insure that both high and low items, various brands and sizes were adequately represented. Since the meeting of the advisory committees, major emphasis of the OPS-BLS group has been aimed at designing a sample which would be representative of markup practices during the base period 

May 24 - June 24, 1950 for all items covered by Ceiling Price Regulations 14, 15, and 16, and which would therefore be fair to the industry. 

This margin survey was first announced at the time the grocery regulations were issued. In the statement of considerations accompanying each of the three orders, CPR's 14, 15 and 16, OPS declared: "The OPS is now organizing a study of margin and earning figures for food distributors in order to obtain more recent comprehensive data. If the study should indicate that the ceiling prices established under this regulation are either too low or too high, the regulation will be promptly revised to reflect the results of the survey."

In addition to revising margins for food items to reflect base period practices, another objective has been added: to determine margins for a selected list of non-food items sold predominately by grocery distributors, with the objective of bringing such non-food items under the same or similar regulations. 

This survey has been designed to cover almost all items generally sold by grocery departments of food distributors, to include high margin as well as low margin items, varying sizes of products, and private as well as nationally advertised brand foods. 

In this survey, a representative cross-section of distributors, covering the four classes of wholesalers and the four groups of retailers, specified in the regulations will be sampled. OPS officials emphasized that all data collected will remain confidential and will be utilized solely for statistical purposes. Each collection form bears the following statement: "The individual company information reported on this Form is for use in connection with the Defense Mobilization Program. Persons who have access to individual company information are subject to penalties for unauthorized disclosures."

Monday, October 1, 1951 

  Re: SPECIAL PAPERBOARD LAC Moore-OPS-GPR-902  

Detailed recommendations for provisions of a tailored regulation for their industry were made today by members of the Special Paperboard Industry Advisory 

Committee at their third meeting with OPS officials.

It was proposed that dollars and cents ceilings be spelled-out for key items produced by the industry.

Individual manufacturers would determine their ceilings on other weights and grades by applying to the spelled-out prices the same differentials that they charged during a specified base period. Differentials would also be employed to determine ceilings for differences in quality, sizes of rolls, trim, finish, color and other particulars.

The period of January 25 to February 24, 1951, was considered as the base period. 

Members of the committee discussed at what level the spelled-out prices would be applied, and suggested f.o.b. mill with adjustment for the variation in selling practices in the industry.

Committeemen reported that some manufacturers sell f.o.b., mill some on a delivered basis, and some on a maximum freight allowed basis and pointed out the difficulty of adjusting these prices for the purpose of obtaining industry averages. 

Methods of making adjustments were discussed. 

The regulation would apply to food container paperboard, special industrial paperboard and cardboard.

Subcommittees representing the food container paperboard and special industrial paperboard segments were scheduled to meet tomorrow for more detailed discussions. 

The meeting was conducted by C. F. Wiedeman, Jr., industrial consultant for special paperboard products.

COLE-OPS-GPR-903  

PENNSYLVANIA MILK COMMISSION CASE 

The Office of Price Stabilization today asked the United States District Court at Pittsburgh for a preliminary injunction to compel 13 milk distributors in the Pittsburgh milk district to lower their price for retail street sale of milk to consumers. 

Federal Judge Wallace S. Gourley set October 8 at 10: 00 A. M. for a show cause hearing as to why a temporary injunction should not be issued. 

Named in the OPS action were: Cronenweth Dairy Co.; Arthur Rombath, trading as D & M Farm Dairy Co.; Jacob Dressler, trading as Dressler Farm Dairy; 

Evergreen Dairy-Miller Bros., Inc.; Harmony Dairy Co.; H. H. Hattman, trading as Hattman's Dairy; Isaly Dairy of Pittsburgh; Meadowgold Dairy, Inc.; Joseph 

A. Gercken, trading as Merry's Dairy; Otto's Suburban Dairy; Rieck-McJunken 

Dairy Co.; John W. Snee and Clara M. Snee, trading as Snee Dairy Co; and

Valley Dairy Co. 

OPS officials informed the court that prices being charged on street sales as a result of the July 17 order of the Pennsylvania Milk Commission are in violation of ceiling prices. OPS late in July denied the Commission's request for an increase.

The state agency's July 17 increase combined with an OPS-approved one made last April raised the street sale price of milk in Pittsburgh to 23 cents a quart, in Erie to 22 cents, and in Johnstown-Altoona to 22 cents. 1 OPS said the permissible legal street ceiling price of milk in the three areas is 22 cents in Pittsburgh, 22 cents in Erie, and 212 cents in Johnstown Altoona. These prices are calculated under General Ceiling Price Regulation pricing formulas.

OPS officials emphasize that the courts have held that regulations issued by a Federal agency supersede those of a State Commission, in numerous cases brought under Office of Price Administration wartime controls. (more) The July 17 order of the Pennsylvania Milk Commission, increasing the 

Pittsburgh and Erie street price one cent a quart and the Johnstown-Altoona price one half a cent a quart, brought the total of both increases to two cents a quart for Pittsburgh and Erie and one and one half cents a quart for 

Johnstown-Altoona area. 1 GPO-0--OPS 881

Although the total increase of two cents a quart in Pittsburgh and Erie would have represented 92 cents per hundred pounds at the producer level, the actual increase to the producer was only 70 cents with the remaining 22 cents increasing the distributive margin. Likewise in the Johnstown-Altoona area the one and one half cents a quart increase would have represented 69 cents per hundred weight at the producer level. But the producer received only 49 cents with the remaining 19 cents increasing the distributive margin. 

Because the amounts which went to the producer did not justify the increases to the consumer, OPS did not approve the Commission's request for the July 17 increase.

According to OPS officials, the agency under the Defense Production Act has no control over increases in prices paid to producers of milk so long as milk remains below parity or the legal minimum established by the act. 

The General Price Ceiling Regulation automatically permits handlers of farm commodities to pass through to consumers the actual dollar-and-cents increase in the price they have to pay for a below-parity agricultural product by adding that increase to their GCPR ceiling price and rounding it according to Supplementary Regulation 20 to the General Ceiling Price Regulation.

Tuesday, October 2, 1951 

  Re: SHELL EGGS TAC 

Barkley-OPS-GPR-905  

A proposed ceiling price regulation for eggs sold in the shell, which would provide for price differentials by zones and months of the year, was discussed today at a second meeting of the Shell Egg Industry Advisory Committee with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization. 

The proposal to use a zone system follows a preference for this approach which was expressed by committee members at their first meeting with OPS officials last May 21. The zone system was used by the Office of Price Administration during 

World War II. 

Under the proposed system, 44 zones would be set up with fixed price differentials above the midwest base zone. These differentials would be lower during the heavy egg production in the spring and higher during the low production in the fall. 

The proposed regulation, which is in the drafting stage, also would recognize quality premiums insofor as practicable.

OPS spokesmen emphasized that the proposed shell egg regulation is in the drafting stage and in designed to meet a possible tight supply situation should one develop in the future.

They explained that current egg prices, on a seasonally adjusted basis, are below parity. The seasonally adjusted price on September 15 was 93 percent of parity. Under the Defense Production Act, ceilings cannot be placed on the producer price of eggs so long as the price is below parity.

The committee also discussed the question of the level at which the regulation should set prices for procurement grade eggs sold to the armed forces. Quartermaster officials of the Department of Defense participated in this phase of the meeting.

Tuesday, October 2, 1951 

  

Moore-OPS-GPR-907  

Re: FOOD CONTAINER PAPERBOARD SUBCOMMITTEE SPECIAL INDUSTRIAL PAPERBOARD SUBCOMMITTEE Members of the Food Container Paperboard Subcommittee and the Special Industrial 

Paperboard Subcommittee of the Special Paperboard Industry Advisory Committee today discussed with OPS officials details of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry.

The Food Container Paperboard Subcommittee after study emphasized that it was impossible to spell out satisfactory dollars and cents ceiling prices for key items as contemplated in the full committee meeting yesterday.

One difficulty was a disparity in the basis of sale. Some mills sell f.o.b. mill and others on a delivered basis. Price differentials between integrated and nonintegrated mills, and between northern and southern mills, constituted another problem. 

Still another was the cost differences arising from use of different types of equipment. 

Members of the subcommittee advised that the best pricing device would be the employment of industry-wide cost adjustment factors which could be applied to individual manufacturers' prices prevailing during a specified base period, possibly to ceilings established under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR.

It was proposed to develop separate factors for solid chemical paperboard, groundwood paperboard, and paperboard made from a conbination of chemical and groundwood pulp. 

OPS officials undertook to study information available on Forms 8, filed by the industry under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, to see if information thereon was sufficient to determine such factors. 

It was indicated CPR 22 prices were higher on an average than the current market. 

Members of the Special Industrial Paperboard Subcommittee recommended that their segment of the special paperboard industry await issuance of CPR 22-X before attempting to fix ceilings under the proposed regulations. CPR 22-X is the revision of the 

Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation which OPS has been considering in order to make it conform with recent legislative provisions, Members unanimously felt it would be impracticable to attempt to spell out prices for more than a few of the special industrial paperboard products, which approximate 

200, because of the variety of specifications.

Important items include stencil board, tabulating card stock, file folder stock, tag stock, coated tag stock, wallet, patch, jacquard board, coated tympan and plain tympan. GPO-O-OPS 886

--  Committeemen said the total product of their industry was around 500,000 tons annually, but 10 or 12 items would account for 80 per cent or more of the volume. 

Even for these items it would be difficult to spell out uniform prices for the industry, because some manufacturers sell f.o.b. mill and others on a delivered basis, and because of differences in cost dependent on whether the manufacturer is integrated or non-integrated, uses a cylinder of Fourdrinier machine, or uses domestic, Canadian or Scandinavian market pulp.

Committeemen suggested that prices might be spelled out for tab stock, tag stock and possibly some of the other major items. Pricing of the remaining items, they recommended, should be by formula. They suggested that if manufacturers had an option of pricing these grades, either under CPR 22 or CPR 22-X, this might provide the most practical solution. 

The discussion bfought out that some manufacturers of special industrial paperboard had filed Forms 8 under CPR 22 and others had not. 

Forms filed showed CPR 22 ceiling prices were higher than GCPR prices. Committeemen reported some manufacturers who had filed under CPR 22 were not attempting to sell at their CPR 22 ceilings, in some instances for competitive reasons and in others because their customers could not pay the CPR 22 prices and continue to operate profitably, Committeemen stressed the importance of having flexible pricing devices available if severe shortages developed in pulp, requiring substitutions of one raw material for another with consequent changes in costs. They said many of the specialties made in small quantities are vital to important industries. The instance of one grade of armature paper was cited. The largest producer manufactured only 50 tons a year. The largest user was a manufacturer of essential components for the aircraft industry. 

Members recommended against decontrol of small volume items as a means of meeting the difficulties in regulation of prices.

PRESS RELEASE   

Tempo E Wednesday, October 3, 1951 

Washington Re: FLUID MILK IAC 

Barkley-OPS-GPR-908  

Office of Price Stabilization officials today informed members of the Fluid Milk Industry Advisory Committee that the National office is preparing a guide to assist OPS field offices in the handling of petitions for adjustments in fluid milk ceiling prices. 

A recently issued OPS regulation, SR 63 to GCPR, set up a formula for adjusting fluid milk ceilings by marketing areas to allow for labor and certain other costs which have increased since a base period, January 1June 30, 1950, and to pass through producer price increases. Authority to make these adjustments was delegated to OPS field offices within the areas. 

The step was taken because of the perishability and local character of fluid milk and the fact that there are hundreds of milk marketing areas of varying size, each with peculiar local problems. 

The field guide now being prepared, agency officials said, should be of great value in aiding local OPS officials to reach decisions on petitions for adjustments. It is possible, they added, that a model area milk price regulation may be prepared for the guidance of field offices. 

Petitions for price adjustments have already been filed in the Chicago and Gary, Ind., marketing areas.

Committee members had expressed fear at the meeting that, because of the large number of OPS field offices, more than 100 in all, some of them may not be staffed with officials who are adequately familiar with the problems of the fluid milk industry,and that this might delay action on petitions. 

Committee members also recommended that the basic regulations, SR 63, be amended in a number of respects, including the addition of a provision to state that the "specified" producer price, which must be listed in the area regulations, be on an average basis. 

They declared that milk distributors in some areas do not all pay the same prices to producers, and in other areas premiums are allowed which result in different prices to producers by different distributors. GPO-O-OPS 896

PRESS RELEASE    

Wednesday, October 3, 1951 Moore-OPS-GPR-909  

Re: WESTERN SOFTWOOD PLYWOOD AND VENEER MANUFACTURERS SUBCOMMITTEE 

Detailed recommendations on the provisions of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry were made today by members of the Western Softwood Plywood and Veneer Manufacturers Subcommittee at a meeting with OPS officials. 

It was proposed that dollars-and-cents ceiling prices be spelled out for standard dimensions and grades of plywood and veneer by species, f.o.b. mill. 

Pricing of items for which prices were not spelled out would be determined by application to OPS.

The subcommittee recommended that the regulation cover manufacturers west of the 105th Meridian, which cuts through Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, New

Mexico and Texas. This area embraces almost the entire region where such products are manufactured. Subcommittee members also recommended that the regulation cover veneers faced with plastics, metals and other materials when applied by the manufacturer of the veneer. It would not apply to veneers faced with hardwoods, which will be covered by another regulation. 

It was proposed that the ceilings be applicable to so-called mill sales. 

Considerable discussion was devoted to the definition of such sales. 

It was the consensus that sales which moved directly from the mill in carload lots to the consumer should be at the prescribed ceilings, and that wholesalers and commission men who might handle such transactions should obtain their profit or commission from discounts allowed by the manufacturer. 

It was proposed that ceilings for wholesalers, distributors and retailers be fixed in a separate regulation, and that for a wholesaler or distributor to be entitled to a markup over the manufacturer's price, he should, in addition to selling perform other services such as stocking, warehousing, rehandling and deliveries in small lots.

Committeemen discussed specifications for various dimensions and grades for which it was proposed to spell out prices. The proposed ceilings would be based on ceilings determined under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, at levels which would include the bulk of production for each item. 

Members indicated the proposed ceilings arrived at in this manner would be satisfactory if ceilings are established on logs at levels indicated by OPS. GPO-O-OPS 895

NIMPA on Beef Quotas 

The Office of Price Stabilization today made public a bulletin signed by Wilbur La Roe, Jr., general counsel of the National Independent Meat Packers 

Association, calling on association members to oppose granting OPS the right to allocate cattle slaughter quotas in order to destroy the entire price control program. McClanahan-OPS-GPR-911  

The bulletin quoted OPS Director Michael V. DiSalle as saying that price controls on meat will not work without the quota power, and it added: "This makes it terribly important to do everything we reasonably can to defeat quotas, if we want to put an end to price control.' 

Mr. DiSalle, in making the letter public today, declared: "We are releasing the attached letter as evidence coming from meat industry sources confirming our opinion that the fight against slaughter controls is actually a fight against the price control program itself. 11 Mr. DiSalle has declared that the price of beef is a vital element in the housewife's budget, and thus is a key factor in the entire control program. 

He called on members of the meat industry opposing the control program to join with the many others who were doing their best to comply and help keep the 

American economy stable. Today he added: "The fact that the letter was sent to our office by an industry member is further indication that the industry itself is divided. Our invitation still stands to the members of the industry who want to operate legally to cooperate with us in solving our common problems. 11 

The NIMPA bulletin admitted that opinion among association members was divided on the subject of quotas, but declared that it was Mr. La Roe's belief that opinion would be unanimous against quotas "if we could put an end to price control through defeating the restoration of the quota power.' 11 Mr. La Roe called on all members who agreed with his position to write their 

Senators and Representatives in opposition to restoring the quota power.

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers SUNDAY, October 7, 1951

Cole-OPS-GPR-912 . 

DiSALLE'S STATEMENT ON MEAT ENFORCEMENT 

Michael V. DiSalle, director of Price Stabilization, said today that the agency is looking into the possibility of tax disallowal for payments in violations of ceilings, made possible by the amended Defense Production Act. 

Commenting on President Truman's statement Thursday that other agencies of the Government would assist OPS in its meat enforcement drive, Mr. DiSalle said the cooperation of the Internal Revenue Bureau may play a major role in discouraging violators. "The law now declares that the President shall prescribe the extent to which any above ceiling payments made in violation of our regulations, or any resultant fines, shall be disregarded by other government agencies in determining costs or expenses in proving gain for tax purposes," he pointed out. "We intend to consult with other government agencies to work out procedures for implementing this provision, and it could conceivably become a very expensive matter to persons consistently paying above ceilings for goods." 

This penalty may be used against persons in the meat industry found paying above ceilings for live cattle, he explained. 

Meantime, the intensified enforcement drive underway for the past two weeks has uncovered 1,849 alleged violations by 740 meat firms through the country, the director declared. These have already resulted in injunctive actions against 85 slaughterers and four criminal complaints against two slaughterers being filed in U. S. District Courts. A total of 1,953 packing plants have been inspected by OPS agents.

Mr. DiSalle said that the enforcement campaign is already beginning to have an apparent effect on the live cattle market. "Since this drive was started September 24," he said, "top prices for cattle at Chicago have gone down for all grades except prime. "This would indicate that the tendency to bid up cattle above ceiling prices is diminishing. The temptation to go out and bid up cattle prices isn't so tempting as it has been, especially when slaughterers know that a close check is being made on purchases of cattle. "We are confident that as these over ceiling paymonts are ended, the current distortion of marketing channels will be eased," he added, "although without authority to allocate the total marketable supply through normal channels we don't promise to end it entirely. We do intend to keep prices in legal bounds, however, and this should eliminate some of the frenzied competitive buying of live cattle which causes the worst disruption of supplics." 1226-2830 GPO-O-OPS 910

OND · - Am He cited these examples of cattle price changes at Chicago since Sept. 24. "The top price at Chicago for good steers has declined 75 cents a hundred pounds. The top price for commercial grade cows has declined by $2. The top price for utility cows has dropped $1.25. "Only the top price for prime cattle at Chicago has shown an increase since 

Sept. 24 and this has been only 25 cents a hundred pounds. "During the last week in September, however, the average price paid for prime cattle at Chicago was off 3 cents a hundred. The average for choice steers was off 20 cents a hundred. The average for good steers was off 12 cents. The average for commercial cows was off 20 cents."

PRESS RELEASE    

Friday, October 5, 1951 

Scott-OPS-GPR-914 

Re: RETAIL MOTOR VEHICLE IAC SUBCOMMITTEE A subcommittee of the Retail Motor Vehicle Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a draft of a proposed new permanent ceiling price regulation covering retail sales of new passenger cars.

Committeemen reviewed the proposed regulation paragraph by paragraph and took exception to several of its provisions. 

In general, the proposed regulation would establish retail dollarsand-cents ceilings on the basis of "Special Orders" to be issued by OPS to cover each make and each body style, line or series, and for extra, special and optional equipment. To these prices the retailer would be permitted to add transportation, Federal excise taxes, State and local taxes, and customary charges for other items and services furnished to the purchaser.

The proposed regulation would permit dealers to make a charge for preparing and conditioning a new car for delivery based on the charge a dealer had in effect during the period January 25 to February 24, 1951, until such time as OPS establishes a charge based on information to be furnished to OPS by the dealers within 30 days. OPS will thereafter establish a charge for each make of car on the basis of a percentage of the basic price of the car.

The committee felt that dealers would have difficulty in reflecting their over-all costs for conditioning and preparing a car for delivery under this method and that the result in general would not be fair and equitable. The committee renewed the recommendation of the industry advisory committee made on September 14 that this charge be set at 5% of the basic price of the car, or $150.00, whichever is less.

The committee recommended that dealers should not be required to maintain discounts by classes of purchasers, such as fleet owners, etc. 

Committeemen asked that the provision covering transportation charges which may be added to ceiling prices, be restated. They recommended that the dealer be permitted to use the amount paid to the manufacturer for transportation, or an amount not to exceed the rail rate from factory to the dealer on an averaging basis.

Finally, the committee recommended that the provisions with respect to invoicing by the dealer to the purchaser be simplified. 

OPS Officials told the committee that its recommendations would be given further consideration and that it is expected that the new regulation can be issued at a fairly early date.

RE: WIRE SPRING IAC 

Browne-OPS-GPR-915 

 Members of the Wire Spring Industry Advisory Committee, at their first meeting today with Office of Price Stabilization officials, discussed issuance of a proposed tailored, dollars and cents, ceiling price regulation to cover the sale of industry products. 

Old MPR 548, which covered the wire spring industry when the Office of Price Administration was operating, will be used as a framework upon which to build the new regulation. 

The industry, numbering about 70 manufacturers, does an average business of about $50,000,000 a year, and its operations are widespread throughout the country. 

It produces mattress springs, bed springs, automobile seat springs and coil springs for furniture, dual equipment, office chairs and specialty lines such as modernistic furniture.

A sub-committee was appointed by the Committee Chairman to provide OPS with information to help in framing the proposed new regulation. The sub-committee consists of H. T. Products Co., Trenton, N. J.; and H. W. Sternberg, Owen Silent Spring Division, American Chain & Cable Co., Inc., Bridgeport, Conn. 

The sub-committee will have a second meeting with OPS officials, October 22. 

Industry members pointed out that there have been many changes in specifications since OPA days, chiefly in the use of heavier wire and changed construction. It will be the duty of the subcommittee to point out how specifications should be set to fit the projected regulation.

Meanwhile, pending Budget Bureau approval, a questionnaire will be prepared by OPS to be circulated in the industry. The questionnaire will seek information in order to establish prices which will fit the new specifications. 

The Wire spring manufacturers said they have been unable to price adequately under Ceiling Price Regulation 22, the manufacturers' regulation. Prices under this regulation are lower than under GCPR, they said, because, during the entire year prior to the Korean invasion, the industry was in a depressed condition. Price wars were waged in some localities, and many manufacturers operated at a loss. Consequently, the industry has remained under GCPR. GPO-O-OPS 926,

PRESS RELEASE   Monday, October 8, 1951  Re: PERFUME BASES TAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-916  

Members of the Perfume Bases Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials said that a tailored regulation, which would permit them to adjust their ceilings to reflect changes in the cost of imported raw materials, was desirable for their industry. 

The industry compounds perfume bases from aromatic oils, resins and other chemicals for use in the manufacture of perfumes, cosmetics, toiletries, soaps and industrial products to impart pleasant odors that will enchance the sale or mask other unpleasant odors.

These oils and resins are for the most part made of imported raw materials. Some of these raw materials have increased sharply in price in recent months, while others have declined. Prices vary annually with crop conditions, demand and other factors. 

The industry is now pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, although it has the option of pricing under the Manufacturers' General 

Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. 

Committeemen reported that their difficulty under GCPR was that, with recent disparate movements in individual materials prices, the normal relationship between costs and selling prices for perfume bases have become distorted. While, on average, selling prices and raw material costs do not reflect any general squeeze on the profits of any concern, individual products fall between the two extremes of either showing a profit or showing a loss, with the unwholesome condition of the profitable items carrying the unprofitable ones.

The feasibility of setting ceilings upon those imported raw materials for which the American demand might determine the world price was discussed. 

Committee members generally did not believe that the United States made the world price for perfume base materials, and expressed the fear that import ceilings would either divert world supplies to other nations for speculative resale to this country at a later date or encourage foreign growers of essential oil crops to curtail their future production.

GPO-O-OPS 925

The perfume base compounds can be varied to some extent with substitutions to meet price requirements. The industry is constantly producing new compounds, Except for specific instances, committeemen indicated that the mechanics of Section 4 of GCPR for pricing new products was practical. 

This is not the case, however, under CPR 22, because of the number and complexity of the new items. Committeemen said the compounds are trade secrets. The methods of computing and reporting ceilings under CPR 22 would tend to disclose these secrets. Moreover, compounds frequently are made up of other compounds, which would increase the complexity of figuring costs under CPR 22.

Committeemen reported on the average CPR 22 would give them price increases over GCPR prices, but the difficulties in making computations under it would make it undesirable. 

One member suggested the industry's products could be classified into two groups, one representing the bases used in industrial products, soaps and inexpensive cosmetics, and the other the ingredients in exclusive perfumes and cosmetics. The former, it was suggested, would lend themselves to pricing by a formula based on cost plus margin, while the exclusive items would not lend themselves to such pattern pricing.

Committeemen suggested that ceilings be determined under the proposed tailored regulation on the basis of costs plus the percentage markup existing in a pre-Korea base period. If that was not acceptable to OPS, some committeemen said a dollars and cents margin would be acceptable to the industry. 

Committeemen undertook to study the problem of a practical pricing formula and to send recommendations to OPS for study. ..

The meeting was conducted by George W. Strasser, acting assistant director, Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division, assisted by R. M. Stevenson, chief, Essential Oils, Flavors and Perfume Materials Section, OPS.
