Scott-OPS-GPR-924  

Officials of the Office of Price Stabilization said today that an upward revision of ceiling prices for lead and zinc scrap will be authorized at an early date.

This action, OPS officials said, will keep ceiling prices for lead and zinc scrap in the same relationship with primary lead and zinc ceiling prices as has · existed until recently. It was pointed out that, on October 2, OPS authorized ceiling price increases for primary lead and zinc as part of a program announced by the Director of Defense Mobilization on September 29, "designed to assure essential supplies of zinc and lead at stable and reasonable prices". 

In forthcoming orders, OPS will revise applicable regulations to take account of increased costs for lead and zinc in the case of certain commodities and services where lead and zinc comprise a substantial part of the total materials cost. 

No action is contemplated by OPS, officials said, with respect to an upward revision of ceiling prices for primary copper, copper and copper alloy scrap, brass mill scrap, brass mill products, or aluminum scrap. 12641 GPO-O-OPS 949

PRESS RELEASE   ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers WEDNESDAY, October 17, 1951 

Cole-OPS-GPR-925  

Re: BEEF ENFORCEMENT REPORT 

Nearly one thousand additional violations uncovered by office of Price Stabilization agents in the third week of the expanded nation-wide compliance drive against slaughterhouses and packing plants have boosted the total of violations to 2, 804, Michael V. DiSalle, OPS Director, announced today.

Five hundred and twenty-nine more plants have been inspected, bringing the total since September 24 to 2,482, while 217 more have been found in violation, boosting the total number of plants found violating OPS slaughtering regulations · to 957, Mr. DiSalle stated.

At the same time Mr. DiSalle pointed out that during the three weeks that the expanded drive has been under way, prices of live cattle, both steers and cows, have dropped on the Chicago market. OPS Director DiSalle said that while some of the price decline might be seasonal, usually resulting from larger movements of cattle to market at this time of the year, cattle receipts for the past three weeks are still well below last year's figures. For example, total receipts at Chicago last week were 25,000 head, compared with 34,859 for the same week last year.

Thus, it was pointed out, the usual seasonal pressures of abundant supply aren't present, and most of the current price decline must be ascribed to rigid enforcement of regulations.

The average price on prime steers at Chicago has dropped 53 cents per hundred pounds, since launching of the expanded drive September 24, Likewise, the price on choice steers has dropped 72 cents, and on good steers $1.00.

The average prices on cows also dipped sharply for the first two weeks of the expanded compliance drive. Although they showed a small increase last week, they are still selling below the high levels in effect when the stepped-up enforcement drive was launched. The average price on commercial cows has dropped 

94 cents, utility cows 24 cents, and cutter and canner cows 44 cents, in the three weeks period. "We believe the determined enforcement action being taken by our agents throughout the nation is beginning to discourage illegal practices which alone have made it possible for those packers who purchase cattle in violations of ceilings to recoup their losses," Mr. DiSalle said.

GPO-O-OPS 960

. 

"If the illegal operators know that they won't be able to get by with paying above ceilings, and then through falsification of weights, overcharging, upgrading or side payments get their money back at the expense of their customers, the will stop paying above ceilings. "This will eliminate the complaint of legitimate packers that they have been unable to buy their normal number of slaughter cattle at legal prices, and do much to restore normalcy of distribution to the market. This normalcy was more easily maintained when we could allocate quotas to slaughterers equitably. Without this power we must rely on strict and full enforcement to keep the illegal operators in line. "We are encouraged to note that our determined enforcement activities are beginning to show some results and live cattle prices are gradually being eased downward."

Injunctive and criminal actions filed in United States District Courts because of slaughtering violations total 156, with 109 being filed since the compliance drive was expanded on September 24, and 24 during the past week. 

Mr. DiSalle stated that it is anticipated that many more such actions will be. filed this week. 1

PRESS RELEASE    MONDAY, October 15, 1951 Re: LIVESTOCK CEILINGS 

Barkley-OPS-GPR-926 ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 

The Office of Price Stabilization today announced that the provisions relaxing cattle ceilings for slaughterers whose volume is below that in 1950 will not be extended. For November and thereafter, all slaughterers will be expected to be in complete compliance with the cattle ceilings. 

The live cattle ceiling price regulation, CPR 23, places a limit on the amount which a packer can pay for all cattle slaughtered during an accounting period, usually a month or four weeks. 

Amendment 2 to CPR 23 exempted from this ceiling price provision slaughterers whose volume was less than 50 percent of what it was in 1950. 

It also provided that slaughterers whose volume was between 50 and 75 percent of what it was last year could pay one percent over the ceiling. 

Amendment 2 was effective for the months of August and September and subsequently was extended through the month of October. Today's announcement means that it will not be extended beyond its present expiration date of 

November 4, 1951.

Re: BOVINE HIDES, IAC 

Downward revision of ceiling prices of hides and skins at this time would not be advisable, members of the Bovine Hides Industry Advisory Committee told Office of Price Stabilization officials today. It was the second meeting of the industry committee with the agency.

The industry men said that a downward revision would result in disadvantages to suppliers as well as to processors of hides and skins. 

The bovine hide industry operates under Ceiling Price Regulation 2, Revision 1, covering cattle hides, kips and calfskins. 

Committee members told OPS officials that the hide industry has operated satisfactorily under the regulation (CPR 2) since its issuance March 15, 1951. 

They said, however, that there may be misunderstanding within the industry as to the method of computing maximum commissions for brokers. 

OPS officials explained to the committee that, under the regulation, maximum commissions for receiving brokers may not exceed 2 percent of the ceiling price for hides and skins as fixed in the regulation. 

There were no comments or suggestions for changes in additions to those discussed at an earlier Industry Advisory Committee meeting.

PRESS RELEASE   TUESDAY, October 16, 1951  Re: SURVEY REPORT REGULATION I 

Browne-OPS-GPR-928  

The Office of Price Stabilization today issued a clarifying statement explaining the cause and effect of Reporting Regulation 1, issued last week and concerning which there has apparently been some uncertainty. 

The statement points out that the action merely makes mandatory the filing of certain reports with the Securities and Exchange Commission for use of the OPS, and that similar information has been obtained by the SEC in the past on a voluntary basis. 

It also points out that similar action concerning data gathered for the price agency by the Federal Trade Commission was taken under a delegation of authority issued September 1. 

The clarifying statement follows: 

The basic facts with respect to Reporting Regulation 1 are: 

(1) During the war, OPA collected financial information on a broad scale from both manufacturing and distributive corporations for general policy purposes. At the end of the war, the Securities & Exchange Commission and the 

Federal Trade Commission took over the continued conduct of these surveys in so far as manufacturing corporations were concerned. The results of these surveys have been published regularly by these two agencies in a joint booklet which reports selected balance sheet and income statement data for 22 major groups of manufacturing industries, (e.g. food manufacturing, chemicals and allied products, electrical machinery, etc.). (2) When ESA was established, immediate consideration was given to the kinds of data that would be required in connection with any control program. 

General information with respect to financial status and experience of American business was obviously essential as a guide to policy. It was decided that the data currently being collected by FTC and SEC could be used for this general policy purpose in so far as manufacturing was concerned. However, no similar data were being collected with respect to wholesaling and retailing, and it was highly important to close this gap. While SEC did obtain annual reports from distributing corporations, this did not fill the need for more current data on a quarterly basis. Consequently, during January and Feburary 1951, a program was worked out whereby SEC and FTC would extend their quarterly profit surveys to include a representative sample of wholesale and retail corporations, using the same general methods and procedures as had been applied in the past to manufacturing industries. Accordingly, appropriate questionnaires were prepared and GPO-O-OPS 975

SAMINE SCER 

distributed by the two agencies to cover quarterly profits of wholesale and retail corporations. These questionnaires were mailed out by FTC in May and by 

SEC in July and are expected to be continued on a regular quarterly basis here- 

TRAZIER CHARISHI ROYA 

after. (3) FTC has always had statutory authority for the collection of manufacturers' profit data under the Federal Trade Commission Act. However, this authority extended to interstate business only. In order to ensure adequate coverage of intrastate business as well, FTC requested, and OPS granted, early in September, a delegation of authority under the Defense Production Act to the Commission to support its collection of this type of data. The quarterly reporting programs of the Securities & Exchange Commission have always been on at voluntary basis but SEC felt that to ensure adequate coverage its collection should be made with the support of mandatory authority. Consequently, on October 12, 1951, OPS issued its Reporting Regulation No. 1, requiring that these data be reported to the Securities & Exchange Commission. These two actions involve no substantive change whatever in the program which had been agreed 'upon early in 1951 and which had been previously initiated. (4) OPS expects to use the data collected under these programs as a guide to policy in the same general way as price indexes, wage indexes, and the like. 

They will provide information essential to determine the import of the control program upon business in general, and upon major sections of industry and trade, and thus serve as a basis for the prompt adjustment of policy to changing" economic conditions. # # # # # # tula adust lead st

VEGETABLE PARCHMENT LAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-931 Members of the Vegetable Parchment Industry Advisory Committee, at their first meeting today with OPS officials, discussed a proposed tailored regulation for their industry that would spell out dollars-and-cents ceilings on seven basic parchment grades.

Ceilings on related weights and grades under the proposed regulation, would be determined by applying differentials to the spelled out prices. 

The differentials would be determined by the price relationships which existed during a specified base period. The period of January 25 to February 24, 1951, was suggested.

Differentials existing during the base period would also be maintained to cover variations in size of shipments, packing, finishing, terms of sale and other particulars.

It was proposed to spell out ceilings on the following grades: 18 lb. vegetable parchment, 27 lb. vegetable parchment, 35-43 lb. lard liner parchment, 40 lb. parchmentized kraft, 55-60 lb. greeting card parchment, No. 80 Egyptian parchment, and

No. 475-1-T vegetable parchment. 

Related grades to be covered by the regulation would include printed, waxed, colored, puckered, crinkled, opaque, glycerine-treated, mottled greeting card, and can liner parchment.

It was proposed that the spelled out dollars-and-cents ceilings be based on studies of ceilings reported by manufacturers under the Manufacturers' General 

Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. 

There are four manufacturers of vegetable parchment.

The application of CPR 22 pricing formulas resulted in some roll-forwards and some rollbacks from ceilings under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, with the roll-forwards predominating. 

Vegetable parchments are water insoluble and are widely used for wrapping butter, margarine and other moist and oily foods. They are made by treating paper materials with acid, glycerine and other chemicals.

Re: PRIMARY CONSUMERS OF NICKEL FOR CHEMICALS & ELECTROPLATING IAC 

An industry advisory committee representing Consumers of Nickel for Chemicals and Electroplating met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss pricing problems as related to nickel anodes and nickel salts.

The industry is primarily concerned with the production of nickel anodes used in connection with electroplating processes; also, nickel salts used in connection with electroplating and for other chemical processes.

It was explained by the committee that nickel anodes are customarily produced from primary nickel. They are cast or rolled in various shapes and to varying specifications, with borings for hanging and for electrical connections. They are hung in a vat of chemical solution through which an electrical current is passed. this manner, the nickel from the anode is released and deposited on metal products immersed in the chemical solution. Thus, the nickel electroplating process is accomplished. Nickel electroplating is applied to a wide range of metal products. Nickel salts are a compound of nickel and acids and are used in the chemical solution in connection with the electroplating process. They are also used in connection with other chemical processes.

It was pointed out by committee members that nickel anodes are customarily produced from primary nickel and not from nickel scrap, because they must be in accord with exacting specifications for proper and satisfactory electroplating results. Nickel scrap does not readily lend itself to satisfactory anode production. 

The same situation exists with respect to nickel salts. In Nickel anodes and salts are currently being priced under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR). Some prices for these products, established under GCPR, are entirely out of relationship to the ceiling price for primary nickel. However, it was pointed out that, generally speaking, most producers established GCPR prices in reasonable relationship to primary nickel prices. In The committee discussed a proposal to place these products under a separate tailored ceiling price regulation and thus remove them from pricing under GCPR. this manner ceiling prices could be established on the basis of a reasonable relationship to primary nickel ceiling prices and at the same time maintain the general level of prices established under GCPR.

Distorted ceiling prices for anodes under GCPR are disturbing to the industry in their relationship to the ceiling prices for primary nickel and the short supply of the primary metal and nickel scrap. (Over) GPO-O-OPS 986

The committee expressed the feeling that a separate tailored pricing regulation for nickel anodes would be helpful. However, there was some question as to whether it would be practical or necessary to include nickel salts under such a regulation. 

OPS officials told the committee that OPS would give further consideration to the industry pricing problems and to the matter of developing a separate tailored pricing regulation for nickel anodes and salts. 

The meeting was conducted by Charles C. Rieth, Metals Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: George W. Strasser, assistant director, Rubber, Chemicals & Drugs Division; Alfred T. Loeffler, chief, Chemicals Branch; Abner Frank and

Committees.

Re: MEN'S AND BOYS' TAILORED CLOTHING IAC 

Members of the Men's and Boys' Tailored Clothing Subcommittee met today with

Office of Price Stabilization officials to discuss problems involved in recalculation of ceiling prices and relief provisions. 

In order to prevent escalation when recalculating direct costs at the opening of a new selling season, the Subcommittee recommended that, if the increase in direct cost of materials used in any selling season subsequent to the first selling season exceeds 15 per cent, then the division factor shall be adjusted upward as follows: 

Increase of 15 % to 24.9% 

Increase of 25 % to 34.9% 

Increase of 35 % or over 

Coakley-OPS-GPR-933  Com an adjustment of .005 an adjustment of .010 an adjustment of .015 

The division factor, used in determining the ceiling price, represents the relationship of the total direct cost to the total net sales in the base period. 

It was pointed out during the meeting that the proposed technique would tend to limit escalation but would not eliminate it entirely, since it permits a partial markup on cost increases in materials.

To provide relief for manufacturers who claim 1950 to be an inequitable base period, the subcommittee recommended that they be permitted to use an alternate period, 1946 through 1949, if their division factor for the year 1950 was about .015 higher than the average division factor for the period 1946-1949. However, in no event could they adjust their division factor to more than .03 below that of their 1950 base period.

Members of the Subcommittee had studied a proposed draft of a supplementary regulation covering these and other problems relating to the industry and told OPS officials that they would present their recommendations in writing. 

Morris Chandross, Chief of the Apparel Branch, and Joseph N. Matz, Acting Chief,

Men's Clothing Section, presided at the meeting. Other OPS representatives present were: Martha Benenson, Business Analyst; Harold D. Cohen, Division Counsel; Joseph P.

Scott-OPS-GPR-934  Re: ASPHALT AND TARRED ROOFING PRODUCTS IAC The Asphalt and Tarred Roofing Products Industry Advisory Committee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems. 

The industry is concerned with the production of a wide range of roofing products which in general are covered under the manufacturers' ceiling price regulation CPR 22. However, generally speaking, the industry is currently pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR) pending mandatory application of CPR 22.

The committee pointed out that historically the industry has been regarded as a uniform pricing industry.

Some members of the industry are multi-line manufacturers and many others are single-line manufacturers. This situation presents a pricing problem from the standpoint of mandatory pricing under CPR 22. Such pricing, it was contended, would distort the historical uniform price relationship existing in the industry.

The committee suggested that OPS develop a tailored pricing regulation establishing ceiling prices on the basis of an industry-wide price adjustment factor. In this connection it was suggested that separate industry-wide price adjustment factors be developed to cover pricing East and West of the 

Rocky Mountains to conform with the industry pricing practice. The third quarter of 1949 was proposed as a base period.

OPS officials told the committee that OPS would make an analysis of figures submitted by the industry on OPS Public Form 8 with a view of determining whether an industry-wide price adjustment factor could be developed as a basis for a tailored regulation.

WEDNESDAY, October 17, 1951

Re: RADIO AND TELEVISION SET MANUFACTURERS, IAC Members of the Radio and Television Set Manufacturers Industry Advisory 

Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss proposals for a tailored ceiling price regulation for their products. It was the first meeting of the committee with OPS.

The meeting was exploratory and was called by OPS to determine whether the General Ceiling Price Regulation, under which most of the industry is operating, is suitable, and, if not, what type of regulation should supplant it. Since the industry has been selling its commodities well below ceilings established under the GCPR, OPS said, it seemed wise to discuss a tailored regulation to be set at a more realistic price level.

The consensus of the meeting was that its chairman should appoint from the industry at an early date a subcommittee of five to study further a tailor-made celling price regulation. One suggestion was that the old MPR 599, the Office of 

Price Administration radio regulation, be used as the framework for the proposed new radio regulation.

Cost factors affecting consumer prices of radio and television sets were discussed. These included tax, warranties, costs of cabinets, chassis, and other component parts, including tubes. 

Industry representatives pointed out that they are presently operating at a narrow profit margin, that they have large inventories, and that their market took a sudden drop after the first quarter of 1951.

Discussion brought out that there is little uniformity within the industry on handling the warranty problem. Some manufacturers, it was said, grant a threemonth warranty, at no charge; others provide a six, nine, or twelve-month warranty for which a charge is made. OPS officials and industry representatives discussed the possibility of placing ceiling prices on warranty charges. 

Committee members said a tailored regulation might solve many of the problems affecting the television industry, such as lack of uniformity in pricing methods. The consensus, however, was that the industry is highly competitive, presently operates under a slim profit margin, and today excess inventories compared to reduced consumer demand are providing effective price control. A new or tailored regulation, it was said, would accommodate new products or changing conditions. 

Committee members discussed Ceiling Price Regulation 22, the manufacturers' regulation, and there was some expression that, as now written, the regulation is not suitable for an industry in a period of development and rapid growth, such as the television industry.

GPO-O-OPS 996

OPS officials said that in view of the general agreement that CPR 22 is unsuitable for the industry, a tailored regulation seems the only answer.

PRESS RELEASE ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers MONDAY, October 22, 1951 

Re: 

Tempo E 

Washington DEVELOPMENT OF TAILORED REGULATIONS FOR MANUFACTURERS AND PROCESSORS 

Hughes-OPS-GPR-936  

The Office of Price Stabilization has ordered its commodity division directors to proceed at once with the development of tailored regulations for manufacturers and processors. These regulations, wherever possible, will provide "identifiable" ceilings for the benefit of buyers and sellers, with emphasis on dollars-and-cents ceilings. 5. 

The program, contained in a pricing memorandum to all commodity division directors from E. F. Phelps, Jr., Director of OPS' Office of Price Operations, has as its objectives: 

1. Quickly building a more stabilized price structure, to guard the nation against the heavier inflationary pressures anticipated in the winter and spring; 

2. Supplanting present interim regulations, and their unavoidable disadvantages, with tailored regulations adopted specifically for each industry or segment of an industry and based on its own particular problems and practices; 

3. Applying identifiable dollars and cents ceiling prices in every case this can be done, to make clear to the seller and buyer the legal prices that can be charged and paid; 

4. Reducing ceiling prices under those that now prevail wherever permitted by the specific requirements of law and by the over-all requirement that ceilings must be generally fair and equitable to an industry; and

Increasing ceiling prices in instances where, because of cost increases, existing ceilings are no longer generally fair and equitable. 

Various pricing techniques are suggested for the guidance of the division directors. 

While dollars and cents ceilings are to be used wherever possible, it is recognized that they usually must be restricted to standardized goods historically sold at substantially uniform prices. Other techniques available include (1) a straight freeze, where a suitable base period with a satisfactory price level can be found; (2) a modified freeze, where it is possible to find a suitable base period providing prices which can be adjusted to reflect more recent costs; (3) a formula technique, setting ceilings on the basis of some mark-up (seller's own historical mark-up or a specified percentage mark-up). over certain elements of cost.

GPO-O-OPS 997

- General rules for price levels are set out in the standards. 

Where a commodity is under GCPR or similar regulation and is selling at ceiling, the price level should be preserved. If it is an important commodity, however, and if there are indications that ceiling prices are clearly higher than pre- Korean prices plus all cost increases up to July 26, 1951, a cost study should be made looking toward a rollback. 

Where a commodity is under GCPR (or other regulation) but selling well below ceiling, and where the ceiling level nevertheless represents a very substantial advance above June 1950 levels, serious consideration should be given to a tailored regulation rolling back ceilings to or toward present market levels. This should not be done, however, if the present market is clearly depressed. 

Where a commodity is under CPR 22, CPR 30, etc., and ceilings are higher than 

GCPR, the tailored regulation should reduce ceilings to or toward the GCPR level wherever CPR 22 and CPR 30 have yielded inappropriate or excessively high ceilings.

Instances may occur, it is noted in the memorandum, where individual adjustments required by the amended Defense Production Act would establish ceilings which vary from those in industry regulations drawn up in accordance with the standards contained in the memorandum. "At this point," the memorandum says, "it need only be indicated that it is not present OPS policy to raise general industry ceilings merely to avoid or to recognize individual adjustments under the amended Act." "These guide posts for our division directors," OPS Director Michael V.

DiSalle said, "do not represent a major policy change. Rather, we are giving new emphasis to a long-standing policy. From the beginning - when we issued the general freeze order last January - we have been following a three-phase program. "First, was the general freeze to stop the upward rush of prices; next was the 'interim' phase, during which we would get out broad regulations to cure some of the inequities and awkwardnesses of the general freeze; finally there was the third phase, the erection of a stabilized price structure through the issuance of tailored regulations adapted to the needs and practices of separate industries.

Brakes "The first phase, we believe, achieved a large measure of success. were successfully applied to the speeding inflation rocket, and it was slowed down almost at once.

"The second phase, represented largely by the issuance of interim manufacturing regulations, was less successful; it was seriously hampered by the long period of uncertainty when we did not know exactly what changes might be made in the Defense Production Act that would affect various regulations. Nevertheless, there was solid accomplishment during this period. Actually, a fair amount of headway in the issuance of tailored regulations was made. 

It is fact though one often lost sight of that up to September 30, 1951 we had issued a very considerable number of regulations tailored to the specific requirements of various raw commodities, manufactured goods, and wholesaling and retailing activities. 

---

A "Now, we are determined to break through the delays and to move rapidly into the third and final phase. We are instructing our division directors to proceed with all possible speed to the issuance of the rest of our tailored regulations. While these instructions relate particularly to regulations covering manufacturing and processing, their issuance will obviously have a beneficial and stabilizing effect on the entire price structure. Wholesalers and retailers sell what manufacturers and processors produce. The manufacturer's price is the wholesaler's cost, and so on to the retailer. Thus the stepped-up program of issuing tailored regulations is an over-all program which will be felt throughout trade and industry."

The process of tailoring regulations, it is emphasized, is not synonymous with increasing prices.

In fact, in a recent memorandum from Mr. DiSalle to the Office of Price 

Operations he declared: "Our objective must be to keep from increasing prices and to reduce them wherever possible. Any increase should be the exception rather than the rule, and 

I will not sign any regulations increasing prices past GCPR levels unless accompanied by the fullest kind of economic justification." 

The standards to be followed were drawn up by Mr. DiSalle and his principal operating assistants -- Mr. Phelps, Director for Price Operations; Harold

Leventhal, Chief Counsel; and Gardner Ackley, Economic Adviser. These officials describe the standards as "ground rules dealing with a number of basic situations," though not necessarily governing in all cases. -0 Referring to uncertainties connected with the passage by Congress of amendments to the Defense Production Act of 1950 the basic authority for the price stabilization program Mr. Phelps noted that the OPS schedule of work "has been impeded by the lack of clarity which has existed since the end of June," and that some questions are not yet fully resolved. 

Nevertheless, he said, it is imperative that OPS find ways and means of getting back on schedule. There is urgent need, he said, for progress towards identifiable ceilings everywhere possible and towards the establishment of a "If firmer and more refined price structure for manufacturers and processors. inflationary pressures rebuild as indicated during the winter and spring, it is incumbent upon OPS to cut across the delays and confusion which have arisen recently and to erect the kind of price structure which will withstand those pressures. Stabilization policy henceforth will have this goal in mind as a matter of priority importance."

Up to now, ceilings for most manufactured goods have been set under either the General Ceiling Price Regulation (the general "freeze" regulation issued in 

January) or one of the six "interim" manufacturing regulations issued in recent months.

The GCPR froze all prices at the highest delivered price charged by sellers during the base period, December 19, 1950 through January 25, 1951. It was a stop-gap measure, issued to put the brakes on what was becoming a runaway inflation, and to keep the brakes on until new regulations, especially designed to fit various groups of sellers and products, could be issued.

-- · · 

The six interim manufacturing regulations one broad regulation covering many products, and five others covering machinery, apparel, textiles, wool yarns and fabrics, and shoes took OPS into the second phase of the over-all price stabilization plan. These regulations were much more general in scope than the more desirable tailored regulations, but they were a major improvement over the GCPR general freeze technique. Generally speaking, the interim manufacturing regulations allowed manufacturers to add to their base period pre-Korean prices certain increases representing added materials and labor costs. 

Though they have accomplished some of the stop-gap purpose for which they were intended, these emergency and interim regulations, the memorandum on standards says, do not provide satisfactory techniques of control for all the industries covered. While generally fair and equitable, these regulations may be unsatisfactory as continuing regulations for particular industries. Some price levels are too high for effective stabilization; others may be too low to satisfy legal requirements or economic needs. Prices for individual sellers or products or areas may be out of line with each other. No satisfactory way of pricing new goods may exist. Reporting and record-keeping requirements may be inadequate or unnecessarily burdensome. "Frequently," the memorandum points out, "the buyer can have no clear idea of the ceiling, and even the seller may have difficulty knowing what it is" under regulations with poorly identifiable ceilings.

Tailored regulations, it is believed, can correct most or all of these and related problems.

A copy of the memorandum is attached.

ECONOMIC STABILIZATION AGENCY TO: 

PRICE OPERATIONS MEMORANDUM NO. 13 SUBJECT: 

October 18, 1951 

Commodity Division Directors Tentative Instructions for Development of Tailored Regulations for Manufacturers and Processors PURPOSE OF THIS MEMORANDUM 

This memorandum explains the tentative general procedures and standards to be used in the development of tailored regulations to replace the GCPR and the interim manufacturers' regulations. 

A tailored regulation is typically prepared for a particular industry or segment of an industry and takes account of its particular problems and practices. This memorandum does not attempt to state all of the standards which may be involved in price control. It concentrates primarily on the salient task of preparing tailored regulations, and focuses on the discussion of those standards which should be most useful in that task. That leaves for separate instructions various other basic aspects of the price control program, including, e.g., individual price adjustment; or the need for raising ceilings to cover increased costs where necessary to render ceilings generally fair and equitable, etc. 

IMPORTANCE OF TAILORED REGULATIONS 

The program of OPS still gives highest priority to the preparation of tailored regulations. This program has been further delayed, and made more difficult, by the new legislative provisions. But the necessity to conform our program to the new legislation should not be allowed to set aside the basic program of tailored regulations. The extent to which that program has been modified by the new legislation is indicated in part below. The individual adjustment aspects of the new legislation will be dealt with in separate instructions.

Presently, ceilings for the bulk of manufactured products are established either under GCPR (or approximate equivalent) or under one of the series of "interim" manufacturers' regulations. Because of the wide range of commodities and sellers covered by these regulations, they do not provide satisfactory techniques of control for all of the industries covered. While generally fair and equitable, these regulations may be unsatisfactory as continuing regulations for particular industries for any one or more of the following reasons: 

The price levels they establish may be either too high for effective stabili- 1

zation, or perhaps in some cases too low to satisfy legal requirements or economic needs; prices for individual products or sellers or areas may be out-of-line with each other, creating both inequities and possibilities for distortions of production or distribution; provisions for new goods pricing may be inadequate; reporting and record-keeping may either be inadequate or unnecessarily burdensome. Frequently the buyer can have no clear idea of the ceiling, and even the seller may have difficulty knowing what it is. 

Tailored regulations for particular industries can correct most or all of these and related problems.

Obviously, priorities in a schedule of tailored regulations should depend not only upon the seriousness of these problems but also upon the significance of the commodity in the economy and upon the seriousness of existing or expected inflationary pressures. The importance of these latter two criteria in the priority schedule should not be allowed to be obscured either by industry complaints with respect to minor commodities, or by the obvious weakness of regulatory techniques where prices are not under serious pressure. 

ADVANTAGES OF TAILORED REGULATIONS 

The term "tailored regulation" has no unique significance, because degrees of tailoring are obviously possible. However, a tailored regulation has the following characteristics in varying degrees: (1) It applies to a narrower range of products than the regulation it displaces; (2) It provides prices or pricing methods which conform more closely to historical or other reasonable differentials (by grade, location, class of seller or buyer, etc.) and this permits a lower average level of prices or a structure of prices better adapted to maintaining a normal flow of goods than a regulation which ignores or merely freezes such differentials; (3) It removes price inequities as between sellers, to the maximum possible extent; (4) It recognizes and provides specifically for various trade practices, where maintenance of such practices is consistent with effective control; (5) It provides specific prohibitions or other restrictions on the particular evasive practices most likely to occur in the trade or industry affected; (6) It specifies reporting or record-keeping provisions better adapted to OPS and trade needs; (7) It provides more effective procedures for pricing new goods and new sellers; (8) For the above reasons it is more enforceable by buyers and/or OPS.

TECHNIQUES FOR TAILORED REGULATIONS 

A. Dollars-and-cents prices

There are various techniques that can be used in tailored regulations. 

Dollars-and-cents regulations are clearly to be preferred on almost all counts, although the area of their application is somewhat restricted to standardized goods, where substantially uniform prices have historically prevailed. However, what appears to be a wide spread of prices for the same product can often be reduced to uniform dollars-and-cents ceilings by use of appropriate differentials for grade, location, class of buyers or sellers, etc. 

B. The straight freeze

Although the straight freeze technique was often used in OPA tailored regulations, the opportunities for use of this technique are substantially narrower in the present situation. A straight freeze requires a base period which had a level of prices which is still appropriate and a structure of prices which is fair and effective. For most products, the GCPR base period is unsatisfactory on one or both counts. A pre-Korean base period may give an excellent structure of prices, but the level is rarely still appropriate. 

There may be cases, however, in which the present market provides both a proper level and a good structure of prices. In such cases a straight freeze as of a current base period may properly be used, and should be seriously considered where commodities are now selling well below inflated GCPR ceilings. 

C. The modified freeze But even if there is no base period which gives both a proper level and structure of prices, a modified freeze may be used where there is an available base period with a good structure of prices. This may be a pre-Korean period plus permitted dollars-and-cents or percentage increase factors (where possible, separate factors for categories or product lines or principal materials) or it may be the GCPR or a current period freeze plus or minus appropriate factors. 

If the GCPR or other base period gives a generally proper freeze level, but an imperfect structure, the device of maximum and/or minimum cut-offs on prices or margins may provide satisfactory tailoring, or an adjustment provision to take care of out-of-line prices may be used. 

D. The formula regulation 

A formula type regulation establishes ceiling on the basis of some mark-up (seller's own historical or specified) over certain cost elements. This type is particularly appropriate where the goods produced are constantly changing and none of the preceding techniques is possible. Generally this mark-up should not be added to current costs, but should rather permit calculation of costs as of some cut-off date. Current costs may be used only if the mark-up is adjusted

-- · 

when costs rise. As a matter of technique mark-ups should never be measured over total cost, but rather over direct cost, or some elements of direct cost. 

Of course the level of mark-ups must include an appropriate allowance for all other costs and reasonable earnings for the industry.

LEGISLATIVE STANDARDS FOR PRICE LEVELS IN TAILORED REGULATIONS 

The amended Act provides that price ceilings in general regulations may be set no lower than the lowest of the following: (1) The prices prevailing just before the date of issuance of the regulation; (2) The prices prevailing during the period January 25, 1951 to 

February 24, 1951; (3) The prices established in a regulation issued prior to 7:00 p.m., July 31, 1951; or (4) Prices equal to the highest prices between January 1, 1950, and

June 24, 1950 adjusted to reflect unit increases or decreases in all costs between the date of these highest prices and July 26, 1951.

GENERAL RULES FOR PRICE LEVELS IN TAILORED REGULATIONS 

A. Where a commodity is under GCPR or similar regulation and is selling at ceiling, a tailored regulation should: (1) Preserve the prevailing GCPR level; but (2) If, for an important commodity, GCPR prices are clearly higher than pre-Korean prices plus all cost increases up to July 26, 1951, a cost study should be initiated which would permit present ceilings to be rolled back to or toward this standard. Indications that this is the case will generally include the following: an extremely rapid and sharp rise of prices between June 1950 and the GCPR; evidence of speculative attitudes in the market during that period; evidence that the price is determined by market demand rather than "administered" by sellers. Often rough calculations can be made, using known facts regarding changes in material prices, labor rates, changes in volume, etc., to indicate the probability that a rollback is appropriate. Because of the difficulties of a cost study, this must be limited to .commodities of substantial importance, whose prices are significant for the cost-of-living or the cost of the defense program. It should particularly be considered where there is danger that without a rollback, prices of other commodities may need to be increased. (NOTE: It is, of course, not practicable to apply this standard through individual seller calculation of his own changes in total costs. Rather this is a standard for determining the appropriate price level for a tailored regulation.)

5- 

(3) However, where cost increases since GCPR and prior to July 26, 1951, have been significant, and there is reason to believe that some recognition of these increases is necessary, the facts should be presented to the Assistant Director for Price Operations for development of an appropriate policy. 

B. Where a commodity is under GCPR (or other regulation) but is selling well below ceiling, and where the ceiling level represents a very substantial advance above June 1950 levels, serious consideration should be given to the issuance of a tailored regulation rolling back ceilings to or toward present market levels.- 

This should be particularly considered in the cases where present ceiling levels were clearly determined largely by demand and speculative attitudes rather than by costs. Such action will not require a cost study, inasmuch as the Act permits ceilings to be set at or above levels prevailing just prior to their issuance. 

Present market levels should not, however, be used where the market is depressed. 

A market is, of course, not depressed merely because prices are below ceiling. 

Judgment as to whether it is depressed must be made in terms of demand conditions, volume of current transactions, inventories, business failures, available evidence on margins or earnings, etc. This aim should be to establish the lowest level that can be firmly and fairly held in the face of renewed inflationary pressures. 

It is important that action be taken in such cases as promptly as possible, and before inflationary pressures reassert themselves. 

C. Where a commodity is under CPR 22, 30, etc., and ceilings under these regulations are higher than under GCPR, the regulation should: (1) Reduce ceilings to or toward the level of GCPR prices, wherever CPR 22 and 30 have yielded inappropriate or excessively high increases. This course may be particularly appropriate where CPR 22 ceilings are higher than actual market levels. Increases above GCPR levels should be viewed very critically to make sure that they do not represent a freakish result of some feature of the manufacturers' formula, and are truly justified by the spirit and intention of the manufacturers' regulation. The choice of base periods in the manufacturers' regulation, or the provisions for transferred materials may have given much higher prices than are necessary or justified. Likewise there are cases in which the cost changes recognized by the manufacturers' regulation may give an exaggerated measure of changes in all costs - perhaps because overhead costs are significant and there had been large expansion of volume. There are also cases in which materials costs have fallen since the cut-off dates of the manufacturers' regulations. Earnings data, such as a comparison of earnings of the first half of 1950 and 1951, may provide a better measure of true cost increases than the particular formulae in CPR 22. (2) If the branch's analysis of all the data shows that paragraph (1) is not appropriate for the industry, the tailored regulation may accept the lowest level of ceiling prices under the manufacturers' regulation at which substantial volume occurs.

1 (3) There may be a few instances in which the formula of clause (1) of Section 402(d)(4) would yield prices substantially below even GCPR levels (because of volume expansion or reduced materials costs). If so, a cost study should be initiated which would permit prices to be rolled back to or toward that standard.

D. This memorandum does not consider the area where a commodity is under CPR 22, 30, etc., but most producers have exercised their option to remain under GCPR pending the mandatory effective date of these regulations. Further instructions will be issued on this subject.

E. "Prevailing" levels of GCPR prices are normally weighted averages of individual prices. Where GCPR ceilings are above the average of delivery prices in the period January 25, 1951 February 24, 1951, the average of such delivery prices rather than ceiling prices should be used. Physical volume of production or sales, or dollar volume may be used as weights. Absence of precise weighting factors is not serious and should not prevent use of a weighted rather than an unweighted average. However, this method should not be used: (1) Where the distribution of prices shows a wide dispersion, and there is reason to believe that a number of the firms with higher prices than average are high-cost firms whose output might be threatened by use of an average price, and where the commodity involved is of substantial importance, Under these circumstances, some form of differential pricing should be devised. If this is clearly impossible, some latitude may be permitted to select a price slightly above the weighted average, but such deviation from the general rule must receive specific advance clearance before the branch initiates formal action. (2) Where the distribution of individual prices is freakish, a weighted average should clearly not be used. For example, we may have the situation where 90 percent of the firms have a uniform price, but 10 percent have prices substantially lower or substantially higher. In such instances, it may be that investigation would disclose that the prices which are out-of-line represent distinct grades, qualities, locations, or other systematic differentials which would be provided in the regulation.

If this is not the case, the modal (most frequently occurring) price should be used - in the above example, the price charged by the 90 percent. In other cases of distorted distribution, some judgment must be applied in establishing the prevailing price. 

EXCEPTIONS TO GENERAL RULES 

Instances may occur in which the individual adjustments required by the amended Act may make industry regulations in accordance with the above standards untenable. Instructions for such cases will be issued later. At this point it

-. need only be indicated that it is not present OPS policy to raise general industry ceilings merely to avoid or to recognize individual adjustments under the amended Act. 

Other exceptions to the above rules may be required for supply reasons, or to meet the industry earnings standard. Any exception for supply reasons must be carefully justified, and fully cleared within the agency before any formal action is initiated.

Although written instructions for the application of the earnings standard are not yet available, considerable work has been done on such instructions, and details may be provided to any branch which is considering application of the earnings standard or is otherwise concerned with the problem whether the ceilings are generally fair and equitable. /s/ E. F. Phelps, Jr. 

E. F. Phelps, Jr. 

Assistant Director

CUDAHY PACKING COMPANY 

Cudahy Packing Company of Newport, Minn., was named in an injunctive action filed this afternoon in the United States District Court at St. Paul, Minn., by the Office of Price Stabilization. 

C. U. Landrum, United States Attorney at St. Paul, stated that the Cudahy firm is charged with violating Ceiling Price Regulation 24 by including the weight of the wrapping used on portions of beef carcasses as part of the weight of the meat. 

Hearing on the complaint has been set for the special term of 

Federal Court in St. Paul November 26. Special Asst. U. S. Attorney 

Alex Dim is in charge of the case. 

According to Paul A. Thuet, Jr., St. Paul District Enforcement

Officer, OPS regulations permit a processor or packer to charge up to 35 cents per hundred pounds for wrapping and 40 per hundred pounds for delivery within a 35 mile radius of distribution point, but do not permit inclusion of weight of wrapping as part of weight of beef in the celling price.

Mr. Thuet further stated that a computation of the total amount of the overcharges by the Cudahy firm has not been completed, but that it is estimated that it will exceed $10,000. GPO-O-OPS 999

Re: 

Moore-OPS-GPR-939  

COATED AND PROCESSED PAPER TAC Members of the Coated and. Processed Paper Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials recommended that a tailored regulation be written for their industry under which they would determine their ceiling prices by formula.

Committeemen pointed out that their prices were dependent to a large extent on the cost of kraft, book, groundwood and other papers which they coat or process. 

The cost of coating materials, lacquer, casein and other chemicals, some of which are imported and not subject to price ceilings, was suggested as another important element in the price structure of coated and processed papers. 

The committee exemined CPR 84, the new tailored formula regulation for Certain Converted Paperboard Products, as a pattern for a tailored regulation for the coated and processed paper industry.

Under CPR 84, manufacturers employ the formulas they used during the period January 25 to February 24, 1951, to determine their ceiling prices, and they are limited to the margins over costs existing in that period. If and when new dollars-and-cents ceilings are issued covering their raw materials, manufacturers pricing under CPR 84, in computing their ceilings by formula, may include raw material costs up to the levels of the new dollars-and-cents ceilings on the raw materials. 

Manufacturers of coated and processed paper are subject to the Manufacturers' 

General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, but most are still exercising the option of pricing under GCPR. Some committeemen reported they were caught in a squeeze when manufacturers of the paper they coated increased prices under CPR 22, which they could not pass on.

Coated and processed papers have many special uses and include gift wrapping, box cover, pyroxylin coated, flint and friction glazed papers.

Members of the committee undertook to study CPR 84 in detail along lines of which OPS will prepare a skeleton regulation. Another committee meeting will consider the draft on October 30.

The meeting was conducted by Daniel H. Kech, industrial consultant for groundwood and book papers, OPS.

Re: RUBBER CHEMICALS IAC 

Recommendations that a tailored regulation be issued to cover their industry were made today by members of the Rubber Chemicals 

Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting with OPS officials.

Committeemen indicated that a regulation would be satisfactory which employed industry-wide percentage cost adjustment factors, applicable to prices established under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, and which would cover new cost increases. The industry is confronted with rises in the cost of aniline and other raw materials. 

The chemicals concerned are employed in the processing of rubber and add to the life of rubber. They include accelerators of vulcanization, activators of vulcanization accelerators, antioxidants, retarders of vulcanization and peptizers. 

Rubber chemicals are under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling 

Price Regulation, CPR 22. Several manufacturers 'have reported ceilings under CPR 22 but have not put them into effect. Committeemen reported CPR 22 would yield some rollbacks and some rollforwards, with the latter predominating.

Committeemen undertook to study the question of what chemical products should be included in the coverage of the suggested regulation and report to OPS. They discussed the type of information that OPS would need and said it would be made available to assist in preparing the regulation.

PRESS RELEASE  

 THURSDAY, October 18, 1951 

Re: 

Browne-OPS-GPR-941  

SEMI-VITREOUS CHINA DINNERWARE LAC Members of the Semi-Vitreous China Dinnerware Industry Advisory 

Committee met today with Office of Price Administration officials to discuss proposals for a new pricing regulation applicable to their manufactures.

Committee members said that a new pricing regulation for their industry might be either a supplementary regulation to an existing order, a new tailored regulation, or an adjustment based on the 

OPS earnings standard policy. The latter, is known as the Johnston formula. It provides that the level of price ceilings for an industry shall normally be considered fair if the industry wide average return on net worth before taxes amounts to 85 per cent of the average for the industry's best three years during the period 1946 to 1949, inclusive.

The meeting chairmen appointed a sub-committee to consider pricing problems of the industry, which will report to the full committee. 

It was suggested that a survey be made of a segment of the industry which will be submitted to the sub-committee. The survey will consist of financial statements to aid OPS in determining if relief is necessary.

The semi-vitreous china dinnerware industry, which normally does a business annually of close to $50 million dollars, produces table china, at popular prices, used in most American homes. 

The subcommittee includes J. M. Wells, secretary-treasurer, The 

Homer Laughlin China Company, Newall, West Virginia; M. C. Sondles, Vice president, Paden City Pottery Company, Paden City, West Virginia, and David G. Boyce, vice-president and secretary, The Harker Pottery 

Company, East Liverpool, Ohio.

A subject discussed at the meeting involved a 3 percent wage increase for pottery workers agreed to by the industry. OPS Officials made it clear that the agency cannot give consideration to anticipated cost increases, either in material or labor. It is impossible, OPS said to tie price increases to prospective wage increases. 

A Majority of the pottery industry, covered already by the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation, has filed under Ceiling Price Regulation 22, the manufacturers' regulation. Some industry representatives said, however, that the bottom dropped from their market on July 1, 1951, and that profit margins have been considerably narrowed. Increased overhead costs, industry men said, have emphasized their problem. GPO-O-OPS 1002

Tempo E-Washington  THURSDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1951 McDonald-OPS-GCPR-942 ST-4200 Ext. 5518 RE; WOOL GROWERS IAC 

Unanimous opposition to a lowering of ceiling prices on domestic wool was expressed today by members of the Wool Growers Industry Advisory Committee, meeting for the first time with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization. 

The wool growers expressed concern that any reduction in ceiling prices at this time would only result in a decided decrease in sheep numbers and a resultant reduction in wool production.

OPS officials called the wool growers in to discuss the possibility of a downward revision of ceiling prices for wool which would have as their basis the legal minimum prices recently determined by the Secretary of 

Agriculture under the authority of the Defense Production Act. Wool market 

Prices have generally been substantially lower than those extablished under CPR 35 (Wool and Related Fibres) since the issuance of that regulation last May, and are still generally below the prices to which ceilings could be legally reduced. 

Principal objection to a reduction of wool ceilings at this time, wool growers told OPS, would be largely "psychological." They felt that the effect of reduced ceiling price would cause many animals who might otherwise be kept for breeding purpose to be slaughtered. This, the wool growers pointed out, would run counter to the evident need to increase domestic wool production and would have an adverse affect on it.

Wool growers also pointed out that labor, feed and other overhead costs have increased greatly in recent years. The drought in many areas also have created many additional problems, the growers told OPS representatives. view of the many uncertainties in the next few years, OPS was requested to let the present wool ceilings stand undisturbed for the time being. In The growers expressed a real appreciation for the opportunity to make their views known, and also acknowledged that OPS was faced with a most difficult problem. 

OPS officials said other meetings would be held with other segments of the wool industry to give the problem further study. 

Today's meeting was conducted by James E. Robison, chief of OPS's Textile 

Branch. Other OPS officials attending included Thomas L. Karsten, Director, Consumer Soft Goods Division; Solomon Jacobson, Division Economist, Consumer Soft Goods Division; George D. Crosier, Benjamin F. Roeder, Victor Salloway,

Re: ARIZONA MEAT PACKERS IN COURT 

Discovery of thousands of pounds of ungraded, unmarked beef in Arizona, during the Office of Price Stabilzation expanded slaughterhouse probe, led to the filing today of injunctive actions in the United States District Court at Phoenix, Arizona, against three Northern Arizona meat packers.

Named in the complaints, filed by U. S. District Attorney 

Frank J. Flynn at the request of Jack Choisser, OPS District 

Enforcement Director, are the Prescott Packing Company and the

Wingfield Commercial Company both of Camp Verde, Ariz., and the 

Verde Food Locker of Cottonwood, Ariz.

The firms are charged with the following OPS meat regulation 

Prescott-- selling ungraded meat, not marking with OPS registration number, not tagging carcasses, not keeping daily kill records, not filing required OPS forms, and performing custom slaughtering without proper authorization. 

Wingfield-- Grading without authorization, failure to tag and weigh properly, selling ungraded meat, having in possession meat not properly graded, and failure to keep required price forms.

Verde-- selling ungraded meat, having untagged and ungraded meat in possession, failure to stamp with OPS registration number, no serial number on carcasses, self grading of meat, failure to file pricing records, failure to file affidavit as custom slaughterer, and slaughtering cattle without complying with requirements to take statements from customers for whom slaughtering is performed.

According to OPS officials, the three meat cases filed today are the first injunctive actions filed in Arizona by OPS for alleged violation of OPS regulations. # # # # # # # # # # # # GPO-O-OPS 1012

Re: WIRE SPRING IAC SUBCOMMITTEE 

Members of a subcommittee of the Wire Spring Advisory Committee met today with Office of Price Stabilization officials to consider what should be covered in a new, tailored, dollars-and-cents ceiling price regulation for industry products. These will include dimensions, types of construction, basic model specifications, tables and extras. 

OPS economists will conduct a survey in order to determine, the ceiling prices which may be applied in accordance with these specifications. 

The full Wire Spring Industry Advisory Committee met October 8. 

As a proposed framework for the new regulation, the subcommittee took MPR 548 of the Office of Price Administration, wartime predecessor of OPS. 

The old OPA regulation was discussed section by section, looking to its adaptation to the changed specifications of today. 

The wire spring industry, with about 70 manufacturers, does an average annual business of about $50,000,000. Its operations are widespread throughout the country, producing mattress springs, bed springs, automobile seat springs, and coil springs for furniture, dual equipment, office chairs and specialty lines, such as modernistic furniture. 

After considering suggested changes in minimum specifications for all types of products to conform to present industry standards, the subcommittee discussed additional new products to be made to specifications and sold in sufficient volume to warrant their inclusion in the pricing schedules. 

The subcommittee recommended selection of key items in each new type product for which detailed price data can be collected. The meeting reviewed current schedules to determine whether the price ratios in the old schedules are presently applicable.

Tempo E- 

Washington

Moore-OPS-GPR-952  

Re: SOUTHERN HARDWOOD TAC 

Detailed recommendations on the provisions of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry were made today by members of the Southern Hardwood Industry Advisory Committee at their second meeting with OPS officials. 

The regulation would spell out manufacturers' dollars-and-cents ceilings f.o.b. mill, for green and dry lumber of standard grades and dimensions, for yellow cypress and for all hardwoods commonly cut by the lumber industry in 

Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas, Oklahoma and portions of Tennessee, Georgia, North and South Carolina and Virginia.

It was proposed tentatively that variations in price levels which normally prevail in different areas, depending on proximity to major northern markets, should be maintained. This could be accomplished by dividing manufacturers into four groups, in accordance with freight costs for delivery from their mills to either Chicago or Scranton, Pennsylvania.

Group 1 would be composed of manufacturers paying 69 cents or more per hundredweight; Group 2, those paying 64 up to 69 cents; Group 3, those paying 59 up to 64 cents, and Group 4, those paying under 59 cents. Ceilings would be the spelled-out prices for Group 1. To the spelled-out ceilings, Group 2 mills would add $1 per 1,000 board feet, Group 3 mills $2, and Group 4 mills $3. 

Ceilings would be spelled out for the following species: 

Sap sweet gum, red sweet gum, black gum, tupelo, tough ash, yellow poplar, beech, birch, locust, sweet pecan, sycamore, soft maple, red oak, white oak, magnolia, elm, cottonwood, willow, hackberry, hickory, basswood, ash, and all species of cypress except tide water red cypress. 

Differentials would be provided for special or selected dimensions, antistain treatment, bundling, stacking, bulkheading in open top cars and for other particulars. (Over)

The meeting was conducted by J. P. Moyer, acting chief, Hardwood Section, OPS.

Re: BEEF PRICE PROGRAM 

Barkley OPS-GPR-953  

The Office of Price Stabilization is considering a number of alternative measures to strengthen the beef price control program, Michael V. DiSalle, OPS director, said today.

Mr. DiSalle declared that the agency has no intention of removing price controls on beef, but instead is studying additional actions to make them more easily enforceable and to correct some distortions in marketing practice which have developed since the agency's authority to allocate quotas to slaughterers was removed by Congress. "Since Congress adjourned without restoring the authority to OPS to allocate available cattle for slaughtering among the various registered packers, I have been asked several times if we plan to remove price controls from beef", Mr. Disalle declared. "We most emphatically do not! "Beef comprises a very important part of the American family's diet, and we feel it is a major responsibility of ours to do all in our power to see that it costs the housewife no more than it does already", he continued. "I have said several times that enforcement of the beef control program would be much more difficult without the power to apportion the slaughter of cattle coming to market equally among all packers, and that opinion I have not changed. However, the lack of slaughter quota authority does not mean we are going to give up the attempt. 1 "We are encouraged by the results of the enforcement drive now underway, and believe that the violations already uncovered and halted will greatly improve the general marketing situation. Also, we are considering several alternative price control measures which shouldkeep cattle and beef prices down. "Whatever proposals seem feasible and required we will try. For we are determined that the American housewife must not be forced to pay more for a steak or beef roast than she already does." Mr. DiSalle pointed out that, despite the contention of some packers that they have been unable to purchase live cattle at legal prices, the agency's regulations have been able to hold retail prices stable and that no serious shortages of consumer supply have developed.

GPO-OPS 1038

"In a short time we expect to distribute to every butcher shop and meat market in the United States printed wall charts showing the legal ceiling for all cuts and grades of beef they sell. It will then be easy for the housewife to know she is paying no more than ceiling prices, and we are determined to hold these ceilings at the lowest level permitted by law." 

Among the alternative controls methods being considered, the Director said, are the possibility of establishing a priority for a packer's slaughter above that of a comparable figure last year for the benefit of the armed services and institutions; a top ceiling on live animals; and a system under which producers will actually be paid on the basis of grade and yield of each animal after slaughtering. "If our people decide that any of these methods are desirable to improve slaughter and price controls, they will be adopted", Mr. DiSalle said.

Enforcement agents have inspected 1,326 more plants during the past week, finding 432 of them violating OPS meat regulations, and uncovering 1,443 violations in these plants. Sixty-four more injunctive and criminal actions have been instituted in United States District Courts during the past week. 

The totals for the four weeks of the expanded slaughterhouse probe are as follows: Plants inspected, 3814; plants found in violation, 1408; number of violations, 4276; and criminal and injunctive actions, 171. This brings the grand total of court actions brought by OPS for violation of meat regulations to 218. "We are determined to halt these illegal practices," Mr. DiSalle declared, "for it is only through using them that packers can pay above legal ceilings for live cattle and still make a profit."

While this enforcement task is considerably complicated by the lack of authority to see that all marketed cattle are channeled into normal and equitable trade channels through percentage quotas, it was pointed out that the agency still has the right to license slaughterers, and prevent new and unneeded ones, as well as fly-by-night borderline operators, from entering the field, with consequent further dislocation of marketing patterns. 

In addition, Mr. DiSalle said, a seasonal increase in the number of cattle coming to market can reasonably be expected in the near future, with a consequent softening effect on live cattle prices. "However, regardless of the pressures and limitations under which we must operate, we don't intend to eliminate controls on beef, any more than we do on other essential items in the cost of living, as long as the mobilization emergency exists", Mr. DiSalle concluded.

Re: WOOL DEALERS AND TOPMAKERS TAC Members of the Wool Dealers and Topmakers Industry Advisory Committee warned officials of the Office of Price Stabilization today that the proposed downward revision of ceiling prices on domestic wool would result in a decreased production of domestic wool, and possibly have other damaging effects on the wool and textile markets. The Committee, meeting with OPS for the first time today, went on record as being unanimously opposed to any change in wool ceiling prices at this time.

OPS invited the wool dealers and topmakers to discuss the possibility of setting new wool ceilings, since recent wool market prices generally have been substantially below the wool ceiling prices established last May by CPR 35 

(Wool and Related Fibres). 

OPS representatives said they thought apparel and fabric manufacturers could plan better for the future if wool ceiling prices were more "realistic," and expressed the view that lower ceiling prices on raw wool would encourage clothing manufacturers and other users to buy more wool, thus creating a demand for greater domestic production of wool. An estimated 51,000,000 pounds of wool, grease basis, still remains unsold in the hands of wool growers, OPS officials said.

The Committee members said they realized that OPS was confronted with a difficult problem in trying to stabilize prices. It was the committee consensus, however, that future world conditions are too uncertain to risk any possible upsetting of either domestic or world wool markets by revising ceiling prices at this time. Some committee members expressed the desire to wait until next spring and the trend of world developments.

This was the second time an industry group has opposed the downward revision of ceiling prices on wool. Last week members of the Wool Growers Industry 

Advisory Committee requested OPS not to reduce wool ceilings.

OPS representatives promised the wool industry group at today's meeting that no action would be taken with respect to revising the present wool ceilings until other segments of the industry had been heard from, and OPS had had an opportunity to give the problem the fullest possible study.

Wednesday, October 24 1951 

 Re: ROCKY MOUNTAIN MOTOR TARIFF BUREAU RATE CASE 

The Office of Price Stabilization was notified today by the Interstate Commerce Commission that it has suspended, pending hearings, rate increase for hundreds of common motor carriers in the transcontinental freight business. The rate increase was proposed by the Rocky Mountain Tariff Bureau, Inc., Denver. 

OPS, as well as various shipping interests, filed protests and requests for suspension. The Commission will hold hearings in which OPS will participate. Coakley-OPS-GPR-958  

The proposed rate increase would have meant a general freight rate rise of six percent over current rates. OPS explained to the Commission that such an increase would be inflationary, in that it would result in higher prices for many commodities transported by the carriers, with consequent increases in production costs to farmers and business men, and higher consumer living costs. 

OPS pointed out that contract motor carrier rates are directly related to the rates of competitive common motor carriers and that if the common carriers were permitted to increase their rates, the contract carriers, who are subject to price controls, would seek corresponding increases. "It is extremely difficult to meet pressures so generated," OPS said, "because of the necessity of maintaining a fair and equitable relationship among carriers, of avoiding the disruption of the pattern of transportation, and of preventing the diversion of shipments from normal channels, with the consequent risk of shortages in various areas.'

OPS pointed out that the proposed increases were part of a general pattern of requests following the granting by ICC of rate increases to the railroads. 

However, OPS said, it found nothing in the records to show that the needs of the motor carriers justify the proposed increases. GPO-OPS 1043

Scott-OPS-GPR-959 

SHIP REPAIR INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE 

Members of the Ship Repair Industry Advisory Committee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems. 

The industry is concerned with a wide range of repair and conversion work on commercial, Naval and maritime administration craft. In general, such servicing and repair work would be covered by Ceiling Price Regulation 34 (Services). However, on October 11, OPS temporarily suspended the application of price controls on ship repair and conversion work to craft 65 feet or more in length. 

Because of the intricate pricing problems involved in ship repairing, pricing under the applicable regulation has been found, generally, to be impractical. The industry committee, therefore, was invited to assist in developing a tailored pricing regulation.

It was the consensus of the committee that price control of ship repairs and conversion is impractical and should be abandoned. 

Committeemen cited the many pricing problems involved. They said the industry does not follow any general pricing pattern. Pricing is varied by reason of geographical considerations, the type of operation differing greatly between yards. 

Work is done in some cases on a time and materials plus overhead and profit basis. 

Other pricing may be on a cost-plus fixed fee, or profit basis. Pricing based on estimates may vary greatly with actual costs because, in many instances, the extent of repairs is not ascertainable in advance and changes in cost are numerous and indeterminate at the time of pricing. It was pointed out also that base period prices are not generally obtainable.

The committee discussed accounting, pricing and operating practices of the industry, and explored various pricing techniques which might be employed under a tailored regulation. (Over) No conclusions were reached and it was suggested that a subcommittee be appointed to advise with OPS on a tentative draft of a tailored regulation which can later be submitted to the whole committee for further discussion and consideration. OPS officials said such a subcommittee will be appointed and asked to meet with OPS at an early date.

The meeting was conducted by W. Leroy Jordan, chief, Automotive Branch, OPS.

PRESS RELEASE    

Mc Donald-OPS-GPR-960 ST-4200; Ext. 5518 

Re: WOOLEN AND WORSTED MANUFACTURERS IAC 

Office of Price Stabilization officials were requested, today not to make any changes in present ceiling prices for wool, and woolen and worsted fabrics. 

The request was made by the agency's Wool and Worsted Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee, meeting here today with a group of OPS officials who have been studying the possible effect of lowering ceilings on raw wool and wool products. 

Today's meeting was the third wool industry group to consult with OPS and to recommend that no action be taken on wool ceiling prices. 

Among the reasons the Committee gave OPS for not desiring any changes in wool ceilings at this time were: 

1. World wool markets might interpret the new ceilings as a suggested level of "fair" prices since the ceilings being proposed are considerably above prices being paid in world markets. This, the Committee said, might increase world prices. 2. 

Unfavorable publicity resulting from any decrease in wool prices might cause further trouble at distributive levels, retailers having large inventories of apparel at present and are experiencing difficulty in making volume sales at prices ranging below ceiling prices, the Committee said. They felt that further consumer resistance might be encountered from persons who erroneously believe that lower ceilings for wool would mean further reductions in retail prices for clothing. 

3. Because of the international currency situation, a lowering of ceilings might place Russia in a very favorable position to purchase wool competitively with United States buyers who would be unable to bid the ceiling price in foreign markets.

After listening to the detailed objections of Committee members to the proposed changes, OPS officials explained to the industry group that, unless a level of ceiling prices for raw wool could be established on some basis nearer to the level of actual selling prices, it would be almost impossible to set realistic ceiling prices on apparel and wool fabrics. OPS officials strongly recommended the proposed schedule of legal, minima prices recently established by the Secretary of Agriculture.

A downward revision of wool ceilings is believed needed, OPS representatives said, because pricing regulations must be established for the entire wool industry that will effectively hold the price line during a period of national emergency. More realistic ceilings, agency spokesman said, would enable OPS to formulate a price control program for wool and wool products. (Over) GPO-OPS 1044

In answer to a question from the Committee as to whether a decision had been made to roll back wool ceiling prices, the Committee was assured that no such decision had been made, and that all of their suggestions would be weighed adequately before any decisions were reached.
