HARDWOOD DISTILLATION PRODUCTS IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-961 ST-4200; Ext. 2491 

A proposed supplementary regulation to the General Ceiling Price Regulation, under which the hardwood distillation industry could apply to OPS for individual adjustment of price ceilings on charcoal and by-products, was discussed today by members of the Hardwood Distillation Products Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting with OPS officials.

Committeemen reported that, with their prices frozen at levels existing last December and January, they are experiencing a squeeze from the rising costs of labor and hardwood, which have either materialized or are in immediate prospect. 

Most of the industry is confronted with a shortage of wood because it competes with buyers of pulpwood and prices which the industry is permitted to pay will not bring out the required production. Committeemen said that they depended to a large extent on wood produced by farmers and that the industry is entering the season when it normally acquires the bulk of its supplies, but the wood is not forthcoming in sufficient quantities. They also cited the drain of labor to nearby cities, munitions industries and pulpwood operations.

Committeemen pointed out that the proposed supplementary regulation would provide relief on their price problems but not on their supply problems. 

To apply for ceilings under the suggested supplementary regulation, manufacturers would propose ceilings reflecting the margins they experienced in an accounting period of their choice between January 1, 1948, and June 30, 1950. Committeemen said their industry was depressed during this period, so that it was doubtful whether the comparison would provide the required relief. Other means of determining a more equitable base period were discussed. 1 Some members of the industry produce only charcoal; others charcoal and an important list of by-products, including acetic acid, wood alcohol and various pyroligneous products.

Charcoal itself is used in the production of castings, essential chemicals and explosives, and the by-products have wide chemical use.

The meeting was conducted by George W. Strasser, acting assistant director, Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division, OPS.

PRESS RELEASE   

Thursday, October 25, 1951

Washington APPALACHIAN HARDWOOD IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-963  

Members of the Appalachian Hardwood Industry Advisory Committee today reviewed in detail a tentative draft of a proposed tailored regulation for the industry at their second meeting today with OPS officials. OPS. 

The regulation would spell out dollars-and-cents ceiling prices on standard dimensions of hardwoods produced in the Appalachian area, green and dry, f.o.b. mill. The ceilings would approximate ceilings established under the General Ceiling Price Regulation when prices were frozen 

January 26, 1951.

The Appalachian area includes all of West Virginia and parts of 

Kentucky, Tennessee, Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia and Maryland.

It was proposed that ceilings be spelled out on the following species: 

Ash, basswood, beech, birch, buckeye, butternut, cherry, chestnut, elm, black gum, red gum, sweet gum, hickory, hard maple, soft maple, red oak, white oak, poplar, sycamore and walnut.

It was proposed that mills in the area be divided into five groups, to be determined in accordance with the different brackets of freight rates to Cleveland, Ohio, a major northern market.

The spelled-out ceiling prices would be the ceilings for the group of mills most remote from Cleveland. Manufacturers in the four other groups would add differentials to the spelled-out ceilings, graduated from one group to another, with the group closest to Cleveland enjoying the largest differential. 

This device was proposed as a means of providing appropriate ceilings in different geographical areas that would reflect the differentials in price normally enjoyed by mills closest to the major northern markets, based on their freight advantage.

J. P. Moyer,

deputy chief, Hardwood Section; David G. White, economist; Max Hirschman, attorney; Ralph E. Platter and Carl Abenfroth, business analysts; George

Thursday, October 25, 1951

Re: SUBCOMMITTEE AUTOMOTIVE REPLACEMENT PARTS MANUFACTURERS IAC A subcommittee of the Automotive Replacement Parts Manufacturers Industry 

Advisory Committee concluded a three-day meeting late yesterday with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization, for the purpose of reviewing a tentative draft of a proposed tailored pricing regulation for manufacturers of automotive parts.

In essence, the proposed tailored regulation is patterned along the general lines of Ceiling Price Regulation 30 (CPR 30 - Machinery) with modifications to meet specific industry pricing problems and trade practices.

Scott-OPS-GPR-964 

The subcommittee examined the tentative draft of the proposed regulation in detail and made numerous suggestions and recommendations for changes and clarifications in order to make it more workable and better suited to industry pricing practices.

The group also reviewed the old OPA pricing regulation MPR-452, used by the industry for pricing during World War II. 

The subcommittee made the following specific recommendations:

I. That the definition of "manufacturer" as well as other specific provisions used in the old OPA pricing regulation MPR-452, be incorporated in the proposed regulation.

II. 

That cost adjustment factors be incorporated in the proposed regulation to meet industry pricing problems and practices as follows: (a) Modify methods prescribed under CPR 30 1. Re: WOOL STOCK, WASTE MATERIALS, AND TEXTILE FIBRES PROCESSORS TAC'S 

Immediate issuance of a tailored regulation for wool stock, waste material, and textile fibres was strongly advocated today by a joint meeting of the Office of Price Stabilization's Wool Stock, Wool Waste Material, and Wool Textile Fibres Processors Industry Advisory Committees. Urging OPS to take steps to set definite dollars-and-cents ceilings as soon as possible, members of the three groups pointed out that a similar recommendation was made as early as last May when dollars-and-cents ceiling prices were established for raw wool and mohair.

The three committees further recommended that OPS announce its policy with regard to raw wool prices and to establish ceilings for wool stocks, waste and textile fibres which would have a definite relation to the schedule of ceilings set up for raw wool. 

Only in the case of a few wool waste dealers did any criticism come of the possible action which OPS may take to lower present raw wool ceilings. 

Most committee members expressed the opinion that the more "realistic" level of ceiling prices for raw wool currently proposed by OPS would be completely satisfactory for wool stock, waste and textile fibres as long as the proper differentials are maintained between these products and raw wool. 

To facilitate the preparation of a dollars-and-cents regulation to cover the three wool product industries, subcommittees were appointed to work with OPS officials in drafting the regulation. Two of these groups - wool stock and wool waste- met with OPS representatives following the regular meeting of the combined committees. The program to be followed, as outlined by these subcommittees, was, the establishment of raw wool prices by OPS, and rag and waste prices based on that level of wool prices. These actions are to be followed by a meeting with OPS and subcommittee members, who will make a final study of the proposed ceiling prices before the issuance of the regulation. 

Both committee members and OPS felt a great deal had been accomplished and the meeting was marked by a very cooperative and business-like approach to the problems on the part of both groups.

THURSDAY, October 25, 1951 Re: RADIO AND TELEVISION SET MANUFACTURERS IAC SUBCOMMITTEE 

A temporary subcommittee of the Radio and Television Set Manufacturers 

Industry Advisory Committee met today with Office of Price Stabilization officials to discuss a proposed tailored ceiling price regulation for those industries.

The discussion covered a wide area, ranging from the general form of the regulation to inclusion of wholesale and retail ceiling prices, warranties and uniform pricing. The consensus was that all these factors should be incorporated in a single regulation. 

It was suggested that the new regulation adopt a modified freeze technique, one of several offered as alternatives under the new price operations memorandum on tailored regulations recently issued by OPS. Under this technique, a recent base period, using the higest price at which radio and TV sets were sold, would be adopted. An automatic adjustment factor would be applied so as to remedy inequalities or hardship cases. 

Industry representatives said that, generally, the modified freeze technique should prove satisfactory if provision were made for the adjustment factor. Subcommittee consensus was that the adjustment factor is most important in adoption of such a regulation.

Some industry members said that dollars-and-cents ceiling under the tailored regulation would not fit the radio and television industry, and that, if the modified freeze technique were adopted for determining manufacturers' ceiling prices, a formula method of arriving at price ceilings should be used for wholesalers and retailers.

The subcommittee will conclude its discussions Friday. Its findings will be turned over to the full IAC for further discussion. 

Several industry members said that, under a tailored regulation, one problem will be the pricing of television sets now in warehouses. These sets have been selling at below ceiling prices since the buyers' market dropped last March.

OPS officials said they did not want to establish uniform warranties in a regulation, but they are faced with the problem of establishing warranty ceilings if a warranty is to be regarded as a commodity, apart from the price of the set itself.

Industry members said several companies have insisted on mandatory warranties, since they provide a measure of control over retail practices. GPO-OPS 1055

The meeting was conducted by Lee McCanne, Chief, Home Furnishings Branch, and Earl R. Smith, Acting Chief, Electronics and Musical Instrument Section, Consumer Durable Goods Division. ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 Re: PAPER SHIPPING SACK INDUSTRY SUBCOMMITTEE 

Effect on their industry of Ceiling Price Regulation 88, covering unbleached kraft paper, was discussed today with OPS officials by members of a subcommittee of the Paper Shipping Sack Industry Advisory

Committee, preparatory to the drafting by OPS of a tailored regulation for the industry.

Committeemen reported that ceilings on 40 pound kraft paper, determined under CPR 88 by applying specified differentials to ceilings spelled out for 50 pound paper, would tend to increase their material costs, and would squeeze them if an attempt is made to maintain prices for paper shipping sacks established under the General Ceiling Price Regulation. 

Kraft paper manufacturers, in their committee meeting yesterday, asserted that the differentials allowed for 40 pound paper and other lighter weights were not adequate to cover the difference in cost between these weights and 50 pound paper.

The paper shipping sack subcommittee also discussed the definition of paper. shipping sacks in contrast with paper bags. It was brought out that in the industry consumer flour and sugar pockets are commonly bracketed with shipping sacks, while coffee sacks are bracketed with paper bags. 

The subcommittee pointed out that the industry normally sells at closely competitive prices and said that the proposed tailored regulation should be drawn so as not to result in divergent prices. Committeemen urged that OPS take into consideration any increase in their costs for lightweight paper that might be experienced under CPR 88.

PRESS RELEASE    FRIDAY, OCTOBER 26, 1951 Re: EXCISE TAXES 

Crist-OPS-GPR-972 

ST-4200; Ext. 5518

In response to a number of inquiries, the Office of Price Stabilization today clarified its proposals to govern pass throughs by wholesalers and retailers of changes in certain manufacturers' excise taxes which become effective November 1.

OPS pointed out that where excise taxes have traditionally been listed separately by resellers and passed on to the customer only on an actual dollars and cents basis, no percentage markup will be permitted on the tax increase.

However, the recent Herlong amendment to the Defense Production Act and other factors require OPS to allow wholesalers and retailers a percentage markup on such taxes in those cases where such sellers have customarily treated the amount of excise taxes as part of the cost for markup purposes. 

Also, when excise taxes are eliminated or reduced the wholesale and retail ceilings must be reduced in the same manner either on a dollarsand-cents basis or percentage--wise, according to the traditional practice in the industry. 

The OPS pointed out today that under the Herlong amendment the agency is required in any new regulation "or amendment thereto" to reflect the customary percentage margins over cost of the pre-Korean period, May 24June 24, 1950.

In view of the Herlong amendment, wholesalers and retailers who have customarily taken markups on costs including excise taxes must be permitted to continue to do so. Further, any new regulation of OPS, it was pointed out, also will have to permit markups on excise taxes, if such markups have been customary in the industry. 

Where the tax pass through was straight dollars-and-cents during the base period, however, it did not affect percentage margins, and thus the increase can be passed along without any markup on it. An example of this dollars and cents pass through arrangement is the historic treatment of excise taxes by retail gasoline dealers.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers THURSDAY, November 1, 1951  Crossley-OPS-GPR-973 

Re: COLLECTION OF STATE OR LOCAL GROSS INCOME, GROSS RECEIPTS TAXES (General Interpretation 4Collection of State or Local Gross Income or Gross Receipts Taxes in Addition to Ceiling Prices.) 

A legal interpretation to acquaint sellers with their responsibilities in the collection of State and local gross income and gross receipts taxes and to prevent over-collections from consumers was issued today by the Office of Price 

Stabilization. 

In brief, the interpretation says, a seller may collect from a purchaser or consumer, in addition to the ceiling price for a commodity, the dollars-andcents amount of the taxes with the usual half-cent provision for handling fractions of a cent, OPS explained. 

Basically, today's interpretation applies to Section 402 (j) of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as recently amended by Congress, which provides that a seller may, in certain cases, collect, in addition to the seller's ceiling price for a commodity, an amount equal to State and local gross income or gross receipts taxes.

OPS explained that the interpretation was issued in response to numerous inquiries from merchants in Indiana. However, it applies throughout the United 

States wherever there are gross income taxes, gross receipts taxes, or taxes similar to the Indiana Gross Income Tax which is used as an example. Because there are thousands of tax statutes throughout the country, it is not feasible for OPS to list every State and local tax situation to which today's interpretation applies, the agency added. 

Commenting on today's announcement, Director of Price Stabilization Michael 

V. DiSalle urged sellers and consumers alike to familiarize themselves with

State and local tax provisions so that over-collections may be prevented. "The overwhelming majority of merchants knowingly would not collect more than the exact amount of the taxes", Mr. DiSalle said. "However, to prevent the rare instances of deliberate over-collection of taxes, every consumer should know the reason for paying more than ceiling prices and, if in doubt, should call on the local OPS District Office for advice," Mr. DiSalle added. 

Today's interpretation covers three basic points of interest to merchants all over the country:

GPO-OPS 1073

--  

(1) Method of computing the amount of tax under Section 402 (j): 

Example under the Indiana Gross Income Tax 

A housewife buys groceries amounting to $4.50. To this amount, the grocer applies the tax of 5/8 of one per cent. The amount of the tax in this instance is 2.8 cents. The grocer may collect 

3 cents above the $4.50, or $4.53.

If the housewife bought five different articles at the same time, each costing 90 cents, the amount of the tax collection would still be 3 cents. The grocer could not collect one cent each on the five articles, or five cents. 

(2) Treatment of fractions of a cent: 

11 Where the total amount collected in addition to ceiling prices involves a fraction of a cent, Section 402 (j) provides that the fraction "shall be disregarded unless it amounts to one-half cent or more.' For example, if the amount of a tax is 1 3/8 cents, the seller would collect 1 cent. If the amount of the tax is anything from 1 1/2 up to 2 cents, the seller will collect 2 cents from the customer. (3) OPS regulations which already give effect to Section 402 (j): 

The seller may not collect these taxes in addition to ceiling prices where commodities are priced under regulations which already give effect to these taxes in establishing ceiling prices. Among these regulations are the General Ceiling Price Regulation, Ceiling Price

Regulation 7 (Retail Ceiling Prices for Certain Consumer Goods), 

Ceiling Price Regulation 31 (the imports regulation), Ceiling Price 

Regulation 34 (the services regulation), and Ceiling Price Regulation 

61 (the exports regulation).

However, the food regulations do not take into account these taxes in the establishment of ceilings and, therefore, a seller may collect the taxes in addition to ceiling prices.

This is required under Section 402 (j) of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended.

Such regulations include CPR 14 (Ceiling Prices of Certain Foods Sold at Wholesale), CPR 15 (Ceiling Prices of Certain Foods Sold at Retail in Group 3 and Group 4 Stores), CPR 16 (Ceiling Prices of Certain Foods Sold at Retail in Group 1 and Group 2 Stores), CPR 24 (Ceiling Prices of Beef Sold at Wholesale), CPR 25 (Ceiling Prices of Beef Items Sold at Retail), and CPR 26 (Revised Ceiling Prices of Kosher Beef Items Sold at Retail).

Re: SOUTHWEST MOTOR RATE INCREASE PROTEST 

The Director of Price Stabilization has filed with the Interstate Commerce Commission a protest against, and a request for a suspension of, a 6 percent freight rate increase proposed by the Southwestern Motor Freight Bureau, Inc.

OPS maintained that the carriers have not yet proved there is need for the increase and asked for public hearings and an opportunity to participate in them. 

The proposal involves some 70 large common carriers and 250 smaller carriers in Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas.

In its petition, OPS contended that the proposed higher rates would be inflationary in that they would increase the cost of commodities carried, would raise production costs of farmers and industry, and would result in higher living costs. 

Furthermore, OPS said, an increase in common carrier rates, which are not subject to price controls, would bring demands for similar increases for contract carriers, now under price controls.

Re: METAL BED & BEDSPRINGS SUBCOMMITTEE OF BEDDING INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE 

Members of the Metal Bed and Bedsprings subcommittee of the Bedding Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss proposals for a tailored ceiling price regulation under which their products will be sold. The full IAC committee met March 

30, 1951, but today's was the first meeting of the subcommittee with OPS. 

After considering all possible techniques which might be employed for price control, industry members said a tailored dollars-and-cents ceiling regulation will be acceptable. The wartime Office of Price Administration regulation MPR 213, which covered these manufacturers during World War II, was accepted by industry members as a basic framework for the new OPS regulation. 

It was suggested that the new dollars-and-cents regulation should have as its pricing base a weighted average in effect at the time of the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation freeze.

The approximately 100 bed spring and metal bed manufacturers in the United States make all-steel bed springs and metal beds of various types and sizes. 

Suggested changes in minimum specifications for all types of products to conform to present industry standards were considered, and the subcommittee discussed additional new products being made to specifications and sold in sufficient volume to warrant their inclusion in the pricing schedules. 

The subcommittee members said they will submit to OPS a new list of specifications covering goods they currently manufacture. 

They described their business as being "sick," and presently operating at a depressed level. Some subcommitteemen contended that control is unnecessary at this time, since the industry is operating in a "soft" market. 

OPS officials explained that it would be wise to have a tailored regulation ready under which the industry could operate in the event of a material shortage. 13428 GPO-OPS 1075

MONDAY, October 29, 1951  

Re: HOME LAUNDRY EQUIPMENT IAC 

McDonald-OPS-GPR-976 ST-4200; Ext. 5518 

A proposal to draft a tailored regulation for the home laundry equipment industry was considered by members of the Home Laundry Equipment Industry Advisory Committee who met here in an all-day session with Office of Price Stabilization officials. After agreeing to the broad outline of OPS's proposed new regulation, the Committee decided that specific points under discussion should be reviewed by a special task group of industry technicians and Committee members who will meet at some later date with OPS representatives. 

The personnel of this group and the time of the meeting will be announced later. 

Some of the problems with which OPS must deal in establishing a tailored regulation for the home laundry equipment industry were discussed by the Committee. These problems as summarized by the Committee follow: 1. 

Individual manufacturers vary greatly in the manner they operate at various distributor levels and care should be taken not to disturb these historic relations. 

2. An industry-wide standard of pattern of distribution would not be accepted by most manufacturers. Ho In addition to labor, many manufacturers are having to pay more for parts, raw materials, and for transportation. 

3. The Capehart amendment does not give full relief to many manufacturers who have given wage increases since July 26 and expect to grant further increases in the near future. 

5. Conversion steel amendment has been of real benefit to the industry but some manufacturers objected to recomputing ceiling prices and filing new ceilings each quarter with OPS. Some Committee members suggested that ceilings could be recalculated once every six months or longer. 

6. The reduction in volume of units because of material shortages poses a problem since unit production costs will increase relatively. 

Some concern was expressed by the Committee that the new Federal excise tax on electric ironers and clothes dryers might create a hardship on some manufacturers since only a few days remain to get their new list prices including the tax into distributor hands.

Scott-OPS-GPR-977 

NICKEL SCRAP INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE The Nickel Scrap Industry Advisory Committee held its second meeting with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization today to discuss pricing problems related to nickel scrap and nickel alloy ingot.

Pure nickel scrap, Monel metal scrap, stainless steel scrap, and certain other nickel scrap materials are covered by Ceiling Price Regulation 29, issued May 3, 1951. Nickel alloy ingot, shot, etc., produced from nickel scrap, are priced under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR).

When CPR 29 was issued, the basic ceiling price for pure nickel scrap was established at 40 1/2 cents a pound. At the same time, primary nickel was selling at 50 1/2 cents a pound. Currently, primary nickel is selling at a ceiling of 56 1/2 cents a pound.

The committee discussed the possibility of adjusting scrap ceiling prices under CPR 29 to a closer relationship to the ceiling price for primary nickel, but officials informed the committee that no conclusions have been reached by 

OPS in this connection.

Officials told the committee that it seemed desirable to issue a separate tailored pricing regulation to cover nickel alloy ingot, shot and waffle.

The committee explored various pricing techniques that might be employed and reviewed in detail the pricing practices and specification standards of the industry. No conclusions were reached and it was agreed that the committee should meet again for the purpose of making specific recommendations for a tailored pricing regulation covering these products. Other

The meeting was conducted by Charles C. Rieth, Metals Branch, OPS.

PRESS RELEASE    Tuesday, October 30, 1951 Coakley-OPS-GPR-978  Re: KEROSENE AND DISTILLATE FUEL DEALERS MEETING 

Officials of the Office of Price Stabilization met today with representatives of the kerosene and distillate fuel oil industry to discuss the problem of supplying the East Coast, and particularly the New England States, with sufficient fuel oil for the winter. 

0. D. Judd, Chief of the OPS Petroleum Branch and chairman of the meeting, told the industry men that OPS has taken no position and made no recommendations in the situation. He said the purpose of the meeting was to get the ideas of the industry on the problem. "Nothing in the law or in our approach to the pricing problem says we must guarantee everyone a profit," he said, "but we do not want to issue any regulation which does not give everyone a chance to stay in business. 

Mr. Judd pointed out the OPS has met with various segments of the oil production and transportation industries in the hope of finding some mechanism within the industry to take care of the situation without raising consumer prices. These efforts had not been successful, he reported, and as a result, about 6 percent of the eastern seaboard market is likely to be affected by a shortage situation.

Independent dealers present said that the General Ceiling Price Regulation froze their prices at low rates which under winter conditions are unrealistic. They estimated that it would take a minimum of 1/2 cent per gallon increase in terminal prices to keep the independent operators in business and to assure adequate supplies of heating oils to the householders in their areas. 

The oil dealers told OPS officials that consumer demands are increasing because of a growing number of householders converting to oil heat. The demands, they said, will increase even more if the weather proves to be normally cold this winter. 

Replying to a query, the dealers assured OPS officials of an adequate supply of oil if ceiling prices were increased. They insisted that the increase should apply to all dealers and not to the independents only. The independent dealers said they feared that if their prices, only, were increased, public reaction would be such as to affect, adversely, future sales. 

The dealers also were unanimous in opposing any subsidy plan. 

Mr. Judd said that further meetings would be held with committees selected from industry representatives attending today's meeting. He said that the committees be set up on a geographical basis so that the problems considered would be common to all component members.

PRESS RELEASE    

Tuesday, October 30, 1951. 

Re: COATED AND PROCESSED PAPER IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-981  

Members of the Coated and Processed Paper Industry Advisory Committee, at their second meeting today with OPS officials, checked over in detail provisions of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry under which they would price their products by formula. 

The formula would include material, conversion and delivery costs plus margin.

It was proposed that manufacturers use the formulas they had in effect during the base period of January 25 to February 24, 1951, and employ the same margins that they utilized during this period. 

Their material and conversion, or manufacturing, costs used in the formula would be actual costs, except that in no event might the material costs exceed the ceilings existing during the base period, until such time as OPS might issue dollars-and-cents ceilings covering the materials. When such ceilings are issued by OPS, the spelled out ceiling prices would be used as the material costs.

The regulation, patterned after CPR 84, covering Certain Converted Paperboard Products, would apply to about 35 manufacturers whose products were valued in 1947 at $25,000,000.

Coated and processed papers include metallic coating, pyroxylin coating, mica coating, suede, dullcoat, semi- and top-size waterproof, friction glazed, flint glazed, fancy cover and decorated foil papers, and laminated combinations of these with paper and cloth.

The regulation would not cover coated book paper and coated paperboard, which are priced under other regulations. 

The meeting was conducted by Daniel H. Keck, industrial consultant for groundwood and book papers, OPS.

PRESS RELEASE    

Wednesday, October 31, 1951

Re: PROCESSED BEEF Barkley-OPS-GPR-982 ST.4200; Ext. 3491 

In order to lessen the workload on processors, the Office of Price Stabilization today announced that the cost and price filing requirements of the processed beef ceiling price regulation will be modified. 

Instead of filing these figures for the entire three-months base period of the regulation, April 1 to June 30, 1950, processors will be given the option of filing the required data for only the first week in each of the months.

OPS said the alternative filing method provide a representative sampling of costs and prices during this period adequate for the purpose of computing adjusted ceiling prices.

The processed beef regulation, Supplementary Regulation 61 to the General Ceiling Price Regulation, became effective September 22, 1951, and establishes an interim ceiling price method for cured, corned, cooked, smoked, dried and barbecued beef products.

The cost and price filing requirements will be modified in a forthcoming amendment to the regulation. GPO-OPS 1084

PRESS RELEASE

Washington Moore-OPS-GPR-984 

PRIVATE BRAND DRUG MANUFACTURERS SUBCOMMITTEE PRIVATE BRAND COSMETIC MANUFACTURERS SUBCOMMITTEE Members of the Private Brand Drug Manufacturers Subcommittee and the Private 

Brand Cosmetics Manufacturers Subcommittee today discussed with OPS officials the type of tailored regulation that would be suitable for their industries. 

Committeemen said the industries were still in need of a tailored regulation that would relieve them of a squeeze on certain products between their frozen ceiling prices under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, and rising costs, and would also provide new product pricing techniques tailored to meet their peculiar problems.

They reported that certain of their raw materials had increased in price under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, that raw botanical drugs had been decontrolled, and that others of their raw materials were imported and not subject to control at the source. On the other hand, some raw materials have declined in price and provided a few offsetting decreases in costs. 

OPS officials indicated that a regulation embodying the Capehart formula would be issued shortly. Committeemen expressed the belief that, if their industries are permitted to reflect cost increases and decreases to July 26 in their prices, this would remedy their cost squeezes. 

OPS officials also indicated that the former

NPA MPR 282 would be reviewed and modified and the modification incorporated in an OPS regulation to eliminate the waiting period on price reports covering new products. 

Committeemen stated that this would solve the bulk of the new product pricing problems. 

They requested, however, that provision be made to permit special new product pricing problems to be called to the attention of OPS whenever the generally applicable formulas derived from MPR 282 produced incongruous or inequitable result. 

Because of the number and complexity of the formulas their industries produce, committeemen said that the new product pricing methods prescribed in CPR 22 would not be practical for them.

It was indicated that the proposed regulation will apply to the manufacture and packaging of drugs for private brand owners in accordance with the latter's formulas. 

The private brand manufacturers reported that, in addition to making drugs and cosmetics packaged under another's brand or trade name, they also produced these products for bulk sale and for sale under their own brand or trade names. OPS officials noted that the proposed regulation would cover only the pricing of products packaged under another's brand or trade name for sale to the brand or name owner.

THURSDAY, November 1, 1951 Tempo E 

Washington Re: ARMY BEEF Secretary of the Army Frank Pace and Office of Price Stabilization Director 

Michael V. DiSalle announced today a program to assist the Armed Services in securing adequate supplies of beef.

Barkley-OPS-GPR-985 

Beginning with the month of December, slaughterers will be required each month to fill military orders for the three top grades of beef to the extent that their slaughter of all beef in the preceding month exceeded a specified percentage of their 1950 kill.

The OPS regulation establishing priorities for Army orders will be issued before the end of November and will be effective during the December accounting period and thereafter, Mr. DiSalle said. A packer's obligation to make deliveries to the Army in December will be determined by the amount of his slaughter in the 

November 1951 accounting period, compared to his November 1950 slaughter. beef must be offered to the Army at no premium above ceiling prices, OPS said. 

In the past few months the Army, which procures meat for all the Armed Services, has had difficulty in obtaining beef, Mr. Pace said. Its current immediate requirements are 56,000,000 pounds boneless weight and it has received offers for only a small portion of this amount, Mr. Pace added. 

The planned OPS action, by making excess beef from packers available to the Army at ceiling prices, is expected to provide most or all of these requirements by the military.

Mr. DiSalle stated that the program had been discussed with Secretary of 

Agriculture Brannan and Secretary Brannan has advised OPS that the Department stands ready to lend its assistance in working out the program. 

The OPS staff is presently working out details of the priority system and expects to complete the regulation in the latter part of this month, Mr. DiSalle said.

Since the abolition of slaughter quotas there has been a serious distortion in normal patterns of livestock slaughter.

The military priority plan to help combat this situation was evolved at a meeting between Mr. Pace, Mr. Brannan, Mr. DiSalle and Economic Stabilization

Director Eric Johnston. 

The proposed priorities are being made applicable only to plants slaughtering in excess of a specified percentage of 1950 volume in order to minimize the effect of military procurement on civilian distribution, Mr. DiSalle stated. GPO-OPS 1092 13554 

(Over)

The Army needs beef on the East Coast particularly, according to Mr. Pace. 

OPS figures show that many packers there are killing at a rate above normal and they can afford to supply the Army without adversely affecting their normal civilian trade, Mr. DiSalle said.

For the present the priorities will be applicable only to the three top grades of beef--prime, choice and good--Army and OPS officials explained. 

Packers who are already making deliveries of these grades to the military on a voluntary basis will be credited with these deliveries in the proposed priority program, they added. 

The percentage of the 1950 slaughter which packers may kill without being subject to the priorities will be set each month and fixed at a level low enough to assure the military of its requirements, OPS officials stated. 13554

Re: WESTERN SOFTWOOD PLYWOOD AND VENEER MANUFACTURERS TAC Members of the Softwood Plywood and Veneer Manufacturers Industry 

Advisory Committee, at their second meeting today with OPS officials, discussed in detail a tentative draft of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry.

It was proposed that dollars-and-cents ceiling prices be spelled out for standard dimensions and grades of plywood of various species, produced west of the 105th Meridian, which cuts through Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico and Texas. 

Species covered in the regulation would include Douglas fir, west coast hemlock, noble fir, white fir, western pine, western red cedar, redwood, Englemann spruce and Sitka spruce.

Ceilings would also be spelled out for rotary cut Douglas fir veneer of standard dimensions.

Differentials would be provided for extra lengths, widths and thicknesses of plywood, and also for cutting to special dimensions, bundling, treating and other particulars.

The spelled out ceilings for plywood and veneer would apply to sales f.o.b. mill in carload lots. Ceilings on less than carload lots would be 

10 per cent higher. The meeting developed considerable discussion as to the definition of a carload and how to apply the definition in cases where plywood is moved by truck or with other lumber products. 

The regulation would apply to softwood plywood surfaced with plastics or metallic faces, but not to plywood with hardwood faces, which will be covered by a hardwood plywood regulation. 

The regulation would provide for establishing ceilings on items not specifically priced on application to OPS. 

The dollars-and-cents ceilings would be fixed at approximately the levels established under the General Ceiling Price Regulation in January. 

The meeting was conducted by Norman 0. Curver, chief, OPS Lumber and 

Wood Products Branch, and Philip Garland, chief, Softwood Plywood section. GPO--OPS 1093

Tuesday, October 30, 1951   Scott-OPS-GPR-987  Re: BRASS MILL SCRAP 

Due to an inter-agency difference in the definition of brass mill scrap, the Office of Price Stabilization finds that some uncontaminated copper scrap has been and is being sold as brass mill scrap at higher ceiling prices determined under Ceiling Price Regulation 47 (Brass mill scrap).

Such copper scrap should properly be priced under Ceiling Price Regulation 

46 (Copper and copper base alloy scrap).

The difference exists as between the OPS Ceiling Price Regulation 47 definition and that contained in National Production Authority Order M-16. 

The OPS definition reads in part, "Brass mill scrap includes all kinds and grades of nonferrous scrap materials which are the waste or by-product of any kind of fabrication of new sheet, tube, wire, rod or other brass mill product."

NPA Order M-16 defines brass mill scrap as being "Uncontaminated scrap which is the waste or by-product of the production or industry fabrication of brass mill products or copper wire mill products"

The distinction is that no mention is made in the OPS definition regarding copper wire mill products.

While OPS feels that CPR 46 and CPR 47 are clear in their coverage, nevertheless, the agency recognizes that some confusion does exist in the minds of buyers and sellers of copper scrap suitable for use by brass mills. 

Accordingly, OPS believes it to be in the public interest to point out that only uncontaminated copper scrap suitable for brass mill use and resulting from the fabrication of copper sheet, rod, tube, extruded or drawn shape, or other brass mill product, qualifies as brass mill scrap within the meaning of CPR 47 and that ceiling prices for this grade of scrap are governed by 

CPR 47. 

All other grades of copper scrap as listed in CPR 46, including No. 1 heavy copper, No. 1 copper wire, No. 2 copper wire, mixed heavy copper, insulated or lead covered copper wire and cable are covered by CPR 46. The fact that NPA might allocate some of these grades of copper scrap to brass mills does not affect the OPS ceiling price procedure. Furthermore, OPS directs attention to the fact that scrap bought or sold under CPR 46 and CPR 47 may not be combined to determine the applicable quantity premium. 13617 GPO-OPS 1096

FRIDAY, November 2, 1951 

Michael V. DiSalle, Director of the Office of Price Stabilization, today issued the following statement: "The Office of Price Stabilization has an obligation to the business community to safeguard business data in its possession by preventing disclosure to unauthorized persons.

In connection with its regulations, OPS must obtain from business firms information in the nature of cost data, profit and loss statements, balance sheets, and product specifications. This information must be treated with the same care which any business or professional man would deem prudent. Business is cooperating in supplying data necessary to the price control program, and OPS must reciprocate by appropriately safeguarding this information. "Other Federal agencies will be permitted access to these data only as required by provisions of law and subject to adequate safeguards. Cases may arise where the withholding of business data will be detrimental to the interests of national defense. If it is necessary for me to make such a determination, I will see to it that OPS releases the information not to a single individual or group of individuals but makes the information generally available to all interested persons. "It is also of greatest importance that the public not be misled by statements of employees regarding OPS actions which have not received final approval. Confusion, inconvenience and even unwarranted financial loss may result to a business man who takes action based upon a personal opinion of an OPS employee if it subsequently develops that the personal opinion does not coincide with the official action of the agency. "These words of caution on the other hand place no restriction whatever on the release of news about OPS actions, decisions and policies. It has always been and will continue to be the policy of OPS to disseminate as widely as possible facts concerning its activities. I fully appreciate that the effectiveness of price stabilization depends upon public knowledge and understanding. "On September 27 an OPS Staff Bulletin was withdrawn by direction of the 

President. That bulletin cautioned OPS employees against disclosure of OPS files and internal memoranda. It was withdrawn to safeguard against erroneous conclusions (1) that it had some connection with the President's Executive Order of September 25, which related strictly to the classification of national security information or (2) that it might be used to suppress news unfavorable to OPS. 

The bulletin had no relation to national security information nor to the President's Executive Order; nor was it intended as a 'news gag.' Its authors were dealing with a matter of records management. When they referred to 'other internal information that might cause embarrassment to OPS,' they meant information in OPS files or passing between OPS officials--such as cost information received in confidence from business firms, or tentative legal interpretations or regulations. There have been cases where disclosure of such documents caused confusion, inconvenience, and embarrassment--not only in OPS but among business men."

FRIDAY, November 2, 1951   Re: OPS GRAND JURY ACTION 

One of the first grand jury actions for alleged violation of Office of Price Stabilization regulations was revealed today in Chicago when the Federal Grand Jury there returned indictments against a Chicago corporation and two of its officers. Cole-OPS-GPR-989  

The indictments charge falsification of records and 31 counts of violation of ceiling price regulations. Possible maximum penalties on conviction are a fine of $10,000 and one year's imprisonment on each count of price violation and not less than five years in the penitentiary or $10,000 fine or both on the falsification indictment.

Named in the indictments returned before Federal Judge John P. Barnes are 

United Enterprises, Inc., 531 West Webster Avenue, Chicago, manufacturer of stainless steel tableware, and two of its officers, Leonard Ratner, president, and Walter 

Ratner, vice-president.

United States Attorney Otto Kerner, Jr., who presented the case to the Grand 

Jury, explained that the indictments are based on charges that the defendant company violated the General Ceiling Price Regulation by selling goods at prices higher than the ceiling prices, and that a price circular dated January 15, 1951, increasing many of the company's prices, actually was printed after the general price freeze of January 

26, 1951, took effect. 

According to Nathan J. Kinnally, Chicago District Enforcement Director, the firm had printed by a Chicago company a price list predated to January 15, 1951, even though it was actually printed after the general price freeze of January 26, 1951. Under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, a company could charge no more than the highest price for which goods were sold or offered for sale prior to the general price freeze. 

Before proceeding with the case, he said, OPS officials called attention of the United Enterprises firm to these facts and recommended that the firm revise its price ceilings, advise its customers of the change, and refund any overcharges. When the firm rejected the recommendation, and still denied it was in violation, Mr. Kinnally said, the case was sent to Washington and then submitted to the Department of Justice for appropriate action. According to OPS officials, ceiling price violations approximate $5,000. 

Edward P. Morgan, OPS Enforcement Director, stated in Washington today that the

United Enterprises case involves particularly wilful violations of OPS regulations. "The very fact that the Chicago firm had the price list predated indicates that its officers knew what they were doing, and, at the same time, were familiar with 

OPS regulations," Mr. Morgan added. 1 GPO-O-OPS 1107

Re: WESTERN HARDWOOD FACED PLYWOOD MANUFACTURERS IAC Members of the Western Hardwood Faced Plywood Manufacturers Industry 

Advisory Committee, at their first meeting today with OPS officials, recommended that dollars-and-cents ceiling prices be spelled out in a tailored regulation at existing price levels for their products, with the exception of plywood faced with 

Philippine mahogany.

Prices would be spelled out for standard grades, dimensions, thicknesses and number of ply for plywood faced with African mahogany, white oak, red oak and birch.

Committeemen reported that the prevailing prices for plywood faced with Philippine mahogany were out of line with costs. Prices have not been adjusted since before the outbreak of hostilties in Korea and substantial increases have occurred in costs of imported materials.

It was proposed that prices be spelled out in carload lots f.o.b. mill, subject to customary discounts to jobbers, and for terms of sale, with perhaps a 10 per cent differential added for less than carload sales.

FRIDAY, November 2, 1951   

Re: 

INDIANA GROSS RECEIPTS TAX 

The Office of Price Stabilization is required by the Halleck Amendment to the Defense Production Act to permit Indiana merchants to increase their prices by the amount of the state's gross receipts tax, OPS Director Michael V. DiSalle said today. McClanahan-OPS-GPR-991

Mr. DiSalle's statement was in response to a protest by Governor Henry F. 

Schricker and other members of the Indiana Revenue Board against permitting merchants to increase prices by the amount of the tax. 

The state board in a telegram to DiSalle, signed by Governor Schrieker, Frank T. Millis, state auditor, and William L. Fortune, state treasurer, requested suspension of an OPS interpretation permitting the pass-on pending a conference on the question with Mr. DiSalle.

The OPS Director replied, however, that Section 402(j) added to the Defense Production Act by Congress July 31 provides that the merchant may increase his ceiling price by the amount of the tax chargeable to this transaction. 

He also cited remarks by Representative Charles A. Halleck of Indiana, sponsor of the amendment, who told the House during debate over the amendment on July 18, that OPS had refused to permit such a pass-on by Indiana merchants, and that his amendment was intended to force the agency to do so. 

Mr. DiSalle pointed out that OPS does not require the merchant to increase prices by the amount of the tax, but is legally prohibited from denying them the right to do so.

He quoted Representative Halleck, as recorded in the July 18 Congressional Record (pages 1577-80), as saying that there was nothing in Indiana law prohibiting merchants from increasing prices to the amount of the tax, although they could not list it and collect it separately, and asserting that the state's merchants had never absorbed the tax and could not afford to do so now. 

The price director pointed out that OPS has no discretion in the matter, but declared that if the State of Indiana has the power to prevent this price increase, "OPS has absolutely no objection, as OPS also prohibited this price increase before its powers were curtailed by the Halleck amendment." 

Mr. DiSalle said he would be glad to meet with Governor Schricker and other state officials, including Congressman Halleck, to discuss the Halleck Amendment, but that meanwhile OPS was compelled to abide by the amendment permitting the tax pass through. 

The Indiana Revenue Board's telegram to Mr. DiSalle and Mr. DiSalle's reply to Governor Schricker are attached. # # # # # # # # # GPO-O-OPS 1105

SATURDAY, November 3, 1951 

 SPECIALTY PORK PRODUCTS 

Barkley-OPS-GPR-992  Tas The Office of Price Stabilization today announced that it is extending the time for filing OPS Public Form 94 from October 31 to December 15, for producers of specialty pork products for which ceiling prices are not now provided in CPR 74.

OPS said the extension is being granted so as to give the industry more time in which to compile the information necessary to complete the form, and because of some delay in distributing the forms. 

The forms, which require producers to describe their products and give price data, must be filed with OPS if the manufacturers are to continue to price their products under the General Ceiling Price Regulation.

Because of the numerous types of specialty pork items, a number of these products, prepared by various manufacturers, are not yet covered by the wholesale dollars-and-cents ceiling price regulation.

The time extension will be officially granted in an amendment soon to be 

Issued to CPR 74.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 3, 1951 

Tempo E 

Washington

Scott-OPS-GPR-993  

Re: RESELLERS OF NEW PASSENGER AUTOMOBILES 

The Office of Price Stabilization today announced postponement until December 10, 1951, of the invoicing and posting requirements under its new passenger automobile resellers ceiling price regulation (CPR 83).

Ceiling Price Regulation 83, covering retail and wholesale sales of new passenger automobiles, was issued and made effective on October 15., It required that every automobile dealer post, within 20 days after the effective date of the regulation, certain information with respect to the several elements entering into the ceiling price of a new automobile, based on Special Orders to be issued by OPS. 

Due to changes in the prices for extra, special or optional equipment, occasioned by the increases in Federal excise tax rates, effective November 

1, 1951, the Special Orders will not be issued in time to permit dealers to comply with the posting requirements of the regulation. Accordingly, the 

OPS posting and invoicing requirements are being postponed until December 10.

The postponement will be formally authorized in a forthcoming amendment. GPO-O-OPS 1111

ADVANCE RELEASE For Morning papers 

Wednesday, November 7, 1951

GRE Washington Cole-OPS-GPR 994 

RE: METAL SCRAP OVERCHARGE PAYMENTS 

Receipt of checks totaling $15,320 for over-ceiling charges in four cases against dealers in non-ferrous metal scrap was announced today by Edward P. Morgan, Enforcement Director of the Office of Price 

Stabilization.

Payments to the United States Treasury in these cases were as follows: Zaslow Iron and Metal Company, Detroit, $720; Harold Lansky 

Company, Detroit, $1,500; H. Schwartz and Company, Detroit, $3,500; and 

Michigan Scrap Iron and Metal Company, Detroit, $9,600.

All of the payments in these cases include a punitive amount in addition to the actual over-ceiling charges involved, Mr. Morgan stated. 

According to OPS officials the Michigan Scrap Iron and Metal

Company had violated the General Ceiling Price Regulation in making overceiling sales of aluminum, copper, brass and nickel scrap, while the other three firms had violated the GCPR in making over ceiling sales of aluminum scrap. "These violations resulted from the fact that the dealers were generally following the same practices which they had followed in an open and free market," Mr. Morgan said. "As a result they appear to have given little or no attention to the OPS regulations." "Many violations of record keeping provisions naturally resulted in other violations. There appears to have been a general feeling in the non-ferrous metal scrap industry that violations of the General Ceiling Price Regulation would be overlooked when the tailored regulation governing the industry was put into effect." "However this is strictly contrary to the policy of the Office of 

Price Stabilization.

All cases in which investigations have been instituted prior to the issuance of the tailored regulation will be completed and, if the facts warrant action, they will be forwarded to the Department of Justice for prosecution." "All non-ferrous metal scrap dealers are now under tailored regulations promulgated since the alleged violations. Future investigations are to be predicated mainly on the tailored regulation. If violations are found, the investigations will also include complete records of business under the 

General Ceiling Price Regulation, and appropriate action will be taken." 30

PRESS RELEASE   FRIDAY, November 9, 1951 

Washington PHILADELPHIA MEAT CASE 

Cole-OPS-GPR-995  

A criminal information against one of the largest independent meat slaughterers in the Philadelphia area was filed in the United States District 

Court in Philadelphia today by United States Attorney Gerald Gleeson of that city. 

The defendants, Cross Brothers Meat Packers, Inc., 3600 North Front

Street, that city, were charges with seven counts of tie-in sales of beef to retailers in that area. Also named in the information were Bernard Cross, vice president, and Fred Schlosser, employee, of the firm.

The case represented the first criminal action in the 35-county 

Philadelphia OPS District, according to Paul B. Hartenstein, OPS District 

Director, who stated that it was one of the most serious cases on the eastern seaboard.

It was developed out of the nation-wide investigation of slaughterers and packers. 

Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Erwin Lodge who presented the case for the Government, disclosed that the charges were founded on practices of slaughterers and packers of forcing retailers to buy some of the highest priced wholesale cuts of beef in order to get lower priced cuts. He pointed out that the expensive cuts were the kind for which the small markets have no sales outlet and become a "loss item" in their stocks. This practice, he said, presents an open invitation for the retailer to mark up prices on certain meat cuts and other items in order to recover their losses. 

Herman L. Mash, District Enforcement Director, stated that the charges against the defendants were based on Ceiling Price Regulation 24 which prohibits "offering, selling or delivering a meat product on condition that a buyer purchase another beef product or any other commodity or service.' 11 He further stated that the defendants if convicted were subject to a fine of up to $10,000 or up to one year in prison, or both on each count. 

Federal Judge Guy K. Bard set bail at $500 for each defendant.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers WEDNESDAY, November 7, 1951  Re: NEW YORK STATE TAX ON MOTOR TRUCKS 

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today that the so-called "ton-mile" tax, levied October 1 by the State of New York on each truck driven in the State, may be added by the trucker to his charges, if all conditions of Section 20 of the General Ceiling Price Regulation are met. 

The New York tax is levied upon each truck for each mile covered, at rates depending upon the wieght of the truck. The 23 weight classifications, established under the tax law, range from 18,000 pounds to the legal gross limit permitted by the State. 

Under Section 20 of the GCPR, excise, sales, or similar taxes, imposed by law and effective after January 26, 1951, may be collected, in addition to the ceiling rates for the service performed, if the collection is not prohibited by the tax law and if the amount of the tax is separately stated on the invoice.

The OPS Office of Chief Counsel has determined that the New York State 

Highway Tax is a "similar tax" within the meaning of Section 20 of the GCPR and that the tax law contains no prohibition against collection in the prescribed manner.

The OPS interpretation was made following numerous queries as to the applicability of the GCPR provision to the new tax law. Coakley-OPS-GPR-996  GPO-O-OPS 1122

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today that the so-called "ton-mile" tax, levied October 1 by the State of New York on each truck driven in the State, may be added by the trucker to his charges, if all conditions of Section 20 of the General Ceiling Price Regulation are met.

Under Section 20 of the GCPR, excise, sales, or similar taxes, imposed by law and effective after January 26, 1951, may be collected, in addition to the ceiling rates for the service performed, if the collection is not prohibited by the tax law and if the amount of the tax is separately stated on the invoice.

The OPS Office of Chief Counsel has determined that the New York State 

Highway Tax is a "similar tax" within the meaning of Section 20 of the GCPR and that the tax law contains no prohibition against collection in the prescribed manner.

The OPS interpretation was made following numerous queries as to the applicability of the GCPR provision to the new tax law. Coakley-OPS-GPR-996  GPO-O-OPS 1122

MONDAY, November 5, 1951  

Tempo E 

Washington 

Browne-OPS-GPR-997 . 

Re: HOUSEHOLD REFRIGERATORS AND FREEZERS IAC Members of the Household Refrigerators and Freezers Industry Advisory 

Committee, at their second meeting today with Office of Price Stabilization officials, agreed that dollars-and-cents ceiling prices to be spelled out in a tailored regulation at the manufacturers', wholesalers' and retailers' levels would be preferred to a general regulation. 

The industry members suggested that a subcommittee of six be appointed by the committee chairman to develop framework within which the regulation can be drawn.

They explained that they are faced with many problems, including material shortages and decreased volume of production. Some household refrigerators and deep freezers are currently selling below ceiling prices, it was said. The Manufacturers currently price either under the General Ceiling Price Regulation or under CPR 22, the manufacturers' regulation.

It was the committee consensus that pre-ticketing of products was undesirable, and that price lists published by the manufacturers should be considered sufficient.

The manufacturers were unanimous agreement that the proposed regulation be simple in character, one which would avoid the necessity of filing voluminous reports with OPS. Another committee suggestion was that an overall heavy appliance regulation be studied and that cooperative meetings of the subcommittee be arranged with similar subcommittees from the Laundry Equipment and Gas and Electirc Range Industry Advisory Committees. This could result in laying groundwork for parallel procedures in all three regulations. The refrigerator and freezer manufacturers also asked that the new ceilings in the regulation be set at other than prevailing levels. Some are selling below cost, they said.

In addition, they pointed out that many are engaged in defense production and have invested large sums in re-tooling and research. 

It was contended that, under present regulations, it is impossible to recover any of these costs.

OPS officials invited attention of the committee to the fact that a possible approach to a new regulation would be to revise CPR 22 in accordance with the so-called Capehart and Herlong amendments to meet the industry's specific needs. In the face of a tailored regulation, this might relieve the industry from 

Coverage under any General Overriding Regulation (Manufacturers') which might be issued subsequently.

Washington AUTOMOTIVE REBUILT PARTS IAC 

Rebuilders of automobile engines and parts should be permitted to reflect in their ceilings the dollar amount of increases granted to original manufacturers, the Rebuilt Parts Subcommittee of the

Crossley-OPS-GPR-998 

Appointed as a permanent subcommittee of the IAC, the group met to discuss a proposed tailored regulation to cover rebuilders, and resellers of their engines and parts, and sales of used engines and parts by wreckers.

Washington Moore-OPS-GPR-1011  Re: PAPER SHIPPING SACK IAC 

Provisions of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry were discussed today by members of the Paper Shipping Sack Industry Advisory Committee at their second meeting with OPS officials.

The regulation would establish prices at the levels existing in the period 

January 25 to February 24, 1951, except for sacks made of 40 pound shipping sack kraft paper.

Manufacturers would be authorized to make specific adjustments in their ceilings to cover the differential for 40 pound basis weight kraft paper, provided for in CPR 88, the Unbleached Kraft Paper Regulation. 

Under the proposed shipping sack regulation, manufacturers who sell according to price lists would use their base period lists except for the adjustment for 40 pound kraft. Those who priced part or all of their products by formula would use the same formulas they employed during the base period with the appropriate adjustment.

The definition of shipping sacks as differentiated from other paper containers was discussed.

It was proposed that shipping sacks be considered to include primary containers of 25 pound capacity or more, overslips for primary containers, and containers (balers) for the assembly of a number of primary containers into a single shipping unit. Sacks would also include plant-packed consumer packages of one pound capacity or more packed in larger shipping containers.

Browne-OPS-GPR-1012 

Members of a subcommittee of the Wool Floor Covering Industry

Advisory Committee met today with Office of Price Stabilization officials to explore the possibility of withdrawing the 15 percent price increase granted carpet mills last March 13. It was the third meeting of the subcommittee.

The increase was granted to offset rapidly rising costs of imported wool.

The industry is currently operating under the General Ceiling 

Price Regulation, SR 11, as revised and amended.

Floor coverings affected are those composed entirely of wool, or synthetic materials, or a combination of both, or which are within the following categories: Chenille, Wilton, Velvet, Axminster and Punched Felt. 

Subcommittee members indicated that a withdrawal of the 15 percent increase would be acceptable at this time. In this connection, it was pointed out, the price of imported wool has dropped, consumer demand has fallen and carpet manufacturers are currently operating at about 50 percent of normal. Members also called attention to the fact that the industry is selling its products at from 25 to 30 percent below ceiling prices.

Industry spokesmen renewed statements that their industry is operating at a loss, generally; that they have at least a six months' supply of raw material on hand, and a heavy inventory of finished goods. They pointed out that since carpet wool, virtually all imported, is on the world market, it is extremely sensitive and subject to wide fluctuation. The spokesmen invited attention to the fact that wool prices are beyond their control or the control of OPS.

They added that transportation charges are another factor contributing to their present situation.

GENERAL SERVICES ADMINISTRATION DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE TENNESSEE VALLEY AUTHORITY

Coakley-OPS-GPR-1017 

RAILROAD FREIGHT RATE INCREASE PROTEST 

Four Federal agencies today filed with the Interstate Commerce Commission an opposition to a petition by the nation's railroads for further hearings on their request for freight rate increases.

Participating agencies are the Office of Price Stabilization, the Department of Commerce, the General Services Administration, and the Tennessee 

Valley Authority. 

The railroads had petitioned the ICC for a 15 percent increase in freight rates. On August 2, 1951 they were awarded a 9 percent increase in the 

Eastern Territory (the area north of the Ohio and east of the Mississippi Rivers) and a 6 percent increase in the Southern and Western Territories and between territories. They have asked that the hearings be reopened on the grounds that the award was inadequate. 

In reply to the railroads' statement that, even with the increased rates granted, their operating income for September 1951 was 41 percent below that of September 1950, the protesting agencies pointed out that a single month of operation is insufficient time upon which to base accurate appraisal of the effects of the granted increases. 

Any judgements of findings predicated on operating data which did not include the last four months of 1951 would be speculative, the four agencies contended, and advocated that data for a still longer period be required. 

Furthermore, the Federal agencies maintained, there exists at this time no condition of general emergency in railroad transportation which requires reopening of the case. They invited attention to the fact that, should such an emergency condition arise, the ICC could order hearings on its own motion.

SMALL ELECTRIC HOUSEWARES MANUFACTURERS LAC Members of the Small Electric Housewares Manufacturers Industry Advisory 

Committee met with Office of Price Stabilization officials today to discuss a proposed tailored regulation for that industry. Browne-OPS-GPR-1018  

Consensus of the meeting was that a tailored regulation is not required at the moment, but committee members agreed that such a regulation might be considered necessary later. Currently, the industry is covered by the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation and by CPR 22, the general manufacturers' regulation. 

The industry does a business of $463,000,000 a year, manufacturing a wide list of small electrical appliances, from vaporizers and hair dryers to toasters and waffle irons.

At today's meeting discussion related to pricing difficulties of the industry. Some committee members voiced the view that a dollars-and-cents tailored regulation would not be suitable. Operating difficulties under ceiling prices in an industry where monthly "special sales" are traditional, were examined. Pre-ticketing requirements under a uniform pricing system were pronounced "unworkable" by the industry group.

Committee members were in agreement that material shortages confront the entire industry and that a shortage of small electrical appliance supplies may result. Members also indicated that profit margins may be slashed and expressed the opinion that the manufacturers face increased wage demands.

PHONOGRAPH RECORD IAC Members of the Phonograph Record Industry Advisory Committee met today with Office of Price Stabilization officials and began discussions looking toward issuance of a tailored, dollars-and-cents, price ceiling for that industry.

Browne-OPS-GPR-1019

In the meantime, a cost survey of the industry will be undertaken by Much of today's discussion centered upon the proposed draft of a tailored regulation, which was taken up paragraph by paragraph. Industry members urged that the final draft provide for adjustment of hardship cases.

WEDNESDAY, November 14, 1951 Tempo E GCPR. 

Washington Re: WOODEN CLOTHESPIN MANUFACTURERS IAC Members of the Wooden Clothespin Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee, at their first meeting today with OPS officials, expressed satisfaction with the provisions of the forthcoming Ceiling Price Regulation for Turned, Shaped and Allied Wood Products, which will be made applicable to their industry. 

Moore-OPS-GPR-1023  

The regulation is a formula type, under which manufacturers will employ their pricing formulas in effect on June 24, 1950, to determine their new ceilings. In computing the formulas, manufacturers will use their suppliers' ceilings on materials and labor rates in effect on July 31, 1951, and other expenses and margins at rates not exceeding the rates used on June 24, 1950.

Clothespin manufacturers are now under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, At present clothespin wholesalers are subject to Supplementary Regulation 29to GCPR, and retailers are covered by Ceiling Price Regulation 7, which applies to many kinds of consumer goods. 

Some committeemen said there had been a squeeze on their retailers, particularly on round clothespins, and suggested as a means of relief that clothespins be included in the proposed wholesale and retail regulation for lumber products. Other members withheld their judgment on this point but agreed to send in their recommendations by letter after study.

Until recent weeks clothespin manufacturers had been under the jurisdiction of the Consumer Durable Goods Division, then they were transferred to the Forest Products Division. Committeemen agreed that the transfer was logical because their operations are similar to other woodworking industries. 

Committeemen recommended that no effort be made for the present to place their products under dollars-and-cents ceilings, suggesting that the question be studied further.

They noted that imported clothespins will continue to be priced under CPR 31, the Import Regulation.

WEDNESDAY, November 14, 1951 

Re: 

 SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA ADMISSIONS 

The Office of Price Stabilization today ruled that symphony orchestras, operas, and ballets are properly considered as theatrical enterprises under the terms of the Defense Production Act, and their admission charges are thus exempt from price control.

McClanahan-OPS-GPR-1025  

The question arose over whether symphonies could continue to charge admission prices which included the amount of Federal taxes formerly in effect, even though the tax was recently removed by Congress. 

OPS had said Tuesday that, if symphonies were determined to be subject to control and not exempt under the Act, they would not be permitted to continue charging the amount of the former tax, in addition to their legal ceiling. 

At that time it was pointed out that the question of symphonies being under control had not been formally raised with the agency, and that no final de termination as to their status had been made. However, in response to a number of requests received today the agency took the question of their exemption under consideration and ruled that they should be considered theatrical enterprises, and thus free of price control. # # # # *# # # GPO-O-OPS 1188'

Thursday, November 15, 1951

  Re: WHITE POTATO IAC 

Barkley-OPS-GPR-1027  

Officials of the Office of Price Stabilization today told members of the newly appointed White Potato Industry Advisory Committee that, if potato prices continue to follow the upward trend of the past few months, it probably will become necessary to impose price ceilings on this important cost-of-living item. 

The committeemen were advised, however, that if ceilings do become necessary they will be set at a level which will meet all legal requirements of the Defense Production Act, as amended, and assure a parity price return to growers. 

They also were informed that the ceilings would permit price differentials for grades and different areas of production. The U. S. Department of Agriculture is now in the process of computing the national parity price on a regional basis. 

The national average price of white potatoes increased from $1.23 a bushel, or 68 percent of parity, on September 15, to $1.39 a bushel, or 76 percent of parity on October 15. OPS has received reports that in some instances prices of some grades are considerably beyond this level. The November 15 average national price with its percent of parity is to be announced by U.S.D.A. at the end of this month.

Committeemen were told by OPS that, if a ceiling price regulation is prepared for white potatoes, it will, in general, follow the pattern of Maximum Price Regulation 271, the potato price regulation in effect during World War II under the 

Office of Price Administration. 

Industry members pointed out that there have been some changes in potato marketing practices since 1946, including more washing of potatoes, more waxing and increased use of consumer size packages. 

They also pointed out that potato bag prices have risen. Although bags are under ceiling price, jute, an imported product from which many bags are made, is subject to fluctuating prices. Committeemen said jute bag prices had increased from $257 a thousand to $346 a thousand in the past four months.

THURSDAY, November 15, 1951  Re: Minneapolis Liquor Case 

Cole-OPS-GPR-1028 

In the first case of its kind in the country, Dudley C.

Ericson, Minnesota 

State Liquor Control Commissioner, and Rose Lang, owner of the Tower Liquor Store, 828 Marquette Avenue, Minneapolis, were named in an Office of Price Stabilization injunctive action in the United States District Court there today. 

C. U. Landrum, United States Attorney, and Alex Dim, Special Assistant U.S.

Attorney, filed the complaint in the Minneapolis court at the request of Paul A. 

Thuet Jr., St. Paul District Enforcement Director for OPS. 

The complaint asks that Mr. Ericson be enjoined from enforcing Chapter 400 of the 1951 Minnesota laws and the regulations issued by Mr. Ericson fixing minimum consumer prices on liquors and wines in excess of OPS ceiling prices. 

The injunctive action also seeks to enjoin Rose Lang from selling liquors and wines at prices higher than permitted by OPS regulations regardless of the fact that the letter of the State liquor regulations permit her to do so. According to Mr. Thuet, the OPS action does not question the right of the State to control liquor prices except insofar as they conflict with Federal regulations. 

Mr. Thuet stated that the OPS position is that the Federal regulations supersede the State regulations where there is conflict. 

Hearing on the motion for a temporary injunction will take place before 

Federal Judge Matthew M. Joyce in Minneapolis on December 10.
