PRESS RELEASE   THURSDAY, November 15, 1951  

Moore-OPS-GPR-1029  

Re: PAPER BAG IAC 

Provision for reflecting the increased cost of certain kinds of paper in the prices for paper bags is a prime need of their industry at present, members of the 

Paper Bag Industry Advisory Committee declared today at a meeting with OPS officials.

A tentative draft of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry was discussed. It would fix dollars-and-cents ceilings on standard sizes and grades of paper sacks normally carried in stock by manufacturers, and provide for formula pricing on items made on order to the buyers' specifications.

It was proposed that prices be spelled out for various sizes of 5 different grades of grocery self-opening bags, 3 grades of grocery flat or square bags, variety bags, 5 grades of bread flat or square bags, 4 grades of candy bags, 8 grades of garment and pants bags, garbage bags, flat and square glassine bags, hardware bags, hotel laundry bags, damp dry laundry bags, liquor bags, 6 grades of millinery and notion bags, 3 grades of shoe bags, and banana bags. 

The proposed ceilings would be determined, in line with the pricing custom in the industry, by specified discounts applicable to the base price lists used in the industry. These discounts are expressed in different numbers of "five", or discounts of 5 per cent. The computation of net price is made by deducting 5 per cent from the base price, then deducting 5 per cent from the resultant figure, and so on until the indicated number of "five" has been used.

When pricing by formula, manufacturers under the proposed regulation would use the formula employed in the period January 25 to February 24, 1951. They would compute their raw material factor on the basis of actual or estimated actual cost of raw materials. In no event, however, could the material costs exceed the suppliers' ceilings existing on February 24, 1951, unless OPS issues dollars-andcents ceilings on the raw materials. Thereafter their material costs could not exceed the latter ceilings.

Conversion costs, covering labor and machine operations, and also margin and delivery costs, would be figured at the same rates existing during the period 

January 25 to February 24, 1951.

The committee discussed the type of information OPS would need from industry to compute the spelled out ceilings, and the extent to which information reported by the industry on Forms 8 under the Manufacturer's General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, could be used. It was pointed out that only a minority of the manufacturers had reported under CPR 22. The majority are still pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR. 

Committeemen recommended that, pending the issuance of a tailored regulation, bag manufacturers still pricing under GCPR be given the choice of remaining under GPO-O-OPS 1202

· that regulation. OPS officials indicated this might be accomplished by an amendment adding their products to items listed under SR 12 to CPR 22, which are temporarily exempted from CPR 22 pending issuance of tailored regulations covering them.

Committeemen noted that non-intergrated manufacturers have tended to experience higher material costs than manufacturers whose paper-making and bag-making operations are integrated. There was some discussion whether two price levels might be established, one for integrated and the other for non-integrated converters, following the pattern of pricing under the unbleached kraft paper regulation. 

Several converters expressed doubt as to the value of two ceiling levels, pointing out that, except in a tight market, the lower ceilings would set prices through competition.

The regulation would cover about 200 manufacturers. It was estimated that an annual production of about 700,000 tons of paper bags, valued at $200,000,000, would be covered by spelled out prices, and about 90,000 tons of paper bags, valued at $100,000,000, would be covered by formula pricing. 

The meeting was conducted by M. C. Walsh, chief, Pulp, Paper and Paper board 

Branch, and Edward F. Melia, business analyst for grocers, variety and specialty bags.

 Coakley-OPS-GPR-1030 

Re: DOMESTIC COOKING APPLIANCES IAC Members of the Domestic Cooking Appliance Industry Advisory Committee, meeting for the first time today, were asked by officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to consider the advisability of a tailored regulation covering their industry and to make recommendations for the pattern of such regulation.

Lee McCanne, Acting Assistant Director of the Durable Goods Division, told the meeting that OPS does not want to change established merchandising practices and suggested that industry representatives present their ideas on what a fair and equitable regulation should contain. 

The industry members, who favored, generally, a tailored regulation, said that, while inventories presently are high, they anticipate a reduction as their allocations of critical materials are cut. They asked that OPS make allowances for rising costs, which, they said, would accompany reduced volume of production.

Industry representatives also requested that they be permitted to maintain their historic margins of profit under the proposed tailored regulation, which should take into account, also, the development of new materials and changes in models, they said. 

Postponement of the December 19 mandatory filing date under CPR 22 was requested by committee members so as to eliminate the possibility of changing ceiling prices at that time and again when a tailored regulation is issued. 

OPS officials said extension of the deadline is not contemplated. Industry representatives said the element of uncertainty under OPS regulations made it difficult for them to quote prices to their distributors, and asked that ceiling prices, approved by OPS, be not made subject to review and possible change at a later date. Prompt action by the Agency on appeals and request from the industry also was requested. 

Miles E. Magargel, Acting Chief of the Appliance and Equipment Branch, conducted the meeting. Other OPS officials attending were W. E. Kirby, Chief, Stove Section; Kenneth Abel, Acting Branch Economist; Helen Nies, attorney;

Re: VITRIFIED CHINAWARE MANUFACTURERS IAC Members of the Vitrified Chinaware Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee, at their first meeting today with Office of Price Stabilization officials, agreed to file for new ceiling prices under Supplementary Regulation 17 to Ceiling Price 

Regulation 22, the general manufacturers' regulation.

Currently, the industry is pricing either under the General Ceiling Price 

Regulation or CPR 22. 

SR 17 will permit these manufacturers to calculate adjustments of their ceiling prices under the Capehart Amendment, taking into account almost all cost changes from pre-Korea to July 26, 1951. The prices will become effective when filed with OPS, without the usual 15 day waiting period. 

OPS officials suggested that, after the new prices are filed, a survey may be necessary to determine whether the so-called Johnston industry earnings standard will apply, or a tailor-made ceiling price regulation should be issued. Under the Johnston standard, and industry is entitled to 85 percent of its earnings for the three best years, 1946 through 1949.

Committee members described the state of their industry as "deplorable," and said it is operating at only about 50 percent of capacity. They pointed out that higher prices will be necessary in order to sustain their lowered volume of production. Current operations, they said, average no more than 33 work hours a week. to 1500.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers SUNDAY, November 18, 1951  

Re: ENFORCEMENT ROUNDUP Cole-OPS-GPR-1032 

New investigations of complaints alleging violation of office of Price Stabilization regulations opened during the month of October totaled 13,363, Edward P. Morgan, OPS Enforcement Director, revealed today in discussing the nation-wide activities of the Office of Enforcement.

Investigations pending on October 1 totaled 14,463. During October 

6,483 investigations were completed. The total number of cases pending on 

November 1 was 21,343. Enforcement agents assigned to investigations during 

October were 981, giving an average case load of 21.7 per investigator for the month.

During October, Mr. Morgan stated, 4,091 cases were closed as a result of no violations being found. In October 265 complaints with requests for injunctions were filed in United States District Court throughout the country. 

Twenty-three complaints were dismissed or withdrawn, 155 injunctions were granted, and injunctions were denied in seven cases. 

Informations were filed in seven criminal actions, and indictments returned in two during October. Pleas of guilty or nolo contendre were entered in two cases, and convictions secured in two others. Fines assessed in criminal actions totaled $1,000.

A total of 3,317 compliance conferences were held during the month and 2,153 cases were closed following conferences. Settlements were effected in 

43 other cases, totaling $64,499.60.

During the month, OPS enforcement agents contacted a total of 36,247 establishments of various kinds. The number of these found in violation of 

OPS regulations totaled 7,102. The number of minor complaints closed in 

October was 648. A total of 197 surveys was planned and 34 surveys were completed during the month. Retail stores led the list of establishments contacted with a total of 13,603. Other categories of establishments with totals of more than one thousand are as follows: restaurants 8,082; services 6,812; automobiles 

3,881; and meat and livestock 1,868.

PRESS RELEASE    

Friday, November 16, 1951

Coakley-OPS-GPR-1033 

Re: INTERMOUNTAIN-COAST MOTOR RATE INCREASE PROTEST 

The Office of Price Stabilization today filed a protest with the Interstate Commerce Commission against a proposed 4 percent increase in common carrier rates in five western states and asked that hearings on the increase be held by ICC.

The proposal to increase rates was made by the Intermountain-Coast Motor Freight Tariff Bureau, Denver, Col., on behalf of 54 carriers. States affected are, primarily, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Montana and Oregon.

In requesting a hearing OPS stated: "that no increase should be allowed to go into effect unless it is conclusively demonstrated at a full public hearing that an increase is essential to the continued economical and efficient operation of the carriers concerned."

OPS further said that the proposed increase would be inflationary in that it would result in increases in the delivered prices of many of the commodities transported by the carriers involved and that these increases would be reflected in production costs of farmers and industry. Ultimately it would mean increased consumer living costs, the agency said. # # # # # # # # # # # # GPO-O-OPS 1213

Saturday, November 17, 1951

Tempo E 

Washington USED MACHINE TOOLS 

A six man group, representing approximately 66 dealers in used machine tools and metalworking machinery in this country, met today with the Office of Price Stabilization Officials to discuss proposed changes in Ceiling Price Regulation 

80, the used machine tool regulation.

BROWNE-OPS-GPR-1034 

The group had submitted to OPS in advance a list of suggested changes in the regulation, which was adopted as the agenda for the meeting. At least 11 changes were recommended in the OPS price regulations. The group meeting with 

OPS today represented "rebuilders", and "reconditioners" of machine tools, as well as those who sell on an "as is" basis. They do not constitute a formal 

Industry Advisory Committee to the agency. 

GPO-O-OPS 1220 The group was selected to represent the 66 dealers following an emergency meeting" of industry members early in November in New York City. The meeting with OPS officials today was held at their request. 

Committee members at today's meeting contended that the Industry Advisory Committee which assisted in the issuance of CPR 80 was not truly representative of the used machine tool industry group, which numbers at least 750 dealers throughout the country. A preponderance of dealers who rebuild these tools constituted the committee, whereas few "as is" dealers were included, OPS officials were told. 

OPS officials said they would take this under consideration, with a view to altering the committee to give a broader view of problems confronting the industry. 

Industry members present said they could not estimate the annual dollar volume of their business, but they did say that their business equals, if it does not exceed, the amount of new machine tools sold in this country. 

OPS officials stated, in opening the meeting, that it would be impossible at this time to commit the agency to suggested changes in CPR 80, which the industry members present sought.

The complaints registered by the committee members included the contention that the percentage tables used in the regulation, which set up age groups and condition categories for tools, is not in accordance with general industrial practice. 

They argued that the regulation's percentage tables, governing prices at which these tools may be sold, are inequitable. (over) 14394

- OPS officials asked for the submission of new, proposed, substitute percentage tables and industry members said these would be supplied the agency as soon as possible. 18 Industry members agreed there is need for price control in the industry, but insisted they require a "workable regulation. CPR 80, in many respects, is not workable, they insisted.

OPS officials asked that the used machine tool industry members present a list of prices of these commodities at the General Ceiling Price Regulation level, for comparison with present prices. Industry members agreed to do so. 

The industry group also:

Questioned the requirement in CPR 80 that the "condition" of a machine tool be stated before its sale. Industry men argued that theirs is the only industry selling used goods which has a "condition" requirement. 

Asked that the percentages be applied to the manufacturers' list price as of the date of sale of the used machines, and that OPS issue an OPS price list to be used by them as a guide, with the right reserved to OPS to call upon dealers to justify their selling prices. Industry men suggested that a supplement to such a guide be issued every six months to accommodate changing prices. OPS officials said this would be impossible, because of both the expense and personnel involved. 

Asked that the OPS eliminate provisions in CPR 80 requiring that a used machine tool, "reconditioned", be tested before it is sold. In many instances, it was said, electric power connections are not available for such testing. 

Asked that requirement of CPR 80 that a certificate be given a buyer that a machine tool has been actually reconditioned be eliminated. 

Asked that the required 30-day guarantee or rebuilt used machine tools be revised in CPR 80. They argued that this had resulted in some buyers taking a machine tool, such as a lathe, for the 30-day period, and then returning it at the end of that period as "unsatisfactory". OPS asked for submission of a new proposed guarantee section from the dealers.

Asked OPS to consider elininating from CPR 80 the requirement that they furnish buyers with information regarding the age or age group of the machine tool sold for pricing purposes.

Asked deletion of a CPR 80 requirement that all invoices carry a description of the most comparable new machine tool against which the used item has been priced. They argued that they keep this information in their own files under the terms of CPR 80, and that it is unnecessary to give a buyer information which he does not seek. Industry men said the requirement implies that they are trying "to put something over" on the customer. Sellers of machine tools to dealers, the latter said, frequently refuse to give this information to their buyers. 

Protested a requirement in CPR 80 that they keep "time" records involving rebuilding or reconditioning a machine tool. 14394

Asked for rules to govern auctioning of machine tools. They protested the practice of advertising auctions without saying whether the tools are rebuilt, reconditioned, or offered "as is". 

OPS officials said they would consider a complaint against CPR 80's requirements on descriptions of precision tolerances in used machine tools, and asked the industry men to submit a substitute requirement. At the save time, OPS said it would consider new definitions of what constitutes "worn parts. 11 The industry asked exemption from price control of items they sell that are priced at $100 or less. They said that the paper work involved in such a transaction sometimes costs more than the part itself. OPS officials promised to take it under consideration.

Moore-OPS-GPR-1036  

Re: ORIGINAL EQUIPMENT TIRE AND TUBE MANUFACTURERS SUBCOMMITTEE 

An OPS proposal to establish dollars-and-cents ceilings on their products at current market levels was questioned by members of the Original Equipment Tire and 

Tube Subcommittee of the Tire and Tube Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee at a meeting with OPS officials today.

Committeemen reported that original equipment tires and tubes are now selling below ceilings established under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR. 

They said prices were reduced October 1, 1951, in anticipation of a further reduction in the government price of natural rubber which has not materialized. 

However, they pointed out that they were confronted with actual and prospective wage increases, and declared that their industry may need the spread between their present selling prices and the ceilings on original equipment tires and tubes to cushion any possible increase in the government price of rubber. They pointed out that original equipment tires and tubes are sold on very narrow margins, and said the action of the industry in voluntarily lowering prices on original equipment tires and tubes in October was evidence it was not contributing to inflation. 

Committeemen pointed out further that the prices for replacement tires and tubes representing the bulk of the tire manufacturing business had not been lowered, but were still at GCPR ceilings.

Tire and tube manufacturers are at present under GCPR, having been exempted from the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, by Supplementary 

Regulation 10 to CPR 22. This exemption, however, was made in anticipation that a tailored regulation would be written for the industry, and OPS undertook to sound out the industry representatives as to the type of regulation that would be the most suitable.

The proposal to fix dollars-and-cents ceilings on original equipment tires and tubes at current market levels conforms with one of the alternatives provided in the Capehart Amendment--ceilings at market levels prevailing immediately before the issuance of a regulation. 

The alternate possibility of making another cost study in the industry, to determine cost increases since pre-Korea on the basis of the Capehart formula, also was discussed.

Members of the subcommittee undertook to study the question and send in their recommendations by November 30, when a meeting of the whole committee is scheduled.

Re: TOOL AND DIE INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE 

The Tool and Die Industry Advisory Committee met for the first time yesterday with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems. 

The industry generally is pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation 

(GCPR) pending mandatory application of Ceiling Price Regulation 30 (Machinery) on December 19. 

The industry is engaged in the production of a wide range of tools, jigs, attachments, dies, etc., used in connection with manufacturing machinery and machine tool equipment. Several thousand tool and die manufacturers comprise the industry, but most of them represent small job shop operations employing a relatively small number of persons, in many cases less than twenty. On the other hand, there are a few comparatively large producers in the industry. 

Committeemen pointed out that the industry for the most part has found it utterly impractical to price under CPR 30. Their main difficulty is in connection with computing materials cost adjustments. Members estimate that only from 3 to 15 percent of the cost of tools and dies is represented by materials cost, and, since the products are built to individual specifications, a varied list of materials are required for each job in consequence, the accounting facilities of most producers are such that it is practically impossible to check material cost increases against base period prices without an almost insurmountable bookkeeping burden. 

It was suggested that the industry be permitted to use current materials costs with a reduction in the customary markup under a tailored regulation. A majority of the committee favored such an application of material costs, but some members said it would not be acceptable.

Some committeemen recommended that ceilings be established on the basis of January 1951 labor costs and current materials costs, with adjustments to reflect increases in labor costs plus overhead costs as provided under the so-called Capehart amendment to the Defense Production Act. 

Some committeemen expressed the opinion that the tool and die industry should be granted the same pricing incentives that have been granted to machine tool manu facturers under Supplementary Regulation 2 to CPR 30 and under General Overriding 

Regulation 15 (GOR 15). They said out that a large part of the current production of tools and dies is used in connection with the production of machine tools. 

OPS officials pointed out that these special pricing provisions for machine tool manufacturers were issued by OPS under a directive from the Office of Defense Mobilization and cannot be applied to other industries. (Over) GPO-O-OPS 1234

- D - The officials told the committee OPS would give full consideration to its suggestions and recommendations. A subcommittee will be appointed to consult further with OPS in the drafting of a tailored pricing regulation for the industry. 

The committee recommended that the industry be given the action of pricing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR) or CPR 30 until such time as a tailored commendation can be issued. 

The meeting was conducted by Edward L. Norman, chief, Cutting Tools and In dustrial Supplies Section, Machinery Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: Leslie J. Carson, chief, Machinery Branch; Leo Wasser, legal staff; Eleanor

Re: OFFICE MACHINES LAC Members of the Office Machines Industry Advisory Committee met today with 

Office of Price Stabilization officials to discuss a proposed tailored ceiling price regulation for the industry.

Supplementary Regulation 17, CPR 22, to their requirements. SR 17 would permit the manufacturers to calculate adjustments of their ceilings under the Capehart Amendment, taking into account almost all cost changes from pre-Korea to July 26, 1951.

Regulation or CPR 22. 

Manufacturers represented at the meeting produce a wide variety of items, including cash registers, adding and calculating machines, typewriters, dictaphones, business machines of all types, addressing machines and duplicating machines. Some also set up bookkeeping systems for their customers.

Distribution costs also are increasing, they said.

It was added that other cost increases result from personnel training, from sales force maintenance in the face of lower production volume, from freight, and from service maintenance. PRESS RELEASE 

I 

   WEDNESDAY, November 21, 1951 Re: TALLOW 

Barkley-OPS-GPR-1041  

Edward F. Phelps, Acting Director of the Office of Price Stabilization, today issued the following statement in regard to the resignation of seven members of the Tallow and Grease Industry Advisory Committee: 

There is no justification or basis in fact for the statement that the 

Committee was called to meet Tuesday to "rubber stamp" a price action. Nor is there any justification or basis for the statement that "political interests" were involved.

This committee was called in to consider some type of appropriate adjustment of an unrealistic ceiling price situation and to give advice on technical problems relating to the industry.

The problem arises from the fact that OPS is seeking to establish a workable and realistic ceiling price level for industry generally with a view to providing necessary stability in the event of renewed inflationary pressures next year. 

This can only be accomplished in the public interest by permitting such upward adjustments as are required by law and reducing such ceilings as have been shown to be unrealistically high, again to the extent the law and full facts permit. 

No decision has been reached on any proposal to reduce the ceiling prices on tallow to any particular level. It is true that we are giving serious consideration, and the committee was so informed, to issuance of a more realistic regulation. 

This action is being considered for the following reasons:

The present OPS ceiling price of tallow, approved last March as a stop-gap measure, is 15 cents a pound, or 200 percent above the pre-Korean price of 5 cents a pound. This ceiling is now completely out-of-line with a realistic price for this product, especially in the light of substantial market stability which has replaced the sharp upward movement of prices during November and December, 1950, and January, Tallow is now selling on the open market for 8 and 9 cents a pound. 1951. 

The decline in tallow prices was recognized last September when the ceiling price of beef was raised one cent a pound to compensate for a 40 percent decline in the price of tallow, a by-product of beef packing. There is no intention on the part of 

OPS to reduce the ceiling price of tallow as much as this compensation warrants.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers 

Tuesday, November 26, 1951

Re: 

 Crossley-OPS-GPR-1043 

FILING AND REPORTING BY RETAILERS 

The first report of initial percentage markups by many retailers of apparel and home furnishings, who price under the general retail regulation (Ceiling Price 

Regulation 7), was due on November 14, 1951, the Office of Price Stabilization said today. Together with this reminder, the agency provided a clarification as to filing and reporting requirements under CPR 7.

Major reason for today's clarification is widespread misunderstanding on the part of retailers as to the three months period on which they must report to OPS when their markups during that period exceeded those reported for the base period. 

OPS emphasized the fact that, for retailers who keep records on a quarterly basis, this report covers the first complete quarter AFTER May 31, 1951, the effective date of CPR 7. The regulation does not call for reports on a complete quarter of their sales operations BEFORE May 31, 1951, OPS added. 

By May 31, 1951, all retailers pricing under CPR 7 were required to file with

OPS, along with their pricing charts, a report of their base period initial percentage markups or gross margins. A "pricing chart" is a listing of the costs of commodities that a merchant offered for sale on certain specified days (list dates), the prices at which he offered them for sale and the percentage markups. Thus the pricing chart shows the merchant's customary margins, which he cannot exceed as long as CPR 7 is in effect. "Initial percentage markups" are the markups for pricing an individual article. 

A "gross margin", generally used by smaller merchants with simpler accounting records, is a markup that applies to a line of merchandise. The "base period", generally, is the period of a merchant's sales operations from July 1, 1949 to June 

30, 1950, or fiscal 1950.

As a check on the effectiveness of CPR 7, the regulation requires merchants to file reports with OPS whenever their current markups exceed those in the base period. 

Retailers who keep records on a quarterly basis are required to file a report on a three months basis whenever their current initial percentage markups or gross margins exceed those that they reported for their base period. Those who keep records on an annual basis are required to make this report on an annual basis. 

Where a merchant maintains records on a quarterly basis, he must file for each complete quarter after May 31, 1951, in which his current markups exceeded those that he reported for the base period, The report of initial percentage markups is due within 45 days after the end of the reporting period. The report of gross margins is due within 75 days after the end of the reporting period. GPO-O-OPS 1250

OM 

2. 

Where a merchant maintains records on an annual basis, the report of initial percentage markups is due within 45 days after the end of the annual reporting period. The report of gross margins is due within 75 days after the end of the annual reporting period. 

Many retailers keep records permitting them to report on a quarter extending from July 1 to September 30, 1951. Where their initial percentage markups exceeded those reported for the base period, this report was due on November 14, 1951, which was 45 days after the close of their reporting period. The report on gross margins is due by December 14, which will be 75 days after the close of the July 

1 to September 30, 1951, quarter.

Monday, November 26, 1951   Re: NATURAL GAS MEETING 

Coakley-OPS-GPR-1045  

Representatives of the Natural Gas industry met with Office of Price Stabilization officials today in Washington to consider a proposal to use area pricingin establishing ceilings at well head for dry gas in new fields. 

OPS officials reported 16 applications for ceilings on new offerings of gas representing, in general, the same type gas in the same general area and subject to the same marketing conditions. A majority of the industry men present agreed as to the feasibility of an area pricing plan. 

It was proposed that North Louisiana, South Louisiana, East Texas, the Gulf

Coast and South Mississippi be considered as a single area for the purpose of studying prices on new gas and that the Permian Basin in West Texas be considered as a separate area. No formal recommendations were made, however. 

Industry representatives told OPS officials that transportation and development costs make it impractical to develop and market available gas in some areas and said that this factor should be weigned in setting ceilings for new gas if supplies are to be increased.

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers FRIDAY, November 30, 1951 

Washington Re: SERVICE TRADES ENFORCEMENT SURVEY 

Cole-OPS-GPR-1046  

A nation-wide enforcement survey in the service trades covered by Ceiling Price Regulation 34 will be launched by the Office of Price Stabilization immediately, Edward P. Morgan, OPS Enforcement Director, announced today.

While compliance on the part of firms and individuals selling services of many kinds is satisfatory in some areas, non-compliance is quite widespread in other areas, Mr. Morgan said. Ignorance of the existence of the regulation and its requirements, particularly the filing and posting provisions of Section 18 of CPR 34, can no longer be given as an excuse because the regulation became effective last May 16, Mr. Morgan pointed out. "The service trades represent about 12 per cent of the average consumer's budget and cannot be overlooked," Mr. Morgan said. "Every effort has been made throughout the country to publicize the regulation, both through the daily and weekly press and through trade journals. Vigorous enforcement action will now be taken to bring about greater compliance with the regulation." 

Authorization has been secured from the Department of Justice, Mr. Morgan stated, for the Special Assistant United States Attorneys attached to the OPS District Offices, and the United States Attorneys to file injunctive actions in the field immediately in connection with the new compliance drive without securing pre-clearance from Washington. This step should speed up the survey and bring many violators of CPR 34 into compliance without further delay.

Among the types of establishments coming under CPR 34 are power laundries, banks, linen supply and diaper services, hand and self service laundries, shoe repair and hat cleaning shops, cleaning and dyeing plants, rug cleaning and repairing plants, pressing altering and garment repair shops, fur repair and storage shops, radio and television service and repair shops, automobile repair shops, refrigerator and other electrical apparatus service and repair shops.

Also bowling alleys and billiard and pool parlors, parking lots, operators of juke boxes, golf courses and automobile storage firms. 

Under the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended, barbers and beauty shops are exempted from price control.

GPO-O-OPS 1263

TUESDAY, November 27, 1951   

Hughes-OPS-GPR-1047  

Re: FILING OF FORM 8: Elimination of Waiting Period 

Taking note of some misunderstanding among industry groups, the Office of Price Stabilization today emphasized that Form 8 must be filed with OPS by December 19 regardless of whether a manufacturer may also have filed Form 100 to obtain a so-called Capehart adjustment of his ceiling prices. Form 8 is the form on which manufacturers report calculations under Ceiling Price Regulations 22 or 30, as well as any ceiling prices which are higher than their General Ceiling Price Regulation "freeze" prices.

At the same time, OPS announced that a manufacturer filing Form 8 no longer will have to observe a 15-day waiting period before putting into effect the higher ceiling prices listed on the form, Amendments to CPR 22 and 30 eliminating the 15-day time lag will be issued within a few days, OPS said. Advance announcement is made for the convenience of manufacturers preparing to meet the December 19 mandatory effective date of the two regulations.

The formal action to be taken will provide that, after filing a Form 8 by registered mail, a manufacturer may put his higher CPR 22 or 30 ceiling prices into effect as soon as he receives his return postal receipt confirming OPS receipt of his report.

Form 100 must be filed in connection with SR 17 to CPR 22 and SR 4 to CPR 30-two of the supplementary regulations permitting filing of applications for adjusted ceilings under the so-called Capehart amendment to the Defense Production Act. 

Before elimination of the waiting period, a manufacturer reporting higher CPR 22 or 30 ceiling prices on Form 8 had to comply with the 15-day waiting period before using his adjusted prices reported on Form 100. But a manufacturer whose Form 8 showed no higher ceilings could put his adjusted prices into effect immediately. 

Today's action was taken to put both manufacturers on the same basis. 

In explanation of the requirement that Form 8 must be filed even though a manufacturer elects to seek a Capehart adjustment, OPS pointed out that the form is needed from those manufacturers using the supplementary regulations so that the agency may have information on the general level of prices under CPR 22 or CPR 30 in a particular industry. With this information, OPS can determine whether ceiling prices of particular sellers who remain under CPR 22 or CPR 30 are in line with the general level of ceiling prices under those regulations. (Over) GPO-0-OPS 1272

.2. 

A further reason for requiring the filing of Form 8, OPS said, is that the information supplied may be used as a basis for establishing a manufacturer's cellings in cases where proposed Capehart adjustments are questioned or rejected by the agency. 

The requirement, OPS added, ahould not be burdensome on manufacturers. Many have already filed Form 8. Others, anticipating that CPR 22 and 30 would go into effect on July 2, presumably had completed their calculations by June 30 but withheld filing when, as a result of action on that date and later dates, OPS indefinitely postponed the mandatory effective dates.

SR 17 to CPR 22 and SR 4 to CPR 30 are optional regulations, and Form 100 which is used under both regulations need not, of course, be filed by December 19. 

Manufacturers who have any problems concerning the filing of either Form 8 or Form 100 are urged to get in touch with their OPS regional or district offices. 

Copies of the forms can be obtained at these offices.

Distributors Industry Advisory Committee.

ERWIN LERTEN APPOINTMENT 

Erwin Lerten has been appointed Chief, Co-ordination of Adjustments and Procedures Division in the Office of the Chief Counsel, Office of Price Stabilization, it was announced today by Harold Leventhal, Chief Counsel of 0.P.S. Mr. Lerten had served as Branch Counsel for the Machinery Branch, Industrial Materials and Manufactured Goods Division of OPS since March, 1951. 

He will direct coordination of established standards for adjustments, ing of adjustments for adherence to those standards and coordination of the application of standards to adjustments. His Division also will establish and maintain internal procedures and procedural regulations.

Mr. Lerten began the practice of law in Philadelphia in 1941 and in February of 

1942 joined the Office of Price Administration, serving until June, 1945. During the greater part of that period he served as Chief Counsel of the Machinery Branch. In During the year following, he served with the U.S. Air Force in the Judge Advocate General's Office and then as counsel with the War Assets Administration. 

January, 1948, he was appointed Senior Field Attorney for the National Labor Relations 

Board at Pittsburgh and resigned from that post to join OPS.

Mr. Lerten, 35, is a native of Philadelphia and was graduated from the University of Pennsylvania Law School in June, 1940. He was awarded the Gowen Memorial Fellowship of Law which he completed in 1941. He was associate editor of the University of 

Pennsylvania Law Review and a member of the Order of Coif. He is married and has two children. 14832

TUESDAY, November 27, 1951  Re: PLASTIC PRODUCTS IAC 

Browne-OPS-GPR-1053  

Members of the Plastic Products Industry Advisory Committee, at their fourth meeting with Office of Price Stabilization officials today, asked for decontrol of their industry.

Ceilings for the industry are currently established under both the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation and Ceiling Price Regulation 22, the general manufacturers' regulation. Committee members, however, expressed firm opposition to continued controls, and said there is no need for them at the present time. 

Some members expressed resentment at proposals to continue price controls for their industry, and several charged that the government agency has singled out the plastic manufacturing industry as a particular target in this connection. 

J. H. Randolph, Jr., Acting Chief of the Houseware and Accessories Branch of the Consumer Durable Goods Division, OPS, said in reply that OPS "has attempted to give the plastic industry the same treatment as industries, and has no intention of putting free enterprise in a strait-jacket."

Committee members disagreed as to their profit condition. Some represented the plastic market as being soft and said they are currently losing money on some of their products. Others said they are pushing their established ceilings. 

The meeting was called to explore application of existing regulations to manufacturers' ceilings for plastic articles, and to discuss the proposed revision of Supplementary Regulation 14 to CPR 22. SR 14 provides a pricing method for custom molded and fabricated plastic products. 

CPR 22, committee members said, is not suited to the establishment of ceilings for custom molded products, but is satisfactory for plastic articles commonly known as "proprietary," which are produced as part of a manufacturer's regular line. 

OPS officials asked the industry representatives to consider possible use of Supplementary Regulation 17 to CPR 22, which provides methods whereby manufacturers under CPR 22 may obtain adjustments in ceilings as required under the so-called 

Capehart Amendment. 

Industry members manufacture a wide variety of products, many in the houseware and accessory field. Novelties, buttons, certain typewriter parts, dinnerware sets, knives, forks, spoons, cups and saucers are in the list. (Over) 14831 GPO-O- -OPS 1276

- Industry men opposed what they called the burden of filing large numbers of reports in connection with price control, but agreed that since the Defense Production Act is the law, industry must cooperate. OPS officials stated that no industry has been singled out for price control. 

Some of the manufacturers said that in recent months their profit margins have narrowed considerably. This, they pointed out, has been due to increased labor and raw material costs.

WEDNESDAY, November 28, 1951  

Scott-OPS-GPR-1054  

Re: INSULATION BOARD INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE Members of the Insulation Board Industry Advisory Committee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems.

The industry manufactures insulation board, plank lath, insulation tile board, panel board and panel tile, building and utility board, and asphalt coated and impregnated sheathing.

Generally, the industry is pricing currently under the General Ceiling 

Price Regulation (GCPR) pending mandatory application of Ceiling Price Regulation 22 (Manufacturers') on December 19. However, one large manufacturer is now pricing under CPR 22 which has resulted in a rollback in his ceiling prices for insulation board. He is a multi-product manufacturer and it was reported to the meeting that he found it desirable to price under CPR 22 in order to obtain price adjustments for other products being manufactured by him, although his company can ill afford taking a rollback on insulation board prices.

Committeemen pointed out that the insulation board industry is a uniform pricing industry which operates on close profit margins. They said the rollback in ceiling prices by the one producer has had a demoralizing effect on the industry as a whole and that the industry cannot indefinitely maintain the GCPR ceilings with lower ceilings being maintained by one producer under CPR 22. 

It was reported that the industry generally is in an over-production position and that labor and materials cost increases have jeopardized industry's profit situation under existing GCPR ceilings. It was also stated that industry pricing under CPR 22 would distort historically uniform price relationships as between products and companies. 

The committee discussed the drafting of a tailored pricing regulation, based on an industry-wide price increase adjustment factor to be applied to prices established by the industry under the General Ceiling Price Regulation 

(GCPR): 

The committee stressed the urgency for the issuance of such a tailored regulation. 

OPS officials reviewed with the committee figures compiled by OPS from OPS Public Form 8 information submitted by companies in the industry as provided for under CPR 22. These figures indicate that some industry-wide price increase adjustment would be justified, although a wide variance in cost increases exists as between individual companies. GPO-O-OPS 1285

The committee favored a tailored regulation based on an industry-wide price increase adjustment factor, although some members felt that the price increase adjustment indicated would not place them in a satisfactory profit position. However, members stated that it was important to the industry that price relationships as between products and companies be maintained. 

The Committee members asked that consideration be given to the matter of increased costs due to freight rates. It was pointed out that practically all producers sell on a delivered basis and that outbound freight costs run to between 15 to 25 percent of the delivered price. Inbound freight also represents a substantial part of production costs. 

The meeting was conducted by Walter H. Acheson, chief, Building Materials 

Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: Charles W. Moore, division economist; Irving Rubenstein, branch economist; David M. Fishbein, economist;

Re: WOOL GREASE PRODUCERS TAC 

Prompt preparation of a tailored regulation which would iron out disparities in prices between producers was recommended today by members of the Wool Grease Producers Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting with OPS officials. 

Committeemen suggested that a dollars-and-cents regulation, following closely the pattern of MPR 53, issued by the wartime Office of Price Administration, be prepared, with a uniform upward adjustment of 7 cents per pound from the prices appearing in that regulation. 

Members said this adjustment would result in prices near the average levels under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, under which producers in the industry with perhaps a few exceptions are now pricing. 

Committeemen reported price distortions frozen under GCPR were such that some producers had withdrawn their product from the market, despite the demand, hoping for a more favorable price regulation. They estimated an equitable adjustment of prices would stimulate production and augment supplies by about 

10 per cent.

Wool grease, obtained from processing raw wool, is widely used in industry. 

Committeemen estimated that about one-third of the production goes into the manufacture of lanolin, which in turn is used in making cosmetics and medicines. 

Other important uses are in paints, varnishes, soap, lubricants and in refining processes. 

Committeemen said the price of wool grease, a by-product, in no way reflects the price of wool, but rather the cost of processing the grease. 

Committeemen proposed that the spelled out ceilings be applicable to wool grease in returnable drums, carload lots, f.o.b. plant, and that differentials be provided for tank car and less than carload quantities. 

The forthcoming General Overriding Regulation embodying the Capehart 

Amendment, which will be available to those pricing under GCPR, was suggested as a means of relief for the industry. But some committee members expressed doubt whether the Capehart amendment would provide the relief they need. 

However, committeemen said they would examine the GOR as a means of meeting the industry's problems, and would file promptly under it if they found it useful. 14882 GPO-O-OPS 1284

The question of the type of information OPS would require in order to prepare a tailored regulation was discussed. OPS officials suggested that if sufficient representative filings were made under the GOR, the information contained might be adequate. Otherwise, preparation of a questionnaire for the industry would be undertaken by OPS. 

The meeting was conducted by George W. Strasser, acting assistant director, Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division, OPS.

Re: RAW COTTON INDUSTRY MEETING 

Technical changes in the raw cotton order (Ceiling Price Regulation 8) which will not have any overall effect on the level of ceiling prices to farmers or on retail ceilings of cotton goods were discussed at a November 27, 1951, meeting of raw cotton industry representatives with the Office of Price Stabilization. 

This was a representative industry group but not a formal Industry Advisory 

Committee, OPS explained. 

Major part of the discussion was devoted to the relationships between the ceiling price on cotton futures contracts and ceiling prices on spot markets for mixed lots and even running lots. A "mixed lot" is a sale of no more than two bales of cotton of the same grade. Sales of larger quantities of the same grade are "even running lot" sales and take a higher ceiling price than do sales in mixed lots. 

Most sales, in the currently tight market for cotton, are being made on an even running lot basis.

The industry pointed out that, when spot market prices are high in relation to futures ceilings, persons in a short position on the futures market may be forced to default rather than to make delivery on contracts. This situation occurred in 

March of this year.

The industry recommended that the level of ceilings now provided in CPR 8 be unchanged except that cotton futures ceilings should be brought more in line with spot ceiling prices.

Another proposal by the industry was that California producers be provided with a ceiling on export sales which would be equivalent to the ceiling on export sales of cotton from a Gulf port. The regulation now provides that California producers must figure their ceilings by deducting the freight differential that would apply on shipments from Carolina mill points. The industry proposal would eliminate the requirement for this deduction and would give the California producers the advantage of their location for making export sales to the Orient. 

Other points of discussion were the pricing of split grades, the grade differentials now provided in the regulation and an allowance for additional expenses incurred in making export sales. OPS proposed that, on certain split grades, ceilings be set at the midpoint between the ceilings applying to the official United States Department of Argiculture grades. The regulation currently provides that the seller may price only at the lower of the ceilings applying to an official grade. (Over) GPO-O-OPS 1291

These and other technical changes in the raw cotton order will be worked out with OPS through subcommittees of the Raw Cotton Industry Representatives. Announcement will be made in the near future as to the membership and the time of meeting of these subcommittees.

Presiding at the Raw Cotton Industry Representatives meeting was James E. Robison, Chief, Textiles Branch, Consumer Soft Goods Division, OPS.

Re: BEDDING IAC 

At their second meeting with Office of Price Stabilization officials today, members of the Bedding Industry Advisory Committee agreed that a tailor-made regulation to establish ceiling prices for that industry would be advisable.

Committee members said that a regulation utilizing a formula method to arrive at ceilings would be preferable to a regulation providing specific dollars-and-cents prices. Discussions centered about the particular pricing formula to be used, and the period upon which the pricing should be based. 

Bedding manufacturers currently are pricing under either the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation or Ceiling Price Regulation 22, the general manufacturers' regulation.

The industry has now been covered by Supplementary Regulation 12 to CPR 22. OPS officials told industry representatives that SR 12 was today extended indefinitely. It covers by name the products they manufacture. These are mattresses, box springs, coil springs, Hollywood beds, metal beds, cots and dual equipment.

SR 12 is a regulation for extending controls at current ceilings, pending issuance of a tailor-made regulation. 

Thus, the manufacturers will be relieved of the necessity of computing and filing with OPS, prices under CPR 22, which is mandatorily effective December 19, next.

Preparatory to issuance of the tailored regulation, committee members said they will submit cost information on a selected list of key products important to the industry. This will aid OPS, agency officials said, in framing the proposed new regulation. Upon receipt of the information, OPS will begin drafting of the tailor-made regulation. No date was set for a further meeting.

THURSDAY, November 29, 1951 

Washington Re: LANOLIN PRODUCERS IAC 

GPR-1062 Moore-OPS-GPR-1062 . 

Members of the Lanolin Producers Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials recommended that a tailored dollars-and-cents ceiling price regulation be prepared that would establish uniform prices for their industry in equitable relationship to prices of wool grease. 

They recommended that dollars-and-cents ceilings be fixed on wool grease as well. Lanolin is refined wool grease and is widely used in cosmetics, medicines and for industrial uses. Ceilings on both wool grease and lanolin are now determined under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR.

Committeemen said there was considerable disparity in their suppliers' wool grease ceilings. They said for some producers the ceilings on technical or industrial grades of lanolin were not sufficient to return a profit, particularly if their wool grease was obtained from higher priced suppliers. They declared a lanolin producer could not arbitrarily decide the grade he wished to produce, and only after processing wool grease could he determine whether it would yield technical grade or more profitable grades of lanolin.

Committeemen said there was a shortage of wool grease, and that some producers of wool grease were withholding it from the market in the hope of obtaining higher ceilings. They said the shortage was due not only to price, but also to the low level of activity in the wool industry. Wool grease is a by-product of the processing of raw wool and its availability is directly related to the volume of wool processed.

Committeemen said they would like to see wool grease producers get higher ceilings, for the beneficial effect it would have on supply, providing their lanolin ceilings were adjusted to reflect the increase on their raw materials. 

They also acknowledged that it would affect the costs of those using wool grease for industrial products other than lanolin. (over) Committeemen suggested that ceilings be spelled out for both wool grease and lanolin in the same tailored regulation, as was the case under the Office of Price 

Administration during World War II in MPR 53. 

The possibility of producers obtaining relief under the forthcoming General Overriding Regulation embodying the Capehart Amendment, which will be available to those pricing under GCPR, was discussed. OPS officials pointed out that OPS would require certain information before a dollars-and-cents ceiling price regulation could be prepared for the industry. They said this information might be obtained from filings under the GOR if they were sufficiently numerous, otherwise OPS would have to prepare a questionnaire for the industry. GPO-O-OPS 1298

The question was raised whether OPS, when it placed wool grease under the GCPR, intended to include lanolin as well. Committeemen reported the industry universally understood lanolin was subject to GCPR, since it was merely refined wool grease, and asked that any doubt on this point be specifically clarified.

The meeting was conducted by George W. Strasser, acting deputy director, Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division, OPS.

Members of the Retailers Problems Subcommittee of the Retail Industry

Advisory Committee met today (Nov. 29) with officials of the Office of Price

RETAIL INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE SUB-COMMITTEE 

Agenda of the meeting included provisions of forthcoming regulations to relieve retailers of hardship conditions due to the lack of certain seasonal stocks of merchandise when CPR 7 became effective last February. It was proposed that a different base date be set in the establishment of ceilings for such seasonal merchandize.

Committee members were unanimous in recommending that dollars-and-cents ceilings for certain categories of merchandise at retail, such as major appliances and bedding items should be avoided. They advised that instead OPS should use an approximation of the CPR 7 technique.

In the matter of changes in service rates, the committee members were of different views but the consensus was that OPS action is inadvisable at this time. All seven members were present and they expressed belief that the session was a constructive benefit to their business.

Re: FOOD CONTAINER PAPERBOARD SUBCOMMITTEE Members of the Food Container Paperboard Subcommittee of the Special 

Paperboard Industry Advisory Committee today discussed in detail with OPS officials provisions of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry which would establish prices at the current market level. 

The proposed regulation would cover special paperboards used to make milk cartons, cups, lids, meat trays and other containers for liquid, moist and oily foods.

Committeemen reported that prices of various manufacturers and on various grades are below the ceilings permitted under the Manufacturers' General 

Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22.

Committeemen pointed out that the proposed regulation contained no provision for adjustment of prices to meet future changes in costs. They cited, for example, the effect of different rates of production on unit cost, including instances when decreased runs for certain grades reduced or wiped out profit margins.

The tentative draft of the proposed regulation provided for adjustment of individual ceilings by OPS so they may be in line with other ceilings established by the regulation or other paper and paperboard regulations. The adjustment could either be made on the manufacturer's application or initiated by OPS. GPO-O-OPS 1308 OPS officials pointed out that this provision would provide means of relief for manufacturers who might be in distress because their ceilings were out of line.

Under the proposed regulation a manufacturer would determine base prices for his various grades of paperboard for various classes of customers. These would be the prices in effect during a 30 day period to be determined, possibly the period ending November 15, 1951, before the application of freight allowance and differentials.

He would be permitted to add and required to subtract the differentials employed during the base period for quantity and special caliper, strength, dimensions, finish, sizing and other particulars. He would have to grant the same freight allowances as in the base period. 

Provision would be made for application to OPS for base prices on grades not specifically covered in the regulation or not made by the manufacturers during the base period. (over) 15033

The meeting was conducted by C. F. Wiedeman, Jr., industrial consultant for paperboard products.

PRESS RELEASE ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers MONDAY, DECEMBER 3, 1951  

Tempo E 

Washington Crossley-OPS-GPR-1068 

ST-4200: Ext. 3491 

Re: APPAREL IAC's 

The Office of Price Stabilization, in a roundup of industry advisory committee meetings in the apparel field, reported today on a single tailored regulation to cover women's and children's outerwear manufacturers. 

The proposed regulation affects a $4 billion segment of the apparel industry in which 11,000 manufacturers account for about 40 percent of the total apparel sales volume in the U. S. The proposed regulation would cover practically all women's and children's outerwear with the exception of knitting mill products, heavy outerwear, and plastic and leather apparel.

The industry advisory committee meetings reported on in this roundup are: 

Dress IAC, Home and Utility Dress IAC, Women's, Misses' and Junior Blouse, 

Skirt and Sportswear IAC, Women's, Misses' and Junior Coat and Suit IAC, and

Children's and Infants' Wear IAC. They were held this week and last. 

OPS proposed a division factor type of regulation. A "division factor" is a ratio of total direct costs to net sales in the same (annual) period. 

Use of this factor results in an historic markup over direct costs by which the selling price for a garment can be arrived at.

OPS officials proposed using the year 1950 as the base period for determing the division factor. The industry recommended some alternative to 1950, including averages of preceding years. The industry representatives also recommended some type of adjustment of the division factor to compensate for markdowns and closeouts.

OPS also proposed a highest price line limitation, at a cut-off point representing 95% of the sales volume in the year 1950 within a category. The manufacturer can take a full markup on costs which would give him prices within the cutoff point. Prices beyond that point would reflect only dollar-and-cents pass-throughs in excess of the cut-off points. 

The industry representatives recommended that the highest price line have a cut-off point at a higher percentage than 95 percent. They also recommended some provision for relief from squeezes on one-price line and two-price line manufacturers. 

It was suggested that use be made of exemption levels below which the highest price line limitation would not operate.

An arriving at material costs, the industry recommended that the unit direct cost of a garment should be the acquisition cost. 

Use of a special averaging table to cover each selling season selected by the manufacturer was proposed by OPS. During this period, the manufacturer must average out to his division factor.

GPO-O-OPS 1309. (Over) 15038

OPS proposed a 45-day period in the next selling season to allow a manufacturer to work off any excess above his permissible markup. The industry recommended that it be allowed the next full selling season as a "mark-up" period.

Generally the question of issuance and effective date of the proposed regulation was recommended for determination by a subcommittee. Ka 15038

PRESS RELEASE    FRIDAY, November 30, 1951 

Re: 

SLIDE FASTENER MANUFACTURERS IAC 

Browne-OPS-GPR-1069  

Office of Price Stabilization officials and members of the Slide Fastener Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee, at their first meeting today, explored the possible issuance by OPS of a tailored regulation for that industry. The Consensus of industry members was that neither Ceiling Price Regulation 22, nor Supplementary Regulation 17 to that regulation, will serve them. industry, which manufactures zippers and zipper components, is currently pricing its products under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, (GCPR). 

Committee members said they would rather continue to price under GCPR, instead of computing prices and filing under CPR 22, which becomes effective December 19, next. They inquired whether they could be covered by Supplementary 

Regulation 12, to CPR 22, while a tailored-regulation is in process of preparation. SR 12 is a manufacturers' regulation for extending controls under GCPR ceilings, pending the issuance of a tailor-made regulation. 

The committee chairman said that the agency could make no commitment on this suggestion. OPS, it was said, has no cost data for the zipper industry which will justify any recommendation that such a step be taken at this time. 

No date was set for a further meeting of the group. 

The committee was representative of approximately 170 manufacturers in the industry. These produce "hundreds of millions of zippers a year, an industry member said. Bulk of the production is bought by the apparel industry. 

Less than 4 percent of the output is sold direct to consumers. Zippers are used in novelties, leather goods and tents, as well as in clothing. 11 Committee members explained difficulties confronting the industry. Under allocations cut-backs in metal ordered by the National Production Authority, they said, they will be reduced to turning out only 35 percent of their average 

NPA base period production.

They painted this picture in a plea for an increased price: The most popular zipper currently sold, the committee members said, is one seven inches long and 7/16th's inches wide. In 1941 this sold for .071 cents. In 1946, after an Office of Price Administration authorized increase, it went to .078 cents. 

In 1951, under CCPR, it sells for .073 cents. (Over) On the other hand, an industry member said, brass used in zippers has increased in cost nearly 100 percent; cotton tapes, twisted cords and threads are up 50 percent over 1941, and labor costs have increased by a similar 50 percent.

PRESS RELEASE    Friday, November 30, 1951 Coakley-OPS-GPR-1070 

Re: ASPHALT AND ASPHALT PRODUCTS LAC Members of the Asphalt and Asphalt Products Industry Advisory Committee, meeting today for the third time with Office of Price Stabilization officials, recommended unanimously that no effort be made at this time to spell out dollarsand-cents ceilings for their products.

They told OPS officials that there would be no positive advantages in such a change in CPR 66 which now sets their ceiling prices, generally, at the highest prices charged during the base period, August 1, 1950 to January 25, 1951. 

They said, further, that dollars-and-cents ceilings would not be feasible because of the administrative difficulties they would impose. 

However, industry representatives asked that CPR 66 be modified to permit the pass-through of increased transportation costs. At the present time 

CPR 66 has a cut-off date on transportation cost additions to ceiling prices of May 15, 1951, so that rate raises after that date cannot be added. It was pointed out that while some producers sell their products f.o.b. refinery and are not concerned directly with transportation costs, others sell on a destination price basis and must absorb increases in transportation rates. 

OPS officials said the agency currently is studying the problem of transportation cost increases from the standpoint of the impact of such costs on the asphalt segment of the petroleum industry. They said consideration would be given to the industry recommendation to retain formula type ceiling prices.

PRESS RELEASE    

Friday, November 30, 1951 

Coakley-OPS-GPR-1071  

Re: MOTOR OILS INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE Members of the Motor Oils Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to explore some of the technical, marketing, and price aspects relating to the introduction of new lubricating oils. 

The meeting discussed the manner in which retail prices for these new products should be handled in relation to wholesale costs. OPS pointed out that increased costs at the wholesale level were in some cases around 5 or 6 cents a gallon above other premium oils which were sold during the base period, but application had been made for increases of 20 cents a gallon at a retail level for the new products by some marketers.

OPS representatives expressed concern that the introduction of these oils at the prices requested might result in general advance in price of all premium oils. They also pointed out that approval of retail prices requested by some applicants would result in prices higher than those of many sellers who had sold similar oils during the base period at lower prices. 

Committee members suggested that it was customary practice at the retail level to pass along price increases in multiples of 5 cents, or 20 cents a gallon, even though the increase at the wholesale level was considerably less. 

Industry members also pointed out that the May 15 cut-off date which applies to transportation cost increase additions to ceiling prices should be extended to permit addition of such cost increases since that date. 

OPS officials indicated that the problems outlined in the meeting would continue under study and that this study would include an examination of customary practices in the industry with respect to reflecting cost increases in selling prices. 

0. D. Judd, Chief of the Petroleum Branch, and Benjamin Goldberg, economist, conducted the meeting. Other OPS officials attending were:

Re: GUMMING IẠC 

Provisions of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry were discussed in detail by members of the Gumming Industry Advisory Committee today at their second meeting with OPS officials.

The industry manufactures gummed tapes and papers, including sealing tape, waterproof tape, reinforced tape, corrugators tape, flat gummed paper, stay paper, veneer tape, "Hollands" and gummed specialties.

The products are widely used in the manufacture of paperboard and corrugated boxes, packaging, binding and various manufacturing operations. Stay tape is used to fasten the corners of set-up boxes. Hollands are used in binding tablets, printed forms and similar products.

Under the proposed regulation base prices would be spelled out for two basic grades of gummed papers, and provision would be made whereunder manufacturers would determine their ceilings on related grades by adding or subtracting the differentials existing during a specified base period between the basic grades and the related grades. 

Prices to be spelled out would be on the following items: Standard gummed kraft sealing tape, 30 inches wide, standard size rolls, 60 lbs. basic weight, 600 feet to the roll, per bundle; 16 to 499 bundles; 500 or more bundles. 

2. Regular sisal tape in rolls, 1,000 one-inch yards, carload lots and less than carload lots.

It was proposed that the base prices be determined before the application of differentials covering different sizes of orders, terms of sale, freight, and differences in color, weight, finishes and other specifications. 

OPS proposed that ceilings for gummed flat papers, veneer tapes, stay paper and gummed specialties be fixed at the individual manufacturer's highest prices as frozen under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR. (Over) Committeemen objected that their increased costs were such that GCPR prices would not be satisfactory. They stressed the importance of the cost of adhesives as an element in their total costs. 15102 GPO-O-OPS 1331

They suggested that action by OPS be delayed until the industry had an opportunity to figure ceilings under Supplementary Regulation 17 to the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. They predicted that these calculations would show the industry was entitled to substantial increases over present prices which are at GCPR levels. 

The meeting was conducted by John E. Becker, industrial consultant on coarse papers.

 TUESDAY, December 4, 1951 

Re: 

Tempo E 

Washington PLASTICIZERS (ESTER-TYPE) IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-1074  

Members of the Plasticizers (Ester-Type) Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting today with OPS officials recommended that a tailored regulation be written for di-octyl phthalate type plasticizers that would spell out dollars-and-cents ceiling prices on standard items. 

It was proposed that ceilings be established on the basis of weighted averages of ceilings established under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22. An alternative of developing industry-wide percentage cost adjustment factors, applicable to prices established under the 

General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, was also considered.

Committeemen reported that some firms in the industry are still selling at prices frozen January 26, 1951, under GCPR, which did not reflect recent substantial increases under CPR 22 in the raw materials costs of phthalic anhydride and various alcohols. 

Part of the industry has already established CPR 22 ceilings, but committeemen reported that CPR 22 yielded disparate prices. Current market prices are not up to CPR 22 levels. Committeemen said if CPR 22 ceilings were averaged, it would permit some increase in prices to offset the increased cost of raw materials, and permit the industry to sell as is its custom at uniform prices.

The plasticizers which the committee proposed to price in this manner are di-capryl phthalate, di-2-ethylhexyl phthalate, di-normal octyl phthalate, di-iso-octyl phthalate and di-normal octyl-decyl phthalate.

Plasticizers are materials that impart pliability and flexibility to synthetic resins and plastics, and are important to a wide range of industrial products, many of which are important in the defense program. 

Committeemen suggested that their industry be described as the manufacture of monomeric and polymeric ester-type plasticizers used in the processing and compounding of synthetic resins, plastics and synthetic rubbers.

Committeemen said there is a demand for increased production which it is impossible to meet in view of the present squeeze resulting from increased prices of their raw materials, and urged that, in fairness to their industry, adjustments be permitted to reflect increased materials costs. 

They discussed the Johnston formula for industrial relief, which requires adjustment of ceiling prices if the rate of earnings of an industry is less than 85 per cent of the best three out of four years from 1946 to 1949, inclusive. 

Members pointed out that most manufacturers in the industry were not making the plasticizers concerned in the 1946-49 period. (Over) GPO-O-OPS 1345

. 

Committeemen suggested that similar relief be studied for various sebacic esters made by their industry, for which there are disparate prices. Manufacturers of sebacates complained of being squeezed by increases in the price of castor oil derived from imports not subject to price control. 

OPS officials indicated that some of the information needed for computing the ceilings on the di-octyl phthalate plasticizers would be obtained from Forms 8 filed under CPR 22, and the industry would be called upon to supply any additional information that was necessary. 

The meeting was conducted by George W. Strasser, acting assistant director, Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division.

RED CEDAR AND INTERMOUNTAIN POLES AND PILING IAC Members of the Red Cedar and Intermountain Poles and Piling Industry 

Advisory Committee at their first meeting with OPS officials today discussed in detail proposals for a tailored regulation for their industry that would fix dollars-and-cents ceilings on standard grades of their products, f.o.b. normal loading points. With the purpose of revising and bringing them up-to-date for their industry, the committee checked over paragraph by paragraph MPR 544 and MPR 555, regulations issued by the wartime Office of Price Administration, which covered poles, piling and their treatment with wood preservations in the western part of the country.

It was proposed that prices established be based on an adjustment of prices frozen under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, the adjustment to reflect the fact that the industry was in a depressed position during the base period under that regulation. Moreover, these prices were out of line with log prices which had a tendency to divert production to sawmills. 

Part of the committee's work was to make recommendations that would keep the regulation in line with a companion regulation being prepared covering 

Pacific Northwest poles and piling.

The latter will embrace the area west of the Cascades, where the production is mainly Douglas fir poles and piling, which normally are pressure-treated. 

The Red Cedar and Intermountain Poles and Piling committee covers the mountain area from the Pacific Coast eastward to the 100th Meridian. Treatment in this area normally is by dipping. But the product of the inter-mountain area is also shipped east and west and pressure-treated on the coast, in Minnesota or at other eastern points.

It is the objective of OPS and the committees to relate the two regulations in a realistic way.

The meeting was conducted by A. L. Helmer, chief, Western Softwood Section, OPS.  Norman O. Cruver, chief, Lumber and 

Wood Products Division; Harold M. Cleland and 0. C. Miller, economists; William 

S. McKinley, attorney, and Walter R. Moulton, Office of Advisory Committees.

Re: Delegation to OPS Regional Offices of 

Authority to Act on Applications for

Adjusted Ceiling Prices Filed Under General Overriding Regulation 21 (Delegation of Authority No. 39) 

OPS field offices were given broad authority today by the Office of Price 

Stabilization to act on applications for "Capehart" ceiling price adjustments filed with them by individual businesses under General Overriding Regulation 21. 

Delegation of Authority 39, effective December 7, includes authority to issued "letter orders" establishing ceiling prices of individual applicants. Washington

The delegation is to OPS' 14 Regional Directors, but Regional Directors are empowered to redelegate to District Offices. 

General Overriding Regulation 21, which went into effect December 5, is the regulation under which most producers, manufacturers and processors have the option to apply for ceiling price adjustments, based on changes in their costs from the pre-Korean period to July 26, 1951. OPS is directed by the Defense 

Production Act, as amended in 1951, to allow such applications. 

GOR 21 says that all applicants whose gross sales in the last complete fiscal year ended not later than July 31, 1951, were less than $1,000,000 shall make application to their OPS District Offices, rather than to Washington. It is these applications filed with the District Offices which will be fully processed in the field. The only exceptions (as provided in Section 4 of GOR 21) will be in cases where the field offices are directed to forward applications to Washington for action. These, generally, will be applications covering commodities for which OPS has established dollars-and-cents ceiling prices. Hughes-OPS-GFR-1077  GPO-O-OPS 1870

WEDNESDAY, December 5, 1951 Tempo E 

Washington Moore-OPS-GPR-1079  Re: PRIVATE BRAND TIRE AND TUBE IAC 

Ceiling Price Regulation 62, covering manufacturers' prices for private brand tires and tubes, is proving a workable and practical regulation from their standpoint, members of the Private Brand Tire and Tube Industry Advisory 

Committee said today at a meeting with OPS officials.

The committee endorsed a proposed amendment to the regulation which would permit private brand owners, if it had been their practice, to continue selling to their affiliated distributors on the basis of existing cost-plus contracts. 

It would also authorize them to buy, if it was their practice, at their pre- 

Korean discounts from the manufacturers' list prices.

The committee discussed the possibility of OPS issuing a tailored regulation for tire dealers which would authorize them to sell tires against manufacturers or private brand owners' suggested selling prices, as has been the custom in the industry. 

Under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, each dealer is required to sell at the prices he individually was charging at the time of the general price freeze on January 26, 1951.

Committeemen indicated that a regulation along the suggested lines would be desirable if means could be found of maintaining under it prices at approximately the GCPR level.

The committee discussed the growing practice of painting white sidewalls on black tires. Members expressed the opinion that such painting should be considered as a service performed at the dealer's level, and not by the manufacturer or private brand owner.

The meeting was conducted by Hubert H. Peterson, chief, Tire Section, OPS.
