Wednesday, December 5, 1951

 Re: WHOLESALE FOOD DISTRIBUTORS IAC Barkley-OPS-GPR-1080 

A proposed interim survey of price markups in the wholesale food distribution business was discussed today at a meeting between officials of the Office of Price Stabilization and members of the Wholesale Food Distributors 

Industry Advisory Committee. 

The survey has been proposed so as to get an idea of how markups used in the wholesale grocery ceiling price regulation, CPR 14, compare with historical markups used in the trade. Industry members have contended that some of the 

CPR 14 markups are out of line with those normally taken in the past. 

OPS said that information obtained in the interim survey may be used as the basis for possible temporary adjustment of markups, pending completion of a more thorough survey which is to be made jointly by the Bureau of Labor Statistics and OPS.

This exhaustive survey had been scheduled to get underway this year, but it was delayed due to reservations on selection of some of the items proposed. 

The committee was called in to review the entire operation of the wholesale grocery markup regulation and the effect of its impact on the industry. Some members reported that earnings had been affected adversely by the regulation. 

They suggested that consideration be given to consolidation or adjustment of the categories for canned fruits and vegetables, and contended that, with softness in the market for some commodities, merchandising flexibility has been unduly impaired.

The interim survey is designed to appraise the validity, in general, of the reported decreases in earnings and further to determine what remedial action, if justified, should be taken through adjustment of specific markups or of categories.

It was agreed that the general structure of the regulation should be maintained. The committee concensus was that price control in the dry grocery field must be continued for the present.

A few other technical adjustments also were considered. 

Representing OPS at the meeting were Edward F. Phelps, Deputy Director of the agency; George L. Mehren, Acting Director, Food and Restaurant Division; 

Emmerson Brown, chief, Food Distributor Branch; Jerry Foytik, division economist;

Washington Re: WHOLESALE MEAT DISTRIBUTORS IAC 

Proposed revision of the Office of Price Stabilization's livestock distribution regulation was discussed today at a meeting between officials of the agency and members of the newly-appointed Wholesale Meat Distributors Industry Advisory Committee.

Barkley-OPS-GPR-1081  

The Committee has been appointed to advise OPS on livestock distribution regulations, without reference to pricing. Its membership represents the entire wholesale meat distribution business, including slaughterers, wholesalers, nonslaughtering processors and frozen meat locker plants.

OPS is now considering revision of Distribution Regulation 1, which includes a provision requiring slaughterers to register. The regulation originally set up machinery for OPS livestock slaughter quotas, but these provisions have been eliminated because of the Congressional prohibition against quotes. 

John Bell

Among proposed revisions of the regulation is one which would shorten the time limit for the filling of meat orders placed by institutions, such as hospitals, orphanages and asylums. This time has been deemed too long. 

Also under consideration by OPS is a reclassification of "occasional slaughterers", persons who are neither commercial nor farm slaughterers, but who occasionally slaughtered livestock in the 1950 base period of Distribution Regulation 1, and thus are able to qualify for registration as slaughterers,

The reclassification has been proposed to permit the OPS to keep a closer check on occasional slaughtering.

Thursday, December 6, 1951

Washington Barkley-OPS-GPR 1082 ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 INSTITUTIONAL WHOLESALERS TAC 

Wholesale food distributors who specialize in sales to institutions, both public and private, today submitted a list of recommendations to the Office of Price Stabilization which, they said, would ease the impact of the wholesale grocery ceiling price regulation, CPR 14, on their operations.

The recommendations were offered at a meeting of OPS officials and members of the Institutional Wholesalers Industry Advisory Committee. The session was one of three called for this week by OPS to review the wholesale grocery regulation and the effect of the regulation's price markups on the food distribution industry.

The Wholesale Food Distributors Industry Advisory Committee met with OPS 

officials yesterday. The Retail Food Distributors Committee will meet with agency officials on Friday (Dec. 7).

The institutional wholesalers told the OPS officials that their earnings had been adversely affected by the institutional sales markups in the grocery regulation. They recommended adjustments to restore these markups to what they said were the normal operating practices prevailing before the present emergency. 

Among other changes they proposed were inclusion of allowances for special packaging for sales to institutions; for sales in less than case lots; for "inbound cartage" (cost of transporting goods from point of receipt to warehouse), and for increased labor costs.

The industry committee also recommended that provision be made for special markup adjustments in high-cost operation areas; for new zone price allowances, and for inventory depreciation.

OPS officials told the industry representatives that their recommendations would receive full and early consideration, but emphasized that no definite commitments could be made at this time. 

They explained that an interim survey of price markups has been proposed for the food distribution industry so as to get an idea of how the markups listed in 

CPR 14 compare with historical markups in the trade.

This survey is designed to appraise the validity, in general, of the reported decreases in earnings of food distributors and further to determine what remedial action, if justified, should be taken through markup adjustments. THURSDAY, December 6, 1951   

Browne-OPS-GPR-1084  

Re: FOUNTAIN PEN AND MECHANICAL PENCIL LAC Members of the Fountain Pen and Mechanical Pencil Industry Advisory 

Committee met today with Office of Price Stabilization officials to explore the possible issuance of a tailored regulation for that industry. 

While there was difference of opinion among committee members as to the need for a tailored regulation at this time, all agreed that they would study existing ceiling price regulations, and return to Washington later for further discussion. 

Fountain pen and mechanical pencil manufacturers currently are pricing under either the General Ceiling Price Regulation, (GCPR) or Ceiling Price 

Regulation 22, the general manufacturers' regulation.

The committee devoted itself to an examination of costs, pricing methods, possible material shortages, the use of substitute materials, the burden of preparing reports for OPS, and the need for price control. 

Some members said that price control under a tailored regulation is necessary to meet possible inflationary trends which threaten during the first half of 1952. Such a regulation, they said, would be especially helpful as an aid to the stabilization of prices and production, in the event a material shortage develops.

They pointed out that a cut-back in production by 25 percent or more early next year is anticipated because of expected shortages in allocations of copper, brass and stainless steel. This, they said, would decrease volume and boost production costs, and that a tailored regulation would provide price adjustments. 

Those members who voiced the opinion that no additional price control or a tailored regulation is necessary, argued that the industry is operating satisfactorily under GCPR or CPR 22; that fountain pens and mechanical pencils are plentiful; that these commodities are now selling at below ceilings; that they do not affect the cost of living, and that competition is keeping consumer prices down.

The committee discussed possible pricing methods if the National Production Authority should shut down suddenly on use of stainless steel for pen points, forcing manufacturers to turn to more expensive metals in order to remain in business.

GPO-O-OPS 1373

OPS officials said that dollars-and-cents ceilings are preferred by the agency in the preparation of a tailored regulation, although the suggestion was made by committee members that a formula pricing method might be favored by the industry. 

OPS spokesmen advised that the industry think in terms of the first quarter of 1952, when inflationary pressures may be greater, and materials scarcer. They pointed out that a tailored regulation could deal with prices at not only the manufacturers' level, but also at that of the wholesaler and retailer. It could also include provisions for uniform pricing and pre-ticketing. 

No date was set for another meeting.

The meeting was conducted by Lee McCanne, Acting Assistant Director, Consumer 

Durable Goods Division and William S. Miller, Chief, Business Equipment Section of that division. Other OPS participants were Herbert Raskin, Attorney; A. D. Holzman, Branch Counsel; Kenneth N. K. Industry Advisory Committees. F. K. Johnston, Office Supply and Personal Goods Section, National Production Authority, also attended.

Re: 

 TIRE AND TUBE DEALERS IAC 

A majority of the members of the Tire and Tube Dealers Industry Advisory Committee today expressed opposition to OPS plans, disclosed at a meeting of the committee, to lower the spelled-out ceiling prices on passenger car tire Moore-OPS-0-1085  

The proposed reduction would be from $3.50 to $3.00 retail and from $2.60 to $2.40 wholesale, in conformity with findings of an OPS survey. 

Carcasses are worn tires to which camelback is applied to make recapped or retreaded tires.

Committeemen, however, felt that if the cuts were necessary, it would be better to take the lesser cut on the wholesale price as proposed than on the retail price, even though it would reduce the spread between wholesale and retail prices. They pointed out that the wholesale price should be as high as possible to bring out supplies.

Members recommended against fixing dollars-and-cents ceilings on truck tire carcasses. They pointed out that most trucking companies recap or retread their good carcasses and said there was no uniform market on the available truck tire caracsses.

The committee approved the proposal of OPS to establish a premium of $1.00 per carcass on 6-ply passenger car tire carcasses, as compared with 4-ply carcasses which would take the proposed new $3.00 and $2.40 ceilings. About 5 percent of passenger car tires are 6-ply.

Members recommend that no attempt be made to put dollars and cents ceiling prices on the services of recapping and retreading. 

Committeemen indicated that a tailored regulation for dealers would be satisfactory which would price new tires at levels now prevailing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, based on manufacturers' list prices.

PRESS RELEASE  

Tempo E 

Friday, December 7, 1951 Re: 

Washington USED MACHINE TOOLS IAC 

Scott-OPS-GPR-1087  

The Used Machine Tools Industry Advisory Committee met yeaterday with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems under the used machine tools ceiling price regulation CPR 80. 

This was the third meeting of the committee. 

The committee recommended that the base date of January 25, 1951, for determining ceilings be changed to a more recent date so as to reflect a closer relationship between the current ceilings for new and used machine tools. 

Committeemen pointed out that ceiling prices for most new machine tools have increased substantially since January 25, 1951, and that adjustment of used machine tool ceilings in relation to the more current level of ceilings for new machine tools would be fair and equitable, and would act as an incentive for bringing more used tools into the market.

Committee members said that new machine tool ceilings have now leveled off and have become relatively static and that a more current base price date than January 25, 1951, would reflect a more realistic basis for determining ceilings for used tools.

It was the committee consensus that the percentage rates applied under the regulation for determining ceilings for used machine tools, are sound and fair, provided the base price date for the new tools is advanced to a date more current than January 25, 1951. However, the committee felt that the percentage rate to be applied in connection with used machine tools manufactured before 1916 should be eliminated and make such tools subject to the same percentage rate as now applied to tools manufactured after 1916 and before 1922. This would have the effect of bringing more of the older machine tools into the market, they said.

Consensus of the committee was that the category of "reconditioned" machine tools should not be eliminated from the regulation. The members said there is a definite necessity for the pricing of "reconditioned" machine tools as now provided by the regulation, but suggested that it might be desirable to provide for some kind of guarantee provision in connection with the sale of "reconditioned" machine tools, similar to the guarantee that is now required in connection with the sale of "rebuilt" machine tools. ("Rebuilt" machine tools are required to be guaranteed to perform satisfactorily after 30 days from date of delivery.) 

The committee recommended that the regulation be changed to give sellers optional methods of determining ceilings where difficulty is experienced in learning current prices for comparable new machine tools. This could be accomplished by permitting sellers to use published prices issued earlier than January 25, 1951, or the acquisition cost to the original purchaser of the 

GPO-O-OPS 1386

machine tool when new. In nearly every case, committeemen said, applying the percentage rates to such earlier new machine tool prices would result in lower ceilings for the used tools, but would facilitate pricing and expedite completion of sales.

The committee agreed that it would be desirable and practical to eliminate ceilings for obsolete types of machine tools having only a nominal value. It was suggested that such tools having a value of less than $300 be exempted from price control.

It has been proposed that OPS issue a price guide book on new machine tools for use in determining ceilings for used machine tools. If such a price guide book is prepared, committee members said, it is important that it include methods and instructions for establishing comparability of new machine tools to obsolete and discontinued models of used tools. 

A subcommittee was appointed to advise with OPS in developing such instructions and methods. Members of this subcommittee are: Louis Botwinik, Harvey H. Goldman, Thomas H. Price, Thomas J. O'Brien and Edwin Johnson, Jr.

Two new members have been appointed to the committee since the last meeting: 

They are: C. Lee McDonald, Jr., McDonald Machinery Company, St. Louis, Mo., and 

Alex Zeeve, Jr., Alex Zeeve & Company, Inc., New York City.

The meeting was conducted by Ralph R. Irwin, business analyst, Machinery 

Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: Leslie J. Carson, chief, Machinery Branch; C. W. Moore, division economist; C. G. Parson, branch economist; 

Harrison C. Thompson, Jr., and Gerald Mazier, legal staff; Robert R. Teates, Office of Enforcement; and Harry Speck, Office of Industry Advisory Committees.

 Re: DENTAL EQUIPMENT AND SUPPLIES MANUFACTURERS LAC Members of the Dental Equipment and Supplies Manufacturers Industry Advisory 

Committee, at their first meeting with Office of Price Stabilization officials today, said that issuance of a tailored ceiling price regulation would be advisable for their industry.

Committee members said they are currently pricing under either the 

General Ceiling Price Regulation, (GCPR) or under Ceiling Price Regulation 22, the general manufacturers' regulation. They stated that they will file under 

CPR 22 before December 19, next, the effective date for that regulation.

OPS officials made no commitments as to issuance of a tailored regulation. 

They said today's session was exploratory in purpose, and that it probably will be necessary to hold another meeting. No date was set. 

Manufacturers represented at today's meeting produce over 15,000 items, including dental equipment, chairs, false teeth, denture base material, cements, fillings, steel instruments, burrs and many others. 

Committee members said that a tailored regulation would solve the problems of 75 percent of their industry. They asked that any such regulation provide for adjustments in hardship cases. Another request was that a tailored regulation be made as simple as possible, so as to reduce reporting requirements. 

One member suggested, that, in establishing ceilings, a modified freeze be adopted, with January, 1951, as the base period. 

Division of opinion developed among the industry members as to whether the Capehart adjustments would be of aid. All agreed that there will be rollbacks under CPR 22, but stated these will be minor, compared to the task of issuing new price lists. The committee members asked that any tailored regulation preserve historic trade practices. They stated that the pricing of new items is a minor problem.

Committee members observed that many of the items they manufacture are selling at below established ceilings. They stated that prices in the dental manufacturing industry have increased less than in any other industry. In the last 10 years, they pointed out, selling prices have increased only 45 percent, while wages have been hiked by 110 percent. All said they have granted récent wage boosts, competition forcing them to hold their selling price line.

Another problem facing the industry, a spokesman declared, is in meeting. competition from the $1,000,000 worth of burrs imported every year. The imports equal the domestic production.

Friday, December 7, 1951   

Re: 

RETAIL FOOD DISTRIBUTORS IAC Barkley-OPS-GPR-1089 

The Retail Food Distributors Industry Advisory Committee today proposed that Office of Price Stabilization ceiling price markups on groceries be adjusted to permit the Nation's half million retail grocers to realize an increase of two percent in their overall margin on grocery sales. 

Members of the committee told the agency at a meeting called by OPS that the markups now provided in the retail grocery ceiling price regulations, CPR 15 and CPR 16, are inadequate in the face of present operating costs and that thousands of grocers are being squeezed.

OPS officials told the committeemen that an overall markup survey is to get underway the first of next year to determine whether the grocery ceiling price regulations have had an adverse effect on the earnings of grocers, or whether in some cases they are too high. 

The committee was informed that the agency must have a factual picture of conditions under the regulations before any adjustment procedure can be under

In the meantime, OPS has proposed that an interim study be made to determine what emergency relief, if any is shown to be justified, could be granted. 

Agency officials were told by committeemen that the large volume stores, which have smaller markups than low volume stores, were in the worst squeeze because, they said, their markups are too low on many lines of food items. 

Committeemen said many low volume stores, with the higher markups, also were being squeezed. They explained this by saying that while the large volume stores are mostly able to get their markups because of lower sales prices, low volume stores, in many cases, are unable to get theirs because they have to compete with the selling prices of the large volume stores. 

They suggested that the squeeze which the grocers complained of, could be remedied by increasing the markups of the large volume stores. If this were done, committeemen said, the big food stores could raise their prices and the low volume stores realize their present margins and still compete pricewise with the large volume stores. 

The meeting was the third consecutive session this week between OPS officials and members of the food distributive advisory committees. 

The three committees were called in by OPS to review the impact of the regulations on the three branches of the trade-- wholesalers, institutional wholesalers and retailers. 

GPO-O-OPS 1381

Wholesalers met with agency officials Wednesday, Dec. 5, and the Institutional Wholesalers were heard Thursday, Dec. 6.

Differentials would be provided for extra lengths, including switch ties, and for various services such as loading, handling, stacking, drying and other particulars.

Browne-OPS-GPR-1092  

Re: BUTTONS SUBCOMMITTEE OF THE PLASTIC PRODUCTS LAC Members of the Buttons Subcommittee of the Plastic Products Industry Advisory 

Committee, at their second meeting with Office of Price Stabilization officials today, asked that OPS exempt plastic buttons from price control.

OPS officials stated that they would give consideration to any reasons the industry could present on behalf of decontrol, but that to date no decontrol of complete industries had been justified.

Plastic buttons are used on men's shirts, women's blouses, and children's clothing. Plastic button manufacturers, some of whom manufacture pearl buttons as well, currently price under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, (GCPR.)

Possibility of issuance of a tailored regulation was discussed. Four committee members said they will submit cost data by the end of next week to assist OPS in preparing such a regulation. Possible base periods were discussed. 

OPS officials declined to commit the agency either to a recommendation for decontrol, or for a tailored regulation. Subcommittee members, however, said that, pending an OPS decision, they will file under Ceiling Price Regulation 22, the general manufacturers' regulation, before its effective date, December 19, but expressed hope that OPS would act fast enough to eliminate the need of putting 

CPR 22 prices into effect.

Two committee members suggested that, pending issuance of a tailored regulation, plastic button makes be granted coverage under Supplementary Regulation 12 to CPR 

22. SR 12 is a "postponement" or "interim" type regulation, and relieves manufacturers from making computations under CPR 22 when a tailored regulation is in the making. 

OPS representatives gave no encouragement to the committee that this could be done, because SR 12 has been restricted to industries where tailored regulations are in process.

The subcommittee asked that a tailored regulation set ceiling prices as close to GCPR prices as possible. They said CPR 22 will work hardship on the industry, since, under this regulation, rollbacks to distressed prices would be inevitable. 

Button manufacturers said they are currently selling close to GCPR ceilings. 

They contended that the cause of over-capacity. cic button is in a distressed state, largely be- 

Production zoomed during World War II, stimulated by defense orders, they said, but new firms entered the manufacturing field. The result is a disproportionate supply of plastc butons. (Over) GPO-O-OPS 1392

Subcommittee members explained that they seek decontrol of buttons because the industry is "unimportant," "dollars-and-cents-wise", to the national economy. 

OPS officials asked the industry members whether, if the plastic button industry is decontrolled, other segments of the plastics industry might seek similar decontrol. Re: EFFECTIVE DATES OF CPR 22 AND CPR 30: NO EXTENSION 

There will be no further extension of the mandatory effective date of Ceiling 

Price Regulations 22 and 30, Office of Price Stabilization Director Michael V.

DiSalle said today. As scheduled, these regulations will become fully effective on Wednesday, December 19, 1951.

Mr. DiSalle made the statement in answer to rumors, current in the trade, that a further extension was being considered. 

CPR 22 is the manufacturers' general ceiling price regulation issued last April, covering many durables, such as furniture, household appliances, hardware and hand tools, many processed foods, chemicals, rubber products and other manufactured goods.

CPR 30, the machinery order, governs ceilings on many automotive and truck parts, aircraft parts, machinery of all kinds, farm equipment, fabricated structural steel shapes and bars and similar products. 

The effective dates of the two regulations have been postponed several times-first because manufacturers felt they had not had enough time to make their calculations of ceilings, and then because of uncertainties connected with the delay in passage of the amended Defense Production Act. Then, on November 9, OPS 

announced that all affected manufacturers will have to price under the regulations by December 19. 

"These regulations have existed since last spring," Mr. DiSalle said, "and manufacturers have known all along that a mandatory effective date was in prospect. 

We believe that all affected businesses have had ample time to make their calculations, especially since the first extension was granted only two days before all filings were due. Since it is imperative, in the development of a sound stabilization program, that the regulations become fully effective, we will make no further extension. 

The reporting form used in both regulations--Form 8--must be on file with OPS by December 19."

Mr. DiSalle pointed out that he was speaking only of ceiling price calculations made in normal course, and not of calculations, filed on Form 100, based on 

It is optional the so-called Capehart amendment to the Defense Production Act.

Re: Barkley-OPS-GPR-1095  

CANNERS BORROWED CEILINGS (CPR's 55 & 56, Interpretation 1--Recalculation of Ceiling Prices under Section 4, as Amended) 

The Office of Price Stabilization ruled today that certain fruit and vegetable canners subject to the amended Sec. 4 of Ceiling Price Regulations 55 and 

56 must recalculate their ceiling prices, including canners who formerly used borrowed or individually authorized ceilings. 

The OPS ruling was made in an interpretation issued by OPS Chief Counsel, Harold Leventhal, to clear up doubts existing in the industry as to whether recalculation was required.

As originally issued, the regulations allowed canners selling items not sold during the base period to borrow prices or to apply for individually authorized ceiling prices where they were unable to determine a price under the basic provisions of the regulations. Subsequently, Sec. 4 of the regulations was amended to provide pricing methods that eliminated in nearly every case the necessity for borrowing ceiling prices or securing individual authorizations. 

Mr. Leventhal ruled today that processors who used borrowed or individually authorized ceilings before October 20, 1951, the effective date of the amendments, together with those who priced under Sec. 4 before the amendment, must recalculate their ceilings. # # # # # # GPO-0-OPS 1411

Re: OPHTHALMIC GOODS MANUFACTURERS LAC Members of the Ophthalmic Goods Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee, at their first meeting with Office of Price Stabilization officials today, said they did not believe that a tailored regulation, at the manufacturers' level, is required for their industry at the present time.

These manufacturers' current ceilings are governed either by the General

Committee members cited several reasons why they do not believe a tailored regulation is necessary. The ophthalmic industry, they said, is highly competitive, and profits have been fragmentary. They added that they are getting along well under present ceiling regulations, but asked whether, in the event no tailored regulation is issued, they might later seek adjustments for relief. 

OPS officials said that a further meeting of the committee could be called at the request of any three members of the committee.

Labor costs were described by members as the greatest problem presently facing the industry. One committee member described recurring wage increases as a "creeping paralysis." (Over) Several members posed the direct question as to whether they would receive more benefits under a tailored regulation than under CPR 22.

OPS officials said this could not be guaranteed, but that generally it was doubtful.

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers THURSDAY, December 13, 1951 

Re: 

McClanahan-OPS-GPR-1097

DISALLE STATEMENT AT COMPLETION OF ONE YEAR AS PRICE STABILIZATION DIRECTOR 

The following statement on his first year as Director of Price Stabilization was issued last night (Wednesday, December 12) by Michael V. DiSalle. 

Mr. DiSalle was sworn into the price stabilization post December 12, 1950.

Today marks one year since I was sworn in as Director of Price Stabilization. It certainly seems longer. It gives me an occasion for expressing my gratitude to the thousands of people who have worked so hard in spite of many obstacles to make this a real program. 

Looking back, it has been a job marked with many periods of frustration, many days when I felt that I could not go on another day; but just when it looked darkest encouragement would come with a new indication of support from people in Government, from consumers, from the President, from Members of Congress, and one could go on to do another day's work. 

It has been an enjoyable year from the standpoint of feeling that there has been accomplishment. Occasionally, I have gotten a critical letter from some person who felt I was not taking the job seriously enough. Actually, there has never been once that I did not realize the seriousness of the responsibility. I just refused to take myself seriously, since I realized that the man who held the office was a very expendable person, and that it was the job that had to be done that was important and not the person who was doing it. No person not having had the opportunity of living with the job could possibly realize how many times a smile or a quip covered a heartache or a feeling of great frustration.

But it has been a splendid experience of twelve months of working with people, a great experience in finding thousands upon thousands of loyal Americans who placed the welfare of their Nation ahead of what might be their own immediate gain. Certainly we have had disagreements with business men and with Members of Congress, but, on the whole, disagreements have been resolved for the welfare of the country. 

There is a great deal to be said on the side of those people who have a basic objection to controls, and yet I have felt quite sincerely that the fight against inflation could not succeed without direct controls. It has been a heart-warming experience to meet with a great many people who, though GPO-O-OPS 1416

fundamentally opposed to controls, yet realize that they are the law of the land and, consequently, are willing to cooperate in an effort to make those controls work.

It has been a twelve months' period that I would not possibly want to relive, for the strain, the pressures and the operation of special groups have created tremendous difficulties. Yet, it has been a twelve months' experience that I would not trade for any other. For these past twelve months have demonstrated again how a democratic nation can, within the framework of government, organize its resources for the benefit of its citizens.

In order to insure that the emergency production effort would not materially damage the Nation's economy, the Production Act provided the power to establish certain controls to be used in the fight against inflation. After much debate and expression of differing views, which are so much a part of a democracy, a price freeze was issued on January 26. The effect was immediately to arrest the psychological factors that were at work, that had driven up the cost of living in the United States more than 8 percent in only seven months. The latest BLS figures indicate that the rise in the last nine months has been held to less than 2 percent. 

A good many people were injured by the effects of the rapid 8 percent rise, and many of them have not been able to completely recover. However, today we have a stabilization program which is better organized than ever before. There is every hope that a complete structure will soon be in place to resist successfully the inflationary pressures that will continue to develop as our defense effort continues to expand. 

The Defense Production Act of 1950 provided the means by which our Government could gear its productive facilities for the great defense effort that became so obviously necessary as a result of the invasion of Korea. 

The work that has been done over the past year in putting together an organization and developing a program will stand the Nation in good stead. 

True, there are still many rough spots; there are still many areas in which work has to be done; but the future of stabilization looks good. 

We cannot overlook the fact pointed out this week by the Defense Department that billions of dollars have been lost as a result of increases in prices. We cannot overlook the fact that the Office of Defense Mobilization estimates that defense production will rise steadily from the present $2 billion a month now being spent to the $4 billion a month contemplated for 1953.

Much of the buying power of these projected expenditures will be dissipated unless the stabilization program is fully developed. 

There are several factors that stand in the way of a complete job:

(1) The necessity for absorbing the price increases resulting from the 1951 amendments to the Defense Production Act. A good many of these increases are, in my opinion, unjustifiable. Since they were provided for by law, they must be allowed. Offsetting this particular difficulty is the fact that for those cost increases occurring after July 26, the OPS is in a position to require reasonable cost absorption. (2) The parity provision of the Act makes it impossible to impose ceilings on agricultural commodities before those commodities reach parity. This, combined with increases in costs occurring at the distributive levels, still makes our food problem a most difficult one. On the brighter side is the progress that has been made in the stabilization of meat prices and the prospects for betterment in that area. (3) Since world prices in many fields are much higher than domestic prices, the necessity for importing strategic items at these higher prices will have to be reflected in a good many areas of production. On the brighter side is the growing realization that the free nations of the world must work together in allocating these necessary materials and the attempts that are being made to work out equitable price relationships. (4) Some adjustments are necessary in a fast moving economy to compensate for weather conditions, droughts, other natural phenomena, but these, all told, will have no significant effect on the general level of prices. Once we have made the adjustments necessary under the new Act there is every reason to believe that we can have effective stabilization.

Whatever has been accomplished has been accomplished as the result of a great many hours of hard work by a good many conscientious employees, as a result of a great deal of cooperation from the consumer, agriculture and business. Thousands of people have contributed advice and hard labor in putting together the program.

There have been a great many misunderstandings in the course of the year, but generally there has been fine support for the program. There has been a great deal of encouragement from people in all segments of society both verbally and by mail. There has been an excellent realization of the need for the program, even though there hasn't been as complete an understanding as desired of the reasons why some of the actions had to be taken. 

With increased citizen understanding of the whys and wherefores of it, the price program can continue to develop as an integral part of the Nation's over-all mobilization program.

WEDNESDAY, December 12, 1951 

Re: 

 CONSTRUCTION MACHINERY SALES, SERVICE & RENTAL LAC Members of the Construction Machinery Sales, Service and Rental Industry 

Advisory Committee met for the first time yesterday with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems. Scott-OPS-GPR-1099  

OPS officials outlined for the committee the general provisions of the forthcoming ceiling price regulation (CPR 105) covering sales of used industrial and construction machinery which becomes effective on December 17. 

In general, CPR 105 establisnes ceiling prices for used equipment on the basis of a percentage of manufacturers' current published list prices for the same or comparable new equipment. Ceilings for "rebuilt and guaranteed" equipment are set at 85 percent of such list prices and, in the case of equipment which is sold "as is" and not rebuilt and guaranteed, the percentage rate is 55 percent. Also, a depreciation method of determining ceilings is provided. 

Consensus of the committee was that the spread between the ceilings for "rebuilt and guaranteed" equipment and "as is" equipment, as applied to used construction machinery, is not sufficient and that the ceilings on "as is" equipment will have the effect of putting a floor as well as a ceiling on prices for such equipment. Also, industry members said that ceilings set for rebuilt and guaranteed equipment is somewhat low. 

It was suggested that current freight costs be added to published list prices for new equipment before applying the percentage rates for determining ceilings for used equipment. Members said that in many cases freight cost is a substantial part of the total delivered cost of new equipment and that the delivered cost of new equipment should be reflected in the ceilings for used equipment.

The committee expressed the opinion that ceilings for "as is" equipment could well be dispensed with and that then the ceilings for rebuilt and guaranteed equipment would have the effect of permitting prices for "as is" equipment to seek a proper market level in relation to the ceilings for rebuilt and guaranteed equipment. They said that, generally speaking, there is an ample supply of new equipment on the market and that consequently there is little, if any, need for controlling prices for "as is" equipment. 

OPS officials said that such a basis for controlling prices for all used construction machinery would not be feasible. 

Some members of the committee suggested that "as is" equipment might be broken down into two or more categories as to age, condition, etc. (Over) GPO-O-OPS 1420

. 

Committeemen said the guarantee of 90 days on rebuilt and guaranteed equipment as provided for under CPR 105 is too long a period of time. They pointed out that 30 days is the period generally used by the construction industry as a guarantee on rebuilt construction machinery. 

The committee reviewed industry pricing practices with respect to charges for rental of construction machinery, and said that, in general, prevailing rental charges in the industry are too low in relationship to the cost of new equipment. 

They suggested that some upward adjustment of rental rates be affected in order to keep the rental business on a sound basis. Rentals, they pointed out, represent a substantial and important part of the construction machinery industry and permit maximum use and availability of equipment. 

The committee asked that OPS consider the advisability of issuing a tailored pricing regulation covering sales of used construction machinery, designed to fit the pricing practices and conditions existing in the industry, and also, that a tailored dollars-and-cents pricing regulation be developed covering rental charges for construction machinery.

A subcommittee was appointed to advise further with OPS in this connection.

CAMELBACK AND TIRE REPAIR MATERIALS IAC Members of the Camelback and Tire Repair Materials Industry Advisory

1, to the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, effective

Re: FRESH VEGETABLE GROWER-SHIPPER IAC

Friday, December 14, 1951 

Re: 

  Eastern Central Motor Carriers Rate Case 

The Office of Price Stabilization, through its Director, Michael V. DiSalle, yesterday, December 13, filed with the Interstate Commerce Commission a protest against and a request for suspension of motor carrier rate increases of 9 percent for carriers operating between the New England and Middle Atlantic States and the Middle West. The increases, to become effective December 24, were proposed by the 

Eastern Central Motor Carriers Association. 

GPO-O-OPS 1441 OPS said that the 915 carriers involved have not demonstrated a need for a 9 percent increase and asked that public hearings be held before any increase is granted. The Agency also asked for an opportunity to participate in the hearings. 

A study by OPS of operating costs of a large group of the carriers, in relation to their income, reveals that a 9 percent increase would reduce their operrating ratio from 95.37 percent to 87.50 percent in the case of 46 single line carriers and from 94.87 percent to 87.04 percent in the case of 442 Class I carriers. OPS said that this would put the carriers in a far better profit position than the Commission has recognized as "reasonable" on numerous occasions. 

The proposed increase would have a significant impact on the national economy, OPS pointed out, since the 442 Class I carriers under study received 51.21 percent of the total operating revenues for Class I motor carriers in the United States during the second quarter of 1951.

Increased freight rates granted the motor carriers would be reflected in the cost to consumers of the commodities they carry and hence in the general cost of living, OPS maintained.

Saturday, December 15, 1951

Re: CANNED MEAT AND DRY SAUSAGE 

The Office of Price Stabilization today announced that it soon will revise the ceiling price regulation for sterile canned meat, the type most commonly found on grocery shelves, and for dry sausage, sausage that has been air dried.

Barkley-OPS-GPR-1103 

The revision will revoke the pricing method presently in effect under this regulation, Supplementary Regulation 15 to the Manufacturers General Ceiling Price Regulation, CPR 22, and again make ceiling price provisions of CPR 

22 applicable to canned meat and dry sausage.

OPS said SR 15 ceilings had never been made mandatory and many canned meat manufacturers had continued to price under the General Ceiling Price Regulation. After issuance of the regulation last August, a substantial segment OPS of the industry said they found its pricing formula unsuitable to them. now feels it desirable to let the manufacturers price under CPR 22, where they were originally placed, until a regulation more directly tailored for this segment of the industry can be issued.

OPS said the action would result in slight ceiling price increases of those manufacturers who had not adopted ceilings under CPR 22 before June 30.

The Consumer Advisory Committee of the Office of Price Stabilization was assured at a meeting Friday by Price Stabilization Director Michael V. The Committee approved recommendations drawn up at a recent joint meeting of its Policy and Regulations Subcommittee and its Steering Committee. 

Among these recommendations was the suggestion that "community dollar and cents pricing be established as soon as possible so that the consumer may be aware of ceiling prices and so can participate effectively in the Stabilization Program and help hold the line if and when anticipated greater inflationary pressures develop." 

A further recommendation was that "community pricing be put into effect for a selected list of (grocery) items in selected areas and where the regional director has a special interest in the program. The data presented to the Committee would seem to indicate that a detailed study would show certain items where market prices and ceiling prices are sufficiently close to permit community pricing." 

Mr. DiSalle told members of the committee that a major problem of OPS is lack of public understanding of the complexities of price controls and of the limitations upon such a program. 

Committee members said that this might well be a function of local consumer committees, which, working through member organizations, could disseminate information about the program. 

The absence of such committees weakens the controls program, committee members said, and makes it difficult for consumers to participate. 

Mr. DiSalle said that community participation programs are under consideration by OPS. However, he stressed the difficulty of getting people to serve on voluntary committees and participate in a sustained program. 

Reference was made to the problem of low-end merchandise, which members of the committee said may be taken off the market entirely or may be subject to an increase in price. Mrs. Chase Going Woodhouse, special assistant to Mr. DiSalle and chairman of the meeting, said she would try to arrange a report on the problem, which also is of concern to OPS, for the mext meeting. Franz B. Wolf, Director, Research and Statistics Division of the OPS Office of Economic Policy, spoke on the relationship between OPS ceiling prices and current market prices, which in many commodities are lower than ceiling prices.

PRESS RELEASE    MONDAY, December 17, 1951 

Barkley-OPS-GPR-1106  

Re: CORN TAC 

Members of the Corn Industry Advisory Committee today expressed preference for a dollars-and-cents ceiling price regulation for corn should the price of this important grain crop reach a level that would make necessary the imposition of controls by the Office of Price Stabilization. 

OPS officials, meeting with members of the Committee, outlined two alternatives which could be used in the event of controls. 

One would be the dollars-and-cents approach. The other would be the freeze technique by removing corn from the parity exempt list of agricultural commodities in the General Ceiling Price Regulation. Under the latter method, prices which sellers could legally receive would be frozen at the highest prices they received during the five weeks immediately preceding imposition of control.

Committee members said they believed it would be impossible for the industry to operate under a freeze technique since sellers would have different ceiling prices. Such a system, they contended, would stop all trading. 

OPS spokesmen informed the industry representatives that the agency is of the opinion that it will be more practical to issue a tailored regulation. 

They are working towards this end, should it become necessary to place ceiling prices on corn. 

As of November 15, corn, the major feed grain for livestock and poultry, was selling at 92 percent of parity. OPS cannot impose ceilings on any agricultural commodity at less than 100 percent of parity or a specified legal minimum. OPS officials said, however, that the agency is maintaining a constant check on corn prices and is ready to act if and when, in the agency's judgment, ceilings become necessary. 

The agency is using the corn regulation of the wartime Office of Price Administration as the starting point for drafting a new regulation. Officials said they thought it best to employ this old regulation, bringing it up-todate. It set specific ceiling prices on corn at country shipper points and at the various distributive levels, authorizing allowances for the moist condition of the grain, shrinkage, premiums and discounts. 

OPS officials said any proposed ceiling price for the current crop would take into full consideration the proper relationship between the price of corn and its value as a feed for livestock and poultry.

Representing OPS at the meeting were Francis C. Jones, Assistant Director, Food and Restaurant Division; A. H. Krueger, Acting Chief, Grains Branch;

PRESS RELEASE    MONDAY, December 17, 1951 

Re: 

MIXED FERTILIZERS TAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-1107  

Recommendation that no attempt be made to prepare a tailored regulation for their industry for the 1952 season, because the season shipments already have begun, was made today by members of the Mixed Fertilizers Industry Advisory Committee at their third meeting with OPS officials.

They said the industry would be satisfied to price during 1952 as is now their choice, either under the Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regu lation, CPR 22, or the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR. Manufacturers of mixed fertilizers have the option of remaining indefinitely under GCPR by the provisions of Supplementary Regulation 12 to CPR 22, pending issuance of a tailored regulation for the industry. 

Last August the committee said CPR 22 prices were satisfactory, but expressed a desire for a tailored regulation that would take into consideration prospective additional increases in the cost of their materials and freight. 

OPS initiated a survey in line with the committee's suggestions and sent questionnaires to 325 plants selling mixed fertilizers and bagged superphosphates. 

The survey contemplated taking weighted averages of the highest prices occuring during the year ending June 30, 1950, in 49 so-called sub-areas, and adjusting them to reflect cost increases since that period up to September 30, 1951. 

At today's meeting, sample computations from the survey for New England and Alabama were discussed by the committee. It was found that these computations resulted in prices lower than many CPR 22 ceilings. 

The reason for this was attributable in part to the definition of base period raw materials costs and selling prices for mixed fertilizers in a manner different from CPR 22. The possibility was suggested that some producers in the industry did not fully understand the questionnaire, and had submitted incomplete reports.

This left the committee with the question whether it wanted the study continued. The committee proposed that the survey be dropped, at least for the present, since any changes in prices, now that the season is already begun, would adversely affect the industry as commitments are made months ahead. 

Committeemen said that prices higher than those produced by the study already were being quoted. OPS officials stressed that any attempt by manufacturers to reflect in their quotations recent increases in the cost of materials and freight, merely because these had been covered in the questionnaire, would be illegal. The highest prices which the industry could legally quote for immediate deliveries of mixed fertilizers, OPS officials said, were either the CPR 22 or GCPR ceilings, whichever they had elected to make effective. As to future deliveries, they may contract to sell at a fixed price or the ceiling price in effect at the time of delivery, whichever is (Over) GIO-O-OPS 1470

lower. In no event may a contract for future delivery require the payment of prices in excess of the ceilings in effect for the producer at the time the mixed fertilizers are delivered to the buyer. 

By Amendment 4 to SR 12, CPR 22, issued November 29, 1951, producers of mixed fertilizers were given the option of retaining GCPR ceilings for mixed fertilizers, even though other commodities which they manufacture must be priced under CPR 22 beginning December 19. OPS officials explained that this does not give producers the right to charge GCPR prices after December 19 for some grades of mixed fertilizers and CPR 22 prices for others. Instead, the producer must retain either GCPR for all mixed fertilizers as a group, or adopt CPR 22 prices for all. Where a producer has put CPR 22 into effect for mixed fertilizers prior to December 19, because that regulation, before the issuance of Amendment 4 to SR 12 made him price mixed fertilizers under CPR 22 if he elected it for other products, the producer may now revert to GCPR prices for mixed fertilizers as a whole. 

OPS representatives pointed out that manufacturers who were dissatisfied with the level of ceiling prices under either GCPR or CPR 22 could now apply for individual relief under the so-called Capehart formula. This could be done under Supplementary Regulations 17 or 18 if a manufacturer priced under 

CPR 22, or under General Overriding Regulations 20 or 21 if he priced under 

GCPR, they said.

  TUESDAY, December 18, 1951 

RE: Tempo E 

Washington FUTURES CONTRACTS DEFAULTS 

The Office of Price Stabilization has declined to modify an agency opinion that settlement prices for defaults on futures contracts in excess of the spot ceiling price for the commodity involved are not permissible. under the Defense 

Production Act, it was announced today.

Barkley-OPS-GPR-1108 

ST. 4200; Ext. 3491 

Modification of the ruling was requested by the Chicago Board of Trade, which proposed a settlement price of $79 a ton for defaulted contracts for delivery of soybean meal last November. The spot ceiling price for this commodity is $74 a ton, f.o.b., Decatur, Ill. 

In denying the request for modification, Harold Leventhal, OPS Chief

Counsel, in a letter to the Board's attorneys quoted from General Interpreta tion 1, issued last June 20, that Section 707 of the Defense Production Act precludes the establishment of a settlement price for default on futures contracts in excess of the spot ceiling price for the commodity involved. To require a person defaulting to pay damages based on a market value in excess of the ceiling price would be to assume as a basis for settlement an illegal market price, he declared.

Mr. Leventhal said section 707 was "an appropriate provision in the 

Defense Production Act since it tends to eliminate the inflationary impact resulting from the allowance in a tight market of prices above ceilings in the form of settlements."

He added that there might be some cases where the Board may require those defaulting on delivery under futures contracts to pay an amount equal to the special or consequential damages actually incurred and directly attributable to the default. In such cases there would have to be an actual showing of such damages. "This letter," wrote Mr. Leventhal, "sets forth what we consider to be the principles which should be applied as relevant principles of law by the representatives of the parties involved or by the appropriate forum or tribunal. 

OPS does not undertake to determine the application of these principles to the facts of each particular case."

A copy of Mr. Leventhal's letter to counsel for the Chicago Board of 

Trade is attached. GPO-O-OPS 1466 15838

DECEMBER 15, 1951 

Kirkland, Fleming, Green, Martin and Ellis, Esqs. 

33 North LaSalle Street 

Chicago 2, Illinois

Attention: 

Gentlemen: 

Bennett E. Bates, Esq.

At your request we have considered the settlement price proposed by the Board of Directors of the Chicago Board of Trade in its resolution of December 3, 1951, for defaulted contracts for delivery of soybean meal in November 1951. The price of $79.00 per ton proposed to be fixed is in excess of the ceiling price of $74.00 per ton, f.o.b. Decatur, Illinois, prescribed by Supple mentary Regulation 3 to the General Ceiling Price Regulation. 

is understood that the Chicago Board of Trade does not have a rule in effect fixing a predetermined amount as a penalty in the event of default. Such a rule, you have stated, might be in violation of the laws of the State of Illinois. It 

You have indicated that the proposed $79.00 settlement price takes into account the price for substitutable commodities which the "longs" would be required to buy to replace the undelivered soybean meal, as well as "the nature of the defaults and the extent of damages suffered by the buyers as a result thereof." 

It has been recognized by you that the contemplated action of the Chicago Board of Trade is inconsistent with General 

Interpretation 1, issued by the Chief Counsel of OPS on June 20, 1951. For that reason you have requested that this interpretation be modified so as not to preclude the Board from settling out defaults at a price in excess of the spot ceiling price for the commodity involved. 

In addition to the arguments advanced by you at our conference on December 6, we have considered carefully your brief dated September 6, 1951, which contends, among other things, that OPS ceiling prices have no applicability to the settlement price for defaulted futures contracts. 

It is our opinion, based on all the data, written and oral with which you have provided us, that General Interpretation 1 should not be so modified. As was stated in that interpretation: 

...section 707 of the Defense Production Act of 

1950 precludes the establishment of a settlement price for default on futures contracts in excess of (Over) 15838

the spot ceiling price for the commodity involved.

The legal maximum market value for the commodity is fixed by ceiling price regulations. To require a defaulting seller to pay damages based on a market value in excess of the ceiling price would be to assume as a basis for settlement an illegal market price.

In our view these considerations are equally applicable here. Section 707 prescribes a controlling principle which prohibits general use of a settlement price exceeding the ceiling price. This is an appropriate provision in the Defense Production 

Act since it tends to eliminate the inflationary impact resulting from the allowance in a tight market of prices above ceilings in the form of settlements.

There may be some cases where a court (or a commodity exchange or other tribunal) may require those defaulting on delivery under futures contracts to pay an amount equal to the special or consequential damages actually incurred and directly attributable to the default. This would not be inconsistent with General Interpretation 1 because the doctrine of special or consequential damages is not predicated on the market value of the commodity. However, the application of this doctrine would, of course, depend upon an actual showing of such damages.

This letter sets forth what we consider to be the principles which should be applied as relevant principles of law by the representatives of the parties involved or by the appropriate forum or tribunal. OPS does not undertake to determine the application of these principles to the facts of each particular case. 

Sincerely yours, /S/ Harold Leventhal

TUESDAY, December 18, 1951 

Re: 

  

Scott-OPS-GPR-1114  

INDUSTRIAL DIAMOND IMPORTERS & MANUFACTURERS TAC The Industrial Diamond Importers and Manufacturers Industry Advisory Commit tee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems. 

Industrial diamonds are used primarily as cutting or abrasive agents, and their principal classifications are as follows: Core drilling stones; grinder stones; tool stones; grinding wheel dressers; shaping, boring and turning tools; elongated stones; flats; die stones; indenters; ballas; carbons; and crushing bort. 

Imported industrial diamonds are covered by the imports ceiling price regulation CPR 31, which, generally speaking, establishes ceiling prices on the basis of a commodity's landed cost plus the same dollars-and-cents markup obtained on deliveries between July 1, 1949, and June 30, 1950.

The committee discussed the situation with respect to prices for imported crushing bort. Crushing bort is a material consisting of imperfectly crystallized or coarse diamonds, or fragments made in cutting good diamonds.

At the present time there is a serious shortage of crushing bort, which is used extensively as an abrasive dust in wheels, for die-making, diamond-set shaping tools, for cutting precious stones and in some drills. 

It was pointed out by OPS that tool makers and die makers are complaining that they are not getting sufficient bort to meet their needs and, in many instances, they are paying prices well above normal levels. Approximately 95 percent of the total world production of industrial diamonds is marketed by a foreign syndicate which fixes the price. Accordingly, the difference between the landed and the selling price to the user (including markup) is readily ascertainable.

The larger manufacturers get an allotment from the syndicate, but the smaller ones must buy in the open market at reportedly exorbitant prices.

OPS officials discussed with the committee the feasibility of setting dollars-and-cents ceilings for importers and sellers of imported diamonds, and the committee reviewed industry pricing practices in this connection.

Re: LEATHER IAC 

A proposed bovine leather regulation under which tanners will base their new ceilings on recent hides ceiling rollbacks, but may reflect increased labor and materials costs as of July 31, 1951, was discussed at a Leather Industry Advisory Committee meeting today with the Office of Price Stabilization. 

The proposed regulation, to be made effective 45 days after issuance, will cover tanners' sales of bovine leather and unfinished splits, produced in this country from domestic and imported cattle hides, kips and calfskins. Separate regulations will cover contract tanners of leather, finished splits, cut stock and leather finishing services.

Major objection on the part of committee members to the proposed regulation was to the base period to be used in determining a tanner's average markup factor to be applied to tannery cost for each type of leather. OPS proposed use of three consecutive fiscal years within the periods January 1, 1947, to June 30, 1951, as the base period. Committee members recommended that the base period include some part of 1946 when the tanners' profit position was substantially better than in the years following.

Committee members also objected to use of the first half of 1950 for determining selling expense, as proposed by OPS, and recommended use of a fiscal year rather than a six months period. OPS indicated it would consider this recommendation.

Committee members further recommended that the year 1951 be used as a base for figuring each tanner's yield factor instead of the year 1950, as proposed by OPS. OPS representatives expressed the opinion that the industry might find fewer distortions through the use of 1950 but agreed that some provision might be made in the proposed order for review of yield factors from time to time. 

Designed to conform as closely as possible tò customary pricing practices in the tanning industry, the proposed order would result in the determination of an average price for each type of leather. This average price would be employed in the preparation of a price list of ceiling prices for the leather items. This average price will be obtained by adding to a constructed January- 

June, 1950, average price, certain increases in costs from that period to June 1951. 

Presiding at today's meeting of the Leather Industry Advisory Committee was 

Dickson S. Stauffer, Chief, Hides, Leather and Shoes Branch, Consumer Soft Goods

Division, OPS. 

Members of the Leather Industry Advisory Committee are: (Over) GPO-O-OPS 1479 15916

Washington Re: OPS FIRST STEEL DRUM CASE Cole-OPS-GPR-1116 

In the first case involving the steel drum industry, the B & F Cooperage Company, Trenton Avenue and Rush Street, Philadelphia, was placed under injunction to comply with the regulations of the Office of Price Stabilization, in the United States District Court, Eastern District of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia this afternoon.

A consent decree was filed in the OPS injunctive action before Federal Judge James P. McGranery. The cooperage firm and its owner, John Joseph Butler, were charged with violating Ceiling Price Regulation 36, requiring firms in that business to maintain for OPS inspection records of prices paid for materials as well as prices charged customers.

Specifically, the firm which conditions used steel drums for reuse, was charged with failure to issue invoices to customers stating types of drums sold, delivery charges, quantities, prices charged, and whether the drums were raw or reconditioned. The firm was also charged with failing to secure invoices on 

Edward P. Morgan, OPS Enforcement Director, stated in Washington that the

Philadelphia case is the first of several which are under investigation as a result of the failure of some members of the steel drum industry to comply with 

OPS regulations. 

Mr. Morgan pointed out that maintenance of complete records is required by 

OPS and is necessary for determination of compliance. OPS, he said, will also vigorously enforce the price schedules provided under CPR 36.

Re: FISHING TACKLE MANUFACTURERS IAC Members of the Fishing Tackle Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee, at their first meeting today with Office of Price Stabilization officials, explored the possibility that a tailored ceiling price regulation may be issued covering the 25,000 or more items the industry produces. 

The chairman of the meeting, J. Hepner Randolph, Jr., Chief of the Housewares and Accessories Branch, Consumer Durable Goods Division, OPS, appointed a subcommittee of three to study the situation. The sub-committee will meet here at a later date not yet named.

Consensus of the IAC group was that the fishing tackle industry should be decontrolled. The industry has been pricing under the General Ceiling Price Control regulation (GCPR), or CPR 22, the general manufacturers' regulation. Committee members cited among their complaints against control what they called burdensome reporting requirements, the difficulty in establishing prices for new commodities, and the problem of keeping low price items in production. 

OPS officials said that, while the decontrol plea of the fishing tackle manufacturers would be given consideration, they could hold out little hope that the industry would be decontrolled.

Committee members said they had all filed under Ceiling Price Regulation 22, December 19 is the mandatory effective date of CPR 22. They said that, with the exception of reels, which are pushing ceilings, most of the other items they produce are selling below ceilings. Because of competition, and a soft market, most committee members declared, they do not currently take advantage of increases permitted under CPR 22.

The industry makes flies and lures, leaders and leader material, snaps and swivels, hooks, rods, lines, reels, complete fly casting outfits, landing nets and accessories.

Committee members discussed application of Section 43 to CPR 7, the industry's retail regulation, under which some of the manufacturers have filed. Section 43, now undergoing revision by OPS, covers uniform pricing, pre-ticketing of merchandise and covers situations where manufacturers historically have suggested prices that retailers and wholesalers shall charge for their branded articles. 

Pre-ticketing, they contended, is impractical for their industry because of the minute size of thousands of their products, such as hooks, flies and lures. addition, they said, pre-ticketing imposes a great burden of expense. In (over) GPO-O-OPS 1493

OPS òfficials explained that the agency feels strongly about pre-ticketing requirements, because they are the "heart and soul" of Section 43. 

Urging decontrol, some committee members predicted that a tight market resulting from material shortages would force low-end merchandise off the market. 

They declared that manufacturers then would turn to higher-priced merchandise because of greater profits. Some manufacturers have already done so because of increased material costs. 

OPS officials expressed concern at possible loss of lower priced items and asked whether incentive adjustments would prevent this. Committee members expressed the opinion that competition would result in effective price control. 

The consumer, they said, is the best price controller. OPS officials stated that the agency is not receptive to general price decontrol, and that only a few items, minor in their impact on the national economy, have been exempted. Early 1952, they said, will have a great inflation potential, with materials short in supply. For this reason, controls other than indirect controls, are necessary. OPS officials then explained the advantages of a tailored ceiling price regulation.

Re: WILSON SUBSIDIARIES PROTESTS DENIED Michael V. DiSalle, Director of the Office of Price Stabilization, has denied the protest of five wholly-owned subsidiaries of Wilson & Co., Inc., one of the nation's largest slaughterers, to their classification by OPS as combination distributors and not as hotel supply houses. 

Filing protests with OPS were Davidson Meat Co., Inc., of Chicago and Los 

Angeles; Gotham Hotel Supply Co., Inc., of New York City; Williams Meat Co., Inc., of Kansas City; Jepsen Hotel Supply Co. of Washington, D. C., and Ed Heuck Co.,

Inc., of San Francisco. 

Each of the Wilson subsidiaries prepares and prefabricates beef cuts which it sells along with other meat and food products to hotels, restaurants and others. 

Such sales are subject to Ceiling Price Regulation 24. Under this regulation these firms being wholly-owned subsidiaries of a large slaughterer must use price schedule II (b) for combination distributors. The firms have been pricing their prefabricated meat cuts under schedule II (a) for independent hotel supply houses, which permits roughly a three per cent greater markup than schedule II (b) for combination distributors.

The OPS regulation does not permit wholly-owned subsidiaries to qualify as hotel supply houses because savings effected all along the line as a result of their affiliation do not entitle them to Schedule II (a) higher prices. CPR 24 is written to preserve the normal distribution channels in the meat industry and thus guarantee availability to the housewife of beef at the lowest possible prices. 

Traditionally, according to OPS statistics, independent hotel supply houses have received a higher markup than affiliated combination distributors. 

In denying the protest of the Wilson subsidiaries and upholding the right of the Director of OPS to classify such firms as combination distributors instead of as independent hotel supply houses, Director DiSalle leaves the way open for petitions for reconsideration filed for the purpose of challenging and rebutting data compiled by OPS. Such petitions, he pointed out, must be filed within 30 days of the denial order date of December 19.

Still pending before the United States District Court in the District of Columbia is the OPS test case against the Jepsen firm which has now been set for a hearing on January 9. It is an injunctive action brought to restrain alleged continuing violations. This case involves the same contentions as those in the 

Wilson subsidiaries' protests now denied by Director DiSalle. In the enforcement case, OPS alleges that the pricing practice of the Jepsen firm has caused higher prices in restaurants and hotels serviced by the firm. GPO-O-OPS 1499

OPS AND DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE AGREEMENT ON COST CURBS FOR MILITARY CONTRACTS 

Details of the recent agreement between the Office of Price Stabilization and the Munitions Board, covering the broad problem of military procurement pricing, and designed to obtain the greatest possible value for the defense dollar, was announced today.

The agreement was explained in a joint statement issued by the agencies, and is implemented in an exchange of correspondence between Michael V. DiSalle, Director, Office of Price Stabilization, and J. D. Small, Chairman, Munitions 

Board.

The understanding was based on the present plan to continue the present broad exemption program under which certain strictly military items have been free from price ceilings since February 1951. It is considered undesirable during the present period to impose price ceilings on such items if reasonable prices can be maintained through military contracting and pricing methods. "We do not look upon this as a departure from price control, but rather as the substitution of a price control method better tailored to the conditions and circumstances under which some military goods are priced," Mr. DiSalle said. 

The understanding provides for creation of a small, inter-agency committee for the consideration of pricing and re-pricing policies, procedures and practices at all military procurement levels. OPS, officials will also visit military procurement offices to review contract pricing and re-pricing. Recommendations will be made from time to time by OPS to the proper procurement officials in connection with such pricing and re-pricing. 

The Department of Defense has also agreed to supply OPS with information and data on the pricing aspects of the Department of Defense procurement programs. 

Director DiSalle pointed out that the OPS would "necessarily reserve the right to reconsider any exemptions or suspensions of military items from ceiling price regulations if experience should prove this to be desirable." 

Correspondence between Director DiSalle and Chairman Small establishes and understanding similar, in some respects, to that of the so-called Henderson- Patterson-Forrestal Agreement of World War II. OPS noted, however, that the present understanding provides a basis for supplying the Office of Price Stabilization with considerably more thorough information or procurement pricing and re-pricing than was made available to the price control agency during World War II. This is because the present understanding provides for collaboration in the review of procurement pricing and re-pricing policies, procedures and practices, as well as statistical data on prices and costs. (Over) GPO-O-OPS 1504

ܝ 

OPS pointed out that Section 401 of the Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended, declares the Congressional intent to be "to assure that defense appropriations are not dissipated by excessive costs and prices." 

Therefore, in a letter to Chairman Small, dated December 7, 1951, Director DiSalle wrote that "we have felt the need for a means of assuring the OPS of the effectiveness of procurement pricing and re-pricing methods in achieving the stabilization objectives of the Defense Production Act, especially for military items exempted from ceiling price regulations." 

Director DiSalle continued: 

"As the military procurement program swings into high gear and inflationary pressures increase, the need for the very best defense contract pricing increases. A slight reduction in average prices paid for defense goods could not only save billions of dollars over a period of several years, but, more importantly, would result in the obtaining of more implements of national security for the dollars spent. "In fact, it is perhaps the only means of reconciling budgetary economy and maximum national security. This point has been reflected in statements by the Secretary of Defense regarding the effects of inflation upon defense appropriations. Close contract pricing also provides incentive for efficient use of materials, manpower, and other resources in short supply." 

The committee being formed by OPS will concern itself with the pricing of defense goods, basic, intermediate and finished. In addition to the 

Munitions Board, the Defense Production Administration, the Atomic Energy 

Commission and the General Services Administration are expected to name representatives. 

1 In connection with the visits proposed to be made to military procurement offices to review pricing practices and policies, Director DiSalle said: 

It seems to us that it would be logical and helpful for staff members of the Munitions Board to join with OPS staff members in making such visits. 

The Office of Price Stabilization feels that it must have the right to recommend procurement policies, procedures or practices which it deems essential to accomplish the objectives of the price stabilization program." 

OPS has already arranged a series of meetings, to be attended by its key personnel, at which representatives of the Department of Defense, including each of the three armed services, have been invided to explain and discuss military procurement pricing policies, procedures and practices. "It is felt," Director DiSalle added, "that such meetings will serve to orient both the price stabilization and the military agency staffs to their mutual advantage. 11

OPS said it would like to have the Department of Defense supply to it statistical data on the amount of procurement under each major type of contract; on prices for commercial-type items of military procurement; and on prices, costs, profit allowances, and explanations of trends therein, for a list of selected, representative, military-type end items, components, parts and subassemblies.

In his reply of December 14, 1951, Chairman Small of the Munitions Board declared that "we agree in the concept of collaborating with your agency in reviewing all aspects of the complex and vitally important problem of defense contract pricing and price regulation." "To this end," he continued, "we would welcome at any time suggestions or recommendations from you with respect to our own procurement pricing policies, procedures and practices as they may support the objectives of the price stabilization program. Furthermore, we will be glad to make available to the OPS information and data on the pricing aspects, including policies and procedures of the Department of Defense procurement programs. 

Chairman Small suggested, that in developing the need for, and making requests for data, OPS staff members should consult with Munitions Board and Military Department representatives, "so as to make certain that what you might desire will serve a useful purpose, and that we may avoid unnecessary administrative burdens upon the very busy and already overburdened staffs of the military departments. 

11 "Members of your (OPS) staff," Chairman Small wrote, "are more than welcome to visit our military procurement offices, observe the ways in which we conduct our purchasing and pricing activities, and submit directly to those offices or to me and the Munitions Board, any recommendations that your people may have with respect to improving our procurement pricing policies and practices, which I agree have a close and important bearing upon the entire price stablization program. 

11 Department of Defense officials indicated their full support of the price stabilization program and stated their desire to continue every effort, as in the past, to integrate with defense policies the policies promulgated by OPS in carrying out its responsibilities.
