WHOLESALE LAMB: CORRECTION 

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today that omission of a sub-head in the wholesale lamb ceiling price regulation (CPR 92) is being corrected as speedily as is mechanically possible.

In the printed copies of the regulation, issued November 8, the sub-head "hundredweight" was inadvertently omitted in Section 45, which enumerates dollarsand-cents additions that may be added to lamb ceiling prices for this type of meat packed in containers.

These dollar-and-cents additions are for hundred-pound sales of the products. 

They range from $1.80 a hundred pounds for lamb packed in heavy wood, metal or solid fibre containers to 50 cents a hundred pounds for lamb packed in lightweight crates. 

OPS said that the agency's attention had been called to the fact that some wholesalers of lamb have been applying the addition to sales of less than hundredweight quantities.

As a consequence, the regulation is being amended immediately to state specifically that the additions apply on a hundredweight basis. 1 GPO-O-OPS 1502

PRESS RELEASE    FRIDAY, December 21, 1951 

Re: 

McDonald-OPS-GPR-1122 

PROTESTS OF PORTS OF SEATTLE AND TACOMA AND BOARD OF HARBOR COMMISSIONERS OF HAWAII DENIED--PORT OF OLYMPIA GRANTED PRICE INCREASE. 

Claims of the Port of Seattle, the Port of Tacoma and the Board of Harbor Commissioners of Hawaii that their services are exempt from price control have been denied by Price Stabilization Director Michael V. DiSalle.

The two municipal corporations and the territorial agency had contended that they are public utilities under the provisions of Section 402 (a) (v) of the Defense Production Act and therefore were exempt by law from selling their services in accordance with regulations issued by the Office of Price Stabilization. Section 402 (d) (v) restricts OPS from establishing rates for public utilities./ "Neither the Ports of Seattle and Tacoma or the Board of Harbor Commissioners of Hawaii meet the statutory requirements to be classified as public utilities," Mr. DiSalle ruled. "Comprehensive control by an independent regulatory agency over the prices charged by a business is required before it may be considered a true public utility. Such control cannot be merely nominal or superficial but must be penetrating and complete. Before a business can qualify as a customary public utility, it must be under the complete regulatory jurisdiciton of an independent rate fixing authority," Mr. DiSalle said. "As mere sellers of services, regulating their own rates under statutory authority does not qualify the Ports of Seattle and Tacoma or the Board of Harbor Commissioners of Hawaii to claim exemption from price control since, in the statutory sense, they are not public utilities," Mr. DiSalle emphasized. 

All of the port facilities affected by today's actions engage in marine storage, wharfage, dockage, and similar services. The three protesting facilities objected to OPS establishing ceiling prices for their services either under the provisions of the General Ceiling Price Regulation or Ceiling Price 

Regulation 34 (Services). 

Today's action was taken only after a careful consideration was given to the arguments presented by each of the three port facilities, Mr. DiSalle said. 

At the request of the two Washington ports, Mr. DiSalle appointed a Board of 

Review to hear oral arguments on the protests at Yakima, Wash. A subcommittee of the Board heard argument at Yakima on September 6. Its findings and recommendations were later submitted to the OPS Director. 

GPO-0-OPS 1520

After considering the full record, the Board of Review found that neither the Port of Seattle nor the Port of Tacoma could be appropriately classified as public utilities because neither is regulated by any independent governmental authority exercising rate regulatory powers. Mr. DiSalle adopted the opinion of the Board of Review and ruled that neither port facility could claim the 

"public utility" exemption of the Defense Production Act. 

The protest of the Board of Harbor Commissioners of Hawaii was filed on September 27. In denying the petition of the territorial agency, Mr. DiSalle ruled that it had failed to show that any local, territorial or other federal authority regulated or controlled the Board in its fixing of rates and charges. 

The port facilities of the Board are not within the "public utility" exemption of the Defense Production Act, Mr. DiSalle said. 

In another action today, Mr. DiSalle authorized the Port of Olympia, Wash., a 17-percent rate increase for marine terminal handling and storage services. 

The Port of Olympia, in a letter to Mr. DiSalle on October 29, stated that unless its rates were raised, there was a possibility it might be forced to discontinue its services since it had sustained substantial increases in operating costs. 

The Port of Olympia has steadily been losing money on its overall operation for some time, it was pointed out. The earthquake of 1949, placed the facility in debt for more than $200,000 required to make repairs. Port authorities told 

OPS that unless some relief was given, the facility might have to go out of business inasmuch as further credit could not be obtained unless its rates were raised to a level that would enable the port to pay its own way. 

The financial problems of the facility were increased further this year by a labor increase of 16.9 percent, port authorities said.

REORGANIZATION OF DISTRIBUTION BRANCH AND CONSUMER SOFT GOODS DIVISION 

The Office of Price Stabilization today announced a comprehensive reorganization of its handling of consumer goods distribution pricing problems. The Consumer Soft 

Goods Division is redesignated the Consumer Goods Distribution, Textile, and Apparel 

Division. The Distribution Branch, which formerly was a single component of the Division, has been organized into two new branches, the Retail Branch and the Wholesale and Central Pricing Branch. Thomas L. Karsten who has been Director of the Consumer 

Soft Goods Division will continue as Director of the new Division. 

Morris L. Chandross, who has been Chief of the Apparel Branch, has been designated as an Assistant Director of the new Division, for Distribution, and will be responsible for the direction of the two distribution branches.

This action, the Agency explained, is in recognition of the tremendously important role of retail and wholesale distribution in the national economy and of the very considerable workload involved in preparing and administering distribution regulations. 

Mr. Chandross had served as Chief of the Apparel Branch since January. Prior to joining OPS, he was Vice President of the Lynchburg Garment Company and Production Manager of the BVD Corporation. He had also been an executive with the Manhattan Shirt 

Company after serving as Chief of the Textile Products Branch of the War Production 

Board during World War II. Prior to this Mr. Chandross had been associated with 

Abraham & Straus as Director of Testing Laboratories and for seven years prior to this, with R. H. Macy & Company. Mr. Chandross is a graduate of Brooklyn College with a B. A. degree.

Lester A. Ferguson, who has been Acting Chief of the Distribution Branch will serve as Chief of the Wholesale and Central Pricing Branch. 

Mr. Ferguson has been with OPS since February.

He formerly served as head of the 

Furniture Section, Consumer Durable Goods Division and then as Chief of the Hardlines and Home Furnishings Section of the Distribution Branch. He has been Acting Chief of the Distribution Branch since July.

Mr. Ferguson has had 16 years of merchandising experience which began in Cleveland, Ohio, where he had attended Western Reserve University. During the war he was an officer in the U. S. Coast Guard. Before coming to OPS he was sales manager of radio, television and major appliances for the Hect Company, Washington D. C., department store. Earlier, he was employed as store manager and buyer for the P. J. Nee Furniture 

Store, Washington; assistant general manager, E. A. Filene Department Store, Arlington,

Va., and furniture, bedding and floor covering buyer for Mayer & Company, Washington, (over) GPO-O-OPS 1511

.- 

George Price has been designated Chief of the Retail Branch and will have responsibility in the working out of new regulations in the distribution field. One of Mr. Price's immediate responsibilities will be development of the Small Retailer 

Regulation on which the Distribution Branch has been working. A new section, the 

Small Retail Section, has been established under Mr. Price's general supervision to complete the new regulation, administer it, and consult with small retailers, generally, on their pricing problems.

Mr. Price, who has been with the OPS since May, has been heading the Accessories and Furnishings Section. Prior to his OPS service, Mr. Price had operated and managed his own retail apparel business, and brings to this post an intimate knowledge of the operations and problems of independent retailers. During World War II, Mr. 

Price was Head of the Women's Accessories Section of the Office of Price Administra tion. Mr. Price is a graduate of George Washington University with a B. A. degree. 

Charles H. Sevin who has supervised the economic work involved in the entire distribution area will be designated Associate Divisional Economist in charge of the economic problems of the two branches.

Mr. Sevin cane to OPS from the Department of Commerce in March, 1951. He began his career there in 1938 as assistant economic analyst in the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, Marketing Research Division. His last position there was economic analyst in the Office of Civilian Requirements. He was graduated from the University of Chicago with Ph.B. and M. B. A. degrees.

The Retail Branch will have three sections. A Soft Goods Section headed by Frank 

F. Strunk, Jr., and a Durable Goods Section headed by Leland McCarthy, will cover pricing activities for larger retail outlets, except centrally pricing chain and mail order establishments. The Small Retail Section, headed by John H. Waite, will be concerned with the special problems and requirements of small retailers.

PRESS RELEASE   FRIDAY, December 28, 1951 Re: 

Tempo E 

Washington CLARIFICATION OF TV SET WARRANTIES (GCPR, Int. 45 Parts Warranties by Manufacturers of Television Sets) 

Cole-OPS-GPR-1125 

Substitution by television set manufacturers of a compulsory, longer warranty at an additional charge, in place of the base period, 90-day warranty would constitute a tie-in sale in violation of Section 18 of the General Ceiling Price Regulation, the Office of Price Stabilization has announced in Interpretation 45, GCPR. 

OPS points out that the dropping of the former 90-day warranty does not justify the proposed compulsory, longer warranty at an additional charge sought by some manufacturers.

The desire of some other manufacturers to increase the duration of a base period compulsory warranty and make an additional charge for such service would also result in a tie-in sale and be a violation of OPS regulations, according to Interpretation 45. 

OPS officials stated that the proposal of some manufacturers to increase their base period compulsory warranty charge, and reduce the price of the television set by like amount would also constitute a violation of ceiling price regulations. # # # # # # The general rules, the interpretation states, are that a seller may not require a tie-in sale and may not increase his ceiling prices. This, however, OPS continues, does not prohibit any seller from offering something in addition to that which he offered during the base period and from making an appropriate and reasonable charge for the item, determined under the applicable ceiling price regulation, provided that the purchaser has a full option to take or leave the additional item.

PRESS RELEASE   ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers MONDAY, December 31, 1951 Hughes-OPS-GPR-1128  Re: TEST PROGRAM FOR COMMUNITY FOOD PRICING 

The Office of Price Stabilization announced today that it is about to try out "community food pricing" in three test cities. "Community food pricing" is a program of posted ceiling prices in grocery stores, a program that was highly successful in World War II. 

OPS Director Michael V. DiSalle said the trial plan is based in part on a recommendation of the OPS Consumer Advisory Committee, and also in recognition of the fact that identifiable ceilings are best from the standpoint of both buyer and seller. Many consumers have complained that they have no way of knowing what the ceilings are in the stores where they shop for groceries. 

The tests will take place shortly in Fresno, California; Fargo, North 

Dakota; and Jacksonville, Florida.

In each of the three test areas, the program will take in all food stores in the city itself and in the immediately adjacent counties. 

Mr. DiSalle emphasized that community pricing is not designed to change prices. OPS is simply requiring the posting of dollars-and-cents ceilings, figured on the basis of existing regulations which provide varying percentage markups for groceries.

The price posters will be furnished by OPS. Each poster will give ceiling prices--the highest prices that the housewife can be asked to pay--for a selected list of 350 to 400 items, including some items from each of the 36 dry grocery categories in the OPS food markup regulations, and some packaged butter and cheese items. 

The first printed list of ceiling prices is scheduled to be posted in the grocery stores of the test areas around the end of January or the beginning of 

February. 

A revised poster will go up every two weeks thereafter during the life of the experiment. Procedures are being worked out to take care of any necessary changes in the two-week interval between printed posters. 

There will be four different community pricing posters in each city--one for each of the four groups of stores listed in the OPS grocery regulations. 

These stores range from the smallest corner groceries to the large chains and super-markets. 

(Over) 

GPO-O-OPS 1534

-  Under the OPS grocery regulations, Groups 1 and 2 are the smaller "independent" stores; Groups 3 and 4, the chain stores and supermarkets. Stores of different sizes and classes, giving different kinds of service, customarily charge different prices for the same goods, as all shoppers know. In recognition of this, the OPS grocery regulations fix different percentage markups for the four store groups.

Thus, the ceiling prices will not be the same in all stores. But they will be identical in all stores of the same group in a given city. 

What Community Pricing Accomplishes 

The grocery posting program is called "community pricing" because it establishes a ceiling price which is community wide for each listed commodity. 

The ceiling is the same in all stores of the same class throughout the community pricing area. Though it may sell for less, no store may sell for more than the flat, community-wide price.

In the OPS instructions to its field offices, community pricing is described as "essentially a technique for translating ceiling prices figured under the wholesale and retail food markup regulations into dollars-and-cents prices which are established on an area basis. The community prices are made available to the purchasers, as well as the sellers, by posting published price lists in retail stores." "Community pricing," Mr. DiSalle said, "was the best-liked and most effective form of price control developed out of wartime experience. "It was popular with housewives because it told them, in easy-to-read charts, the exact ceiling prices of their market-basket foods, and thus protected them from overcharges. It appealed to the trade because it reduced their own figuring and record keeping to a minimum. It had the further advantage that it was the type of control easiest to enforce. "The structure of community pricing is a simple one, though many complex problems may come up in actual operation. "Posting of dollars-and-cents ceiling prices is the main feature of the program. The other principal change is that grocers in Groups 1 and 2 (that is, the smaller independent stores) no longer figure their own maximum prices for items on the chart. That is done for them by the local OPS District Office. "First the Office visits a representative group of wholesalers to find the actual prices that retail grocers are paying to their suppliers. A representative wholesale price is found for each commodity. This wholesale price is then marked up by the percentage amounts allowed for the commodity in OPS retail grocery regulations. "The result of the calculations is a list of ceiling prices. These prices are printed on a poster which is distributed to the stores. The grocer puts the chart on his wall on the appointed day. Thereafter, until OPS authorizes changes in the chart, the prices listed are the highest ones the grocer can charge. He can always charge less, of course.'

· - 

Problems of Community Pricing 

Since the grocery regulations were issued, last March, Mr. DiSalle added, OPS has wanted to put nation-wide community pricing into operation. 

But strong obstacles have stood in the way. One of them was the fact that 

OPS lacks authority to control farm commodities selling below parity, and therefore has been unable to prevent frequent food price changes. Prices must be reasonably stable to get the most out of community pricing, since it takes time to print the charts. With frequent price changes, charts might be out of date almost from the moment they are posted.

Community pricing has been postponed also because many actual selling prices have been somewhat below permitted ceilings. Thus there has not been a compelling need for consumer protection from overceiling charges. 

Looking to the period ahead, however, OPS' Consumer Advisory Committee has urged for some time that dollars-and-cents ceiling prices for groceries be established at the earliest possible moment, so that consumers may be aware of ceiling prices and can help hold the line. 

Recently the Committee, while recognizing the difficulties involved in starting full-scale community pricing now, nevertheless recommended that a program be put into effect for a selected list of grocery items in selected The limited test of community pricing will permit OPS to determine how useful the posting of ceiling prices is both to the consumer and the food retailer under existing conditions. Thus the test will provide a basis for deciding whether such a program should be extended to other cities and towns. areas. 

Posted ceilings, Mr. DiSalle said, may be higher than actual prices marked on some food items. OPS has been surveying prices in about 2,000 stores for several months, and results of the survey indicate that many prices, nationally, are below allowable ceilings.

On the average, the OPS survey indicates, prices have been about 4 percent below ceilings. Four percent is equivalent to a one-cent difference on a 25-cent item.

Since this is an average, it means that actual prices for many items will be at ceilings while prices of other items may be further below ceiling than this average. 

Prices tended to "soften" (decline), Mr. DiSalle pointed out, after the 

OPS price freeze of last January stopped the "scare psychology" which followed the Korean outbreak.

Even though many prices are below ceilings, the grocery trade is asking for an increase in ceilings, particularly for commodities selling at or close to ceiling. The chain stores and supermarkets, especially, have contended that the operation of ceilings has brought their margins and net earnings to a depressed and inequitable level. These contentions are presently under consideration by OPS. # # # # # #

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers WEDNESDAY, January 2, 1952 Re: 

 MANDATORY FILING OF OPS PUBLIC FORM 8 

Officials of the Office of Price Stabilization today estimated that between 5,000 and 10,000 manufacturers had failed to file proposed ceiling prices by December 19, as required by OPS general manufacturers' and machinery manufacturers ceiling price regulations (CPR 22 and CPR 30).

Scott-OPS-GPR-1129  

These regulations became mandatorily effective on December 19, and manufacturers of commodities covered by them were required to file OPS Public Form 8 by December 19 to establish proposed ceilings by applying labor and materials cost adjustments to pre-Korean prices. Manufacturers, who failed to file Form 

8 as required, have not established legal ceiling prices for their commodities. 

Edward P. Morgan, Director of the OPS Office of Enforcement, stated that immediate compliance by these manufacturers will be sought. Mr. Morgan said that plans are being considered for a compliance survey and in the event of noncompliance, for the immediate filing of injunctive actions in United States 

District Courts without preclearance in Washington.

OPS officials reported that approximately 120,000 Forms 8 had been filed with OPS up to December 19, the effective date of the regulations. 

It was pointed out, however, that some manufacturers filed more than one Form 8 to cover separate commodity categories or product lines, and, therefore, the figure of 120,000 does not mean that 120,000 individual manufacturers have filed.

Officials pointed out also that manufacturers of a fairly wide range of commodities have been given the option of continuing to price under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR) pending early issuance by OPS of specific tailored pricing regulations covering these commodities. Commodities subject to such optional pricing are listed under Supplementary Regulation 12 to CPR 

22 and Supplementary Regulation 3 to CPR 30.

Re: OPS CRIMINAL ACTIONS IN SCRAP METAL FIELD 

The first criminal actions involving alleged violations of Office of Price Stabilization regulations by scrap metal dealers were brought today. 

Criminal informations were filed in the United States District Court at Norfolk, Virginia, before Federal Judge Albert V. Bryan against Joseph

Jacobson, doing business as the American Iron and Metal Company, 2529 County Street, Portsmouth, and Norman Gutterman, one of the partners of S. Gutterman & Company, 1206 E. Brambleton Avenue, Norfolk.

The defendants are charged by OPS with violating the Defense Production 

Act, Ceiling Price Regulation No. 5, by upgrading iron and steel scrap.

The court set January 17 as the date for arraignment. 

Edward P. Morgan, OPS Enforcement Director, stated in Washington that "The upgrading of scrap metal is a very serious matter in view of the huge quantities of scrap needed for the defense effort at the present time. 

Scrap constitutes a very large percent of the raw material used in making steel, and the cost of scrap is therefore a major component in the cost of finished steel. "Increased costs are reflected sooner or later in increased prices. 

A rise in the price of finished steel would set in motion inflationary forces that would be felt in every home in America. We are investigating numerous other cases in which shipments of iron and steel scrap have been upgraded. 

In the American Iron and Metal Company case, a shipment was made to the 

Brake Shoe and Castings Division of the American Brake Shoe Company at 

Portsmouth on June 21, 1951, through the Norfolk office of the Luria Steel and Trading Company, scrap brokers.

In the Gutterman case, the American Brake Shoe Company was also the purchaser and the Luria firm the broker.

WEDNESDAY, January 2, 1952 Tempo E 

Washington Coakley-OPS-GPR-1131 

Re: EXCEPTIONS TO ICC EXAMINER'S FINDINGS IN MOTOR RATE CASE 

The Office of Price Stabilization today filed with the Interstate Commerce Commission exceptions to findings of an ICC examiner which would permit rate increases of 4 percent for motor common carriers represented by the Pacific Inland 

Tarif Bureau, Inc. 

The Bureau, representing carriers operating in Washington, Oregon, Idaho, California, Western Montana, and Utah, proposed a 6 percent increase in rates to be effective August 30, 1951. This increase was suspended by the ICC upon protest of shippers and associations of shippers. A hearing was held before Examiner Paul Coyle, October 15, 16 and 17 in Portland, Ore.

Mr. Coyle recommended that the suspended rate schedules, calling for a 6 percent increase, be cancelled and that proceedings be discontinued without prejudice to the establishment of rates increased by 4 percent over present rates. 

OPS recommended a 2 percent rather than a 4 percent increase and pointed out that, while the agency did not object, generally, to the findings of the examiner, it was seriously concerned because of the "unique and unsupportable recommendation" that the Commission should include Federal income taxes and surtaxes as an operating expense in computing operating ratios for motor carriers. 

OPS maintained that the increase in rates recommended by the ICC examiner would adversely affect the stabilization program. Further, OPS said, if Federal income taxes were included in operating costs, each new tax levy by the Congress would result in increased motor rates, thus nullifying the indirect control of inflation exerted by Federal taxation.

FILING BY APPAREL MANUFACTURERS 

Apparel manufacturers who have been pricing and selling their products under the Apparel Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation (Ceiling 

Price Regulation 45, Revision 1) will be required to file the report required under Section 3 of that regulation by January 11, 1952, the Office of Price 

Stabilization announced today.

This announcement is a reminder of the filing deadline as set by Amendment 

1 to CPR 45, Rev. 1 issued on December 7, 1951 (See Press Release OPS-0-557).

Before this action, no specific filing date was provided for apparel manufacturers who voluntarily priced under CPR 45, Rev. 1. A manufacturer may put this regulation into effect for himself by pricing and selling under it, and he must file his report within 30 days after he first sells an article priced under it. 

Those who were pricing and selling under the regulation before the effective date of Amendment 1 (December 12, 1951) are given until January 11 to file their reports. 

Until a mandatory effective date is set for CPR 45, Rev. 1, apparel manufacturers who have not used that regulation are given the option to remain under the General Ceiling Price Regulation. However, OPS pointed out that those who voluntarily have elected to make CPR 45, Rev. 1 effective for their products must file their reports; those who fail to do so within the required time are prohibited from selling or delivering their articles unless and until the report is filed. 

OPS reported that only 1,200 such filings have been received to date.

Although the agency has no overall information as to how many apparel manufacturers have elected to price under CPR 45, Rev. 1, OPS believes that a considerable number of manufacturers pricing and selling under that regulation have not filed. # # # # # # # # # GPO-O-OPS 1563

PRESS RELEASE    TUESDAY, January 8, 1952 

Moore-OPS-GPR-1135 

Re: WIREBOUND BOX IAC 

Recommendation that a formula type of regulation be prepared for their entire industry was made today by members of the Wirebound Box Industry Advisory 

Committee at their second meeting with OPS officials.

The committee considered proposed drafts prepared by OPS of tailored regillations for two segments of their industry. 

One proposal contemplated establishing spelled out dollars-and-cents ceilings for standard items, produced for the packaging of fruit, vegetables and other agricultural commodities, at levels prevailing under the General Ceiling 

Price Regulation, GCPR. 

A formula type of regulation was proposed for Wirebound boxes made for industrial useres because the products of this segment of the industry lack uniformity and do not lend themselves to dollars-and-cents pricing. 

A pricing formula would include as elements material costs, conversion costs, margin and delivery costs. Because the industry was in a depressed period immediately prior to the outbreak of fighting in Korea, it was proposed that January 25 to February 24, 1951, be selected as a base period. Manufacturers would compute their prices by using the formulas and margins they had in effect during that period, and using February 24 as the cut-off date on their material and conversion costs.

Committeemen asserted that margins in their industry were still narrow and that the prices thus arrived at would not be adequate to permit absorption of subsequent increased costs.

They suggested that a formula type of regulation be prepared at this time for the entire industry to facilitate pricing in accordance with industry practice. Furthermore, they urged that studies be made of costs to justify higher ceilings than would be obtained from the proposed formula pricing or dollars-and-cents ceilings obtained from averaging GCPR prices. 

They reported that increased costs for logs and labor were major considerations to them. Logs were tight against ceilings, they said, and manufacturers were being forced to go father afield and pay higher freight costs to obtain them. They suggested that a study of wage increases also would show justification for more favorable prices.

The committee recommended that the wire-bound box regulation be written for manufacturers, and that resellers be covered by the prospective regulation for resellers of lumber and other wood products. 

The meeting was conducted by Stanley C. Craven, chief, Wood Container Section, OPS. GPO-O-OPS 1608

Tuesday, January 8, 1952

  Re: RESALE OF MERCHANT TRADE STEEL PRODUCTS IAC Members of the Resale of Merchant Trade Steel Products Industry Advisory 

Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems under Ceiling Price Regulation 98 (CPR 98) covering resellers of iron and steel products. 

Scott-OPS-GPR-1137 

This was the second meeting of the committee, it having met previously with OPS on April 13, 1951.

The industry is composed principally of warehouse jobbers of merchant trade wire and tubular steel products, including iron and steel standard pipe, corrugated or formed galvanized or coated siding and roofing, wire nails, barbed wire, wire fence, fence posts, bale ties and wire hoops, etc. These products when sold by jobbers are subject to pricing under CPR 98, issued on 

November 30, 1951. 

It was the consensus of the committee that, generally speaking, CPR 98 is a sound and workable pricing regulation as applied to the industry which the committee represents and should have a stabilizing effect on industry pricing. 

The committee indicated, however, that some provisions of CPR 98 needed minor changes and clarifications with a view to making the regulation more clearly understood by the industry generally. The committee discussed in detail the need for these changes and clarifications.

In general, CPR 98 provides for a jobber markup of 20 percent over base mill prices and transportation costs for merchant wire and roofing and siding products. Committeemen said this 20 percent markup is somewhat low and does not realistically reflect the overall historical markup which most jobbers have had in effect. They recommended that OPS consider the fairness of increasing the markup, possibly to 25 percent, with a somewhat higher markup to be applied in the New York City metropolitan area.

The meeting was conducted by John H. Congdon II, consultant, Metals Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: William Kerber, chief, Metals Branch;

Tuesday, January 8, 1952

  

Coakley-OPS-GPR-1138  

Re: CONTRACT MOTOR CARRIER IAC The Contract Motor Carriers Industry Advisory Committee made several re commendations to the Office of Price Stabilization in a two-day meeting which concluded here today.

Following a discussion of Supplementary Regulation 39, covering adjustment of contract rates, and Supplementary Regulation 40, covering pick-up and delivery service rate adjustments, it was agreed that, if more information were supplied on the forms specified by the regulations in filing applications, delays in OPS action would be avoided. Requests by the agency for further information before action could be taken, it was pointed out, would not be necessary.

In the case of contract carriers, this would mean inclusion of dollars-andcents increases which would result from specific rates applied for, particularly in cases where the application covered rates with varying amounts or percentages of increase.

Committee members expressed the opinion that amendment of SR 39 and SR 40 to cover adjustments under the so-called Capehart amendment is not necessary and recommended that the industry seek such adjustments under General Overriding Regulations 20 and 21 which provide for adjustments under the Capehart formula. 

Committee members reported they would not oppose delegation to field offices of OPS the authority to process adjustment applications, but urged that if such delegation is made, the field offices be adequately staffed with personnel trained in transportation problems. However, they indicated a preference for OPS to continue to handle such applications in the national office. 

Committee members opposed any change in the present provisions of SR 39 and SR 40 which permit rate adjustments applied for to go into effect automatically upon the expiration of a 30-day period, if OPS takes no action in the interim. 

They asked that it be continued regardless of whether the applications are processed in Washington or in the field offices. 

Another Committee recommendation would require motor carriers and pick-up and delivery carriers to make their books and records available to OPS, rather than to file a list of all ceiling prices with the Agency. Committee members objected to the amount of clerical work which would be required in the latter procedure and the expense it would entail. 

Today's meeting was the third held by this committee and was attended by 13 of the 17 industry members. Lester R. Conley, Acting Chief of the OPS Transportation Branch, and Dewey C. Wayne, Chief of the Highway Section, conducted the meeting.

Re: NATURAL GAS RATE CASE INTERVENTIONS 

The Office of Price Stabilization today filed petitions to intervene in three natural gas rate cases before the Federal Power Commission which propose rate increases totaling some $26,000,000 and affecting most natural gas users in the Eastern and Southern section of the country. 

The Transcontinental Gas Pipe Line Corporation proposes to increase its rates to wholesale customers by approximately $13,900,000 for the year 1952. 

This company supplies 52 resale customers in the states of New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, North Carolina, South Carolina and

Virginia. 

Alantic Seaboard Corporation and Virginia Gas Transmission Corporation of which Atlantic is a parent company, have requested rate increases estimated at $3,036,976 or 15.3 percent over present rates. These two pipeline companies own and operate an integrated, interstate, natural gas transmission system extending from Boldman, Ky., to a point on the Maryland-Pennsylvania state line. They supply 8 resale customers.

An estimated increase of $9,718,949 in rates is proposed by the United Fuel Gas Co., Charleston, W. Va. This company serves 77 communities in the 

West Virginia-Ohio-Kentucky area and has 11 resale customers, most of which are subsidiaries of the Columbia Gas System. 

These three bring to 9 the cumber of natural gas cases before the FPC in which OPS is taking part.

All together, they involve increases of approximately $80,000,000 per year in the wholesale price of gas. 

These rates are not subject to direct price control by OPS but must be approved by the Federal Power Commission. However, under the Defense Production 

Act, public utilities making application for an increase in wholesale rates must notify OPS and must consent to intervention by the agency in proceedings before the regulatory body. 

Michael V. DiSalle, Price Stabilization Director, in filing today's petitions on behalf of OPS, pointed out that these increases, if granted, would be paid by countless smaller utilities who would in turn seek to add the increase to their prices to household and industrial customers. "OPS is well aware of the importance of utility rates in the cost of living picture," Mr. DiSalle said. "We fear that, as is so often the case, these proposed wholesale increases, if granted, would be pyramided by resale markups at the retail level with consequent increases to consumers of considerably more then $80,000,000. We have an example of the chain reaction of one increase here: Atlantic Seaboard and Virginia Gas are seeking increases because of the petition for higher rates filed by their affiliated supplier, United Fuel Gas GPO-O-OPS 1630

Company. This company in turn claims it must charge higher rates because of recent increases granted by FPC to Tennessee Gas Transmission Company, United 

Fuel's supplier. 

11 1 "It is evident,' he said, "that in many cases the wholesale pipeline companies are seeking to pass on to the consumer recent federal income tax increases, levied to help meet the costs of the defense program and to combat inflation. Many are also attempting to raise the level of profit on their investment above that prevailing before Korea, and to translate every cost increase into a rate increase. We do not believe this is justified in a period of national emergency and we feel that disproportionate increases in natural gas rates would adversely affect the price stabilization program.' 11

Thursday, January 10, 1952

 Re: REUSABLE IRON AND STEEL PIPE LAC Scott-OPS-GPR-1141 Members of the Reusable Iron and Steel Pipe Industry Advisory Committee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss problems of industry pricing under Ceiling Price Regulation 98 (CPR 98) covering resellers of iron and steel products.

This was the second meeting of the committee, it having met previously with 

OPS on April 19, 1951.

The industry is concerned with sale of re-usable iron and steel pipe, casing and tubing, structural pipe, etc., including used pipe contained in pipe lines, oil wells, or similar pipe assemblies whether or not it is sold in place. 

Generally, CPR 98 establishes ceiling prices for re-usable iron and steel pipe on the basis of 80 percent of the jobber ceiling price for new pipe of the same type.

Committeemen said the industry is experiencing difficulty in buying reusable pipe at a price which will permit it to be resold at a ceiling price representing 80 percent of the jobber's ceiling price for new pipe. In order to make more re-usable pipe available, the committee recommended that the ceiling price be increased to 95 percent of the jobber's ceiling price for new pipe. 

The committee discussed in detail the need for changes and clarification in some of the provisions of CPR 98, paricularly with reference to definitions, so that the regulation will be more clearly and precisely understood by the industry generally.

OPS officials told the committee that its suggestions and recommendations will be given full and careful consideration.

Tempo E- RE: 

Washington STEAM POWER GENERATING EQUIPMENT TAC Members of the Steam Power Generating Equipment Industry Advisory Committee met for the first time yesterday with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems under the machinery ceiling price regu lation (CPR 30). 

Scott-OPS-GPR-1143 

The industry is concerned with the manufacture, facrication, installation and erection of large individually engineered and designed steam power generating equipment and related equipment such as coal pulverizers, economizers, air heaters, etc. 

The equipment involves installations that range from relatively small portable steam generating boilers to huge generating plants up to 14 stories in height. It is estimated that the industry's annual volume of sales will exceed 250 million. dollars.

The industry generally is required to price under the formula pricing provisions of Ceiling Price Regulation 30 (CPR 30) both as to equipment manufactured and the installation and erection services furnished in connection with its sale. 

The pricing formula, in general, provides for use by the manufacturer of his pricing method in effect during his base period, as applied to labor and material costs in effect on March 15, 1951. (In some cases materials costs as of December 31, 1950, are used.)

Committeemen said the industry has been squeezed somewhat by increases in labor and material costs since March 15, 1951, as applied to manufactured equipment. 

In this connection, they added, it has become increasingly necessary to purchase steel from steel warehouses rather than direct from the mill and in many cases it is necessary to subcontract with the steel warehouse for fabrication of steel in order to obtain the steel.

With respect to pricing of installation and erection services, they said, the industry is experiencing serious difficulty because of increased and varying labor and materials costs since March 15, 1951, and because the industry is in an inequitable competitive position with other contractors who price under the construction ceiling price regulation (CPR 93), using a restricted markup applied to current labor and material costs, while the industry is required to price under CPR 30, using March 15, 1951 labor and materials costs for performing the same type of installation and erection services.

The committee recommended that installation and erection services performed in connection with the sale of equipment be priced under the construction ceiling price regulation CPR 93, rather than under CPR 30. They said that such action would be fair and equitable and would place the industry on a sound pricing basis with respect to charges for installation and erection service. 

The meeting was conducted by Warren B. Leland, chief, Auxiliary Machinery Sec tion, Machinery Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: Archie A. Stone, chief, Machinery Branch; C. W. Moore, division economist; C. Parson, branch economist;

Leo Wasser, legal staff; and Harry Spack, Office for Industry Advisory Committees.

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers WEDNESDAY, January 16, 1952 

Washington Re: GOVERNMENT SALES Crossley-OPS-GPR-1144 

The Office of Price Stabilization today issued a clarification as to the coverage of the temporary suspension from the General Ceiling Price Regulation of sales of certain United States government property. 

In Amendment 1 to Supplementary Regulation 72 to the GCPR, issued on Dec ember 29, 1951, temporary suspension from the GOPR was continued from December 

31, 1951, to February 29, 1952 (See Press Release OPS-0-618). This continuation of the temporary suspension applied to the identical United States government property covered in Supplementary Regulation 72 to the GCPR, issued on October 

4, 1951 (See Press Release OPS-0-425). Today's OPS announcement is made to correct misunderstanding on the part of some buyers of government property as to the extent of the temporary suspension. 

Included in the suspension order is government property consisting of any commodity, material, article, product, process, or other item of personal property, whether new, used, waste, salvage or scrap. It must have been bought originally for use by, and be owned at time of sale by, an agency or instru mentality of the United States. 

Not included in the temporary suspension from the GCPR, where applicable, are the following: (1) Property which was originally bought by the government for the purpose of resale or stockpiling. (2) Sales by the government which are covered by any other Supplementary Regulation to the GCPR or by any numbered ceiling price regulation. (3) Sales of any commodity produced or manufactured by the government or by any person for the account of the government. (4) Sales for which a ceiling price has been established for government sales under Sections 3 or 7 of the GCPR. 

Before suspension from price control can be made effective for any sale of government property, two requirements must be met: (1) A copy of the invoice or other evidence of sale must be retained by the sales agency for inspection by OPS; and (2) the buyer of the property must have been notified in writing in advance of the sale that resale of the property is subject to any applicable ceiling price regulation.

Tempo E-Washington WEDNESDAY, January 16, 1952 Re: WHITE POTATOES Barkley-OPS-GPR-1147  

Michael V. DiSalle, Director of the Office of Price Stabilization, today announced that maximum OPS retail markups for sales of white flesh potatoes to consumers will be announced shortly and will become effective not later than 

January 28, 1952.

These markups will supplement the OPS regulation establishing dollars-andcents ceiling prices for white potatoes at country shipping points and at wholesale levels. This regulation, CPR 113, was issued January 5 and becomes effective January 19.

The retail markups, which will be issued in the form of amendments to the retail grocery ceiling price regulations, CPR's 15 and 16, will provide specific percentage margins over cost of white potatoes for each of the four classes of grocery retailers-small independents, large independents, chains and supermarkets.

There will be different retail markups for bulk and prepackaged sales of potatoes. Retailers will be able to apply these markups to their legal acquisition costs in the preceding week. This will make unnecessary any protracted time-lag between the effective date of CPR 113 on January 19 and the retail markups on or about January 28.

In stating that retail markups would be announced shortly, Mr. DiSalle emphasized that CPR 113 would become effective as scheduled, but said that a series of adjustments, additions and possible amendments is under study. Every effort will be made to issue these adjustments as near to the January 19 effective date as possible, he added.

The OPS Director pointed out that, as in all other regulations, the agency will make adjustments in the potato regulation as necessary to protect consumers, producers and distributors against unnecessary dislocation of trade practices.

Seasonal Adjustments 

Mr. DiSalle said that seasonal state additions to the f.o.b. shipping point base ceiling prices, for each state for each month from February through May, would be issued shortly.

GPO-O-OPS 1071

February, 10 cents; March, 10 cents; April, 5 cents; and May, 5 cents.

Mr. DiSalle said these additions are consistent with the seasonal state differential prices as computed by the Secretary of Agriculture.

Mr. DiSalle said that requests have been made to consider extra allowance for washing and waxing potatoes, and this matter will be studied further by the OPS staff.

Distributive Margins 

Mr. DiSalle also said that CPR 113 will be amended within a few days to specify the exact amounts which may be added for specified distribution funetions. This will avoid squeezes on intermediate handlers or distributive channels. The technique will be similar to that used in the final wartime Office of Price Administration orders governing fresh fruits and vegetables. 

Producer Prices 

The OPS Director reemphasized that CPR 113, as first issued, is a temporary regulation. It came out within a few days after the Secretary of Agriculture had announced that the national average price for potatoes at the farm level exceeded parity. At that time potato prices at shipping points for only a very few states were below the state differential prices based on computations by the Secretary of Agriculture. Prices in most states exceeded these levels. 

The basic prices in the regulation were designed to give producers at least the parity price. Congress had established parity as the general fair price for producers.

The statement of considerations to CPR 113 emphasized that a more detailed regulation would be developed if continued pressure on potato prices justified. 

An upward adjustment was made in the Idaho differential price, as determined by the Secretary of Agriculture, in order to compensate farmers and handlers for the unusually high percentage of lower-grade potatoes produced in that state this year.

A margin from the farm gate to f.o.b. shipping point of at least 75 cents a hundred pounds was allowed in all areas, with minor upward adjustments in a few areas to assure normal flows of the product. The U. S. parity price and the state differentials are so calculated that price benefits to producers from all special marketing services between the farm gate and shipping point are reflected for each region.

The regional adjustments from the U. S. average parity price also explicitly include allowances for the particular practices in each region. 

Distributor Allowances

A margin of at least 60 cents a hundred pounds was allowed in all areas to cover distribution costs between shipping points and retail stores.

·4Freight costs between shipping points and wholesale stores also can be reflected. 

Additions may be made to ceiling prices for any potatoes 2 inches in dianeter or 4 ounces in weight. For round or intermediate varieties, additions in ceiling prices may be made for specified increases in size of the potatoes. 

The same additions to ceiling prices may be made for long varieties of potatoes as average weight increases.

Addition to ceiling price is authorized for the highly uniform sizes and weights in special packs put up for hotel, restaurant or other similar outlets. 

Finally, a set of additions to ceiling prices is allowed for packaging of potatoes in various consumer size bags or containers. 

The packaging allowance may be added to ceiling prices in accordance with Table 3 in CPR 113 by any shipper or distributor, except retailers, who performs this service.

Future Adjustments 

Thus, Mr. DiSalle said, there is recognition in CPR 113 of the differences in regional production and pricing patterns and of distributive practices of the potato industry. 

He stressed that parity price levels increase proportionately with increases in costs incurred by farmers. Thus, potato producers are protected against squeezes from rising costs because parity prices below which OPS cannot set ceiling prices rise at least as much as do costs paid by farmers. # # # # #

 PRIVATE MOTOR CARRIER IAC The Private Motor Carrier Industry Advisory Committee, meeting for the first time today with Office of Price Stabilization officials, recommended that, where a seller uses his own transportation equipment and adds transportation costs, as a separate item, to the cost of his goods to the consumer, adjustments of ceilings to reflect increased transportation costs be handled by the Commodity Divisions of 

OPS rather than by the Transportation Branch. 

Committee members maintained that because private carrier transportation is an integral part of a firm's business operation, its cost should be considered by the Commodity Divisions, along with other manufacturing and distribution costs, in setting ceiling prices.

The Committee further recommended that provisions for adjustment of ceilings to reflect transportation cost increases be incorporated in commodity regu lations issued by OPS. 

Lester R. Conley, Chief of the Transportation Branch, and Dewey C. Wayne, Chief of the Highway Section, who conducted the meeting, told the committee that officials of the Transportation Branch would consult with representatives of the Commodity Divisions in an effort to work out the problem.

Re: RESALE OF OIL COUNTRY TUBULAR GOODS LAC Members of the Resale of Oil Country Tubular Goods Industry Advisory Com mittee met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss pricing problems under the ceiling price regulation covering resellers of iron and steel products (CPR 98).

This was the second meeting of the committee. It met with OPS officials on April 18, 1951.

The industry is concerned with the sale of casing, tubing, drill pipe and drive pipe, and other similar products customarily referred to as Oil Country 

Tubular Goods. 

It was the consensus of the committee that pricing unddr CPR 98 has been generally satisfactory and has not presented any industry difficulties. They said that the ceiling price determining provisions of the regulation as applied to Oil Country Tubular Goods fairly well carries out the historical pricing practices prevailing in the industry. 

This industry group is also somewhat concerned with the purchase and sale of re-usable pipe in a reconditioned and un-reconditioned state. 

Reconditioned and re-usable pipe is priced under CPR 98 at 80 percent of the price for comparable new pipe. Un-reconditioned pipe when sold to a reconditioner is not subject to price control, but when sold to a person other than a reconditioner, the ceiling price is $65 a ton. 

It was the consensus of the committee that the ceiling price for re-usable pipe should be set at 95 percent of the price for comparable new pipe in order to provide an incentive for bringing more re-usable pipe into the market. It was also suggested that ceilings for un-reconditioned pipe be controlled on the basis of the ceilings established for all re-usable pipe. 

The meeting was conducted jointly by William Kerber, chief, Metals Branch and John H. Congdon II, consultant, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were:

Re: BLOTTING AND IMPREGNATING PAPERS IAC 

Recommendations that a tailored regulation be prepared for their segment of the paper industry were made today by members of the Blotting and Impregnating Papers Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting with OPS officials. 

Committeemen suggested that dollars-and-cents ceilings be spelled out for standard grades of blotting paper, and that formula pricing be provided to cover impregnating and saturating papers which are treated with plastics and other chemicals to make special papers for decorative and industrial uses. 

Manufacturers of blotting and impregnating papers are still pricing their products under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR, which froze prices at the levels existing from December 19, 1950, to January 25, 1951. 

Committeemen indicated that a regulation which would maintain these levels would be acceptable.

It was suggested that the proposed regulation follow in general the provisions of MPR 450, issued during the war by the old Office of Price 

Administration. 

Committeemen examined the pricing formulas contained in several new OPS regulations with the view of finding a formula suitable for saturating papers. Regulations examined included CPR 84, covering converted paperboard products; CPR 115, covering paper shipping sacks, and a draft of the forthcoming printing services regulation.

OPS officials undertook to prepare a tentative draft of a regulation for blotting and impregnating papers in line with the committee's suggestions. 

A subcommittee was named to be on call to advise on details of the draft, which will be submitted at a future meeting of the committee for consideration.

Re: DOMESTIC WOODPULP CONSUMERS TAC 

Whether adjustments should be made to woodpulp ceilings established by Ceiling Price Regulation 49, and the possible effect on supply of any such adjustments, were discussed today by members of the Domestic Woodpulp Consumers Industry Advisory Committee at a meeting with OPS officials and representatives of other government agencies.

The regulation, which became effective June 30, 1951, established dollarsand-cents ceilings on overseas woodpulp substantially higher than the ceilings it fixed for domestic woodpulp. The overseas ceilings were the lowest prices paid for overseas woodpulp imported during the second quarter of 1951. No ceilings have been imposed on Canadian woodpulp, which is priced somewhat higher than domestic ceilings, but well below the ceilings on overseas pulp.

Re:  

SMALL PNEUMATIC COMPRESSOR TAC 

The Small Pneumatic Compressor Industry Advisory Committee met today for the second time with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization for a further discussion of industry pricing problems. The committee previously met with OPS officials September 6, 1951.

The industry is concerned with the manufacture of small air compressors of 1/4 horsepower up to and including 15 horsepower, but not including compressors used in connection with condensing units. Small compressors are used as a vital component in a wide range of commercial and industrial applications and in connection with military, naval and Air Force equipment and facilities. Many mechanical devices and installations are dependent upon these compressors. They are also vital to the operation and maintenance of transportation by truck, rail, water and air, committeemen said.

Committeemen said the industry generally has suffered a serious price squeeze under ceiling prices established by the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR), and that computation of ceilings under the machinery ceiling price regulation CPR 30, even after applying adjustments permissable under the so-called Capehart amendment, will not give the industry sufficient price relief. In some cases a rollback from GCPR prices will result, they said. This situation is due to the drepressed price level prevailing in the industry during the pre-Korea base period provided for under CPR 30, according to committee members.

Some manufacturers had increased prices by varying degrees above pre-Korea levels, before the issuance of GCPR, which froze prices prevailing during the period December 19, 1950, to January 25, 1951. Committeemen said, however, the

GCPR prices established in the industry still reflect a generally depressed price situation. 

Committeemen said, that because of the general price squeeze many manufacturers are restricting and diverting production and are making plans to divert more production facilities to other products. They said this restriction and diversion of production will increase progressively under the existing squeeze. 

A survey made by OPS indicates that the level of prices prevailing during the pre-Korea base period, even though depressed, did reflect a relatively uniform price level as between companies due to competitive conditions. OPS officials said a further study will be made of industry data with a view of determining whether an industry-wide price adjustment ratio can be applied to the pre-Korea base period price levels prevailing in the industry. 

A subcommittee was appointed to confer with OPS in an effort to develop a GPO-O-OPS 1680

Guy  tailored pricing regulation that will alleviate the present price squeeze.

Re: BAKING IAC 

Barkley-OPS-GPR-1156  

A tentative draft of a proposed ceiling price regulation for bakery products was reviewed today at a meeting between officials of the Office of Price Stabilization and members of the agency's Baking Industry

Advisory Committee. 

The meeting, the third held by OPS with representatives of the industry, was called to obtain the committee's views and recommendations. 

Bakery product ceiling prices now are governed by the General Ceiling 

Price Regulation.

As outlined to the committee members, the tentative regulation provides percentage factors which bakers may apply to base period prices to reflect cost changes, other than for raw materials. 

Changes in raw materials costs would be reflected by pass-through provisions with a minimum of record-keeping requirements. 

OPS officials told the committee that, while the percentage factors would not be announced until the regulation is issued, they were worked out after a representative sampling of the industry.

Agency spokesmen expressed the opinion that the trade would be much better off with OPS factors, which are equitable to all segments of the industry, rather than to have the industry do its own calculating. 

The committee was informed also that OPS proposes to make a special provision for commission sales since it does not appear that a general percentage factor would be feasible in such cases because there is no uniformity of commissions in the industry.

The industry committee recommended that small retail bakers be excluded from the regulation and continue to price under provisions of GCPR. GPO-O-OPS 1693 khu

PRESS RELEASE   

Tempo E 

THURSDAY, January 17, 1952 

Washington 

Crossley-OPS-GFR-1157  

Re: RETAIL LAC 

Progress reports to the Retail Industry Advisory Committee on proposals concerned with reporting requirements, pricing of pre-ticketed brand-name merchandise, a small retailer regulation, freight costs and averaging of prices featured the third meeting of the Office of Price 

Stabilization with retailers today.

In a departure from the usual plan of Industry Advisory Committee meetings, William C. Truppner, an Assistant Director of the National

Production Authority, reported on NPA policies and programs affecting the future supply of consumer durable goods. Mr. Truppner indicated that, as the military stockpiling program gets into full swing in 1952, demand may exceed supply in the consumer durable goods field. This situation may be expected to continue through the first part of 1953, Mr. Truppner added.

In a roundup of actions affecting chain and department stores and new sellers, OPS reported issuance of two amendments, in accordance with IAC recommendations, and indicated issuance in the near future of an action taking into account certain normal internal rearrangements of departments within department stores. 

On Section 53 of Ceiling Price Regulation 7, OPS announced that current reporting requirements will be suspended in the near future. 

Section 53 requires a report of base period initial percentage markups. or gross margins and a current report for the retailer's accounting period whenever the current markups exceed those in the base period. 

These reports were intended as a guide to OPS as to the effectiveness of the retail regulation in controlling margins. As the data have not proved currently useful to OPS, the agency indicated its intention to relieve the trade of the current reporting requirement. 

Reporting on a forthcoming regulation to provide methods and standards of obtaining uniform retail ceiling prices for brand-name merchandise, OPS indicated that the latest revision of this order had been completed and would soon be issued. The agency advised that the forthcoming order will place primary responsibility for notification of price changes and (Over) GPO-O-OPS 1695

for marking and tagging on the manufacturer or wholesaler. As owners of brand names, either manufacturers or wholesalers may set uniform retail ceiling prices in accordance with the coming order. Currently, OPS explained, authority to set uniform retail ceilings on branded merchandise is provided by individual letter order under Section 43 of CPR 7. 

On the work of the Small Retailers' Subcommittee toward a Small Retail Regulation, OPS reported that the agency plans to present various alternative proposals to small merchants at their places of business. 

OPS District Office personnel will be asked to call on small merchants and get their comments and reactions.

On the problem of increased freight costs, especially on furniture, OPS presented four subcommittee recommendations for applying these increases to costs of merchandise. Generally, these methods would involve some sort of averaging device with use of a factor to allocate increased freight costs to articles of merchandise. 

To meet the pricing situation of retailers who receive, at lower cost, merchandise identical with goods inventory, an optional ceiling price averaging method, as worked out by a subcommittee, is proposed for future issuance by OPS. Also, in the draft stage is an amendment to provide an alternative list date for certain seasonal merchandise. 

This proposal would enable a retailer to file an amended price chart setting a base date within the normal selling season for that merchandise. 

Members of the Retail Industry Advisory Committee who were present at today's meeting were the following:

 FRIDAY, January 18, 1952 

Washington 

Barkley-OPS-GPR-1159  Re: RETAIL MEAT TAC 

Plans to include dollars-and-cents ceiling prices for all retail sales of meat in one master regulation were discussed today by officials of the Office of Price Stabilization at a meeting with members of the 

OPS Retail Meat Industry Advisory Committee. 

The committee was called into session to consider proposed regulations establishing specific retail dollars-and-cents ceiling prices for veal, lamb and pork, as well as to obtain from them, their experience under the dollars-and-cents ceilings for retail beef during the last two or three months.

While sales of veal, lamb and pork are under specific dollars-andcents ceilings at the wholesale level, individual retailers now compute their ceilings for their own stores by applying their General Ceiling 

Price Regulation markup to their wholesale costs.

When the retail dollars-and-cents ceilings are issued, retailers will no longer be required to compute their ceilings but will use the OPS prices. Agency spokesmen assured the committee members that these ceilings would meet all the legal requirements of the Defense Production 

Act, as amended. 

As retail ceilings are issued for veal, lamb and pork, OPS officials said the present plan is to put out a master regulation which would include the retail beef ceilings as well as ceilings for the other meats. 

Thus, retailers would operate under a single OPS regulation rather than have a separate regulation for each type of meat.

The committee was told that consideration would be given to the use of different pricing zones for the various meats to conform to sales patterns of the trade.

The retail ceilings will vary according to the distance of the sale from the source of supply and according to groups of stores. This is to allow for transportation costs and the historical differences in margins among various types of retail outlets. 

Representing OPS at the meeting were Arval Erikson, Assistant Director of the Food and Restaurant Division; Irvin L. Rice, Chief, Meat and

MONDAY, January 21, 1952

 Richardson-OPS-GPR-1161 

Re: COSMETICS & TOILETRIES MANUFACTURERS IAC 

At their third meeting today with officials of the Office of Price 

Stabilization, members of the Cosmetics and Toiletries Manufacturers 

Industry Advisory Committee suggested that issuance by OPS of a tailored regulation for the industry be postponed pending further agency development of industry-wide and individual product price adjustment standards. 

The committee discussed current pricing problems under GCPR and stated that current market prices were generally at GCPR ceilings. Most members reported continuing cost increases for raw materials, labor, freight, warehousing and advertising. They pointed out that increases in sales volume in 1951 over 1950 had helped to offset increased direct costs in more or less satisfactory fashion. 

George W. Strasser, Assistant Director, Chemicals and Drugs Division,

OPS, who presided, informed the committee that the agency was studying the problem of price relief on individual products and the development of a product standard.

Most of the session was occupied by a detailed examination of the price control implications of a recent Federal Trade Commission ruling applying to the Cosmetics and Toiletries industry's trade practices. 

The industry members expressed the view that manufacturers' sales promotion allowances which are conditioned upon the performance by the retailer of certain advertising or other services to promote the sale of the product and which are not a part of the contract for the sale of the commodity should not be considered as price differentials within the OPS meaning of the term. 

After a detailed analysis of the several services concerned, OPS promised that due consideration would be given to the views advanced by the industry committee members.

A majority of the industry members lodged a recommendation that the FTC ruling become effective on the date as scheduled, February 1, preferably with a prompt clarification of the OPS press release dated January 17 on the FTC ruling.

Monday, January 21, 1952 Re: 

  CONSUMER ADVISORY COMMITTEE Coakley-OPS-GPR-1162  

The National Consumer Advisory Committee today asked for a statement of policy from officials of the Office of Price Stabilization on the question of setting ceiling prices at figures closer to current market prices.

Members of the committee referred to a recent statement by Edward F. 

Phelps, Jr., Assistant Director of OPS, that "Contrary to widespread gossip, we have no intentions whatsoever of pursuing a general policy of reducing ceilings in the case of most soft market or depressed situations. Such action will be confined to a limited number of commodities where early ceilings have proved clearly excessive and the balance of our efforts will be directed to holding the general level of ceiling prices where it now exists, to the extent consistent with the law or essential supply.' 

Virgil Zimmerman, special assistant to Mr. Phelps said that the statement referred to OPS policy of setting ceilings that are fair and equitable rather than merely seeking to effect rollbacks which might produce distortions and future inequities in the economy.

In explaining why OPS has not, generally, reduced ceilings to the level of present market prices, Mr. Zimmerman said that in some areas prices are lower than those which would yield a fair and equitable level of profits in a normal market. In other areas, he said, they are lower than the minimum which could be established under the Defense Production Act. 

Further, he said, a system of ceiling prices does not work well unless all prices are in line, as they relate to each other, and that a new freeze of present market prices would in most commodity areas lead to distortions and inequities which would need immediate correction. 

The Advisory Committee asked that it be given specific information as to what rollbacks have been effected, what the result has been and what future actions are contemplated so that they can evaluate the price controls program and incorporate the information into educational material for consumers. 

J. Russell Boner, Chief of the Apparel Branch, OPS Consumer Soft Goods 

Division, told the Committee that a tailored regulation covering apparel is being prepared and that its release would be timed to coincide with that of related regulations.

He pointed out that special problems are involved in writing a regulation in this field because of constantly changing styles, materials and similar factors. 

Charles M. Gilbert, Consumer Durable Goods Division spoke on the problem of keeping low-end merchandise on the market under a price control system. He said that currently there is no shortage of these low price items, alothough manufacturers are cutting out items which have a low volume of sales.

TUESDAY, January 22, 1952   

Re: DOUGLAS FIR DOOR IAC 

Moore-OPS-GPR-1163  

Provisions of a proposed tailored regulation for their industry were discussed today by members of the Douglas Fir Door Industry Advisory Committee at their first meeting with OPS officials.

It is proposed to spell out dollars-and-cents ceilings on standard grades and dimensions of doors, including house doors, cupboard doors, French and rim doors, garage doors, solid exterior doors and hollow core doors. The regulation would cover manufacturers in the Pacific Northwest Douglas fir area. 

Committeemen recommended that doors made of hemlock, spruce and certain other fir species be included in the regulation for doors made of Douglas fir, which is the predominant species. Members suggested that the regulation be drafted especially for manufacturers, and that resellers be covered by other regulations.

Committeemen checked over in detail provisions of MPR 44, the war-time Office of Price Administration regulation covering such doors, which they said would provide a logical pattern for a new regulation. Committeemen reported that the industry was still pricing by discounts applied to the basic price lists set up by the old regulation. They suggested that prices in the new regulation be determined by specified discounts applied to the same basic prices. 

The problem of pricing hollow core doors, because of the lack of uniform industry-wide specifications, was discussed.

Committeemen said it would not be realistic to determine ceilings on doors before ceilings are fixed on the raw materials, plywood and shop lumber. They said even if OPS fixes ceilings on these materials, as planned, at approximately the levels prevailing under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, their GCPR ceilings on doors would still not cover recent increases in labor costs. 

The meeting was conducted by Norman O. Cruver, chief of the Lumber and 

Wood Products Branch, and Glen Converse, chief of the Millwork Section, OPS.

PRESS RELEASE

'ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Afternoon Papers MONDAY, January 28, 1952 

Washington Cole-OPS-GPR-1164 

Re: SERVICE TRADES INJUNCTIONS FILED 

Approximately 75 injunctive actions have been filed by the Office of Price Stabilization against service trades establishments throughout the country, for failure to keep and file records and reports as required by Ceiling Price Regulation 34, Edward P. Morgan, OPS Director of Enforcement, stated today.

Service trades establishments, according to Mr. Morgan, have thus far paid to the United States Treasury more than $60,000 in single, double and treble damages as a result of overcharges, and have also made restitution to customers in the amount of approximately $140,000. 

Among those making restitution were two New York banks, which repaid nearly $78,000, and a Maryland oil burner service firm which paid back approximately $36,000.

Preliminary reports received in Washington, as a result of the 

CPR 34 compliance survey, indicate that, while the initial filing of reports was very low, the survey activities and the institution of court injunctive actions have resulted in greatly increased filings. 

To date more than 130 cases have been referred to the Department of Justice with recommendation that injunctions be sought against the alleged delinquent service establishments. Similar action is contemplated against more than 425 other concerns, Mr. Morgan said.

Of the 75 injunctive actions already filed in the U.S. District 

Courts, the requested injunctions already have been granted in 16 cases, according to Mr. Morgan. The remainder are expected to be acted upon, shortly. 

Injunctive actions have been instituted in Buffalo and Rochester, N. Y., Raleigh, N. C., Atlanta, Ga., Memphis, Tenn., Jacksonville, Fla., Fargo, N. D., Duluth, Minn., Wichita, Kans., Green Bay, Wis., Helena, Mont., Tulsa, Okla., and San Francisco, Calif. The filing of a number of similar actions in other cities throughout the United States is expected shortly, Mr. Morgan stated. He did not elaborate. 

The compliance survey of establishments coming under the service trades regulation, CFR 34, has already had a good effect in that it has not only stimulated an awareness of the existing regulation on (Over) GPO-O-OPS 1732

BRAZ HOT 

the part of many who had not yet filed, but it has resulted in mumerous establishments rolling back their prices and making restitution to customers or payments to the United States Treasury, the enforcement chief said.

Service establishments are required under CPR 34 to post a statement of their ceiling prices in a conspicuous place, and to file a copy of it with the OPS District Office within a 30-day period. They are required to keep records showing the prices, rates or pricing methods used during the base period, and to make them available to 

OPS agents for inspection.

Service trades against which OPS has already taken injunctive action include laundries and dry cleaning establishments, garages and service stations, jewelers, watch repairers and camera supply firms, shoe repair and hat cleaning shops, and radio and television firms, the agency said.
