WEDNESDAY, January 23, 1952 Re: 

PAPER NAPKIN IAC Moore-OPS-GPR-1167  

Members of the Paper Napkin Industry Advisory Committee, at their first meeting with OPS officials today, expressed belief that the use of industrywide percentage cost adjustment factors was the only practical method of price regulation to employ in a tailored regulation for their industry. 

They favored the development of such factors, which each manufacturer would apply to his ceiling prices established under The General Ceiling 

Price Regulation, GCPR. 

Committeemen said there was such a lack of uniformity in the products of the industry that it would be impractical to attempt to spell out dollarsand-cents ceilings on a list of standard products, or even on certain key items. 

OPS officials reported that manufacturers had filed Forms 8 under the 

Manufacturers' General Ceiling Price Regulation, CFR 22, covering about half of the industry's production, which totals $50,000,000 in value annually. 

These forms showed that manufacturers who reported were entitled to price increases under CPR 22 of from three to 15 percent over their GCPR prices, with the average around seven percent. 

However, it was brought out that only a few CPR 22 prices had been put into effect, and that prices generally remained at the GCPR level. 

Committeemen explained this was due to competitive conditions, and because prices had been soft in the face of substantial reductions in inventories of distributors. Those who filed new CPR 22 ceilings, they said, were unable to obtain them if some competitors continued selling at GCPR ceilings, as was generally the case. 

Committeemen expressed the opinion that separate factors should be developed for different categories. However, because of the lack of uniformity of their products, there was some question as to the definition of the categories which should be established. 

The following four general categories were discussed: Packaged regular household items, packaged multi-ply and specialty items, bulk regular items and bulk multi-ply and specialty items. (over)

GPO-O-OPS 1733

A subcommittee was named to study the definition of categories and work with OPS officials on a tentative draft of a tailored regulation. 

Committeemen pointed out they were facing additional cost increases since the cut-off dates provided for in CPR 22, and prior to the cut-off date of July 26, 1951, as provided for in the Capehart Amendment to the Defense Production Act. They also said that the ceiling price of papers used in the manufacture of paper napkins "logically" should be stabilized before new ceilings are fixed for napkins. They pointed out that their suppliers were not obtaining generally the maximum prices for paper to which they were en titled under CPR 22. 

Committeemen reported a substantial part of the production in their industry was by non-integrated converters who purchased their paper from paper manufacturers.

They suggested, also, that the sale and lease of dispensing machines used in their business should be controlled in the regulation covering the products made by them.

WEDNESDAY, January 23, 1952 Re: 

Tempo E- 

Washington G Richardson-OPS-GPR-1168  PHARMACEUTICAL DRUG MANUFACTURERS LAC 

Meeting today for the third time with officials of the Office of Price 

Stabilization, members of the Pharmaceutical Drugs Manufacturers Industry 

Advisory Committee reported that the industry's situation is such that issuance of a tailored regulation for the industry is not necessary at this time. They declared their willingness to remain under the General Ceiling Price Regulation, GCPR. 

In the discussion of pricing problems under GCPR, it developed that current market prices generally were at GCPR ceilings, except for reductions below ceilings in the case of a few products such as antibiotics. Industry members said that their major problem has been the increasing cost of labor and in some areas the increased cost of such items as glass ampules and corrugated containers. 

The committee advised that GOR 20 and GOR 21 would have virtually no effect upon current price ceilings for pharmaceutical drugs since these regulations recognized cost increases only to July 26, 1951, and required manufacturers to make their calculations on a category basis. Such relief as this industry required was on individual products rather than on product categories. 

Industry members explained that a more specific definition of the term "category" in a manner generally acceptable to the industry, would present difficulty because of the great disparities in number and types of products handled by the firms in the industry as well as their widely different methods of production. This problem was left open for further study and comment by committee members.

Members explained that the industry market prices have been relatively constant, as pharmaceutical products do not generally fluctuate as they do in certain other basic industries. 

A sad note was struck at the meeting by announcement that Robert C. Gasen, one of the committee members, had met his death in the air liner crash yesterday at Elizabeth, N. J. Mr. Gasen, Treasurer, Bristol Laboratories, Syracuse, N. Y., was en route to today's meeting aboard the ill-fated plane. He had attended both previous meetings of the committee.

Other OPS officials present at the meetings: Thomas H. McCormack, Director, Rubber, Chemicals and Drug Division; Hugh Weisberger, Division Economist; Eugenia 

Keller, Branch Economist; Joseph P. Folsom, chief, Drug, Cosmetics and Perfume

WEDNESDAY, January 23, 1952  Hughes-OPS-GPR-1170 

WHOLESALE CONSUMER (SMALL) DURABLE GOODS TAC WHOLESALE CONSUMER (LARGE) DURABLE GOODS LAC 

Representatives of wholesalers in the consumer durable goods fields met today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss a proposed wholesale price regulation. The proposed regulation would supplant the General Ceiling 

Price Regulation (CCPR) and Supplementary Regulation 29 to the GCPR which now govern pricing in the industry.

The occasion was a joint meeting of the Wholesale Consumer (Small) Durable 

Goods Industry Advisory Committee and the Wholesale Consumer (Large) Durable Goods Industry Advisory Committee. Chairman of the meeting was Lester A. Ferguson, Chief, Wholesale and Central Pricing Branch, Consumer Goods Distribution, Textile and Apparel Division. 

In their introductory remarks, OPS officials pointedout that wholesaling in the consumer goods industry represents an enormous volume. Some 43,000 wholesalers in the field do an annual volume of business of approximately $32 billion. Lines handled are of extremely diverse types, and there are great variations in operating methods, types of outlets, accounting systems, warehousing, and the like. 

There are many small wholesalers in the industry, often with elementary accounting methods.

These differences, it was pointed out, pose many problems in the drafting of an effective regulation fair to all elements of the industry. 

The proposed regulation, OPS officials said, would cover all commodities customarily considered to be consumer soft goods, large durable goods, and small durable goods. All goods within the general classification of such goods would be included, except foods, certain forest products, imported articles, antiques, petroleum products, drugs and chemicals, industrial machinery and other commodities now or hereafter specifically covered by other regulations. 

The proposed regulation would be a margin type regulation, giving each wholesaler his own historic markups by categories of goods. The pricing chart technique would be used. The chart would be similar in principle to the pricing chart provided in the retail regulation, Ceiling Price Regulation 7. That is, the wholesaler would show on his chart what his goods cost him as of a designated base period, what he sold them for, and what his margin was between cost and selling price. This procedure would establish his allowable margins for pricing goods currently. 

A major difference between the chart proposed in the wholesale regulation and the charts used under CPR 7 would be that the wholesaler would establish his own categories, rather than to use categories prescribed in the regulation. GPO-O-OPS 1734 wwwww

Discussion of the proposed regulation brought out four main industry viewpoints: 

1. Committee members were unanimous in their feeling that a pricing chart requirement should be avoided if at all possible. In view of the thousands of items handled, it was said, the preparation and use of a chart would impose a heavy burden on individual sellers. 

2. In connection with the question of a suitable base period, most committee members expressed their belief that the base period established in the GCPR--December 19, 1950 through January 25, 1951--would be preferable to a current base period. 

3. Committee members expressed doubt that one regulation to govern all wholesaling in the consumer goods fields can be successfully devised and administered. It was suggested that instead of a single regulation, there might be several covering different fields. It was suggested, for example, that there might be separate regulations for hardware and furniture. 

4. There was general agreement among committee members that landed costs should be the basis for computing chart markups and for determining current ceiling prices. This question arose in relation to statements by OPS officials present that the treatment of freight in arriving at costs was one involving general agency policy.

Some committee members also expressed concern over an OPS proposal that two separate wholesale regulations--one for small wholesalers and one for large concerns--might be issued. Fears were expressed that this would put large operators at a disadvantage, since pricing by small companies might be more loosely controlled. OPS officials explained, however, that there would simply be a difference in techniques, and that certainly the agency would not be disposed to put any segment of the industry at a competitive disadvantage. 

At the conclusion of the meeting the Chairman expressed the Agency's appreciation for the cooperative spirit uniformly in evidence at the meeting, and for the valuable information which had been gained by all present. All industry viewpoints will be carefully weighed, he said, before final decisions are reached.

The Chairman expressed the hope that similar good results will come from the meeting with representatives of wholesalers in the consumer soft goods fields which OPS has scheduled for Friday, January 25. 

OPS officials present, in addition to Chairman Ferguson, included: Thomas 

Karsten, Division Director; M. L. Chandross, Assistant Director; Harold D. Cohen, Division Counsel; Charles H. Sevin, Division Economist; Philip J. Hummel, Acting

Chief, Wholesale Section; Bernard A. Goodkind, Chief Counsel, Distribution Branch; 

Robert J. Rosthal and Howard E. Smith, Jr., of Distribution Branch counsel; Milton 

A. Kolar, wholesale consultant; Maurice C. Piatt, business analyst, Wholesale Section; 

Paul Guggenheim, economist, Apparel Branch; Reuben Losner, assistant branch counsel, Retail and Wholesale Branch; and William R. Thomas from the Office for Industry

Advisory Committees.

Re: AUTOMOTIVE REPLACEMENT PARTS MANUFACTURERS TAC Members of the Automotive Replacement Parts Manufacturers Industry Advisory 

Committee met with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization today. to discuss further the pricing practices in the automotive parts industry and the problems involved in developing tailored ceiling price regulations for that industry. The industry, comprising about 2,000 separate manufacturers, to a large extent, is still operating under Ceiling Price Regulation 30 (Machinery and Related Manufactured Goods). 

Today's meeting was the fourth which the Committee has held with OPS officials, the last being on November 10.

Committeemen urged OPS today to continue to study the problems in the industry as a result of pricing under CPR 30 before issuing any additional ceiling price regulations. 

OPS agreed to develop further statistics concerning cost increases in the industry, and to confer again with industry representatives before taking further pricing actions. It was announced that a subcommittee appointed from the over-all group would again confer with CPS in the near future to continue discussions concerning the pricing problems within the industry. 

Although no definite agreement was reached today on several proposals laid before the Committee, discussion did revolve around an optional method which would permit individual manufacturers to continue to reflect in their ceiling prices the provisions of the so-called Capehart amendment to the Defense Production Act. 

This method would be of particular benefit to those manufacturers who have not already filed for Capehart adjustments under existing OPS regulations. Under this proposed pricing method, manufacturers' ceiling prices would be their pre-Korean prices plus a fixed percentage increase for each special category of automotive parts. Such percentage increase factors would be developed by OPS. 

(Over)

Re: VITREOUS CHINA PLUMBING FIXTURES TAG Members of the Vitreous China Plumbing Fixtures Industry Advisory Committee today asked the Office of Price Stabilization to establish an industry-wide price adjustment to be applied to ceilings established by the industry under the General 

Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR). 

Currently, the industry is pricing under the general manufacturers' Ceiling 

Price Regulation 22 (CPR 22). 

Committeemen pointed out that this industry, like other segments of the plumbing supply industry, has historically maintained a uniform pricing pattern as between products and among producers, and that this uniform price relationship prevailed during the GCPR base period December 19, 1950, to January 25, 1951. 

They said that industry pricing under CPR 22, as between individual companies, has caused a serious distortion of the historical price relationship within the industry. This situation, they said, has resulted in a disruption of normal distribution and has caused many buyers to withhold orders because of the uncertain and fluctuating price structure. 

The committee asked that the industry be permitted to use ceilings established under the GCPR pending the establishment by OPS of an industry-wide price adjustment factor.

Members stressed the urgency of the situation and asked that OPS take appropriate action as quickly as possible.

Officials told the committee that OPS would ask the industry for sales and price data for the GCPR base period and would review this data in relation to data submitted by the industry in the filing of OPS Public Form No. 8 under 

CFR 22. It will then be possible, officials said, for OPS to determine an appropriate basis for an industry-wide price adjustment in relation to GCPR ceilings. 

The meeting was conducted by Walter H.

Acheson, chief, Building Materials 

Branch, OPS. 

Other OPS officials attending were: Irving Rubenstein, branch economist;

HOUD BY Re: LOCAL CONSUMER ADVISORY COMMITTEE PROGRAM A Local Consumer Advisory Committee Program is being initiated on a test basis by the Office of Price Stabilization as part of the OPS Consumer Re-3000 lations Program, Michael V. DiSalle, Price Stabilization Director, announced today. Ten pilot cities have been selected for the test. boos OPS has been working on such a program for some time, Mr. DiSalle said. 

The project was recommended by the OPS National Consumer Advisory Committee which will cooperate in setting up the local committees. 

The pilot cities, selected to give as wide a range as possible for the test are: 

Fresno, Calif.; Fargo, N. D.; Jacksonville, Fla.; Los Angeles, Calif.; Spokane, Wash.; Salt Lake City, Utah; Detroit, Mich.; Cincinnati, Ohio; Binghamton, N. Y.; and Hartford, Conn.

The test group includes cities in which there are OPS District Offices and one without a District Office; a small city, large cities and a metropolitan area; and in the case of Hartford, Conn., an entire OPS District which is co-extensive with the State and covers large, medium and small cities, rural and semi-rural areas. Fresno, Fargo and Jacksonville also are pilot cities for the OPS community pricing project.

The objective of the Local Consumer Advisory Committee pilot program is to work out a more effective mechanism for assuring that the consumer has a full understanding of price stabilization as part of the National Defense Program and for providing the consumer with a channel through which to comment on the program, advise on it and assist in its implementation, Mr. DiSalle said. The committee will act in an advisory capacity to the District Director and submit its recommendations and a report of its activities to him. 

Cooperating with the District Offices, the consumer advisory committees will assist cooperating organizations and other groups to hold meetings, forums, debates and competitions on the subject of stabilization and the defense program. Another function will be to assist the District Directors in fostering cooperation between the community and OPS. 

Size of a committee is left to the discretion of the District Director, but will include persons nominated by the organizations cooperating with the National Consumer Advisory Committee, in addition to persons nominated by local organizations interested in consumer problems. OPS expects to make 

(Over) GPO-0-OPS 1740

GSD  each committee representative of a cross section of the community, including various income levels, religious and minority groups. 

Members may be nominated by the cooperating organizations but will be appointed by the District Director and serve on the committee as individuals rather than as representatives of the nominating organizations. 

In Spokane, Salt Lake City, Detroit and Binghamton, volunteer committees already exist, although not all of them are exclusively consumer committees. 

Some contain representatives of business and industry as well as consumer groups and it is proposed that these will set up sub-committees of exclusively consumer interest representatives to participate in the pilot test. # # # # # # #

Re: CAST BRASS PLUMBING FIXTURES LAC Members of the Cast Brass Plumbing Fixtures Industry Advisory Committee met for the first time today with officials of the Office of Price Stabilization to discuss industry pricing problems.

Committeemen pointed out some of the operating difficulties with which they said the industry is currently confronted. The industry, generally, has had to cut-back on production because of reductions in the allocation of raw materials ranging as high as 73 percent. On the other hand, distribution channels are buying on a hand-to-mouth basis because of the uncertainty of demand due to reported and contemplated restrictions on construction and housing, and due to the uncertainty and fluctuation in prices caused by recent industry ceiling price changes under the general manufacturers' Ceiling Price Regulation 22.

With respect to pricing, members said that the industry has historically maintained a uniform price relationship pattern as between products and between producers. They said this historical pattern is generally reflected in ceilings established by the industry under the General Ceiling Price Regulation (GCPR). 

However, they said that pricing under CPR 22 has resulted in a serious distortion of the industry's historical pricing pattern, both as between products and as between companies. This has resulted in a demoralized pricing situation within the industry, causing buyers to withhold orders and generally disrupting normal distribution. 

It was the concensus of the committee that the application of an industrywide price adjustment factor to GCPR ceilings would alleviate the current pricing difficulty and restore the normal historical industry pricing pattern. 

OPS officials told the committee that the industry will be asked to furnish detailed sales and price data in relation to GCPR sales and prices. These data will be reviewed in connection with data furnished by the industry in its filing of OPS Public Form 8 in establishing ceilings under CPR 22. With this information at hand OPS will consider the desirability of establishing an industry-wide price adjustment factor to be applied to GCPR ceiling prices as established in the industry.

A sub-committee will be appointed to advise with OPS in this connection. 

The meeting was conducted by Walter H. Acheson, chief, Building Materials 

Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: Lee M. Keller, business analyst; 

D. M. Fishbein, economist; H. R. Gluck, legal staff; J. A. Murray, accountant; 

P. C. Roots, economist; and Harry Spack, Office for Industry Advisory Committees.

Tempo E-Washington Scott-OPS-GPR-1175 TUBULAR BRASS PLUMBING GOODS TAC 

The Tubular Brass Plumbing Goods Industry Advisory Committee today asked the 

Office of Price Stabilization to develop a tailored pricing regulation for the industry.

Committee members told OPS officials that the industry generally is confronted with an extremely abnormal pricing and operating situation. 

They said the industry is suffering from a substantial cut-back in allocation of raw materials and a limitation on production of many items, as imposed by the 

National Production Authority. They pointed 

They pointed out that the NPA limitation has resulted in the elimination of production of many profitable items, leaving the remaining production largely on low-end-profit items which are essential to the civilian and defense economy. This situation, they said, has placed the industry in a depressed pricing, operating and profit position. 

Pricing under the general manufacturers' Ceiling Price Regulation 22 (CPR 22), and the so-called Capehart Amendment, does not give the industry pricing relief because of a depressed industry price position during the pre-Korea base period, particularly with respect to low-end-profit items, members said. 

It was the consensus of the committee that an industry-wide price adjustment factor based on CPR 22 criteria would not give the industry relief and the committee recommended that OPS make a survey of the industry's pricing position with a view towards developing an appropriate tailored pricing regulation. 

Officials told the committee that such an industry survey will be proposed and that a subcommittee will be appointed to advise with OPS in this connection. 

The meeting was conducted by Walter H. Acheson, chief, Building Materials 

Branch, OPS. Other OPS officials attending were: Lee M. Keller, business analyst; 

David M. Fishbein and Peter C. Roots, economists; Harry R. Gluck, legal staff; 

Joseph A. Murray, accountant; and Harry Spack, Office for Indus try Advisory Committees. # # # # # # #

PRESS RELEASE   ADVANCED RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers TUESDAY, January 29, 1952 

Cole-OPS-GPR-1176  

Re: ROUNDUP OF LUMBER PAYMENTS, COURT ACTIONS 

Payment to the United States Treasury of $6,086.05 by the Brunswick Lumber

Company of Alberts, Va., as a result of overceiling charges to its customers, was announced today by Edward P. Morgan, national Enforcement Director for the 

Office of Price Stabilization. 

The payment by the Brunswick lumber firm, a manufacturer and wholesaler, represents one and one quarter times the overcharges, according to Mr. Morgan. 

Two other firms, the Builders Lumber and Supply Company of Villa Platte, La., and Chandler Wrecking Company of Memphis, Tenn., have paid $232.50 and $200, respectively, to the U. S. Treasury, which amounts were more than the actual overcharges. The Louisiana firm's check was accepted by the Department of 

Justice, with OPS concurrence, after injunctive action had been filed. 

At Raleigh, N. C., consent orders and judgment for injunctions have been entered in the U. S. District Court in the cases of several lumber companies charged by OPS with failure to maintain records at the actual place of operations rather than in another state where company headquarters may be located. 

Included in this group are the Mills Lumber Company, Aurora, N. C.; C. 

Warren Waters Company, Pinetown, N. C.; and Orvie B. Alligood Co., Washington,

N. C. 

The Bate Lumber Company of Newburg, N. C., has also signed a consent order. A similar case against the Roper Milling Company of Roper, N. C., has been continued to January 31, at the request of the defendant. 

OPS is seeking treble damages of over $21,000 in an injunctive action filed in the U. S. District Court at Tallahassee, Fla., against Clark Howard Belvin, doing business as the C. H. Belvin Lumber Company of Thomasville, Ga. OPS charges the firm, a wholesaler, with more than 125 overceiling sales. 

Substantial damages for overcharges and injunctions are also sought in three actions filed in the U. S. District Court at Norfolk. The defendants are: W. C. 

Barnes Lumber Company, Suffolk, Ga., more than 190 overceiling sales totaling $3,889.63; Thomas E. Coale Lumber Company, Norfolk, Va., overceiling charges totaling $2, 546.86; and the S. E. Barnes Lumber Company, Suffolk, Ga., over 

330 overceiling charges totaling $2,804.60. Treble damages are sought in all 

Hearings are scheduled for February 18 at Norfolk. three cases.

Washington WILLIAM P. DRAKE APPOINTMENT 

William P. Drake, Vice President of the Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Co.,

Philadelphia, has been named Director of the Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division of the Office of Price Stabilization, OPS Director Michael V. DiSalle announced today. Coakley-OPS-GPR-1177  

The new director succeeds Thomas H.

McCormack who is returning to his duties as Director of Sales of the Grasselli Chemicals Division, E. I. duPont de Nemours. 

& Co., Wilmington, Del. 

Mr. Drake will serve as director until next July 1, Mr. DiSalle said. 

As "Pennsalt" Vice President in Charge of Sales, Mr. Drake has headed the chemical company's mine sales departments which serve a great many of the nation's industries. He joined the company in 1934 in its student training course. Then, successively, he was a salesman, a manager of sales, and assistant vice president in charge of sales, before his appointment as vice president in 1949. 

Mr. Drake is a member of the Manufacturing Chemists Association, the American 

Electroplaters Society, the Armed Forces Chemical Association, the Midday Club of 

Philadelphia and Psi Upsilon. He is a director of the Main Belting Co., Philadelphia. He is a vestryman of St. David's Episcopal Church, Radnor, Pa.

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers MONDAY, January 28, 1952 RE: 

COMMUNITY PRICING TEST PROGRAM BEGINS 

Ceiling price posters listing dollars-and-cents ceilings for many standard grocery items will be put up Monday morning, January 28, in three areas where the Office of Price Stabilization is testing a "community food pricing" program, the agency announced today. 

The three test areas are Fargo, North Dakota; Fresno, California, and

Jacksonville, Florida. Posters will be on the walls in all stores in the three areas at the opening of business on Monday morning. 

In the Fargo area, the smallest of the three areas, posters will be in 123 retail food stores. Four hundred and fifty-one stores are included in the Fresno program, and 1,566 in the larger Jacksonville area.

The ceiling price posters will list the maximum price that grocers may charge for between 350 and 400 "dry" grocery items, plus butter and packaged cheese.

While grocers may always charge less, they may not legally charge more than the price listed on the poster. 

The posters have been prepared and printed by OPS. The main distribution is taking place by mail from the Regional Office for the test area (Minneapolis for the Fargo area; San Francisco for the Fresno area, and Atlanta for the

Jacksonville area). Additional copies of the posters may be had at the District 

Offices in the test cities.

Under the test program, grocers no longer figure their own ceiling prices for the items listed on the poster. This is done for them by the local OPS District 

Office. For some time these offices have been making surveys to determine representative wholesale prices. To these wholesale prices the OPS office has applied the standard retail markups fixed in the OPS grocery regulations. The resulting ceiling prices are printed on separate posters for each store group recognized in the grocery regulations. These groups range from the smallest stores to the largest chains and supermarkets.

The program is called "community pricing" because it fixes a community-wide price for each grocery item. This price is the same in all stores in the same store grouping.

GPO--O-OPS 1752

Reports from OPS District offices in the test areas indicate great local interest in the test program. Wholesalers and retailers, individually and through their representatives, have given whole-hearted cooperation, it is reported. Many retailers express the opinion that the program will relieve them of considerable work in computing their own ceiling prices, and will improve their relations with customers, since it will eliminate unfounded suspicion of over-ceiling charges. 

Housewives have aldo received the program with enthusiasm. Now, for the first time, they will know definitely what the maximum legal prices are for many of their market basket foods.

During the test program a limited number of items will be on the ceiling price posters. These, generally, will be items which are of greatest importance in the cost of living, and which are selling at or near the ceiling price. 

New posters will be printed and displayed every two weeks, to take into account any changes in wholesale prices which may have occurred. If any such changes are necessary within the two-week period, these will be printed on postcards or sheets which the grocer can attach to his ceiling price posters. 

Grocers are required to post one ceiling price chart for each 1500 square feet of selling space. The charts must be put up in such a way as to be easily read, and so that customers can come within two feet of them. 

The principal purpose of the test program, OPS said, is to discover whether community pricing if feasible under present conditions. If it develops that there now is sufficient stability in grocery prices to make the program feasible and desirable, consideration will be given to extending it to other areas and perhaps throughout the nation.

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers 

MONDAY, January 28, 1952

 Tempo E-Washington Re: SEPARATE PARCEL POST CHARGE ON SHIPMENTS TO RETAILERS Crossley OPS GPR-1179 

The Office of Price Stabilization today provided an official ruling on a proposal by the National Association of Shirt, Pajama and Sportswear Manufacturers to make a separate charge to retailers for parcel post shipments, reflecting the recent increase in postal rates.

The ruling is contained in a letter of January 25, 1952 to 

M.J. Lovell, Executive Director of the National Association, from

Harold D. Cohen, Assistant Chief Counsel, OPS. 

Mr. M. J. Lovell

The National Association of Shirt, Pajama & Sportswear Mfrs. 

276 Fifth Avenue 

Dear Mr. Lovell:

In brief, OPS indicated that if a manufacturer's current selling price for an article is below ceiling, he may increase his selling price, for any cost increases, within the ceiling. However, the agency emphasized, the manufacturer who did not charge separately for parcel post shipments during the base period may not separately state a charge for packaging in addition to the price for the article.

The complete text of the letter follows: 

I have your letter of Jamary 8, 1952, in which you request an interpretation of the General Ceiling Price Regulation and Ceiling Price 

Regulation 45, Rev. 1, on the following question: "Where pursuant to Federal legislation enacted after manufacturers' pricing regulations, limiting the size and weight of a parcel post package, it now becomes necessary to use more cartons in making the same size of shipment than was formerly required, may a manufacturer (a) charge for the additional cartons and handling, (b) charge for all of the cartons and handling?"

GPO-O-OPS 1751

At a conference with representatives of this Agency on January 4, 1952, you stated the following: At all times prior to January 1, 1952, the mamufacturer made no separate charge for preparing articles ordered for shipment. 

Whether a purchaser requested that the articles he ordered be shipped by parcel post, freight, express or any other means, the mamfacturer prepared these articles for shipment without making any charge, other than his prices for the articles, to cover cartons and handling. Now that recent postal regulations have reduced the permitted size and weight of parcel post packages, the manufacturer will have to use more cartons and incur additional handling costs in making parcel post shipment of the same mumber of articles as he formerly was able to ship in one carton. He wishes to recover his additional costs in making such a shipment by making a separate charge for some or all of the additional cartons and handling costs involved. 

This is to advise you that if the manufacturer's current selling price for an article is below his ceiling price, he is at liberty to increase the former to an amount not in excess of his ceiling price, whether he wishes to do so to compensate for additional handling costs or for any other reason. 

It must be emphasized, however, that the manufacturer may not separately state a charge for packaging in addition to the price for the article. That is, any expense which he may incur in preparing articles for shipment must be covered by the selling price. He may not make any separate charge for cartons or handling, regardless of whether that charge would cover all cartons and handling or only the additional cartons and handling involved in operating under the new postal regulations.

The 

The manufacturer's ceiling price for an article, both under the GCPR and CPR 45, Rev. 1, includes all services which he customarily included with the articles in the base period; and it appears that during the base period of both regulations the manufacturer included in his price the service of packaging for parcel post shipment, and made no special charge for it. 

GCPR contains no provision for increasing a ceiling price to compensate for increased costs since the base period. CPR 45, Rev. 1, does permit adjustment of base period prices to reflect changes in indirect material and labor costs, but such adjustments are confined to changes in cost which occurred between the base period prescribed date and March 15, 1951, in the case of labor, and June 4, 1951 in the case of materials; the permitted adjustments will have been included in the manufacturer's calculated ceiling price, and further adjustments are prohibited.

This interpretation is limited, of course, to our understanding, as stated above, of the facts supplied by you. If I can be of further assistance, please do not hesitate to call upon me. 

Very truly yours, eurod 

Bow Brand

Harold D. Cohen Assistant Chief Counsel, OPS Division Counsel, Consumer Soft Goods Division

January 25, 1952 Re: enforcement.

  UNDERWEAR, LINGERIE AND NEGLIGEE IAC 

Discussing a proposed regulation to cover women's outerwear and underwear manufacturers, the Office of Price Stabilization today suggested to the Underwear, Lingerie and Negligee Industry Advisory Committee an alternative highest price. line limitation offering advantages from the standpoint of use, administration and Generally, OPS explained, the highest price line limitation is a means of encouraging the continued manufacture of relatively inexpensive articles by the provision of more liberal markups on articles priced below the highest priced articles. 

Crossley-OPS-GPR-1180 

OPS suggested that the period from February 28, 1951 to February 29, 1952 might be considered for determination of highest price lines. This period could be broken down to arrive at spring and fall highest price lines. For each selling season for garments in separate categories and made of different basic fabrics, a manufacturer would find the highest price line at which he delivered. In the sense that this suggestion would not permit a pass-through of actual cost increases on each line, it would represent a so-called "absolute" highest price line limitation. 

Committeemen generally favored the tentative proposal, although they felt that some provision should be made for increasing the highest price where basic fabric costs reached ceiling.

In addition to the highest price line feature, the proposed regulation arrives at an historic markup for manufacturers through use of a ratio of base period direct costs to net sales, known as a "division factor". There was considerable discussion as to whether manufacturers should be required to average out to this division factor once or twice a year. OPS felt that effective price control required that the industry should average out twice a year. 

Presiding at today's meeting was Jules Walder, head, Women's Wear Section Apparel Branch, Consumer Goods Distribution, Textiles and Apparel Division, OPS.

Members of the Proprietary Drug Manufacturers Industry Advisory Committee, at their third meeting with OPS officials today, recommended that agency consideration be given to some liberalization of regulatory provisions applying to their industry. They pointed out that, due to historical peculiarities native to proprietary drugs, certain provisions of GOR 20 and GOR 21 make it impractical for them to file for price adjustment under the Capehart formula. 

Industry representatives estimated that sales for the industry as a whole have increased as much as 10 to 15 percent since the pre-Korean period. However, they said, sales of certain items such as antihistamines have declined. They added that the industry today is faced with rising costs of raw materials, labor, freight, advertising etc., which have increased an over-all average of 65 percent since December 31, 1944. (Over) They expressed the belief that GOR 20 and GOR 21 furnish little possibility for price relief for them because of the difficulty of determining categories of their products. Accordingly, they requested an amendment to the General Ceiling 

Price Regulation, GCPR, to permit adjustment of their ceilings on an individual branded commodity basis. 

The industry members declared that with provision for such an adjustment applications for relief would be received by OPS only for a limited number of products in their line which have been caught in a costs squeeze. They explained that they are committed to absorb certain cost increases in their advertised brand products because of competitive market conditions.

FRIDAY, January 25, 1952 

Washington EAST COAST DISTILLATES 

Coakley-OPS-GPR-1183  

Michael V. DiSalle, Director of Price Stabilization, today told the Petroleum Administration for Defense that the Office of Price Stabilization could not accept the PAD recommendation that ceiling prices for middle distillates (including kerosene, No. 2 fuel oil and diesel oil) on the East Coast be increased by amounts ranging from four-tenths to six-tenths of a cent per gallon. Roger 

Putnam, Administrator for Economic Stabilization Agency, concurs in the decision, Mr. DiSalle said in a letter to Bruce K. Brown, Deputy Administrator of PAD. "This conclusion does not reflect any determination upon our part that there "To be sure, is no threat of shortage on the East Coast," Mr. DiSalle wrote. 

I am informed that the latest report shows East Coast fuel oil inventories 31.8 percent above those of a year ago. Likewise, we have been assured by several of the so-called independents that they can see no threat of shortage, although a few of their competitors may have gambled unwisely in accepting contracts in excess of their supply commitments. Nevertheless, we must accept your determination that a shortage remains a possibility, in the event of colder weather in the remaining months of the heating season. "Our conclusion rests, rather, upon the view that the price increase which you propose is both an inefficient and costly way of solving whatever shortage problem may develop. This agency obviously cannot rule out the occasional use of But in price adjustments to achieve some production or distribution objective. view of the mandate which we have been given to strive for the maximum stabilization of prices, we can use price increases for supply reasons only where it is clear that there is no reasonable alternative means to achieve the supply objective." 

Mr. DiSalle pointed out that, in this case, alternative means are available. 

These include the powers of allocation and direction, and, in addition, the authority, where necessary, for the government to buy and resell, or to subsidize private transactions. These powers are conferred by the Defense Production Act. 

Mr. DiSalle said that officials of OPS had made certain proposals to PAD along these lines and had offered their services to PAD to help work out effective arrangements. PAD is now considering these suggestions, but, Mr. DiSalle indicated, further announcement on these matters would have to be made by the supply agency. GPO-O-OPS 1757

GPR 

East Coast Distillates 

TRIMINAL 

Increasing the ceiling prices of distillates one-half cent per gallon would mean an additional cost to East Coast fuel oil consumers, for the remainder of this heating season, amounting to more than $14,000,000 even if milder-thannormal weather entirely eliminated the shortage threat. The threatened shortage would amount roughly to a six day's supply Mr. DiSalle pointed out and stated that a $14,000,000 increase seems a high price to pay on what is at best an estimate.

ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers SUNDAY, January 27, 1952  

McClanahan-OPS-GPR-1184  

DISALLE STATEMENT ON THE ANNIVERSARY OF THE GENERAL CEILING PRICE REGULATION 

Price Stabilization Director Michael V. DiSalle today issued the following statement as OPS marked the first anniversary of the General Ceiling Price Regu lation. 

The General Ceiling Price Regulation, freezing most prices at levels then prevailing, was ordered by the Office of Price Stabilization one year ago today. 

It is gratifying to realize that, after a full year of operating under our price control system, the cost of living has been held to a very moderate increase.

The latest Bureau of Labor Statistics figures show that the cost of living went up only 2.9 percent from last February 15, when the freeze was first reflected in their report, through December 15, the latest date on which figures are available.

When this relatively small increase in the Consumer Price Index is compared to the 10 percent rise that took place in 1950, I feel we can certainly say that a great deal has been accomplished in stabilizing the nation's economy. 

It is also significant that the latest increase in the cost of living index is attributed to rising food costs and to higher prices for miscellaneous goods 

Under and services, such as medical costs, hair cuts and beauty shop services. the law, OPS cannot prevent increases in the price of foods which are selling In addi- below parity at the farm level, and most foods are still below this. tion, professional services are exempt from control, and the right to control prices of barber shops and beauty parlors was taken from the agency by the Congress last summer. 

This was

When Congress enacted legislation to provide for a check rein on inflation, it expressly ordered that voluntary controls and indirect measures, such as credit restrictions, taxation and encouraged savings, be tried first. done, but the cost of living for you and me and our neighbor continued to climb. 

From June 1950 to January 1951, this sensitive indicator of what it costs to pay the butcher, the baker and the clothing maker had surged up by eight percent. 1 GPO-O-OPS 1761

This was a clear indication that the voluntary methods were not sufficient, and on January 26, 1951, the General Ceiling Price Regulation was issued, freezing most prices of what you buy and sell.

This served as an immediate brake on the spiral. People realized a positive program was underway, and the disastrous wave of scare buying ended almost at Meantime, other factors, such as credit controls, voluntary savings, and the like also began to exert their influence. With the pressures thus relieved, prices eased and we started immediately to eliminate the various inequities in cost-price relationship which any blanket freeze must inevitably bring. 

In the past 12 months, much of this program has been accomplished. 

Special regulations are in effect for nearly all major types of industry-food, dry goods, manufacturing, services, and the like. In addition, we have made pretty good progress toward breaking these major regulations down into specially tailored ones for various segments of industry and trade. Well over 

100 of these tailored regulations are now issued, and others are being developed and issued daily.

As we have previously said, we sincerely feel that the cause of stabilization was hampered by certain restrictions placed in the amended controls act last There can be no denying that the Herlong and Capehart amendments, which prevented us from forcing certain cost absorptions by industry which we felt they could stand better than the consumer, have resulted in higher price ceilings. 

Also, with beef selling at 152 percent of parity--the farm price set out by the law as fair based on the costs the farmer has to pay--it had seemed to us that it was only logical and just to roll cattle prices back to a more reasonable figure to force the price of beef down at the consumer level. We did compel one roll back and announced that two additional ones were planned, but Congress felt these should not be permitted and banned them by law. 

However, our job is to administer the law as passed by Congress as best we can, for the greatest good and fairest treatment of all, and this we have done. 

All of us at OPS realize, of course, that this is no time to sit back and coast on what has been accomplished. There can be no doubt that as defense spending rises to the rate of $65 billion dollars a year, which it is soon to do, the great amount of money flowing into the economy will create heavier inflationary pressures. These we must be prepared to meet. 

Although I am leaving the government shortly, I have every confidence that my successor, whoever he may be, with the wholehearted support of the great majority of patriotic Americans will be able to keep prices reasonably stable despite these pressures. # # # # da bra s

Re: DISTILLED SPIRITS AND WINES 

The Office of Price Stabilization today announced that the February 1 mandatory effective date of the alcoholic beverage ceiling price regulation will be extended insofar as it applies to retailers and "on-premise licensees" selling packaged distilled spirits and wines for off-premise consumption. 

OPS said that many reports have been received which indicate that the methods by which retailers and on-premise licensees must calculate their ceiling prices under the regulation, SR 2 to CPR 78, require considerably more paper work than had been anticipated. 

The mandatory effective date of SR 2 for all sellers other than retailers and on-premise licensees, as well as the date by which the OPS Public Forms required of them are to be completed, will not be changed and will remain 

February 1, OPS said. # # # # # # # # # GPO-O-OPS 1765

PRESS RELEASE  Tempo E ADVANCE RELEASE For Use in Morning Papers WEDNESDAY, January 30, 1952 

Washington Re: CHICAGO FUTURES CONTRACTS Barkley-OPS-GFR-1186  

The Office of Price Stabilization, through an opinion of Harold Leventhal, Chief Counsel, has informed the Chicago Board of Trade that the agency cannot provide a definitive ruling on a modified proposal presented by the Board as a method of handling settlement of defaults last November on future contracts for delivery of soybean meal.

The action was made public today when OPS released a letter from Mr. 

Leventhal to Bennett E. Bates, Attorney for the Board. Mr. Bates, in outlining the proposal of the Board, expressed the hope that "this approach to the problem will fit in with the program of OPS." 

Last December, the Board advised OPS that it proposed to set a settlement price of $79, $5 a ton in excess of the spot ceiling. OPS then ruled that 

Section 707 of the Defense Production Act precluded such a settlement price. 

"To require a person defaulting to pay damages based on a market value in excess of the ceiling price would be to assume as a basis for settlement an illegal market price," Mr. Leventhal informed the Board at that time.

More recently, Mr. Bates explained that the Board was not acting upon the basis of any black market prices, and would clarify its intention by providing a "settlement price" of $74 a ton, "plus $5 liquidated damages." Attorney Bates assured OPS that the amount of liquidated damages has "no relationship whatsoever to the presence, or absence, of a black market for a commodity in question, nor of a relationship between closing prices and black market levels, if any exist." 

Mr. Leventhal replied that there is no violation of the Act where there is both (1) no assumption or use of value in excess of ceiling price, and (2) the assessment is a determination of actual damages or an exaction to promote the integrity of exchange contracts. But he further stated that although it may be that in this case the amount of liquidated damages ($5) is intended only to promote the integrity of Board of Trade contracts, the amount is not set in a way which makes it possible to state affirmatively that the amount involved is definitely collectible under the Act. Such an affirmative ruling was made in 

General Interpretation 1 where the amount was predetermined by a penalty rule. 

Mr. Leventhal's letter noted the circumstance that the $5 liquidated damages comes out to exactly the same result as the previous $79 settlement price, and also amounts to a figure as high as seven percent of the ceiling, but he stated that such factors were not necessarily controlling. In the absence of a rule predetermining the amount of exaction, Mr. Leventhal confined his letter to a clarification of the applicable legal principles and stated that OPS could not provide an affirmative ruling on the transaction. (More) 1 GPO-0-OPS 1766

. 

Mr. Leventhal's letter follows: 

ANTIK DANCE 

Bennett E. Bates, Esq. 

Kirkland, Fleming, Green, Martin and Ellis 

33 North LaSalle Street 

Chicago 2, Illinois 

Dear Mr. Bates:

This will acknowledge your letter of January 9, 1952 with reference to assessment of charges by the Chicago Board of Trade against defaulting short sellers of soybean meal. The subject was previously considered in my letter of December 15, 1951. I further discussed the matter in conversation with 

Mr. Carl Bostrom, then President of the Chicago Board of Trade, and Messrs. 

Ailes and Farmer on January 16, 1952. d-^ Your letter of January 9, 1952 advises that the Board proposes to amend its resolution of December 3, 1951, which fixed a settlement price of $79 a ton for defaulting shorts, $5 a ton in excess of the spot ceiling price. The proposed amended resolution would provide that all futures contracts in default shall be settled for the closing market price of $74 per ton, plus $5 a ton as liquidated damages. You indicate that the determination of this amount of liquidated damages would be governed in no way by an assumption that the market value for the commodity is in excess of the spot ceiling price of $74 per ton. 

It is clear also that the assessment of liquidated damages is not predicated on special or consequential damages actually incurred for the reason, as you point out, that the scope of the Chicago market makes it difficult, if not practically impossible, to determine the extent of such damages. 

In General Interpretation 1 we expressed the view that Section 707 of the Defense Production Act of 1950 precludes an assessment which requires a seller, defaulting in delivery on a futures contract, to pay damages based on the market value in excess of ceiling price. We further stated that if the rules of an exchange in effect at the time the futures contract was entered into require the assessment of a predetermined amount as a penalty for defaulted futures contracts, the assessment of such a penalty would not be in contra vention of the Defense Production Act or of applicable price regulations for the reason that it was clear that the penalty bore no relationship whatever to possible overceiling prices.

The difficulty with the problem which you present to us is this: We do not know the basis on which the Chicago Board of Trade, or its appropriate committee, has acted in this matter. 

Our letter of December 15, 1951, assumed that the December 3, 1951 resolution, in setting a "settlement price" had proceeded on an assumption of value of the soybean meal. We had been asked to reconsider General Interpretation 1. (More)

3 1 2 les! 40 tel kare late of ps You state in your letter of January 9 that the settlement price was not based on any such assumption of value, and you propose to make your approach clear by using the term "liquidated damages." That term is somewhat more appropriate to reflect the basis or approach where in fact there has been no consideration of value in excess of ceiling. But to avoid any misunderstanding it should be noted immediately that use of such a term is not controlling or conclusive. 

It may be that the amount of liquidated damages is set at an amount intended only to promote the integrity of Board of Trade contracts. But since the basis of the determination of the amount of liquidated damages is not definite it is not possible to state affirmatively, as we were able to do in General Interpretation 1, that the amount involved is collectible without any possible problem of violation of the Defense Production Act. The exaction can be demonstrated to be only a penalty to promote integrity of exchange contracts where the amount is predetermined by rule. 

As we have previously advised, we are not undertaking to rule upon the facts of this case. It is noted that the $5 liquidated damage here proposed results in a total amount of $79 per ton, an amount identical with that previously set forth as a settlement price. The $5 figure amounts to almost seven percent of the ceiling price, a percentage figure substantially greater than that actually involved in connection with General Interpretation 1. These factors, while relevant, are not necessarily controlling. 

Under present regulations, there is no violation of the Defense Production Act of 1950 in a case where both (a) the assessment is a determination of actual consequential damages, or an exaction to promote the integrity of exchange contracts, or both, and (b) there is in fact no use or assumption of value (whether market value, fair value, true value) in excess of ceiling price.

For the reasons stated we cannot provide an affirmative ruling in this particular case. However, we trust this further statement of the applicable principles is helpful. 

Very truly yours, Harold Leventhal

Chief Counsel etati

Monday, January 28, 1952   

Re: 

RUBBER CHEMICALS TAC Richardson-OPS-GPR-1187 

Members of the Rubber Chemicals Industry Advisory Committee today, at their second meeting with OPS officials, discussed the scope and form of a tailored regulation for rubber processing chemicals.

Agency representatives explained that, under the Capehart amendment, the industry would be required to absorb cost increases occurring subsequent to July 26, 1951, the cut-off date for adjustment set by that amendment. 

OPS officials advised the committee that study of the industry's Form 8 filings on rubber chemicals showed that a uniform increase of 3.767 percent in its GCPR price level for these products would be appropriate in lieu of widely disparate percentage adjustments by individual firms.

After discussion by committee members, the OPS proposed list of specific rubber chemicals for which individual ceiling prices were to be set was adjusted to reflect tonnage items, and excluded minor specialties.

The OPS proposal that ceiling prices of all other rubber chemicals be adjusted to 103.767 percent of their respective GCPR ceilings was generally acceptable. This factor is subject to revision.

It was also recommended by the committee that adjusted prices be rounded to the nearest half-cent per pound, and apply to sales to ultimate consumers in the rubber industry. 

For purposes of the proposed price regulation, the following definition for rubber chemicals was presented by OPS:

Synthetic organic chemicals used in the compounding and processing of rubber, including accelerators of vulcanization, activators of vulcanization accelerators, antioxidents and stabilizers, retarders of vulcanization and peptizers. At the suggestion of the committee synthetic organic vulcanizers were added to the list. 

Excluded under the definition are such products as plasticizers and softeners, aromatic odors, blowing agents, organic pigments, lubricants, extenders and rubber substitutes. 

After some discussion, the industry members recommended that in the projected tailored regulation, one manufacturer's specialty items be allowed those price increases which already have occurred under CPR 22. It was suggested that this be offset by a corresponding reduction in the industry average increase factor. (over) GPO-O-OPS 1767

OPS officials explained that calculations would be made in terms of prices per pound for sales in ton lots. The customary dollars-and-cents differentials in effect for each company and all other terms and conditions of sale in effect under GCPR would apply. New products would be priced in accordance with CPR 22. 

The meeting was conducted by George W. Strasser, acting assistant director of the Rubber, Chemicals and Drugs Division, OPS.  

Hugo E. Weisberger, division economist; H. E. Mordan, accountant; Wilhelm Hirschkind, consultant; G. J. Dowd, consultant; Philip Travis, branch counsel; H. I. Cramer, consultant; R. M. Joslin, chief, Aliphalic Organic Chemicals Section; H. J. Koenig, section economist; and W. R. Thomas, Jr., business specialist, Office of Industry 

Advisory Committee. E. E. Neyland, Rubber Division, National Production Authority, also attended.

Re: GENERAL STEEL PRODUCTS INDUSTRY ADVISORY COMMITTEE Members of the General Steel Products Industry Advisory Committee today told officials of the Office of Price Stabilization that the industry's voluntary agreement with OPS to hold the line on steel prices has operated satisfactorily and that price control or any change in ceiling prices for the steel producing industry should be continued on a voluntary basis. 

The committee met with OPS to discuss a tentative draft of a proposed pricing procedure for determination of price adjustments under the so-called Capehart amendment to the Defense Production Act, which permits producers to reflect changes in labor, materials, and overhead costs up to July 26,1952 

OPS Director Michael V. DiSalle told the committee that the voluntary price agreement which OPS has had with steel producers has proven to be a highly satisfactory operating agreement and an outstanding and fine example of industry cooperation with Government. He pointed out, however, that the present discussion of steel price adjustments must be entirely independent of any wage negotiations and that the discussions need not be in conflict with a continuance of the voluntary price agreement. He said OPS needed industry's help in determining the most practical and fair procedure for giving industry price relief under the Capehart amendment and to give full effect to the purpose of the amendment. 

Edward F. Phelps, Jr., Director for Price Operations told the committee that, contrary to published reports, OPS does not have any precise or even general estimate as to what price increase, if any, the application of Capehart adjustments would have on steel prices. He said that the matter of continuance of the voluntary agreement or the writing of a new freeze order would be given further and full consideration. Mr. Phelps also pointed out that if price adjustments under the 

Capehart amendment resulted in price distortions in relation to the historical pricing pattern of the industry, it might be possible to develop a regulation which would overcome this difficulty and still accomplish the purpose of the Capehart amendment. He said that the advice, recommendations and suggestions of the committee are desired on these matters as well as on the procedure for determination of Capehart adjustment as tentatively proposed. 

The committee reviewed the proposed Capehart price adjustment procedure in detail. 

Committee members asked that they be permitted to make a further study of the proposed procedure as related to the industry's accounting practices, and that the committee be permitted to meet again with OPS on February 7 for a further discussion of the problems involved. At that time, members said, they will be better prepared to make sound recommendations and suggestions with a view toward making the Capehart price adjustment procedure more readily adaptable to the accounting practices of the industry.

It was tentatively agreed that the committee will meet again on February 7. (More) GPO-O-OPS 1778

TUESDAY, January 29, 1952   

Cole-OPS-GPR-1189  

Re: NATIONAL TODDLE HOUSE COURT ACTION The National Toddle House Corporation, operator of a nation-wide chain of small restaurants, was named defendant in a civil action filed in the U. S. 

District Court at Memphis, Tenn., by the Office of Price Stabilization this afternoon.

The corporation, owner and operator of 159 restaurant units, with headquarters at 5 North Third Street, Memphis, is charged with violating the 

General Ceiling Price Regulation in charging overceiling prices. OPS seeks treble damages approximating $88,000.

OPS alleges that the defendant firm, incorporated in Delaware in 1935 and now doing a business of several million dollars a year, not only increased its prices but also decreased its portions for pie, hamburgers and other food items.

The investigation started with a routine check regarding record keeping in Columbus and Cleveland, Ohio, and spread to other cities throughout the nation where the firm operates. 

Federal Judge Marion F. Boyd stated hearing would be held in case 20 days following service.

PRESS RELEASE  ADVANCE RELEASE 

For use at 11 a.m., EST

THURSDAY, January 31, 1952  Re: RESIGNATION OF ARNOLD F. SHAW Cole-OPS-GPR-1190 

Arnold F. Shaw, special assistant to Michael V. DiSalle, Director of the

Office of Price Stabilization, has resigned, effective tomorrow, February 1, He has held the post for the last 13 to re-enter private practice of law. months.

Mr. Shaw, a native of Chicago and graduate of Northwestern University law 

School, will be associated as a partner with the Washington law firm of Donohue and Kaufmann.

He has practiced law in Chicago where he is a member of the Chicago Bar Association, and has also been engaged in the manufacturing business in that city for some years.

He served with the United States Navy as a lieutenant in the Philippines and the South Pacific during World War II. 

Before coming to the Office of Price Stabilization, Mr. Shaw was with the 

Department of Justice as a special assistant to the Attorney General.

WEDNESDAY, January 30, 1952 

Re: Scott-OPS-GPR-1191  

KAISER-FRAZER AND ALLSTATE AUTOMOBILES 

The Office of Price Stabilization said today that it has approved an application of the Kaiser-Frazer Corporation for ceiling price adjustments on its line of Kaiser, Henry J and Allstate passenger automobiles, under the so-called Capehart amendment to the Defense Production Act. 

The ceiling price adjustments approved by OPS are required by the Capehart amendment and reflect labor, material and overhead cost changes to July 26, 1951, as shown by detailed figures and information submitted to OPS by the company. However, the amount of adjustments approved are somewhat less than applied for by the company, due to a lack of information to completely support the full amount of overhead cost increases claimed.

Under the partial OPS approval of its application the company is authorized to increase its present f.o.b. factory wholesale ceiling prices by the percentage figure indicated for each line of passenger automobiles and factory installed extra, special or optional equipment as follows; 

Henry J line 

Allstate line 

Kaiser line 

11.68 percent 

11.68 percent 

11.12 percent

The company has not indicated to OPS whether it will put the increases into effect immediately. However, under OPS regulations, the company is required to file with OPS its proposed new wholesale ceiling prices, and its suggested new factory retail price lists.
